    Proposal runtime-types

    Stage 0 Draft / October 17, 2026

    Runtime Types

    Introduction

    This proposal adds an optional static type system to ECMAScript. Its types are values at run time and are enforced there: a typed binding rejects a value outside its type, a conversion between numeric types is written explicitly rather than performed silently, and the type of a value is available through reflection. Annotations are optional and additive, so a program that does not use them keeps its current meaning.

    The system is deliberately close to the value-type discipline of systems languages. It adds sized integers, floats, and decimals; value-type classes with a defined in-memory layout; operator overloading; generics specialized by monomorphization; and types as first-class, interned values that ordinary code can compute with and reflect on. None of this is visible to a program that does not opt in.

    This document is the normative specification. It is written against the design, which, together with the rationale, the full set of extensions, and worked examples, is maintained in the design repository. Readers new to the proposal should start there; this document formalizes what that material describes.

    Note

    The specification is under active construction. The clauses below establish the shape of the document; normative text is added phase by phase, following the specification plan in the design repository. Until a section is filled in here, the corresponding behaviour is defined only by the design documents.

    1 Runtime Types

    This clause and its subclauses define the runtime type system as a set of additions to and revisions of the ECMAScript specification. The work is organized into the phases described in the design repository's specification plan: the static type-checking framework; the grammar of type expressions; the type universe; conversions; runtime enforcement; typed declarations, operators, functions, and classes; the type-object and reflection API; and the numeric library. Extensions (SIMD, generics, decorators, primitive metadata, and the rest) are specified as independent additions layered on this core.

    Each addition is expressed as an insertion into or revision of the edition of ECMAScript that 1.1 pins, so that this document reads as a patch against that specification rather than a restatement of it. Clauses appear in the order of the underlying ECMAScript specification, cross-referenced to the sections they modify, and the extension clauses follow the core, each of them named in Table 39.

    1.1 Conventions

    This document is a diff. It is written against ECMA-262, 16th edition (ES2025), which is the pinned edition, and it should be re-pinned and re-diffed at each subsequent edition rather than left to drift. Within a grammar block, a production shown with inserted text is that edition's production with the marked additions; a production shown entirely as an insertion is new to this proposal. A cross-reference whose target is not defined here is a reference to the pinned edition and resolves against it. Where a later clause extends a production an earlier clause has already patched, the later block restates the production in full, marking only its own additions as inserted; the blocks are one production, and the latest restatement is its complete form.

    The design is the collection of documents in the ecmascript-types repository: a README specifying the core and a set of extension documents specifying SIMD, generics, decorators, primitive metadata, memory layout, type programming, and the rest. This specification is that design rendered as a patch against the pinned edition. A note that cites the design is pointing at the source of a requirement, at a case the design works through, or at a question this specification decided and the design should record; as the proposal advances, each such citation should become a link to an issue in that repository, so that a reader can follow a decision to the discussion that settled it.

    Three conventions govern the semantics. The relations of the type system, SameType, IsSubtype, IsAssignable, and the operations over Type Records, are abstract operations rather than syntax-directed operations, because they relate types to types and not Parse Nodes to values; the syntax-directed part of the type system is the Static Type of an expression (1.2.6), which each clause that adds an expression form extends. The static semantics that attach to a production are Early Errors, and this document states one with the phrase “it is a type error if”, which 1.2.8 defines as an Early Error rather than a thrown error; they are stated at the rule they belong to rather than gathered into one block, because a type error is a condition on types and reads where the types are. A thrown TypeError or RangeError is reserved for a check that could not be resolved statically.

    Note

    The editorial state of this document is worth stating plainly. Its structure, cross-references, and grammar are complete and it builds clean, and every obligation the design records is either specified here or named in Table 39 as belonging to an extension. What it has not had is the multi-editor review that turns a complete specification into an approved one, and the decisions it records, marked as such in the notes, are this specification's answers rather than the design's, offered so that a reader can disagree with a stated position instead of guessing at an unstated one.

    1.2 Type System Foundations

    This clause defines the machinery the rest of the specification builds on: the representation of a type, the structural identity that interns types into unique values, the subtyping and assignability relations, the static type of an expression, compile-time evaluation of a type expression, and the reporting of type errors. It introduces no user-facing syntax; the productions and library that use this machinery are added by later clauses.

    Note

    ECMAScript defines runtime behaviour through abstract operations and a limited set of static semantics, chiefly Early Errors, but it has no framework for assigning a type to an expression or relating two types. This clause establishes that framework. Because a type in this proposal is also a value, a single notion, the Type Object, serves both as the entity the type checker reasons about and as the value a program observes.

    1.2.1 Types and Type Objects

    A Type Record is a Record used by this specification to describe an ECMAScript type. Each Type Record has a [[Kind]] field and the additional fields listed for that kind in Table 1.

    Note 1

    The structured fields referenced above, a Property Type Record, an Index Signature Record, a Signature Record, and a Tuple Element Record, are defined by the clauses that introduce object types, function types, and arrays and tuples. This clause depends only on Type Records being comparable and canonicalizable, which the operations below provide for every kind.

    A Type Object is an ECMAScript object that denotes a type. Every Type Object has a [[TypeRecord]] internal slot whose value is a canonical Type Record (1.2.2.8). A type name or type expression in expression position evaluates to a Type Object, and reflection returns one.

    Type Objects are interned. 1.2.2.9 maps each canonical Type Record to a unique Type Object, so two Type Objects denote the same type if and only if they are the same value. Consequently comparing two Type Objects with IsStrictlyEqual returns true exactly when they denote the same type, and a Type Object may be used as a property key or a key in a Map or Set to key on a type.

    Note 2

    The observable behaviour of a Type Object, including how it exposes its own structure to reflection, is defined by 1.12. The remainder of the type system uses only its [[TypeRecord]] and its identity.

    1.2.2 Structural Identity

    Two types are the same when they have the same structure, with one exception: a nominal type is identified by its declaration, so two classes with identical members are still different types. This clause defines that notion and the canonical form that makes it decidable and internable. A pair of Type Records is carried through the recursive comparisons as a List so that comparison of a recursive type terminates; each such pair is represented as a Record with a [[First]] field and a [[Second]] field.

    1.2.2.1 SameType ( s, t )

    The abstract operation SameType takes arguments s (a Type Record) and t (a Type Record) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether s and t denote the same type. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s, t, « »).
    2. If IsSubtype(s, t, « ») is false, return false.
    3. Return IsSubtype(t, s, « »).

    SameType is MUTUAL SUBTYPING. It is therefore reflexive, symmetric, and transitive wherever IsSubtype is reflexive and transitive, which is to say it is an equivalence relation - and callers that de-duplicate, intern, or otherwise treat it as equality may rely on that.

    Note

    It was previously defined as SameTypeWithAssumptions, whose algorithm carries three steps keyed on s alone - for an enum, a literal, and a parameterized type - with no mirror for t. That made a relation named for equality ASYMMETRIC: SameType("a", string) answered true where SameType(string, "a") answered false. Callers treating it as equality inherited an order dependence; de-duplicating a union by it discarded string from "a" | string while leaving string | "a" intact, so the same type written two ways admitted different values.

    The refinement those steps provided is not lost. It is what IsSubtype computes, and a caller asking "does s refine to t" should call IsSubtype rather than a relation named for sameness.

    1.2.2.2 SameTypeWithAssumptions ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation SameTypeWithAssumptions takes arguments s (a Type Record), t (a Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether s and t denote the same type, treating each pair in assumptions as already established so that comparison of recursive types terminates. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s and t are the same Record, return true.
    2. If assumptions contains a Record p such that p.[[First]] is s and p.[[Second]] is t, return true.
    3. If s.[[Kind]] is not t.[[Kind]], return false.
    4. Set assumptions to the list-concatenation of assumptions and « the Record { [[First]]: s, [[Second]]: t } ».
    5. If s.[[Kind]] is any or s.[[Kind]] is void, return true.
    6. If s.[[Kind]] is primitive, then
      1. If s.[[Name]] is not t.[[Name]], return false.
      2. Return SameArgumentList(s.[[Arguments]], t.[[Arguments]], assumptions).
    7. If s.[[Kind]] is literal, then
      1. If SameValue(s.[[Value]], t.[[Value]]) is false, return false.
      2. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Base]], t.[[Base]], assumptions).
    8. If s.[[Kind]] is parameterized, then
      1. If s.[[Metadata]] and t.[[Metadata]] are not structurally equivalent (1.2.7.2), return false.
      2. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Base]], t.[[Base]], assumptions).
    9. If s.[[Kind]] is deferred, then
      1. If s.[[Operator]] and t.[[Operator]] are not the same - a core or built-in operator by its name, a function by identity - return false.
      2. Return SameArgumentList(s.[[Operands]], t.[[Operands]], assumptions).
    10. If s.[[Kind]] is nominal, then
      1. If s.[[Declaration]] and t.[[Declaration]] are not the same Parse Node, return false.
      2. If either s or t has a [[DeclarationIdentity]] field, then
        1. If either lacks that field, return false.
        2. If s.[[DeclarationIdentity]] and t.[[DeclarationIdentity]] are not the same identity, return false.
      3. Return SameArgumentList(s.[[Arguments]], t.[[Arguments]], assumptions).
    11. If s.[[Kind]] is union or s.[[Kind]] is intersection, return SameTypeList(s.[[Members]], t.[[Members]], assumptions).
    12. If s.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. If s.[[Elements]] and t.[[Elements]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
      2. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the number of elements of s.[[Elements]], do
        1. Let p be s.[[Elements]][i].
        2. Let q be t.[[Elements]][i].
        3. If p.[[Rest]] is not q.[[Rest]], return false.
        4. If p.[[Initial]] is none or q.[[Initial]] is none, then
          1. If p.[[Initial]] is not none or q.[[Initial]] is not none, return false.
        5. Else if SameValue(p.[[Initial]], q.[[Initial]]) is false, then
          1. Return false.
        6. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
      3. Return true.
    13. If s.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. If s.[[Extent]] is not t.[[Extent]], return false.
      2. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Element]], t.[[Element]], assumptions).
    14. If s.[[Kind]] is reference or s.[[Kind]] is shared, return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Target]], t.[[Target]], assumptions).
    15. If s.[[Kind]] is function, return SameFunctionType(s, t, assumptions).
    16. Assert: s.[[Kind]] is object.
    17. Return SameObjectType(s, t, assumptions).
     Note

    SameTypeList holds when two Lists of Type Records have the same length and are position-wise the same under assumptions. SameArgumentList is SameTypeList extended to compare non-type arguments, such as an array extent, with SameValue. SameObjectType (1.11.1.2) and SameFunctionType (1.10.2.1) compare the members of an object or function type. Because a canonical union or intersection has its members in a fixed order (1.2.2.8), position-wise comparison of members is sufficient.

    1.2.2.3 SameTypeStructural ( s, t )

    The abstract operation SameTypeStructural takes arguments s (a Type Record) and t (a Type Record) and returns a Boolean.

    It determines whether s and t are the same type CONSTRUCTION, rather than whether they denote the same values.

    It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s, t, « »).

    This is a STRICTER relation than SameType. Two Type Records may denote the same values and still differ in construction - most importantly in the metadata they claim - so an implementation that interns Type Objects must use this relation and not SameType. Interning by SameType merges records whose claims differ, and the claim of whichever record is discarded is lost with it.

    Note

    It is the relation SameType was defined as before that operation became mutual subtyping, kept here under a name that says what it computes. The two are separated because they answer different questions: SameType asks whether a value of one is acceptable where the other is required, and SameTypeStructural asks whether the two were built the same way.

    1.2.2.4 SameTypeList ( a, b, assumptions )

    The abstract operation SameTypeList takes arguments a (a List of Type Records), b (a List of Type Records), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether a and b have the same length and are position-wise the same type under assumptions. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If a and b do not have the same number of elements, return false.
    2. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the number of elements of a, do
      1. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(a[i], b[i], assumptions) is false, return false.
    3. Return true.

    1.2.2.5 SameArgumentList ( a, b, assumptions )

    The abstract operation SameArgumentList takes arguments a (a List), b (a List), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether a and b have the same length and equal elements, comparing Type Record elements as types under assumptions, Parse Node elements by being the same Parse Node, compound compile-time constants by structural equivalence (1.2.7.2), and other elements with SameValue. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If a and b do not have the same number of elements, return false.
    2. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the number of elements of a, do
      1. Let x be a[i].
      2. Let y be b[i].
      3. If x is a Type Record and y is a Type Record, then
        1. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(x, y, assumptions) is false, return false.
      4. Else if x is a Type Record or y is a Type Record, then
        1. Return false.
      5. Else if x is a Parse Node and y is a Parse Node, then
        1. If x and y are not the same Parse Node, return false.
      6. Else if x is a Parse Node or y is a Parse Node, then
        1. Return false.
      7. Else if x and y are compound compile-time constants, then
        1. If x and y are not structurally equivalent (1.2.7.2), return false.
      8. Else if SameValue(x, y) is false, then
        1. Return false.
    3. Return true.

    1.2.2.6 AreDisjoint ( s, t [ , active ] )

    The abstract operation AreDisjoint takes arguments s (a Type Record) and t (a Type Record) and optional argument active (a List of Records) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether no value is of both s and t. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If active is not present, set active to a new empty List.
    2. If active contains a Record whose [[First]] is s and whose [[Second]] is t, return false.
    3. Set active to the list-concatenation of active and « the Record { [[First]]: s, [[Second]]: t } ».
    4. If s.[[Kind]] is any, parameter, or deferred, return false.
    5. If t.[[Kind]] is any, parameter, or deferred, return false.
    6. If s.[[Kind]] is shared, return AreDisjoint(s.[[Target]], t, active).
    7. If t.[[Kind]] is shared, return AreDisjoint(s, t.[[Target]], active).
    8. If s.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. For each element m of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If AreDisjoint(m, t, active) is true, return true.
      2. Return false.
    9. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. For each element n of t.[[Members]], do
        1. If AreDisjoint(s, n, active) is true, return true.
      2. Return false.
    10. If s.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element p of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If AreDisjoint(p, t, active) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    11. If t.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element q of t.[[Members]], do
        1. If AreDisjoint(s, q, active) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    12. If s.[[Kind]] is void or t.[[Kind]] is void, return true if s.[[Kind]] is not t.[[Kind]], and false otherwise.
    13. Let sb be s; while sb.[[Kind]] is parameterized, set sb to sb.[[Base]].
    14. Let tb be t; while tb.[[Kind]] is parameterized, set tb to tb.[[Base]].
    15. If sb.[[Kind]] is literal and tb.[[Kind]] is literal, return false if SameType(sb, tb) is true, and true otherwise.
    16. If sb.[[Kind]] is literal, set sb to sb.[[Base]].
    17. If tb.[[Kind]] is literal, set tb to tb.[[Base]].
    18. If both sb and tb are composite types (23.2), then
      1. If either is the top composite type, return false.
      2. Return CompositeShapesAreDisjoint(the shape of sb, the shape of tb, active).
    19. If exactly one of sb and tb is a composite type, then
      1. Let other be the one that is not a composite type.
      2. If other.[[Kind]] is primitive, array, or function, return true.
      3. If other is an enum type, return true.
      4. Return false.
    20. If sb.[[Kind]] is primitive and tb.[[Kind]] is primitive, return false if SameType(sb, tb) is true, and true otherwise.
    21. If sb.[[Kind]] is primitive and tb.[[Kind]] is object, function, array, or tuple, return true.
    22. If tb.[[Kind]] is primitive and sb.[[Kind]] is object, function, array, or tuple, return true.
    23. Return false.
     Note

    This is the judgment 1.8.5.3 already made in prose, given a name so that canonicalization, the Early Error of 1.4.2.1, and the narrowing rows decide it once and the same way. Everything it answers true for that clause's note had already committed to: two distinct non-composite primitive types have no common values, since each value belongs to exactly one of them (1.5.1), and neither does a non-composite primitive type share values with an object or a function type.

    An intersection of exactly two parameterized Type Records over one base reduces to their MEET, where a governing meta type gave one: the constraint its meet hook returned (Table 42), which is satisfied by exactly the values satisfying both. So uint8<{ bounds: 1..=10 }> & uint8<{ bounds: 5..=20 }> is uint8<{ bounds: 5..=10 }>, and the two spellings intern to one Type Object — the reason the reduction is here and not at each use, since a type reached by two spellings must answer ===.

    The hook runs USER CODE and this operation does not, so the meet is computed by the checking pass and read here. A meta type declaring no meet, or returning undefined, leaves the intersection standing, which is what keeps two differently-branded parameterizations of one primitive distinct: 1.2.2.6 decides on the base and leaves them overlapping, and a meta type with nothing to prove says nothing here either.

    The operation is CONSERVATIVE: where the values of a type are not yet known it answers false, never true. any, a parameter, and a deferred computation whose operands have not closed therefore overlap with everything, which is what keeps a generic body from being rejected for a disjointness that only some instantiation would have. It is likewise silent about two object types, two nominal types, and a nominal against an object: two object types may share a value, which is the case intersections exist for, and whether two unrelated nominal CLASSES are disjoint is a question this operation deliberately does not answer, there being no need of it and a subtyping cost to deciding it. That question is answered instead by an Early Error on the syntax (1.4.2.1) and by a step of NarrowTo (1.8.5.3), both run by the checking pass, which is already running IsSubtype, so the interning path this operation sits on is not disturbed. A written P & Q of two unrelated classes and a narrowing to the same pair therefore receive one answer.

    Disjointness is decided on the BASE of a parameterized type and never on its metadata, which is what keeps a layered brand a type rather than an empty one: string.<{ brand: 'E' }> & string.<{ brand: 'V' }> is two refinements of one string, inhabited by every String granted both, while string.<{ brand: 'E' }> & uint8 is empty because the bases are. A rule phrased over "two value types" rather than over their bases would have destroyed the first along with the second.

    The walk to the base is a LOOP and not a single step, because parameterizing an already-parameterized type nests: the outer [[Base]] is the inner type, so string.<{ brand: 'E' }>.<{ brand: 'N' }> reaches string only by walking through the layer between (1.5.20). A single step would have compared one nested brand against another and found two parameterized types it could not relate, and reading that as disjoint would have emptied every layered type in the language.

    The base a walk arrives at need not be a primitive. A literal base is decided by the primitive beneath it, so a brand on 'a' and a brand on string may share a value while a brand on 'a' and a brand on 'b' may not. An object or array base carries a brand as a mark on the value, so two brands over one object shape are two refinements of it exactly as over a string, and a brand over an object is disjoint from a primitive for the ordinary reason rather than because it is branded.

    1.2.2.7 CompositeShapesAreDisjoint ( s, t, active )

    The abstract operation CompositeShapesAreDisjoint takes arguments s (a Type Record), t (a Type Record), and active (a List of Records) and returns a Boolean. It proves selected contradictions between two composite shapes without evaluating values or treating a membership contract as a construction schema. An unresolved case returns false. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If one of s and t has [[Kind]] object and the other has [[Kind]] tuple or array, return true.
    2. If both s.[[Kind]] and t.[[Kind]] are object, then
      1. For each Property Type Record p of s.[[Properties]], do
        1. Let q be the Property Type Record of t.[[Properties]] with the same [[Key]] as p, or none if there is none.
        2. If q is not none, at least one of p.[[Optional]] and q.[[Optional]] is false, and AreDisjoint(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], active) is true, return true.
      2. Return false.
    3. Let sFixed be true if s.[[Kind]] is tuple and none of its elements is a rest element, and false otherwise.
    4. Let tFixed be true if t.[[Kind]] is tuple and none of its elements is a rest element, and false otherwise.
    5. If sFixed is true, let sMin be the minimum length admitted by the declared defaults of s.
    6. If tFixed is true, let tMin be the minimum length admitted by the declared defaults of t.
    7. If sFixed is true and tFixed is true, then
      1. Let required be max(sMin, tMin).
      2. If required is greater than the smaller of the numbers of elements of s and t, return true.
      3. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i < required, do
        1. If AreDisjoint(s.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], t.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], active) is true, return true.
    8. Else if sFixed is true and t.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i < sMin, do
        1. If AreDisjoint(s.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], t.[[Element]], active) is true, return true.
    9. Else if tFixed is true and s.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i < tMin, do
        1. If AreDisjoint(s.[[Element]], t.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], active) is true, return true.
    10. Return false.

    Record membership permits extra keys by width subtyping. Two conflicting optional properties can both be absent; if either is required, their common value must satisfy both property contracts. Likewise, only tuple positions required at every common admitted length can prove an element conflict. Two array composite shapes can share the empty tuple even when their element types are disjoint; an array shape denotes the variable-length tuple composite. A declared tuple default establishes possible omission without evaluating its initializer. Rest-containing tuple shapes, index-signature interactions and other unresolved shape constraints retain a conservative result unless the kind distinction already proves failure. Repeating an active Type Record pair supplies no proof of disjointness; other independently established conflicts are still checked.

    1.2.2.8 CanonicalizeType ( t )

    The abstract operation CanonicalizeType takes argument t (a Type Record) and returns a Type Record. It returns the canonical form of t, reading no [[Origin]] (21) in deciding it. Canonical Type Records that denote the same type are the same Record, which is what lets 1.2.2.9 intern them. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t.[[Kind]] is union or t.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. Let members be a new empty List.
      2. For each element m of t.[[Members]], do
        1. Let c be CanonicalizeType(m).
        2. If c.[[Kind]] is t.[[Kind]], then
          1. For each element n of c.[[Members]], append n to members.
        3. Else,
          1. Append c to members.
      3. Remove from members each element that is the same type (SameType) as an element occurring earlier in members.
      4. Let kept be a new empty List.
      5. For each element m of members, do
        1. Let subsumed be false.
        2. For each element n of members other than m, do
          1. If t.[[Kind]] is union, let wider be n and let narrower be m; otherwise let wider be m and let narrower be n.
          2. If IsSubtype(narrower, wider, « ») is true, and either IsSubtype(wider, narrower, « ») is false or n occurs before m in members, set subsumed to true.
        3. If subsumed is false, append m to kept.
      6. Set members to kept.
      7. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection and members contains an element whose [[Kind]] is union and whose [[Members]] is empty, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « » } (the never type; see 1.5.18).
      8. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection and members contains two elements a and b such that AreDisjoint(a, b) is true, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « » } (the never type).
      9. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection, members has more than one element, and every element of members has [[Kind]] object, then
        1. Let properties be a new empty List.
        2. Let signatures be a new empty List.
        3. For each element m of members, do
          1. For each Property Record p of m.[[Properties]], do
            1. Let q be the Property Record in properties whose [[Key]] is p.[[Key]], or empty if properties contains no such Record.
            2. If q is empty, then
              1. Append a copy of p to properties.
            3. Else,
              1. Set q.[[Optional]] to true if q.[[Optional]] is true and p.[[Optional]] is true, and false otherwise.
              2. Set q.[[Readonly]] to true if either q.[[Readonly]] or p.[[Readonly]] is true.
              3. Set q.[[Type]] to CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: intersection, [[Members]]: « q.[[Type]], p.[[Type]] » }).
          2. For each Index Signature Record ix of m.[[IndexSignatures]], append ix to signatures.
        4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: object, [[Properties]]: properties, [[IndexSignatures]]: signatures }).
      10. If members has exactly one element, return that element.
      11. Order the elements of members according to the total order of 1.8.5.2.
      12. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: t.[[Kind]], [[Members]]: members }.
    2. If t.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. Let elements be a new empty List.
      2. For each element e of t.[[Elements]], do
        1. Let c be CanonicalizeType(e.[[Type]]).
        2. If e.[[Rest]] is true and c.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
          1. NOTE: A rest element whose type is itself a tuple is that tuple's elements in place, [...[uint8, string], T] being [uint8, string, T], which is what lets a spread of a bound variadic parameter (4.4) intern as the tuple it spells.
          2. For each element n of c.[[Elements]], append n to elements.
        3. Else,
          1. Append the Tuple Element Record { [[Type]]: c, [[Rest]]: e.[[Rest]], [[Initial]]: e.[[Initial]] } to elements.
      3. For each Tuple Element Record e of elements, do
        1. If e.[[Rest]] is false and e.[[Type]] is never, return never.
      4. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: tuple, [[Elements]]: elements }.
    3. If t.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. Let element be CanonicalizeType(t.[[Element]]).
      2. If t.[[Extent]] is a Number greater than 0 and element is never, return never.
      3. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: array, [[Element]]: element, [[Extent]]: t.[[Extent]] }.
    4. If t.[[Kind]] is reference, then
      1. Let target be CanonicalizeType(t.[[Target]]).
      2. If target is never, return never.
      3. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: reference, [[Target]]: target }.
    5. If t.[[Kind]] is shared, then
      1. Let target be CanonicalizeType(t.[[Target]]).
      2. If target is never, return never.
      3. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: shared, [[Target]]: target }.
    6. If t.[[Kind]] is literal, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: literal, [[Value]]: t.[[Value]], [[Base]]: CanonicalizeType(t.[[Base]]) }.
    7. If t.[[Kind]] is parameterized, then
      1. Let base be CanonicalizeType(t.[[Base]]).
      2. If base is never, return never.
      3. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: parameterized, [[Base]]: base, [[Metadata]]: t.[[Metadata]] }.
    8. If t.[[Kind]] is deferred, then
      1. Let args be a new empty List.
      2. For each element a of t.[[Operands]], do
        1. If a is a Type Record, append CanonicalizeType(a) to args.
        2. Else, append a to args.
      3. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: t.[[Operator]], [[Operands]]: args }.
    9. If t.[[Kind]] is object, then
      1. Let c be the canonical form of t defined alongside that kind, with each contained Type Record canonicalized.
      2. For each Property Record p of c.[[Properties]], do
        1. If p.[[Optional]] is false and p.[[Type]] is never, return never.
      3. Return c.
    10. If t.[[Kind]] is function, return the canonical form of t defined alongside that kind, with each contained Type Record canonicalized.
    11. Return t.
     Note 1

    An earlier draft forbade absorption, on the ground that folding by IsSubtype would make the canonical form depend on a relation that READS canonical forms, and that the unabsorbed union cost nothing because membership and assignability answer identically either way. Neither holds.

    The circularity does not arise, because the fold runs on members ALREADY canonicalized by the loop above it: IsSubtype is asked about canonical forms that exist, never about the form being built. The order-independence the clause needs survives it — "a" | string and string | "a" are one Type Object, as are "a" & string and string & "a" — and so does termination through recursive and MUTUALLY recursive members, where the relation simply declines to relate the pair and both members stay.

    The unabsorbed form does cost something, and the cost is not in the judgments. Membership and assignability do answer identically, but a union with a subsumed arm still has that arm, and an implementation lays out and TAGS what a type says it holds. string | (number & bigint) describes one inhabited arm and would be given a tagged two-arm representation; absorbed, it is string, and a slot of it holds one kind of value. The saving is in shape and inline caches rather than in what the relation answers, which is precisely where a canonical form is supposed to pay.

     Note 2

    An intersection every member of which is an object Type Record is ONE object type, and is returned as one. An intersection requires every member, so a value of it has every member's properties, and a name more than one member declares must be satisfied for each of them at once — which is what an intersection of the types they give it denotes. The merged member is built as an intersection and handed back to this operation rather than decided here, so the three answers already defined are the three it gets: two identical types deduplicate, a subtype pair subsumes to the narrower, and a disjoint pair reduces to never. A member REQUIRED by any one arm is required, an intersection requiring all of them, and one declared readonly anywhere is readonly for the same reason.

    Distribution reaches the case whole-object subsumption cannot. { a: number } and { a: 5 } are already related, { a: 5 } being a subtype, so their intersection folded to the narrower before this step existed; in { a: uint32 } & { a: string } neither object is a subtype of the other, so the pair stood as an intersection whose emptiness was discovered at every use of the annotation rather than stated once in the type. It also removes a disagreement between a type and its own identity: { a: number } & { a: 5 } interns as { a: 5 }, and an operation that read the members as written could accept a value at one spelling and refuse it at the other.

    The step is gated on EVERY member being an object Type Record. A member of another kind has values the merge cannot describe — an array shares values with an object type, being a subtype of Iterable, so [].<uint8> & { length: uint32 } is inhabited and is not the object type the properties alone would give — and such an intersection is left standing.

    An object Type Record a REQUIRED property of which is never has no values, since a value of it would have to hold a value of a type that has none, and is never. An OPTIONAL property of never does not empty the type: it declares a member that may never be present, which every value omitting it satisfies. The test is one level deep and on the CANONICAL property types, which is what makes it terminate without an inhabitation judgment or a fixpoint: canonicalization is bottom-up, so { a: { b: never } } reduces because the inner record reduced first. A recursive type closes its cycle through a reference position — an array element, a nullable union — and neither propagates, so a cycle cannot drive a type to never through this step.

    A reference, a shared type, and a parameterized type reduce with their target or base for the same reason: a ref names a location and there is no location of the empty type, a shared marker is not observable in the value (1.2.2.6), and metadata narrows a base's values and cannot add one.

    A tuple and a fixed-extent array are products too, and reduce for the reason an object does: a value would have to hold a value of a type that has none. The rule must be the object's rather than a weaker one, because a program can write the same shape either way — type Pair<A: type, B: type> = [A, B] and type Result<T: type, E: type> = { value: T, error: E } are one shape with two spellings, and an instantiation at the empty type that answered differently for them would make inhabitation a property of how a shape was written.

    A REST position does not empty a tuple, and neither a variable-length array nor a zero-extent one is emptied by its element type. Each supplies no element, so the empty array or the empty tuple inhabits it; this is the boundary 1.8.3.1 also draws, where a zero extent is answered before the element is consulted.

    What the reduction costs is that a type-level list cannot be a tuple type when one of its positions is the empty type. It costs nothing in practice: the type-programming extension's list currency is an array of types rather than a tuple type — elementTypes returns one and tupleOf consumes one — so a program that filters never out of a list reads the array and builds the tuple from the result, which has no such position left in it. TypeScript keeps such a tuple, but keeps { a: never } as an object too, so it is not evidence for treating the two products differently; Rust reduces both, (i32, !, char) and a struct with an uninhabited field being equally uninhabited.

    Flattening merges a nested union into its parent, and likewise for intersection; de-duplication and the fixed order make member order insignificant, so A | B and B | A canonicalize to one Record and, after interning, one Type Object. A nominal, primitive, any, or void Type Record is already canonical apart from canonicalizing the Type Records in its [[Arguments]], which the recursion reaches when they occur. Recursion terminates because a cycle in a type passes through a nominal position, which is canonical without descending into its declaration. Flattening is also what removes a never member from a union: the member is an empty union, so it contributes nothing, and T | never canonicalizes to T with no rule naming the case. The first intersection step above is the one algebraic fact about never that does not fall out this way (1.5.18). The second is what makes never the ONLY empty type rather than one of many: an intersection two of whose members are disjoint has no values, and a type with no values is that type. Without it number & bigint interned as a Type Object of its own - uninhabited by the reasoning of 1.8.5.3, with no default value and no assignable source, and yet neither never nor assignable to it, so IsAssignable could not equate two empty types. Reducing also removes a dead arm from a union that has one, flattening then dropping the never, so string | (number & bigint) is string: a slot of that type holds one kind of value and an implementation need not tag it as a union to discover so. Canonicalization ABSORBS by subtyping, and the two kinds keep opposite survivors: a union keeps the WIDER member, so "a" | string is string, and an intersection the NARROWER, so "a" & string is "a". A single rule for both would fix one and break the other.

    1.2.2.9 GetTypeObject ( t )

    The abstract operation GetTypeObject takes argument t (a Type Record) and returns a Type Object. It returns the unique Type Object that denotes the type described by t. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If type evaluation is active, charge one type-construction request as specified in 1.2.7.5.
    2. Let canonical be CanonicalizeType(t).
    3. If the type-object intern table contains a Type Object existing such that SameTypeStructural(existing.[[TypeRecord]], canonical) is true, return existing.
    4. Let obj be a new Type Object whose [[TypeRecord]] internal slot is canonical.
    5. Add obj to the type-object intern table.
    6. Return obj.
     Note

    The intern table is a specification device; an implementation may realize it in any way that yields the same identities. It is a property of a heap: Type Objects, like other objects, are shared by the agents that share one and are not shared with an agent that does not (40).

    1.2.3 Subtyping and Assignability

    Subtyping relates a more specific type to a more general one. Assignability is the relation the type checker applies at an assignment, an argument, or a return: it is subtyping, widened at the boundary with the any type. Because this proposal performs no implicit numeric widening, a primitive type is a subtype of no other numeric type. It is a subtype of itself, of the any type, and of the same primitive bearing fewer metadata arguments, since a metadata parameterization refines the type it parameterizes rather than being a different type: Meter is a float32.<{ m: 1 }> and is a subtype of float32, which is what makes m instanceof float32 true.

    1.2.3.1 IsSubtype ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation IsSubtype takes arguments s (a Type Record), t (a Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether every value of the type s is a value of the type t, treating each pair in assumptions as already established so that comparison of recursive types terminates. The initial call passes an empty List for assumptions. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s.[[Kind]] is function and t.[[Kind]] is function, then
      1. If s is t, return true.
      2. If assumptions contains a Record p such that p.[[First]] is s and p.[[Second]] is t, return true.
      3. Let next be the list-concatenation of assumptions and « the Record { [[First]]: s, [[Second]]: t } ».
      4. For each Signature Record b of t.[[Signatures]], do
        1. Let matched be false.
        2. For each Signature Record a of s.[[Signatures]], do
          1. If IsSignatureSubtype(a, b, next) is true, set matched to true.
        3. If matched is false, return false.
      5. Return true.
    2. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(s, t, assumptions) is true, return true.
    3. If assumptions contains a Record p such that p.[[First]] is s and p.[[Second]] is t, return true.
    4. Set assumptions to the list-concatenation of assumptions and « the Record { [[First]]: s, [[Second]]: t } ».
    5. If t.[[Kind]] is any, return true.
    6. If s.[[Kind]] is nominal and s.[[Declaration]] is an enum declaration and IsSubtype(the underlying type of s.[[Declaration]], t, assumptions) is true, return true.
    7. If s.[[Kind]] is literal and IsSubtype(s.[[Base]], t, assumptions) is true, return true.
    8. If s.[[Kind]] is parameterized, then
      1. If IsSubtype(s.[[Base]], t, assumptions) is true, return true.
      2. If t.[[Kind]] is parameterized and SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Base]], t.[[Base]], assumptions) is true and the metadata subtype judgment of 1.5.20 holds of s.[[Metadata]] and t.[[Metadata]], return true.
    9. If s.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element m of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(m, t, assumptions) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    10. If t.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element m of t.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(s, m, assumptions) is true, return true.
      2. Return false.
    11. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. For each element m of t.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(s, m, assumptions) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    12. If s.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. For each element m of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(m, t, assumptions) is true, return true.
      2. Return false.
    13. If s is a composite type (23.2), then
      1. If t is the top composite type, return true.
      2. If s is not the top composite type, then
        1. Let sShape be the shape of s.
        2. If t is a composite type that is not the top composite type, then
          1. Let tShape be the shape of t.
          2. If sShape.[[Kind]] is tuple and tShape.[[Kind]] is array, then
            1. NOTE: Between two composite shapes both sides are frozen, so the reason a tuple is not a subtype of an array type (a mutable container) does not arise; the array shape is the variable-length tuple composite, and a tuple composite is of it when every element is of the element type.
            2. For each element e of sShape.[[Elements]], do
              1. If IsSubtype(e.[[Type]], tShape.[[Element]], assumptions) is false, return false.
            3. Return true.
          3. Return IsSubtype(sShape, tShape, assumptions).
        3. If t.[[Kind]] is object and sShape.[[Kind]] is object, return IsObjectSubtype(sShape, t, assumptions).
        4. If t.[[Kind]] is tuple and sShape.[[Kind]] is tuple, return IsSubtype(sShape, t, assumptions).
        5. If t is an interface type with a structural form, return IsSubtype(s, that form, assumptions).
      3. Return false.
    14. If t is an interface type and s does not refine t, then
      1. Return IsSubtype(s, the structural form of t, assumptions).
    15. If s.[[Kind]] is function and t.[[Kind]] is object, and both t.[[Properties]] and t.[[IndexSignatures]] are empty Lists, return true.
    16. If s.[[Kind]] is nominal and t.[[Kind]] is object, then
      1. If s is an interface type, return IsSubtype(the structural form of s, t, assumptions).
      2. Return false.
    17. If s.[[Kind]] is parameter or t.[[Kind]] is parameter, then
      1. If s.[[Kind]] is parameter and t.[[Kind]] is parameter, then
        1. If s.[[Name]] is t.[[Name]] and s.[[Arity]] is t.[[Arity]], return true.
        2. Return false.
      2. If s.[[Kind]] is parameter and s has a [[Constraint]] field, return IsSubtype(s.[[Constraint]], t, assumptions).
      3. Return false.
    18. If s.[[Kind]] is shared and t.[[Kind]] is not shared, return IsSubtype(s.[[Target]], t, assumptions).
    19. If t.[[Kind]] is shared and s.[[Kind]] is not shared, return IsSubtype(s, t.[[Target]], assumptions).
    20. If t.[[Kind]] is array, t.[[Extent]] is dynamic, t.[[Element]].[[Kind]] is any, and s.[[Kind]] is either array or tuple, return true.
    21. If s.[[Kind]] is not t.[[Kind]], return false.
    22. If s.[[Kind]] is nominal, then
      1. If t.[[Declaration]] is s.[[Declaration]], return SameArgumentList(s.[[Arguments]], t.[[Arguments]], assumptions).
      2. If t.[[Declaration]] is an ancestor of s.[[Declaration]] in the class and interface hierarchy, then
        1. Return the result of comparing t.[[Arguments]] against the arguments s supplies to t.[[Declaration]] through the hierarchy, with SameArgumentList.
      3. Return false.
    23. If s.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. If t.[[Extent]] is not s.[[Extent]], return false.
      2. Return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Element]], t.[[Element]], assumptions).
    24. If s.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. If s and t both have established positional domains as described in 1.14.1, return true if the source length range is included in the target length range and every occupied source position is a subtype of its corresponding target position at every admitted source length, and false otherwise.
      2. If one of s and t has an established domain involving finite or nested rest expansion and the other has no established positional domain, return false.
      3. If the minimum length of s is less than the minimum length of t, return false, where a tuple's minimum length counts the elements whose [[Rest]] is false and [[Initial]] is none.
      4. If the maximum length of s exceeds the maximum length of t, return false, where a tuple's maximum length is unbounded when any element's [[Rest]] is true and its element count otherwise.
      5. If t has more than one element whose [[Rest]] is true, then
        1. If the element counts of s.[[Elements]] and t.[[Elements]] differ, return false.
        2. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the element count of t.[[Elements]], do
          1. If s.[[Elements]][i].[[Rest]] is not t.[[Elements]][i].[[Rest]], return false.
          2. If IsSubtype(s.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], t.[[Elements]][i].[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
        3. Return true.
      6. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the greater of the element counts of s.[[Elements]] and t.[[Elements]], do
        1. If s cannot supply position i, continue, where a tuple can supply each position below its maximum length.
        2. If IsSubtype(the type at position i of s, the type at position i of t, assumptions) is false, return false, where the type at a position of t is the [[Type]] of the element that receives it and the type at a position of s is the union of the [[Type]] fields of every element of s that could receive it, an element receiving a position when some assignment of that many values to s.[[Elements]] gives it that one (1.10.4.2).
      7. Return true.
    25. If s.[[Kind]] is reference or s.[[Kind]] is shared, return SameTypeWithAssumptions(s.[[Target]], t.[[Target]], assumptions).
    26. If s.[[Kind]] is function, return IsFunctionSubtype(s, t, assumptions).
    27. If s.[[Kind]] is object, return IsObjectSubtype(s, t, assumptions).
    28. Return false.
     Note 1

    A refinement is a subtype of what it refines, and the three steps above are where that is decided. They were carried by 1.2.2.1, which this operation consults before any rule below, and that placement made them unreachable: a relation named for sameness answered true for two object types whose members merely refined each other, so this operation returned there and 1.11.1.3's writable-member invariance was never consulted. { a: "x" } was a subtype of { a: string }, and the write that clause warns of - "a bare float32 could be written through the supertype view into a slot the program believes holds a Meter" - was admitted. SameType decides sameness; this operation decides refinement.

     Note 2

    A type parameter is OPAQUE within the declaration that binds it: it is a subtype of itself and of its constraint, and nothing else is a subtype of IT. The asymmetry is the point. T: string says every value of T is a String, so a T may be returned where a String is wanted — but it does not say a String is a T, because T may be bound to a literal type: f.<"abc"> satisfies that constraint, and "s" is not a value of "abc". So function f<T: string>(x: T): string { return x; } is well typed and function f<T: string>(x: T) { let v: T = "s"; } is not.

    Without the [[Constraint]] step a constrained parameter would be LESS usable than an unconstrained one, since writing the constraint would buy its author nothing inside the declaration while still restricting the caller. With it, the constraint is what it reads as: a statement about every binding the parameter can take, available wherever the parameter is.

     Note 3

    A function type describes callable Objects, so every value of it satisfies an object type with no properties or index signatures. This is a subtype relation, not type identity: reflection retains the function's signatures. A signature alone establishes no named property or index signature, and an empty object contract does not establish callability.

    Three of the steps above are one relation. A type refines another when it is a parameterized type whose [[Base]] is that type (1.5.20), an enum whose underlying type is that type (1.11.8), or a nominal type whose declaration extends or implements that type's declaration. A type is a subtype of every type it refines and of everything that type is a subtype of; the converse never holds without a crossing, a construction boundary for a parameterization, a validated call for an enum, and nothing at all for a class. The three steps are that rule's cases.

    Note 4

    A literal type is a subtype of its base and of everything its base is a subtype of, which is what makes 'on' usable where a string is required while string is not usable where 'on' is. A tuple's defaults take part in identity but not in subtyping, and tuples relate by the arity window: s is a subtype of t when every length s admits, t admits, and every position s can supply is a subtype of the position of t that receives it. Where s has several rest elements a position may be supplied by more than one of them, so the type s can put at that position is their union, and requiring each to be within t's position is what makes the rule sound.

    Where t has more than one rest element, its positions are not determined by their index and the exact relation is inclusion between two regular languages, which a product construction decides and which a subtyping check cannot afford to run at every use. The rule above is conservative there: it requires the two element lists to correspond one for one, which is sound and is exact whenever they do. A program wanting a relation the conservative rule refuses writes the two tuple types in corresponding shapes, and the case is narrow, since the target of a subtyping check is a declared type and a declared type with two rests is already an unusual thing to write.

    A deferred computation is a subtype of itself, of the any type, and of its operator's BOUND where the operator has one: the key universe string | symbol | uint32 for keyof, T[keyof T] for an indexed access whose index is a subtype of keyof T, and the declared return type of a function builder. A builder with no return annotation, like an operator over operands nothing is known about, has no bound and is a subtype only of itself and any. Before specialization nothing finer than identity is known about its result, so nothing finer is assumed: two mentions of one deferred call are one type by interning, and two different calls are unrelated until they evaluate. No step above names the kind because none needs to; a deferred source reaches the final step for every target but itself and its operator's bound and any.

    A generic class is invariant in its arguments, so Map.<string, uint8> is a subtype of no other instantiation of Map. This is the conservative choice and the only one that is sound for a mutable container, since a Map.<string, uint8> used as a Map.<string, number> would accept a Number into storage typed uint8. A parameter may be declared covariant or contravariant, as it may in C# and Kotlin, and 4.11 states what such a declaration means; the step above is what it relaxes. Invariance is what a parameter carrying no such declaration has.

    A position declared covariant admits an argument the position's own type is ASSIGNABLE FROM, not merely a subtype of. The two differ for any, which is assignable in both directions — let e: Error = a for an any a is admitted, and so is the reverse — while being a subtype only of itself and upward. Reading a covariant position by subtyping alone therefore answers one way at the top level and another one position in, for the same pair; that is one relation asked two ways rather than two rules, and the assignable reading is the one that agrees with every other position a value passes through.

    This does not reach an INVARIANT parameter, which is what a mutable container has and what the paragraph above requires of it: Map.<string, uint8> remains usable as no other instantiation, Map.<string, any> included, since its storage is written THROUGH the view and an any there would admit a write the storage does not hold. A covariant parameter is one whose values the type only ever PRODUCES, so a wider reading of it can be wrong about a value but cannot corrupt one.

    A consequence worth stating, because it decides how a generic's statics are written: a type argument fixed to a CONCRETE type in a signature's return admits only that argument. Promise.resolve written (value: R): Promise.<R, any> would produce a value assignable to Promise.<R, any> and to no other instantiation — not because any is special, but because invariance makes every instantiation unrelated. A static whose result is meant to satisfy a caller's declared type states that position as a PARAMETER and lets the contextual type fix it, as Promise.reject does with its E.

    Note 5

    [ ] . < any > is the top of the array family: an array of some element type, which every array and every tuple type is a subtype of. any is already the type of which every value is a value, and this is that reading carried to the array types; the extent rules are unchanged, so a fixed-length target still fixes the length and admits any element type within it.

    Element invariance is untouched for every other element type, for the reason given above: a [ ] . < uint8 > used as a [ ] . < number > would accept a Number into storage typed uint8. What makes any admissible where a general covariance is not is that a store to an element is checked against the array's own element type at run time (Table 23), so a write through the wider view is refused whatever the static type permitted. A language whose containers are invariant and whose elements are unchecked supplies this as a wildcard or a star projection and forbids writing through it; the check here is what takes the place of that prohibition.

    Without this the bound a generic writes over the array family, T extends [ ], is satisfied by an array whose element type is written any and by nothing else, since no array is declared that way.

    The keyed collections have the same top, by the same reasoning one step along: Set.<any> is a set of some element type and Map.<any, any> a map of some key and value types, and every instantiation is a subtype of its family's top. What makes any admissible here is what makes it admissible above - a store into a collection is checked against the receiver's own declared types at run time (1.14.10), so a write through the wider view is refused whatever the static type permitted.

    A collection's top is decided ARGUMENT BY ARGUMENT rather than all at once, so Map.<string, any> is the top of the maps keyed by String and a Map.<uint8, uint8> is not a subtype of it. The array has one type argument and so never had to say this.

    A BARE type name is not a top. Set is the unparameterized type - a collection carrying no type arguments, whose behaviour is 1.15.7 - and a Set.<uint8> is not a subtype of it, exactly as a [ ] . < uint8 > is not a subtype of a bare [ ]. The top has a spelling, and it is the one that composes: Map.<string, Set.<any>> says what a bare Set in that position could not.

    Note 6

    This resolves an inconsistency rather than adding a rule. A specialization of a LIBRARY generic was formerly a subtype of its bare name while a specialization of a USER generic was not, so Set.<uint8> reached Set and G.<uint8> did not reach G - two readings of one rule, with nothing in this specification choosing between them. The array chooses: a bare name is the unparameterized type, and the erased form is written with any.

    The kind-specific steps record the variance chosen by this proposal: a nominal type is a subtype along its declared inheritance; an array is invariant in its element and in its extent, a fixed-length array being neither a subtype nor a supertype of the dynamic-length array of the same element (11.1 gives Span.<T>, the one type that accepts either, and 1.7.7 states the same rule for instanceof), with the array whose element is any a supertype of every array and tuple type (Note 5); a tuple is covariant position-wise, which is sound only because a store to a position is checked against the type the value carries for it (1.14.10), as the same rule makes [].<any> a supertype of every array, and makes Set.<any> and Map.<any, any> supertypes of every instantiation of theirs; a reference is invariant in its target, as is a shared (41.4); a composite type is covariant in its shape, which the frozenness of every composite makes sound (23.2). IsObjectSubtype (1.11.1.3) applies width subtyping to properties and depth subtyping through a readonly one; IsFunctionSubtype (1.10.2.4) applies contravariant-parameter, covariant-return subtyping to signatures. An enum type is additionally a subtype of its underlying type (1.11.8). The justification for each choice is given by the clause that introduces the corresponding feature.

    1.2.3.2 IsAssignable ( s, t )

    The abstract operation IsAssignable takes arguments s (a Type Record) and t (a Type Record) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether a value of the type s may be assigned where the type t is expected. This is the relation checked at bindings, arguments, and returns. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s.[[Kind]] is any or t.[[Kind]] is any, return true.
    2. Return IsSubtype(s, t, « »).
     Note

    When s is the any type and t is not, assignability holds but the value's membership in t is not known statically; a check is inserted at the boundary (1.7.3.1) that throws a TypeError if the value is not of the type t. When t is the any type, no check is required. This two-part treatment, static where the types are known and a run-time check at the any boundary, is the gradual character of the system: it is why an untyped program keeps its behaviour while a typed one is checked.

    1.2.4 Strict Mode for Annotated Code

    A Script whose own body contains a TypeAnnotation is strict mode code. A function-like unit whose parameters, return position or own body contains a TypeAnnotation is strict mode code, including its parameters and all code that inherits its strictness. This classification applies to the entire unit independently of source order. Annotation discovery for an enclosing unit excludes nested function-like units, including their parameters and return annotations, and nested class bodies. A method's computed name and decorator expressions belong to their enclosing evaluation scope. Classes and Modules retain their existing strictness.

    The trigger is syntactic and includes an annotation denoting any; it does not resolve or evaluate the annotated type. Conversion expressions, inferred types and other type syntax do not independently activate this rule. Nested functions inherit strictness downward, but a nested function's annotation does not activate strictness in its parent or siblings. The strict-code Early Errors are Syntax Errors, and the usual strict runtime semantics apply, including the unbound this value, unmapped arguments and direct eval's scope. An implicit strict unit does not contain a synthetic use-strict directive, so it does not acquire the separate prohibition on such a directive with non-simple parameters. A dynamically constructed function classifies its own combined parameter/body source; it does not inherit the caller's mode.

    Checked code (1.2.5) is classified the same way from a wider set of syntax, and adds type errors only.

    1.2.5 Checked Code

    A unit is a Script, a Module, a function-like unit or a class. Proposal syntax is any production this specification adds to the grammar of the pinned edition, a decorator included. A unit is checked code when its own syntax contains proposal syntax, or when it is nested in checked code. Discovery for a unit excludes nested units, including their parameters and return positions; a method's computed name and the decorators on a unit belong to the enclosing unit. The classification applies to the entire unit independently of source order, and it does not resolve or evaluate any type.

    Direct eval code is checked code when the code containing the direct eval is checked code, as it inherits that code's strictness; otherwise it classifies its own source. Indirect eval code classifies its own source. A dynamically constructed function classifies its own combined parameter and body source and does not inherit its caller's classification.

    Outside checked code, the judgments of 1.8.5.4 and 1.8.5.1 produce no type error, though the facts they establish still hold. A rule this specification attaches to a built-in, operator or declaration form of the pinned edition likewise produces no type error outside checked code, and keeps the behaviour of the pinned edition, including any error it throws when evaluated: the typed signatures of existing built-in methods, which also give their arguments no contextual type there; a store to a built-in accessor; the object operand of in and instanceof; a call of a value that is not callable; and overload sets formed from function declarations. Function declarations of one name form an overload set only where at least one of them is checked code, and an unannotated declaration then joins the set as a fallback.

    A rule about a declared type, or about a binding or global this specification introduces, applies everywhere. A program written for the pinned edition cannot reach one: it contains no proposal syntax, and its own definitions of those names shadow the new globals.

    Note

    Checked code and strict mode code are classified alike but from different triggers. Strictness changes run-time semantics and follows annotations only (1.2.4); checked code adds type errors only and follows all proposal syntax. A unit using match without an annotation is checked code but not strict mode code.

    1.2.6 The Static Type of an Expression

    A resolved typed super property read participates in immutable-binding inference just as the corresponding typed this property read does. This applies to an established computed key as well as a dotted name. The inherited member supplies its readable type without executing a getter. Extracting a method preserves its signature and receiver requirement; storing it in a binding does not bind its receiver. Unknown members, any and ordinary unannotated mutable bindings retain their existing treatment.

    The Static Type of an expression is the Type Record the type checker assigns to it. It is a syntax-directed operation defined by cases over the expression grammar. Each later clause that adds or modifies an expression form gives the Static Type for that form; the cases established by this clause are those that do not depend on a feature introduced later, listed in Table 2.

    Established evidence for an unannotated immutable String constant is preserved through an unannotated immutable copy, including parentheses and finite alias chains. Such evidence may determine a built-in concatenation's normal String result without creating an annotation-derived binding or return contract. Keep the value evidence distinct from the source-form judgment names a literal type: copying a literal name does not itself make the copy one. An explicit any view, mutable or reference alias, or unknown initializer supplies no such immutable-copy proof.

    When a source text uses an already initialized immutable binding, retain its established declared or inferred contract and any eligible constant evidence by that binding's identity in its declaration environment. A nearer declaration blocks fallback even when it supplies no evidence. Follow an import to its exporting binding; local import immutability does not establish that the target is immutable. Reading retained evidence does not invoke an environment method, ordinary getter or initializer, inspect a runtime value to manufacture a type, or execute earlier statements to obtain future evidence. Checking alone does not publish a program binding. A successfully initialized binding remains eligible after a later abrupt completion, while an unreached or abruptly failed initialization supplies no completed binding evidence.

    An initialized immutable binding whose value is a Symbol supplies that Symbol's identity as computed-property-key evidence, independently of whether its readable contract is symbol or any. An immutable copy and an import retain the identity of the actual target value. An uninitialized binding, mutable target, reference binding or opaque object-environment lookup supplies no such evidence. This key evidence does not manufacture a binding contract or annotation-derived participation, evaluate an initializer, or read a reference's current referent. At a Module's required checking boundary, use its declaration environment and the exporting bindings that have actually initialized; linking alone supplies no value identity.

    Where source analysis establishes that an immutable local declaration will receive a fresh Symbol, repeated visits to that declaration within the same checking unit retain one private key identity. Immutable aliases of that declaration retain that identity. Distinct declarations, including those with equal description text, remain distinct. A private checking identity is not an evaluated Symbol or a published binding value; it neither initializes the declaration nor substitutes for the actual Symbol when evaluation supplies it. Unknown initializers and shadowed intrinsic names supply no fresh-Symbol proof. Reconsider dependent computed-key judgments when the actual binding identity becomes available.

    Apply those retained facts in the environment the source text uses: an ordinary Script and a dynamically constructed function use their target realm's global environment, direct eval uses the caller's lexical environment, and indirect eval uses its eval realm's global environment. A binding in a different realm or activation, a same-spelled property, or an opaque object-environment lookup supplies no substitute. Retained type or constant evidence does not change the temporal dead zone, ordinary evaluation order, or reference permissions and liveness.

    An OptionalExpression is typed along its live chain. At each optional boundary, remove null and undefined from the base type and apply the ordinary member-access or call judgment to the remaining type and the subsequent chain segments. If that boundary can short-circuit, canonicalize the union of the live result type with undefined. An entirely nullish base contributes only undefined; a known non-nullish base introduces no additional absent result; a result whose Static Type is unknown remains any. Parentheses end the chain: (o?.a).b is an ordinary access to the optional result, whereas o?.a.b keeps the latter access on the live path. Redundant optional access on a non-nullish base is permitted. Keys, arguments and nested expressions are still checked, and the ordinary argument-binding rules apply to optional calls.

    A tagged template uses the ordinary call judgment with its template-strings object as the first argument and its substitution expressions as the remaining arguments. Each known first-argument position contributes the exact cooked String value produced by TemplateStrings, or undefined for an invalid escape; it is not a lexical lookup of the name undefined. The position count and cooked literal facts participate in overload selection. The raw positions remain Strings. This judgment changes neither GetTemplateObject, the frozen arrays and site identity it provides, nor the syntax errors for untagged templates. A constructor call uses its resolved constructor signature, including explicit type arguments, before applying the same argument-binding judgments.

    Computed names of object methods and accessors, and class methods and fields, are checked using the ordinary expression and property-key conversion judgments. This includes generator, async and async-generator methods. Check each name in its enclosing evaluation scope before entering the member parameters, body or instance/static this scope, retaining the class self-name and type-parameter scopes. The expressions are checked even in an unused body; no key is evaluated during this traversal. Assignment, reference permissions and liveness retain their ordinary rules.

    A setter body is checked with its PropertySetParameterList bound in the setter's parameter scope, including binding patterns and the enclosing class's type parameters. Its parameter annotations, assignments and shadowing obey the ordinary parameter-binding judgments. The computed property name is checked before entering that scope.

    A member read whose key is a statically established Symbol identity uses the declared member's type, just as a read with a known String key does. The identity is resolved in the expression's lexical scope; a shadowing declaration does not inherit an outer constant's key. This judgment includes inherited members and substitutes the receiver's type arguments. An optional member contributes the union of its declared type with undefined, including when combining the member types of a union receiver. An unknown key or a key no alternative declares remains governed by the ordinary dynamic read rules; in particular, an array's Symbol property is not an indexed element.

    A write through a union receiver must satisfy the write permissions of every reachable known alternative at that operation, after narrowing. It is a type error if a selected member is readonly in any such alternative and the operation lacks that member's constructor or initializer permission (1.11.2). This applies to simple, compound and update assignments and to assignment targets in destructuring and iteration. Write permission is separate from assignability of the stored value. This rule does not freeze an object, deepen readonly, or change intersection member judgments.

    A store through a union receiver or a statically established finite set of property keys must satisfy each reachable known destination's write type separately. This includes array and tuple elements, simple and compound assignments, destructuring and iteration targets, and stores through reference aliases whose origins are known. Fresh literals receive each destination's contextual type independently; a union of read types is not a replacement for these write obligations. A single location declared with a union type remains one destination. The same alternatives determine write permission and whether a member belongs to closed typed-class storage (1.7.6); open structural objects are not thereby closed. Unknown alternatives retain their runtime checks and do not erase separately known obligations. Key expressions are not evaluated by this judgment, and correlations are used only where independently established.

    A call through a union of function types is checked separately against every reachable known function alternative, after narrowing and optional-chain short-circuiting. Argument mapping, ref requirements, generic inference and overload resolution are performed within each alternative, using that alternative's contextual types. It is a type error if a known alternative refuses the call; the signatures of distinct union alternatives do not form one overload set. When each selected return is known, the call's Static Type is their union. A contextual result requirement applies independently to each alternative. Unknown arguments and spreads retain the existing gradual checks; uncertainty about a spread's suffix does not erase a known incompatible prefix. Per-alternative checking does not select a runtime callee or transfer one alternative's inferred bindings to every callee. Function intersections are not governed by this union rule.

    new.target is any DELIBERATELY, and the reason is worth stating so that a later reading does not take it for an omission. Its value is a constructor or undefined, and the constructor is not bounded by the enclosing function: Reflect.construct(_target_, _args_, _newTarget_) supplies an arbitrary one, so a type naming the enclosing class or a subclass of it would be unsound. The honest type is therefore a union of a callable type with undefined - and a union with undefined cannot have its members read without narrowing, which new.target ? new.target.name : *undefined* requires and which this specification defines only for references: a binding, and a member access through one. new.target is a meta-property rather than a reference, so no narrowing applies to it.

    Note 1

    A union type here would refuse a program that ECMAScript admits, which is worse than saying nothing: any claims nothing and so cannot license an elision (1.7.5) that a value contradicts. Should narrowing ever extend to meta-properties - import.meta has the same shape - the union becomes both sound and usable, and this row should be revisited then. Widening any to a type is a compatible change; a wrong type is not.

     Note 2

    Reading a member of a UNION gives the union of that member's type across the union's members, and is a type error where ANY of them does not declare the keySOME of them declare the key and others do not.

    The accessible keys are therefore the INTERSECTION of the members' keys, and the type of a read is the UNION of what each declares for it. _c_.x at { x: int32 } | { x: int8 } is int32 | int8, so reading it AS an int32 is an error: the program cannot know which member _c_ holds. _c_.x at { x: int32 } | { y: string } is an error outright, and a null member - which declares nothing - makes every read of a nullable object one.

    Narrowing is how a program reads a member a single member declares (1.8.5.3). A key EVERY member declares still reads without narrowing, which is what makes a discriminated union usable: the discriminant is readable, and reading it is what narrows.

    A key NO member declares is not this case either, and the distinction is the reasoning above: uncertainty about which member is held decides nothing where every member agrees the key is absent. Such a read is an ordinary absent read, governed by the note in 1.7.6 - it yields undefined on every value the union admits, exactly as it does on a single object type, and if (u.maybe), typeof u.absent and _u_.absent === undefined are as ordinary here as anywhere. Reading u.toString() is the same case: no member's structure declares it, and it is reachable on every value the union admits.

    An INTERSECTION is not this case. Every value of one satisfies all its members, so each member's type is known and a read of it needs nothing.
    Note 3

    An element of a destructuring pattern is a binding, and its annotation is a boundary like any other: let [a: uint8] = [300] throws, and let [a: uint8] = [1] binds a uint8 rather than a Number. The design writes this form throughout, and a pattern is where the annotation has nowhere else to go — there is no second place to say what a is.
