    A plain formal parameter is a different case with its own entry above: its type is enforced once, where the arguments are bound and a generic call's type arguments are known. A pattern ELEMENT inside a parameter has no such entry, which is why it needs this one.

    A destructuring pattern preserves the known read contribution of the declared property it selects, for String and Symbol keys alike. If every alternative of a union source declares that key, the contribution is the union of those read types, including undefined for optional members. An element annotation is checked against that contribution, and typed parameter patterns and participating const patterns retain it under their existing inference rules. This does not infer a type for an otherwise untyped let binding, impose a new missing-key rule, or establish a property contribution from an unknown key or a possibly overwriting unknown spread.

    Where those existing rules give an extracted non-reference binding an inferred contract, initialization of that binding is a boundary at that contract, as for a plain inferred binding. Read the property or iterator value, evaluate its default if selected, then perform the required admission before initializing the binding or proceeding to the next extraction. A failure preserves earlier effects and already initialized bindings, leaves that binding uninitialized, and follows ordinary iterator-closing rules where applicable. Substitute generic parameters in the same runtime context as the enclosing binding. Successful admission establishes the binding's contract for later uses, captured reads and retained binding evidence. This does not infer a contract for an otherwise gradual binding, deepen readonly, promote an already conforming plain aggregate into typed storage, or grant a reference borrow permission. Explicit annotations and reference bindings retain their existing separate rules.

    Note 4

    A compile-time constant is a literal, a name denoting a constant of literal or enumerator type, or a compile-time numeric constant expression over those, so its value is fixed by the source alone; every clause that names the term reads this definition.

    The Static Type of a numeric literal given here is its type in the absence of a contextual type. Literal propagation, by which a literal takes the type its context requires, so that 0 in a uint8 position is a uint8, refines this and is defined by the conversions clause. The Static Types of the remaining expression forms, including operators, calls, array and object literals, and this, are given by the clauses that specify those forms; until a form is specified, its Static Type is the any type. An unannotated let or var binding has the any Static Type unless it uses a typed initializer. An unannotated const preserves a type supplied by a typed feature in its initializer: a typed construction, call result, conversion, binding, member or element read, or an expression composed from such contributions. Parentheses are transparent. An explicit annotation takes precedence, including any; an initializer whose Static Type is any leaves the binding dynamic. Literal-only untyped initializers do not acquire binding types under this rule. The preserved type describes the value held by the binding and does not make its fields or elements readonly. Initialization is a boundary at the inferred type, subject to the same stability conditions as an explicit annotation (1.7.5.1); immutability of the destination alone does not establish that its initializer produces a value of that type. Literal propagation nonetheless reaches a USE of an unannotated const whose initializer is a compile-time numeric constant expression, which produces the value the initializer would have produced had it been written at that position: const K = 3.14 yields a Number where nothing requires a type, a float64 in a float64 position, and a float32 in a float32 one. This infers no type for the binding, and adds none: it decides which VALUE a use produces, which is the question propagation already answers one position earlier. A let is excluded, because a binding that may be reassigned must have a type its assignments are checked against; an annotation on a const excludes it for the same reason. The constants of the Math object named by 21.3.1 participate as such a const does, since none of them can be written as a literal that denotes it.

    1.2.7 Compile-Time Evaluation

    Because a type is a value, a type annotation may be an expression that computes one (1.4.2.4); an expression whose computation can be carried out during type checking is compile-time evaluable. This clause defines when such an expression may be evaluated, when it is, what its evaluation may do, and what carries its result before it can run: the evaluability discipline, the deferred application that stands for a call whose generic arguments are not yet bound, the evaluation of a call with memoization and a fixpoint for recursion, and the budget that bounds the whole.

    Evaluation is confined to the admitted compile-time-evaluable fragment. A top-level type-position expression required by pre-evaluation checking is evaluated at the source-checking boundary of 1.2.8. For a Module, that boundary follows the module evaluation order and dependency availability specified in 1.3.8; it is not a graph-wide requirement to finish computed type checking before any module body runs. A type-position expression inside a generic declaration evaluates at each specialization, once every generic parameter it reads is bound. A call may resolve through imports to a compile-time-evaluable function declaration. Resolving that call does not execute an imported module body on demand or admit reads of ambient mutable state; the evaluability restrictions below continue to apply.

    No operation of this specification evaluates such an expression before every generic parameter it reads is bound. The invariant this serves is stated exactly: the inference fixpoint is builder-free, and every checker-visible effect of user type code is declarative data, a forward-verified proposal, or a per-instantiation-checked contract. Those three are the whole of what user code may contribute to checking, and each is closed: the declarative data are a signature's [[ThisType]] and [[Narrows]] (8) and the hooks of a meta type (6), which the checker reads and calls at named seams; a forward-verified proposal is a trial candidate or a declared inverse (15), which binds nothing until forward evaluation and assignability confirm it; and a contract is checked at every evaluation before it is believed at any (14). The computed constraints of 1.4.3.4 are the measure of the boundary rather than an exception to it, since a constraint over T runs after T is bound and before the parameter it constrains is, which is after everything it reads.

    Note

    The blunt form of this invariant, that a builder never runs during inference at all, is what a reader expects and is not quite what holds, so it is worth being precise about which part is load-bearing. A trial evaluates a builder while a parameter is being inferred; what it does not do is let the builder into the fixpoint. Each evaluation is of a builder whose arguments are already bound, to a candidate rather than to an inference variable, and its result is checked rather than solved against. Nothing runs backwards, nothing is unified, and no builder observes a partially-solved state. That is the difference between a proposer the checker verifies and a participant the checker trusts, and this proposal admits only the first. It is stated so that later ergonomic pressure has something to push against, and the sentence to push against is the one this note follows, not the slogan.

    1.2.7.1 IsCompileTimeEvaluable ( expr )

    The abstract operation IsCompileTimeEvaluable takes argument expr (a Parse Node) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether expr can be evaluated during type checking, reading only values known at that time. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If expr is a literal, return true.
    2. If expr is a reference to a binding, then
      1. Let binding be the binding to which expr resolves under the ordinary lexical and module binding rules.
      2. If binding is an indirect import binding, follow its target bindings to the binding in the exporting module and set binding to that binding. Use its declaration and initializer in the following steps.
      3. If binding is a parameter of the function under evaluation, or a local binding of that function, return true.
      4. If binding is a function declaration binding whose source text contains no assignment to that binding and no direct eval, and the declared function is compile-time evaluable, return true.
      5. If binding is immutable and its initializer is compile-time evaluable, return true.
      6. If binding is a value generic parameter or a type generic parameter, return true.
      7. If binding is an enumerator of the enum under evaluation that is declared before the enumerator whose initializer is being evaluated, return true.
      8. Return false.
    3. If expr is a function call, then
      1. Let callee be the expression that expr calls.
      2. Let args be the List of argument expressions of expr.
      3. If IsCompileTimeEvaluable(callee) is false, return false.
      4. If callee does not denote a compile-time-evaluable function, return false.
      5. For each element arg of args, do
        1. If IsCompileTimeEvaluable(arg) is false, return false.
      6. Return true.
    4. If every operand of expr is compile-time evaluable and the result of expr's operator is determined by its operands, return true.
    5. Return false.

    A compile-time-evaluable function is one whose body reads only its parameters, its own local bindings, immutable bindings whose initializers are compile-time evaluable, and other compile-time-evaluable functions. It may create local state and mutate it. Its body contains no await, no yield, no direct or indirect eval, no use of the Function constructor, and no construction of a Proxy; regular expressions are within the fragment. It performs no input or output and reads no ambient mutable state, none of which it can name under the reading rule above, which is why the discipline is a property of what the code can name rather than a wall around what it does.

    A function declaration creates a mutable binding, yet it is the callee this operation exists to admit: the callee of a builder call resolves to a function declaration. Its binding is therefore treated as immutable here where the source text contains no assignment to it and no direct eval. A function the program reassigns is not the function the checker would read, so a call through its name is not evaluable, and a let or var binding is not immutable whether or not the program writes to it.

    An import's local immutability does not make the exported binding immutable. This judgment follows the resolved export, including re-exports; a read of an exported let or var remains a read of mutable state. A module namespace member that resolves to an exported binding is subject to the same judgment. The declarations and initializers consulted by this judgment retain their original lexical scopes. In particular, free references in a builder and in its helper functions resolve in the environments of those functions, not in the importing source text or a temporary environment reconstructed from their signatures. A known Static Type is not the value of a binding: a function signature must not stand in for the function, nor may a namespace's structural type stand in for the namespace value. These rules neither initialize an unavailable binding nor execute a dependency body; availability and failure timing remain those of 1.3.8.

    Note 1

    This is the same notion the where clauses and metadata annotations of the extensions require, and it is what lets a switch over a generic parameter be evaluated to a type during checking. A function that is not compile-time evaluable remains an ordinary function in expression position; only its use in type position is restricted. Local mutation is admitted because an accumulator array or a visited Set is how a walk over a type is written; shared module-level mutable state is not evaluable and is rejected statically, which also disposes of the hand-rolled memo cache, since the memoization of 1.2.7.3 is the supported mechanism and is observably equivalent. Fixing the fragment's grammar and semantics as a normative implementation target in its own right, with a conformance suite, is A; the discipline above is the boundary it pins.

     Note 2

    A preprocessor module and every export of it used as a replacement decorator are required to be evaluable, for the reason a type builder is: both are user code an implementation runs while compiling, and the discipline is what makes the run deterministic. There is one notion here, not two.

    1.2.7.2 Deferred Applications

    A call whose arguments involve an unbound generic parameter cannot evaluate yet, and is carried as a type: the deferred Type Record of Table 1. The deferred application Type Record of a ComputedType is the deferred Type Record whose [[Operator]] is the function its callee resolves to and whose [[Operands]] holds, for each argument in order, an element that is: the TypeParameter Parse Node where the argument is a reference to an unbound generic parameter; the deferred Type Record where the argument is itself a ComputedType reading one; and otherwise the argument's compile-time value, a Type Object contributing its [[TypeRecord]].

    Identity is by that key. SameTypeWithAssumptions compares two deferred Records by operator identity and SameArgumentList, and Type Objects are interned, so two mentions of partial(T) in one generic body are one Type Object before anything is known about T. At specialization, each TypeParameter Parse Node among the [[Operands]] is replaced by the parameter's binding, and the application evaluates by 1.2.7.3.

    Two compound compile-time constants, arrays or plain objects of compile-time constants, are structurally equivalent when they have the same shape and their leaves are pairwise SameValue, a Type Object comparing by identity and a RegExp by its source and flags. A compound constant argument contributes to an application's identity by structural equivalence rather than by reference, so pick(User, ['id', 'name']) written twice is one application although the array is a fresh object at each occurrence.

    Note

    An unbound parameter is represented by its declaring Parse Node rather than by a Type Record kind of its own, because a parameter is never a type by itself anywhere this specification currently reaches; what a bare parameter annotation denotes inside a generic body belongs to the generics work, and the hook for it is recorded in Table 39. Structural equivalence for compound constants is the value semantics the Composites proposal gives tuples and records; it is stated directly here so that the rule does not depend on that proposal, and 23, which specifies composites for this design, coincides with it by construction.

    1.2.7.3 EvaluateBuilderCall ( f, args )

    The abstract operation EvaluateBuilderCall takes arguments f (a compile-time-evaluable function) and args (a List) and returns either a normal completion containing a Type Object or a throw completion. It evaluates one type-level call, with memoization and a fixpoint for recursion, and checks the contracts of 14 against its result. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let key be CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: f, [[Operands]]: args }).
    2. If the evaluation memo contains an entry for key, return that entry's Type Object.
    3. If the in-flight List contains key, then
      1. If no placeholder exists for key, let the placeholder for key be a fresh Type Object, created without interning and distinguished from every other value.
      2. Return the placeholder for key.
    4. Append key to the in-flight List.
    5. Let result be Completion(the evaluation of the body of f with the elements of args as its arguments under the semantics of this clause).
    6. Remove key from the in-flight List.
    7. Let value be ? result.
    8. If value is not a Type Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    9. If a placeholder exists for key, then
      1. If value is the placeholder for key, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Let final be the Type Record obtained from value.[[TypeRecord]] by replacing each position that holds the placeholder with a reference back to the type being defined, forming a cyclic Type Record.
      3. If no replaced position is a reference position, throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Set value to GetTypeObject(final).
    10. Record value in the evaluation memo for key.
    11. Return value.

    The evaluation memo is a specification-level map from canonical deferred Type Records to Type Objects, and the in-flight List tracks the keys under evaluation. Each distinct key evaluates once per program; every later occurrence, in any module, yields the same interned Type Object. An implementation may realize both devices in any way that yields these results.

    Evaluation of the body of f uses f's ordinary function environment and the applicable parameter binding, generic specialization, receiver and return contracts. Permission to evaluate a function during checking does not remove any of these contracts. An imported name that denotes f denotes that same function for this operation; importing it does not instantiate a new function in the importer's environment. A failed contract or a result that is not a Type Object fails the containing type computation under 1.2.8. Reuse of a memoized result must preserve these requirements and the accounting rules of 1.2.7.5.

    Note

    The fixpoint is what makes a builder work on a recursive type with no API surface: a builder mapping over a type that references itself re-enters itself with the same key, receives the placeholder, and the placeholder resolves at return into the same kind of named-back-edge cyclic type that a recursive alias produces from syntax, validated by the same cycle rule (1.8.1). The two throws distinguish the two failures: a call whose entire result is its own placeholder learnt nothing and is unproductive recursion, and a cycle resolved at a position that embeds the layout inline would demand an infinite layout. A recursion that never repeats a key, a genuinely infinite family, is not caught here; it runs into the budget of 1.2.7.4. This mechanism is the computational twin of the coinductive assumption Lists that SameTypeWithAssumptions and IsSubtype already carry.

    1.2.7.4 The Evaluation Budget

    Evaluation under this clause is metered by two host-defined limits: a count of evaluation steps and a count of type-construction requests, each per top-level type-position evaluation. Every operation that evaluates a type is metered, the instantiation of a generic type alias among them, since an unmetered one is a way to recurse without spending the budget; so is BindTypeArguments (4.3), and with it the specialization of a declaration over a variadic parameter, since a declaration applying itself to a pack one element longer is the recursion a type alias performs with one more field. For a given source text, two hosts either produce, position for position, the same interned types, or at least one reports a type error: the limits decide whether compilation fails, never what it produces.

    The budget bounds a computation, which either completes or is abandoned and reported. A rule requiring a SEARCH — over the types an argument could take, rather than over a fixed evaluation — is not metered by it and is refused where it would otherwise arise (4.12), because truncating a search under a budget yields a wrong answer where truncating a computation yields none.

    A limit must be one the implementation can actually reach. An implementation whose own resources — a native stack, a heap — are exhausted before the limit is has not met this clause, whatever the limit's value: the evaluation ends in a way no program can observe and no diagnostic names, which is the outcome this clause exists to prevent. Where an implementation cannot raise its own capacity, it lowers the limit instead. A limit above what an implementation can reach is not a limit.

    Note 1

    This bears on any floor a host is asked to meet. A step count in the millions bounds a computation that widens as it runs, and bounds nothing about one that RECURSES: a self-referential type alias reaches an implementation's native stack in thousands of steps, not millions, so an implementation meeting a high floor and reporting nothing has satisfied the number and failed the requirement. The requirement is that exhaustion be reported, and a host chooses limits low enough that it is.

    Lowering the STEP limit is the wrong remedy, and a host is not asked to. A step count low enough to stop a recursion would stop a wide computation that was going to finish, and the two failures are unrelated: one exhausts a stack, the other a clock. A host that meters NESTING separately — a third count, of type-position evaluations open at once — bounds the resource that is actually scarce and leaves the step floor where it is. The value is not a floor this specification fixes, because the depth a native stack affords differs between implementations and between the constructs a recursion passes through: a recursion through an array or a function type walks further per level than one through an object member, so a host measures its own worst case rather than trusting a shared number.

    Exhaustion is not an abrupt completion the evaluated code can observe. No try statement within the evaluation handles it; the evaluation is abandoned, and EvaluateToTypeObject of the containing type-position expression is empty, with a diagnostic naming the outermost call and the deepest frames. The containing source check reports a StaticTypeError for evaluation-limit exhaustion. An incidental hook exception or lack of a result after exhaustion does not instead establish an ordinary type mismatch, select an overload fallback, or supply an unknown type.

    Note 2

    "Not an abrupt completion the evaluated code can observe" is a requirement on how exhaustion is REPRESENTED, not only on what it means. An implementation that reports exhaustion by throwing gives a where predicate or a builder a try that catches it, and the evaluation then continues on a budget it has already overrun. Recording exhaustion as a state of the evaluation, so that every metered operation after it does nothing and the containing evaluation fails whatever the evaluated code does with what it caught, has the behaviour this clause describes. The diagnostic belongs at the containing evaluation for the same reason: the operation that spends the last step is wherever the budget happened to run out, which is not the outermost call this clause asks to name.

     Note 3

    Making exhaustion catchable inside evaluation would let a program's types depend on the host's limits: the same source would elaborate differently under a large budget and a small one, and the memo would cache whichever answer came first, which is nondeterminism through the error channel. Graceful degradation therefore has to be deterministic and structural: a builder takes an explicit cap as an argument and computes the identical type on every host, rather than falling back when fuel runs out. Bounding a deliberately Turing-complete type language by limits has precedent; the magnitudes are fixed here as floors a host meets or exceeds: ten million evaluation steps and one million type-construction requests per top-level evaluation, ten thousand automaton states for the pattern decision procedure, and sixty-four specializations for a trial, calibrated against the erased-system limits the design cites. A host exceeding a floor can only turn a failure into a result, never a result into a different one, so the invariant above is undisturbed.

    1.2.7.5 Type Evaluation Accounting Boundaries

    A type computation includes the complete evaluation it invokes: builder and declared inverse bodies, their callbacks, generic arguments and defaults, object member and tuple element defaults, array extents, refinement predicates, and metadata hooks. Charging only the entry to a user function does not bound that computation. Nested evaluation shares the enclosing computation's resource state and cannot reset its remaining allowance. When an implementation imposes the nesting limit of 1.2.7.4, that limit includes ordinary ECMAScript function-body invocations made during the computation, including mutual recursion and calls through callbacks; tail-call optimization does not remove a logical invocation from this accounting. Suspension retains that state; evaluation by another agent has a distinct state. Evaluating ordinary program code outside such a computation does not consume its allowance.

    A type-construction request is an invocation of GetTypeObject while type evaluation is active. Charge one request on entry, before canonicalization, lookup, or allocation, whether the result is already interned or requires a new Type Object. Reading an existing Type Object without invoking this operation is not a construction request. Physical allocation, garbage collection, interning order, and a previously populated intern table do not determine this charge. A tuple candidate enumerated by trial specialization consumes the additional request specified in 15.2, even if that candidate has no materialized Type Object.

    Each counter begins at zero. A request whose charge is no greater than the remaining allowance succeeds and reduces that allowance by its charge; a larger request marks the computation exhausted before the requested evaluation proceeds. Exactly consuming the allowance is permitted. Exhaustion is sticky until the outermost computation ends: unwinding a nested call, handling an incidental exception, or returning a fallback does not clear it. A result obtained after exhaustion must not be published as a successful specialization, inverse proposal, resolved type, or successful evaluation-memo entry.

    The enclosing checking boundary tests exhaustion before interpreting the computation's result. Exhaustion takes precedence over an incidental hook exception, an absent result, an assignability mismatch, or a candidate-selection failure produced while abandoning that computation. The diagnostic identifies evaluation-limit exhaustion as specified in 1.2.7.4. An implementation failure of its own stack or heap is not evidence that a language type is invalid and must not be translated into an ordinary type-mismatch proof.

    Note

    These rules distinguish logical requests from physical allocation and define containment of exhaustion. The host-defined limits and the remaining evaluation-step accounting in 1.2.7.4 still permit acceptance differences. This clause does not by itself establish a portable total fuel model or authorize a host to report native failure as semantic exhaustion.

    1.2.7.6 EvaluateToTypeObject ( expr )

    The abstract operation EvaluateToTypeObject takes argument expr (a Parse Node) and returns either a Type Object or empty. It evaluates expr, which appears in type position, to the Type Object it denotes, or defers it, or returns empty if it does not evaluate to one. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If IsCompileTimeEvaluable(expr) is false, return empty.
    2. If expr is a ComputedType and expr reads a generic parameter that is not bound, return GetTypeObject(the deferred application Type Record of expr (1.2.7.2)).
    3. Let result be Completion(the evaluation of expr during type checking in which each call of a compile-time-evaluable function is performed by EvaluateBuilderCall).
    4. If result is an abrupt completion, return empty.
    5. Let value be result.[[Value]].
    6. If value is not a Type Object, return empty.
    7. Return value.

    It is a type error if an expression appears in type position and EvaluateToTypeObject of it is empty (1.2.8). When the empty arises from an abrupt completion whose value is an Error, the type error's diagnostic carries that Error's message, prefixed by the source text of the type-position expression; when it arises from the budget, the diagnostic is the one 1.2.7.4 describes. Diagnostic content is not observable to the evaluated program.

    Note

    Evaluation during type checking uses the ordinary evaluation semantics of the operators and calls involved, restricted to the compile-time-evaluable fragment, so no separate evaluator is defined. Because enum and sealed-class exhaustiveness is checked, a switch used to map a value to a type covers every case its argument can take and therefore yields a Type Object rather than undefined. A thrown exception becoming the diagnostic is the design's authored-error story: a builder states its own misuse message, which an erased type language cannot.

    1.2.8 Type Errors

    Type errors fall into three families (1.2.5). A judgment that reads a type inferred from code, and a rule attached to a built-in, operator or declaration form of the pinned edition, apply only in checked code. A rule about a declared type, or about a binding or global this specification introduces, applies everywhere.

    Implicit protocol calls check their actual receiver against each applicable signature's [[ThisType]], alongside that signature's argument and result obligations. The receiver is the resource for disposal, the iterable for an iterator entry hook, the iterator for next or return, the original object for primitive conversion and the thenable for promise assimilation. The ordinary method receiver marker denotes that receiver and is not an unrelated nominal requirement. A failure proof combines receiver, argument and result failures per signature and per reached alternative; an unknown or viable alternative prevents that proof. Preserve generic substitution, nullish fallback, skipped stages, iterator closing and completion precedence. The checking pass invokes none of these methods.

    A reached optional call applies the same argument-spread eligibility rules as an ordinary call. Short-circuiting alternatives do not evaluate or check an otherwise skipped argument operation. A possibly reached call still checks an established invalid spread; any, named object spreads and unknown iteration counts retain the ordinary call rules.

    A type error is a violation of the type system detected by the type checker: an assignment whose source is not assignable to its target, a call whose arguments match no signature, a type annotation that is not compile-time evaluable, and the like. The clauses that follow state such a violation with the phrase “it is a type error if”.

    A constructor reached through a stable lexical value origin retains its argument contracts, including named, optional, reference and generic parameters. A conditional constructor target is checked against each established alternative independently; it is not an overload set. Shadowing, explicit any, reassignment, decorators or an unresolved origin prevent transporting a contract without further evidence. No constructor or getter is executed to recover an origin.

    A type error that is determinable before a source text runs is an Early Error: a source text that contains one is rejected rather than evaluated. Detection is the work of the checking pass, the logical source check specified here and in 1.3. An implementation may divide this work into several physical traversals or reuse validated results when it preserves the required judgments, applicability, failure timing and effects. The purely syntactic type rules are applied together with the other Early Errors at parse; the rules that evaluate — a computed type, a builder call, a hook of the metadata protocol (6) — are applied by the checking pass, under the discipline and budget of 1.2.7. For a Script the pass runs when evaluation of the script would begin, before the first step of its body; for a Module it runs at the per-module boundary of 1.3.8, before that module's own body and after the dependency prerequisites required by the ordinary module evaluation algorithms. A cycle does not require every dependency body to have completed. The source text of an eval is a Script and is checked as one. The source text CreateDynamicFunction builds is checked as one unit, in the global scope where that function is created, at the point where CreateDynamicFunction enforces its other Early Errors, and a type error is thrown there as they are. Before applying any judgment that consults them, the pass processes the source text's own type declarations — its type aliases, its interfaces, its meta declarations, the implicit cast operators of its primitive blocks (6.5), and the inverse decorations of its compile-time-evaluable functions (15.3) — in source order, which is what makes a meta type declared in a source text govern a judgment in the same source text; a declaration the pass has processed is not processed again when evaluation reaches its position. Type alias and interface declarations inside export wrappers participate under 1.3.7.

    A check that cannot be resolved statically, because a value reaches a typed position only as the any type, is deferred to run time. 1.7 specifies where these deferred checks are inserted and what they throw: a TypeError when a value is not of the required type, and a RangeError when a numeric value is outside the range of its type.

    Note

    The design documents sometimes describe a statically-determinable violation, such as assigning a uint32 to a uint8 binding, as a “TypeError”. This specification realizes such a violation as an Early Error, and reserves a thrown TypeError for the any boundary and other genuinely dynamic checks. The distinction is observable: an Early Error rejects the source text before any of it runs, whereas a thrown TypeError occurs during evaluation. Treating a statically-determinable type violation as a whole-source rejection matches a strict, check-before-run type system; whether some violations should instead be deferred to a thrown error at the offending operation was a decision left open when this clause was first written and is now settled, in this direction, for the reason that follows: the compile-time evaluation phase (1.2.7) already commits every implementation to the per-module checking pass this clause now names, so the cost that once made deferral attractive is sunk, and a diagnostic at the declaration is strictly better than the same diagnostic at first execution. For a module the rejection is observable after the module's dependencies have evaluated, which is when the pass runs; that two-phase timing is not new, being exactly how an error thrown by a module's own evaluation already behaves.

    1.2.8.1 Proved Library Operations

    A proved Map.groupBy result retains the established callback key contract and the source iteration contribution as the element contract of each fresh group array. A proved Object.groupBy result retains the same group contract and the callback result after ToPropertyKey: Symbol keys remain Symbols, while established non-Symbol primitive keys become Strings. These are facts about fresh results, not invariant type stamps placed on ordinary collections. Check a receiving annotation using its normal adoption and conversion rules. No non-empty group is inferred from an empty or unknown source, and unknown callback, key-conversion or iteration effects retain the runtime boundary.

    At proved intrinsic String.prototype.replace and replaceAll operations, a callable replacement is checked against each established invocation's actual argument list and undefined receiver. A string search supplies the matched String, its numeric offset and the entire input String; a RegExp or another replacement protocol may supply a different list and requires its own proof. Use ordinary parameter conversion, omission, defaults and rest binding. A proved absence of matches establishes no callback invocation. A custom @@replace method, a replacement method or unknown lookup effects do not inherit the intrinsic contract.

    At an established implicit ToString stage of a proved library operation, a participating operand necessarily containing only Symbols is a type error. This includes a string search operand of String.prototype.includes and an Array.prototype.join separator when their preceding stages are established. The examples are not a list: an operation is proved by its origin, so every proved intrinsic that converts an operand with ToString has the stage, among them the search operands of startsWith, endsWith, indexOf, lastIndexOf and localeCompare, each argument of String.prototype.concat, the filler of padStart and padEnd where the target length exceeds the receiver's, and the first argument of parseInt, parseFloat and the URI functions. Array.prototype.join and toString also convert each element after the separator; that stage is established where the receiver's type fixes a length of at least one, as a tuple or an array of fixed extent does, and not for an array that may be empty. Do not replace ToString with a String-only parameter requirement: numeric and other ordinarily convertible primitives remain admitted. The explicit String function's Symbol conversion is unchanged. A proved Object.is is a test whose answer the types may already know: it is a type error where a participating operand's type cannot hold the other operand's value, as a search with a needle its element type cannot hold is (1.14.10, 1.15.4.1). A proved Array.isArray declares a narrowing of its argument (8.2) to the ~array~ and ~tuple~ members of its type, whose every value is an Array and stays one, and away from its primitive members, none of which is one; a proved Number static declares a narrowing to the Number-valued members, answering false for any other value as its existing signature does. Classify the established argument-domain members independently by each proved intrinsic predicate's answer: a true member survives only on the true edge, a false member only on the false edge, and an unknown member on both. In particular, a Number-valued floating domain may still answer false to Number.isInteger. Publish an argument fact only to its preserved captured origin; lexical shadowing or replacement of the intrinsic defeats its origin proof. A test of either is therefore judged by 1.8.5.4. A proved Object.is supplies only SameValue-compatible branch evidence under 1.8.5.1. It is not rewritten as strict equality: zero signs and decimal cohort identity retain their distinct semantics. Unknown earlier protocol effects retain runtime checks.

    At a proved typed array or window set operation, read the source as an array-like object, not as an iterable. Establish its length, the converted offset, the destination bounds and the reached indexed reads before checking a copied value against the corresponding destination storage type. An incompatible established store is a type error under the same rules as a direct typed store. An empty copy creates no element obligation; an earlier range failure does not establish a store. Overlap, conversion order, source getters, range errors and reference liveness retain their runtime semantics.

    At proved Object.create or Object.setPrototypeOf, a participating prototype argument necessarily outside Object or null is a type error. Preserve Object.setPrototypeOf's preceding RequireObjectCoercible stage and its ordinary handling of non-nullish primitive targets. This is a prototype-argument judgment, not structural adoption or a requirement that the target itself be an Object.

    A proved synchronous Array.from result carries the element contract established by the same operation, source and callback proof used for its input checks. With a supplied mapper, use its established result contract; with an omitted or undefined mapper, use the source's established iteration contribution. Check a receiving type against that result at the ordinary conversion boundary. Do not infer elements from mutable indexed storage, infer an incompatible element from an empty source, or turn initial result length into fixed storage extent. An unknown callback result or lost intrinsic proof retains the runtime boundary. This rule introduces no synchronous result contract for Array.fromAsync.

    At a proved intrinsic Reflect.apply, check the selected target's callability, the supplied receiver and the forwarded argument list at its ordinary callable contract. Build the list using the operation's array-like positional reads, not iteration; establish the relevant count, entries and effects. Preserve ordinary overload selection, defaults, rest binding and conversions. Reference Values decay under the built-in rule; forwarding does not manufacture references for reference parameters.

    At a proved intrinsic Reflect.construct, check the construction capabilities of the target and of an explicitly supplied newTarget independently. Check the established array-like argument list against the target's construct signatures, not newTarget's parameters. Preserve overload selection and ordinary binding. The restriction on directly instantiating an abstract class is not a prohibition on its use as a constructible newTarget or base. A different newTarget does not establish that the result has the target's ordinary instance type. Unknown capabilities, argument reads, specializations or effects remain dynamic. These judgments allocate no instance and change no reference-liveness rule.

    A proved selected function contributes its declared generic capability independently of its result signature. Applying explicit type arguments to a function declared nongeneric, such as the original Object.keys, is a type error. Generic statics such as Object.values, Object.entries, Array.from and Array.of retain their declared parameters. A mutable property's spelling does not establish this capability; aliases require the same origin and effect proof.

    At a proved intrinsic Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.any or Promise.allSettled, it is a type error when a participating input's established type cannot satisfy the synchronous iteration protocol the operation requires. Ordinary iterable values are admitted; elements need not themselves be Promises. Preserve every viable or unknown alternative. Where no early proof applies, the original rejection and completion behaviour remains in force.

    At proved Array.from, Array.fromAsync, Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy calls, check the supplied callback's callability and each established invocation against its ordinary value-parameter and receiver boundaries, including omission, defaults, rest binding and permitted conversions. An omitted or undefined Array mapper selects identity mapping; a grouping callback is required. A known empty source does not establish an invocation with an incompatible element, although the operation still checks callability. Use the selected operation's own await stages: Array.fromAsync awaits the values it supplies to the mapper and its mapped results. Do not infer iteration from mutable indexed storage. Immutable tuple Composites can establish ordered positions; unknown iteration or callback alternatives retain runtime checks.

    The judgments in this clause require establishing the actual selected intrinsic or descriptor and the relevant argument, receiver and storage facts. A spelling or nominal receiver type is insufficient. Account for prior source texts, lexical shadows, own properties, prototype changes, argument evaluation, implicit conversions and other effects that could invalidate a dependency, including concurrent interference where possible. An annotation's boundary is such an effect only where it can run user code for the value that reaches it: checking a construction of the annotated class, a keyed collection constructed empty against type arguments whose checks run no user code, or a literal of plain scalar data against an object type whose members' checks run none, runs no user code. A construction is such an effect unless it runs no user code, as for an intrinsic Map or Set constructed without arguments, or a class of the source text with no heritage, decorators, type parameters or constructor, whose instance fields take scalar initializers or primitive defaults, constructed with scalar arguments. A runtime identity guard cannot justify an Early Error. Unknown dependencies retain runtime checks; checking invokes no ordinary getter, setter, conversion, callback or thread body. Permitted compile-time type evaluation remains governed by its existing rules.

    It is a type error to perform an established write to an accessor with no setter, such as the original typed-array capacity or collection size accessor. A fresh receiver with established descriptors may justify the proof; a receiver type alone does not exclude a writable own shadow or a replacement setter. Compound assignments and updates use the same judgment. A logical assignment whose store is skipped performs no write and is not rejected by this rule. Capacity reservation, storage relocation and reference liveness are unchanged.

    At a proved intrinsic Function.prototype.call or apply, check the forwarded arguments and receiver at the selected target's ordinary callable contract. apply uses array-like positional reads, not iteration; count, entries and their effects must be established independently. At a proved bind, check the fixed prefix and receiver, without demanding the arguments left for the eventual call, and retain a residual signature only where the remaining mapping is established. Reference Values decay on entry to these built-ins as specified by 2.3; forwarding does not recreate references. Overload and generic argument binding retain their ordinary rules.

    At a proved typed Atomics operation, it is a type error if the known target category cannot satisfy 41.6's operation-specific restriction, or an established operand boundary necessarily fails its prescribed conversion. Integer-only operations remain distinct from operations admitting floating-point targets; shared is not an eligibility requirement. The first reference argument retains the Atomics exception to built-in decay. A conditional replacement conversion, such as the replacement of compareExchange, is not established solely by the presence of its argument; a possibly skipped conversion prevents that failure proof. No memory-order, blocking or liveness rule is changed.

    At a proved callThread, apply 41.3.2 to established facts, then check the forwarded inputs at the target's callable contract. A non-Object first argument is not an options bag. A first parameter admitting an Object takes precedence over bag classification. If several classifications remain possible, reject only when every relevant mapping fails; otherwise retain the runtime classification. Built-in reference decay remains in force. This judgment launches no work and changes neither Promise settlement nor cancellation.

    At a proved Object.assign, Reflect.set, Object.defineProperty, Reflect.defineProperty or Object.defineProperties, an established write to typed own data obeys the ordinary storage boundary. It is a type error when that write necessarily fails. The proof must establish ownness, enumerability, keys, descriptors and the actual receiver as needed by the selected helper. For example, the original Object.assign({ (x: uint8): 0 }, { x: "s" }) has a statically incompatible write. A later source cannot erase an earlier failed write, while duplicate definitions within one source obey ordinary final-property semantics. Structural membership alone does not enumerate copied properties, and a distinct Reflect.set receiver is not assumed to be the target. Unknown getters, proxies, descriptors and explicit any remain dynamic. Reflection gains no ability to replace protected typed storage or extend a reference's lifetime.

    Descriptor adapters preserve the selected operation's staging. Reflect.defineProperty does not bypass a typed storage conversion because it returns a Boolean. Object.defineProperties collects and validates the complete descriptor list before applying any definition; a malformed later descriptor or an unknown descriptor getter prevents a proof that an earlier store is reached. Final duplicate-property semantics and each applied definition's order remain unchanged.

    1.3 Static Type Checking

    This clause defines the common inputs, applicability and composition of the type judgments in this specification. A judgment uses only the evidence admitted by its defining clause. An implementation must not reject an additional program by using a stronger proof procedure, runtime feedback, speculative object shapes, or an optional optimization. It may issue an informative diagnostic for such a program without changing its acceptance or evaluation. A judgment that lacks an admitted proof is unresolved; it is not a proof of failure.

    1.3.1 Static Semantics: Checked Unit Ownership

    The checked unit of a Parse Node is its innermost owning Script, Module, function-like unit, or class, with the ownership exceptions in the following table. Ownership includes parameter and return positions. A function-like unit is a function declaration or expression, generator declaration or expression, async function declaration or expression, async generator declaration or expression, arrow function, async arrow function, method (including a getter, setter, generator method, async method, or async generator method), or operator definition (including a signature without a body). A class declaration or expression owns its heritage, modifiers, fields, static initialization and other class syntax, excluding the own syntax of its methods and other nested units.

    To classify a parsed source, first determine every node's owner and whether each unit owns any proposal syntax. Proposal syntax is determined by the added grammar alternatives, including alternatives added to existing productions; it is not determined by a list of implementation AST class names. Next, in outer-to-inner order, mark a unit checked if it owns proposal syntax or its enclosing unit is checked. The Script of a direct eval whose caller is checked is marked checked before this second operation. Indirect eval and dynamically constructed functions receive no such inherited mark. The combined parameter and body source of a dynamically constructed function has one owning function unit even if an implementation parses its fragments separately.

    The classification does not evaluate annotations, decorators, computed keys, or any other expression. Moving proposal syntax within its owning unit cannot change that unit's classification. Strictness is a separate classification; neither strictness nor a typed import activates checking by itself. Classification and ownership may be cached. A cache must include inherited direct-eval classification and must not reuse a result for a different source or ownership graph.

    1.3.2 Type Rule Applicability

    Each type-checking obligation identifies its rule, responsible source node, and, where relevant, the contract from which it arises. The checked status used by a rule is the status of that source node's owning unit. A deferred obligation retains that ownership when type evaluation resolves its inputs; the unit containing the resolution machinery is irrelevant. A synthesized node retains the source obligation it represents.

    The following precedence resolves the three families in 1.2.8. A rule enforcing a declared type or a contract on a proposal-introduced binding applies everywhere. This remains so when its source value was inferred, when an existing built-in forwards the value to typed storage, or when the contract is reached through an established import or alias. Otherwise, an added rule on an existing built-in, operator or declaration form applies only in checked code. An inference-based impossibility or flow diagnostic also applies only in checked code. Ordinary ECMAScript Syntax Errors and runtime errors are unaffected.

    A diagnostic family can describe several obligations with different applicability. For example, an inadmissible constructor can be an existing JavaScript value used with new, or a Type Object introduced by this proposal that supplies conversion but no construction. The first added static rejection is checked-only; the latter contract applies everywhere. The rule and contract origin determine applicability, never a diagnostic's English wording or its family code.

    For an implicit Symbol.hasInstance call, distinguish the existing operator's callability requirement from the selected callable's declared receiver and parameter contracts. A proof of non-callability (including the nullish-hook fallback) is checked-only. A proof that every selected callable violates its declared receiver or parameter contract applies everywhere. Outside checked code, a union alternative that fails only the added callability rule cannot contribute to that latter proof. No hook or getter is executed to classify the obligation.

    Applicability does not erase analysis. Outside checked code, the transfers of 1.8.5.1 still establish their specified facts and distinguish impossible predecessors. They withhold only an inapplicable diagnosis. An empty meet is still empty, including when established by metadata evaluation. An unresolved or failed optional knowledge-producing hook follows its own specified fallback; it must not be confused with a successful empty result.

    Existing built-in contextual signatures and overload formation require earlier applicability decisions. Outside checked code the added existing built-in signature supplies no contextual argument type. A declared callable or typed storage obligation still supplies its declared context. Declarations form an overload set under exactly the checked-declaration condition of 1.2.5. Suppressing a final message cannot undo a contextual conversion or an overload set that should never have been formed.

    1.3.3 Checking State and Evidence

    A checking state consists of the declaration environment, current value facts, origin facts, reference facts, and the reachable completion alternatives. These are specification data, not properties of program objects. Lexical bindings are identified by their declarations, not by the spelling of their names. A property path includes the captured receiver origin and the established keys; the same spelling on another receiver is a different path.

    Joining reachable predecessors retains a fact only to the extent it holds on every predecessor contributing to that result. Value domains are joined by the specified type union; exclusions and relations retain only common evidence about the same surviving identities. An absent fact on a reachable predecessor is not an impossible predecessor. Joining no reachable predecessors produces an impossible result. Abrupt alternatives are joined separately by completion kind and target. Leaving a scope projects away its local binding identities; it does not erase a captured value that the existing capture rules preserve.

    The checker must use the defined finite domains and transfers. It does not solve arbitrary predicates, assume purity from a return annotation, or enumerate possible runtime objects. A recursive type judgment uses its specified assumptions or cycle rule. A transfer for which this specification supplies no value proof preserves the applicable declared contracts and treats the missing value evidence as unknown; that absence cannot justify an impossibility rejection.

    1.3.4 Recursive Declaration Validation

    The cycle rules of 1.8.1 and 9.4 apply to a closed declaration independently of whether execution reaches a use of it. A bare alias cycle denotes no type. A cycle requiring infinite inline layout is invalid. A cycle passing through the reference positions admitted by those rules remains eligible; the existence of a cycle alone is not a rejection predicate.

    When checking establishes either violation, the responsible source is the declaration that contains the cycle. The source check fails without evaluating its candidate body, including when the declaration occurs in an uncalled nested function. The invalid graph is not an input on which subsequent contextual typing, canonicalization, member lookup, or narrowing may establish a successful checking result. An implementation may stop after that diagnostic or recover to collect further diagnostics, but recovery supplies neither an accepted program nor a fallback language type.

    Completing declaration information may precede this judgment. An unresolved generic parameter or unavailable computed type is not proof of a cycle violation. The rule is applied when its inputs are established under the existing declaration and specialization rules; a resource limit is not a substitute for this structural judgment.

    1.3.5 Declaration Preparation State

    Each invocation of source checking has its own declaration-preparation state. A group of type aliases and interfaces prepared together in one lexical declaration scope identifies the bindings created for those declarations in that scope. These are binding identities, not identifier spellings. Resolving a name still follows the applicable lexical-environment and module-import rules. A same-spelled binding in another scope, realm, agent, or earlier source-checking invocation is not a member of the group.

    When preparation encounters an uninitialized binding read while resolving a type reference, that read is eligible for deferred recursive resolution only if the binding read is the binding of a declaration in the currently active preparation group. An unresolvable name, an uninitialized assignment, a read of an unrelated value binding, or an arbitrary thrown value does not establish such eligibility. An indirect module binding identifies the binding actually read in the exporting module; the local import spelling does not establish membership. An exception's class, properties, or formatted message is not evidence of binding identity or recursive resolution.

    Eligibility for deferred resolution is not proof that a recursive type is valid. The declaration's type must still be determined under the applicable declaration rules, including 1.3.4, default-value requirements, and compile-time evaluability. A temporary unresolved reference supplies no fallback language type, successful member contract, or narrowing fact. A runtime-dependent type expression retains its specified runtime behaviour; failure to prepare it does not by itself turn its eventual runtime exception into an Early Error.

    Nested source checking has a distinct active preparation group while the enclosing invocation is suspended. On every exit from the nested invocation, the enclosing state is restored. On every exit from an outermost invocation, its temporary preparation evidence is discarded. These requirements apply to success, rejection, abrupt completion, resource exhaustion, and host interruption. Reusing a parsed source or a type cache must not reuse an earlier invocation's temporary membership evidence.

    This state creates no program reference, extends no reference lifetime, and adds no observable property to an exception or Type Object. Equivalent internal representations are permitted. Discarding temporary preparation evidence does not itself undo declaration instantiation or observable effects; those remain governed by their respective evaluation algorithms.

    1.3.6 Recursive Interface Resolution

    Interface formation preserves every declared member contract across self-reference, mutual reference and forward reference. The rule applies in every lexical declaration scope, including a block, switch statement, function body or other nested scope, as well as during source checking. Moving an otherwise valid recursive declaration into such a scope does not make its type references ordinary uninitialized value reads.

    1. Resolve a type reference under the ordinary lexical binding rules. If it refers to an already initialized binding, use that binding's type value under the existing rules. Otherwise, only a binding identified with an actual interface declaration is eligible for declaration-based interface formation. An unrelated uninitialized value, a shadowing parameter, an unresolvable name or a thrown lookalike supplies no such declaration.
    2. Identify the declaration, its binding in the current lexical activation, and the generic arguments established by the ordinary binding rules. Retain the interface declaration identity specified in 1.11.7.1 in every node and application for that binding. If formation of that declaration is already in progress for this activation, retain a reference to the corresponding node of the type graph. Otherwise, begin its formation in the declaration's environment. Resolving an outer declaration from an inner scope must not substitute the inner scope's same-spelled captures.
    3. Form the interface's complete structural contract, retaining recursive edges in property types, method and call signatures, index signatures and compound types. Generic applications retain their bound arguments; a reference to one specialization does not become a reference to the unspecialized declaration or another specialization. Complete the recursive graph before using it as a successful type result. An unfinished edge is not the type any, an unconstrained object, an absent property, or a function with no signatures.
    4. Apply the existing declaration, recursive-validity, evaluability and specialization judgments to the resulting graph. A recursive reference is evidence of graph identity, not permission to ignore a member obligation. Subsequent membership, assignability, reflection and typed boundaries consult the completed contract.
    5. On success, expose the completed type through the existing declaration and Type Object rules. On failure, propagate the applicable completion and discard temporary formation evidence. Restore the prior lexical and generic environments on every exit, including abrupt completion, resource exhaustion and host interruption. Evidence from a failed formation, another activation, realm or agent cannot complete a later graph.

    Resolving a forward declaration in type position does not itself initialize that declaration's ordinary value binding or mark its ordinary Evaluation as completed. It does not execute intervening statements or an enclosing body. Expression-position reads retain their ordinary initialization and temporal-dead-zone rules. Source preparation may still initialize declarations at its existing checking boundary; this rule does not undo that preparation or process an already completed declaration twice.

    The reference retained during graph formation is specification data, not an ECMAScript Reference or a program value. It introduces no storage, object property, reference permission or extended lifetime. Implementations may use shared graph nodes, handles or an equivalent representation, but a successfully formed recursive contract cannot lose information because one declaration was visited before another.

    These rules do not authorize evaluating a genuinely runtime-dependent input before its environment exists, entering an uncalled function, or reading a required cyclic import through a fabricated local declaration. Imported binding availability and checking failure still follow 1.3.8. Closed invalid declarations remain subject to the pre-body judgment of 1.3.4; an unrelated native runtime error retains its existing phase and class.

    1.3.7 Exported Declaration Preparation

    For the declaration preparation required by 1.2.8, an ExportDeclaration of the form ExportDeclaration : export Declaration whose Declaration is a TypeAliasDeclaration or InterfaceDeclaration contributes that declaration in the same lexical declaration scope and at the same source-order position as the corresponding declaration without the export prefix. The export wrapper introduces neither a separate preparation group nor a later checking phase.

    Every preparation stage that consults these declarations uses this selection, including establishing the preparation group, resolving recursive references and computed types, making metadata shape aliases available before their governing meta declarations, and completing a type whose result depends on the registered metadata protocol. The declaration retains its original binding identity, lexical environment and source location. Its exported binding is the same binding used by ordinary module resolution; preparation does not create a second declaration or a snapshot of that binding.

    A named export or re-export clause contributes no additional local type declaration to preparation. In particular, exporting the name of a declaration already selected does not process it twice, and a re-export does not process a dependency's declarations in the importing module's preparation group. Nested declarations remain subject to their own scope and checking rules; the export wrapper does not move them into the enclosing group.

    The declaration's existing success, failure, runtime-dependence and specialization rules still apply. A declaration successfully processed during preparation is not processed again when ordinary Evaluation reaches it through the export wrapper. Failure to prepare a genuinely runtime-dependent declaration does not mark it as successfully processed. A required unavailable imported input fails as specified in 1.3.8; an eligible recursive reference still requires the validity judgment in 1.3.4.

    This selection does not perform Evaluation of the export wrapper or of other export forms. It does not execute an ordinary exported value initializer, class initializer, default-export expression or decorator application. Those operations retain their specified evaluation order and effects. The restricted computations that an existing type-preparation rule requires remain subject to 1.2.7 and its budget. No export grammar, reference lifetime or ordinary module dependency order is changed by this rule.

    1.3.8 Module Type Checking Order

    Parsing and linking apply the rules assigned to those phases before module evaluation. For the remaining judgments that require type evaluation, each Source Text Module Record has a pre-body checking boundary at the point where its ordinary module evaluation would enter its own code. Checking does not introduce a separate traversal that executes dependency bodies. InnerModuleEvaluation, ExecuteAsyncModule and AsyncModuleExecutionFulfilled continue to determine when that boundary is reached, including cycles and asynchronous dependencies.

    In Source Text Module Record ExecuteModule, replace the Evaluation of the module's [[ECMAScriptCode]] in the branch without top-level await with EvaluateModuleBodyWithTypeChecking of that code. Retain the surrounding context suspension, restoration and abrupt-completion propagation. In AsyncBlockStart, when asyncBody is a Module Parse Node, replace its Evaluation with EvaluateModuleBodyWithTypeChecking of asyncBody inside the async evaluation closure, after its context becomes current. The existing rejection path handles an abrupt result. This change does not apply to an ordinary async function body.

    A module with no top-level await of its own can still have pending asynchronous dependencies. Its body and pre-body checking wait until the ordinary dependency prerequisites are satisfied. A checking failure follows the existing module evaluation rejection paths and prevents bodies whose execution depends on the failed evaluation from starting. Effects of dependency bodies that already ran are retained. Failure does not restart a dependency or undo its effects.

    Within a cycle, a required imported binding may still be uninitialized when this boundary is reached. If preparation of a type declaration or another required pre-evaluation type judgment attempts to read that imported binding and cannot complete for that reason, checking fails with a StaticTypeError for type-evaluation failure before the candidate module body starts. Binding identity follows the resolved import target, including re-exports, as in 1.3.5. Do not treat this failure as permission to retry after body entry, wait for every member of the cycle, or substitute a fallback type. This does not require evaluating an expression whose evaluation is deferred by a generic or other explicit deferral rule, and it does not reclassify an unrelated runtime exception.

    The existing Module Record evaluation state governs repeated evaluation requests and shared dependencies. Checking must not re-enter an already evaluated module body or repeat its type computations in response to another request to evaluate the same record. A still-pending evaluation is neither successful nor rejected. Cached checking results may be reused only when their semantic inputs and required observable phase are preserved.

    1.3.8.1 EvaluateModuleBodyWithTypeChecking ( code )

    The abstract operation EvaluateModuleBodyWithTypeChecking takes argument code (a Parse Node) and returns a Completion Record. It applies the module's required pre-evaluation type judgments before entering its body, in the module execution context selected by the ordinary module evaluation algorithms. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Assert: code is a Module Parse Node.
    2. Let checkResult be the Completion Record obtained by applying the pre-evaluation checking of 1.2.8 to code in the running execution context, including its required declaration preparation and type judgments.
    3. If checkResult is an abrupt completion, return ? checkResult.
    4. Return Completion(Evaluation of code).

    1.3.9 Effects and Evaluation Order

    Transfer follows the language's evaluation order. It captures a value before subsequent effects where evaluation does so, and invalidates facts about a mutable location when the specified effect can change that location. A definite lexical write invalidates the binding's current-value facts and dependent relations, then installs only the facts established by the new value. A write through a known alias has the same effect on the aliased location. Replacing a path prefix invalidates dependent suffixes. Declared store contracts survive these invalidations.

    An unknown call, accessor, conversion, proxy operation, callback, iterator operation or direct eval cannot supply an effect-free proof. Invalidate the mutable facts that the operation can affect under the existing origin and escape rules; retain facts about immutable captured primitive values and other identities those rules establish as independent. A known intrinsic is used only while its identity and the relevant receiver/descriptor facts remain established. No ordinary operation is executed merely to discover these facts. Compile-time type evaluation is the separate, restricted operation of 1.2.7.

    Suspension, iterator closing, resource disposal and a finalizer apply their specified invalidations and completion replacement before a successor receives facts. A runtime identity guard or an inline-cache observation is not a static proof. The origin and effect preconditions in 1.2.8.1 remain requirements for every transferred library fact and contract.

    1.3.10 Transfer Composition

    An expression analysis has a value result, a state after each reachable normal result, and abrupt alternatives. A deciding analysis additionally separates true and false results, or nullish and present results for the nullish operators. Reporting an impossible deciding alternative and computing the alternatives are distinct operations. The exemptions for explicitly written constant tests remain those of 1.8.5.1; an empty alternative does not by itself authorize a new diagnostic in every expression position.

    Statement analysis sequences only normal predecessors into the next statement and transports abrupt alternatives to their actual targets. An if joins its reached arms. A switch separates label selection from body fallthrough, uses the captured discriminant, and includes labels on both sides of a default when deciding whether that default is selectable. A label's evaluation effects precede subsequent label tests.

    Loops use the bounded write-discovery and widening rules of 1.8.5.1. The entry alternative is not a repeated-iteration alternative. A while or ordinary for loop includes its possible zero-iteration exit; a do-while first executes its body. A continue reaches only its designated loop's update/test, and a break reaches only its designated exit. For-in, for-of and for-await-of apply their specified enumeration, iterator, assignment, closing and suspension effects. An established empty iteration has no body predecessor, whether or not its diagnostic applies.

    A catch receives only the throw alternatives its filter admits and preserves its declared binding contract. A finalizer is analyzed for each pending completion alternative; a normal finalizer preserves that pending completion with the finalizer's resulting facts, while an abrupt finalizer replaces it. Return, throw, break and continue retain their values and targets, with UpdateEmpty where the ordinary semantics requires it. Unreachable source still undergoes the ordinary syntactic and declared-contract checks specified for it; it supplies no outgoing execution facts to a reachable join.

    1.3.11 StaticTypeError Objects

    The initial value of the global object's StaticTypeError property is the intrinsic object %StaticTypeError%. The property has the attributes { [[Writable]]: true, [[Enumerable]]: false, [[Configurable]]: true }. Each realm has its own %StaticTypeError% and %StaticTypeError.prototype% objects. They are created with the realm's other intrinsic objects.

    The %StaticTypeError% intrinsic is a built-in function object with [[Call]] and [[Construct]] internal methods. Its [[Prototype]] is %Error%. Its name is "StaticTypeError" and its length is 1𝔽, with the usual built-in function property attributes. Its prototype property has value %StaticTypeError.prototype% and attributes { [[Writable]]: false, [[Enumerable]]: false, [[Configurable]]: false }.

    1.3.11.1 StaticTypeError ( message, options )

    1. If NewTarget is undefined, let newTarget be the active function object; else let newTarget be NewTarget.
    2. Let O be ? OrdinaryCreateFromConstructor(newTarget, "%StaticTypeError.prototype%", « [[ErrorData]] »).
    3. If message is not undefined, then
      1. Let msg be ? ToString(message).
      2. Perform CreateNonEnumerableDataPropertyOrThrow(O, "message", msg).
    4. Perform ? InstallErrorCause(O, options).
    5. Return O.

    1.3.11.2 Properties of the StaticTypeError Prototype Object

    The %StaticTypeError.prototype% intrinsic is an ordinary object. Its [[Prototype]] is %Error.prototype%. It has no [[ErrorData]] internal slot. Its own constructor, name, and message properties have values %StaticTypeError%, "StaticTypeError", and the empty String, respectively. Each has attributes { [[Writable]]: true, [[Enumerable]]: false, [[Configurable]]: true }.

    A StaticTypeError instance has an [[ErrorData]] internal slot. No diagnostic identifier, source location, or other host diagnostic record is an additional required own property of the instance. A required type rejection creates the error using the intrinsic of the checking realm, independently of changes to the global StaticTypeError binding.

    1.3.12 Diagnostic Identity

    Normative rejection predicates are the rules of this specification, with applicability determined by 1.3.2. The accompanying diagnostic registry supplies stable references to those rules and developer-facing diagnostic families. It does not replace the predicates, enlarge the required rejection set, or authorize suppressing an applicable error.

    Diagnostic text, presentation order, number of reported consequences, and host transport are implementation-defined. No diagnostic code property is added to ECMAScript Error objects by this clause. A host may expose structured diagnostics containing a family identifier, responsible rule, phase, source location, structured arguments, and related declaration/origin locations. The identifiers are independent of section numbering, message wording, and source filenames. A stable identifier is never reassigned to a different meaning; a retired identifier remains reserved. A provisional identifier must be identified as such in the registry.

    The registry's index links rule identities to their defining clauses. Several rule identities may share a diagnostic family, including rules with different applicability. Implementations must determine the applicable rule and its source/contract provenance before rendering a diagnostic. Changing diagnostic wording must not change program acceptance, required facts, or the phase of rejection.

    1.3.13 Diagnostic Rule Index

    This informative index identifies rule families and links to their normative clauses. It does not define an additional rejection predicate. Provisional identifiers may be refined; stable and retired identifiers are never repurposed.

    1.4 Grammar

    This clause adds the syntax for writing a type. It is grammar only: it defines what may be written and where, while the meaning of each form is given by the clauses that follow. Every production here is additive, and every construct it introduces is a syntax error in the current language, so no source text changes meaning.

    Note

    The type grammar is a separate grammar from the expression grammar, reached from expression contexts only through the annotation and operator productions of 1.4.4 and 1.4.5. Keeping the two apart is what lets a type use |, &, {, and ( with meanings unrelated to their expression counterparts.

    1.4.1 Lexical Grammar

    1.4.1.1 Punctuators

    Two punctuators are added. Neither token sequence occurs in any currently valid source text, which is what allows them to be added without changing the meaning of an existing program.

    Punctuator :: OptionalChainingPunctuator TypePunctuator OtherPunctuator TypePunctuator :: one of .< := Note

    .< introduces a type argument list (1.4.2.2). Today a . must be followed by an identifier name, a private name, or a numeric part of a literal, so .< is never produced by valid source text. The leading . is what distinguishes generic application from a comparison: a.<b>(c) cannot be read as a < b > (c), which is the ambiguity that prevents the bare angle-bracket form. Because a numeric literal is lexed by longest match, 1.<2 still lexes as the literal 1. followed by <, and so continues to mean a comparison.

    := introduces a typed initializer or a conversion (1.4.5). A : immediately followed by = does not occur in valid source text.

    1.4.1.2 The InputElementType Goal Symbol
