    A type argument list is delimited by < and >, and type arguments nest, so a source text may end one list immediately inside another. Under the ordinary lexical goals the two closing punctuators would be lexed as a single >> token. A goal symbol is therefore added in which > is always a single punctuator.

    InputElementType :: WhiteSpace LineTerminator Comment CommonToken RightBracePunctuator

    The InputElementType goal symbol is used in all syntactic grammar contexts where a TypeArguments or a TypeParameters is being parsed, between its opening .< or < and its closing >. When this goal symbol is used, the punctuators >>, >>>, >=, >>=, and >>>= are not recognized; a > is lexed as the single-character punctuator >.

    Note

    This is the same device the specification already uses to lex / differently where a regular expression may appear. It resolves the nesting problem lexically rather than by a parser rule, so Map.<string, [].<uint8>> closes both lists. A shift operator inside a type argument list must be parenthesized, which is only relevant to a value argument, since a shift cannot otherwise appear in a type.

    1.4.1.3 Imaginary Literals

    An imaginary literal is a numeric literal with the suffix i, denoting a value on the imaginary axis. The suffix occupies the slot a numeric literal followed immediately by an identifier start occupies today, which is a syntax error, and is the slot the n suffix of a BigInt literal already uses.

    NumericLiteral :: DecimalLiteral DecimalBigIntegerLiteral DecimalImaginaryLiteral NonDecimalIntegerLiteral[+Sep] NonDecimalIntegerLiteral[+Sep] BigIntLiteralSuffix LegacyOctalIntegerLiteral DecimalImaginaryLiteral :: DecimalLiteral ImaginaryLiteralSuffix ImaginaryLiteralSuffix :: i Note

    Unlike the BigInt suffix, which attaches only to an integer literal, the imaginary suffix attaches to any DecimalLiteral, so 4i, 2.5i, and 1e3i are all imaginary literals. The rule that the source character following a numeric literal must not be an identifier start continues to apply, so 4if remains a syntax error. The type of an imaginary literal is defined by the complex numbers extension.

    1.4.2 Type Expressions

    A Type is the syntax of a type. Union and intersection compose types, and the remaining forms are primary.

    Type[Yield, Await] : UnionType[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionType[?Yield, ?Await] UnionType[Yield, Await] : |opt IntersectionType[?Yield, ?Await] UnionType[?Yield, ?Await] | IntersectionType[?Yield, ?Await] IntersectionType[Yield, Await] : &opt PostfixType[?Yield, ?Await] IntersectionType[?Yield, ?Await] & PostfixType[?Yield, ?Await] PostfixType[Yield, Await] : PrimaryType[?Yield, ?Await] IndexedAccessType[?Yield, ?Await] ParameterizedType[?Yield, ?Await] IndexedAccessType[Yield, Await] : PostfixType[?Yield, ?Await] [ Type[?Yield, ?Await] ] ParameterizedType[Yield, Await] : PostfixType[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await] PrimaryType[Yield, Await] : shared PrimaryType[?Yield, ?Await] PredefinedType LiteralType TypeReference[?Yield, ?Await] ComputedType[?Yield, ?Await] KeyOfType[?Yield, ?Await] ArrayOrTupleType[?Yield, ?Await] ObjectType[?Yield, ?Await] ReferenceType[?Yield, ?Await] CoverParenthesizedTypeAndFunctionTypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await] PredefinedType : one of void null undefined LiteralType : NumericLiteral - NumericLiteral Infinity - Infinity NaN - NaN StringLiteral true false ReferenceType[Yield, Await] : ref PrimaryType[?Yield, ?Await] KeyOfType[Yield, Await] : keyof PrimaryType[?Yield, ?Await] Note

    The optional | and & above are a leading SEPARATOR and carry no meaning: | _T_ is the type T, whether or not T is itself a union, and likewise for &. They exist so that a type written across several lines can align its members, as the design writes type Shape = followed by a | on each line. Being on the base case of each production rather than a production of their own, they may appear at most once and only before the first member, so _A_ | | _B_ has no parse. A leading token with no type after it has none either, the token being a separator that happens to come first rather than a prefix operator.

    FunctionType is an alternative of Type rather than of UnionType, because a function type's return extends as far to the right as it can: (string) => uint32 | null returns uint32 | null. A function type is therefore not by itself a member of a union or an intersection, and putting one in a union requires parenthesizing it. That is true on either side, so the order of a union's members never matters.

    void and null are reserved words and so cannot be reached through TypeReference, which is why they are given their own production. undefined is not a reserved word but a global binding, an ordinary identifier; it is given its own production here as well, so that undefined in type position always names the undefined type rather than depending on the global binding being in scope, matching the treatment of null. The other built-in type names, uint8 and the rest, are ordinary identifiers and are reached through TypeReference; they are shadowable, so a program that declares its own binding named uint8 is unaffected.

    ReferenceType takes a PrimaryType operand, so ref uint8 | null is a union of ref uint8 and null. ref is a contextual keyword: it is a valid identifier today, so ref followed by a token that cannot begin a type is an identifier.

    keyof is likewise a contextual keyword, and a KeyOfType binds tighter than union and intersection, so keyof A | B is the union of keyof A and B. Its result is the union of the operand's key types, one literal type per named member. The full definition over each kind is given by 1.4.2.5, producing a union of the literal types of 1.5.19.

    1.4.2.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors for Intersection Types

    An intersection with callable constituents retains their signatures for calls, including optional calls and tagged templates. Applicable signatures use ordinary signature selection and argument, reference-parameter and result checks. Non-callable constituents still constrain the same value through their members and membership rules; they do not erase the callable contract, and the intersection is not treated as a union of possible callees.

    IntersectionType : IntersectionType & PostfixType
    • It is a type error if the Type Records denoted by two of the members of this IntersectionType are disjoint (1.2.2.6), unless one of the members denotes never.
    • It is a type error if two of the members of this IntersectionType denote object Type Records that declare a property of the same key, neither declaration is optional, neither property type denotes never, and the two property types are disjoint (1.2.2.6).
    • It is a type error if two of the members of this IntersectionType denote nominal Type Records whose [[Declaration]]s are both class declarations, neither member denotes never, and neither is a subtype of the other (1.2.3.1).
    • It is a type error if two of the members of this IntersectionType denote parameterized Type Records over one base and a governing meta type's meet hook (Table 42) returns null for their portions, unless one of the members denotes never. A meta type that declares no meet, or whose meet returns undefined, decides nothing here and the intersection stands.
    Note

    The second rule reaches THROUGH a member, and is the same rule as the first rather than an addition to it. Canonicalization distributes an all-object intersection and gives a shared member the intersection of the types its arms declare (1.2.2.8), so a disjoint pair there empties the object exactly as a disjoint pair of arms empties the intersection. Without it the case would be reported nowhere useful: 1.2.2.6 is silent about two object types, so the whole-arm rule answers false and the emptiness reaches the program as a refusal at every use of the annotation.

    The exemptions are the first rule's, for the first rule's reasons. A member written never states the emptiness deliberately, so { a: never } & { a: never } is the annihilation identity of 1.5.18 at a property rather than a mistake. An OPTIONAL declaration on either side is exempt because it does not empty anything: a value omitting the property satisfies both arms, so { a?: uint32 } & { a: string } is inhabited by every value with a string a and by none with a uint32 one, which is a narrowing rather than a contradiction.

    The message names the property as well as the two types, since a reader given only the types has to find which of the arms' members they came from, and an intersection of wide object types may declare many.

    The third rule decides what 1.2.2.6 declines. No value is an instance of two classes neither of which extends the other: this language has single inheritance, and 1.7.1.1 gives a value the nominal Type Record of ONE class. Symbol.hasInstance may be overridden so that instanceof answers otherwise, which does not bear on this: the override does not reach Reflect.typeOf or the is operator, which are what the type system reads.

    It is decided HERE and not in that operation, and the reason is the cost that clause names. AreDisjoint runs from 1.2.2.8, which runs whenever a type is interned, while IsSubtype's nominal arm recurses into type arguments and re-enters canonicalization; putting the judgment there would make interning depend on subtyping for a diagnostic. This pass is already running IsSubtype, so the same judgment costs nothing, and the type is left as written rather than reduced — which is also why an implementation is free to keep AreDisjoint conservative.

    The rule is restricted to CLASS declarations, and must be: nominal covers an interface and an enum as well, and both overlap freely. A value satisfies any number of interfaces, so I & J is inhabited by any value with the members of both; a class may implement any of them, so A & J is inhabited by an instance of a class that does; and a class intersected with an object type is inhabited by an instance of a subclass carrying the member. A base and its subclass are exempt by the subtype test, sharing every value of the subclass.

    Canonicalization already reduces such a type to never (1.2.2.8), so this rule changes no type; it changes where a program hears about one. Reduction alone would report the mistake at every USE of the annotation, as an assignment refused by a type no value inhabits, rather than at the & that made it - which is how an erasure checker reports it and is the least useful place to say it. The members are written right there, and the message names them.

    This is the call 1.8.5.3 already makes with its empty sentinel, which reports a test that cannot succeed as a mistake rather than narrowing to the type with no values, and it is made here for the same reason and with less doubt: a narrowing row at least has a live value flowing through it, while a written empty intersection has nothing that could ever reach it. & written where | was meant is the mistake this catches, and it is the common one.

    The rule is on the SYNTAX, so a never a computation reaches is untouched. Reflect.makeType (1.12.4) constructing a disjoint intersection returns never and does not throw, because canonicalization is total and the kit computes with the empty type: union(« ») and an exclude that removes every member are never, and a builder that threw instead would put a guard in every kit function. A generic body is likewise not rejected: in type F<T: type> = T & string; the member T is a parameter, over which AreDisjoint is conservative, so the declaration stands and an instantiation at number reduces to never silently.

    The reduction and this rule are decided over the same types, but only where the members have been RESOLVED. Canonicalization reduces every disjoint intersection whatever the shape of its members; this rule is decided over what the checking pass has resolved, and where a member is not resolved far enough there to be judged, AreDisjoint answers false and no error is reported. The type is never either way, so the failure mode is a MISSED diagnostic and never a wrong one: such a program hears about its mistake from the use site, as it did before this rule existed.

    An implementation should resolve as far as it can, and the reach is easy to underestimate. A parameterization is resolved by its BASE, and the base may be named rather than written — a nested brand, a brand over an object, an array or a literal — so an implementation that consulted only the built-in names diagnosed string.<{ brand: *"E"* }> & uint8 and missed E.<{ brand: *"N"* }> & uint8, two annotations differing in nothing but what named the base. What an implementation may not do is report on a member it has NOT resolved, an unresolved type being one that may still turn out to be anything: a base that declares type parameters is being applied rather than refined (1.5.20), and its object-shaped argument is a type.

    A member that denotes never is exempt because writing it says what the rule is for saying. uint8 & never is the annihilation identity of 1.5.18 spelled out rather than a mistake, and an author who wants to write the empty type has never itself, which is admitted as a type name on the same terms as every other. The exemption is on a member DENOTING never, so an alias for an already-reported empty intersection is reported once at its own declaration and not again at each mention of it.

    1.4.2.2 Type References and Type Arguments

    A type reference names a type, optionally applying type arguments to it. Generic application always uses .<, in a type and in an expression alike.

    TypeReference[Yield, Await] : TypeName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeName[Yield, Await] : IdentifierReference[?Yield, ?Await] TypeName[?Yield, ?Await] . IdentifierName TypeArguments[Yield, Await] : .< TypeArgumentList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt > .< > TypeArgumentList[Yield, Await] : TypeArgument[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArgumentList[?Yield, ?Await] , TypeArgument[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArgument[Yield, Await] : Type[?Yield, ?Await] BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] : Type[?Yield, ?Await] ... Type[?Yield, ?Await] Note 1

    Because .< is a single punctuator, a qualified name and an application are told apart lexically: in Temporal.Unit the . is followed by an identifier, while in Map.<string, uint8> the .< opens an argument list, so a TypeName cannot extend across it.

    A type argument is written as a Type even when it is a value, as the width in int.<8> and the lane count in vector.<float32, 4> are. A numeric or string literal argument is a LiteralType, and a name that resolves to a value generic parameter is a TypeReference, so the syntax need not distinguish the two; the clause on generics decides which a given parameter expects. A value argument that is a computed expression, such as an arithmetic combination of value generic parameters, is written through a ComputedType (1.4.2.4): the builder call is the spelling for a computed argument, evaluated once its parameters are bound, and the argument position takes no further computation syntax of its own. A where clause (4.9) constrains the values a variadic or value parameter admits.

    A TypeArgument may NAME the parameter it supplies, Box.<Element: uint8>, which lets an application skip a parameter that has a default rather than repeat it: given Grid<T = float64, Rows = 4, Cols = 4>, Grid.<Cols: 8> says what differs where Grid.<float64, 4, 8> repeats what does not. The separator is : rather than = to match the named ARGUMENT form of a call, and because = already means "the default if none is supplied" in the declaration - the opposite sense at the same position.

    Arguments bind to parameters by BindTypeArguments (4.3), the one operation every application site performs, whichever spelling the list uses: a parameter takes its positional argument where one reaches it, otherwise the named argument bearing its name, otherwise its TypeParameterDefault, and a parameter left by all three is an error, as it is for a positional application. A TypeArgument of the third form spreads a tuple: its Type must resolve to a tuple type or to an array type whose extent is stated, and it is a type error otherwise, since a spread whose length is not known cannot say how many parameters it fills; the elements are spliced into the list, in order, before anything binds, so swizzle.<...Pair> for type Pair = [0, 1] is swizzle.<0, 1> and names the same specialization.

    It is a type error for a TypeArgumentList to contain a TypeArgument of the second form whose BindingIdentifier does not name a TypeParameter of the type or function being applied. It is a Syntax Error for a TypeArgument of the second form to appear in the TypeArguments of an ArrayOrTupleType, a form that takes TypeArguments WITHOUT declaring parameters, such as [4].<uint8>, whose extent and element the grammar does not name - so a named argument there names nothing, and the form alone shows it. The first is a type error rather than a Syntax Error because it turns on the declaration applied, which may be imported, an alias, or computed, and is known only when the checking pass resolves it. A name that matched nothing would otherwise be discarded silently and the parameter would take its default, which makes a misspelling change what a program means.

    It is a Syntax Error for two TypeArguments of the second form in one TypeArgumentList to have the same BindingIdentifier. It is a type error for one to name a TypeParameter already supplied positionally, and a type error for a TypeArgument of the first form to follow one of the second, so the positional arguments are exactly the leading ones and a positional argument's meaning does not depend on the names used after it — except where the second-form argument names a variadic parameter, in which case the first-form arguments after it, up to the next second-form argument, join its run: q.<I: 0, 1, N: 8> binds I to [0, 1], since a name that could supply a pack only one element would not be able to supply it at all. Both need the applied declaration, the second to know whether the name is variadic, and so are type errors for the reason the unknown name is; only the duplicate name is visible in the list alone.

    The standard library's generic types carry the parameter names their signatures are written with, listed in Table 7, so Map.<V: uint8, K: string> means what it says and Map.<Z: uint8> is the error a user declaration's unknown name is.

    Note 2

    The table is the names the clauses cited already write, collected so an application can use them; a generic whose signature names nothing, such as an ArrayOrTupleType, is in it by omission and refuses every name. A standard library declared in the language's own syntax would carry these names on its declarations and retire the table.

    1.4.2.3 Library Type Argument Binding

    A dependent built-in application retains its family-specific formation obligations. When substitution closes an application, validate it before publishing the resulting type, including through nested aliases, object members, container arguments and function signatures in unused declarations. In particular, the shape restriction on Composite and the lane and count restrictions on vector apply equally to direct and substituted applications. An open application remains deferred; it does not authorize a closed invalid application. Traverse recursive type graphs with cycle detection and distinguish parameters by their binding identities. These checks form types without evaluating a value constructor or changing conversion rules.

    Explicit applications of the following library declarations use these parameter lists. Every parameter has domain type. A blank default entry means that an explicit application must supply the parameter. Bare names and constructions without TypeArguments retain their existing untyped, adoption or inference behaviour.

    Expand stated-extent spreads, bind positional and named arguments and fill declared defaults before interning a type or consuming its arguments. Excess arguments, a missing required argument, an unknown label, a parameter supplied positionally and by name, or a positional argument after a non-variadic named argument is a type error. Duplicate written labels remain the Syntax Error of 1.4.2.2. Existing constraints, including weak holdability, still apply. Annotation and expression applications use the same declaration metadata. Expression judgments require the actual generic declaration's origin, and a shadowing declaration supplies its own parameter list. None of these declarations is variadic. Other library families retain their own declarations, including Iterator's wrapper parameter.

    1.4.2.4 Computed Types

    A type position admits a call. The callee is written as a type reference and the arguments as ordinary expressions, so partial(User) and pick(User, ['id', 'name']) are types, as is a call of a call where a function returns a function that computes one.

    ComputedType[Yield, Await] : TypeReference[?Yield, ?Await] Arguments[?Yield, ?Await] ComputedType[?Yield, ?Await] Arguments[?Yield, ?Await]

    A ComputedType is a compile-time type expression and is governed by 1.2.7: the call must be compile-time evaluable, and the type the ComputedType denotes is the Type Object that EvaluateToTypeObject returns for it. A call that is not evaluable, that completes abruptly, or that does not produce a Type Object is a type error by the rule stated there.

    Note

    The form is additive twice over. Every position in which a Type may appear is new syntax, so no existing program contains one; and within the grammar of this specification a TypeName followed by ( derived nothing before this production, so no program written against the earlier grammar changes meaning either. Disambiguation costs one token: after a type reference, .< opens type arguments, ( opens a call, and any other token ends the reference.

    Only a call is admitted, deliberately. The design's rule is that an expression evaluating to a Type Object during checking is a valid type, and the call is the one expression form the type grammar needs to reach all of it: a conditional over IsAssignable, a map over a union's members, or any richer computation is a function away, written inside the builder rather than inline in the annotation. Keeping the surface to one form also keeps the evaluability requirement attached to one production.

    The same call in expression position is an ordinary call and needs nothing from this clause: a builder is an ordinary function, and calling it at run time yields the same interned Type Object the type position denotes. This production makes the call writable where a type is required; it does not change what the call is.

    1.4.2.5 Static Semantics of keyof

    A KeyOfType denotes GetTypeObject of the Type Record that KeyTypesOf returns for the Type Record its operand denotes.

    1.4.2.5.1 KeyTypesOf ( t )

    The abstract operation KeyTypesOf takes argument t (a Type Record) and returns a Type Record. It returns the type of the keys of t, which is never where t has no keys. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t involves an unbound parameter, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: keyof, [[Operands]]: « t » }.
    2. If t.[[Kind]] is object, then
      1. Let keys be a new empty List.
      2. For each element p of t.[[Properties]], do
        1. If p.[[Key]] is a String, let base be the Type Record of the String type.
        2. Else, let base be the Type Record of the Symbol type.
        3. Append the Type Record { [[Kind]]: literal, [[Value]]: p.[[Key]], [[Base]]: base } to keys.
      3. For each element x of t.[[IndexSignatures]], append x.[[KeyType]] to keys.
      4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: keys }).
    3. If t.[[Kind]] is intersection, then
      1. Let keys be a new empty List.
      2. For each element m of t.[[Members]], do
        1. Let k be KeyTypesOf(m).
        2. Append k to keys.
      3. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: keys }).
    4. If t.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. If t.[[Members]] is empty, return t.
      2. Let first be KeyTypesOf(t.[[Members]][0]).
      3. Let kept be a List of the union members of first: the elements of first.[[Members]] where first.[[Kind]] is union, and « first » otherwise.
      4. For each integer i such that 1 ≤ i and i < the number of elements of t.[[Members]], do
        1. Let k be KeyTypesOf(t.[[Members]][i]).
        2. Remove from kept each element that is not assignable (IsAssignable) to k.
      5. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: kept }).
    5. If t.[[Kind]] is parameterized, return KeyTypesOf(t.[[Base]]).
    6. If t.[[Kind]] is nominal and t has a [[Structure]] field, return KeyTypesOf(t.[[Structure]]).
    7. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « » }.
     Note

    The first step is the one that makes K: keyof T a constraint with content: within the declaration that binds T nothing is known about its keys, so they are UNKNOWN rather than absent, and the operator is carried as a deferred record until a specialization closes its operand - the treatment 1.4.2.6 gives T[K] and 1.2.7 gives a call, stated once for all three as the deferred kind. Without it a parameter reached the final step and keyof T was the empty type, which made the constraint empty and every body written against it unwritable. These are the rules of the operator, and the only statement of them: keyof is a primitive of the core (B), not a spelling of a kit function, so there is no second definition to keep in step. A union's keys are the common keys, computed by keeping the first arm's keys that remain assignable to each further arm's, which is what lets the literal 'x' survive against an arm whose keys come from a string-keyed index signature. An intersection's keys are the union of its members' keys. A Symbol key contributes its own literal type (1.5.19), so the operation is total over the keys an object type can have. A refinement has its base's keys, so keyof sees through a brand and through the where of a dependent record type (5) to the properties underneath, which is the only reading on which keyof and the property mappers agree about a refined object. An interface has the keys of its structural form, for the same reason and by the same unwrapping IndexedTypeOf performs. A kind with no keys is never, the empty union, rather than an error: the set of keys of a uint8 is empty, which is a thing this operation can say, and saying it is what keeps keyof T usable in a generic whose T is later bound to such a type — the alternative reported the fault inside the generic's own declaration rather than at the call that chose T. keyof never is the same answer by a different route: never is the empty union, so the union step above returns it unchanged. A keyof written directly on a type with no keys is almost always a mistake and is worth flagging as one, but it is not a type error and the operator stays total. IndexedTypeOf is unaffected and still returns empty for its three failures, since indexing a type by a key it does not have is a different question. An implementation folding over the arms must include the empty-union base case, since an arm-intersection fold does not otherwise reach it.

    1.4.2.6 Static Semantics of Indexed Access

    A deferred indexed access retains its formation obligation through aliases, nested types and generic substitution. When substitution closes its operands, apply IndexedTypeOf again. It is a type error if the result is empty, even when the containing declaration is unused. A failed closed projection does not become any, never or an unknown annotation. Unresolved operands remain deferred; this judgment executes no ordinary property lookup.

    An IndexedAccessType denotes GetTypeObject of the Type Record that IndexedTypeOf returns for the Type Records its PostfixType and Type denote. It is a type error if IndexedTypeOf returns empty.

    Note

    It is stated as an abstract operation, as 1.4.2.5 is stated as KeyTypesOf, so that one operation has one normative statement and the two spellings cannot drift. The kit's indexed (B) computes the same function, and is a convenience rather than a necessity: the syntax reaches every position, including a generic return — function pluck<T: type, K: keyof T>(o: T, key: K): T[K] — a Type Object held in a variable, and an expression position through the type operator, type T["n"]. What the builder gives is what any kit function gives: a value to pass, compose, and map with, which syntax cannot be.

    Reading a property that a declaration marked optional yields the union of its type with undefined, which is what reading an absent property gives. { a?: string }["a"] therefore admits a String and *undefined*, and { a: string }["a"] admits only a String.

    The form is POSTFIX, so it binds tighter than the prefix operators and than union and intersection: keyof T["a"] is keyof (T["a"]), and T["a"]["b"] chains left to right. That is why it sits at its own level between IntersectionType and PrimaryType rather than among the primaries.

    Only a String literal key is admitted in this edition. A numeric key, an index signature, and a tuple index are each a type error rather than an unspecified corner, so a program that writes T[number] is told that this edition does not cover it rather than discovering an implementation's guess. The restriction is a floor and not a ceiling: a later edition may admit them, and could not have taken them away.

    That restriction is also what keeps this form clear of the INDEX ACCESSORS (1.9.9), and the two do not overlap today. An index accessor applies where the base is an instance of a class that declares one and every index is a value of a NUMERIC type, and an index that is not numeric makes the access an ordinary property read; this syntax is a TYPE position, takes a String literal key, and reads a declared property. Different position, different key type, and this form does not reach a class instance type at all.

    Where a later edition admits a numeric key here, it meets the accessor's domain exactly, and the question it must answer is what Grid[uint8] denotes for a Grid declaring operator [](i: uint8): string — the accessor's RETURN type is the only reading that makes the two spellings describe one operation, as T["a"] and a property read already do. Deciding it then rather than now is the point of stating the restriction as an error: nothing has to be un-said.

    1.4.2.6.1 IndexedTypeOf ( t, k )

    The abstract operation IndexedTypeOf takes arguments t (a Type Record) and k (a Type Record) and returns either a Type Record or empty. It returns the type of the members of t named by the keys k, or empty where there is no such type. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t mentions a parameter type or k mentions a parameter type, then
      1. Let tName be t.[[Name]] if t.[[Kind]] is parameter, and the display form of t otherwise.
      2. Let kName be k.[[Name]] if k.[[Kind]] is parameter, and the display form of k otherwise.
      3. Let name be the string-concatenation of tName, "[", kName, and "]".
      4. Return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: parameter, [[Name]]: name }.
    2. Let arms be t.[[Members]] if t.[[Kind]] is union, and « t » otherwise.
    3. Let keys be k.[[Members]] if k.[[Kind]] is union, and « k » otherwise.
    4. Let results be a new empty List.
    5. For each element arm of arms, do
      1. Let shape be arm.
      2. Repeat, while shape.[[Kind]] is parameterized, or shape.[[Kind]] is nominal and shape has a [[Structure]] field,
        1. Set shape to shape.[[Base]] if shape.[[Kind]] is parameterized, and to shape.[[Structure]] otherwise.
      3. If shape.[[Kind]] is not object, return empty.
      4. For each element key of keys, do
        1. If key.[[Kind]] is not literal, or key.[[Value]] is not a String, return empty.
        2. Let p be the element of shape.[[Properties]] whose [[Key]] is key.[[Value]], or empty if there is none.
        3. If p is empty, return empty.
        4. If p.[[Optional]] is true, append CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « p.[[Type]], the Type Record of the undefined type » }) to results.
        5. Else, append p.[[Type]] to results.
    6. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: results }).
     Note

    Where a type parameter is involved the access is DEFERRED rather than computed or refused - IndexedTypeOf returns the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: indexed, [[Operands]]: « t, k » } - : within the declaration that binds T, nothing is known about it, so T[K] names an access that will be performed at each specialization. It is a type of its own, and its opacity is the deferred kind's - it relates to itself, to any, and to its operator's bound T[keyof T], and nothing concrete relates to it - which is what makes function pluck<T: type, K: keyof T>(o: T, key: K): T[K] { return o[key]; } well typed while return 5 from the same signature is not. The EXPRESSION o[key] reaches this operation too, so both spellings of one access answer one type; that agreement is the whole reason the deferred form is stated here rather than left to each resolver.

    Returning empty rather than raising is what lets the three failures - a key that is not a String literal, an operand with no properties, and a property that does not exist - be reported as one type error by the clause above, while the kit's indexed reports which of them it was. A class instance type is not reached: it is nominal without a [[Structure]] the loop unwraps to, so C["n"] is empty where I["n"] for an interface is not.

    1.4.2.7 Array and Tuple Types

    A declared tuple default is evaluated and converted to its position type when that type is formed, whether the initializer is a literal, a folded expression, or another compile-time-evaluable expression. An incompatible closed default is a type error even if no value ever demands it. A default depending on a type parameter is checked when specialization closes the obligation. Evaluation uses the existing evaluable fragment and budget; the converted value is the default used for construction, identity and reflection.

    For a tuple access with a proven singleton numeric key, a required position before any rest has that position's declared Static Type. The proof may be a numeric literal, a numeric literal type, or the established value of an unannotated compile-time numeric const (1.2.6). It respects lexical shadowing and explicit annotations, including any, and preserves exact integer values rather than rounding a key to select a different position. It is a type error if the proven index is negative, fractional, or beyond the positions of a fixed tuple. The selected type participates in the ordinary call, assignment and borrow judgments. This rule establishes no type for a general dynamic index or for a newly recognized key whose position depends on a default or rest; it does not remove a runtime storage, bounds or reference-liveness check.

    An array type is a fixed or dynamic count of elements of one type, and a tuple type is a fixed count of individually typed positions. Both are written in brackets, and are told apart by whether a type argument list follows the closing bracket.

    ArrayOrTupleType[Yield, Await] : [ ] [ ] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await] [ ArrayExtent[?Yield, ?Await] ] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await] [ TupleElementList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt ] ArrayExtent[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] TupleElementList[Yield, Await] : TupleElement[?Yield, ?Await] TupleElementList[?Yield, ?Await] , TupleElement[?Yield, ?Await] TupleElement[Yield, Await] : Type[?Yield, ?Await] Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt ... Type[?Yield, ?Await] Note 1

    [] alone is the EMPTY TUPLE. The array of any is written [].<any>, and it is the bound of the array and tuple family, so a type parameter constrained by it is satisfied by any array or tuple. Each structural family has such a bound and each is written in that family's own syntax: {} for objects, [].<any> here, and (...a: [].<any>) => any for functions. A bound admits every member of its family and nothing outside it, so a function is not assignable to {} and an array is not assignable to the function bound; and each composes, (...a: [].<any>) => string being every function that returns a String, which a bare name for the family could not express. [] denoted that bound in an earlier draft, which left the empty tuple with no spelling at all and gave the terse form to the role that turned out never to be written: across this proposal's design documents and its 190-program challenge corpus, [] in bound position appears zero times, [] meaning the empty tuple about thirty, and the builder call that was the only way to denote an empty tuple zero. The reassignment also removes a silent misreading rather than a diagnostic - [] was not an error under the old reading, it was a DIFFERENT type, so a program written by a reader who expected the empty tuple compiled and meant something else. [].<T> is a dynamic array, [N].<T> a fixed one, and [T1, T2] a tuple. What the brackets carry is the EXTENT — whether it is stated, and what it is. Whether the value owns its storage is a different question and is not asked here: Span.<T> (11) is the type of a value that does not, and every form above is assignable to it. A tuple's trailing position may carry a default through Initializer, and a tuple may spread another tuple or an array type at either end.

    The first three alternatives and the fourth are distinguished only after the closing ], by whether a TypeArguments follows, and their bracketed contents belong to different grammars: an extent is an expression and a tuple element list is a list of types. A single-element case such as [uint8] therefore cannot be resolved by bounded lookahead. This specification resolves it with a cover grammar, as it does for parenthesized expressions and arrow parameters: the bracketed text is parsed under a cover production and refined to an extent expression or a tuple element list once the token after the closing ] is known, an extent when a TypeArguments follows and a tuple otherwise. The committee may still prefer to distinguish the two forms by their opening bracket, which would remove the cover grammar rather than change the meaning of any program it already accepts; this is a decision worth taking before the syntax is final.

    Determine default placement in the effective ordered sequence after expanding tuple rest operands. A finite array rest contributes exactly its extent in required positions; a zero extent contributes none. It is a type error if a required position follows a defaulted position, or if a defaulted position follows an unbounded rest. A trailing unbounded rest may follow a defaulted fixed prefix. An unresolved operand defers the affected formation obligation until specialization; a closed specialization must satisfy it. A tuple is positional: an unsupplied defaulted position is selected only when the input stops before that position, never because a supplied value fits a later element better. In particular, [number = 7, ...[].<string>] admits an empty input but does not admit a one-element String input. The latter supplies position zero and cannot skip it to reach the rest. A shape wanting to omit a member in the middle names its members, which is an object type.

    A tuple element's Initializer is its position's default, and [[Initial]] is that default's value. The Initializer must be compile-time evaluable (1.2.7) and it is a type error otherwise: a tuple type is interned, so one Type Object serves every use of the type and the value in it is shared by all of them. A compile-time evaluable default is a value type, a string, or an enumerator, each of which is copied where it is used, so the sharing is unobservable; a default that allocated would hand every value of the type the same object. Evaluability does not by itself ensure this, since a compile-time-evaluable function may create local state and return it (1.2.7.1), so the rule is stated on the value as well: it is a type error for a default's value to be an Object unless the position's type is a value type (1.5.1), whose values copy. [[2].<uint8> = [1, 2]] is therefore a default and [any = []] is not.

    For a ... TupleElement, canonicalize the resolved operand type. It is a type error unless that record is an array or tuple. An operand dependent on an unbound type parameter retains this requirement, which is checked when substitution determines the operand, including at a generic application. A closed any, scalar, or union that remains a union is not a sequence record; an unbounded homogeneous rest is written ...[].<T>. A union canonicalizing to a single array or tuple is judged as that record.

    Expanding a tuple rest preserves every element's formed [[Initial]] value. A still-pending initializer obligation retains its original source and lexical/generic environment through expansion, canonicalization and substitution. A same-spelled parameter in the spreading or receiving context does not rebind it; a parameter's constraint is not its argument value. Validate each closed default's evaluability and conversion at type formation even if uses supply the position. Receiving construction consumes the already formed values under the existing fragment-budget, value-copying and admission rules; spreading itself does not re-evaluate the initializer. A pending generic input is identified by its parameter declaration; a consumer's same-spelled parameter does not supply that input. Source nodes and checking environments are not additional public Type Record identity fields.

    An array in a tuple position is converted position-wise, as one in an array position is converted element-wise: each element is converted to the type of the position it occupies, and an element past the declared positions is converted to the element type of the rest that collects it. A position the array does not supply takes its default, converted to that position's type as a supplied value would be, so the length may fall anywhere from the number of positions carrying neither a rest nor a default up to the number of positions, and beyond it only where a rest collects the surplus. Conversion rather than a bare check is what every boundary of this specification performs, and a tuple literal builds a new Array, so no storage another binding holds is rewritten by it.

    A fixed extent is part of the type and does not change. An operation that would give an array of such a type a length other than its extent is a TypeError exception, whether it is a store to an index at or past the extent, an assignment to length, or a method that appends or removes. A request for capacity past the extent is refused for the same reason although it changes no length: the storage of a fixed extent holds exactly that many elements for the life of the array, so reserve past the extent is a TypeError exception, reserve within it is a no-op, and the capacity of such an array is its extent rather than any allocation's. Stating the rule in terms of length alone would miss this, reserve being exactly the operation a length comparison cannot see (2.10). The extent is a compile-time constant: the layout computes a byteLength from it and an array view's byteElementLength defaults from it, so an extent that an ordinary store could change would not be constant for either. A growable [ ] . < T > has no extent to hold and grows as an Array does.

    One type describes every count a CONTAINER reports or accepts: an array's length, its capacity (2.10), an index used to read or write an element, the length of a view over a buffer, and the size of a keyed collection (1.15). That type is the index type, and it is uint64. Its full range is ALLOCATABLE AND USABLE: an array type is not bounded by the maximum length of an ordinary Array, since a count type wider than what the container can hold would describe lengths no program could reach. An instance is an Array in its methods and its element behaviour and not in its extent limit. The width is uint64 rather than uint32 because a view's length comes from its buffer and is not bounded by the maximum length of an Array (12); typed owned arrays and views use the same full count range. %TypedArray% is unaffected: its counts are Numbers and remain so (1.14.10.4). It is a property of the language and not of an array: an array type takes ONE type argument, its element, and there is no per-array spelling that varies the counts' type. Naming it once rather than repeating uint32 at each site is what lets the width be stated in one place, and what keeps capacity comparable with length without a conversion — the invariant that a capacity is at least a length is unstateable if the two are not one type.

    A store to the length property of an array carrying an array or tuple type is a typed store whose target is the index type. A numeric literal takes that contextual type; it is a type error if a statically known source is not assignable to the index type or a literal cannot be represented by it. It is also a type error if a statically known literal length violates the array's fixed extent or the tuple's permitted lengths. Where the source is unknown, the store performs the ordinary checked conversion to the index type: a value of the wrong type throws a TypeError exception and a numeric value not exactly representable throws a RangeError exception. An untyped Array retains the base language's length conversion.

    The fixed-extent judgment also applies to a built-in update or compound assignment whose result can be determined from the exact storage extent and its operands. For example, a.length++, --a.length and a.length += 1 on a [2].<uint8> are type errors, whereas a.length += 0 preserves the extent. The computation uses the index type's arithmetic, including its integer wrapping, without making length a literal type. A tuple whose positions are all required and have no rest similarly supplies an exact length. Where the current length or an operand is unknown, or a declared operator supplies different semantics, the corresponding judgment is deferred; a successful count judgment never removes a reference-liveness check.

    For such a typed array, ArraySetLength converts a supplied [[Value]] to the index type before changing the array. It uses that count as the requested length, checks the fixed-extent or tuple constraint, and then performs the applicable length and element-removal operations. Checking the count does not discharge a reference-liveness obligation: resizing during reference iteration and removal of a borrowed element remain subject to 2.10, including when the count check is statically elided.

    Note 2

    The uint64-over-uint32 argument above is about a VIEW, and does not reach the keyed collections, which have no view form. The other property does, and is why their size is this type rather than one of its own: counts have to be comparable ACROSS containers as well as within one. _map_.size < _array_.length is a sentence a program wants to write, and it is unwriteable if the two are different types, exactly as "a capacity is at least a length" is unwriteable if those two are. A per-container count type would make that comparison impossible by construction, which is the defect naming the type once exists to prevent, and no language that has been surveyed has one: Rust reports usize from both Vec::len and HashMap::len, and C++, Java, Swift and C# each use a single integer type across their containers.

    An array type may be written where an expression is expected, and there denotes the type's constructor: new [100].<uint8>() constructs an array of that type, and class G extends [16].<uint8> { } derives a class from it. A construction of a fixed extent has that many elements, each the default value of the element type (1.8.3); a construction of a dynamic one has none and grows. An instance is an Array carrying the element type, so a store to an element is checked against it and the methods of Array.prototype apply, and a class deriving from an array type has instances that are Arrays in the same way. Its [[Prototype]] is not %Array.prototype% itself but an object that INHERITS from it and adds the capacity operations (2.11), so every method of Array.prototype reaches an instance unchanged while capacity, reserve, and shrinkToFit reach only an array that has an element type. Placing them on Array.prototype would put three members on every array in the language that exist to refuse the receiver they will usually have: 'capacity' in [] would be true for an ordinary array and reading it would throw. Two mentions of one array type denote the same constructor, since the types are interned and the constructor is the type's.

    Note 3

    The bracketed form is an array literal where an expression is expected, so the two readings meet at [100].<uint8>`: an array literal cannot be followed by a type argument list, which is what tells them apart. The reading as a type is taken before the brackets are evaluated as a literal, since evaluating them is the reading being replaced.

    shared before a type marks a type whose storage is shared between the threads of one heap, as let a: shared [4].<uint8>, a fixed-length array so placed. It is a type error if the operand of shared is itself shared. Which types admit the modifier, what it places where, and what a checker may assume of a slot that carries it are given by 41.4; the grammar is stated here because it is the type grammar, and the grammar is the core's.

    1.4.2.8 Intrinsic Array Method Contracts

    For a proved intrinsic tuple mutation, check the values stored at each established destination slot against that slot's declared type. The union of tuple element types is not a write contract for each position. Apply the selected operation's index coercion, clamping, overlap order and reads before stores: reverse exchanges paired positions, copyWithin copies in its prescribed direction, fill writes only its selected range, and splice checks its established shifts and inserted positions. Account for permitted value conversions and subsequent reads of converted values. A no-op range performs no stores. Unknown indices, effects or source values retain runtime checks; a comparator's mere presence does not establish a sort permutation. These store checks do not prove fixed extent, deletion permission or reference liveness.

    At a proved intrinsic push, pop, shift, unshift or splice on a fixed-extent array or a tuple, it is a type error when established arguments and length prove that the operation necessarily changes the extent or leaves the tuple's permitted lengths. Apply the operation's index coercion, clamping and deletion rules before computing that effect. A zero-item push or unshift, a pop or shift on an empty array, or a splice with equal inserted and removed counts is not rejected by this extent judgment. Unknown counts, including the count a spread argument supplies, and replacements remain dynamic. Equal extent does not waive element, storage, bounds or reference-liveness checks.

    The judgments in this clause apply only when the selected operation is established to be the corresponding Array intrinsic. A receiver's array type and a familiar member name alone do not establish that fact: own methods, prototypes, accessors, argument evaluation and user conversions may change the selected operation. A bounded proof may use engine-owned intrinsic identities, lexical origins and source effects; an unresolved dependency defers the judgment. A lexical origin follows 1.4.2.10: a let binding qualifies while no assignment, assignment pattern, captured write or direct eval can replace it, and a declaration without an Initializer holds its type's default, which for a stated-extent array is a new array. A guard executed by an inline cache cannot justify an irreversible Early Error. These judgments never prove reference liveness.

    For with, the replacement value is checked at the receiver's element type, or at the selected tuple position. A known negative index is relative to the current length. When several tuple positions remain possible, a statically known replacement must satisfy each possible destination; unknown values and unresolved indices retain their runtime checks. The base language's index coercion and out-of-range behaviour are unchanged.

    A supplied comparator for sort or toSorted must be callable and accept the two element values supplied by the intrinsic. Omission or undefined selects the default comparison. The callback result follows the base language's numeric coercion; it is not required to have a declared number return type, and no ordering law is proved. A callback for reduce or reduceRight must accept the accumulator, element, index and receiver actually supplied. The initial value and callback results determine the accumulator contract independently of the element type. These rules do not require an unused callback parameter to be written.

    An intrinsic that creates an ordinary array copy, including slice, filter, toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with, splice and concat, does not give that copy the receiver's fixed storage extent. A homogeneous copy has a dynamic array type with the element contract that the operation establishes, and an item the operation inserts, as with and toSpliced do, is converted to that contract and checked against it where it is established. Knowledge of its initial length is a value fact, not a fixed storage type. Mutating sort and reverse return the receiver. A tuple result retains positional information only where the operation guarantees the resulting positions; otherwise no positional shape is invented. Receiving boundaries enforce the created container's actual type even when its current length happens to equal a required fixed extent.

    1.4.2.9 Object Types

    A computed member read whose key is a statically established finite set retains the read contract of each selected key. For each key, a named property takes precedence; only a key not declared by name uses an applicable index signature. Join the established read types, preserving optionality and any missing outcome established by the ordinary exact-key rule. If an alternative remains unknown, the read remains unknown. This does not establish that an index-signature key exists. General non-finite computed reads retain the dynamic treatment below. Neither key expressions nor getters are evaluated by this judgment.

    Every closed declared property default, including one in an interface, is evaluated and converted to its declared property type at type formation, under the same rules as a tuple default. Failure is a type error even for an unused type. A dependent default is checked after specialization supplies its dependencies. The readonly modifier is admitted only on named properties; readonly before an IndexSignature is a Syntax Error. An ordinary property whose name is readonly is unaffected.

    At a fresh object literal, a property not declared by name must satisfy every index signature admitting its established key. Its one produced value has one representation; contextualize at the conjunction of those value types, rather than converting independently for each signature. It is a type error if no such value can be produced. Named properties retain precedence. Compatible overlaps and an empty object remain valid, and an unknown contribution retains runtime checking. Apply the same obligation to established shorthand, method and final spread contributions under the existing property-replacement rules.

    An object type describes a value by its members. It is the inline form of an interface.

    It is an early error for a TypeMemberList to declare the same PropertyName twice, whatever the two members say. { n: int32, n: string } and { n: int32, n: int32 } are both refused, the second although its halves agree.

    Note 1

    The rule is about the DECLARATION and not about inhabitability: a repeated member is a mistake at the point it is written, and refusing only the contradictory spelling would accept the redundant one while a duplicate BINDING name a scope out is refused whatever it is bound to.

    Merging two declarations is a separate question with its own answer (1.11.7): members arriving from different declarations of one interface are merged, and it is only within a single list that a repeat is an error.

    The relationship runs both ways, and the reverse direction needs a name. The structural form of an interface type is the object Type Record whose [[Members]] are the members the interface declares, taken together with those it inherits, and with the interface's type arguments substituted. Every interface has one. A class has none: a class states a construction and an identity as well as a shape, and it is the identity that its type is for.

    Note 2

    This is what lets a value satisfy an interface by having its members, which 1.2.3.1 reads. Without it the rules would refuse f({ a: 'a' }) for interface IExample { a: string; }, since an interface is a nominal type (Table 1) and an object literal's type is object, and the step separating the kinds would answer before any member was inspected. The composite types have relied on the notion since they were specified, naming it in their own subtype rule; this clause is where it is defined rather than assumed.

     ObjectType[Yield, Await] : { } { TypeMemberList[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberSeparatoropt } TypeMemberList[Yield, Await] : TypeMember[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberList[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberSeparator TypeMember[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberSeparator : one of , ; TypeMember[Yield, Await] : PropertyName[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt PropertyName[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt MethodSignature[?Yield, ?Await] MethodSignature[?Yield, ?Await] IndexSignature[?Yield, ?Await] MethodSignature[Yield, Await] : TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FunctionTypeParameterList[?Yield, ?Await]opt ,opt ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt IndexSignature[Yield, Await] : [ BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] ] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] Note 3

    Members are separated by either , or ;, and a trailing separator is permitted, so both { x: float32, y: float32 } and { x: float32; y: float32; } are written. A ? marks an optional member.

    A MethodSignature with no PropertyName is a call signature. An object type or interface whose members are all call signatures denotes the function Type Record whose [[Signatures]] are those signatures in declaration order, so { (uint32): uint32 } is (uint32) => uint32 written with braces, { (uint32): uint32; (string): string } is the overloaded function type the arrow form cannot spell, and { <T: type>(x: T): T } is a generic one (1.4.2.10). A call signature's TypeParameters are subject to the same early errors as a function type's. It is a type error for an object type to mix call signatures with named members or an index signature: this specification gives a callable value a function type and a keyed value an object type, and the design writes no shape that is both.

    A member may be declared readonly, which sets the [[Readonly]] field of the Property Type Record it contributes. A write to a readonly member is a type error, at compile time where the type of the base is known and at run time otherwise. A form that stores back to the member, including a compound assignment's binary fallback and an increment or decrement, is a write. A declared compound operator instead invokes a method without replacing the member (1.9.9), so that invocation is permitted through a readonly member. readonly is shallow here as it is for a field (1.11.2): it fixes the member, not the object the member refers to.

    Note 4

    This is what makes the depth covariance of 1.11.1.3 sound. That clause admits a subtype through a readonly member "since a value read from it and never written through it need only be of the required type", and the second half of that sentence is a rule rather than an observation.

    The guarantee is weaker than a field's, and the difference is where each belongs. A class's readonly is a property of the OBJECT: the declaring class says so, the instance carries it, and a write is refused however the instance was reached. An object type's readonly is a property of the REFERENCE, since one object may be viewed through both a readonly and a writable type and the two views are the same object. The refusal is therefore what the type of the base expression supports, and a write through a base of type any is not refused.

    An IndexSignature constrains the properties an object type does not declare by name: { [key: string]: uint32 } is the type whose remaining string-keyed properties, beyond those declared, are uint32. It is a type error if a TypeMember's Initializer appears without ?, since a default belongs to an optional member, the design's c?: uint8 = 0. A member default's value copies, under the rule and for the reason 1.4.2.7 gives a tuple element's, so c?: any = [] is a type error: an array the type shared would be one array in every value built at it. The Initializer must be compile-time evaluable (1.2.7) and it is a type error otherwise, for the reason 1.4.2.7 gives of a tuple element's: an object type is interned, so a member's default is one value shared by every use of the type rather than a computation performed per construction. A language that evaluates a default at each construction may admit any expression there; this one evaluates it once, which is what makes “the default is part of the contents that intern” a coherent statement and what lets a typed composite creation write it before freezing. A default is a construction feature: it is written where a value of the type is being built, an object literal taking the type, a typed parse (43.1), and a typed composite creation (23.5.2), and never by a check of a value that already exists. A check reads; an object lacking an optional member satisfies the type with the member absent, whether or not the member declares a default, and no check writes the default onto its subject. The line between the two is the one 15.1 already draws. An object literal written AT the position is fresh and is being built there, so the type supplies what the literal omits; a value that reached the position through a binding is not fresh and is only read, so nothing is written onto it. let v: S = { id: 1 } fills a declared default and let o = { id: 1 }; let v: S = o; does not, which is the same distinction freshness already makes about excess members and about literal types, rather than a second rule to learn. A default is therefore never written onto an object a program can already observe: the only object it reaches is one coming into existence at the type. It is a type error if the key type of an IndexSignature is not string, symbol, uint32, or a union of these. A key domain dependent on an unbound parameter retains this well-formedness obligation. Recheck the resolved domain when substitution closes it, including through nested aliases and interface applications, before publishing the resulting type. An open parameter is not evidence that a closed invalid domain is admissible. A member the ObjectType declares by name is NOT constrained by a signature whose key type admits its key: the signature governs the remaining properties, as the first sentence of this paragraph says, and the declared member governs its own. Each signature contributes an Index Signature Record to the [[IndexSignatures]] field of the object Type Record the type constructs (1.11.1).

    Note 5

    An earlier draft of this clause required a declared member to be assignable to the signature's value type, the rule TypeScript applies, in the same sentence that gave the signature the properties "beyond those declared". The two cannot both hold, and the second is the one this specification keeps, for a reason stronger than which sentence came first: IsOfType (1.7.2.1) decides membership by walking the members, checking a declared member against its own type and every other key against the signature, so { name: *"n"*, x: 1 } IS of { name: string, [k: string]: number }. A rule refusing that annotation would leave a type no program can write whose membership predicate nonetheless accepts values, and 1.11.7 points at IsOfType for exactly this question. The two would also disagree about a fresh literal, which 1.4.2.9 fills member by member by the same division.

    What TypeScript buys with its rule is a sound type for a read through a computed key, o[k] for a k of the key type, which under this reading may land on a declared member of another type. This specification does not need it: a general non-finite read is not given the signature's value type statically, and reaches the boundary check of 1.7.3 like any other read whose type is not established. The cost TypeScript is avoiding is one this proposal does not pay, so the constraint it pays for is one this proposal does not need.

    1.4.2.10 Function Types

    Calling a Type Object for conversion does not by itself grant [[Construct]]. It is a type error to use a proved conversion-only Type Object as the target of ordinary new, or as the target or newTarget of a proved Reflect.construct. Preserve the actual value's capability through established aliases and specializations. A class constructor remains constructible when held in a binding annotated type; that annotation alone proves neither constructibility nor non-constructibility. Explicit array construction and placement construction retain their own rules. Unknown identities and explicit any remain dynamic.

    A function type is a parameter list and a return type. Its parameters may be named or unnamed, and may carry the ref and rest modifiers a declaration's parameters carry.

    The collected-container well-formedness rule of 1.4.4 applies to every annotated rest in a function type, object or interface call signature, method signature, and abstract method. Resolve the annotation before publishing the signature. It is a type error unless it denotes an array or tuple; a type parameter must have an array-or-tuple constraint. Aliases and unnamed parameters obey the same rule. A genuinely deferred type-resolution obligation is retained until resolution. This check is independent of whether an implementation or call is present and does not change reference-rest permissions.

    A signature does not establish whether its function value can be constructed. It is a type error to construct a statically identified typed arrow, generator, async function, or async generator, and it is a type error to invoke a statically identified typed class constructor without new, including through an optional call or a tagged template. Ordinary function construction remains admitted. A function participates in this judgment through its parameter or return annotations, reference parameters, type parameters, or a non-any annotation on the binding holding it. A class participates through its typed members, declared operators, type parameters, class modifiers, or implemented interfaces. An annotation elsewhere in the enclosing body does not make an unrelated invocation participate.

    An optional call applies the invocation-kind judgment to the selected callee value on its executing edge. A nullish split does not erase an established class-constructor origin merely because the Static Type used for another judgment is unknown. A skipped edge performs no invocation. Subsequent member access or a call result needs its own origin proof; the original callee's identity does not transfer to that different value. A diagnostic belongs to the original optional expression and its checking unit, not to a synthetic expression used by an implementation.

    A conditional selection is a ConditionalExpression or an expression of the ||, && or ?? operator, and its possible selected origins are the operands it can yield: each of these yields one of its operands unchanged, except that && yields its left operand only when that operand is falsy. The left operand of && therefore contributes the falsy part of its Static Type (1.9.5) rather than itself: a falsy part made only of primitive types is known to be neither a constructor nor callable and counts as such without participating, while a falsy part that may hold an Object is an unknown alternative. A conditional selection and an immutable alias of it preserve a conservative summary of these invocation capabilities. It is a type error to construct such a selection when every possible selected origin participates and is known not to be a constructor; apply the corresponding rule to calling only known typed class constructors. A possible supported or unknown alternative prevents the negative proof. Capability facts are independent of signature identity, so canonicalizing equal signatures does not discard them. This judgment evaluates neither the condition nor a selected function.

    Identification uses the function or class expression itself, or a lexical binding whose value origin is established. Parentheses and immutable aliases preserve that origin. A mutable origin is usable only while replacement is excluded; assignments, including assignment patterns and captured writes, and direct eval withdraw an otherwise unproved origin. Shadowing uses the binding's lexical identity. An open property, an unknown function value, a signature alone, an overload dispatcher of unknown invocation kind, or a decorator that can replace a class supplies no negative capability proof. These facts are separate from signature identity and subtyping. A class constructor has [[Call]], whose class-constructor guard rejects ordinary invocation; it is not classified as an object lacking [[Call]].

    These are typed-source judgments under 1.2.8. Pure JavaScript such as new (() => 1)() retains its runtime exception, as do unknown values and values deliberately exposed through any. The checking pass does not execute a function, decorator or property getter to determine an invocation capability.

    FunctionType[Yield, Await] : TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt FunctionTypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await] => Type[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionTypeParameters[Yield, Await] : CoverParenthesizedTypeAndFunctionTypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await] CoverParenthesizedTypeAndFunctionTypeParameters[Yield, Await] : ( ) ( FunctionTypeParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt ) FunctionTypeParameterList[Yield, Await] : FunctionTypeParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionTypeParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] , FunctionTypeParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionTypeParameter[Yield, Await] : refopt Type[?Yield, ?Await] Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt refopt BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt refopt ... BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] refopt ... Type[?Yield, ?Await]

    A FunctionTypeParameter may carry an Initializer, a default for the parameter, as a TupleElement may (1.4.2.7): (a: uint8 = 1) => void, or in an interface of call signatures (string = '5', named: uint32). The Initializer is evaluated once, when the function type is resolved, and its value is converted to the parameter's type; it is compile-time evaluable and its value copies, under the rule 1.4.2.7 gives a tuple element's default, since the function type is interned with it; the Parameter Record's [[Initial]] holds the result and the parameter is optional. A parameter with an Initializer need not be named: the default fills its position, and a name is needed only to be addressed by a named argument. It is a type error if a parameter without an Initializer, without a BindingIdentifier, and not marked ? follows one with an Initializer, save a rest parameter. A parameter with a name may follow one: a named argument (1.10.4) fills it and leaves the default to be taken, which is what the example (string = '5', named: uint32) relies on. A parameter without a name is reached only by position, and a call that reaches it has supplied the defaulted position too, so that default could never be taken; this is the reason 1.4.2.7 gives for a tuple's defaults. The default is data the type supplies for a position; it is read by the call site (1.10.4) and never by the callee, whose own parameter list is unaffected.

    When the production PrimaryType : CoverParenthesizedTypeAndFunctionTypeParameters is recognized, the interpretation of CoverParenthesizedTypeAndFunctionTypeParameters is refined using ParenthesizedType : ( Type ) ; it is a Syntax Error if the cover does not match that refinement, the judgment reading the cover alone: a FunctionTypeParameter that carries a BindingIdentifier, an Initializer, a ?, or a ... is not a Type, while a lone ref PrimaryType is the ReferenceType it spells and refines to a parenthesized one.

    ParenthesizedType[Yield, Await] : ( Type[?Yield, ?Await] ) Note

    (uint8) is a parenthesized type and (uint8) => uint8 is a function type, and the two are told apart by the token after the closing parenthesis, exactly as a parenthesized expression is told from arrow parameters. The cover grammar is the same device the specification already uses there.

    A function type may declare type parameters, <T: type>(x: T) => T, and is then the type of a generic function: its Signature Record's [[TypeParameters]] are the Type Parameter Records of the declared list (1.10.1), and its parameter and return types may name them. The list is subject to the early errors of 1.4.3.1 as a declaration's is, and its parameters bind by BindTypeArguments when a call through a binding of the type supplies type arguments. A function type declares no where clause: a where belongs to a declaration and is not part of a signature's identity, so it is checked at the specialization a crossing performs (4.6) and never read by the relations on types. Identity and subtyping of generic function types are given by 1.10.2.1 and 1.10.2.3.

    1.4.3 Type Parameters

    An established upper bound supplies operational contracts inside a generic body: member reads, store types and permissions, callable signatures, primitive operations and narrowing tests (1.8.5.4) are checked using the applicable bound. It is a type error when those contracts establish that an operation cannot succeed, even if no specialization invokes the body. This projection does not identify a parameter with its bound: assignment to the parameter, reference invariance, type identity and dependent type expressions retain the opaque parameter. Admitting a store under an upper bound alone does not prove it valid for every narrower specialization. A value parameter's domain supplies the same contracts: in the unspecialized body the parameter reads as a value of its domain, the type 1.4.3.3.3 checks every argument for it against. Cyclic, dependent or unknown bounds do not authorize evaluation of a builder or an assumed closed shape; unresolved obligations remain for specialization or runtime checking.

    A generic declaration introduces its parameters in angle brackets. Declaration uses <, while application uses .<, so the ambiguity that application avoids does not arise at a declaration, where no expression may appear. The same brackets after a declared name hold the PARAMETERS of a primary declaration or the ARGUMENTS of a specialization of one (1.4.3.2), and which an entry is follows from its syntax alone: an entry written as a name followed by : declares a parameter, and every other entry is an argument. Whether a name is in scope never decides it.

    TypeParameters[Yield, Await] : < > < GenericEntryList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt > GenericEntryList[Yield, Await] : GenericEntry[?Yield, ?Await] GenericEntryList[?Yield, ?Await] , GenericEntry[?Yield, ?Await] GenericEntry[Yield, Await] : TypeParameter[?Yield, ?Await] SpecializationEntry[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameter[Yield, Await] : VarianceModifieropt BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterHolesopt TypeParameterDomain[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterConstraint[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeParameterDefault[?Yield, ?Await]opt VarianceModifieropt ... BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterDomain[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterConstraint[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeParameterDefault[?Yield, ?Await]opt VarianceModifier : one of in out TypeParameterHoles : < TypeParameterHoleList > TypeParameterHoleList : _ TypeParameterHoleList , _ TypeParameterDomain[Yield, Await] : : Type[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterConstraint[Yield, Await] : extends Type[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterDefault[Yield, Await] : = Type[?Yield, ?Await] Note 1

    Every parameter states its domain. T: type declares a type parameter, since type is the domain of Type Objects and a type parameter is a compile-time constant whose value is a type, which is what it evaluates to in an expression position (4.1). V: uint32 declares a value parameter, and N: uint32 = 4 gives it a default. A bound follows the domain, T: type extends Ordered.<T>. A variadic parameter's domain is its collection type, ...I: [].<uint32> for a pack of uint32 constants and ...Ts: [].<type> for a pack of types, and a bound on a pack of types bounds the tuple, ...Cs: [].<type> extends [].<Component>. A higher-kinded parameter writes its holes before its domain, W<_>: type, and the domain describes what an application of it yields (4.12). The _ of a TypeParameterHoleList is the IdentifierName _.

    Earlier drafts declared a type parameter with a bare name, <T> or <T extends B>, and treated a name that resolved to a type as a specialization. A bare name is now always an argument, so neither <T> nor <T extends B> declares anything: the first is a reference to whatever T is in scope, and the second is a Syntax Error, since extends does not follow an argument. An implementation's diagnostic for either offers T: type or T: type extends B.

     Note 2

    A VarianceModifier declares the parameter's variance, whose meaning is given by 4.11: out declares it covariant and in contravariant, and a parameter carrying neither is invariant. The words name the positions the parameter may occupy, out for the output positions a covariant parameter is restricted to and in for the input positions of a contravariant one, which is the spelling of C# and Kotlin whose variance this is.

    in is a reserved word, so it can only be a modifier here. out is not: it remains an ordinary identifier everywhere, INCLUDING as a type parameter's own name, and is a VarianceModifier only where a BindingIdentifier follows it immediately. So <out: type> and <out: type = T> each declare a parameter NAMED out, while <out T: type> declares a covariant T, and <out out: type> declares a covariant parameter named out. One token of lookahead separates the two readings, and no program that does not write a modifier changes meaning.

     Note 3
