    A parameter written with ... is a variadic parameter, collecting any number of arguments as a rest parameter collects any number of values, and its TypeParameterDomain is the type of what it collects — ...I: [].<uint32> for a pack of uint32 values, ...Ts: [].<type> extends [].<Bound> for a pack of types, ...I: [4].<uint8> for exactly four — the habit the rest-parameter annotation of 1.4.4 already teaches. What a variadic parameter binds is a tuple Type Record (4.4); the ... is only the collection marker at the application, so <...Ts: [].<type>> applied .<uint8, string> and <Ts: type extends [].<any>> applied .<[uint8, string]> bind the same thing.

    1.4.3.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors

    A TypeParameters is a parameter list when every GenericEntry of it is a TypeParameter, a specialization list when none is, including <>, and a mixed list otherwise.

    TypeParameters : < GenericEntryList ,opt >
    • It is a Syntax Error if, within any maximal sequence of consecutive TypeParameters of the list that are not of the ... form, a TypeParameter that has no TypeParameterDefault follows one that has a TypeParameterDefault.
    • It is a Syntax Error if two consecutive TypeParameters of the list are both of the ... form and the first has no TypeParameterConstraint and a TypeParameterDomain whose Type is [].<type>.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this TypeParameters is a mixed list and it is not the TypeParameters of a function declaration, a method definition, or an operator definition.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this TypeParameters is a mixed list and a GenericEntry of it is a SpecializationEntry that is a CaptureBinding or of the form ... CaptureBinding.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this TypeParameters is not a parameter list and it belongs to a function type, a call or method signature of an interface or object type, a function, arrow, or class EXPRESSION, a MetaDeclaration, or the declaration of a variable, a constructor, an accessor, or an enumeration.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this TypeParameters is a parameter list and it belongs to a partial class or interface declaration or to a primitive operator block (6.5).
    • It is a Syntax Error if the BoundNames of two TypeParameters of the list are the same.
    • It is a Syntax Error if a TypeParameter of the list has a TypeParameterConstraint and the Type of its TypeParameterDomain is neither type nor, for a TypeParameter of the ... form, [].<type>.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this TypeParameters belongs to a function declaration, a method definition, or an operator definition and any element of the BoundNames of its TypeParameters also occurs in the BoundNames of that definition's formal parameters, or in the LexicallyDeclaredNames or the VarDeclaredNames of its body.
    Note 1

    The last rule is the rule ECMAScript gives an ordinary parameter, function f(a) { let a; }, closed over the one case it leaves open. A var of a parameter's name aliases the parameter's binding, which is why ECMAScript permits it; a type parameter has no binding to alias, so a var of its name, hoisting to the top of the body from any block, would replace it for the whole body, lines above the var included. A scope nested in the body may shadow a type parameter as it may shadow an ordinary parameter: { let T = 5; }, a callback (V, K) => V inside class M<K: type, V: type>, or a nested function's own declarations. A type written in the shadowing scope reads the shadowing binding too, since a type name resolves lexically, so a name keeps one meaning at each level. A class's type parameters need no such rule, since a class body binds no names.

     Note 2

    The rule on a constraint states what 15.2 assumes, that a value parameter has a domain and no bound. The kind is read from the domain as written (1.4.3.3), so the rule needs no name resolved, and a value parameter's values are narrowed by a where clause instead (4.9).

    The first rule is the trailing-defaults rule stated per run: a variadic parameter counts as defaulted, since an application may leave it empty, and it ends the run, so <...A: [].<uint32>, N: uint32> is legal with N required — the parameter after a pack is what stops the pack's run positionally, and is otherwise reached by name. The second is the syntactic half of the rest-parameter sentence "two rests with nothing typed between them are an error": a pack of types with no bound admits everything, so a pack adjacent to it could never receive an argument positionally. The half that needs a domain or bound resolved — one that resolves to [].<any> admits everything too — is the type error of 4.4.

    The mixed-list rules place selector-prefixed overloads. A function, method, or operator may mix fixed arguments with parameters, write<float32, maximum: float32, bits: uint32>(value: float32), and the list is then its own overload whose fixed positions are unnamed; a class, interface, alias, partial, or primitive block has one primary per family and may not, so class Box<uint32, N: 8> {} is refused where class Box<uint32, 8> {} was meant. A capture at the top level of a mixed list would observe nothing a caller could not already name, so it is refused in favour of a parameter.

    1.4.3.2 Specialization Lists

    A specialization list after a declared name specializes the family that name already declares: its entries are ARGUMENTS for the primary declaration's parameters, in order, and each is a fixed argument, the wildcard _, or a capture that binds the argument standing in its position.

    SpecializationEntry[Yield, Await] : Type[?Yield, ?Await] CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] ... CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] CaptureBinding[Yield, Await] : const BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameterHolesopt TypeParameterDomain[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeParameterConstraint[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeArgument[Yield, Await] : CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] ... CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] : CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] ArrayExtent[Yield, Await] : CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] TupleElement[Yield, Await] : CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await] ... CaptureBinding[?Yield, ?Await]

    The additional TypeArgument forms let a capture stand inside a nested application of a specialization entry, positionally, Map.<string, const Element>, or under the nested constructor's own parameter name, Map.<K: string, V: const Element>. The fixed extent of an array type within a specialization entry may likewise be a CaptureBinding, [const N].<const Element>, and so may an element of a tuple type, [const Head, ...const Tail], where a ... capture binds the tuple of the elements its run covers. A SpecializationEntry that is the Type _ is the wildcard, which matches any argument and binds nothing; any in the same position is the exact argument any.

    Within a generic class's body, meaning its instance and static members but not its heritage or its own parameter list, the class's bare name in a type position denotes the class over its own parameters, as this does: begin(): PacketWriter { return this; }. A static member's are those of the specialization it is reached through. A nearer declaration's type parameter of the same name shadows it. Elsewhere, and in a value position anywhere, the bare name keeps its meaning.

    In a value position within the body the bare name keeps its JavaScript meaning, the class's inner binding, and each specialization's body is evaluated with that binding naming the specialization. So new B(args) there constructs the specialization being evaluated: its parameters are the class's own, it is typed as the class over its own parameters, as the name in a type position is, and each argument is checked against the constructor at those parameters with the relation of a binding or a return. In the body of B<T: type>, new B(x) for an x of type uint16 is therefore an error, since the body is checked for every T, and a parameter the arguments do not determine takes the class's own value rather than its default. new B.<X>(args) names its specialization explicitly and is unaffected, and outside the body a construction infers its arguments as any generic call does.

    An intrinsic family follows the declared-default rules of 1.5.25 in ordinary concrete type positions, including constraints. Thus complex denotes complex.<number>, and bare int, uint, rational, and vector lack required arguments. A family-wide constraint uses positional anonymous arguments, such as T: type extends uint.<_>, as specified in 1.5.26.

    A primitive's value parameter, the width of int.<N> and uint.<N> and the lane count of vector.<T, N>, has the domain uint32; the range its type imposes, from 1 to 216 for a width, is a bound apart from that domain. A capture in such a position therefore restates its domain as uint32 when it writes one. The intrinsic argument of rational instead admits either such a width or the type bigint; this intrinsic domain does not introduce mixed type/value domains for user-declared parameters.

    A capture's domain is its position's: a primary declaration's parameter at the top level, and the nested constructor's parameter within an application. A written TypeParameterDomain restates that domain and must be the same type, except in a metadata position, where it selects the meta type whose metadata the capture binds, float32.<const D: Dimensions>. A TypeParameterConstraint bounds a type capture. A capture has no default and no variance, which the grammar does not provide: both are promises a primary declaration makes to its callers, and a capture only observes an argument that primary binding has already supplied.

    A primary binds before its specializations are matched (1.4.3.2.4), so a specialization list reaches only applications whose arguments the primary can bind. It is a type error, at the declaration, for a fixed argument of a class specialization, or of a partial class or interface target, to stand in a primary position that could not bind it: a type where the parameter is a value parameter, a value its domain cannot represent, or a type its bound does not admit where that bound is closed. This is the test 1.4.3.2.2 applies to decide whether a callable declaration attaches; a class family has no standalone case to receive a list that fails it, so the list could match no application. It is likewise a type error, reported at the later declaration, for two class specializations of one family that are not partial to admit the same applications, compared with captures canonicalized by binding identity and an omitted entry read as its position's default. Two such declarations could never be told apart by an application, and the specialization for their intersection that resolves an ambiguity between two different lists would be a third copy of the same list.

    1.4.3.2.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors

    CaptureBinding : const BindingIdentifier TypeParameterHolesopt TypeParameterDomainopt TypeParameterConstraintopt
    • It is a Syntax Error if this CaptureBinding is not contained in a SpecializationEntry or in a type-subject pattern (24).
    • It is a Syntax Error if the TypeParameters or type-subject pattern containing this CaptureBinding contains another CaptureBinding with the same StringValue of BindingIdentifier, even where the two annotations agree.
    • It is a Syntax Error if this CaptureBinding is contained in the Arguments of a ComputedType, or in the TypeArguments of the TypeReference that is the callee of a ComputedType.
    Note

    A capture is declared once and may then be used any number of times, as a bare reference, and each further use requires the argument in its position to be the same: SameType for a type and SameValue for a value. Two declarations of one name are refused rather than read as an equality, since a reader could not tell whether equality or two unrelated bindings was meant. A capture's scope is the whole list, the specialized signature or heritage, and the body, so a use may precede its declaration, which keeps Map.<V: T, K: const T> meaning Map.<K: const T, V: T>.

    A builder is evaluated forward and never run backwards, so a capture among its arguments would observe nothing, and a ComputedType is a builder call by its syntax alone: class S<Make(const T)> {} is refused before any name is resolved. A capture REFERENCE there is not refused, class S<const T, Make(T)> {}, since it reads a capture bound at a structural position and is checked forward. Whether some other position exposes a component depends on what its name denotes, and is the type error of 1.4.3.2.3.

    1.4.3.2.2 Callable Overload Contracts

    A function's, method's, or class operator's generic list declares an overload contract, so its declaration group may hold several same-named declarations whose lists differ; a class operator's group is keyed by its operator and whether it is unary, and it is static or not as a method's is. An interface's operator, and a primitive block's, declares parameters only. An owner is one whose list holds parameters only. A declaration whose list holds only fixed arguments, captures, and _ attaches to the owner of its group whose list accepts it: each entry lands in one of the owner's parameters by position, a fixed argument there is of that parameter's kind and admitted by its domain and bound, and a capture or _ takes the parameter's domain. It borrows the owner's parameter names. A declaration no owner accepts, and one whose list mixes arguments with parameters, is standalone: its unlabeled positions are positional only, and it takes part only in ordinary overload resolution.

    An attached declaration whose parameter list is the owner's instantiated at its entries (the same parameter types, optionality, rest element, and reference permissions; parameter names and initializers are not compared) is a replacement. It keeps the owner's contract, and is reached through the owner's generic function value. Its return type must be a subtype of the owner's instantiated return type. An attached declaration with another parameter list is additive, and is never reached through the owner's generic function value.

    An owner may omit its body. A bodyless owner declares only the labels and generic contract its attached declarations keep, and an application no attached declaration matches is then no viable overload. In a class declared abstract, a bodyless method with no attached declaration is an abstract member instead.

    An explicit application of a group's name to type arguments selects, in order: the most specific attached declaration whose list matches the arguments, by 1.4.3.2's specificity; otherwise a standalone declaration whose list matches them, a position its list fixes being more specific than one an owner's parameter reaches; otherwise the owner's body, bound as any generic call binds it; otherwise there is no viable overload, a static type error where the arguments are known statically and a TypeError otherwise. Two applicable declarations neither of which is more specific than the other are an error at that application only, which names both and the arguments. Source order never decides. A declaration whose parameters cannot receive the call's arguments is not applicable, whatever its list admits: an additive declaration taking one more parameter than the owner is not the case of a call that supplies the owner's.

    The fixed type fragments of a specialization list are declaration obligations, including those nested beside captures or wildcards. They are checked in the declaration's lexical environment with its parameters and captures in scope, whether or not an application of the declaration occurs and whether or not an enclosing body is invoked. A capture binding or wildcard is pattern syntax and is not itself evaluated as a closed type. References to bound parameters or captures may resolve symbolically; their presence does not exempt an independently checkable fixed fragment from its obligation.

    Resolve each name at its source position to the binding selected by lexical resolution before obtaining that binding's type or declaration. A same-named declaration in a sibling function, a completed inner block or another unrelated source environment supplies no type and does not shadow an intrinsic or outer binding at this position. This applies equally to a bare name, an applied generic name and a name nested in a fixed fragment. Forward references follow the existing declaration and initialization rules; checking a type does not initialize a binding.

    When following an alias, resolve its body in that alias's declaration environment, preserving recursive declaration identity and the applicable parameter bindings. A caller's same-named alias cannot replace it. Retain the selected source bindings and declaring environments for deferred obligations, including builder dependencies and imported or previously established bindings. An index keyed only by identifier spelling does not establish visibility, availability or reference liveness. Apply the query-input requirements of 1.6.2.7 to any retained answer.

    After the dependencies required by such an obligation have been resolved, failure to resolve its type is a static type error in that fragment. A dependency not yet completed is not a failed resolution, and a dependent computation remains subject to the ordinary specialization rules. A failed resolution required by static selection is not an unsuccessful match and does not permit selection of a fallback. This applies to direct calls and stored applications as well as declaration checking; it does not require an open application to become concrete.

    A named type argument reaches each candidate through that candidate's own labels: an attached declaration's are its owner's parameter names, a mixed declaration's are its parameters' names (its fixed arguments are positional), and a declaration whose list holds only fixed arguments, captures, and _ has none. A capture's name is never a label. A candidate that does not know a label is not applicable; a position a named application leaves open takes its parameter's default. A value parameter admits a literal that its domain can represent. It is an error, naming the label, if no candidate knows a label the application uses.

    A call of a group's name without type arguments selects by ordinary overload resolution among its owners, each with its binding inferred from the arguments as any generic call's is, and its additive and standalone declarations, each by its own parameters. A replacement takes no part in that resolution itself: when an owner is chosen, its inferred binding selects among its replacements as an explicit application of those arguments would, and otherwise the owner's body runs, or there is no viable overload if the owner has no body. The call's contextual type does not filter out an owner whose replacements the resolution would reach, since the owner's return type is not the call's when a replacement is chosen; the call produces the chosen declaration's own return type.

    An application of a group's name to type arguments that is not called is a value: it selects as a call would, with no arguments to count. A chosen declaration's value calls it with its captures bound; applications that choose the same declaration with the same bindings evaluate to the same value, and the declarations of two evaluations of one scope are two. A group with an owner is, as a value, that owner's generic function: a replacement is reached through it, an additive declaration never is, and it conforms to a function type as the owner does. A group whose declarations are all standalone is an ordinary overload set, and conforms to no generic function type.

    An application inside a generic body whose arguments name that body's open type parameters is selected for each specialization when it is evaluated, and is checked once for every binding: through an owner that takes the arguments, against the owner's signature; or else through the one declaration whose list admits every binding the arguments' bounds allow, where a capture or _ admits any binding and F.<…> of captures and _ admits every binding of a bound that is the family F. Each other declaration that some such binding would select instead, and whose parameters can receive the call's arguments, must then have that declaration's parameter list instantiated at its arguments. An application satisfying neither is a static error.

    Standalone declarations whose lists hold only fixed arguments, captures, and _, of one length, are ordered by specificity as an owner's attached declarations are, a fixed position being more specific than an open one.

    A method's group is the same-named methods of one class body or object literal, however many; the selection rules above apply to a call, an application, or a stored application of a method as to a function's. The group a method call names is found from its receiver: in the nearest class of the receiver's class and its superclasses whose body declares the name, in the receiver's object literal, or, for super, from the enclosing class's superclass.

    A binary use of a class operator whose group holds a specialized declaration selects as an implicit call of that group would, its right operand the one argument, and the operation has the chosen declaration's return type. A use with no right operand to select by, a unary, compound-assignment, or index operator's, is a static error when its group holds one. A class operator's owner has a body.

    A declaration whose where clauses do not all hold for an application is not applicable to it: its clauses are evaluated with its bindings, and a method's with its class's bindings too, before any body runs, and selection then proceeds among the rest.

    A group's type is its owner's generic function, and a type's reflection is its structure, which reconstructs the type. The group's declarations are reflected from the group value: Reflect.getReflection given a function value that holds specialized declarations, or a value one of their applications produced, returns an object whose signatures has one entry per declaration, each with its role ("owner", "replacement", "additive", or "standalone") and its typeParameters: for each position, its label (an owner's parameter name, borrowed by an attached declaration; a parameter's own name in a mixed list; or undefined for a position that takes none) and either its kind or its pattern's text. A capture's name is never a label. For an application's value, selected is the entry it selected, the owner's for its body. A selected declaration's value has that declaration's type with its captures bound.

    Declarations told apart by their lists are not duplicate overloads for sharing parameter types: a replacement shares its owner's by definition. Their duplicates are judged by the applications their lists admit.

    BodylessOwnerDeclaration[Yield, Await] : function BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await] ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[~Yield, ~Await]opt ; BodylessOwnerMethod[Yield, Await] : ClassElementName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await] ( UniqueFormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[~Yield, ~Await]opt ;

    1.4.3.2.2.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors

    BodylessOwnerDeclaration : function BindingIdentifier TypeParameters ( FormalParameters ) TypeAnnotationopt ; BodylessOwnerMethod : ClassElementName TypeParameters ( UniqueFormalParameters ) TypeAnnotationopt ;
    • It is a Syntax Error if TypeParameters holds anything but parameters.

    A BodylessOwnerDeclaration is a function declaration of its declaration group, and a BodylessOwnerMethod a method of its class body. For each declaration group of a StatementList, ClassBody, or object literal, and each name declared in it by functions, methods, or class operators, it is an early error if:

    • A declaration whose list holds only fixed arguments, captures, and _ is accepted by more than one owner of the group.
    • A bodyless owner has no attached declaration in the group, and is not a method of a class declared abstract.
    • A replacement's return type is not a subtype of the owner's return type instantiated at its entries.
    • Two attached declarations of one owner admit the same applications, compared with captures canonicalized by binding identity, or two standalone declarations do.
    • A capture at the top of a standalone declaration's list has no written domain, since its position belongs to no owner whose domain it could take.

    1.4.3.2.3 Capture Scope

    The captures of a specialization list are collected before anything in it is resolved. Their scope is the whole list, the specialized declaration's signature or heritage, its constraints and where clauses, and its body, under the ordinary rules for class and static scope. Within that scope a bare IdentifierReference whose StringValue names a collected capture is a capture reference, including where it precedes the capture's declaration, and a capture shadows any outer binding of its name throughout the scope. The declared name, Pair in class Pair<const T, T>, is resolved before the capture scope is entered. A nested constructor, Map in Map.<string, const E>, is resolved within it, so a first-order capture named Map makes that application a type error rather than a lookup that falls back.

    1.4.3.2.3.1 CollectCaptures ( list )

    The abstract operation CollectCaptures takes argument list (a TypeParameters Parse Node or a type-subject pattern) and returns a List of Capture Records. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let captures be a new empty List.
    2. For each CaptureBinding c contained in list, in source text order, do
      1. Let variadic be true if c is the CaptureBinding of a ... CaptureBinding form, and false otherwise.
      2. Append the Capture Record { [[Name]]: the StringValue of the BindingIdentifier of c, [[Declaration]]: c, [[Variadic]]: variadic } to captures.
    3. Return captures.

    A capture's domain is the domain of the position it declares, as 1.4.3.2 says: the primary declaration's parameter at the top level, and the resolved nested constructor's parameter within an application. It is a type error, at the declaration, for a written TypeParameterDomain to denote a type other than that domain, except in a metadata position; for a capture to stand in a position that exposes no component, such as an argument of an application whose name denotes no constructor; for a capture of kind constructor to occupy a first-order position; or for a capture whose position takes a value to carry a TypeParameterConstraint, since a value is narrowed by a where clause (4.9) and not bounded, as a value parameter is (1.4.3.1). The kind of a capture's position is known only once the primary or the nested constructor is resolved, which is why this is a type error where the parameter's own rule is a Syntax Error.

    1.4.3.2.4 Matching a Specialization List

    Matching compares a specialization list with the ordered bindings BindTypeArguments (4.1) produced for an application of the primary declaration. The primary is bound first, by explicit, named, and spread arguments, then the expected type, the value arguments, and the defaults, and the list is then matched against that result. So a capture's name is never an argument a caller can supply, and Box.<uint32, N: 8> and Box.<uint32, 8> meet the same specializations. Matching evaluates no capture as an argument and runs no code other than the forward computations described below. A match that fails binds nothing, and the next candidate starts from an empty environment.

    A callable group containing a specialization case remains eligible for explicit type arguments even if its ordinary callable signatures have no type parameters. An unresolved case input does not establish that the callee is nongeneric, that a case matches, or that a default portion may replace a supplied portion. Retain the selection dependency until the required inputs are available, using established String or Symbol key identity for metadata captures. A completed no-match retains its ordinary failure, and a known nongeneric callable without such a group retains its type-argument error.

    1.4.3.2.4.1 MatchSpecializationList ( list, bindings )

    The abstract operation MatchSpecializationList takes arguments list (a TypeParameters Parse Node) and bindings (a List of Records with fields [[Declaration]] and [[Value]]) and returns either a normal completion containing either a List of Records with fields [[Capture]] (a Capture Record) and [[Value]] (a Type Record) or no-match, or a throw completion. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let env be a new empty List.
    2. Let deferred be a new empty List.
    3. Let runs be the GenericEntry Parse Nodes of list assigned to the primary declaration's parameters, one run per parameter, by the positional and variadic rules of BindTypeArguments, with no CaptureBinding or capture reference evaluated.
    4. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k < the number of elements of bindings, in ascending order, do
      1. Let run be runs[k].
      2. If the primary parameter at k is variadic, then
        1. Match run against the elements of the tuple bindings[k].[[Value]] as MatchSpecializationPattern matches the elements of a tuple type, and return no-match if it does not match.
      3. Else,
        1. If run is empty, let pattern be the Type of the primary parameter's TypeParameterDefault, evaluated over bindings; otherwise, let pattern be the sole element of run.
        2. Let r be ? MatchSpecializationPattern(pattern, bindings[k].[[Value]], env, deferred, specialization).
        3. If r is no-match, return no-match.
    5. For each Parse Node d of deferred, do
      1. Let computed be ? the Type Record d denotes, evaluated over env by 1.2.7.
      2. If SameType(computed, the subject recorded with d) is false, return no-match.
    6. For each Record b of env, do
      1. If b.[[Capture]].[[Declaration]] has a TypeParameterConstraint, then
        1. Let bound be ? the Type Record its Type denotes, evaluated over env.
        2. If IsAssignable(b.[[Value]], bound) is false, return no-match.
    7. Return env.
     Note

    The entries are arguments of the primary as an application's are, so a variadic parameter of the primary takes a RUN of entries: with class Tup<...Ts: [].<type>>, the list <uint8, ...const Rest> matches every application whose first type is uint8 and binds Rest to the tuple of the others. The list is positional only, so no run is opened by a name. An omitted trailing entry stands for the primary's default at that position, not for a wildcard, so with class FixedBuffer<T: type = uint8, N: uint32 = 16> the list <uint8> matches only an extent of 16. Structural positions are matched first and computations over captures are checked afterwards, which is why a computation may read a capture bound at a later position. A computation that throws, or that exhausts the evaluation budget, is an error, not a failed match.

    1.4.3.2.4.2 MatchSpecializationPattern ( pattern, subject, env, deferred, mode )

    The abstract operation MatchSpecializationPattern takes arguments pattern (a Parse Node), subject (a Type Record), env (a List of Records with fields [[Capture]] and [[Value]]), deferred (a List of Parse Nodes), and mode (specialization or type-subject) and returns either a normal completion containing either matched or no-match, or a throw completion. It matches one position. mode is type-subject for a slotted type-subject pattern (24), which shares this operation and differs only in how a fixed leaf is compared. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If pattern is the wildcard _, return matched.
    2. If pattern is a CaptureBinding or a capture reference, then
      1. Let c be the Capture Record the capture scope associates with pattern.
      2. If c is declared in a metadata position with a written TypeParameterDomain, then
        1. Let M be the meta type that TypeParameterDomain names.
        2. Let m be the metadata carried by subject, or undefined if it carries none.
        3. Set subject to MetadataPortion(m, M).
      3. If env contains a Record whose [[Capture]] is c, then
        1. Let b be that Record.
        2. If c is declared in a metadata position, then
          1. If subject and b.[[Value]] are equivalent metadata values (Table 43), return matched.
          2. Return no-match.
        3. If SameType(subject, b.[[Value]]) is true, return matched.
        4. If subject is a literal type, b.[[Value]] is a literal type, and SameValue(subject.[[Value]], b.[[Value]].[[Value]]) is true, return matched.
        5. Return no-match.
      4. Append the Record { [[Capture]]: c, [[Value]]: subject } to env.
      5. Return matched.
    3. If pattern is an application whose arguments contain a CaptureBinding, a capture reference, or the wildcard _, then
      1. Let C be the declaration the application's constructor denotes, resolved in the capture scope.
      2. If pattern is a metadata application of a primitive that declares no type parameters and subject is that bare primitive, treat subject as an application of C supplying one metadata position with no carried metadata for the following steps. This does not construct a parameterized Type Record.
      3. If subject is not an application of C, return no-match.
      4. Let slots be the arguments of pattern assigned to C's parameters by the positional, named, and variadic rules of BindTypeArguments, with each omitted parameter taking its default and with no CaptureBinding or capture reference evaluated.
      5. For each parameter position q of C, in order, do
        1. Let r be ? MatchSpecializationPattern(slots[q], the argument of subject at q, env, deferred, mode).
        2. If r is no-match, return no-match.
      6. Return matched.
    4. If pattern is an array or tuple type whose extent or elements contain a CaptureBinding, a capture reference, or the wildcard _, then
      1. If subject is not a Type Record of the same form as pattern, which is a tuple for a tuple type, an array with a fixed extent for an array type whose extent is written, and an array of dynamic extent for one whose extent is not, return no-match.
      2. Match the extent and each element of pattern against those of subject by MatchSpecializationPattern, a ... CaptureBinding binding the tuple of the elements its run covers under the variadic rules of BindTypeArguments, and return no-match if any does not match.
      3. Return matched.
    5. If pattern reads a capture, append pattern to deferred, recording subject with it, and return matched.
    6. Let fixed be ? the Type Record pattern denotes.
    7. If mode is type-subject, return matched if subject matches fixed by 20, and no-match otherwise.
    8. If SameType(subject, fixed) is true, return matched.
    9. Return no-match.
     Note

    A fixed position compares by identity and not by assignability: Pair<uint32, _> matches Pair.<uint32, string> and not a Pair whose first argument is a refinement of uint32, and any in a list is the exact argument any. A repeated capture is an equality under SameType, so Pair<const T, T> matches Pair.<uint8, uint8> and not Pair.<uint8, uint16>, and a repeated value capture compares by SameValue, so NaN repeats and 0 and -0 do not. A repeated pack requires the same length and elementwise identity, and a run of one sequence holds at most one ..., since two leave no boundary between them. The wildcard makes a position structural as a capture does, so Map.<_, uint8> matches every Map whose value type is uint8 and is never resolved as a type named _. The form of an array is part of what matches: [const N].<const E> matches only an array of fixed extent and [].<const E> only a dynamic one. Only structural positions expose a component: a builder is never run backwards to find a capture, and is instead evaluated forward, as a deferred check, from captures bound elsewhere.

    Callable selection, the relationship of a specialized callable to its owner, and the contract a callable replacement preserves are specified in 1.4.3.2.2. Class replacement contract preservation is specified in 4.10. Class replacement selection and replacement contracts for alias and interface families remain extension hooks. An implementation reports a specialization it cannot select as an error rather than accepting it and ignoring it.

    1.4.3.3 Parameter Kinds

    A parameter's kind is decided by how its domain is written: the Type type declares a type parameter, [].<type> on a parameter of the ... form a pack of types, and TypeParameterHoles a constructor. Any other domain declares a value parameter, and is judged by what it denotes, so an alias of a value type is a value domain as that type is. An alias of type is refused rather than read as type.

    Note

    The kind decides how an argument binds, a type or a constant, so it is read where it is written: a reader, a tool, or an implementation knows it from the declaration alone, without resolving a name that may be declared later or imported from a module not yet linked. Rust marks a value parameter syntactically, const N: usize, and C++ distinguishes typename T from int N the same way. The diagnostic for an alias of type offers the spelling, T: type or ...Ts: [].<type>.

    1.4.3.3.1 ParameterKind ( p )

    The abstract operation ParameterKind takes argument p (a TypeParameter Parse Node) and returns either a normal completion containing one of type, value, or constructor, or a throw completion. It is evaluated once, at the declaration; a domain that reads an earlier parameter is evaluated as a deferred application (1.2.7.2) and classified by its operator. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let written be the Type of the TypeParameterDomain of p.
    2. If p has a TypeParameterHoles, then
      1. If written is not the Type type, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Return constructor.
    3. If p is of the ... form and written is the Type [].<type>, return type.
    4. If p is not of the ... form and written is the Type type, return type.
    5. Let d be ? the Type Record written denotes.
    6. If p is of the ... form, then
      1. If d is not an array or tuple Type Record, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Set d to the element type of d.
    7. If d is the type type, throw a TypeError exception.
    8. If IsPermittedValueDomain(d) is true, return value.
    9. Throw a TypeError exception.
     Note

    The final step is where a bound written as a domain is caught at its declaration. T: Ordered.<T> declares a value parameter whose values would be objects, which no generic argument can be, and the diagnostic offers T: type extends Ordered.<T>; Rust, Swift, and Kotlin write a bound as T: B, so this is the mistake a reader from those languages makes first. A domain that admits both Type Objects and other values, any or type | uint32, reaches the same step, since a binding from an argument could read it either way.

    1.4.3.3.2 IsPermittedValueDomain ( d )

    The abstract operation IsPermittedValueDomain takes argument d (a Type Record) and returns a Boolean. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If d is a primitive Type Record other than the type type, return true.
    2. If d is an enumeration type or a literal Type Record, return true.
    3. If d is the Type Record of a union, then
      1. For each member m of d, if IsPermittedValueDomain(m) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    4. If d is a meta type's constraint shape, or an application of one (6.1), return true.
    5. If d is an array Type Record, return IsPermittedValueDomain(the element type of d).
    6. If d is a tuple Type Record, then
      1. For each element type e of d, if IsPermittedValueDomain(e) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    7. Return false.

    An array or tuple of value domains is itself one, though its values are Objects: a value parameter binds the LITERAL type of its argument (1.4.3.3), and an array's literal type is the tuple of its elements' literal types, so what a generic argument is identified by is that content and never the array's identity. It is what join<D: string, P: [].<string>> relies on to bind the strings a call passes. An array whose elements are objects is not a value domain, for the reason no other object type is.

    Note

    A meta type is the one record-shaped value domain: its values are the normalized, immutable metadata records its hooks accept, compared by that facility's identity rather than by object identity, which is why decimal128.<{ currency: To }> names one type however the record is spelled. No other object type is a value domain, since a generic argument's identity would then turn on object identity.

    A union is a value domain when each of its members is one, so V: uint8 | string declares a parameter over constants of either type, the case C++ writes template<auto V>. any is not a value domain: it admits Type Objects, which would make a binding from an argument ambiguous between the argument's type and its value, and it admits objects, which no generic argument can be. Neither is type | uint32, for the first reason. A parameter over types is written T: type, and one over several kinds of constant is written as the union of their types.

    1.4.3.3.3 EffectiveConstraint ( p )

    The abstract operation EffectiveConstraint takes argument p (a Type Parameter Record) and returns a Type Parse Node or none. It returns the type an argument for p is checked against: a value parameter's domain, and a type or constructor parameter's bound. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If p.[[Kind]] is value, return p.[[Domain]].
    2. Return p.[[Constraint]].

    This operation selects source; it does not resolve that source in the caller's environment. Its denotation at an application, including a completed description retained by a substituted signature, is determined by 4.2.

    A parameter is bound from a call's argument by its kind. Where a formal parameter's annotation reads a parameter p, the argument contributes to p its Static Type if p.[[Kind]] is type, and the literal type of its value if p.[[Kind]] is value, which requires the argument to be a compile-time constant as every value argument must be. So function id<T: type>(x: T): T called as id((3 := uint16)) binds T to uint16, while function init<C: Component>(component: C) called with Component.Transform binds C to that constant. A pack binds elementwise by the same rule.

    1.4.3.4 Computed Constraints and Literal Inference

    The Type of a TypeParameterConstraint or a TypeParameterDefault may be a ComputedType (1.4.2.4) that reads parameters declared earlier in the same TypeParameters. It is a type error for it to read the parameter it belongs to or one declared later in the list. The rule on a later parameter holds of every form a constraint or default takes, since the later parameter has no binding when this one's constraint is evaluated or its default substituted. The rule on the parameter's own name holds of every default, and of a constraint where the read is within a ComputedType, a KeyOfType or an IndexedAccessType, the forms that evaluate over their operand. A bound that names its own parameter as a type argument, as T: type extends Ordered.<T> does, is an F-bounded constraint and is not refused: it is checked against the binding once the binding exists, which is how Rust reads T: PartialOrd<T>. The list owns its names, so a later parameter shadows an outer binding of the same name throughout the list and a read of it is the forward read above.

    Parameters bind left to right. At a use of the generic declaration, whether through explicit arguments or through inference from a call, the first parameter is bound, then the next parameter's constraint is evaluated by 1.2.7 over the bindings so far, then that parameter is bound and checked against its evaluated constraint, and so on down the list. Within the declaration itself, before any parameter is bound, such a constraint is carried as the deferred application of 1.2.7.2.

    Where a parameter has an evaluated constraint at all, the binding inferred for it from a call argument is the LITERAL type of the argument's value, not the widened base. This was stated for a constraint that is a literal type or a union of literal types (1.5.19) and holds for any constraint: the constraint is a contextual type, and 1.6.6 gives a literal in a position with one the type of that position. An UNCONSTRAINED parameter widens, which is the case its example describes. The binding is then checked against the constraint as any binding is, admitting a literal - or a union or tuple of them, which is what several arguments contribute - that fits it.

    Note

    This is the one placement of a builder call that needs a sentence of new specification, and the one inference rule builders ask for. function pluck<T: type, K: keyof T>(o: T, key: K): indexed(T, K) reads in order: infer T from o, evaluate keyof T over that binding, and infer K from the second argument literally, so pluck(user, 'name') binds K to the literal type 'name' and the return type evaluates to that property's type. The constraint does double duty, checking the argument and cueing the literal inference, which is the cue K extends keyof T gives an erased system. It is a rule about constraints rather than a hook: no user code runs inside the inference of the parameters the constraint reads, and a mistaken argument fails the ordinary constraint check, with the evaluated union available to the diagnostic.

    A constraint that is a value type binds a value, as the note above says of W: uint32; a constraint that is a union of literal types binds a literal type, whose value is recoverable from it. The design's kit reads that value back out constantly, which suggests these are one mechanism seen from two sides, a binding to the literal type with the value as its view, and the decision is that the literal-type binding is primitive with the value as its view, executed by the generics clause.

    1.4.4 Type Annotations

    An annotated rest parameter whose target is a BindingPattern uses the same collected-container contract as a named rest. The written annotation takes precedence over a contextual signature. After argument distribution and reference decay, enforce the collected array or tuple type, including element conversion and extent, before binding the pattern. Statically, pass that contract to the ordinary pattern contribution judgment; an object pattern reads indexed storage members, while an array pattern uses the iteration contribution and does not acquire a protocol guarantee from storage alone.

    When checking a function's parameter initializers, all parameter binding identities and their effective declared or contextual contracts are in scope, including bindings introduced by destructuring. Initializers are then checked in declaration order. Recording a contract does not initialize a binding or remove its temporal dead zone. A closure written in an earlier default may therefore be checked against a later parameter's contract; invoking it before that parameter is initialized still throws a ReferenceError. Declarations in the function body are not in the parameter-initializer environment.

    A type annotation attaches a type to a binding, a parameter, a return, or a class member. This clause adds the annotation and the positions that accept it; the meaning of an annotation in each position is given by the declarations, functions, and classes clauses.

    TypeAnnotation[Yield, Await] : : Type[?Yield, ?Await] : BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] [no LineTerminator here] is Type[?Yield, ?Await] TypedInitializer[In, Yield, Await] : := AssignmentExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await]

    A binding may carry an annotation, or a typed initializer that infers the binding's type from its initializer. The binding of a for-of or for-in head takes the same annotation, as for (const a: int32 of f()), and a BindingPattern in any of these positions annotates its elements through SingleNameBinding.

    FormalParameter[Yield, Await] : refopt BindingElement[?Yield, ?Await] SingleNameBinding[Yield, Await] : BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt BindingElement[Yield, Await] : SingleNameBinding[?Yield, ?Await] BindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt BindingRestElement[Yield, Await] : ... BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ... BindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt

    A DESTRUCTURED binding takes its annotation the same way a named one does, before its initializer: function f({ a, b }: Point) annotates the object being destructured, not the names taken out of it, and each name's type follows from the annotated type's members. Without this a pattern could carry an annotation only as a REST element - ...{ a, b }: T was admitted where { a, b }: T was not - which is a distinction the grammar drew and nothing else did.

    A rest element's annotation is the type of what it collects, an array or tuple type rather than an element type, so ...args: [].<uint32> collects uint32 values into a [].<uint32>. It is a type error if the annotation does not RESOLVE to an array or tuple type, and the rule is on what it resolves to rather than on how it is written: a name, a type parameter and a computed type are each judged by what they denote. A type parameter used this way must therefore be constrained to [].<any> or to a narrower array or tuple type, so that the error is reported where the rest is declared rather than at every application. Where the annotation states an EXTENT — [2].<uint8>, or [N].<uint8> for a value parameter N — the extent is part of the type and the call must supply that many arguments; for a value parameter this is checked where N is supplied. Its Parameter Record's [[Type]] holds that type, and the element type of a rest is the [[Element]] of an array type and the union of the [[Type]] fields of a tuple type's elements; an operation comparing a single argument against a rest compares against its element type. The production is restated because a rest reaches its binding through BindingRestElement rather than through SingleNameBinding, so without this the design's function f(a: string, ...args: [].<uint32>) {} and let [a: uint8, ...b: [].<uint8>] = [1, 2] have no parse.

    The array-or-tuple annotation requirement applies to every annotated BindingRestElement, including one in an array binding pattern or a nested parameter pattern. It is a declaration well-formedness judgment independent of the source's Static Iteration Contribution: an unknown source, element type or count does not validate an annotation of a different kind. In particular, any or object alone is not an array-or-tuple rest annotation; an unannotated rest and an array with [[Element]] any remain admitted. Resolve aliases and type parameters by the same rules as for formal rests, retaining the existing deferred type-resolution rules. Object rest retains its separate rule in 2.2. This judgment does not replace element, position or extent checks at known contributions or at run time.

    A parameter list may hold more than one rest parameter, and a rest may appear anywhere in it rather than only last, which the pinned edition's FormalParameters does not admit. The productions are restated so that a rest is an ordinary element of the list.

    FormalParameters[Yield, Await] : [empty] FunctionRestParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] , FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] , FunctionRestParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt FormalParameterList[Yield, Await] : FormalParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] , FormalParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterElement[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterList[?Yield, ?Await] , FormalParameterElement[?Yield, ?Await] FormalParameterElement[Yield, Await] : FormalParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionRestParameter[?Yield, ?Await] FunctionRestParameter[Yield, Await] : refopt BindingRestElement[?Yield, ?Await]

    ref on a rest parameter, in a declaration and in a function type alike, distributes over the run: each parameter the rest collects is a ref parameter. References are not values, so a ref rest binds no array. Its name is usable in exactly three forms, each a direct use of one collected reference and none a store — spread into another call's ref rest position, name[k] with a compile-time-constant k, and name.length (whose count has the index type) — and any other use is the escape error a single ref parameter already has, applied per element. The rule is static: the checker refuses every other form where it can see the name — an index that is not a constant, a property, a bare read, a store, a whole pass — and the run time, which cannot tell a constant index from another, refuses a store of the run, a pass of it to a parameter that is not a ref rest, and an index out of range. A callback whose type carries a ref rest is satisfied by a function whose parameters are individually ref; the run is matched by 1.10.4.2 as any rest is.

    Reference-run forwarding retains an occurrence independently of its expanded entries. Evaluate the written arguments once in source order and record the source boundary of every zero-length reference-run spread. The occurrence contributes no argument, Reference Value, argument rank or count. Include forwarding permissions in the named and positional binding judgment. Among assignments satisfying the ordinary type, reference and forwarding requirements, select the lexicographically greatest parameter-count List as in SequenceAssignment. Every non-empty forwarded entry must reach a reference-rest position. For an empty occurrence preceding all named contributions, require a reference rest whose selected positional interval contains the occurrence's boundary, including either endpoint or a zero-length interval. Groups supplied by names or by a named rest's returned suffix do not advance that positional cursor. After named contributions have begun, require the currently open named rest to be a reference rest; an empty occurrence does not reopen a rest closed by a fixed named contribution. Multiple qualifying zero-length intervals need no selection, since the occurrence assigns no value.

    Apply this forwarding permission to the effective callable signature in view. A compatible implementation with individual reference parameters, or with no parameters for an empty reference-rest view, receives the already admitted actual argument sequence without a second requirement that its own declaration spell a rest. Without such a view, the actual selected signature supplies the contract. An ordinary value boundary, including a reflective built-in with no reference rest, does not admit the run even when it is empty. For an overload set, forwarding compatibility participates in each candidate's binding and viability; it contributes no additional ranking preference. A partition that violates forwarding permission does not exclude a candidate if another assignment satisfies all requirements. A forwarding failure is a TypeError exception before parameter initialization or callee body evaluation. Earlier argument effects and abrupt completions retain their ordinary order. Omitted positional arguments remain omitted, and final binding and later accesses retain all reference-liveness checks.

    The forwarding permission is also a static judgment under 1.2.8. If the spread operand is established to name a reference-rest binding and the effective callable contract has no signature containing a reference-rest position, it is a type error even in an uncalled body and even if the run is empty or its length is unknown. An ordinary rest, individual reference parameters, and an empty parameter list do not supply that position. Use lexical binding identity and the effective substituted callable contract, including a callable view, rather than the implementation's parameter syntax. All parameter binding conventions are available while checking defaults, including later reference-rest bindings, without initializing them or changing their temporal dead zones. An unknown callable retains its runtime check; the presence of a potentially eligible overload signature prevents this absence proof but does not establish successful routing, admission or liveness.

    Checking also rejects forwarding when every effective candidate has no possible route from the written occurrences to reference-rest positions. Preserve established named pinning and source order: a fixed named contribution closes named-rest scope, while a potentially named spread makes that scope unknown until a later established name determines it again. A required callable iteration hook establishes positional routing without establishing a count; array or tuple storage and an optional hook do not by themselves establish that fact. Do not evaluate arguments, iterators, getters or initializers to decide this judgment. A length-independent negative proof may contract every forwarded run to a zero-width occurrence, relax collected extents and element admission, and ask whether any assignment to the remaining fixed, optional and rest positions admits every occurrence at a reference rest. Ordinary positional spreads range over all finite lengths. Account for permitted omission and possible named-rest suffix giveback when forming this relaxation. If even this relaxed routing has no solution, the call is a type error, including in an uncalled body. A solution to the relaxed judgment is not a proof of full admission, overload selection or liveness, and cannot replace their required checks.

    UniqueFormalParameters and the arrow forms are defined over FormalParameters and so admit the wider list without restatement; the duplicate-name early errors of the pinned edition apply to it unchanged. It is a Syntax Error for a FunctionRestParameter to carry an Initializer, as it is today. Adjacent rest parameters must each carry a type annotation; a missing annotation in an adjacent pair is a Syntax Error. Each annotation must resolve to an array or tuple type, and it is a type error if either adjacent rest has an element type of any, including through an alias or a substituted type parameter. Adjacent constrained rests may have the same element type. Arguments are distributed by 1.10.4.2: the leftmost rest takes the greatest run that leaves the remaining parameters satisfiable, including required trailing parameters. Assignment preserves each reference argument and does not copy its referent or remove its reference marker.

    Note 1

    Every language admitting a rest away from the end pairs it with something that marks the boundary. Swift allows several variadic parameters and requires the first parameter after one to carry an argument label; Ruby allows def f(a, *b, c) and binds the fixed parameters from both ends before the splat takes the middle; TypeScript reaches a non-final rest only through a tuple type with a middle rest element. This design has two such markers already, the declared types of the parameters and the named arguments of 1.10.4, and the adjacent-pair rule above excludes unrestricted neighboring runs. Greedy assignment determines the boundary even when constrained rests have the same element type.

    A function may carry type parameters and a return annotation.

    FunctionDeclaration[Yield, Await, Default] : function BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] } [+Default] function TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] }

    A class field may carry an annotation.

    FieldDefinition[Yield, Await] : ClassElementName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt Note 2

    The positions above are representative rather than exhaustive: the remaining function forms, including methods, arrow functions, generators, and class constructors, take the same annotations and are patched by the clauses that specify them (1.10.8). An arrow function's parameter list and return annotation interact with the arrow cover grammar and are given by 1.10.7.

    ref before a parameter is a contextual keyword. A parameter named ref remains valid, since an identifier that is not followed by a token that can begin a binding element is a parameter name; function f(ref) therefore continues to declare a parameter named ref, while function f(ref a: int32) declares a reference parameter named a. The claim rule this shares with every other borrowing form, and the Early Errors of the ref parameter — no BindingPattern and no Initializer — are stated with the rest of the borrowing syntax in 2.1.

    1.4.5 Types in Expression Position

    A type name is already an expression, since a type is a value, so uint8 and Map.<string, uint8> may be written where a value is expected. The type forms whose syntax collides with the expression grammar cannot: a function type reads as an arrow function, an object type as a block, a tuple type as an array literal, and a union as a bitwise or. The type operator resolves the collision by parsing its operand as a type.

    UnaryExpression[Yield, Await] : UpdateExpression[?Yield, ?Await] delete UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] void UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] typeof UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] + UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] - UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] ~ UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] ! UnaryExpression[?Yield, ?Await] [+Await] AwaitExpression[?Yield] TypeOperatorExpression[?Yield, ?Await] TypeOperatorExpression[Yield, Await] : type [no LineTerminator here] Type[?Yield, ?Await]

    A conversion converts the value of its left operand to a type, and is written after the value.

    RelationalExpression[In, Yield, Await] : ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] < ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] > ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] <= ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] >= ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] instanceof ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] [+In] RelationalExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] in ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] [+In] PrivateIdentifier in ShiftExpression[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] := Type[?Yield, ?Await] RelationalExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] [no LineTerminator here] is MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] Note

    Placing a conversion at RelationalExpression gives it the precedence of instanceof, so a + b := uint8 converts the sum, and the right operand being a Type means x := A | B converts to the union rather than taking the bitwise or of a conversion.

    type is a contextual keyword, since a program may already bind the name type, and this leaves an ambiguity: type (uint8) => uint8 is a type operator applied to a function type, while type (x) is a call of a function named type, and the two agree until the token after the closing parenthesis. This specification resolves it with a cover grammar, as the grammar already does for arrow parameters and parenthesized expressions: the parenthesized text is parsed under a cover production and refined to a function-type operand or a call argument list once the token after the closing parenthesis is known. The type declaration form raises no ambiguity, since its type is followed by a binding identifier, and the computed types of 1.4.2.4 do not widen it: type f(x) was a syntax error and is now the operator applied to a computed type, so the only covered case is an operand that begins with (. The committee may still prefer to avoid the cover grammar by restricting the operand or by requiring the operator only where a type cannot otherwise be written; that would remove the covered case rather than change the meaning of any program the cover grammar already accepts, and is a decision worth taking before the syntax is final. It does not reach the two operands below, which stay ambiguous however the operand is restricted.

    Two operand tokens are ambiguous in a way no cover production can resolve. type [0] is the operator applied to the tuple type [0], and a member access on a binding named type; type -1 is the operator applied to the literal type -1 (1.5.19), and a subtraction. Unlike the parenthesized case the two readings do not diverge at a later token: each is complete and ends where the other does, so a refinement has nothing to look at and the ambiguity must be decided rather than covered. It is decided here in the operator's favour: type [0] is the tuple type, type -1 is the literal type, and a program that means the value writes (type)[0] or (type) - 1. This is the treatment ECMAScript already gives let [ at the start of a statement, which is a destructuring declaration rather than a member access on a binding named let. A property access such as o.type[0] is unaffected, since only a bare type reaches the operator, and the [no LineTerminator here] restriction means a line break before - 1 leaves it a subtraction. Deciding the two tokens differently is the hazard worth naming: - given to the operator and [ left to member access would admit type -1 while refusing type [uint8], and a tuple type would then have no spelling in expression position at all. If the change of meaning is judged too high a price, the alternative that keeps a tuple operand writable is to make it an early error for such an operand to appear where the name type is also bound, so that the program is refused rather than reinterpreted.

    The operand of type is a full Type and so extends as far as one reaches: type A | B is the union of A and B, not the bitwise or of type A and B. A bare name is a type expression, so type uint8 is a redundant spelling of uint8. The extensions that introduce type-position operators use the Type production defined here, sharing this precedence; is takes the wider MatchPattern (24), of which a Type is one form, so x is A | B tests the union exactly as before.

    is is a contextual keyword rather than a reserved word, and the [no LineTerminator here] restriction is what that costs. a is b on one line is a Syntax Error today, so the new production takes syntax no program can be using; but a, is, and b on three lines is three statements today, by automatic semicolon insertion, and must stay three. The restriction keeps it so, at the price that a program cannot break the line before is. This is the treatment async already receives before an arrow's parameters, and the alternative, reserving the word, is not available.

    1.4.6 Type Arguments and Placement new in Expression Position

Arguments[?Yield, ?Await] CallExpression[Yield, Await] : CoverCallExpressionAndAsyncArrowHead[?Yield, ?Await] SuperCall[?Yield, ?Await] ImportCall[?Yield, ?Await] CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] Arguments[?Yield, ?Await] CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] [ Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ] CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] . IdentifierName CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] TemplateLiteral[?Yield, ?Await, +Tagged] CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] . PrivateIdentifier CallExpression[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await]

    A MemberExpression or CallExpression followed by TypeArguments evaluates the expression and specializes the result by the listed types. The value must be generic: a generic function, a generic class, or a parameterized type; the arguments bind by BindTypeArguments (4.3) — positional, named, and spread alike — and the substitution is that of 4.7, of which this production is the explicit written form. For a generic function the result is the specialization as a value (4.5): one interned function object per function and ordered bindings, whose where clauses ran once at its creation, so f.<uint8> may be stored, compared, passed to map, and called later exactly as the function it specializes, and evaluates its type arguments once rather than at each call. Where the expression's Static Type shows a value that is not generic it is a type error, and otherwise a specialization of a non-generic value throws a TypeError exception. The OptionalChain productions are not extended; a specialization does not follow ?..

    The placement forms allocate into an existing buffer rather than into fresh storage. The first argument is the buffer, the second, when present, is the byte offset and otherwise 0, and the third, when present, is the byte length reserved for each element and otherwise the constructed type's byteLength. Construction stores each field of each instance at its laid-out position (Table 39, memory layout); a third argument larger than byteLength leaves padding between elements, a smaller one makes elements overlap, and bytes the layout does not assign keep the buffer's contents, since reusing storage is what the form is for and the zero-fill rule of fresh allocation does not apply. It is a RangeError exception when the extent so computed exceeds the buffer's length. Over a resizable buffer the extent is recorded: shrinking the buffer below a live allocation's extent detaches those instances, touching a detached instance throws a TypeError exception, and growing never invalidates.

    Each written placement AssignmentExpression and its nested bodies is subject to the ordinary type-error judgments in its lexical, generic, private-name and reference context. Placement syntax does not exempt a subexpression from checking, even in an unused body. This requirement adds no static buffer-category, offset, layout or extent judgment. Evaluation order and multiplicity, runtime extent checks, detachment and reference liveness are unchanged.

    Note

    new ( begins both a placement form and an ordinary new whose constructor is parenthesized. Source that continues with a MemberExpression after the closing parenthesis is the placement form; under the base grammar such source has no parse as a single expression, so the added reading changes no existing program. The array form of the design, new(buffer, byteOffset, byteElementLength) [10].<Type>(0), needs no further production: [10].<Type> is an ArrayLiteral specialized by TypeArguments, which the alternative above already admits as the target MemberExpression.

    new . Arguments is TARGET-TYPED CONSTRUCTION: it constructs the type its position requires, so the type is not named. It is told apart from new.target by the token after the dot, an Arguments against an IdentifierName, and from both forms above by the dot itself; under the base grammar new . ( has no parse, so the added reading changes no existing program.

    The type comes from the position rather than from the expression, so a position requiring no type gives nothing to construct: it is a Syntax Error for this form to appear where the contextual type is absent. A Syntax Error rather than an inference, because inferring the type would be the binding-type inference this proposal does not perform. It is a type error where the contextual type is not constructible, as in let n: uint8 = new.(1). Among a constructible type's signatures the ordinary ranking chooses, with no rule of its own, and nesting follows without further rule, an inner form taking its type from the outer constructor's parameter.

    1.5 The Type Universe

    This clause adds the value types of this proposal to the ECMAScript language types of 6.1. For each type it fixes the set of values the type contains and the Type Record (1.2.1) that describes it. The operations over these values, the conversions between them, and the literals that produce them are specified by later clauses. This clause settles only what the values are and what the types are called.

    1.5.1 Value Types

    A value type is a type whose values are ECMAScript language values that are not Objects. A value of a value type has no identity: two values of the same value type that are the same value are indistinguishable, and nothing observable distinguishes one occurrence of such a value from another. The existing primitive types are value types in this sense, and every type this clause adds is one.

    The values of distinct value types are distinct. Where two types are described below as containing the same mathematical values, each contains its own values representing them: the uint8 representing 0 and the uint16 representing 0 are different values of different types, as the Number 1 and the BigInt 1 are today. Every value therefore belongs to exactly one type, which is what lets 1.7.1.1 report it.

    Every type added here is described by a Type Record whose [[Kind]] is primitive, whose [[Name]] is the String naming the type, and whose [[Arguments]] is the List of its type and value arguments. uint8 is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: primitive, [[Name]]: "uint", [[Arguments]]: « 8 » }, and vector.<float32, 4> by { [[Kind]]: primitive, [[Name]]: "vector", [[Arguments]]: « the Type Record for float32, 4 » }.

    Note

    Because Type Records are canonicalized and interned (1.2.2.9), a type written two ways is one Type Object: int8 and int.<8> name the same Type Record and therefore compare strictly equal. The shorthand names of 1.5.27 are consequently aliases rather than separate types.

    1.5.2 Integer Types

    For each positive integer N, int.<N> is a value type whose values are the integers from -2N-1 through 2N-1 - 1 inclusive, and uint.<N> is a value type whose values are the integers from 0 through 2N - 1 inclusive. Each has exactly 2N values. Neither has a negative zero, an infinity, or a NaN.

    N is a value argument, so int.<8> and int.<16> are distinct types, and the width of a type is recoverable from its Type Record.

    Note

    N is bounded: it lies in the inclusive interval from 1 to 216, and a width outside it is a type error. The bound is a specified constant like the budgets, generous enough for any hashing or cryptographic width and small enough that a computed type cannot demand an unbounded layout for one Type Record of cost. The design gives shorthands only through 128 and uses uint.<1> as the lane type of a boolean vector, but nothing above restricts N, and an unbounded N obliges every implementation to provide arithmetic at arbitrary width, which is a substantially larger commitment than the named widths imply. Fixing N to a bounded set, to the powers of two, or to a range up to 128 are all defensible; the choice belongs with the committee, and it interacts with the bit-field widths of the memory layout extension, which are the reason a width such as 3 is meaningful at all.

    1.5.3 Binary Floating-Point Types

    float16, float32, float64, and float128 are value types whose values are those of the corresponding IEEE 754-2019 binary interchange formats, with the same treatment of NaN the Number type receives: the many NaN encodings of the format are represented as a single NaN value. Each therefore has 2w - 2p + 3 values, where w is the width of the format in bits and p its precision in bits, as given in Table 9.

    Each of these types has a positive zero and a negative zero, a positive infinity and a negative infinity, and a single NaN, as the Number type does.

    Note

    float64 and the Number type have the same set of values but are distinct types, so neither is assignable to the other without a conversion. This is the rule stated for every pair of value types and is not a special case: Number is the type an untyped program computes with, and float64 is the type a program asks for when it wants that format by name.

    1.5.4 Decimal Floating-Point Types

    decimal32, decimal64, and decimal128 are value types whose values are those of the corresponding IEEE 754-2019 decimal interchange formats. A finite value of a decimal type is a triple of a sign, an integer coefficient, and an exponent, drawn from the ranges in Table 10. Each type additionally has a positive infinity, a negative infinity, and a single NaN.

    An arithmetic result whose exponent falls outside the range of its type is a RangeError exception. This is where a decimal parts company with a binary float, which saturates to an infinity instead: a decimal's range is a property of the TYPE rather than of the format, so a result the type cannot hold has no value of the type to be, and an infinity would claim the operation merely grew large rather than left the type behind. The same rule governs a conversion into a decimal (Table 19), so a value arrives out of range by no route.

    Two finite values of a decimal type that have the same numerical value but different exponents are distinct values of the type. The values written 1.0, 1.00, and 1.000 are three values of decimal128, one for each exponent, and a decimal type therefore preserves the significance of the quantity it was given. IEEE 754 calls such a set of values a cohort.

    Note

    Preserving trailing zeros is the point of the decimal types: a price given to two places prints to two places, which is what the money types of the primitive metadata extension depend on. The consequence is that the numerical order and the value identity of a decimal type come apart, and the equality operations must choose between them. The design settles two of the three: == compares numerical value, so 1.0 == 1.00 is true, and SameValueZero compares numerical value, so 1.0 and 1.00 are one key in a Map or a Set rather than two. Identity follows the representation: SameValue distinguishes the cohort members 1.0 and 1.00, so they are distinct map keys and distinct literal types, while === and == compare numerically and find them equal, the same split Number already has for +0 and -0.

    This specification settles SameValue the way the paragraph above already uses it: SameValue distinguishes cohort members, so Object.is(1.0, 1.00) is false for two decimal128 values of different exponents, while SameValueZero and == compare numerical value and find them equal. This is the split the design records for ===/== versus identity, and it is the parallel with negative zero, where SameValue distinguishes +0 from -0 and SameValueZero does not. The alternative, SameValue comparing numerical value, was rejected because it would make Object.is unable to distinguish values that print differently, which no other type permits; its cost, that SameValue and SameValueZero then differ on a case unrelated to zero, is the same cost negative zero already imposes and is judged the lesser one. This remains a decision the committee owns, recorded here because the type universe is where the cohort becomes observable.

    An operation with a decimal NaN operand gives the NaN, and one with an infinite operand gives the IEEE 754-2019 result; an operation IEEE 754-2019 signals as invalid, such as the difference of two infinities of one sign or the product of zero and an infinity, and one that would make a NaN or an infinity from finite operands, throws a RangeError exception.
