NaN and the infinities therefore arrive by conversion and from the bytes of an encoding, and the arithmetic carries them without making them.

    1.5.5 Rational Types

    For each positive integer N, rational.<N> is a value type whose values are the exact rational numbers representable as a quotient of two values of int.<N>. A value of rational.<N> is a pair of a numerator and a denominator, both values of int.<N>, such that the denominator is greater than 0 and the greatest common divisor of the numerator and the denominator is 1. Every value of the type is therefore in lowest terms, and each rational number has at most one representation in the type.

    A rational type has no negative zero, no infinity, and no NaN. An operation whose exact result is not representable, including one whose normalized numerator or denominator falls outside int.<N>, throws a RangeError rather than rounding.

    rational.<bigint> is a value type whose values are all the rational numbers, each as a quotient of two bigint values in lowest terms with a denominator greater than 0. No value is outside it, so an operation on it throws no RangeError for want of range; a zero denominator is still one. It has no layout, as bigint has none. Its numerator and denominator are bigint values, and Math.floor, Math.ceil, Math.round and Math.trunc of one return a bigint.

    For parse, a literal of a rational type is a decimal numeric literal — digits, with an optional fraction and exponent — or two decimal integer literals separated by /, the second unsigned: 0.1 is 1/10 and 3/4 is 3/4, as a literal in a rational position denotes. A literal whose denominator is 0 is a literal whose value no rational type can represent, so parse throws a RangeError for it, as the constructor does for a zero denominator.

    rational.<N>.approximate(_x_, _maxDenominator_) returns the value of rational.<N> nearest the Number x whose denominator does not exceed maxDenominator. Of two values equally near, it returns the one with the smaller denominator, and of two with the same denominator, the one nearer zero. It throws a RangeError if x is not finite, if maxDenominator is less than 1, or if x lies outside the range of rational.<N>, which is overflow rather than approximation; rational.<bigint> has no range to lie outside, and bounds only the denominator. The explicit alias rational64.approximate is that of rational.<64>; there is no bare rational application.

    Note

    Normalizing on construction is what makes the type a value type in the ordinary sense: without it, one half would have many representations and equality would have to normalize before comparing. It is also what makes the RangeError unavoidable, since a sum of two representable rationals can have an unrepresentable normalized denominator. Refusing to round is the distinction between this type and a float; a rational that cannot be represented exactly is an error, not an approximation.

    1.5.6 Complex Types

    For a value type T that is number or one of the binary floating-point types, complex.<T> is a value type whose values are the ordered pairs of a real part and an imaginary part, each a value of T. The number of values of complex.<T> is the square of the number of values of T.

    Note

    The width-named shorthands of 1.5.27 count total bits rather than component bits, following the convention of NumPy and Go, so complex64 is a pair of float32 and not a pair of float64.

    1.5.7 Vector Types

    For a value type T that is an integer, binary floating-point, or vector type, or a metadata parameterization of one, and a positive integer N, vector.<T, N> is a value type whose values are the sequences of exactly N values of T. T is the lane type and N the lane count. The number of values of vector.<T, N> is the number of values of T raised to the power N.

    Note

    A vector's lane type may itself be a vector, which is how the boolean vectors of the design are built: boolean8 is vector.<boolean1, 8>, where boolean1 is the design's name for uint.<1>, eight one-bit lanes, and boolean8x16 is vector.<boolean8, 16>. The lane counts an implementation can hold in a register are a matter for the SIMD extension; the type exists for every positive N.

    It is a type error to form vector.<T, N> where T is not a lane type or N is not a positive integer, since neither denotes a vector type. Where the lane type is itself a vector, this applies to it in turn.

    A parameterized lane type is how a vector's lanes carry metadata: vector.<float32.<{ m: 1 }>, 3> is a vector of meters, its lanes read as float32.<{ m: 1 }>, and it has the representation of vector.<float32, 3>, since a parameterization has exactly the representation of its base. A lane enters the parameterization as a scalar does, through a declared cast. Such a vector is a subtype of the vector of the same count over its lane's base, as the lane is a subtype of its base, so a vector of meters is accepted where a float32x3 is; a lane type that differs in representation, uint8 against uint16, relates no vectors.

    1.5.8 Vector Lanes

    A vector's lanes are reached by two pairs of operations, and the pairs differ in when the lane is chosen. Where the lane is a compile-time constant the choice is checked, and where it is an expression it is not; a design uses the first wherever it can (design, simd.md).

    For a vector type vector.<T, N>:

    • lane.<I>() has the Static Type T. It is a type error if I is not a non-negative integer less than N.
    • withLane.<I>(value) has the Static Type vector.<T, N>, and takes a value of type T. It is a type error if I is not a non-negative integer less than N. Its value is the receiver's, with lane I replaced by value; the receiver is unchanged, since a vector is a value type (1.5.7).
    • A member access with a computed key of type uint32 has the Static Type T, and an assignment to one takes a value of type T. The key is an expression, so no static rule bounds it: reading or writing a lane whose index is not less than N throws a RangeError.
    Note 1

    The asymmetry is the reason both forms are given. lane.<I>() is refused at check time for an index out of range and v[i] is not, because an index that is an expression is not known until the access happens. The design's rule is to write the constant form wherever the index is a constant, and the specification's part is only that the two differ in when the bound is enforced.

    withLane.<I>(value) returning a new vector rather than modifying the receiver is not a rule of this clause; it follows from a vector being a value type, and is stated because a reader arriving from an array is likely to expect otherwise.

     Note 2

    The assignment is asked about because withLane expresses the same intent and returns a value, where v[i] = value mutates one in place, which is what a value type is meant not to do (simd.md, Open Questions). It is kept, and the reason is not the consistency one: an array does already permit a value type's element to be assigned, but the decisive point is that withLane`'s index is a COMPILE-TIME CONSTANT. The two operations therefore do not overlap where it matters — refusing the assignment would leave a lane whose index is computed with no way to be written at all — so the redundancy the question supposes does not exist.

    Note 3

    An operation taking a computed index and returning a new vector would restore the redundancy and reopen the question honestly. Nothing here proposes one; a revision that added it could then refuse the assignment without leaving the computed case unwritable, which is the only ground on which refusing it would be complete.

    vector.<T, N> declares a cast operator from T, so a value of the lane type converts to a vector by filling every lane with it, and the conversion is one of the user-defined casts of 1.6 rather than a rule of its own. A value whose type is not the lane type does not convert: for a float32 s, float32x4 accepts s and float64x2 does not, and a design that wants the second converts s to float64 first. An operator applies this cast to a scalar operand whose numeric base is the lane type's, so for a float32 s, v * s scales every lane of a float32x4 v, and a literal beside a vector adopts the lane type (1.9.4); a scalar of another numeric type is a type error there. A vector type called with its lanes constructs the vector, taking one argument per lane or one argument broadcast to every lane, and each argument is judged at the lane type as an argument is: a literal the lane type cannot represent is a type error (1.6.6), so uint8x16(300, …) is refused rather than wrapped. A single argument that is itself a vector is an explicit conversion instead (1.6.7), and a single argument to a vector of uint.<1> lanes is a bitmask.

    Where the lane type is uint.<1>, a lane and a bit coincide: lane i of a vector.<uint.<1>, N> is bit i of an N-bit integer, counting from the least significant. The conversion between such a vector and an integer type is that correspondence read in each direction. An integer value converted to the vector type gives the vector whose lane i is bit i of the value, and a value of the vector type converted to an integer type gives the integer whose bit i is lane i.

    Note 4

    This is what makes a bit vector a bitfield rather than a name for a byte. A boolean8 initialized from 0b00000010 has lane 1 set and the rest clear, so a[1] is 1 and a[0] is 0; assigning 1 to lane 3 and reading the value back as an integer gives 0b00001010.

    The numbering is the one 17 states for the masks a comparison produces, and it is stated here as a rule because that clause states it as a remark about hardware. A bit vector converts whether or not a comparison produced it.

    A bit vector is not a bit-field. The sub-byte integer members a class may declare, with their own bit order and offsets, are 9's and are a different feature: they pack members of differing widths into a layout, where a bit vector is N lanes of one width that permute, compare, and select like any other vector. The two are stated in different clauses because they answer different questions, and a reader meeting boolean8 here is not meeting the other.

    sum() has the Static Type T and is the sum of the receiver's lanes. Its result is that of adding the lanes in an implementation-defined order, which for a binary floating-point lane type is observable: addition is not associative there, so two implementations may return different values for one receiver.

    Note 5

    The order is left to the implementation because fixing it would forbid the instruction that makes the operation worth having: a pairwise horizontal add is what the hardware provides, and it associates differently from a left fold. A design needing a fixed order writes the fold it wants over lane.<I>().

    1.5.9 Vector Permutation

    A permutation names a lane of a source for each lane of its result, so it reorders, repeats, narrows, and widens in one operation. Two forms draw from one source and from two (design, simd.md).

    For a vector type vector.<T, N> and indices I₁ through IL, each a compile-time constant:

    • swizzle.<I₁, …, IL>() has the Static Type vector.<T, L>. Lane j of the result is lane Ij of the receiver. It is a type error if any Ij is not a non-negative integer less than N, or if L is not a positive integer.
    • shuffle.<I₁, …, IL>(other) has the Static Type vector.<T, L> and takes an other of type vector.<T, N>. An index below N selects that lane of the receiver, and an index from N to 2_N_-1 selects lane Ij-N of other. It is a type error if any Ij is not a non-negative integer less than 2_N_, or if L is not a positive integer.

    L need not equal N. A permutation of fewer indices than the receiver has lanes narrows, and one of more widens: swizzle.<0, 1>() on a four-lane vector has the Static Type vector.<T, 2>.

    Note 1

    Each index is a compile-time constant because that is what the instruction this form compiles to takes: the lane selector of shufps and its kind is an immediate operand. Other instructions take a selector in a register, pshufb, tbl, and vrgather among them, so a permutation whose selection is data is possible and is a DIFFERENT operation. It would be named swizzleDyn here, and it is an open question of the design (simd.md) rather than an omission from this clause.

    What is open about it is one rule: an index that is data may be out of range, where an index that is a constant is refused before the program runs, and there is no answer to defer to. Rust's swizzle_dyn and WebAssembly's i8x16.swizzle yield zero for such an index; x86's pshufb wraps; ARM's tbl and RISC-V's vrgather zero; and Java's VectorShuffle does neither, wrapping an invalid index into a negative band that a later operation may use to steer a second source. WebAssembly specified zero and then added a relaxed form whose result is implementation-defined, because upholding zero on x86 costs instructions. Each answer has been chosen by a real design and the hardware disagrees with itself, so whichever this specification chose would be extra work on some target — which is why the operation waits on a decision rather than on a clause.

    The two-source numbering is the one place a reader is likely to err. For a four-lane receiver, indices 0 through 3 name the receiver's lanes and 4 through 7 name other's, so a.shuffle.<0, 1, 4, 5>(b) takes the first half of each.

    swizzle is how the eight- and sixteen-lane vectors permute, since the component accessors of 1.5.10 name only a vector's first four lanes.

     Note 2

    The design writes the index list as a variadic value generic parameter, swizzle<...I: [].<uint32>>(), whose length gives the result's lane count. Value generics and their variadic form are specified by 4 and 4.4; the rules above are what that spelling means.

    1.5.10 Vector Component Accessors

    A vector of four or fewer lanes has names for its lanes, drawn from two sets, and a sequence of those names is a permutation written as a property (design, simd.md). xyzw and rgba name the same lanes in that order, so v.x and v.r are one lane and v.wzyx and v.abgr are one permutation.

    A property key is a component accessor of a receiver of type vector.<T, N> when all of the following hold:

    • N is at most 4.
    • The key is a sequence of 1 to 4 characters, each drawn from xyzw or each drawn from rgba. A key mixing the sets is not a component accessor.
    • Each character's index within its set is less than N.

    Such an accessor has the Static Type T for a key of one character, and vector.<T, L> for a key of L characters. L is independent of N: a two-lane vector's xyxy has the Static Type vector.<T, 4>.

    An accessor whose key names no lane twice is assignable, and takes a value of the accessor's own Static Type. An accessor whose key names a lane twice is not assignable, since an assignment to it would give one lane two values; it is a type error to assign to one.

    For a union receiver, assignment must be permitted by every known alternative. A known vector alternative for which the key is a repeated-lane component accessor therefore makes the assignment a type error. This includes compound assignment and a statically known computed key. A repeated-lane read remains valid; an ordinary object property with the same spelling retains its declared permissions. Unknown receivers or keys retain their runtime checks. This rule does not grant a component a reference capability.

    The value stored through a component accessor must satisfy the selected accessor's type under the ordinary conversion and contextual literal rules. This judgment applies to dot access and a statically known String key alike, and the lane-value judgment of 1.5.8 applies to a computed key of type uint32. Distribute destination contracts over reachable known receiver alternatives rather than checking against their joined read type. Two effect-free component projections of the same vector binding retain the same receiver alternative, so v.xy = v.yx remains valid for a vector union; independently obtained receivers do not acquire that correlation. The same destinations govern compound and logical assignment, destructuring and iteration targets. Unknown keys or receivers defer to run time. This changes neither numeric computed bounds checking nor reference eligibility.

    Note 1

    A vector of more than four lanes has no component accessors, because the two sets have four characters each. Such a vector permutes with 1.5.9, which is why that clause takes indices rather than names.

    That limit is a decision rather than a gap awaiting names. Every shading language that has these accessors stops at four, and no language with wider vectors has invented a set for them: Rust and Java give wide vectors indices and permutations and no names at all. Extending a set would collide, since a and b already name lanes in rgba and would name different lanes at a different width; adding a second pair of sets for lanes 4 through 7 does not reach sixteen; and numeric names in the manner of OpenCL's s0 through s7 would spell what lane.<I>() and swizzle already spell. The four names exist because geometry has conventional names for its axes, not because permutation wants sugar, so a vector with no such convention has no names and loses nothing.

    The design writes the third set GLSL provides, stpq, as deliberately absent: HLSL and WGSL dropped it, and two sets already name every lane.

    A component accessor is a property, not a syntactic form, and the distinction is observable. The names are non-enumerable properties of the vector's prototype, shared by every value of that shape, so:

    • v['xyz'] reaches the same value the dotted access does, since the key is looked up rather than parsed.
    • Reflection over the object a vector converts to sees the accessors: Object.getOwnPropertyNames(v) includes every accessor name of that vector's lane count.
    • Object.keys(v) is empty, since the accessors are not own properties.
    • Object.getOwnPropertyNames(C.prototype) for a four-lane vector type C includes every accessor name, of which there are 680 counting both sets and every result length from 1 to 4.
    Note 2

    in and Reflect.get are not among these, and the reason is the language's rather than this clause's: both require an Object, and a vector is a value type. A String behaves the same way — '0' in 'abc' is a TypeError though 'abc'[0] reads — so an accessor being a property does not make these operations reach it. An earlier draft of this clause listed them, which was an error about JavaScript rather than about vectors.

    A form keyed on the receiver's static type would satisfy neither: a computed access could not reach it, and reflection could not see it. Making the accessors properties is what keeps a vector an ordinary object, at the cost of several hundred prototype names that Object.getOwnPropertyNames reports. None of them collides with a method of the vector prototype, since every accessor name is drawn from xyzw and rgba alone.

    A component accessor is equivalent to the permutation of the same lanes:

    • A read through a key of one character is lane.<I>() for that character's index I (1.5.8).
    • A read through a key of L characters is swizzle.<I₁, …, IL>() for their indices (1.5.9).
    • An assignment through an assignable key replaces the named lanes with the corresponding lanes of the assigned value, leaving the receiver's other lanes unchanged.
    Note 3

    The equivalence is why this clause adds no operation. v.xzzw is v.swizzle.<0, 2, 2, 3>() and v.x is v.lane.<0>(); the names are how a program reads, and the permutation is what an implementation compiles. A compound assignment such as v.xy += w is the read, the operation, and the assignment in the order any compound assignment takes them, and needs no rule here.

    1.5.11 Lane-wise Math

    The function properties of the Math object apply lane-wise to a vector argument, returning a vector of the argument's shape. Where a function takes more than one argument, the arguments are vectors of one shape and the function applies at each lane; a scalar argument beside a vector one broadcasts (1.5.8).

    The set divides by whether the scalar function is exactly specified. min, max, abs, sqrt, floor, ceil, round, and trunc are exact, and lane j of the result is the scalar result for lane j of the argument. The remaining functions - the trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, and hyperbolic families and pow, cbrt, and hypot - are implementation-approximated as their scalar forms are, and the vector form is approximated independently of the scalar form: lane j of the vector result is not required to equal the scalar function applied to lane j.

    Note

    The independence is deliberate. A vector math library computes a transcendental to a different accuracy than the scalar library does, so requiring the two to agree would forbid an implementation from using the vector instruction at all, which is to forbid the reason the operation is offered here. A program requiring bit-identical results between the two spellings applies the scalar function lane by lane, which is what it is asking for.

    1.5.12 Mask Operations

    Reading any, all, or select from a statically known mask produces the corresponding function type. The any and all functions return boolean. The select function is generic in the selected lane type: both arguments and its return are vector.<U, N> for the receiver's lane count N. A known scalar argument is incompatible even before U is inferred. These callable contracts apply to method values as well as direct calls and do not change eager argument evaluation.

    17 states what a comparison between vectors produces. This clause states what consumes one. A mask is a vector whose lane type is uint.<1>, which is what the design names booleanN (1.5.8), and a vector whose lane type is itself such a vector is a mask too: that is the wide form a comparison yields, so a float32x4 comparison's boolean32x4 result is a mask as much as a boolean4 is. The operations below are declared on a mask in either form and on no other vector. A lane of the compact form is set when its bit is set, and a lane of the wide form when every bit of it is, which is what a comparison writes into one: all-set or all-clear.

    For a mask of N lanes:

    • all() has the Static Type boolean, and is true when every lane is set.
    • any() has the Static Type boolean, and is true when at least one lane is set.
    • select(whenSet, whenClear) takes two vectors of one type vector.<U, N> and has that Static Type. Lane j of the result is lane j of whenSet where lane j of the receiver is set, and lane j of whenClear otherwise.

    U is not the receiver's lane type. A mask selects between vectors of any lane type, so long as they share its lane count.

    Note 1

    select over an arithmetic result is how a program computes some lanes and leaves the others, which a target with predicated instructions performs in one instruction rather than two. m.select(_a_ + _b_, _src_) is the write-masked form, whose untaken lanes come from src, and m.select(_a_ + _b_, _zero_) is the zero-masked form. An implementation may lower either to such an instruction, computing only the lanes the mask takes, when the arm whose lanes it elides is an expression whose evaluation has no effect an ECMAScript program can observe; arithmetic over vectors is such an expression.

    That condition, and not the shape of the call, is what bounds the permission. select is an ordinary method, so its arguments are evaluated before it is entered: an argument that calls a function, reads an accessor, or otherwise has an effect is evaluated whatever the mask holds, and only lanes of an arm an implementation can show to be pure may go uncomputed. No syntax is added for the masked forms, because this composition already denotes them, and a per-operation mask parameter would give every operator a second spelling for what it already says.

    select is an ordinary call, so **both arguments are evaluated** before it is made, whichever lanes of the receiver are set. It is not a conditional and does not have a conditional's evaluation.

    Note 2

    That is the trade select exists to make. A branch evaluates one side and costs a misprediction where the condition varies per lane; select evaluates both and costs neither, which is why branchless code is written with it. A design that must not evaluate one side writes a branch.

    A mask is a vector and nothing about these operations makes it a separate kind of value: a lane of it is read by index, it permutes, and it carries component accessors like any other vector of its shape, so m.x is a lane of it and m.xyxy is a four-lane mask.

    1.5.13 Vector Widths

    vector.<T, N> admits any positive lane count, which is what lets one kernel be written against a width. The width a target executes in one instruction is a property of the target, and float32.preferredLanes is that width for the lane type float32, and every lane type carries the same property.

    Its result is a compile-time constant, so a type may be formed from it and a generic declaration may specialize on it. Its value is host-defined.

    Note 1

    The operation is on the LANE type rather than on vector, and the reason is that a bare parameterized primitive is not a value: uint, int, and vector denote types only when applied, so const x: uint = 5 is refused for the same reason const x: vector = ... is. A vector.preferredLanes(T) would need vector to be a value, which would single it out among the three. complex declares a component default, so it is complex.<number> in a concrete type position. This supplies the type of an imaginary literal and keeps complex distinct from complex128. rational has no default; rational64 is its explicit 64-bit alias. A lane type is already a Type Object and already carries statics — byteLength and the parsing operations among them — so float32.preferredLanes is one more property on a surface that exists, and it reads as what the operation asks: how many lanes of this type fill a register.

    This is the one operation of this specification whose result may differ between hosts, so it is the one place a program's TYPES may differ between hosts: a vector.<float32, vector.preferredLanes(float32)> is a different type on a target with four lanes and on one with eight. That is the point of the operation rather than a defect in it — a program written against it is portable in the sense that matters, which is that it compiles to the target's own width rather than to a width chosen for another machine.

    It is also why a design that needs one type across hosts writes the lane count rather than asking for it. The determinism this specification fixes elsewhere is determinism for a given host (1.2.7.4), and this operation does not weaken it: two evaluations on one host agree.

    A vector whose lane count exceeds the target's width is formed and used as any other, and an implementation executes it in as many instructions as it needs.

    Note 2

    Gather, scatter, and masked load and store are not specified. The design defers them (simd.md), and they are named here so that their absence reads as a boundary rather than an omission: they are the operations that vectorize an indirect access, and they need an addressing model this specification does not have.

    1.5.14 Wrapping a Vector

    A type alias of a vector type is that vector type, so a value of it has the component accessors of 1.5.10 and the operations of the clauses above. A class holding a vector as a member is a distinct nominal type, and does not have them: a class does not acquire the members of its own field's type.

    Note

    This follows from the rules for aliases and classes rather than adding one, and is stated because it decides a design question the design document poses. A Vector4 written as an alias swizzles and a Vector4 written as a class does not, unless it declares the accessors it wants. The trade is nominal distinction: two aliases of vector.<float32, 4> are one type, so a Quaternion and a Vector4 written that way are mutually assignable, where two classes are not.

    1.5.15 The any Type

    any is the type of every value. Every ECMAScript language value is a value of the any type, and a binding whose type is any accepts any value. It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: any }, and it is the type of a binding that carries no annotation, which is what makes an untyped program a program whose bindings are all of the any type.

    1.5.16 The void Type

    void is the type with no values. It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: void }, and it is written as the return type of a function that returns no value. No value is a value of the void type, so no binding may have it.

    It is a type error if an actual binding declaration resolves to the void type, independently of whether it has an initializer or that initializer is statically known. This includes local and parameter bindings, bindings within destructuring patterns, and catch bindings, including through a type alias. A binding whose type depends on a generic parameter is checked when an application resolves that binding's type; an application that makes it void is a type error. A parameter name in a function-type signature does not itself declare a runtime binding. This rule does not prohibit void return types or occurrences inside protocol types such as Generator.<Y, void, void>, and it does not reinterpret void as undefined.

    It is a type error for a program to depend on an expression whose Static Type is void: for it to be a test (1.8.5), the left operand of &&, || or ??, the receiver of ?. or of a property access, the operand of a unary operator other than void, delete and typeof, an operand of an arithmetic, bitwise, shift, relational or equality operator, the right operand of a compound assignment other than a logical one, or a template substitution. Such an expression may be an expression statement, the operand of void, an operand of the comma operator other than its last, a value returned where the return type is void, the right operand of &&, || or ?? or an arm of a conditional expression, whose value is judged where it is used, or a value reaching an untyped binding, an untyped parameter, Reflect.typeOf or typeof, the positions the note below names, typeof reporting the value as Reflect.typeOf does.

    Note 1

    A call of a function whose return type is void evaluates to undefined, as a call of a function with no return statement does today. The void type is the statement that a program must not depend on that result, not a claim that no result exists.

    Note 2

    The sentence is about the FUNCTION'S OWN return type, and it holds because such a function cannot return a value at all: 1.7.4 refuses a body that contradicts its annotation, so every call it describes already answers undefined.

    A call reaching a function through a void-returning TYPE is a different case. 1.2.3.1 makes a void return required of nothing, so const _h_: () => void`` may hold a function returning a String; _h_() then evaluates to that String. What void promises is that no TYPED position will accept it: the Static Type of _h_() is void, so let _s_: string = _h_() is refused, and every position that demands a type refuses it likewise.

    The value is therefore observable only where nothing was declared - an untyped binding, an argument to an untyped parameter, Reflect.typeOf. That is the same reach any has everywhere else in this specification, and it is why the promise is stated over the STATIC reading rather than over the value.

    Erasing the value at the call was considered and is not specified. It would require the checking pass to compute a Static Type for EVERY call, including the ones no position asks about, since a call whose value nothing wants is exactly where the erasure would have to act; and it would not close the gap, because Reflect.typeOf is itself such a position.

    It follows that a void return type constrains the CONSUMER of the result and not the value leaving the function: the check it installs is the one that refuses a binding, and no check is performed on the returned value itself. return; and falling off the end are the same function written two ways, so testing undefined against a type with no values would refuse one and admit the other. undefined is the type to write for a function that returns the value undefined and whose caller may hold it (1.5.17).

    1.5.17 The null and undefined Types

    null is the type whose one value is null. It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: primitive, [[Name]]: "null", [[Arguments]]: « » }, and it is written with the PredefinedType null.

    undefined is the type whose one value is undefined. It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: primitive, [[Name]]: "undefined", [[Arguments]]: « » }, and it is written with the PredefinedType undefined. It is distinct from the void type: void is the type with no values, written to say that a result must not be depended on, whereas undefined has the one value undefined and a binding may hold it.

    Note

    These are the types 1.7.1.1 reports for null and undefined. The reject type of a typed promise is undefined by convention when the promise never rejects, which is one place the undefined type is written directly; another is a union such as uint32 | undefined for a value that may be absent, the position an erased system reaches with an optional. null and undefined are ordinary members of the type universe and may appear in a union, an intersection, or any other type position.

    Resolving the undefined type name to void looks like it keeps the name and RuntimeTypeOf in agreement, and an implementation of this specification did so. They agree on a type with no values, so undefined is not a value of the type its own RuntimeTypeOf reports, and with it every uint32 | undefined becomes a union no value can inhabit. The agreement to keep is at the undefined type: RuntimeTypeOf(undefined) is undefined, the name denotes that same type, and void remains a return type that no binding may hold.

    1.5.18 The never Type

    never is the type with no values: the union of no members, described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « » }. It is not a new kind of type; it is the empty case of a kind the type system already has, admitted as a type in its own right because computation reaches it regardless. A union filtered of its every member is this type, whatever this clause says.

    Expression-position access to it is the type operator, type never, as it is for every other type name (1.5.27). No separate name is provided for it: a Reflect.never beside the general bridge would be a second spelling of one value, with nothing to say when to prefer which, and the construction it saves - Reflect.makeType({ [[Kind]]: ~union~, [[Members]]: « » }) - is equally reachable through the operator.

    Its algebra follows from the operations already defined, with no rule specific to it except the one noted last.

    • never is a subtype of every type. In IsSubtype (1.2.3.1) a source of the union kind is a subtype when every member is, and a quantification over no members holds.
    • No type other than never is a subtype of never. A target of the union kind requires some member to accept the source, and there is none.
    • never is the identity of union. Canonicalization (1.2.2.8) flattens a member of the same kind into its parent, and flattening an empty union contributes no members, so T | never canonicalizes to T with no rule naming the case.
    • never annihilates intersection: an intersection with a never member is never. This is the one fact that does not fall out, and CanonicalizeType carries the step for it.
    • An intersection two of whose members are disjoint (1.2.2.6) is never, which is the general case of the preceding: a never member is disjoint from every member, itself included. CanonicalizeType carries this step too, so number & bigint, uint8 & string, and 'a' & 'b' are all this one type. A program that WRITES such an intersection is reported at the annotation rather than left to discover it downstream (1.4.2.1).

    No value is a value of the never type: IsOfType (1.7.2.1) over a union with no members is false for every value, and DefaultValueOf (1.8.3.1) of it is none, so a binding of the type can be neither defaulted nor, since no expression's value can satisfy it, initialized. A value of the any type reaching a position of the never type fails its boundary check (1.7.3.1) for every value. That vacuity is the point: never exists to be computed with, as the result of removing every member from a union, not to be inhabited.

    Note

    Because the empty union canonicalizes to itself and Type Objects are interned (1.2.2.9), every computation that produces the empty union produces one Type Object, so never has the same identity story as every other type. The name is admitted through 1.5.27 on the same terms as every other built-in type name, so let x: never; is writable, and the name is shadowable exactly as uint8 is. Admitting it does not extend switch exhaustiveness, which remains reserved to enums and sealed hierarchies (1.11.9). It is also distinct from the empty sentinel of the narrowing operations (1.8.5), which reports a test that cannot succeed as a mistake rather than narrowing to the type with no values.

    1.5.19 Literal Types

    A literal type has exactly one value. It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: literal, [[Value]]: v, [[Base]]: b }, where v is a String, Number, Boolean, BigInt, or Symbol and b is the Type Record of the existing language type of which v is a value. A LiteralType (1.4.2) denotes the literal type of the value it writes: a StringLiteral with base string, a NumericLiteral with base number or bigint as the literal is written, and true or false with base boolean. Infinity and NaN are Numbers that are written with a name rather than a numeral, and a LiteralType may write either, negated or not: Table 43 admits any Number as a metadata value and says that a NaN is equivalent to a NaN, so a meta type whose constraint is a bound could otherwise not state its own default in a parameterization. A Symbol has no literal syntax, so no LiteralType writes a symbol literal type: one arises through construction (1.12.4) or through keyof over a symbol-keyed object type (1.4.2.5), and a program names it with an ordinary binding.

    The one value of a literal type is a value of its base, so the type is a subtype of its base (1.2.3.1), 'on' is usable where a string is required, and a value is of a literal type exactly when it is that value. A union of literal types is the closed set the design's discriminated unions select on, and keyof produces one (1.4.2.5). boolean and true | false have the same values and are distinct types: true | false is a subtype of boolean through the literal rule, and boolean is deliberately not a subtype of the pair, because completing the relation over value-set equality is the road to deciding language equivalence, which the pattern judgment already declines.

    A literal expression whose contextual type (1.6.5) is a literal type, or a union or intersection with a literal type among its members, takes the literal type of its own value where that literal type is assignable to the contextual type, so let a: 'on' | 'off' = 'on'; gives a the literal type 'on'. A contextual type of any other shape leaves the literal to the rules already given for untyped literals, so let s: string = 'on'; still gives s a string and let x: uint8 = 5; is unchanged.

    Note

    The base of a numeric literal is number however the literal will be used, matching the Static Type a literal takes with no contextual type; a literal type over another numeric type, the uint8 3 as a type, is expressible through construction but not through syntax, and its interaction with literal propagation is settled where it was needed: a : constraint naming a value type gives a literal argument the literal type over that base, the contextual rule above extended to the constraint's context, so W: uint32 binds the literal type of 4 over uint32 with 4 as its value view, and propagation elsewhere keeps base number. A Symbol is a literal type's value like any other, compared by SameValue, which for a Symbol is identity, so a symbol's identity is already its type's identity and the unique symbol of an erased system has nothing left to do. Any Symbol qualifies, well-known, registered, or freshly created, and no declaration form distinguishes them because none is needed. A symbol literal type is reproducible outside its Agent exactly when its Symbol is: one from Symbol.for names itself by its key, while one from Symbol is Agent-local, so a type carrying it cannot be shared, and the extension that shares types across Agents reports that rather than inventing an identity (Table 39).

    1.5.20 Parameterized Types

    A metadata parameterization refines a base type with a metadata value: the Type Record { [[Kind]]: parameterized, [[Base]]: b, [[Metadata]]: m }. Over a primitive base it is written float32.<{ m: 1 }>; over any base it is reachable through construction (1.12.4), so an object, class, or function type may carry a brand or a pattern. A width or lane argument such as the N of int.<N> is not a parameterization: structural arguments live in a primitive Record's [[Arguments]], and metadata rides this wrapper.

    A parameterized type has exactly the representation of its [[Base]]. Metadata never changes layout, alignment, or size.

    A metadata record is the value of [[Metadata]]: a record whose keys are meta keys claimed by meta types (6.1), and whose values are each either a leaf — an ECMAScript language value, such as a brand's tag — or another metadata record, such as the structural form a pattern or a range takes (Table 43). Two metadata records are the same when their keys are the same and, for each key, their values are the same leaf or the same record, however either record was constructed: one written in source, one built by 1.12.4, and one read back from a reflected node are indistinguishable if they describe the same metadata. That sameness is what interning uses, so it is what decides whether two parameterizations are one type.

    The default relation is the branding rule. A parameterized type is a subtype of its base, so the brand is shed freely on the way up; the base is not a subtype of the parameterization, so the way down is a crossing: calling the Type Object, as UserId(7), is the construction boundary, and the metadata's validation judgment runs there where one is defined. Two parameterizations of one base with structurally equivalent metadata are one type by interning; two with different metadata are related only as the metadata subtype judgment admits. A metadata value's fields are governed by the meta types that claim them, which supply that judgment and the validation judgment below, and which are required to be pure, compile-time evaluable, and deterministic; 6 defines them all.

    A TypeArguments following a PostfixType supplies TYPE ARGUMENTS when the type it follows declares type parameters, and is a METADATA RECORD otherwise. A TypeArguments whose TypeArgumentList is empty supplies no argument, so every parameter takes its TypeParameterDefault; it is a type error where a parameter has none, and the error names that parameter. Supplying more arguments than the base declares is likewise a type error against the parameter list. Where the TypeArguments is a metadata record, it is a type error for its TypeArgumentList to be empty, since .<> after a type that declares no type parameters supplies neither an argument nor a record, and for an argument of it to denote a type other than an object type, since a type is not a metadata value (Table 43): P.<uint8> for such a P names no metadata. A base-form meta type receives a leaf, as uint8.<7> does (6.2); a class or an interface, which no base-form meta type governs, takes exactly one argument, and it denotes an object type. Whether the record's keys are claimed is decided by 6.2 whatever names the base, a class or an interface as much as a primitive or an alias.

    The same rule reaches every parameter no written argument supplies, in three spellings that are therefore one type: a trailing position left empty, so Grid.<8> for a Grid<Rows: uint32 = 4, Cols: uint32 = 4> is Grid.<8, 4>; the empty list A.<>; and the BARE NAME of a generic declaration in a type position — an annotation, a parameter or return type, a heritage clause, a concrete generic bound, the operand of is or a when pattern, a type expression — so A for a class A<T: type = uint8> is A.<uint8>, and Box for a class Box<T: type> is a type error naming T. A bare generic name denotes its declaration rather than an application in one position only: as an argument whose receiving parameter explicitly requires a higher-kinded declaration (4.12), and where an argument that is not such a declaration is refused by that clause. In expression position the name evaluates to the constructor, which stands for the declaration wherever a declaration is a value, as in the base of a generic node (1.12.4).

    Note 1

    There is no bare instantiation for a bare name to denote. A construction of a generic class yields a specialization (4.8), so a type that admitted only instances of the unapplied declaration would admit nothing; and a name that meant the family would make a default meaningless in a type position, since let a: A = new A.<uint32>(1) would then be accepted for a class whose author wrote T = uint8. The family has a spelling of its own: an argument written any admits any instantiation in its position (1.15.6), so Box.<any> is a Box of some element type, and Pair.<any, string> a Pair of some first type and a string second.

     Note 2

    The argument's own form cannot decide this, and no rule reading it can. A metadata record is WRITTEN AS AN OBJECT TYPE, so Box.<{ a: uint8 }> is the same text whether { a: uint8 } is a type being supplied to a parameter or a record refining a base — the collision is total rather than partial. A rule keyed on the argument makes every generic applied to one object type unreachable, and is arity-dependent besides: two object arguments cannot be one record, so Pair.<{a}, {b}> would read as an application while Box.<{a}> would not.

    Deciding by the declaration is what this specification already does for the two neighbouring ambiguities in this same bracket. Whether an argument is a type or a VALUE is not read off the argument — "the syntax need not distinguish the two; the clause on generics decides which a given parameter expects" (1.4.2.2) — and which parameter a NAMED argument supplies is decided against "a TypeParameter of the type or function being applied". This is that rule, applied to the one case it had not been.

    Where the base is a type parameter the reading cannot be decided where it is written, since it depends on what the parameter is bound to; it is DEFERRED with the application and decided at instantiation. So type F<T: type> = T.<{ brand: 'B' }> is a declaration, and F.<string> is string.<{ brand: 'B' }>. A reading that dropped the arguments instead would make the brand its own base, which 1.5.20 describes as the worst shape a brand can fail in.

    A form that takes TypeArguments WITHOUT declaring parameters is unaffected, because it does not reach this rule: an ArrayOrTupleType such as [4].<uint8> carries its arguments in its own production.

    A parameterization applies to any PostfixType and composes with itself and with an indexed access in EITHER ORDER: T.<_A_>.<_B_> refines a parameterized type, O["a"].<_A_> parameterizes an indexed access, and T.<_A_>["a"] reads an index of a parameterized one. Attaching arguments only to a TypeName would make the rule turn on whether a type had been NAMED — an array, a generic application, an indexed access, a parenthesized type and a function type each denote an ordinary type, and each could be parameterized the moment it was bound to a name. Each spelling denotes the same type its named form does.

    A value is of a parameterized type when its runtime type is that type or a subtype of it, or when it is a value of the [[Base]] and the validation judgment holds of the value and the metadata (6). A brand, whose meta type defines no validation, therefore admits no bare value of its base except through the construction boundary, which is the point of a brand. That admission rests on the first limb above, and so on the value having a discoverable runtime type: a Number carries its Type Record, and so do an object and an array, while a String, a Boolean and a BigInt do not. On a String the value carries the parameterization as it does a literal string type, so a brand there behaves as one on a Number does. A BigInt carries one likewise. A Boolean does not: true and false are single values, so a Boolean that carried a mark would not be those values, and on a Boolean a brand is checked where it is DECLARED and cannot be recognised from a value in hand, so an implementation must discharge the boundary statically where it can prove the value's type — the check it would insert can never pass otherwise, and a brand on such a base would be declarable and uninhabitable. An object or an array carries one as a MARK ON THE VALUE, the way an array's element type travels with it: their runtime type is otherwise derived from the shape, and two structurally identical object types are one answer to 1.7.1.1, so a brand — which is deliberately not structural — is recorded rather than inferred, and the mark is read in preference to the derived answer. A brand so recorded survives a mutation of the value, which is correct: a brand records PROVENANCE, where a judgment that VALIDATES records a predicate and is therefore re-run at every boundary. A class instance is nominal and mutable in exactly the same way. The two readings of that absence are deliberate and opposite: the MEMBERSHIP test reads "defines no validate" as admitting nothing, and the CONSTRUCTION BOUNDARY reads it as having no judgment to run. So UserId(7) produces a value and let x: UserId = 7 is refused, and a pattern - which does define a judgment - is decided by that judgment at both. An implementation that applies the membership test at the boundary makes a brand a type nothing can inhabit; one that skips it at an annotation makes a brand a claim the language does not check.

    Note 3

    A parameterization is shed at a BOUNDARY and preserved through an OPERATOR, and the two are different questions. A boundary — an argument, an annotation, a return — is where a declared type says what is wanted, and that is what "shed freely on the way up" governs: UserId is assignable to uint32, so passing one where the base is declared succeeds and the brand is gone. An operator is arithmetic WITHIN a type: UserId + UserId is a UserId, and UserId + uint32 is a type error. Were the brand shed at the operator instead, those two expressions would produce the same type and the operator would erase exactly the distinction the brand was introduced to draw; a caller who wants the base writes the conversion.

    RuntimeTypeOf reports the parameterization, not the base, WHERE THE VALUE CARRIES ITS TYPE — a Number, an object and an array do; a String, a Boolean and a BigInt do not, and on those it reports the base, there being nothing else to read, and 1.7.1.1 reports what a value IS. It follows that a branded value is not the same value as its base — UserId(7) is not 7 — while carrying no wrapper: typeof answers as the base does, and an array of them has the base's footprint. The saving is representational, not identity.

    Parameterizing an already-parameterized type NESTS: the outer parameterization's [[Base]] is the inner type, and each layer's metadata is its own. So T.<{ brand: a }>.<{ brand: b }> is a third type refining the second, both judgments run at a crossing, and a brand composes with a pattern on the same value. A parameterization written with several keys at once merges them into one portion, which is the same type by 1.2.2.1.

    A union naming both a parameterization and its base is the base: a parameterization is assignable to what it refines, and a union drops a member a preceding one is a supertype of. So UserId | uint32 is uint32 and admits any uint32, which is rarely what the writer meant. Two parameterizations of one base do not collapse, neither being assignable to the other.

    The StringPattern meta type carries a pattern as metadata, a source and flags rather than a RegExp object, so that one pattern written in two modules is one type; a hook that reads it is handed a RegExp built from those. Its validation judgment holds of a String exactly when the entire String matches the pattern, the whole-string discipline 1.13.5 already uses; its subtype judgment holds only of patterns whose source and flags are identical, which structural equivalence already makes one type, so the floor is reflexivity and the conservatism is intentional. No template-literal type kind exists or is planned: a finite string family is ordinary code over a union of literal types, and an infinite one is a pattern.

    Note 4

    Interning is what makes a brand a real newtype: brand(uint32, 'UserId') written in two modules is one type with no registry, because the metadata compares structurally and GetTypeObject does the rest. The brand is not a lie told to the checker, as an intersection with a phantom symbol is in an erased system: the parameterization is visible to reflection, participates in validation, and can carry conversion semantics when the brand is a unit rather than a tag. Builders still cannot mint a nominal type, a class, an enum, or a sealed hierarchy, and this clause is why they do not need to: the thing nominal minting is wanted for is a brand.

    The sanctioned sharpening of the pattern subtype judgment is the design's decision procedure over the regular fragment: pattern pairs free of backreferences and lookaround, within a fixed automaton size, get the exact language-inclusion answer, and pairs beyond the bound get the syntactic one. The tier is decided by syntactic size and never by remaining fuel, so the judgment is identical on every host, the same invariant 1.2.7.4 enforces; the size constant is among the design's open budget numbers. A parameterized field with no initializer takes the base's default where validation admits it or none is defined, and has none otherwise; whether a brand should instead always demand an initializer is a policy its meta type states by defining validation.

    1.5.21 The type Type

    type is the type whose values are the Type Objects (1.2.1). It is described by the Type Record { [[Kind]]: primitive, [[Name]]: "type", [[Arguments]]: « » }, and it is the Static Type of a type name or type expression in expression position (1.2.6). A function that computes a type annotates its return with it.

    Note

    type is not a value type: its values are Objects, and they have identity. That identity is exactly what interning fixes, so two occurrences of a type expression that denote the same type are the same Type Object rather than merely equal ones. type is nonetheless a primitive type in the sense of the Type Record kinds, since it is a named type of the language rather than a structural description of an object's members.

    Because type is itself a type, type is a value of type, and a type argument may be constrained to it, which is what a generic parameter written T: type asks for. 1.12 defines what a Type Object exposes.

    1.5.22 The Existing Language Types

    The names number, boolean, string, symbol, object, and bigint denote the existing ECMAScript language types of 6.1: the Number type, the Boolean type, the String type, the Symbol type, the Object type, and the BigInt type respectively. This proposal adds no values to any of them.

    Each is described by a Type Record whose [[Kind]] is primitive and whose [[Name]] is the name above, except object, which is described by { [[Kind]]: object, [[Properties]]: « » }, the object type with no required properties, to which every Object is assignable.

    Note

    number is a value type like the rest, so no other numeric type is assignable to it and it is assignable to no other numeric type. It is nonetheless the type an untyped program computes with, and the type a numeric literal takes in the absence of a contextual type (1.2.6), which is why an unannotated program continues to mean what it means today.

    1.5.23 Numeric Types

    The specification already treats a numeric type as a set of values together with a fixed table of abstract operations over them, and defines Number and BigInt that way in 6.1.6. Each integer, binary floating-point, decimal floating-point, rational, complex, and vector type is a numeric type in that sense, and provides the operations of that table for which it is defined.

    For a numeric type T, the operations are those named in 6.1.6: T::unaryMinus, T::bitwiseNOT, T::exponentiate, T::multiply, T::divide, T::remainder, T::add, T::subtract, T::leftShift, T::signedRightShift, T::unsignedRightShift, T::lessThan, T::equal, T::sameValue, T::sameValueZero, T::bitwiseAND, T::bitwiseXOR, T::bitwiseOR, and T::toString. A numeric type need not define every operation; one it does not define is not applicable to its values, and an operator that would use it is a type error. The definitions are given by 1.9 and 1.13.

    Note

    Reusing this table rather than introducing a parallel one is what lets the existing operator semantics carry over unchanged. The specification generalized these operations from Number to two types when BigInt was added, and the shape it arrived at, an operator dispatching on the numeric type of its operands with no implicit conversion between types, is the shape this proposal needs. What this clause adds is more numeric types, not a new mechanism.

    The table was written for types that are closed under their operations and totally ordered, and not every type here is either. A complex type has no lessThan, since the complex numbers are not ordered. A vector type's comparisons return a vector of lane results rather than a Boolean, which is why the SIMD extension gives them their own return type rather than reusing lessThan. A rational type's operations can fail where a float's would round. These are the cases 1.9.3 settles, and they are the reason the table above is a list of what may be defined rather than what must be.

    Values of two different numeric types are never === and never the same value, as a Number and a BigInt are not; == compares their mathematical values, as 1 == 1n does. Within one type, each type's own sameValue and equal rules hold.

    1.5.24 Typed Promise Executors

    For a proved intrinsic construction participating through declared type arguments or a typed executor operand, check the executor's callability independently of recognizing its inline function syntax. A known non-callable executor is a type error. Its incompatibility must not defeat an otherwise established constructor-origin proof. Unknown values retain runtime checking, and ordinary untyped Promise construction retains its base-language exception timing.

    For an established intrinsic Promise.<R, E> construction, complete omitted type arguments by 1.5.25. The executor receives a resolving function and a rejecting function, both returning void. The rejecting function accepts a value of E. The resolving function accepts either a direct value of R, an intrinsic Promise, or a structural thenable whose callable then can receive the two ordinary resolving callbacks. For R equal to void, the direct no-value input is undefined. Resolution does not require the thenable object itself to be of R: assimilation precedes the result boundary.

    The intrinsic constructor's executor parameter supplies this function type as a contextual type. Unannotated executor parameters adopt it; explicit annotations are checked through the ordinary function relation. A known incompatible direct argument or executor parameter is a type error before execution, including within an unused body. The structural thenable input may be represented by a readonly then member of function type (any, any) => any; its normal return is ignored. This does not infer arbitrary thenable results, and an unknown assimilation path retains its runtime checks.

    Apply the static intrinsic rule only where lexical resolution, the actual intrinsic data binding and a bounded effect analysis establish the constructor origin. A shadowed or replaced constructor retains its own contract. The origin proof may recognize a direct intrinsic construction with a locally supplied executor and scalar resolving/rejecting calls that introduce no unknown user effects; it must defer where user code, an accessor, a thenable or a dynamic lookup may replace the constructor before the selected construction. No executor or thenable executes during checking.

    At an actual intrinsic construction with declared type arguments, record R and E before calling the executor and adopt its callback context through the ordinary function boundary. These are internal type records, not observable properties or changes to the Promise's prototype. An eventual direct fulfillment value, after thenable assimilation, passes through the ordinary R boundary before fulfillment. A supplied rejection reason passes through the E boundary before rejection. An R of void admits fulfillment with undefined.

    If a fulfillment or rejection boundary fails, reject the Promise with that boundary's exception, without checking the exception recursively against E. This is a failed type contract, not a successful fulfillment or a new application rejection payload. Existing intrinsic exceptions, such as self-resolution and a throwing then getter, retain ordinary Promise rejection behaviour. Preserve single settlement, thenable scheduling, eager executor invocation, and all reference-liveness checks. Untyped construction retains the base language's behaviour. Reflection on an explicitly typed intrinsic construction retains its completed type arguments.

    1.5.25 Intrinsic Type Parameters and Defaults

    Lexical declarations and bound parameters are resolved before an intrinsic declaration of the same spelling. In an ordinary concrete type position a bare name and an empty application bind declared defaults, in declaration order, just as an explicit application does. Missing required arguments, unknown labels, duplicate arguments, a positional argument following a named one, excess arguments, and inadmissible domains are type errors at the application, including in an unused body. Defaults and canonical value arguments are completed before canonicalization or interning; an explicit default is never erased from a closed application's [[Arguments]].

    All existing element, component, lane, and layout restrictions still apply. The intrinsic width-or-bigint domain is not a user-declared mixed type/value domain. rational.<int32> is invalid. rational64 and rational.<64> have identical complete arguments and are the same Type Object. complex, complex.<>, and complex.<number> likewise have identical complete arguments.

    Where a receiving parameter explicitly expects a higher-kinded declaration, resolve the declaration without applying its defaults. Intrinsic declarations participate in this context with their stated arity; application of a bound declaration validates its intrinsic domains. This does not introduce a public family-value API. Injected class names and user-class constructor inference retain their existing rules. Intrinsic numeric construction supplies no new inference: an explicit application or a declared concrete default determines its type.

    Range literals retain their existing contextual endpoint rules and metadata's host-base normalization. Requiring an element argument in a concrete range annotation introduces neither a default element type nor a new runtime representation for an endpoint-free literal. A written full range and a full-range metadata default obey the same complete RangeBounds.<T> shape; neither satisfies a two-ended Range.<T> shape.

    Canonical display uses the standard aliases rational8, rational16, rational32, rational64, and rational128; other rational arguments use the explicit family application. Complex display uses complex for the declared default and the standard component-width aliases where defined. User aliases and module order do not affect this choice.

    1.5.26 Anonymous Family Constraints

    Within an argument position in a type parameter's constraint, the bare identifier _ is an anonymous wildcard matching one argument admitted by that parameter's domain. Each written wildcard is independent and declares no source-visible binding. This reading does not apply to storage types or arbitrary type expressions. Omitted positions retain their declaration defaults, including dependent defaults, and missing required positions remain errors. Thus Pair.<_> for Pair<T: type, U: type = T> requires equality, whereas Pair.<_, _> does not.

    A Family Constraint Record contains an application head identifying an intrinsic or nominal declaration and ordered argument entries. An entry is fixed, a wildcard with a private identity, a nested application, or an omitted declaration-default computation retaining its declaration context and earlier argument bindings. Normalization may reduce a default to a fixed entry or a correlated occurrence of an earlier wildcard. Transparent forwarding aliases expand to these entries and preserve repeated parameters. A fixed any entry is the exact type any; the ordinary concrete A.<any> view is unchanged.

    Supported heads are intrinsic families, nominal class or library declarations, and forwarding aliases expanding to those applications using fixed arguments and direct parameter references. Structural-interface existential patterns, computed-alias inversion, named captures in constraints, wildcard packs, and applications of variadic heads are type errors in this version. Ordinary concrete structural constraints remain valid. Intrinsic RangeBounds is supported by the declared range-shape relationship.

    A matching witness is the candidate's canonical application or one of its nominal ancestor applications with substituted arguments. A range shape additionally supplies its RangeBounds application with the same element argument. Metadata wrappers may be examined through their base to find a witness; this examination never alters the original candidate, its metadata, or the type bound to the parameter. A union satisfies a pattern only if every arm does. No conversion or enumeration of possible arguments is performed.

    Match a witness and pattern recursively. Heads must identify the same declaration and have the same completed arity. A fixed argument must be the same canonical type or value as its candidate argument. A wildcard admits a candidate argument of its declared domain; another occurrence of that wildcard requires the same argument. After preceding bindings are available, evaluate each omitted default forward in its declaration context and compare its result with that argument. This evaluation uses 1.2.7.4; failure or exhaustion aborts checking and is never a mismatch permitting overload fallback.

    Specificity is proven inclusion. Treat a source pattern's independent wildcards as opaque arguments and prove that every such binding satisfies the target pattern. Fixed arguments, supported equality correlations, and established nominal ancestry may establish inclusion. A user computation with an unknown result supplies no inclusion proof. Applicable candidates remaining incomparable under the ordinary selection rules are ambiguous, independently of declaration order. Static checking defers a candidate whose default computation cannot yet be evaluated to the ordinary binding check; it does not assume an inclusion fact. A bound neither permits mixed-width arithmetic nor changes invariant reference location types or liveness.

    1.5.26.1 SatisfiesTypeConstraint ( candidate, constraint )

    The abstract operation SatisfiesTypeConstraint takes arguments candidate (a Type Record) and constraint (a Type Record or a Family Constraint Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It checks a generic argument without converting it or changing its identity. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If constraint is a Type Record, return IsAssignable(candidate, constraint).
    2. If candidate.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element member of candidate.[[Members]], do
        1. If ? SatisfiesTypeConstraint(member, constraint) is false, return false.
      2. Return true.
    3. Let witnesses be the canonical applications supplied by candidate as defined above.
    4. For each element witness of witnesses, do
      1. Let matches be ? the result of recursively matching witness against constraint as defined above, with a new empty set of wildcard bindings.
      2. If matches is true, return true.
    5. Return false.

    1.5.27 Type Names

    A built-in constructor is a type name where its family has no other spelling: Promise, Date, RegExp, Map, Set, Error, WeakMap, WeakSet, Symbol, Proxy, ArrayBuffer and DataView all name types. Seven do not, and in each case the language already denotes that family another way. String, Boolean, Number and BigInt are excluded because the lowercase name IS the type. Array, Object and Function are excluded because the family has a structural spelling — [].<T>, { … } and (…) => T — and each of those spellings also provides the family's bound, which a bare name could not: a name gives only the top of the family, where the structural form composes.

    Each type of this clause is denoted by a name. The intrinsic generic names denote types after required arguments and declared defaults have been bound (1.5.25). complex declares the default T = number; rational declares no default. The remaining names in Table 12 are shorthands, each denoting the same Type Record as its expansion and therefore, after interning, the same Type Object.

    Note 1

    The shorthands are aliases, not distinct types, so int8 === int.<8> is true and a value of one is a value of the other. complex expands through number rather than float64, so complex and complex128 are distinct types, as number and float64 are.

     Note 2

    How these names are bound is not settled by the design and is not settled here. Every other part of this proposal is gated by syntax that is an error today, which is the argument that no existing program changes meaning. Type names are not: they are ordinary identifiers, and number, string, object, boolean, symbol, any, and never are among the most common identifiers in existing code. The available answers each cost something, and this specification decides for the one that costs existing programs nothing: the type names resolve, in either position, through the ordinary scope chain first and through the built-in table only where no user binding of the name exists; in a TYPE position always, and in an EXPRESSION position only within a source text that admits type names. A scope that shadows a name loses the short spelling there and writes the type operator form, const T = type uint8;, which is available everywhere and is the only spelling in a source text that does not admit them. So no existing use, assignment, shadowing, or typeof probe of these names changes meaning, because no existing source text admits them; and where one does, its author wrote the syntax that says so. This is the convenience the committee was told could be traded back in later, taken without trading the compatibility away first; a future edition may widen what admits, and could not have narrowed it.

    Resolution finds a name; what it finds must BE a type. A binding that holds an ordinary value is not one, however exactly that value's type is known, so const q: uint8 = 1; let v: q = 2; is a TypeError rather than an annotation meaning uint.<8>. The two spellings that say what such a program meant are already available: const T = type uint8; names the type, and Reflect.typeOf(q) (1.12.1) queries the value's. Both are explicit about which of the two is intended, which an unadorned q cannot be in a language where a name may hold either.

    Note 3

    The error differs from the one an unknown name gets, and the difference is the useful part. Tokne is bound by nothing, so resolution walks the scope chain, finds nothing, and reports a ReferenceError as it would for any unbound name. q IS bound; it simply does not denote a type, which is a TypeError. A reader who mistyped a name and a reader who reached for a value are told different things because they made different mistakes.

    A Script or Module admits type names when its source text contains either a production this proposal adds — an annotation, a type operator, a conversion, an is, a type parameter list, or any other syntax that is an error without this proposal — or an IdentifierReference to one of the built-in type names this clause governs, in any position OTHER than the operand of typeof and the target of an assignment. A reference that is the target of an assignment also does not RESOLVE to a type name, even where the text admits for some other reason: it resolves as it would without this proposal, so a sloppy-mode assignment to such a name creates the global it creates today rather than reaching an immutable binding. The operand of typeof is excepted from admitting only, and resolves like any other reference where the text admits. It is a property of the SOURCE TEXT, determined when the text is parsed and fixed for its lifetime; it is not a property of the realm, and it is not established by anything that happens while the text runs.

    Note 4

    Both halves of that are load-bearing. It is per source text because a realm holds many: a page that loads one typed module beside a hundred untyped scripts must leave the hundred alone, and a realm-wide answer would change typeof string in every one of them — the outcome this clause exists to prevent, reached by the mechanism meant to prevent it. And it is fixed at parse because a text that became admitting partway through its own execution would answer typeof string as "undefined" on one line and "object" on a later one, with a call in between as the only difference. A call written in a branch that never runs still admits, for the same reason: what a name means may not depend on control flow.

    The second clause is stated as an exception rather than as a list of admitting positions, because a list is a losing game: the names are reached as a call, as the object of a member access, as an argument, as a property value, and as an operand of a comparison, and each is the same use of the same name. The exception is short and it is decidable, and it costs nothing that was not already lost. Referencing an undeclared identifier is a ReferenceError today in every position but two: typeof reports "undefined" rather than throwing, and a sloppy-mode assignment creates a global. So a source text that reaches one of these names in any OTHER position was already broken before this proposal, and admitting on it cannot change the meaning of a program that worked. The two exceptions are exactly the idioms this clause's compatibility sentence names.

    The assignment exception governs RESOLUTION as well as admitting, and that second half is what makes the first half worth anything. A text that reads one of these names anywhere admits, so a script that creates an implicit global - string = 5; with no declaration - and then reads it would otherwise have its assignment reach the type name instead of the global, and fail against an immutable binding. The assignment must land where it lands today. var string = 5 was never at risk, because a declaration is found by the ordinary scope walk before a type name ever is. The typeof exception needs no such half: a text that does not admit has nothing bound for the probe to find, which is the whole of what existing code requires, and a text that DOES admit has opted in, so reporting "object" there is what its author asked for.

    What the exception buys is the reason it is needed at all: decimal128("1.0"), float32x4(1, 2, 3, 4) and complex64(1, 2) are how those values are CREATED, uint64.byteLength and decimal128.parse reach a type name as an object, and a program computing with any of them may write no annotation anywhere. Without the clause each would fail on the one name it needs. It is also what makes this specification's own examples consistent with the rule: uint8(1) + uint16(1) and uint8(1) == uint16(1) (1.9.1.1) are written as bare references to type names, and a text containing them admits by this clause alone.

    Two hosts need the rule stated rather than inferred. Code passed to eval or the Function constructor is a source text of its own and admits on its own terms; a direct eval ALSO admits where the text it runs inside does, so a name reached inside it resolves as it would just outside it. An indirect eval and the Function constructor take only their own, since there is no enclosing text they run inside. A console or REPL that evaluates each entry as its own Script carries the state across the entries of one session, so a name declared in an earlier entry keeps its meaning in a later one; a host that did otherwise would have uint8 resolve on one line and not the next.

    Binding them as properties of the global object is what the language does for every constructor it has added, and it keeps var string = "x" working, since a var at global scope reuses an existing property. But the design also asks that these names cannot be reassigned, and a non-writable global property would make that same assignment throw in strict mode and fail silently outside it, so the two requirements cannot both hold. Binding them as immutable lexical declarations of the global scope satisfies the design but makes var string at the top level of an existing script a SyntaxError, which is not acceptable. Requiring them to be imported, which earlier drafts of the design assumed, has no compatibility cost at all and gives up the ambient spelling the rest of the document uses. Resolving them in type position only, as a language with separate type and value namespaces would, is compatible but contradicts types being values, since the same name must denote the type in expression position for reflection to work.

    This is the one place where the proposal's compatibility argument does not reach, and it deserves a decision and a web-compatibility analysis before Stage 2.

    The rule is EVERY name this specification binds as a type, not only the primitives: the intrinsic metadata interfaces of 7.15 resolve the same way, and a partial declaration over one reaches it in type position rather than through an expression-scope binding. Stating it here once is deliberate.
