An implementation that binds these names in expression scope UNCONDITIONALLY, rather than only where the source text admits them, satisfies neither this clause nor its argument - typeof string answers "object" rather than "undefined" in a text that never mentioned a type, an existing var string = 5 does not take effect, and in strict code it throws - and the breakage falls on number, string, and object, which are the names this clause exists to protect. typeof itself is not touched by any of this (1.7.1.1): it reports what its operand resolved to, and what varies is whether the operand resolves to anything.

    1.6 Conversions

    This clause defines when a value of one type becomes a value of another. The governing rule is that it does not: a value of one value type never implicitly becomes a value of another, and every conversion between two distinct value types is written in the source text. This clause states that rule, defines the four things that remain implicit and are not conversions between two typed values, and specifies the explicit conversion that a program writes when it wants one.

    Note

    The rule exists because no widening is lossless for every pair. int64 to float64 loses precision above 2**53, and a language that admits the easy cases has to enumerate the hard ones anyway. Refusing all of them is the rule Rust, Swift, and Go use. It is livable here for the same reason it is livable there: the initializers and arguments that would want a conversion are usually literals, and a literal never needs one (1.6.6).

    1.6.1 The Conversion Rule

    At an assignment, an argument, or a return, the source value's type must be assignable to the target type (1.2.3.2). Since a primitive type is a subtype only of itself and of the any type, no numeric value type is assignable to another, and a program that requires one to become another states the conversion.

    Four things remain implicit. None is a conversion between two typed values.

    1.6.2 Inferred Return Types

    A function whose signature declares no return type may still have one, inferred from what its body returns. The inferred type is then the function's return type for every purpose a declared one serves: it is the Static Type of a call, it is enforced when the function returns, and reflection reports it. What it is not is a second way to declare, and the whole of this clause is the answer to one question — which functions have one — because a rule that answered "all of them" would compute a type for every function in every program ever written, and one that answered "only annotated ones" would lose the type one call away from the annotation that established it.

    Override compatibility consumes published returns after inference has established them. A changed publication requires dependent comparisons to be reconsidered. An unpublished or explicitly any return remains unknown; return inference does not change the parameter-based identification of an override.

    1.6.2.1 Dependent Result Contracts

    A published inferred result can contain parameters bound by its function or by an enclosing generic declaration. Such a result is a symbolic contract in that declaration environment. Determine and use it as follows:

    1. During declaration checking, retain each parameter's binder and effective constraint. A completed symbolic input is not unfinished solely because no runtime type argument has been supplied. Apply the existing subtype and assignment judgments to that input; do not replace the parameter with its constraint or with any. A subtype constraint permits the relations it establishes, but does not identify the parameter with that constraint.
    2. Apply 1.6.2.14 to symbolic inputs as to other completed inputs. When the existing store rule preserves a scalar value's domain without conversion, retain its parameter-dependent domain through the store, subsequent captures and contribution queries. The destination's wider annotation does not replace the stored domain. Preserve all applicable effects, predecessor joins and binder identities.
    3. A nongeneric helper can return a parameter of an enclosing declaration. Establish its call-result contract in that enclosing environment; the helper needs no additional type argument. A completed symbolic result is usable by contribution inference even while its enclosing parameter remains uninstantiated. This does not exempt the call from the replacement judgment of 1.7.5.1.
    4. At a runtime return boundary, instantiate the published contract using the generic arguments of that function invocation and the bindings captured from its declaration environment. Lexically inner binders shadow outer binders; a same-spelled parameter in an unrelated caller supplies no binding. Apply the ordinary return conversion and enforcement to this instantiated contract. Apply the same instantiation when supplying a concise body's result context and the effective result contracts of resumable forms. Do not enforce an unresolved parameter as a closed type, waive an inferred boundary because its declaration was generic, or overwrite a shared declaration contract with one invocation's argument.
    5. Reflection and runtime callable compatibility use the published contract under the function value's captured generic bindings. A still-generic signature retains its own unbound parameters and constraints. Inspecting a closure after its creating call has returned, or from a caller with different generic arguments, does not change its captured contract. Completing or instantiating a type contract does not initialize a captured value or establish reference liveness.

    A returned generic signature introduces its own parameter declarations. Instantiating the enclosing result substitutes only parameters supplied by that enclosing environment, including free occurrences in the returned signature's parameter, result, receiver, narrowing, constraint and default descriptions. It does not apply the returned signature to arguments. A later application of that returned function binds its own parameters by BindTypeArguments. Declaration identities, rather than equal parameter spellings, distinguish the two operations; preserve the returned signature's parameter declarations and unevaluated default and constraint source environments. No signature application or default expression is executed merely to publish or reflect a result.

    Whenever inference resumes a declaration or one of its contributions, use the same generic environment that declaration checking established: parameter declaration identities, effective bounds, value-parameter domains, variadic collection contracts and enclosing bindings. Retaining names alone is insufficient. The resumed environment still contains symbolic parameters until an application supplies their arguments; do not replace a parameter by its upper bound. This requirement applies equally to ordinary, async, generator and async generator functions. Suspending or resuming an inference computation neither initializes a value binding nor establishes reference liveness.

    Note

    For example, both closures below retain their respective captured result types. The final expression evaluates to "1s", and each closure reflects the same result type as an otherwise identical function with the corresponding Number or String return annotation.

    function make<T: type>(x: T) {
  const captured = x;
  function produce() { return captured; }
  return produce;
}
const a = make(1);
const b = make("s");
const x: number = a();
const y: string = b();
String(x) + y;

    In a declaration function f<T: type extends string>(x: T) { let value: string | number = x; const captured = value; }, the stored scalar domain and the captured contract retain T. Its constraint makes it usable as String, but assigning an arbitrary String back to a position requiring T is not justified. Forward helper chains over this capture must complete under 1.6.2.14 before their consumers are finalized.

    1.6.2.2 Anchored Contributions and Participation

    A contribution of a function is what 1.6.3 defines: the Static Type of the operand of each return, or undefined where a return carries no value or the body can complete without one, with a return in a nested function literal belonging to that literal.

    A contribution that reads a LOCAL BINDING which cannot change is the type of that binding's initializer, widened as a contribution is. A binding cannot change when it is declared const, or declared let and never assigned within the function. A binding with a declared or inferred type contributes that type. For a binding that still has Static Type any, this contribution rule gives the binding no type for other purposes; in particular it does not infer a type for an unannotated let. Typed const inference is specified independently in 1.2.6.

    Note 1

    Without this rule, extracting a subexpression into a local — the most ordinary refactoring there is — silently removes a function's inferred return type. function f(x: number) { return g(); } publishes what g returns, and function f(x: number) { const v = g(); return v; } would publish nothing if the local lost its initializer's contribution. A typed const now preserves that information through its binding type as well; the contribution rule remains necessary for an unchanged unannotated let and for untyped constants. Nothing in the second program says that the type was lost.

    Reading THROUGH the binding rather than typing it is the same move 1.2.6 makes for a numeric constant, where propagation "decides which VALUE a use produces" and "infers no type for the binding, and adds none". A binding that cannot change is a name for its initializer's value, and a contribution asks what the function produces.

    The condition is that the binding cannot change, and not that it is const. A let never assigned is as transparent as a const; a let that IS assigned must contribute nothing, because a published type is enforced where the function returns (Table 23) — reading only the initializer of let v = g(); v = 5; return v; would publish the type of g's result and make a program that runs today throw at its own return.

    A contribution is anchored when its Static Type derives from a DECLARED type: a parameter's annotation, a binding's annotation, a field's annotation, a declared return type, or the inferred return type of a function that is itself participating. Anchoring follows the derivation of the value, not control dependence, so in return _flag_ ? 1 : 2 an annotation on flag anchors nothing: the contribution is the join of the arms, and the arms are literals.

    A function or arrow expression contributes its callable contract, not merely the fact that its syntax is a literal. Determine its declaration provenance under the same lexical and contextual environments that determine that contract:

    1. A known parameter, receiver or result position other than any, obtained from a written annotation or an adopted contextual signature, supplies declaration provenance. Preserve symbolic parameter identities and their enclosing substitutions as required by 1.6.2.1.
    2. A completed inferred result supplies provenance when the literal itself participates under this clause. A private contribution result that does not qualify for publication supplies none. For a generator or async generator, determine yield and completion contributions independently: an unknown component does not erase a known declaration-derived component. The existence of a Promise or generator carrier alone supplies no anchor.
    3. A generic parameter list alone, a known literal-only body result, or a signature whose only known positions are any does not supply an anchor. An annotation used only to choose control flow does not supply provenance to literal value-producing arms. An annotation elsewhere in a nested body contributes only through the ordinary derivation and participation rules.
    4. Retain the provenance of the particular contract computation through contribution dependencies. Equal function types need not have equal declaration provenance. Neither another query of the same source under a different context nor an unfinished inference answer establishes an anchor for this query.

    These rules do not execute a literal or its enclosing function, apply generic defaults, initialize a captured binding, or establish reference liveness. A literal's declarations and any published result still undergo the ordinary callable compatibility and runtime enforcement judgments.

    Note 2

    In function make() { return () => "ok"; }, the literal's privately known String result does not anchor make. In function make() { return (x: any) => "ok"; }, the literal participates by its annotated parameter and publishes its String result, which supplies provenance to make. An explicit any result instead remains unknown: function make() { return (): any => "ok"; } gains no anchor from that result.

    For a contribution that reads a binding, determine its type and its declaration provenance separately, as follows. Parentheses around the read do not affect either determination.

    1. Resolve the binding in the function's lexical environment. A local or parameter shadows an outer binding even if the local has no annotation, no initializer, an unresolved type, or the type any. The annotation of the shadowed binding supplies no evidence for this read.
    2. A binding with a known declared type other than any supplies an anchored contribution. This includes a literal type, null, and undefined. Having exactly one possible value does not erase the declaration from which the type derives. An inferred binding type preserves the declaration provenance of the initializer from which it was inferred.
    3. For an unannotated local whose unchanged initializer is read through under the preceding contribution rule, carry both that initializer's contribution type and its anchoring result. Widening the contribution changes its type, not its provenance. A literal-only initializer therefore remains unanchored when named by a local; a declaration-derived initializer retains its anchor.
    4. For a captured binding, use its declared or inferred binding contract. Do not import the enclosing evaluation's current-value narrowing into the function's published result merely because that narrowing holds where the declaration is encountered. The captured storage is read when the function executes. The contribution does not change the binding's permitted stores, capture mode, or reference-liveness requirements.
    Note 3

    In let s: string = "s"; function g() { return s; }, the annotation on s anchors g even when the surrounding flow knows the singleton value "s". In function g() { const s = "s"; return s; }, naming and widening the literal alone do not make g participate. In let s: string | number = "s"; function g() { return s; }, the captured contract contributes string | number; a later valid store of a Number cannot invalidate the published result.

    A conditional contribution derives its anchoring from its value-producing arms in their respective guarded environments. Joining or widening those arms does not create declaration provenance. A cycle of private, unanchored answers cannot make its declarations participate merely by reading one another: without an annotated signature or an independently anchored contribution, each result remains private. A participating external consumer may still ask for those private answers under the following rule.

    A function participates in inference when its signature declares a parameter type or a return type, or when at least one of its contributions is anchored. A participating function whose declared return type is absent has an inferred return type, which is the join of its contributions, and that type is published: it is recorded in the signature's [[InferredReturn]] field and is visible to every other clause. A join of the any type publishes nothing, since a function whose result is unknown is indistinguishable from one that never participated.

    A function that does not participate has no inferred return type and no [[InferredReturn]]; a call of it has the any Static Type, exactly as before. Its contributions are still computed where a participating function's inference asks for them, and the answer is used to type the ASKER without being published for the answerer: function g() { return 'foo'; } remains untyped at its own call sites even where a participating function returns g() and infers string from it.

    Note 4

    Annotations are therefore the only seed. A source text containing none computes no inference, publishes nothing, and is unchanged in every respect, which is the compatibility statement of this proposal made mechanical rather than argued. What annotations buy is reach: the type an annotation establishes travels as far through returns as the returns carry it, and stops where a body stops deriving from it.

    This is a position no shipped language occupies, and the neighbours are worth naming. Inferring for every function is what an erased checker does, and it is affordable there because nothing is enforced and no engine must do the work; here it would compute types for the whole existing web to no purpose. Inferring only where a signature is annotated is simpler still and loses the case that matters most in practice, the wrapper that returns what it called, so an annotation would stop being useful one call from where it was written.

    1.6.2.3 The Inference Fixpoint

    A contribution may be the return type of a function whose own inference is in progress, directly or through a cycle of calls. If that dependency has no provisional contribution result yet, its initial contribution is never. Otherwise use its most recent provisional contribution result, including a completed unknown join, and repeat inference until the required provisional results, participation and published types do not change. Because never is the identity of union (1.5.18), a cycle's initial contribution vanishes from a join that has any other member, so a function whose base case returns a uint32 publishes uint32 and one that only calls itself publishes never, which is what a function that never returns a value has.

    Distinguish an unfinished contribution, a known contribution (including never), and a completed unknown join. An unfinished prerequisite remains a dependency under 1.6.2.9; its absence is not a completed unknown result. Once a contribution computation completes, its result replaces the previous provisional result even when the new join is unknown. Re-entering that computation does not replace an already computed unknown join with the initial never seed. A change to a private provisional result also requires reconsideration of its dependent contributions; the absence of a published result does not make such a change irrelevant.

    Apply the participation and publication rules anew to the updated contribution result. A completed unknown join publishes no inferred result, and a contribution that no longer establishes participation supplies no inferred result merely because an earlier approximation did. Remove the superseded inferred signature result, its declaration-derived provenance and the runtime return contract derived from it. Retain explicit annotations and their runtime enforcement. Preserve any independently specified protocol shape of an unannotated generator; a generic protocol shape does not itself establish participation. These changes neither initialize storage nor change reference capture or liveness.

    Complete finite propagation within a recursive dependency group before concluding that inference does not converge. Copying a previously established result or joining previously established union members does not construct a new recursive type. In particular, when a group's contribution transfers only copy or join members of a fixed finite set of established types, compute their closure under those transfers, with never as the initial contribution and a completed unknown join retaining its ordinary absorbing behaviour. The number of declarations, their source order and the distance from a seed to a consumer are not grounds for a non-convergence error.

    Reconsider a contribution when a required provisional or published input changes, retaining its declaration environment and the applicable type-argument substitution. Dependencies include results read through a function value or an explicit generic application, as well as a direct call. A private answer is such an input even when it supplies no declaration-derived anchor. An implementation may retain an answer while its inputs remain unchanged; invalidating a required binding contract also invalidates answers derived from that contract. Reconstructing an equivalent signature or canonical type is not progress by itself. These requirements permit dependency worklists and component scheduling without prescribing either representation.

    A dependency read may use its available approximation while the recursive group is being solved. Reconsideration must propagate changed inputs until the group is complete; it need not recursively re-evaluate every previously answered dependency at each read. This permission does not make an answer permanent: the input-change and binding-invalidation requirements above continue to apply.

    For a generic result dependency, retain the identity and declaration environment of the generic declaration before applying the caller's bindings. Substitute those bindings into the available provisional answer as well as any published answer. This includes a private answer and the initial never contribution of a recursive reference; an unanswered dependency must not become a completed unknown merely because an application copies a signature. A completed unknown remains unknown after substitution. Specialization does not itself publish a private answer or create declaration provenance, and a receiving context cannot replace explicit type arguments already bound by the application. A final published symbolic protocol result replaces any superseded concrete approximation in the runtime return contract. Instantiate that final contract with the invocation's bindings; dependence on a type parameter does not preserve an earlier approximation.

    Repetition does not always converge: a recursive result can grow under a type constructor at every step, as function _w_(_a_: uint32) { return [_w_(_a_)]; } does. It is a type error where the repetition does not reach a fixpoint, and the program says what it meant with an annotation. Apply the actual contribution transfers, including projection and unknown absorption, before concluding that a constructor makes a cycle grow without bound. The occurrence of a constructor on a recursive path, or a chosen number of changing approximations, does not by itself establish that conclusion. Inference produces no equirecursive types.

    A sufficient proof of constructor growth is a closed contribution equation built only from the recursive result, a finite set of known seed types, finite joins, and type constructors that preserve their operand as a proper structural component. If a recursive occurrence passes through at least one such constructor and survives every normalization of the equation, repeating that equation produces types of unbounded structural depth. This proves non-convergence. Establish the equation from the actual contribution judgment, including declaration identity, participation, contextual typing and any substitution; recognizing a constructor in source syntax alone does not establish the equation. A projection that removes that component, an annotation that replaces it, or an unknown contribution that absorbs it invalidates this proof.

    This sufficient proof is not a restriction requiring every recursive equation to have that form. A different proof may establish non-convergence. A repeated state establishes non-convergence only when it is the complete state of a deterministic contribution computation with unchanged external inputs: include required dependencies, their provisional and published results, participation, environments and the outstanding work. Repetition of the displayed return types alone, or repetition while an external prerequisite remains unfinished, is insufficient. When no proof is established and inference cannot complete within the implementation's checking resources, apply 1.6.2.5.

    The domain of the fixpoint is the participating functions of the linked module graph, computed before any module in the graph evaluates. A function therefore has one inferred type wherever it is called from, and whether a callee is defined in the same source text, in another module of the graph, or in an earlier script of the same realm makes no difference to what a program means. A dynamically imported module has no such relationship to its importer: a call through it has the any Static Type, and the enforcement and reflection of the imported function carry its type instead.

    Note

    "Before any module in the graph evaluates" is a phase that need not exist in an implementation before this clause requires it: a checker may run entirely at parse, where the graph is not yet resolved and an imported name is not yet anything. Such an implementation can satisfy this clause by checking a module twice — once at parse, which sees everything a module says about itself, and once when its imports resolve, with the types of the imported names supplied. Nothing is reported twice, because a module whose first check failed never reaches the second.

    What a module records for its importers is the type of each of its own top-level declarations, keyed by the LOCAL name. Import resolution already answers with a module and a binding name, and that binding name is the local one, so a renamed import, a default export, and a re-export chain all resolve through the same lookup and none needs a rule of its own. A namespace import binds one name to every export, so its type is the object type of what the module declares; without that, the spelling of an import would decide whether a program is checked.

    1.6.2.4 Constructor Growth in Dependency Components

    The sufficient proof in 1.6.2.3 extends to a finite system of contribution equations. Each equation belongs to a declaration and its required result component in its declaration environment. Identify dependencies by their resolved declarations, including applicable type-argument bindings, rather than by identifier spelling or formatted types. An edge denotes a result actually used by the contribution judgment; a name that is shadowed, an unresolved input or a potentially replaced callee supplies no such identity proof.

    For this proof, establish all of the following before classifying a component as growing:

    1. Each equation in the required dependency closure is built from a finite set of known seed types, results of other equations in that closure, finite joins, and constructors preserving their operands as proper structural components. Apply the actual participation, contextual typing, substitution and normalization rules. Every result dependency has an equation in the closure. An unsupported or unfinished outgoing dependency prevents this proof for every equation depending on it, even if an apparent cycle can be drawn without that dependency.
    2. For each occurrence of another equation's result, record an edge from the consuming equation to that dependency. Mark the edge as CONSTRUCTING only when at least one proper constructor enclosing that occurrence survives the complete contribution transfer and normalization. An unwrapped result copy is not constructing. Joining results is not by itself constructing.
    3. Partition the dependency graph into strongly connected components: two equations belong to the same component exactly when each is reachable from the other by following dependency edges. A single equation with no self edge has no cycle. A component is growing under this proof exactly when it contains a constructing edge whose target is in that component. Such an edge lies on a cycle; every traversal of that cycle preserves an additional proper structural component, giving unbounded structural depth.
    4. A growing component has no finite result under these equations and produces the non-convergence type error. The diagnostic identifies a declaration in that component; an acyclic consumer is not itself evidence of a growing cycle. Do not publish an intermediate approximation as a completed inferred contract. A component with only copy/join edges is not rejected by this proof; complete its finite closure under 1.6.2.3.

    A constructor on an acyclic path to a finite result does not prove growth. A projection, a substituting annotation or an absorbing unknown contribution can remove a would-be constructing edge or prevent the closed-equation proof altogether. Merely seeing a constructor in a source expression is therefore insufficient. Failure to establish these premises is not a type error or a completed unknown result; continue the ordinary contribution computation, use another sound proof, or apply 1.6.2.5 on resource exhaustion. An unrelated unsupported component does not invalidate an independently closed proof.

    Note

    This judgment states proof premises and their consequence. It does not prescribe a graph representation, traversal order, source-syntax recognizer, or a resource allowance. In particular, a production implementation can use shared type representations and iterative component algorithms without modifying user-object layouts, runtime call-site caches or reference-liveness checks.

    1.6.2.5 Return Inference Resources

    Resource exhaustion during a required return-contribution computation is distinct from a proof that its equation has no finite fixpoint. An implementation may bound contribution evaluations, distinct provisional answers and the number of contribution queries active at once. These are host-defined resource limits, not alternative rules for inferred types. A source check that exceeds such a limit is abandoned with a StaticTypeError identifying inference-resource exhaustion and the declaration being computed. It supplies no inferred result. In particular, a chosen number of changed approximations establishes only that the implementation spent that allowance, not that further approximations would change forever.

    1. One resource state covers one invocation of the containing source check, including declaration preparation, dependent initializer queries, nested function queries, protocol-component queries and any reconsideration required before the check finishes. Reconsideration does not reset that state. A subsequent independent source check starts a new state; an interleaved check in another agent has a distinct state.
    2. Charge one contribution evaluation before recomputing a function body's contribution for a requested result component. The active-query count includes that query until it returns. Reading a previously available answer without recomputing its contribution is not an evaluation. Required input invalidation still requires reconsideration under 1.6.2.9.
    3. Charge a distinct-answer unit at the completion of a contribution query, before supplying its answer to a consumer or publication step, according to 1.6.2.6. This boundary applies to function declarations, expressions, arrows, methods, accessors, contextual callbacks and protocol-component queries. It is not conditional on publishing a named signature or runtime contract. Recreating a query or signature does not create a new declaration for a per-declaration allowance.
    4. The counters begin at zero. A request that exactly consumes its allowance is permitted. The next request marks exhaustion before performing the charged work or installing the result. Exhaustion is sticky until the containing check ends; unwinding a query does not clear it.
    5. At that checking boundary, exhaustion takes precedence over an incidental result, absent result or mismatch produced while abandoning the computation. Do not publish or retain provisional signatures, inferred runtime contracts, successful checking obligations or inference-cache entries derived from the abandoned check as completed results. Retain explicit contracts and restore the suspended checking environments. Evaluated user code cannot handle exhaustion and select a fallback.

    The limits may decide whether checking completes, but never change a completed result into a different type or into a completed unknown join. Native stack or heap failure is not a non-convergence proof. The implementation must report exhaustion before exhausting its own capacity for the operations it meters, under the same containment principle as 1.2.7.4. A return annotation may remove a required inference; it does not waive the checks required by that annotation. These resource rules change neither ordinary evaluation order nor reference liveness.

    Note

    The accounting units above distinguish recomputation, reuse and distinct answers; they do not prescribe a common dependency schedule, a common acceptance floor, or a total cost model for all static analysis and type evaluation. Different conforming resource limits or schedules can therefore cause one implementation to report exhaustion while another completes the same required judgment. A cache cannot turn an incomplete result into a successful answer, and allocation or formatted type text does not establish input identity.

    1.6.2.6 Return Contribution Answer History

    Distinct-answer accounting associates each answer with its source function declaration or function-producing syntax node and with the requested contribution component. For a generator DoExpression, the expression is the source owner of its body-contribution queries. The components are the ordinary return result, an async function's fulfilled result, a generator's yielded result, and a generator's completion result. Async generator yield and completion queries use the same component distinctions after their specified awaited transfers. A reconstructed signature, a new query object or a repeated preparation pass retains the same source owner for this accounting.

    1. Each source owner has one distinct-answer allowance within the containing source check. Its history contains pairs of a component and an answer. Known types, including never, and a completed unknown join are answers. An unanswered declaration-contract prerequisite is not a completed unknown answer and creates no history entry; the attempted query still consumes its contribution-evaluation allowance. An available recursive approximation, including the initial never contribution, remains subject to 1.6.2.3.
    2. Two history entries are equivalent only when their components are the same and their answers are equivalent. Two completed unknown joins are equivalent to one another, but not to never or an explicit any type. Compare known answers with the existing type-equivalence judgment. Equality of a generator's yield and completion types does not merge those two components.
    3. If an equivalent pair is already recorded, no additional distinct-answer unit is charged. Otherwise request one unit from the source owner's remaining allowance before recording the pair or using its answer. All components and all required checking contexts of that source owner share the allowance. A zero allowance permits no first answer. Returning to a previously recorded answer consumes no new unit.
    4. The history denotes answers as they were when recorded. Later completion or mutation of an implementation's signature, alias or composite-type records must not rewrite earlier entries or make a novel answer appear to have been seen already. Preserve the nominal declarations, activation identities, deferred environments, symbols and other identities required by type equivalence; copying an identity-bearing object does not manufacture an equivalent identity.
    5. Constructing a Promise or Generator carrier from component answers, copying an answer into a provisional signature, or publishing its runtime contract does not itself constitute another body-contribution answer. If one of those operations initiates a further contribution query, that query is accounted for at its own completion. The distinct-answer allowance therefore cannot be bypassed by avoiding signature publication or multiplied merely by representing an answer at several publication sites.

    This history is an accounting device, not a query cache. Equal component answers can arise from different parameter types, substitutions, receiver types, source environments, contextual targets or dependency states. Their accounting equivalence does not authorize reuse in another context, suppress recomputation after input invalidation, or complete an unfinished dependency. Apply 1.6.2.7 when reusing a judgment. Actual recomputation still spends a contribution-evaluation unit. Resource exhaustion uses the containment, precedence and restoration rules of 1.6.2.5; it is not evidence of non-convergence.

    Note

    Implementations may use immutable type records, persistent versions, canonical type graphs or private snapshots to retain history. No particular allocation strategy or traversal schedule is prescribed. These rules do not set a portable acceptance floor or define complete query-input identities for caching, and they change neither runtime object layout nor reference liveness.

    1.6.2.7 Inference Query Identity and Validity

    A logical inference query identifies the judgment being requested, its source owner and its applicable checking context. For a body-contribution judgment, the owner and component are those of 1.6.2.6. For a dependent initializer, expression, flow transfer or checking obligation, retain that judgment's source position and role as well. A query's identity, the validity of a previously computed outcome, and equivalence for answer accounting are separate judgments. A new allocation does not necessarily denote a new query; equal answers do not establish the same query.

    The applicable checking context contains the inputs prescribed by the requested judgment. The following distinctions must be retained whenever that judgment can observe them. An implementation may omit an input only when its irrelevance to that judgment is established; an absent input and an unfinished required input are not interchangeable.

    InputRequired distinctions
    Source and lexical resolutionThe source owner and source position, declaring lexical environments and resolved binding identities, including shadowing, imported bindings and nominal declarations. Identifier spelling alone does not identify a binding.
    Parameters and generic bindingsEffective parameter contracts and binding kinds; names, order, defaults, rest and reference positions where used; generic binder declarations, constraints, value-parameter domains, substitutions and applicable instantiation identities. Pairing generic binders for type equivalence does not replace their identities in a declaration-context query.
    Contextual contractsThe contextual signature or overload alternative, declared result and generator component contracts, and any contextual adaptation required at the source position. An equal current inferred return does not equate different contextual alternatives.
    Receiver and capturesThe applicable receiver contract and its declaring owner, lexical receiver adoption and captured binding contracts. An ordinary nested function does not borrow the receiver of the query that requests it.
    Flow and completionThe source-position current-value domains, effects, places, admitted predecessors and completion state required by the transfer. A captured operand, a later store and a fixed declaration contract remain distinct. Retain any reference-origin, permission or liveness input required by the judgment; a cached declaration contract supplies none of those facts by itself.
    Checking boundaryThe containing source check and its applicable phase, enabled proposal features, checked-code classification, available declarations, imported contracts, realm-dependent intrinsic assumptions and completed host or type-evaluation inputs. A parse-time query with unresolved imports is not a completed link-time query.

    A reusable outcome additionally has a validity relation to every required dependency. A dependency observation identifies the depended-on judgment in its context, the part of its outcome consumed, and whether that part was unfinished, a recursive approximation, or completed. Completed known types, completed unknown joins and absence of a published inferred contract are distinct from an unfinished computation. Participation, declaration provenance, required diagnostics and any dependent transfer outputs are parts of the outcome when the consumer uses them; recording only the displayed return type is insufficient.

    1. Before reusing a completed outcome, establish that the request denotes the same judgment in an equivalent applicable context, and that every dependency observation on which that outcome relies remains valid. Establish equivalence by the existing rules for each input: preserve declaration and other identity-bearing inputs by their required identity, and compare value or contract inputs by the equivalence appropriate to their use. Assignability alone is insufficient.
    2. If a required dependency changes or completes, invalidate the dependent outcome unless its continued validity is established. Reconsider the affected judgment with its source-position inputs under 1.6.2.14. If its validated outcome remains equivalent in every part used by a downstream consumer, that consumer need not be recomputed solely because an upstream computation ran again. Equality of the result type before validating the changed inputs supplies no such proof.
    3. Retain the dependency relation when an outcome is reused. A cache hit must not make a required dependency invisible to a later invalidation, nor make an unfinished dependency appear completed. A recursive approximation can be reused only as an approximation under 1.6.2.3; it cannot be installed as a completed result by a cache lookup.
    4. Keep the meaning of saved inputs and observations stable. Mutating a compiler-owned signature, type record, environment map or dependency record cannot retroactively change what a prior query observed. Preserve source, nominal, activation, deferred-environment and symbol identities. An immutable representation, a snapshot or validated dependency versions may establish this requirement; the specification does not require copying runtime values.
    5. Reuse must retain the requested judgment's complete effect on static checking, including required diagnostics and dependent outputs. Discarding a speculative contextual attempt's diagnostics does not turn its failed checking outcome into a successful one when that same judgment is requested again. Conversely, a failure belonging only to an inapplicable contextual alternative must not reject an applicable alternative. Reusing a scalar expression type is insufficient when the request also requires its source-flow transfer or deciding-test judgment. Restore the suspended checking environment after a nested query. No reuse initializes a binding, executes user code, establishes a runtime effect, extends reference liveness or authorizes check elision.

    These requirements apply to reuse within a check and to any reuse across checking boundaries. An implementation need not retain outcomes across checks. If it does, it must establish the applicable source and dependency identities anew and satisfy all required obligations in the new check. A completed contribution answer imported into a new source check is subject to that check's answer-history allowance before use; a retained cache cannot bypass its first-answer charge. Reading a valid available answer does not spend a body-contribution evaluation, while actual recomputation spends the evaluation specified in 1.6.2.5. This distinction does not prescribe a portable cache, dependency schedule, numeric limit or acceptance floor.

    Note

    These are semantic reuse conditions, not a required key layout, fingerprint algorithm or incremental compiler architecture. A production engine may intern immutable contexts, retain versioned dependency graphs or recompute judgments. Such compiler-owned structures require no change to user-object shapes or runtime inline caches. A cache miss is not a new language error, and an abandoned resource-limited check supplies no reusable completed outcome.

    1.6.2.8 Lexical Environments of Contributions

    The contribution judgments in 1.6.2.2 use the binding environments of the contributing source position. They do not use a single name map for the entire function. Determine these environments as follows, without executing source text.

    1. Establish the function's parameter, variable and body lexical bindings according to declaration instantiation. A VariableDeclaration belongs to its variable environment even when its occurrence is nested in a block, loop, handler or switch. A declaration without an initializer does not replace an existing binding's value. An unannotated var redeclaration, including a destructuring one, does not erase the contract of the binding it reuses. Preserve the parameter/body distinctions required by 1.7.5.1.
    2. On entering a lexical block, establish its declared bindings before reading any contribution in that block. This includes names in destructuring patterns and declarations that follow the contribution in source order. An unknown contract still shadows an outer same-named binding. Establishing a name or contract does not initialize its runtime binding or suppress its temporal-dead-zone checks.
    3. Establish local function declaration signatures throughout the scope that owns the binding, including before their declaration text. All sibling declarations in that scope are available before following a result dependency. Construct the signatures and overload sets by the ordinary declaration rules, using declared information for overload identity and ranking. Resolve signature annotations and body dependencies in their declaration environments. A local declaration with an unknown result still shadows an outer same-named function. Its body supplies a separate inference query when needed; its returns and yields are not added directly to the enclosing function's contributions.
    4. A switch discriminant is outside the CaseBlock's lexical environment. All clauses of that CaseBlock share one lexical environment, including declarations in later clauses. A nested block in a clause has its own environment.
    5. A lexical loop-head binding belongs to that loop's environment; a var loop-head binding belongs to the enclosing variable environment. Preserve the base-language head, iterable-expression and per-iteration binding scopes. Loop-body blocks have their own environments. A loop-local binding supplies no type or provenance to a read outside its scope.
    6. Each catch clause has its own parameter environment and body block environment. Its filter and binding annotations supply contracts according to 1.4.4; an unannotated parameter with no known filter is unknown. Sibling handlers and the finally block do not share these local bindings. Collect each syntactic handler once, regardless of an implementation's representation of a list of handlers.
    7. Associate initializer contribution types, numeric-constant facts and anchoring provenance with the binding identity that supplied them. Leaving a scope removes its local facts from lookup and reveals the enclosing bindings again; it does not remove a surviving variable-environment binding. A nested function's returns and yields belong to that function, and a class body or static block does not contribute to its enclosing function.

    Every contribution computation, including a function literal's contextual result query, may read an unparticipating callee's provisional answer as specified in 1.6.2.2. That use does not publish the callee's result or create a declaration-derived anchor. Apply 1.6.2.9 to required local results and captured binding contracts as to other dependencies. Reconstructing an equivalent signature or temporary inference record is not growth of its result type.

    A transparent initializer contribution is local evidence about that contribution, not an annotation on the captured storage. When querying a nested function, a captured ordinary unannotated let does not acquire a contract from the enclosing contribution walk's initializer alias. A typed constant retains the binding contract supplied by its participating initializer, and a reference binding retains its referent's contract under the existing reference rules. Preserve declaration provenance separately in each case. A constant initialized from a contract-free mutable alias does not acquire a typed capture contract merely because that alias was transparent to the enclosing contribution query.

    Preserve receiver binding as well as named bindings when querying a function's result. An ordinary function declaration or expression has its own this binding and uses its applicable declared or contextual receiver contract, if any. It does not inherit a class or method receiver merely because the query occurs inside that body. An arrow uses its lexical receiver. This judgment changes neither runtime receiver binding nor reference capture or liveness.

    These rules select bindings; the existing contribution, iteration, catch, mutation-stability and dependency rules determine their types. They do not infer a type for an ordinary unannotated mutable binding, make a literal-only contribution participate, establish a path as reachable, or substitute source visitation order for unresolved dependencies. A published inferred result still cannot justify check elision. Reference aliasing, reference liveness, effects and runtime initialization order are unchanged.

    Note

    In function f(x: string) { let g = x; { let g; g = 1; } return g; }, the returned g is the unchanged outer alias and contributes string. The inner assignment changes another binding. Conversely, in function f(g: string) { { return g; let g; } }, the return reads the inner unknown binding and cannot borrow the parameter's annotation. If executed, that read retains its ordinary temporal-dead-zone failure.

    1.6.2.9 Publication Dependencies and Checking Order

    The results required by 1.6.2.3 are independent of declaration visitation order. Establish the lexical identities and available contracts of a declaration scope before finalizing obligations in that scope that consume inferred returns. This applies to Scripts, Modules, function bodies, blocks and switch scopes, including consumers preceding a function declaration or the declaration of a captured binding. It also applies when the consumer is in an uncalled body or a branch whose ordinary Evaluation is not reached.

    1. Resolve each inference dependency in the environment of the declaration whose contribution is being computed, including its parameter and type-parameter environments. A caller that requests the computation does not supply its own same-spelled bindings. Untyped and unresolved bindings still shadow outer bindings.
    2. Read a captured binding's contract as specified in 1.6.2.2. A required inferred binding contract may itself depend on the Static Type of its initializer and on published returns. Establish those dependencies using their existing participation and type rules. If that Static Type depends on flow at the initializer, retain that dependency; replacing it with the broader declared type of an initializer operand is not an equivalent computation. This does not evaluate the initializer, invoke a function, obtain a runtime value, or initialize a binding.
    3. When a contribution requests an unpublished callee result, compute the callee's contributions under the inference-fixpoint rules. A provisional result is available to a participating inference that asks for it, but the mere existence of that provisional result does not make the callee participate and does not anchor the caller. A declared result or a result published by a participating callee supplies declaration provenance under the existing anchoring rule.
    4. Complete the applicable inference dependencies before finalizing a consuming assignability, narrowing or other type-checking obligation. If publication changes an input previously used by an obligation, reconsider that obligation. An unavailable input remains unresolved under its defining rule; declaration visitation order alone cannot be the reason to treat an established contract as any.

    These dependencies cross function forms. Inference of an ordinary return may require an async result or a generator protocol, and inference of an async result or delegated yield may require another declaration's result. Apply the contribution rules of 1.6.2.19 before building the callee's result type: an async result uses its fulfillment contribution, and a generator keeps its yielded and returned contributions distinct. A generic protocol shape alone supplies no annotation-derived anchor. A provisional protocol result remains private on the same terms as a provisional ordinary return; requesting it does not publish it for a non-participating callee.

    For an async fulfillment contribution, apply the established awaited-result projection to each known union alternative before joining the contributions. A conditional union of a direct value and an intrinsic Promise supplying that same value type does not add a Promise layer to the fulfillment result. Apply the same projection to an async generator's returned contribution, independently of its yielded contribution. An unresolved assimilation alternative remains unknown; no hook is invoked by this inference. Joining raw Promise wrappers before projecting them is not an equivalent transfer and cannot justify a recursive-growth error.

    For generator inference, an unknown yielded or returned contribution remains any in that component; it is not replaced by void or by the other component. An empty yielded-contribution set contributes never, while normal completion contributes undefined only to the return join. Declared locals and unchanged initializer aliases use the same contribution and provenance rules in both joins. Delegation supplies its yielded contribution under 31 and retains the provenance of that contribution. Neither a known return nor a known yield makes an unknown component known, and the input component is not inferred.

    An implementation may prepare a declaration group eagerly, resolve dependencies on demand, or use an equivalent schedule. It must produce the same required acceptance and rejection results. An acyclic dependency chain is not non-convergent merely because its declarations are encountered in the reverse order or because it exceeds an implementation's chosen number of whole-scope passes. Module dependency availability and failure order remain governed by 1.3.8.

    Contract preparation does not change ordinary initialization order or reference liveness. If no type error is established, a forward value read still observes its ordinary temporal dead zone or uninitialized value. In particular, preparation neither runs a captured initializer early nor converts an ordinary runtime Reference Error into an inferred-return diagnostic. A known inconsistent typed consumer is rejected at the specified checking boundary even if ordinary execution would first encounter a different runtime error.

    1.6.2.10 Initializer Contracts and Dependent Obligations

    An obligation that consumes an inferred binding contract follows 1.6.2.9. Its inputs include the binding's participation, the Static Type of its initializer, and the incoming flow facts required to compute that type. A dependency identifies a declaration and a source position, not only a name or a type representation. A completed unknown Static Type and a computation whose required inputs are not yet established are distinct: only the former is subject to the ordinary rules for any.

    1. Establish the incoming flow for the initializer under 1.8.5, and compute its Static Type in its lexical, generic and contextual environments. Apply the binding form's existing participation and widening rules. An earlier established branch or store can therefore affect the inferred contract; a later store does not replace that contract with the later value's type.
    2. If an input to this computation is unfinished, retain the dependency and complete that input under its defining rule before the binding contract is final. This includes an inferred callee result used by an earlier test or store. When that result becomes available, recompute the affected flow transfer and its dependent initializer facts; merely completing the callee does not validate the flow facts computed without it. Apply the existing fixpoint rules when these dependencies are recursive.
    3. Recompute a consuming obligation whose input changed, retaining the consumer's own source position, lexical and generic environments, contextual type, receiver and enclosing function context, and applicable incoming flow. Resolve each producer in its own declaration environment. Do not use the environments or outgoing flow at the point when the work happens to be scheduled.
    4. Finalize the obligation only after its required inputs are established. An intermediate acceptance or rejection that depended on an unfinished input is not a final judgment. A completed unknown input retains the existing gradual rules and runtime checks; it supplies neither an annotation-derived anchor nor a proof of incompatibility. A failure to complete required work follows its existing failure rule, and is not converted into a completed unknown type.

    Default-value compatibility is a consuming obligation. Apply these requirements to parameter defaults, defaults within binding patterns, and instance or static field initializers whenever their existing rules require checking the initializer against an established target type. The target is the declared or contextual type required at that source position. The fact that a function is uncalled, a default is not selected by a particular invocation, or an instance is not constructed does not discharge an established incompatibility.

    A parameter default retains the parameter environment in which it is defined, including parameter binding identities and their applicable initialization state. A body declaration does not become visible to that default merely because the body has been visited before the obligation is completed. An untyped or unresolved parameter still shadows an outer declaration. A binding-pattern default retains its pattern context. A field initializer retains its class, type-parameter, private-name and receiver contexts; an instance receiver and a static receiver are not interchangeable. These are requirements on the source judgment, not instructions to evaluate a default or allocate an instance during checking.

    These environment requirements hold through nested dependency requests. Temporarily checking a producer in a different declaration environment does not end a suspended parameter-default judgment or make the producer's body bindings visible to it. On resuming the requesting judgment, retain its original binding identities and source state. A reference in a parameter initializer, including within a closure created there, does not resolve to a body-only var or function declaration. This separation also applies to async and generator functions. A diagnostic's related declaration, when provided, is resolved in the same source environment as the checked reference.

    Completing an obligation does not change the applicable compatibility, participation, conversion, default evaluability or reference rules. In particular, ordinary function parameter defaults do not acquire a new compile-time-evaluability requirement through this clause, and a default already subject to such a requirement remains subject to it. A diagnostic produced by a completed obligation retains the original consuming source location and checking unit under 1.2.8.

    Reconsidering an obligation retains the identity of its consuming source judgment and applicable context. Replace that obligation's unfinished inputs with the dependencies required by the reconsidered judgment; merely reconstructing an environment or revisiting an initializer does not create a distinct obligation or establish progress. Complete newly required producer judgments under their own rules, and finalize the consumer only from established inputs. This requirement does not permit discarding an unfinished judgment, treating it as any, suppressing a required diagnostic, or making completion depend on an implementation retry or time limit.

    A chain of inferred bindings is subject to the same dependency relation as an inferred callee result. Completing one initializer can establish the input of another initializer, whose contract in turn establishes an input of a consuming obligation. Retain each initializer's own incoming flow and contextual environments through that chain. Completion propagates both a known participating contract and a completed unknown result; the latter does not prevent completion of dependent computations, but it supplies no new participation. A cached provisional type or an earlier visit to the declaration does not establish that its prerequisites are complete.

    This dependency relation also applies to inferred local binding contracts requested while computing a nested function's contributions. Before answering such a request, identify the binding in the declaration environments of 1.6.2.8, including when its initializer follows the requesting contribution. Resolve the initializer in the binding's own parameter, type-parameter, lexical and receiver contexts. A requesting local function does not supply its own parameters or receiver to that initializer. The initializer's contextual type and incoming flow are those of its source position.

    1. Where the binding has a declared contract, use that contract under the existing binding rules. Otherwise, determine whether its binding form requires or admits an inferred contract. An ordinary unannotated mutable binding does not acquire a contract merely because its initializer is transparent to an enclosing contribution query.
    2. For an inferred contract, establish the initializer's required binding, result and flow dependencies. Apply typed-constant participation or the typed-initializer rules, as applicable. A provisional callee answer available to a contribution query is not thereby a published contract available to constant inference.
    3. Keep a completed binding contract distinct from any initializer contribution type and provenance that the enclosing function may use locally. An enclosing contribution that reads a transparent initializer need not wait for an unrelated capture-contract computation. Conversely, reading that binding from a nested function requires its binding contract; the local contribution type cannot substitute for it.
    4. Propagate completion through every dependent result and consuming obligation under this clause. Encountering an initializer dependency again while computing it does not establish any or a type error; apply the existing recursive dependency rules. Reconstructing a lexical environment or dependency representation does not create a new source binding or change its contract.

    A required reference-binding contract is also an initializer dependency. Apply 2.5 in the reference declaration's own lexical, parameter, type-parameter and receiver environments, including when the declaration follows a requesting contribution. For an initializer that resolves to a named lexical location, use that location's declared or completed inferred binding contract, not the current-value narrowing of a read. Parentheses do not change this location judgment. An alias chain retains the contracts and declaration environments of its source bindings. A transparent initializer contribution of an ordinary untyped binding does not supply a location contract.

    Keep the value type of a reference binding separate from its current origin, write permission, runtime initialization state and reference liveness. Establishing its contract neither obtains a runtime location nor reads its value, initializes the reference, executes an initializer or permits an otherwise invalid borrow. Rebinding retains the fixed binding type under 2.5; an established type does not prove that every location subsequently selected through that alias admits a store. If selecting the source location requires a receiver, key, call result or other unresolved input, retain that dependency under the existing location rules. Do not substitute the requesting function's flow or turn an unresolved input into a completed unknown contract.

    An unavailable contribution result does not prevent discovery of a declaration on which that result depends. Establish the required declaration and initializer dependencies even when their source text follows the return or yield requesting them, or is unreachable under ordinary Evaluation. A completed unknown contribution affects the join under the existing gradual rules; it does not exempt other source text from its declaration, dependency or checking obligations. Merely encountering one unknown or unresolved result is not a completion criterion for the enclosing source scope.

    If a contribution judgment is performed after its source position has been traversed, retain that position's binding identities, contextual type, receiver, parameter and type-parameter environments, initialization state and incoming flow. Do not use the flow after a later store, a sibling branch or a suspension in place of that source judgment. Traversing a contribution's operand for effects or further contributions is distinct from obtaining its type: deferring a yield's type does not omit a nested yield, delegation input or contribution inside a test, and does not move suspension effects. Completing a required binding contract invalidates any dependent result or obligation that used an unfinished answer. The completed contract remains distinct from contribution-only initializer evidence.

    For a contribution within a switch, use the clause entry formed by the selected-label environment joined with normal fallthrough from the preceding clause. Establish the default selection environment after all failed labels, including those textually following the default. A CaseClause or DefaultClause without a StatementList contributes no declarations or statements, but remains part of label selection and the normal fallthrough relation. Its absence of statements does not discard its label, label effects, or incoming flow. Establish the shared case-block declaration environment before resolving clause contributions.

    Preserve each selected entry while computing subsequent label entries: effects in a later label do not become effects of an earlier successful selection. Conversely, effects in labels actually reached along the failed-selection path are inputs to later selections and to the default. A write that replaces the original discriminant's place prevents refining its new value from the captured discriminant. Apply the existing expression-effect and place-identity rules, and consume only breaks targeting this switch when forming its successor. A contribution query is not permitted to replace these predecessor relations with independent copies of the switch's original entry.

    Contribution inference records and consumes immutable Boolean producer relations under 1.8.5.1 in the same declaration and source environments used by ordinary checking. This applies to direct and composed aliases, tests controlling statements or expression operands, conditional result arms and switch selection, including an initializer contract requested by a nested contribution. Process successive bindings of one declaration in source order, including their initializer effects. A Boolean copy does not freeze a mutable subject or supply a narrower captured storage contract to a nested function.

    A delayed expression-type query retains its source position's normal-completion state as well as its flow facts. A return or yield contribution is queried where its operand is evaluated, before the enclosing abrupt completion or suspension; a later return, throw or sibling branch cannot make its conditional arms lack their original incoming environments. Restore the requesting computation's completion state after the query. This requirement preserves the existing rules for inspecting unreachable source and joining contributions; it does not introduce a new unreachable-code exemption or change runtime initialization.

    A captured switch discriminant retains the result-to-source relations established by 1.8.5.1, including the result environments of a Boolean expression or preserved predicate and the evaluated and skipped alternatives of an optional chain or its typeof result. Apply the effects of each reached label to those relations before selecting its entry. Pass the remaining alternatives along the failed-selection path, excluding only values established to match that label under the applicable selection rule. In particular, a failed singleton label can exhaust an optional result's evaluated alternatives; subsequent labels and the default cannot restore those alternatives. A non-singleton label's type does not by itself exclude its whole domain. This rule applies both to a direct contribution and to an initializer whose contract a contribution consumes; reducing the captured result to its scalar type does not discharge the required source-flow judgment.

    The incoming flow used by a contribution query is the flow at the contributing expression or initializer under 1.8.5.1. In particular, a guarded abrupt completion does not contribute a normal predecessor to a following initializer. Join the remaining normal predecessors, and retain the destinations of breaks and continues. Loop entries and exits, switch selection and fallthrough, exceptional entry and finally transfer use their existing flow rules; syntactic visitation order is not an additional predecessor. An inference query for a nested function has its own completion state and cannot terminate or revive the enclosing query's path.

    Source flow includes the current-value facts established by successful participating initializations and stores under 1.8.5.1. Determine the source value at its production point using the ordinary Static Type judgment and the contracts available to that judgment. Process operand evaluation, required conversions and store effects in the specified order, then establish any permitted destination fact from the resulting stored domain. For sequential expressions and successive bindings, the effects of each preceding expression are inputs to the next expression. A right operand's type before conversion is not necessarily the type of the stored value. Preserve the declared destination view for mutable objects, callable contracts, predicates and contextual void; a more specific initializer shape or signature cannot replace that view.

    A provisional callee result available only to contribution inference does not become an ordinary store or capture contract by being assigned to a local. Likewise, transparency of an ordinary untyped local to an enclosing contribution query does not make that local a typed storage destination or a participating source for constant inference. Apply the existing alias and effect invalidations even when a store establishes no new fact. A reference store is a write to its referent, with that location's contract and alias effects; it does not turn the reference into an immutable copy. If a required source, conversion or flow input remains unresolved, retain the dependency and reconsider its affected transfer and consumers when it completes. A completed unknown supplies no unsupported stored-domain fact.

    Apply the existing effect and invalidation rules in evaluation order, including between bindings in one declaration and across suspension. A fact invalidated before an initializer is not an input to that initializer's contract. Once established, an inferred constant contract is a contract of the new binding: a later store to the initializer's source binding does not alter it. A nested function reads that contract, but does not inherit a narrowing of other captured mutable storage from the point where its result is requested. A reference binding retains the existing location contract and liveness rules; it is not an immutable copy of the referent's currently narrowed value. These requirements do not discard contributions or exempt unreachable source from checking under the existing rules.

    A computation proved independent of incoming flow may be prepared without completing that flow first. This is a scheduling freedom, not a different Static Type judgment. In particular, using a wider declared operand type in place of an initializer's required narrowed type is not such a proof. A flow-independent implementation path does not discharge dependencies left outside that path, and an unsupported preparation path is not a completed unknown type.

    Apply a binding form's validation to the result of its completed initializer computation. In particular, the requirement that a typed initializer have a Static Type other than any is not a requirement that an implementation already possess that type when it first visits the declaration. Conversely, scheduling a later computation does not discharge that requirement: a completed unknown result still fails it. A cycle follows 1.6.2.3; waiting for an unfinished dependency alone establishes neither a completed unknown result nor non-convergence.

    These requirements apply at the checking boundary of 1.2.8, including obligations inside uncalled functions and otherwise unreachable source. They do not execute an initializer, call a function, initialize a value binding, extend reference liveness or authorize check elision. An implementation may store obligations or recompute equivalent judgments; no particular queue, frame representation or traversal count is required.

    1.6.2.11 Completed Binding Contracts at Consuming Positions

    A read of an inferred binding consumes the completed contract required by 1.6.2.10. The binding's first observed type is not a permanent answer when its prerequisites were unfinished. Apply the following requirements to each dependent consuming judgment.

    1. Identify the source binding by lexical identity. Determine its inferred contract in its initializer's source environment, using the binding form's participation and widening rules. Complete required binding and result dependencies under 1.6.2.9; an implementation's cached unavailable answer is not a completed unknown.
    2. Use that completed contract together with the flow facts valid at the consuming source position. Do not replace a subsequent store's current-value fact with the initializer's earlier fact, or compute the initializer under the consumer's later flow. A constant's inferred contract is not changed by a later write to the initializer's source.
    3. If completion changes an input to a judgment already attempted, reconsider that judgment at its original source position. This requirement propagates through chains of inferred constants, typed initializers, inferred function results, and their consumers. Preserve the original lexical, contextual and checked-code environments.
    4. Apply the existing deciding-test and transfer rules to the resulting type and source facts. This includes tests in conditionals, iteration, logical and nullish expressions and assignments, switch selection, and guarded patterns. A value query does not become a deciding test merely because completing its operand establishes a constant answer. An unchecked source position does not become checked through the completion of a dependency.
    5. Retain diagnostics established by completed declaration obligations even when their contracts were requested during a speculative query. A discarded speculative consumer does not discharge an independent declaration requirement. Conversely, an unfinished attempt is not a completed diagnostic. Apply the existing recursion rules where dependencies form a cycle.

    These requirements constrain the final judgments, not the timing of an implementation's internal requests. Eager completion, demand-driven completion and deferred reconsideration are permitted when they give the same required judgments. They neither evaluate initializers nor initialize value or reference bindings, prove reference liveness, permit check elision, change a mutable location's contract, or add participation to ordinary untyped mutable storage.

    1.6.2.12 Dependent Store Facts and Captured Writes

    The completion requirements of 1.6.2.11 apply to source-flow transfers as well as declaration contracts. A store whose result depends on unfinished inference is not a completed unknown source. Determine its required judgment under 1.8.5.1 using the following requirements.

    1. Identify the destination binding or established place and the value produced by this store separately. Retain the source environment at the assignment's evaluation point, including the declared destination contract, required contextual typing and incoming facts. Complete the source's required dependencies in their own environments.
    2. Check the completed source against the declared destination. Apply operand evaluation, conversion and store effects in their specified order. Establish only the stored domain justified after successful completion by the existing transfer rules; the source's pre-conversion domain is not automatically that domain. A completed unknown source retains ordinary runtime boundary handling and supplies no additional refinement beyond an established successful-store contract.
    3. Reconsider each judgment that consumed an unfinished store fact, including initializer contracts and return contributions. A constant capturing that store's value uses the fact valid at its initializer, even when completion is requested after another assignment to the source. Completing the old store does not overwrite a later store's fact or restore a fact invalidated by an intervening effect.
    4. At each flow join use the actual incoming alternatives and their completed transfers. A missing fact is an unknown predecessor; an unfinished fact remains a dependency. Neither is an impossible predecessor. An implementation's internal placeholder is not the any type and cannot discharge a dependent obligation. Complete dependent deciding tests and their result environments at the original source positions before finalizing their consumers. The same requirements apply to normal and abrupt completions, loop widening, switch selection and finally transfer.
