The binding must retain a Boolean value under its ordinary participation and conversion rules; an explicit any view, mutable binding or reference alias establishes no immutable Boolean-copy relation by this rule. No implementation-selected alias-depth cutoff changes these required judgments for an established finite chain.

    A generic value retains its parameter identity for bindings, assignments and results. Alongside that identity, keep a proof domain obtained from an established upper bound and refined by the actual incoming branch facts. Subsequent type-test and truthiness judgments may use that domain, including on a false edge; the domain is not a replacement type argument or store contract. Join proof domains over incoming paths and invalidate them on replacement or uncertain alias effects. An unknown initial bound alone supplies no verdict.

    For a preserved scalar value, a failed established literal comparison or literal-pattern selection also records the exact excluded scalar values internally, even when NarrowFrom returns the same broad Type Record. Subsequent literal tests whose entire success set is excluded are impossible under the existing deciding-position rules; a case label and a literal pattern are such tests. A test over bindings whose operators have no effects records its outcome on each edge in the same way, so the same test before any write to those bindings can never succeed after it failed and can never fail after it succeeded; a case label repeating an earlier effect-free label of its switch can never succeed. Entering the body of a for-of is a test, which can never succeed where the iterated sequence's static iteration contribution guarantees no position or a range with constant endpoints has no interior. Retain an exclusion at a join only when every incoming path guarantees it, and discard affected exclusions on writes, unknown alias effects or loss of the subject's identity. Literal adoption and the actual equality operation determine the excluded values: strict equality identifies the signs of zero, while signed-zero patterns retain their distinct semantics; NaN and distinct numeric identities are not conflated. Coercion without an established equal-value mapping supplies no exclusion. These facts introduce no public complement Type Record, reflected type identity, arbitrary arithmetic relation or interval subtraction.

    A call proved to select the original %Boolean% intrinsic carries the true and false result environments of its captured first argument. Evaluate the callee and arguments once in source order, applying the effects of later arguments before exporting facts about an earlier captured value. A participating argument whose truthiness is established supplies the corresponding Boolean result type; a value query is permitted, and the existing literal-idiom exceptions remain. Construction with new, an unknown argument mapping, a replaced or shadowed intrinsic, and an arbitrary Boolean-returning function supply no such correspondence. The intrinsic proof is a static identity and effect proof, not a speculative runtime guard.

    A participating immutable binding initialized by an established identity-preserving copy of a primitive value retains that value's existing flow evidence, including exact scalar exclusions. It may also retain a same-value relation to the captured source place. Existing narrowing forms on either value propagate their evidence to the other only while both origins remain current. Replacing the source ends the relation to its current value, but does not invalidate the immutable snapshot's own evidence. Equal spellings, unknown incoming origins, reference alias effects, and unresolved conversions establish no relation. Joins and loop widening apply to the origin identities as to other facts. This is not general equality solving or a heap-alias analysis, and it preserves declared storage contracts and reference liveness.

    An immutable binding holding a typeof result may retain the classification's source identity. A recognized tag comparison or switch label selects the corresponding source domain while the current source still denotes the captured value. A tag is a many-to-one classification: "number" retains all admitted numeric families, and "object" retains all admitted Object-tag alternatives, including null. Replacing the source or losing its identity ends the relation; the saved tag is never reevaluated. This rule infers no relationship for arbitrary String-returning functions.

    For a preserved participating numeric value, established original non-coercing Number.isNaN, Number.isFinite, Number.isInteger and Number.isSafeInteger tests refine a finite internal partition: NaN, infinity, finite fractional values, unsafe integral values and safe integral values. Omit cells impossible for the established family. This partition applies to Number, binary float16/32/64 and sized integer domains; a numeric literal contributes its exact applicable cell. Finiteness selects the last three cells, integer selects the last two, and safe integer selects the last; a negative answer retains every other possible cell. For these supported floating domains, proved self-comparison of the same preserved data value produces and consumes the NaN category under its built-in equality semantics. Other domains retain established whole-member classification without assuming this partition: BigInt and complex predicate-admission rules, unresolved metadata and unknown intrinsic identities are unchanged. A join unions possible categories, and replacement or uncertain alias effects discard the affected evidence. Retain numeric-family identity and the public Type Record; these categories introduce neither new public scalar types nor arithmetic propagation. An equality with a numeric constant, and an equality or relational test of a value whose partition is NaN alone, read the partition as well, so such a test whose whole success set the partition excludes can never succeed and one whose whole failure set it excludes can never fail.

    On the equal edge of a proved built-in strict primitive comparison, retain a relation between the two captured value origins as well as their initial compatible domains. Later narrowing forms may transfer only evidence invariant under that equality operation. For String and Boolean values this includes their literal domains and exclusions; for floating values it includes compatible numeric categories and truthiness, but not a particular zero sign. Success excludes NaN. A sign-specific zero exclusion or identity must not cross a strict-equality relation as if it were SameValue. Distinct numeric families, decimal cohorts and unresolved metadata retain their established equality semantics; an unproved mapping contributes no relation. Keep relations only on incoming paths that establish them and while both origins survive replacement, alias effects and suspension. Propagation is bounded by the source's captured relations and finite fact vocabulary; it infers no arbitrary arithmetic relation or heap equivalence.

    A comparison of two established typeof results projects compatible tag domains onto their preserved sources. On equality retain each source member whose tag can occur on the other side. On inequality exclude a tag only when every possible value of the other source has that tag. Unknown tags prevent an exclusion that depends on them. Apply this projection to a nonliteral typeof switch label with the ordinary label-effect and fallthrough joins. A shared tag does not establish equal values or equal proposal types: numeric-family collisions and the Object/null collision remain.

    A call proved to select the original Object.is intrinsic can project compatible known primitive domains onto its preserved data arguments. A singleton String or other supported exact primitive value supplies success evidence and a sign- and family-correct miss exclusion. For the Number domain, success against the original Number NaN selects the NaN category and failure excludes it. Success against negative zero establishes that zero value; failure excludes only that sign, retaining positive zero. SameValue does not contextually adopt a Number argument into a sized numeric family. A broader representable domain is retained where finer identity cannot be expressed; decimal cohort distinctions are not discarded. Both this intrinsic and a later intrinsic consuming its evidence require independent origin proofs. Unknown calls, getters, replacement, argument mapping or conversion supply no unsupported relation.

    For an immutable object binding pattern, apply the primitive-copy rule separately at each established data extraction. Capture the current member domain and evidence at its read point, check the binding conversion and retain a relation only where the copy preserves identity. Renaming does not change that identity. A later computed key, getter, default, rest collection or other effect can break the relation to the current source while leaving the earlier primitive snapshot's own evidence intact. Unknown accessors, alternative origins and unresolved conversions supply no relation. Nested object patterns apply the same rule to each admitted data path. Array binding patterns consume their selected iterator and acquire no indexed-source relation from this object-field rule. Participation, declared binding types and reference liveness are unchanged.

    A successful structural type test or structural member pattern may project its established member evidence onto a corresponding stable data path. Admit only proved data storage, including typed data fields and immutable Composite members, whose identity survives every remaining observation in the test or pattern. Accessors, unknown extractors, refinements that may run code, and unknown iteration supply no such projection. Conjunction sequences evidence, while alternatives retain only evidence common to successful alternatives. Failure of a multi-property test does not establish which member failed. This projection changes neither the declared member store type nor the scope of any pattern binding.

    The internal truthiness evidence for a preserved scalar is related to that scalar's actual falsy values, even where its public truthy and falsy parts both contain the broad member. The only falsy String is the empty String; BigInt has zero; floating numeric domains additionally distinguish both zero signs and NaN. A truthy edge excludes every applicable falsy possibility. Subsequent truthiness is proved only when every possible falsy value has been excluded; an unexcluded NaN or nullish union member prevents that proof. A falsy String observation may retain its existing empty-String literal type internally. These facts follow the same joins, invalidations, numeric identities and equality semantics as scalar exclusions, and create no public complement type. A short-circuit reachability judgment reads this same evidence about the captured left value. Reject a right operand only when the established answer skips it: a truthy left side of && or a falsy left side of || instead selects the right operand. A NaN-only category is falsy. Use the same result feasibility when joining tested expression results.

    An established awaited-result contract supplies the resumed expression's truthy and falsy parts in a deciding position. Awaiting a Promise is not a transparent test of the Promise object, and this result contract carries no arbitrary pre-suspension place relation. Unknown assimilation or fulfillment alternatives remain conservative. Absence of a normal fulfilled result follows 25; rejection and finalization remain separate paths.

    Metadata comparison requests may identify a stable binding or property path through parentheses, with a constant on either side. Mirror the comparison operator when the constant is on the left. Use the current type of that place and carry the request's lexical identity and dependencies through the same joins and invalidations as other facts. Arbitrary expressions and unstable paths establish no place fact, and unresolved hooks retain their existing conservative behaviour.

    A declared call fact refers to the argument value supplied at its target. A tagged template uses the same selected-signature and argument mapping rules, with its cooked template object first and its original substitutions following in evaluation order. Unresolved overload selection supplies no arbitrary predicate or assertion. If a later argument changes the target place or invalidates its fact, that captured value supplies no fact about the changed place. A void assertion establishes its facts at the call's normal completion, including when the call is parenthesized or an operand of another expression. A position reached both through that completion and through a path that skipped the call receives their join. The spelling of a statement body with or without braces does not change this rule.

    Note

    This analysis composes the proposal's existing type tests; it is not general constant folding, satisfiability solving, or proof of a predicate's implementation. The deciding-position restrictions, stable-membership conditions, literal-idiom exceptions and exhaustiveness limits of 1.8.5.4 continue to apply. A constant-answer membership query in a value position remains permitted. Propagating a type fact does not keep a borrowed location alive, permit a relocation, or remove a runtime boundary check otherwise required by this proposal.

    1.8.5.2 The Canonical Total Order

    The total order over canonical Type Records that CanonicalizeType invokes is fixed as follows, so that the member order a program observes through reflection is the same on every host. Records of different [[Kind]] order by the row order of Table 1. Records of one kind order by their fields in that table's order, compared as: a Type Record recursively by this order; a List element-wise and then shorter first; a String by code units; a Number by numeric value with -0𝔽 before +0𝔽 and NaN greatest; a BigInt by value; a Boolean with false before true; a Symbol by the order in which each is first interned into a Type Record within the surrounding Agent; a function, as a deferred record's [[Operator]], by the source position of its declaration, module before offset; and a metadata value by the structural comparison of 1.2.7.2 with its leaves ordered by these same rules. Where one field holds values of two different ECMAScript language types, as a literal's [[Value]] does, they order by type, in the order String, Number, BigInt, Boolean, Symbol.

    Note

    The order is arbitrary and load-bearing at once: nothing about it matters except that every host computes the same one, because canonical order is observable, a union's arms reflect in it and a builder that turns a union into a tuple inherits it, and the determinism invariant of 1.2.7.4 therefore reaches it. A builder wanting a different order sorts. The order among Symbols is Agent-local, because a Symbol is, and it is stable within a program because the same source interns the same symbols in the same sequence; a Symbol never reaches a comparison in another Agent, since a type carrying one cannot be shared.

    1.8.5.3 NarrowTo ( s, t )

    The abstract operation NarrowTo takes arguments s (a Type Record) and t (a Type Record) and returns either a Type Record or empty. It returns the type of a value known to be of the type s and also of the type t, or empty if no value can be of both. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s.[[Kind]] is any, return t.
    2. If s.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. Let kept be a new empty List.
      2. For each element m of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(m, t, « ») is true, append m to kept.
        2. Else if IsSubtype(t, m, « ») is true, append t to kept.
      3. If kept is empty, return empty.
      4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: kept }).
    3. If IsSubtype(s, t, « ») is true, return s.
    4. If IsSubtype(t, s, « ») is true, return t.
    5. If t.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. Let parts be a new empty List.
      2. For each element m of t.[[Members]], do
        1. Let part be NarrowTo(s, m).
        2. If part is not empty, append part to parts.
      3. If parts is empty, return empty.
      4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: parts }).
    6. If s is a class type and t is a class type, return empty.
    7. If AreDisjoint(s, t) is true, return empty.
    8. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: intersection, [[Members]]: « s, t » }).

    A class type is a nominal Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is a class declaration, or the type of a global constructor usable as a type name other than Symbol, Proxy and ProxyHandler. Each is a type whose values are its instances by prototype chain, with the single-inheritance identity a class has, so two class types neither of which is a subtype of the other share no value. Symbol names primitive values, and a proxy takes its target's prototype, so neither has that identity.

    A union t is taken member by member because CanonicalizeType does not distribute an intersection over a union (1.2.2.8): without the step, NarrowTo of a class type against a union of class types it shares no value with would be the intersection C & (A | B), which stands for a type with no values.

    Note

    The disjointness judgment is 1.2.2.6, which this clause once stated in prose and which canonicalization and the Early Error of 1.4.2.1 now share, so a type is empty in one place exactly when it is empty in the others. Two distinct non-composite primitive types have no common values, since each value belongs to exactly one of them (1.5.1), and neither does a non-composite primitive type share values with an object or function type. Two object types, or two nominal types that are interfaces, may have common values, since a class may satisfy both, so an intersection of those is inhabited and is returned. This is the step that yields empty for d ?? 5 where d is a uint8: the narrowed type would be the intersection of uint8 and null | undefined, which has no values.

    empty remains distinct from the never this same disjointness produces in a TYPE, and the difference is what each is for. A narrowing row that cannot succeed is a branch the program wrote and can never take, so it is reported as the mistake it is; a type computation that filters every member away has an answer, and the answer is never. The two are the same judgment put to different uses, which is why they may share the operation without sharing the result.

    1.8.5.4 NarrowFrom ( s: a Type Record, t: a Type Record, ): either a Type Record or empty

    The type errors of this clause apply only in checked code (1.2.5). Outside checked code a test is never refused by them, though their results still narrow.

    description
    It returns the type of a value known to be of the type s and not of the type t, or empty if there is no such value.
    1. If s.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. Let kept be a new empty List.
      2. For each element m of s.[[Members]], do
        1. If IsSubtype(m, t, « ») is false, append m to kept.
      3. If kept is empty, return empty.
      4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: kept }).
    2. If IsSubtype(s, t, « ») is true, return empty.
    3. Return s.

    This operation returns Type Records only. The internal scalar exclusions and generic proof domains of 1.8.5.1 may supply additional flow evidence without changing its result or the identity of a declared type.

    Both NarrowTo and NarrowFrom read a closed set by its members (1.11.8, 1.11.9). Where s, or a member of s, is an enum all of whose enumerators' values are known, it is read as the union of the literal types over the enum of those values, one per value; where it is the type of a sealed abstract class, as the union of the types of its direct subclasses; and where it is boolean, as true | false, a reading inside these operations that leaves the subtype rule of 1.5.19 untouched. A sealed class that is not abstract is a member of its own set and is read as written. Against that reading a literal t whose base is not that enum keeps the enumerators whose value it is, and NarrowFrom removes them, since an enumerator is equal to its value (1.9.2). A result that removed no member of the reading is s as written.

    Both operations return empty where the result they would otherwise return admits no value: a union of no members, a parameterized type whose metadata holds an empty range (6.2), or an intersection of two parameterizations over one base whose governing meta type's meet answers null (Table 42), the last decided by the checking pass, which runs the hook. This is the narrowing counterpart of the Early Error a written intersection of the same pair receives, so the two receive one answer.

    It is a type error to apply a narrowing form where the test can never succeed or can never fail, since the branch it guards is then dead code the program did not intend. These are the branches for which NarrowTo or NarrowFrom returns empty. The sentinel is deliberately not the never type (1.5.18): a test that cannot succeed is reported as a mistake rather than narrowed to the type with no values, because a branch the program wrote and can never take is dead code and not a computation.

    The judgment is made from Static Types, so each direction of it applies only where its answer is a fact no value can lose after it is checked. NarrowTo(s, t) being empty shows a test that can never succeed only where s and t are disjoint across such a boundary: where every value of one is an ECMAScript primitive value - it is a numeric type whose typeof is "number", bigint, string, boolean, symbol, null or undefined, a literal type of one of those, an enum whose underlying type is one of those, a parameterized type over one of those, or a union of such types - and the other is an object, array, tuple, function or nominal type that is not an enum, or a union of those, since a value that is not an Object never becomes one nor the reverse (a vector, complex, rational or composite value is an Object, and type values are Type Objects); where both are primitive, literal or enum types, or parameterized types over one, whose underlying primitive types (an enum's being the type its enumerators have) share no value; or where both are class types (class type), or unions of them, which share no instance; or where s is read as a closed set and every member of that reading meets one of these conditions with t, an enumerator being an immutable value and a subclass a class; or where the result admits no value and both are parameterized types over types whose every value is an ECMAScript primitive value, or unions of those, whose values cannot change. The length and in rows of Table 24 meet it as well, since a fixed shape's length never changes and typed storage cannot be deleted (1.7.6). Disjointness that rests on the members of an object type is not such a boundary, since the object case of 1.7.2.1 is checked at the boundary and not afterwards, and two enums are not disjoint by declaration alone, since their enumerators may share values. NarrowFrom(s, t) being empty shows a test that can never fail only where every member of s and of t is a primitive, literal, enum or class type, or t is any: a value of an object type can stop satisfying it through mutation, and a where refinement is evaluated again by every test. For a pattern test the condition applies to each NarrowTo and NarrowFrom that MatchNarrow and MissNarrow perform (24.3), and an empty produced by one that does not meet it is not a verdict.

    Where a member of s is a parameter with an established upper bound (1.4.3), this judgment reads that member as its bound, since a verdict for the bound holds for every specialization the bound admits. The facts the test establishes keep the parameter, and a parameter with no established bound gives no verdict.

    A relational comparison, <, <=, > or >=, of an operand whose Static Type is a numeric type, a closed set read by its members, or a union of them, with another operand, each contributing limits, a compile-time constant its value and any other operand those of its Static Type, an enum's limits being its least and greatest enumerator values,, in either order, is a test wherever it decides a branch. It can never succeed where no pair of the operands' values satisfies it, and can never fail where every pair does; since NaN satisfies no comparison, a type with a member that can hold NaN is judged only in the first direction. A parameterized member is judged by the metadata row of Table 24 instead. For a proved built-in comparison, apply its judgment separately to existing known source members and remove a member from an edge only where its entire domain proves the opposite outcome. Canonicalize the surviving union. A member that partially overlaps the comparison retains its existing type, and an unresolved member contributes to both possibilities. Respect selected operator dispatch, literal adoption, exact constant representation, NaN and numeric-family admission; no new interval or cross-variable relation is inferred. In a value position a settled comparison remains a question with a constant answer. A comparison of an operand whose Static Type is string, a union of literal String types, or an enum over string, with a String constant, is judged the same way in code-unit order, the empty String being the least String and string having no greatest. A fixed-shape sequence's length (1.4.2.7), a literal String type's among them, is read as its exact length wherever a test reads it, and an index within a literal String's length reads as its own character (27), nothing being claimed past the end, where a read reaches String.prototype: as the limits of this paragraph, as a constant compared with another operand, as the value whose truthiness the truthiness rule settles, and against the case labels of a switch over it.

    An equality, or a case label, whose operand is the global NaN or Number.NaN, unshadowed, can never succeed, and its negation can never fail, since NaN is equal to nothing; where the other operand does not participate (1.9.7), no error results. A proved built-in strict or loose equality of the same preserved data value with itself can never fail, and its negation can never succeed, where its current domain and internal categories exclude NaN. In the supported floating domains, a NaN-only category makes self-equality always false. Self-inequality selects NaN and self-equality excludes it, by 1.8.5.1. Repeated getter reads, unresolved operations and selected user operators establish no such value identity or reflexivity proof.

    A strict equality of two participating operands, neither naming a literal type, can never succeed, and its negation can never fail, where their Static Types share no value under the stability condition, a closed set being read by its members. Two typeof results whose operands' tags (1.12.1) share none are such a pair; two whose operands each have one tag, the same tag, can never differ.

    The disjoint strict-comparison judgment is an operator obligation in checked code: it applies when the result is stored, returned, discarded or used to decide a branch. Determine whether an operand names a literal type from names a literal type, using its resolved source declaration, independently of its current narrowed Static Type. In particular, narrowing an annotated mutable or immutable binding to a literal Type Record does not grant that operand the literal-name exception. This obligation does not make an ordinary pure membership query a deciding test.

    Note 3

    For example, String((5 := uint8) === (5 := uint16)) is subject to that obligation: consuming the Boolean result does not change the operands' contracts. An equality inside a function with unannotated parameters retains its ordinary runtime query where those operands have no participating contracts. Likewise, after let a: uint8 | string = 1, a read of a uses the established current-value fact under 1.8.5.1; a broad union parameter without that fact supplies a different comparison domain. The declared union still permits a later String store. An established current String-key fact is also an input to the ordinary computed-property read judgment: let k: string = "n" can select the uint8 member of { n: uint8 }, whereas a general String parameter without a finite-key fact leaves that selection unknown. These examples do not change the separate rules for type-position indexed access, effect invalidation or reference liveness.

    A test whose value's type settles its truthiness can never succeed or can never fail wherever it decides a branch, including a non-path expression that supplies no place fact. Where the truthy part (1.9.5) of the Static Type of such a test is never, the branch its truth leads to can never be taken, and where the falsy part is never, the other one can never be; it is a type error in either case. A test that is true, false, 0 or 1, under any parentheses and !, is exempt, so while (true), for (;;) and if (false) keep their meaning. The rule reads a test by the Static Type of its value, whatever its form: a conditional expression by the Static Type of the whole and never by the truthiness of an arm, whose value is judged where it is used (1.5.16), though a narrowing form within an arm is still judged where the arm decides the branch, an assignment by its actual returned value after applying store effects, and the producers the tested-expression transfers name by their parts. An operator with a rule of its own keeps it, including the selected-result rule below. A built-in comparison whose result type remains the broad boolean receives no additional settled-truthiness judgment. The left operand of || and && is judged by the paragraph below. The bare-v row supplies the corresponding representable truthy and falsy parts as branch facts. A test whose Static Type is void is refused by 1.5.16 rather than judged here, since it has no value whose truthiness could be settled. An array literal, including one 1.14.8 leaves without a Static Type, has a truthy part only and is never nullish, since it is an Array whatever its elements. So does an untagged template literal any of whose cooked strings is non-empty, since it is a non-empty String.

    After overload resolution and every specified result transformation, an established selected declared operator result is subject to the truthiness judgment in a deciding position. This includes unary, binary and declared compound operators, overloaded negation and derived comparisons. Equality-derived results and derived relational comparisons use the specified ToBoolean and negation, rather than the raw method result or receiver type. A declared compound operator supplies its method result without rebinding the target. Apply ordinary call effects to captured facts; a declared result contract does not prove an operator pure. Unknown dispatch or a result admitting both truth values stays conservative. Do not inspect or execute an operator body to infer a constant answer.

    The established normal Object results of match all, generator do * and async generator async do * expressions are truthy under the same judgment. An empty collection is still an Object; yielded and returned generator values are not the generator object. This does not apply the ordinary match/do scalar-result transfer to these forms, execute a generator body, prove nonemptiness, or discard abrupt completions. An unknown transformed result retains conservative checking.

    switch labels are tested in order, so a case label is a narrowing form over what the earlier labels left, by the case e rows of Table 24. A label whose value an earlier label of the same switch tested can never succeed, and so can a typeof label whose tag is not one typeof produces. The default of a switch over an enum holds the discriminant with every case's type removed (1.11.8), and is a branch that can never be taken where that is empty. So is the default of a switch whose discriminant's every member is boolean, null or undefined, closed sets the language owns, once its labels leave nothing; this requires no case, and a written union of literal types stays outside, as the note below says.

    Note 4

    This is why d ?? 5 is rejected where d is a uint8: the left operand can never be nullish, so NarrowTo of uint8 and null | undefined keeps no member and the test is a mistake rather than silent dead code. A test whose narrowing keeps no member is a mistake WHERE IT DECIDES A BRANCH; elsewhere it is a question with a constant answer, which a program may legitimately ask — a instanceof uint8 for a uint8 a is how one demonstrates what the operator answers, and is not dead code. The ?? above is rejected in a value position for a different reason, and the distinction is worth keeping apart: its RIGHT OPERAND can never be evaluated, so the form contains code the program wrote and cannot reach, where an impossible instanceof merely has a constant result. The same reading applies to || and && whose left operand's type settles the test, and to ||= and &&=, whose right operand is a store that can then never be evaluated. The nullish forms read both ways: ?. on a receiver that is always nullish can never evaluate the rest of its chain, and ??= on a target that is always nullish always stores, so each is rejected as the ?? above is.

    Narrowing on typeof is weaker here than in a type system layered over the language, and deliberately so, because typeof is unchanged: it reports "number" for every numeric type, so typeof v === "number" narrows uint8 | string to uint8 but cannot separate uint8 from uint16, and reports "object" for the SIMD, rational, and complex types. Reflect.typeOf and instanceof are what distinguish those, and instanceof is the form that narrows. A program discriminating a union of numeric types therefore writes instanceof, not typeof.

    Narrowing a binding or stable path relies on the invalidation rules in 1.8.5.1. Assignment to the path or a prefix can end the fact. This does not license narrowing arbitrary repeated property expressions: the path restrictions above and the structural-membership stability conditions remain necessary (1.11.1).

    The switch row covers the exhaustiveness the design reserves to enums and sealed classes. A union of literal types deliberately does not drive exhaustiveness, so it narrows in each case but its default is not proven unreachable.

    1.9 Operators

    For binary arithmetic, bitwise and ordered operators, it is a type error when participating operand contracts establish that every possible selected path fails a required primitive conversion or produces numeric categories incompatible with that operation. Consider declared and derived operator dispatch and contextual literal adoption first. A known Symbol on a selected numeric or ordered-conversion path fails; multiplying BigInt by Boolean fails because the latter converts to Number. Arithmetic's numeric-category exclusions do not apply to ordered comparison or equality merely because the same types occur there. This negative proof does not prohibit otherwise successful coercions. An unknown or viable alternative, or unresolved operator dispatch, prevents the proof. Participation and preservation of ordinary JavaScript exception timing follow 1.9.7.

    Follow established primitive conversion results into the selected operation's own numeric-family rules. On the built-in numeric path, Boolean, null and undefined produce Number and therefore cannot serve as a sized numeric-family operand where that operation requires matching families. This applies to such ordered operations as well as arithmetic and bitwise operations; it does not import BigInt arithmetic restrictions into comparison. Ordinary Number operations, successful String coercions, contextual literal adoption and applicable declared operators are unaffected. Reject only when every selected path fails; an explicit any or unresolved dispatch retains runtime checking.

    The built-in >>> operation is unavailable for the ECMAScript bigint type, including when both converted operands are BigInt. A participating operation, including the built-in operation of >>>=, is a type error when this domain exclusion or the conversion exclusions establish failure on every selected path. Declared dispatch and literal adoption precede this judgment. It does not prohibit BigInt << or >>, Number unsigned right shift, or unsigned right shift in a sized integer value family. An implementation representation using BigInt does not change that family. Unknown alternatives and ordinary untyped expressions retain runtime checking.

    It is a type error for an untagged template substitution, or an operand on a built-in + concatenation path, to require implicit string conversion when its participating Static Type establishes only Symbol values. Participation is the operand-contract judgment of 1.9.7. Applicable declared operators are considered first. A union supplies this negative proof only when all alternatives require the failing conversion; any and unknown coercions retain runtime checking. A tagged template passes its substitution values to the tag without this implicit conversion, but expressions inside its substitutions are checked normally. Explicit String(value) is unaffected. Ordinary JavaScript intrinsic results and unrelated annotations do not change exception timing. No coercion method or getter is executed to answer the judgment.

    This clause specifies what an operator does when its operands are typed. Little new machinery is required, because the specification already has the mechanism: when BigInt was introduced, the operators were generalized from one numeric type to two, and an operator now reduces its operands to numeric values, rejects a pair whose types differ, and dispatches to an abstract operation belonging to the type. This proposal adds numeric types to that mechanism. It does not add a second one.

    Note

    The principle the design states is that typed code changes what a program checks and what its values can represent, and does not change what an operator means. Every rule below follows from it. Where an operator's result is forced by the type rather than chosen, as an integer quotient is, the type decides; everywhere else the operator means what it means today.

    1.9.1 Dispatch

    ToNumeric is revised so that a value of a numeric type of this proposal reaches an operator as itself rather than as a Number.

    1.9.1.1 ToNumeric ( value )

    The abstract operation ToNumeric takes argument value (an ECMAScript language value) and returns either a normal completion containing either a Number, a BigInt, or a value of a numeric type of this proposal, or a throw completion. It returns value converted to a numeric value, preserving the numeric type it already has. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let primValue be ? ToPrimitive(value, number).
    2. If primValue is a value of a numeric type of 1.5, return primValue.
    3. If primValue is a BigInt, return primValue.
    4. Return ? ToNumber(primValue).

    The remaining machinery is unchanged and generalizes as written. In 13.15.3, the step that throws a TypeError when the two operands are not of the same numeric type applies to every numeric type, and the table associating an operator with an abstract operation is read as associating it with T::op for the numeric type T of the operands. The operations are those of 1.5.23.

    Note

    This is the whole of the dispatch. 1n + 1 already throws a TypeError today because the two operands are of different numeric types and neither converts to the other, and uint8(1) + uint16(1) throws for exactly the same reason, by the same step, with no rule specific to it. The shape the committee arrived at for BigInt, an operator that dispatches on the numeric type of its operands and refuses to mix them, is the shape this proposal needs, which is why adding sixteen numeric types costs one inserted step.

    ToNumber is not reached for a typed operand and so is never the vehicle for an implicit conversion, which is what 1.6.10 anticipated. ToNumber keeps its meaning for a value of the any type, whose numeric type is not known statically: the operand arrives as whatever it is, and the same steps apply to it dynamically.

    The string behaviour of + is unchanged and applies before any of this: if either operand is a String after ToPrimitive, the result is the concatenation. uint8(1) + "x" is therefore "1x". This is not an implicit conversion between value types in the sense 1.6.1 forbids, since no uint8 becomes a value of another numeric type; it is the meaning + has always had, and changing it for typed operands would violate the principle above.

    1.9.2 Arithmetic Never Promotes

    In peer-operand literal inference, a literal beside a parameterized numeric value adopts that value's numeric base, not its metadata. This rule precedes primitive-block admission and applies to arithmetic, comparison, equality, and case matching. Explicit binding, argument, return, and cast contexts retain their stated requirements. Integer exponent and shift-count rules retain their own contexts. No unit-polymorphic zero rule is introduced: arithmetic may reject a scalar/quantity pair where strict equality answers false; loose equality retains its mathematical-value rule.

    Two operands of the same value type produce a result of that type. Two operands of different value types are a type error, since neither is assignable to the other. Where one operand is a literal it takes the type of the other (1.6.6), so a literal never forces a conversion.

    The LITERAL rule of the preceding paragraph also reaches ==, !=, ===, !==, and a case label, though the type error of the preceding paragraph does not. A comparison answers rather than computing, so two operands of different numeric types compare unequal instead of being an error; but a literal in one of those positions still takes the other operand's type, so uint8(5) === 5 is true. A binding adopts nothing, so uint8(5) === n for an n of the number type is false, and the values of distinct value types remain distinct. A bigint literal takes no Number-family type, being of a numeric type of its own. A literal the type cannot represent is not equal to any value of it, so the comparison is false rather than an error - unlike an arithmetic position, where the same literal is an Early Error, because there the literal must become a value and here it need not.

    Note 1

    Reaching equality is what makes a typed value usable with the comparisons programs actually write, including inside a callback: a.find(x => x === 65) over a [].<uint16> finds its element, where without the rule it could find nothing. The alternative considered was to leave === strictly identity-based, which is the treatment BigInt receives - but a BigInt has its own literal syntax, 5n, and the types of this proposal have none, so a literal is the ONLY way to write one of their values in a comparison. Declining would have made every such comparison require an explicit conversion.

    It is a type error if the Static Types of the operands of an arithmetic, bitwise, shift, or relational operator are numeric types that are not the same type, except that ordered comparison between the existing unbranded Number and BigInt types retains the base language's mathematical comparison. This exception applies to scalar and union alternatives and does not relax the identity rules for the numeric value types added by this proposal or their brands. A shift's right operand is a DISTANCE rather than a quantity combined with the left one, and is exempt as well: where both operands are of integer types, the distance may be of any of them, the operator takes it as written (1.9.6), and the result has the left operand's type. Converting the distance into the left operand's type could change it, since uint8 of 256 is 0, and would make x << k shift by the wrong amount. Where either operand has the any type the check is deferred, and the TypeError of 1.9.1 is thrown at run time if the selected operation forbids the differing types.

    Note 2

    float32 arithmetic is float32 arithmetic: x * x for a float32 x is computed in float32 and rounds once, rather than widening to float64 and rounding twice. C promotes float to double in many contexts, so the same source can produce different results depending on where a value is used, and the reproducibility this proposal offers across engines depends on refusing that.

    1.9.3 The Operations Each Family Defines

    A numeric type defines the operations of Table 25. An operator whose operation the operand's type does not define is a type error.

    Note

    An update expression, ++ or --, steps its operand by one of the operand's own type, as ECMAScript applies add with the type's unit. An integer, a binary floating-point, a decimal floating-point and a rational number have that unit, the last two stepping in their own type since neither has a Number value. A complex number has none: the complex numbers are the family the table leaves unordered, and an update of one is a type error, as an operation its type does not define.

    The Number type continues to define the bitwise and shift operations, which convert their operand with ToInt32 as they do today, and no existing program changes. A float32 does not, because the same conversion applied to it would be an implicit conversion between two value types: ~x for a float32 x is a type error rather than a silent trip through int32. This is the one place where an operator that works on a Number does not work on the corresponding typed value, and it follows from the conversion rule rather than from a decision about bitwise operators.

    The table is the answer to the three cases 1.5.23 left open. Two of them are absences, complex having no order and a rational having no remainder. The third, a vector comparison returning a vector, is not an absence but a signature the protocol cannot express, since lessThan is required to return a Boolean. Rather than widening the protocol for one family, the vector comparisons are declared operators, which is a path the specification already provides and which admits the return-type overloading they need (1.10.5).

    1.9.4 The Result of an Operator

    1.9.3 states which operations a family has. This clause states what an application of one yields, which Table 2 does not reach: that table gives the Static Type of a literal, a binding, and a type name, and an operator application is none of those.

    Where a declared operator applies (1.9.9), its overload set is resolved using the operand types and the application's contextual return type, as for a call (1.10.3). Its selected signature supplies the result type; that type need not be the receiver's type. Apply any specified Boolean conversion or negation before judging the actual normal result in a deciding position under 1.8.5.4. The declaration does not establish that invocation preserves captured facts. The following rules apply to the built-in operation when no declared operator applies.

    For the built-in in and instanceof operators, including the private-name form of in, it is a type error if the right operand's Static Type establishes that its value is not an Object. This judgment includes non-object primitive types and their literal and qualified forms; a union is rejected by this rule only when every alternative is known to be non-object. Unknown types, open type parameters and unions with a possible Object retain the runtime check. Type Objects and composite objects are Objects for this judgment, irrespective of their Type Record's [[Kind]]. This is an object-eligibility check, not a requirement that an instanceof operand be a constructor: an object with a custom Symbol.hasInstance remains eligible. The normal runtime protocol checks still apply.

    For instanceof, a participating right operand also contributes its effective declared Symbol.hasInstance contract. A typed class constructor contributes its constructor-side static contract, including inherited and specialized members and established immutable lexical aliases. Use actual declaration and well-known Symbol identity rather than the expression's spelling; decorated, replaced or unknown origins retain their existing deferral. It is a type error if every possible selected hook call is known to be invalid: a present non-nullish hook cannot be called, or the actual left operand cannot satisfy its applicable argument signatures. The hook is selected before any ordinary instance-test shortcut for a primitive left operand. Its result is passed to ToBoolean, so an Object result is valid. Nullish hooks retain the ordinary callable-target fallback. An optional hook prevents this hook-call proof unless its fallback also fails under the rule below. Open callable possibilities, unknown contracts and viable alternatives prevent a closed negative proof; missing declarations on open objects do not prove absence. The judgment uses the actual well-known Symbol and inherited and specialized contracts, invokes no getter or hook, and preserves reference decay and liveness. This protocol proof does not replace the separate per-alternative requirements on explicit function calls.

    For the nullish-hook fallback, it is a type error when both the effective Symbol.hasInstance contract is proved nullish and a stable creation origin proves that the participating target is an ordinary non-callable Object. An ordinary object literal and its stable aliases can supply the latter fact. An open structural type or a nominal class name without such an origin does not prove the absence of [[Call]], and an annotation whose conversion may replace the creation result withdraws the origin proof. Every selected alternative must fail; a viable custom hook, unknown origin or undeclared hook prevents the negative proof. A primitive left operand does not skip the target's fallback callability requirement. No getter, hook or reference is evaluated, and runtime reference checks remain required.

    For a numeric operator whose operand Static Types include a union, the same-type and family-availability judgments below are negative proofs over the operand alternatives. It is a type error only when every possible combination is known to have no applicable operation. Consider declared and derived operator dispatch before built-in availability, retain brands when comparing numeric identity, and consider a literal in each applicable numeric context. An unknown alternative or unresolved dispatch prevents this proof. Failed alternatives contribute no diagnostics, literal contexts or result types. This judgment does not require a Cartesian product of result types and does not change the per-alternative requirements on function calls. Where an alternative remains viable, retain the runtime check for the actual operands; do not apply a scalar built-in exclusion to bypass a possible declared operator in another alternative.

    The Static Type of that operator application is determined as follows.

    1. If the operator is &&, ||, or ??, the Static Type is the union of the short-circuiting part of the left operand's Static Type and the right operand's Static Type, where the short-circuiting part is the falsy part (1.9.5) for &&, the truthy part for ||, and, for ??, the result of NarrowFrom (1.8.5) applied to that Static Type and null | undefined; where that part has no members, the Static Type is the right operand's Static Type alone, and where the complementary part has no members, so that the left operand always short-circuits and the right is never evaluated, the Static Type is the short-circuiting part alone.
    2. Else if the operator is an equality or relational operator other than one whose operands are vectors, the Static Type is the primitive type named "boolean".
    3. Else if the operator is +, the built-in operation is established, and either operand is known to contain only String values, the Static Type is the primitive type named "string".
    4. Else if either operand's Static Type is a literal type and the other's is not, the literal adopts the other operand's numeric base, excluding metadata (1.6.6), or beside a vector type the numeric base of that type's lane type, and this rule is applied again.
    5. Else if one operand's Static Type is a vector type and the other operand has the numeric base of the vector type's lane type, the other operand broadcasts: it is converted by the lane cast (1.5.8), and this rule is applied again.
    6. Else if the operands' Static Types are not the same type, it is a type error: an operator does not combine two numeric types (1.9.2).
    7. Else if the operands' Static Type is a vector type, the Static Type is that vector type, the operator having been applied at each lane; except that a relational or equality operator between vectors is overloaded on its result type (17).
    8. Else if the family of the operands' Static Type does not define the operation, it is a type error.
    9. Else, the Static Type is the operands' Static Type.

    The concatenation result judgment reads String category evidence through literal bases, parameterized, shared and reference wrappers, enum underlying types and established type-parameter bounds. Every member of a non-empty union must supply the evidence; one member of an intersection suffices where that member restricts every inhabitant to String. An unresolved member or recursive revisit supplies no evidence. Existing lexical constant evidence may supply a String literal; this does not assign a permanent contract to an unannotated mutable binding. Parentheses are transparent. The resulting string is the type of a normal completion, not a proof that primitive conversion succeeds. Apply the existing conversion-failure judgments and ordinary destination checks; a contextual numeric destination neither changes + to addition nor parses the String. No getter, conversion or operator body is evaluated to obtain this fact, and the operand's actual type, metadata, participation and reference permissions are unchanged.

    A selected declared class operator or primitive-block definition retains its result contract before the built-in concatenation judgment. An open left operand may carry a declared operator whose result is not String. Failure to select a primitive block for an entire compound operand contract does not establish absence of dispatch for each member. Preserve an established selected result; unresolved dispatch or result alternatives do not justify replacing that result with string. This judgment does not change overload admission, evaluation order, abrupt completions or reference liveness.

    The two exceptions in that step are duals, and between them they keep the Static Type to the values the expression can produce: obj && f() is the type of f(), since no object value is falsy and the left cannot be produced, while undefined && f() is undefined, since the right is never evaluated at all.

    The first step is where the short-circuit operators part company with the rest: they produce one of their OPERANDS rather than a value of a common type, so the step that refuses two unlike types does not reach them and a && a < 10 is a uint32 or a boolean rather than an error. A contextual type applies to the operands rather than to the application, since it is an operand that is produced: let c: uint32 = x || 10 puts the 10 at uint32 by literal propagation exactly as let c: uint32 = 10 does. A literal that is a member of a union reaches its target only this way, since assignability compares the union as a whole.

    An untyped numeric literal at a union is adapted toward the member it FITS, by the rule 1.7.3.3.1 applies to a value: narrower before wider, an integer member before a floating one, and a member whose range excludes the value not at all. let _v_: string | uint8 = 1 gives _v_ the uint8 member, and { x: 1 } at { x: int32 } | { x: uint8 } gives its x the same member the scalar position would.

    The members are ordered and flattened first, so which member is chosen is a property of the TYPE and not of how the program spelled it. Where no member accepts the value the literal is refused, as it is at a single type.

    The members need not differ in a NUMERIC type, and the difference need not be at the literal's own level. Where they differ in an object member, an array member, a tuple member, or in a member of one of those in turn, the literal is adapted toward the first member it fits, by the same rule. { p: { x: 1 } } at { p: { x: int32 } } | { p: { x: string } } reaches the first, and so does { p: [1] } at { p: []<int32> } | { p: []<string> }.

    Note 1

    Whether a literal fits a member is decided by ATTEMPTING the adaptation and observing whether it reports, not by comparing types. By the time a member must be chosen the literal has a type in which the values are gone - { p: { x: 1 } } is { p: { x: number } } - so a question about range, which decides { p: { x: 70000 } } against { p: { x: uint8 } }, cannot be asked of it.

    An attempt that reports nothing is a fit whatever it returns. An ARRAY literal adapted against its target returns no type at all - 1.14.9 withholds one so the boundary is not elided, since the boundary is where an Array carrying the element type is built - and it is nonetheless adapted, on the same evidence as any other literal.

    An attempt that reports is discarded together with anything it recorded, so a member that does not fit leaves nothing behind for the members after it.

    An INTERSECTION is not this case: its members must ALL be satisfied, so members that disagree admit nothing and the literal is refused.

    The last step is the substance of it: an operator on operands of one type yields that type, and never a wider one. What follows from that, and is not implied by a type's name, is collected here.

    Note 2

    Three results in the table are worth stating in words, being the ones a type's name does not suggest.

    An integer type divides by truncating toward zero and wraps on overflow, so 7 / 2 at uint8 is 3 and 1 - 3 at uint8 is 254. 1.13.2 gives the forms that trap or clamp instead.

    A one-bit integer is an integer, so 1 + 1 at boolean1 is 0. The name suggests a Boolean, but the family is integer and the arithmetic wraps at one bit as it wraps at eight.

    A relational or equality operator yields a Boolean and not a value of a sized type, because it answers a question rather than computing a quantity and so has no result type to preserve. A comparison between vectors is the exception the fourth step names, and is overloaded on its result type because a lane-wise comparison has more than one useful shape.

    1.9.5 The Falsy and Truthy Parts of a Type

    The falsy part of a type is the union of the members of that type that have a falsy value, and the truthy part is the union of the members that have a truthy value. A member contributes to a part as follows, and where a member contributes to neither the part is a union of no members, the never type.

    Note

    A numeric type, string, and bigint contribute the whole member to both parts, because each has both falsy and truthy values and the falsy one has no type of its own to name: a uint32 zero is a value of uint32, and there is no narrower type this specification can write for it. Naming the member is the widening direction, and a wider Static Type is sound where a narrower one would be a claim the type system cannot support. An implementation that can name the value more precisely, as it can for boolean, may do so.

    These parts are what make the common idioms type as written. s || "anon" at a string is a string, since the truthy part of string is string and both operands are then of one type. x ?? 10 where x is uint32 | undefined is a uint32, since NarrowFrom removes the absent member. obj && f() is the type of f(), since no object value is falsy and the left contributes nothing. And a && a < 10 where a is a uint32 is uint32 | boolean rather than boolean, which is the honest statement: the expression evaluates to a where a is zero. A program that wants the Boolean writes !!(a && a < 10).

    1.9.6 Integer Operations

    For an integer type T of width N, each operation computes the exact mathematical result and then reduces it to a value of T as Table 19 specifies for an integer target: the result is taken modulo 2**_N_ and interpreted as a value of _T_. Overflow therefore wraps, in two's complement for a signed type, and discards the bits that do not fit.

    T::divide returns the exact quotient truncated toward zero. T::remainder returns the remainder whose sign follows the dividend, unchanged in meaning from the Number type. If the divisor is zero, both throw a RangeError exception.

    It is a type error if the divisor of / or % is a known integer operand whose value is zero and the operands are of an integer type of this proposal. A known integer operand is a literal, a const bound to a constant expression over literals and such constants (1.8.2), an explicit conversion of either to an integer type in either spelling (1.6.7), its value being the conversion's result, or a const of an integer value type whose initializer is one of these. uint8(256) is therefore the value 0, and (-1 := uint8) the value 255.

    The shift operators take their distance as written: x << k is the exact x × 2*`k` reduced as above, and `x` `>>` `k` the exact quotient of `x` by 2`k` rounded toward negative infinity, so a distance of _N_ or more shifts every bit out and leaves 0, or -1 where `>>` is applied to a negative value of a signed type. The distance is NOT reduced modulo _N_. If the distance is negative, the operators throw a *RangeError exception, and it is a type error if it is a known integer operand whose value is negative or at least N, the divisor rule one operator along.

    Note 1

    The distance rule is a consequence of the reduction rule above rather than an addition to it, and is stated because three implementations of one operator disagreed about it while that rule sat above them. x << k and x × 2*`k` are the same computation, so they must not part company at any distance; reducing the distance modulo _N_ would make `x` `<<` _N_ answer `x` while `x` × 2*_N_ answers 0. The masking rule is what Java, C# and WebAssembly adopt and what the shift instructions of common hardware do, and it is available to an implementation wherever it can show the distance is below the width, which is nearly everywhere. What it cannot be is the meaning of the operator: a mask is only free where _N_ is a power of two, and `uint.<24>` and `uint.<40>` are ordinary types here.

    A negative distance throws for the reason a zero divisor does: it names no result. Treating it as an exact power would make the answer depend on the operand, since 2*-1 times an even value is an integer and times an odd one is not, and the reduction step has no meaning for a non-integer. The literal rule is the divisor rule one operator along, and both reference designs do the same: a constant shift at or above the width is a compile error in Rust under its default overflow lint, and a negative constant shift count is illegal in Go, whose specification otherwise states this clause's rule exactly — "there is no upper limit on the shift count", and "`x` `<<` 1 is the same as `x`2".

     Note 2

    Truncating toward zero and taking the remainder's sign from the dividend are one decision rather than two, because the identity (a / b) * b + a % b = a holds only when the quotient and the remainder round the same way. Truncated division pairs with a dividend-signed remainder and floored division with a divisor-signed one; mixing them produces an arithmetic that does not add back up whenever the dividend is negative and the remainder is not zero, which is two of the four sign combinations. The floored pair is available under its own name rather than by redefining the operators, as Math.divFloor and Math.mod in 1.13.3.

    That an integer quotient truncates is not a choice. An int32 has nowhere to put 1.5, so the result type decides the answer, and this is the one operator whose meaning the type changes. A floored % would be a choice, since both answers fit the type, which is why the operator keeps the meaning it has for a Number.

    Division by zero throws because an integer type has no infinity and no NaN, so there is nothing to return. A float is unaffected and keeps the answer it has today: float32(1) / 0 is an infinity and float32(1) % 0 is a NaN, because a float has somewhere to put them.

    The literal-zero rule matches the treatment of a literal that does not fit its type (Table 22): it is a mistake visible in the source text, so it does not compile, while a divisor whose value is not known until run time raises a RangeError there. It deliberately does not extend to bigint, where 1n / 0n continues to throw a RangeError exception at run time: that expression is legal today, and rejecting it earlier would break an existing program. The asymmetry is a compatibility constraint rather than a design view, and it is worth stating in the design document, which does not currently note that the rule stops at the new types.

    1.9.7 Unary Operators

    The negative update/store proof includes an established numeric read with a callable, structural object, array, tuple or nominal destination that cannot receive the updated value. Determine the actual setter or reference-location write contract, including applicable inbound conversions and declared operator precedence. Unknown or viable alternatives prevent rejection. This is a conversion-and-store judgment, not ordinary assignment compatibility: the existing numeric-to-String update path remains admitted.

    Unary - applies T::unaryMinus for the numeric type T of its operand. For an unsigned integer type of width N, the result is 2*_N_ minus the operand, modulo 2*_N_, so unary minus on an unsigned value wraps rather than raising an error.

    For a built-in prefix or postfix increment or decrement, it is a type error when the participating operand contract proves that every possible path fails either numeric conversion or storing the updated value in the operand's location. The judgment uses the actual write contract, including a setter parameter or reference referent, rather than assuming it equals the read type. It computes the updated value where needed for a literal destination, respecting the numeric type's rounding and wrapping; the value stored is distinct from a postfix expression's result. An unknown conversion, destination or applicable operator prevents this proof. A union with a successful path retains its runtime check.

    For example, a boolean location cannot receive a built-in increment's numeric result, a symbol value cannot undergo its numeric conversion, and a location of literal type 1 cannot receive 2. A location of 1 | 2 can increment from 1; it is not rejected solely because incrementing 2 fails. Number, BigInt and the proposal's numeric updates, including wrapping, remain valid, as does numeric-to-String conversion on the existing update/store path. This rule does not replace that boundary with ordinary assignment checking. Applicable declared updates precede the built-in judgment and retain their result/store requirements. No location is evaluated, borrowed or pinned to perform the proof; write permission and reference liveness remain independently required.

    Unary + returns its operand unchanged when the operand is a value of a numeric type of this proposal. It continues to throw a TypeError for a BigInt, and continues to apply ToNumber otherwise.

    After applicable user-defined operator dispatch, it is a type error to apply unary + to an operand whose participating Static Type establishes only BigInt or Symbol values, or unary - or ~ to one establishing only Symbol values. Participation here is an operand contract: an annotation, a declared member, a declared or published return, or an inferred contribution carrying such a contract through a constant, pattern, iteration binding or enclosing value expression. An unrelated typed condition or annotation in the surrounding body contributes no operand contract. A union proves this error only when every alternative is forbidden by the operator; any and unresolved alternatives retain the runtime check.

    Knowledge of an ordinary JavaScript literal or intrinsic result is not such participation: +1n, +Symbol(), +BigInt(1), and aliases or patterns derived solely from those untyped values retain their runtime exception timing. An ordinary unannotated mutable binding does not acquire a permanent contract from its initializer. A rejected typed unary-plus expression does not publish a BigInt result. This rule changes no conversion semantics: BigInt still admits unary minus and bitwise NOT, the proposal's numeric types keep their own operations, and declared operators are resolved before the built-in domain is tested. No reference permission or liveness rule changes.

    Note

    Unary minus on an unsigned value is defined rather than rejected because the alternative is worse: an unsigned type is a bit pattern as much as a count, and -x on it is the two's complement negation the hardware computes. Casting to the signed type first is usually clearer, and a program that wants the error uses the checked form.

    Unary + is a decision, and it is recorded here because it splits from BigInt. +x throws for a BigInt because +x is the idiom for coercing to a Number, and returning a BigInt from it would silently defeat that idiom. The same argument applies to a uint8, and would say +x should throw for every type this proposal adds. Against it: operator+() is an overloadable unary operator on a class in the design, so unary + already means more than ToNumber, and an earlier clause of this specification states that +a on a uint8 is a uint8. This clause follows the design. If the committee prefers consistency with BigInt, the change is to this step alone, and it would make +x a TypeError for every numeric type of this proposal.

    1.9.8 Equality and Comparison

    === and !== are not overloadable and retain their identity semantics. What identity means follows from the type. The identity of a reference type is the reference, so two distinct objects are never ===. The identity of a value type is its value, as it already is for a uint8 and a String, so two instances of a value type class are === exactly when their fields are, compared field by field.

    == between two values of the same numeric type applies T::equal. Between two values of different numeric types it is false rather than a type error, as it is today between a Number and a BigInt of unequal value, and IsLooselyEqual continues to compare their mathematical values where both are numeric. A decimal compares by numerical value, so a value with trailing zeros equals one without them (1.5.4).

    The relational operators apply T::lessThan through IsLessThan, unchanged.

    Note

    That === compares a value type class field by field rather than by reference is what makes a value type a value: two Vector2 instances holding the same coordinates are the same value, and a Map keyed on them has one entry. This is the existing rule for a uint8 and a String applied to an aggregate, not a new one.

    == returning false across numeric types rather than throwing is the existing treatment of a Number against a BigInt, and it is deliberately not aligned with the arithmetic operators, which do throw. This specification states the rule the design left open: == and != between two typed values compare by the loose-equality algorithm they already use, so uint8(1) == uint16(1) is true by comparison of mathematical values, while uint8(1) + uint16(1) remains a compile-time type error. The two are deliberately not aligned: an arithmetic operator produces a value and so must fix the type it produces, which is why a cross-type use is rejected rather than silently widened; equality asks a question and produces a Boolean whatever its operands' types, so it has no result type to fix and no information to lose by answering. This is a stated position rather than an inherited one; a committee that prefers equality to throw across typed values, for symmetry with arithmetic, has the alternative recorded here.

    1.9.9 User-Defined Operators

    A class may declare an operator, in which case the receiver is the left operand and the declaration's parameter is the right. Where an operator's operands are of a type that declares it, the declaration is applied in place of the steps above. The overloadable operators are the arithmetic, bitwise, shift, relational, and logical operators, their compound assignment forms, the increment and decrement operators in prefix and postfix form, the unary operators, the index accessors, and the conversion operator of 1.6.8.

    A COMPOUND ASSIGNMENT form that a class declares is invoked as a method call on the left operand, and THE ASSIGNMENT TARGET IS NOT WRITTEN: the value of _a_ op= _b_ is whatever the declared operator returns, and the binding, field or element named on the left is left as it was. Such an operator therefore applies to a const binding.

    Where the class declares the BINARY operator and not the compound form, _a_ op= _b_ is _a_ = _a_ op _b_ as it is today, and the target is written — so that form does not apply to a const binding. Which of the two a program gets is a consequence of what its class declares.

    Note 1

    A declared compound operator exists to update its receiver in place, which is what makes it worth declaring beside the binary form; writing the returned value back over the target would make the form a reassignment and defeat that. It matters most for a value type, whose bindings are usually const precisely because the value is updated through the operator rather than replaced — so writing the target back made the form unavailable exactly where it was meant to be used. Returning this is what allows chaining, and this rule is what allows the receiver to have been mutated by the time it is returned.

    === and !== are not overloadable. An operator that the operand's type already defines through 1.5.23 may not be redeclared for that type, so a program cannot redefine uint8 addition. An operator a built-in type does not define may be declared for it, which is how the SIMD extension gives the vector types their comparisons and how the primitive metadata extension declares operators on a parameterized primitive.

    A relational operator that the class does NOT declare is derived from < where < is declared: _a_ > _b_ is _b_ < _a_, _a_ <= _b_ is the negation of _b_ < _a_, and _a_ >= _b_ is the negation of _a_ < _b_. The result of the declared operator is coerced with ToBoolean before being negated, since it is a user function and may return any value. A DECLARED operator always takes precedence over the derivation, so a class that declares both < and > uses each as written.

    Without this an undeclared relational operator reached the abstract relational comparison, which coerces both operands to "[object Object]" and compares that String with itself - making > always false and <= and >= always true for any class declaring only <. Half of those answers are correct by coincidence, which is why only the reversed operand order reveals it: _M_(2) > _M_(1) answered false.

    Note 2

    Deriving <= as the negation of _b_ < _a_ assumes a TOTAL order. Where neither _a_ < _b_ nor _b_ < _a_ holds - as for a NaN-like value under a partial order - the derived <= answers true where false is meant. A type whose order is partial should declare <= itself, which the precedence rule above permits. Partiality cannot be detected from < alone, so this is a caution to the author of such a type rather than a rule the implementation can enforce.

    An index accessor is applied by a computed member access rather than by an operator between two operands. A computed access may supply more than one index, grid[x, y], which is how the design writes a multidimensional or jagged index. Where the base of a computed access is an instance of a class that declares an index accessor, and every index supplied is a value of a numeric type, the access applies the accessor whose parameter count matches the number of indices, with those indices as its argument list, in place of the ordinary property read or write: the read direction for a value use and the write direction for the target of an assignment, the write direction taking the indices followed by the assigned value. An index that is not of a numeric type makes the access an ordinary property access, so an index accessor does not shadow the string-keyed and symbol-keyed properties, including the methods, of an instance it applies to. Resolution among several index accessors of one class is overload resolution on the number of indices and then on their types (1.10.3), as for any overloaded operator, so a class may declare [i] and [x, y] and each is reached by the access that matches it.

    Where a class declares a read direction whose Static Type is a reference type and declares no write direction for that number of indices, an assignment whose target is such an access stores through the reference the read direction returns. This is the assignment-target rule of 2.8 applied to an index access: the accessor is a call whose result is a reference, and a reference denotes the place a write goes, which is why the design writes such an accessor without a setter. A read direction whose result is not a reference has no location for a write to reach, and an assignment to it is a TypeError exception. It is a type error for a class to declare both a reference-returning read direction and a write direction for the same number of indices, since the write would have two meanings.

    Note 3

    A read-modify-write applies the accessor once per direction, as it does for a declared read and write pair: the read yields the value at the location and the write asks for the location again.

    Where no accessor applies, a computed access supplying several indices has the meaning it has in the base language: the brackets hold one expression, the indices are its comma-separated operands, and the key is the value of the last. Every operand is evaluated, in order, whether or not an accessor applies, so which reading a given access takes is observable only in the value it produces and never in the effects it has. A parenthesized m[(a, b)] supplies one index, as it reads.

    For an applicable index accessor, check each supplied index expression as an argument of its selected signature. Apply the corresponding parameter's contextual type under 1.6.5, retaining the expression's source and numeric adaptation eligibility. Thus m[(effect(), 2)] supplies one argument whose final literal can take the index parameter's type; it does not supply two arguments, adapt the discarded result of effect(), or make (effect(), n) adaptable where n is a stored Number.
