Read and write directions use their own selected parameter contracts. The assigned value and any reference returned by a read direction retain their separate store and liveness obligations.

    Note 4

    Resolution among several declarations of one operator is overload resolution on the operand types, specified in 1.10.3. The operator overloading extension works the rules through a case where the receiver is not the left operand, a scalar multiplying a vector, and states what an engine must guarantee for the result to compile as well as the equivalent C++ would.

    1.10 Functions and Overloading

    This clause defines the structure of a function type, the identity and subtyping of one, and the resolution of a call among several signatures declared for one name.

    1.10.1 Signature Records

    A Signature Record describes one callable signature. It has the fields of Table 28. A function Type Record's [[Signatures]] is a List of them, with more than one element when the function is overloaded.

    A Type Parameter Record describes one declared type parameter, of a signature or of a generic declaration. It has the fields of Table 29.

    The [[Domain]], [[Constraint]] and [[Default]] Parse Nodes retain their declaring environments. Effective constraint and default descriptions may accompany them under 4.2; each description retains its parameter declaration identities and captured substitutions and does not replace per-application evaluation with one declaration-wide concrete result.

    Two Lists of Type Parameter Records are the same up to renaming when they have the same length and, pairwise, the same [[Kind]], [[Variadic]], [[Variance]], and [[Arity]], and constraints and defaults that denote the same types once each parameter of one list is identified with the parameter at the same position of the other. This is how generic signatures compare (1.10.2.1): [[Name]] is never read, so <T: type>(x: T) => T and <U: type>(x: U) => U are one type, and a constraint, a default, a modifier, or the order makes two.

    A Parameter Record has a [[Name]] (a String), a [[Type]] (a Type Record), an [[Optional]] field (a Boolean, true when the parameter is marked ? or has a default), a [[Rest]] field (a Boolean), an [[Initial]] field (an ECMAScript language value or none, the declared default), and a [[Reference]] field (a Boolean). [[Reference]] is true exactly when [[Type]].[[Kind]] is reference: the flag restates the type for convenience, and reflection reads the fact from the type.

    Note 1

    A signature is identified by its parameter types and its return type, so two declarations of one name may differ in the return type alone (1.10.5). Those two declarations are how a name is overloaded, in EVERY goal symbol and every scope: the early error ECMA-262 raises for a redeclared lexical name does not apply to a second FunctionDeclaration of a name a FunctionDeclaration already declared, whose signature differs. A name a let, const or class declaration bound is not one, and is redeclared as it always was.

    Note 2

    Stated for every goal because it was true of only one. A script's top-level function declarations are var-scoped, so a second was already admitted there; a module's and a block's are lexical, so the same two declarations were an early error. Whether a function could be overloaded therefore depended on which file it was written in, which no rule said and none intended.

    Where the signatures do NOT differ, the second declaration is the error this clause already gives — one signature written twice — rather than a redeclaration. The parser cannot tell the two apart, since it has no resolved types; the check that can runs after resolution, and reports at the second declaration either way.

    An export of an overloaded name, named or default, exports the WHOLE set. A name denotes all of its declarations, so an importer resolves against all of them and no declaration is unreachable through the boundary. A parameter's name is carried because the design's named arguments select by it, and is not part of the signature's identity. A parameter's [[Initial]] and a signature's [[ThisType]] are part of the identity, compared by SameValue and as a type; the name is carried from the first occurrence interned, so two structurally identical declarations reflect the first's names. That is an order-of-loading fact, deterministic within a program and tolerated because a parameter has one name and there is nothing else to do with two. It is also the measure of what may be added: no field may be admitted whose value depends on the order modules were reached in, which is a stronger rule than counting fields and is the one 21 satisfies by unioning where a name wins. A decorator's metadata is the case that tests this and does not become an exception to it: two functions of one signature are one type however differently their parameters are decorated, so metadata cannot ride a Signature Record, and 7 reads it from the declaration instead. [[ThisType]] and [[Narrows]] are the design's declarative checker facts: data the checker reads and never code it runs. Both are part of a signature's identity, and both are consumed by 8.

    1.10.2 Identity and Subtyping of Function Types

    These operations complete the cases 1.2.2.2 and 1.2.3.1 defer for the function kind.

    1.10.2.1 SameFunctionType ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation SameFunctionType takes arguments s (a function Type Record), t (a function Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether s and t are the same function type. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s.[[Signatures]] and t.[[Signatures]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
    2. For each integer i such that 0 ≤ i and i < the number of elements of s.[[Signatures]], do
      1. Let a be s.[[Signatures]][i].
      2. Let b be t.[[Signatures]][i].
      3. If a.[[TypeParameters]] and b.[[TypeParameters]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
      4. Let identified be a List whose elements are the elements of assumptions.
      5. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[TypeParameters]], do
        1. Let u be a.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        2. Let w be b.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        3. If u.[[Kind]] is not w.[[Kind]], or u.[[Variadic]] is not w.[[Variadic]], or u.[[Variance]] is not w.[[Variance]], or u.[[Arity]] is not w.[[Arity]], return false.
        4. Append the Record { [[First]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is u.[[Declaration]], [[Second]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is w.[[Declaration]] } to identified.
      6. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[TypeParameters]], do
        1. Let u be a.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        2. Let w be b.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        3. If exactly one of u.[[Constraint]] and w.[[Constraint]] is none, return false.
        4. If u.[[Constraint]] is not none and SameTypeWithAssumptions(the Type Record u.[[Constraint]] denotes, the Type Record w.[[Constraint]] denotes, identified) is false, return false.
        5. If exactly one of u.[[Default]] and w.[[Default]] is none, return false.
        6. If u.[[Default]] is not none and SameTypeWithAssumptions(the Type Record u.[[Default]] denotes, the Type Record w.[[Default]] denotes, identified) is false, return false.
      7. If a.[[Parameters]] and b.[[Parameters]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
      8. For each integer j such that 0 ≤ j and j < the number of elements of a.[[Parameters]], do
        1. Let p be a.[[Parameters]][j].
        2. Let q be b.[[Parameters]][j].
        3. If p.[[Optional]] is not q.[[Optional]], return false.
        4. If p.[[Rest]] is not q.[[Rest]], return false.
        5. If p.[[Reference]] is not q.[[Reference]], return false.
        6. If p.[[Initial]] is none or q.[[Initial]] is none, then
          1. If p.[[Initial]] is not none or q.[[Initial]] is not none, return false.
        7. Else if SameValue(p.[[Initial]], q.[[Initial]]) is false, then
          1. Return false.
        8. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], identified) is false, return false.
      9. If a.[[ThisType]] is none or b.[[ThisType]] is none, then
        1. If a.[[ThisType]] is not none or b.[[ThisType]] is not none, return false.
      10. Else if SameTypeWithAssumptions(a.[[ThisType]], b.[[ThisType]], identified) is false, then
        1. Return false.
      11. If the number of elements of a.[[Narrows]] is not the number of elements of b.[[Narrows]], return false.
      12. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[Narrows]], do
        1. Let m be a.[[Narrows]][k] and let n be b.[[Narrows]][k].
        2. If m.[[Target]] is not n.[[Target]], return false.
        3. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(m.[[Type]], n.[[Type]], identified) is false, return false.
      13. If a.[[Return]] is none or b.[[Return]] is none, then
        1. If a.[[Return]] is not none or b.[[Return]] is not none, return false.
      14. Else if SameTypeWithAssumptions(a.[[Return]], b.[[Return]], identified) is false, then
        1. Return false.
    3. Return true.
     Note

    Two generic signatures are the same up to renaming: the type parameters are identified position by position through assumptions, the mechanism the recursive cases already use, so a parameter of a and the parameter at the same position of b are one type for the comparison, and <T: type>(x: T) => T and <U: type>(x: U) => U are one function type. [[Name]] is never read. Kind, variadic marker, variance, arity, and the constraints and defaults are compared under the same identification, so <T: type extends A> and <T: type extends B> are two, as are <T: type> and <T: type = uint8>.

    Signatures are compared position-wise, so the order in which a name's overloads are declared is part of the function type. Canonicalization does not reorder them, because there is no order over signatures that is both total and meaningful, and because the declaration order is already observable through the reflected signatures list.

    1.10.2.2 EffectiveSignatureReturn ( signature )

    The abstract operation EffectiveSignatureReturn takes argument signature (a Signature Record) and returns a Type Record or none. It returns the completed result contract used by callable conformance. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If signature.[[Return]] is not none, return signature.[[Return]].
    2. Return signature.[[InferredReturn]].

    The publication rules of 1.6.2 store none for a completed unknown join; they do not publish the any type. An explicit any result annotation is retained. This operation does not complete an unfinished inference dependency, and an unfinished result must not be replaced by none merely to discharge a conformance obligation. Complete the dependencies required by 1.6.2.3 and 1.6.2.15 before finalizing that obligation.

    This result is used on both sides of callable conformance, including the signature comparisons reached through interface satisfaction, inherited contracts, callbacks and function-valued results. A target with a published result still describes what its consumers can receive. Identity, interning, overload-set formation, ranking and declared-only viability continue to read the declared signature fields. Declaration identity alone cannot discharge a result obligation that depends on publication. This distinction applies recursively when a comparison reaches a callable contract; it does not relax writable-storage invariance or reference-liveness requirements.

    A published result describes a function value, not an unwritten storage promise on a replaceable function declaration binding. For a store to that binding, including contextual typing of the replacement expression, use its declared signature with [[InferredReturn]] set to none. Preserve its declared parameters, explicit result, receiver and narrowing contracts. This does not erase the published contract of a function value passed to a consumer, or an explicit callable annotation on another binding. The existing binding-stability rules determine whether a later read may use the original function's published result.

    1.10.2.3 IsSignatureSubtype ( a, b, assumptions )

    The abstract operation IsSignatureSubtype takes arguments a (a Signature Record), b (a Signature Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether a function with the signature a may be used where the signature b is required. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If a.[[Untyped]] is true, a.[[InferredReturn]] is none, neither signature has a reference parameter, and b.[[Narrows]] is empty, return true.
    2. If a.[[TypeParameters]] is not empty and b.[[TypeParameters]] is empty, then
      1. Let bindings be the bindings of a.[[TypeParameters]] inferred from b's parameter types by the structural matching of 20.
      2. Let sourceResult be EffectiveSignatureReturn(a) with bindings substituted.
      3. Let targetResult be EffectiveSignatureReturn(b).
      4. If sourceResult and targetResult are not none, targetResult.[[Kind]] is not void, and sourceResult still contains unbound parameters of a, use structural matching against targetResult to infer those remaining parameters. Bindings already established by parameter matching are retained.
      5. Check every inferred binding by IsAssignable against its parameter's constraint after substituting the inferred bindings, including those on which a dependent constraint depends. If a parameter cannot be bound or a binding fails its constraint, return false. A completed result with no remaining inference variable is checked covariantly below, not required to be identical to targetResult.
      6. Set a to the Signature Record whose fields are those of a with each Type Record they hold replaced by the result of SubstituteType applied to it and bindings, and whose [[TypeParameters]] is empty.
    3. Else if a.[[TypeParameters]] is empty and b.[[TypeParameters]] is not empty, then
      1. Return false.
    4. Else if a.[[TypeParameters]] is not empty, then
      1. If a.[[TypeParameters]] and b.[[TypeParameters]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
      2. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[TypeParameters]], do
        1. Let u be a.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        2. Let w be b.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        3. If u.[[Kind]] is not w.[[Kind]], or u.[[Variadic]] is not w.[[Variadic]], or u.[[Arity]] is not w.[[Arity]], return false.
        4. Append the Record { [[First]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is u.[[Declaration]], [[Second]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is w.[[Declaration]] } to assumptions.
        5. Append the Record { [[First]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is w.[[Declaration]], [[Second]]: the parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is u.[[Declaration]] } to assumptions.
      3. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[TypeParameters]], do
        1. Let u be a.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        2. Let w be b.[[TypeParameters]][k].
        3. If u.[[Constraint]] is not none, then
          1. If w.[[Constraint]] is none, return false.
          2. If IsSubtype(the Type Record w.[[Constraint]] denotes, the Type Record u.[[Constraint]] denotes, assumptions) is false, return false.
    5. If an argument sequence admitted by b has a statically established omission that a cannot bind, after the defaults supplied by the crossing have been applied, return false. A rest may supply no arguments; a required parameter whose type admits undefined can bind an omitted argument. Preserve the gradual admission of any. A fixed tuple rest is compared by its positional elements, retaining their defaults.
    6. Let identicalParameters be true.
    7. If a.[[Parameters]] and b.[[Parameters]] have different lengths, then
      1. Set identicalParameters to false.
    8. Else,
      1. For each integer k such that 0 ≤ k and k < the number of elements of a.[[Parameters]], do
        1. Let p be a.[[Parameters]][k].
        2. Let q be b.[[Parameters]][k].
        3. If p.[[Rest]] is not q.[[Rest]], p.[[Optional]] is not q.[[Optional]], or p.[[Reference]] is not q.[[Reference]], set identicalParameters to false.
        4. If one of p and q has a default and the other does not, set identicalParameters to false.
        5. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, set identicalParameters to false.
    9. If identicalParameters is false, then
      1. For each integer j such that 0 ≤ j and j < the number of elements of b.[[Parameters]], do
        1. Let q be b.[[Parameters]][j].
        2. If a.[[Parameters]] has no element at index j and no element of a.[[Parameters]] has [[Rest]] true, return false.
        3. Let p be the element of a.[[Parameters]] that receives the argument at index j, or, where more than one could receive it, the union of the types of those that could (1.10.4.2).
        4. If p.[[Reference]] is not q.[[Reference]], return false.
        5. Let pType be p.[[Type]], or the element type of p.[[Type]] where p.[[Rest]] is true.
        6. Let qType be q.[[Type]], or the element type of q.[[Type]] where q.[[Rest]] is true.
        7. If q.[[Optional]] is true, q.[[Rest]] is false, and q has no default supplied by the crossing, set qType to the union of qType and the undefined type.
        8. If p.[[Rest]] is false and p is optional or has a default, set pType to the union of pType and the undefined type.
        9. If p.[[Reference]] is true, then
          1. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(qType, pType, assumptions) is false, return false.
        10. Else,
          1. If IsAssignable(qType, pType) is false, return false.
    10. If a.[[ThisType]] is not none, then
      1. If b.[[ThisType]] is none, return false.
      2. If IsAssignable(b.[[ThisType]], a.[[ThisType]]) is false, return false.
    11. Else if b.[[ThisType]] is not none, then
      1. Return false.
    12. For each Narrowing Record n of b.[[Narrows]], do
      1. Identify the parameter denoted by n.[[Target]] with the corresponding parameter of a, or identify "this" with "this". Parameter names need not agree.
      2. If a and b do not declare the same narrowing form (Boolean test or void assertion), return false.
      3. If there is no corresponding Narrowing Record m of a.[[Narrows]], return false.
      4. If b declares a Boolean test, the narrowed sets of m.[[Type]] and n.[[Type]] must be equivalent within the parameter domain admitted by b; if that equivalence is not established, return false. SameType under assumptions after substitution is a sufficient conservative judgment.
      5. Otherwise, if IsSubtype(m.[[Type]], n.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
    13. Let bReturn be EffectiveSignatureReturn(b).
    14. If bReturn is none, return true.
    15. If bReturn.[[Kind]] is void, return true.
    16. Let aReturn be EffectiveSignatureReturn(a).
    17. If aReturn is none, return true.
    18. Return IsSubtype(aReturn, bReturn, assumptions).

    Reference modes and narrowing guarantees participate in ordinary callable conformance, including assignments, callbacks, interface satisfaction and overrides. The untyped catch-all does not erase a reference parameter's required location or supply an undeclared narrowing fact. Reference parameters require arguments even when their referent annotation is any; a reference rest may collect an empty sequence. Explicit any at a value boundary retains its gradual meaning. This does not change the decay of a reference passed directly to a by-value parameter, and introduces no adaptation wrapper or additional reference-liveness permission.

    Note 1

    Identical parameter contracts accept the same argument sequences even when a rest precedes a fixed tail. Parameter-list indices are not argument indices in such a sequence. The identical-parameter step establishes only parameter compatibility: receiver requirements, narrowing guarantees, reference modes and effective return covariance are still checked. It does not evaluate defaults, add a wrapper or change SequenceAssignment.

    Omission safety compares effective binding behaviour, not equality of optional flags and not the target's maximum arity. A source default, an undefined-admitting source, or a default supplied by the target crossing can make an omission safe. An optional target without a default cannot stand over a source that requires a value it may omit. Fixed positions after optional/defaulted positions retain their own obligations. The existing sequence-assignment rules govern rest distribution, and explicit reference markers retain their ordinary agreement and liveness checks. These are type-record judgments; no default expression or function body runs to decide them.

     Note 2

    The four directions a generic signature can face follow one question: could a caller reading b be misled? A generic a is usable where a concrete b is required by INSTANTIATION — (uint8) => uint8 holds id.<uint8> — and the bindings the relation infers are the ones the crossing specializes at (4.6). A concrete a is not usable where a generic b is required, since <T: type>(x: T) => T promises every T and (x: uint8) => uint8 would return a uint8 for a string; the untyped catch-all of the first step is the one exception, as it is everywhere. A generic a is usable where a generic b is required when it is at least as general: the same parameters position by position, each constraint of a admitting everything the corresponding constraint of b admits, so <T: type>(x: T) => T satisfies <T: type extends Animal>(x: T) => T and not the reverse. The inference here never runs user code: it is the structural walk the checker already has, and the constraint check on an inferred binding is IsAssignable. A where on a's declaration is not consulted, because a function type has none; it is checked at the specialization the crossing performs.

    A parameter and a [[ThisType]] are related by 1.2.3.2 and not by 1.2.3.1, because a parameter position is a BOUNDARY and any is bidirectional at a boundary. IsSubtype admits any only as its target, which is the right rule for a subtype question and the wrong one here: it made a specific parameter refuse an any-typed position, so (uint8) => void was not usable where (any) => any was declared although the mirror was, and gradual typing broke at the function boundary in one direction only. The two [[ThisType]] steps refuse both mismatches, which is what 8.1 states in each direction: a signature with none is usable nowhere a this is required, and one that has a [[ThisType]] is usable nowhere a this is absent. That is what makes adoption load-bearing rather than decorative — a non-arrow function reaching a position whose signature has a [[ThisType]] is compared as if it had adopted it (1.7.2.1), and an arrow, which adopts nothing, is refused here.

    A return type keeps IsSubtype, and the asymmetry is deliberate. A return is covariant and is a PROMISE the function makes rather than a position a caller supplies, so a known specific result may stand where any is required by IsSubtype's ordinary target rule. A source explicitly returning any does not thereby satisfy a specific result promise.

     Note 3

    Parameters are contravariant and the return is covariant, which is the standard rule and the only one that is sound: a function used where (uint8) => uint8 is required will be handed a uint8, so it must accept at least every uint8, and its result will be used as a uint8, so it must produce only uint8 values. A ref parameter is invariant because it is a location that is both read and written, so a mismatch in either direction is unsound; this is the parameter-level counterpart of the reference rule in 1.2.3.1.

    A function that accepts fewer arguments than the target supplies is admitted, since ECMAScript already ignores extra arguments and rejecting it would make every callback that omits an unused parameter unusable. A void return is required of nothing, since a caller that has declared it will not use the result.

    The catch-all step asks for [[InferredReturn]] as well as [[Untyped]] because the two are not the same question. [[Untyped]] is syntactic, so it is true of function g() { return f(); }, which declares neither a parameter type nor a return type; but g PARTICIPATES in inference all the same, since a contribution of it is anchored by f's declared return, and it therefore publishes a return type. 1.6.2 says subtyping and assignability read "the published one otherwise", and a catch-all asking only about [[Untyped]] returns before that reading can happen - so g would satisfy () => string while publishing uint32. The catch-all is for a signature there is nothing to judge BY, which is what [[Untyped]] alone does not establish. Where a signature is untyped and publishes nothing there is nothing to judge in any position, which is why the step precedes the arity and parameter steps as well: an untyped function naming parameters its caller does not supply is the ordinary shape of existing ECMAScript.

    An UNKNOWN return is required of nothing either, which is the last three steps. A signature reaches them when it declares no return type and publishes no inferred one, and 1.6.2 settles what that means: a join of the any type publishes nothing, "since a function whose result is unknown is indistinguishable from one that never participated". A function that never participated has [[Untyped]] true and is admitted by the first step; one that participates and publishes nothing must be admitted here, or the two would be distinguishable after all - and distinguishable by a BODY, which is what [[Untyped]] being a syntactic property exists to prevent. function f(x: uint8) { let v = 1; v = 5.5; return v; } publishes nothing because a reassigned binding cannot, and it satisfies (uint8) => uint8 exactly as function f(x) { ... } does.

    This is not the same as declaring any. function f(x: uint8): any PROMISES nothing, and a promise of nothing does not satisfy a promise of uint8: IsSubtype(any, uint8) is false and the assignment is refused. The unannotated function makes no promise to break. The two are different signatures for the same reason - which is why [[Return]] is none where none is declared rather than the any type - and an implementation that stored any for both would refuse every function whose body defeats inference, while also reporting the two as one signature declared twice.

    This admission does not agree with the arity rule of 1.10.3.1, and the disagreement is worth stating. A call of f declared as function f(a: uint8) {} with two arguments selects no signature and is an error, because a signature is viable only for an argument list its arity accepts. But f is assignable to (uint8, string) => void by the rule above, and a call through a binding of that type reaches f with the second argument present and is not an error. The same call is therefore rejected when written directly and permitted through a function type. Either extra arguments are acceptable, in which case overload resolution should admit them and prefer the signature that uses the most, or they are not, in which case a function that ignores a parameter should not satisfy a type that supplies it and every such callback needs its parameter list widened. The design states the first rule and not the second, and this specification supplies the second in the shape ECMAScript's existing tolerance of extra arguments suggests. This specification settles it as the two rules answering two questions. A direct call is checked against what the author declared, where an extra argument is a mistake worth catching at the site that made it; assignability answers what a value can safely receive, where an extra argument is ignored by the language itself. Both rules stand as written, and a committee preferring one question's answer for both has each rule's consequences recorded above.

    1.10.2.4 IsFunctionSubtype ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation IsFunctionSubtype takes arguments s (a function Type Record), t (a function Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether every value of the function type s is a value of the function type t. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. For each element b of t.[[Signatures]], do
      1. If there is no element a of s.[[Signatures]] such that IsSignatureSubtype(a, b, assumptions) is true, return false.
    2. Return true.
     Note

    An overloaded function type is the conjunction of its signatures, so a function satisfies it by satisfying each one, possibly with a different signature for each. This is why the quantifiers run this way round: every signature the target promises must be met by some signature the source provides, and a source may provide more.

    1.10.3 Overload Resolution

    An overloaded name evaluates to a single function object that resolves at the call site. Its name is the shared name, its length is the smallest parameter count among its signatures, and call, apply, and bind resolve by the same rules. Individual signatures are not addressable as properties; they are exposed by the function reflection of the decorators extension.

    1.10.3.1 ResolveOverload ( signatures, args, contextualType )

    The abstract operation ResolveOverload takes arguments signatures (a List of Signature Records), args (a List of arguments), and contextualType (a Type Record or none) and returns either a Signature Record, none, or ambiguous. It selects the signature a call invokes. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let viable be a new empty List.
    2. For each element declared of signatures, do
      1. Let sig be declared.
      2. If sig.[[TypeParameters]] is not empty, then
        1. Let bindings be the bindings of sig.[[TypeParameters]] from the call's explicit type arguments by BindTypeArguments (4.3) where the call supplies them, and otherwise, or for the parameters they leave unbound, from args by 15.
        2. If some parameter of sig.[[TypeParameters]] is left unbound, or binding it was a throw completion, then
          1. Continue.
        3. Set sig to the Signature Record whose fields are those of sig with each Type Record they hold replaced by the result of SubstituteType applied to it and bindings, and whose [[TypeParameters]] is empty.
      3. Let argumentBindings be BindArguments(sig, args) (1.10.4.4).
      4. If argumentBindings is unmatched, then
        1. Continue.
      5. If some element of args does not satisfy its receiving contract under argumentBindings as defined below, then
        1. Continue.
      6. If contextualType is not none, sig has a declared return type, and IsAssignable(sig.[[Return]], contextualType) is false, then
        1. Continue.
      7. Append sig to viable.
    3. If viable is empty, return none.
    4. For each element sig of viable, do
      1. Let rank be the greatest rank in Table 30 required by any element of args to match its receiving contract under the bindings that made sig viable.
      2. Let sig's worst rank be rank.
    5. Let best be the elements of viable whose worst rank is least.
    6. If best has more than one element, then
      1. NOTE: Specificity breaks the tie the ranks leave. For each argument, a parameter written as a concrete type is more specific than one written as a type parameter, and a parameter of a fixed position is more specific than an element received by an ordinary rest or a rest typed by a generic pack, read from the declared signature each element of best was instantiated from. Compare the positions actually receiving the arguments under BindArguments; merely containing a rest elsewhere does not make a signature less specific.
      2. Remove from best each element that some other element of best is more specific than for some argument, and that is more specific than that other element for no argument.
    7. If best has exactly one element, return that element.
    8. Return ambiguous.

    For viability, ranking and specificity, each argument's receiving contract is its assigned fixed parameter's type or its actual position within a rest. For a reference rest, retain the positional leaf type selected by the complete collected contract and the lexicographically greatest successful sequence assignment of ReferenceSequenceAdmits (1.10.4.3), including nested rests. Do not replace the leaf with a union of the tuple's element types. Retain the owning declared parameter as well: a leaf within a rest is still a rest position for specificity. Reuse the assignment that established viability when comparing candidates.

    A reference receiving position requires the original reference contribution and the reference-argument judgment of 2.4. At run time, the referent must be live and satisfy the receiving type without conversion, and its available declared location type retains its invariant obligation. The current referent type and the invariant location type are distinct facts; a narrower current value does not narrow the location's contract. Unresolved static facts retain their existing deferred runtime judgment. Rank an admitted reference against its receiving leaf type under the existing ranks. A value receiving position instead judges and ranks the decayed value under the ordinary value rules. An explicit reference contributes no additional preference between otherwise equally ranked candidates; existing specificity and ambiguity rules still apply.

    Overload selection does not evaluate value parameter initializers or create replacement borrowed locations. The dispatcher forwards the original arguments and locations to the selected function; it is not itself a value parameter boundary. Final parameter binding and later accesses retain their independent admission and liveness checks, including after an intervening argument effect or initializer. This does not change the value boundaries of call, apply, or bind.

    Note 1

    Rank 2 separates two ways of matching that are otherwise indistinguishable, and without it a pair of signatures a reader would consider plainly ordered is ambiguous for every call:

    1. interface I { a: uint8 } and type O = { a: uint8 } as two signatures of one name, called with { a: 1 }.

    The argument has the shape exactly, which is rank 1 against O; it satisfies I by having the members, which is what an interface-typed position accepts and is now rank 2. The exact match wins, which is the answer a reader expects and the one the languages that face this question give.

    Rank 2 does not reach a class that DECLARES the interface: such a class refines it (1.2.3.1), so it matches at rank 1 as any subtype does, and a declaring class is not made to lose to an unrelated structural signature. Nor does it order two nominal parameter types against each other: two interfaces of one shape are each satisfied structurally by the same argument, both at rank 2, and the call remains ambiguous - which is correct, since neither is a better answer than the other.

    It is a type error if ResolveOverload returns none, and it is a type error if it returns ambiguous. Where an argument has the any type the resolution is performed at run time on the argument's runtime type, and the same errors are thrown as a TypeError there.

    Two signatures declared for one name must not be ambiguous for any argument list. A declaration that writes no return annotation declares the SAME return as another that writes none, so two declarations of one name that annotate the same parameter types and neither annotate a return are one signature written twice, and are a type error at the second. Declaring nothing is a declaration of nothing, not an unknown. It is a type error to declare a signature that is viable for the same argument list as an existing one at the same rank, after specificity and declared return discrimination leave them tied. Two generic signatures that are the same up to renaming (1.10.1) are one signature written twice, and are the same error: function r<T: type>(e: T) after function r<U: type>(e: U) redeclares, whatever the letters.

    A generic signature is viable when its type parameters bind, from the call's explicit type arguments or by inference from its value arguments, and is then ranked as the instantiated signature it becomes; one whose parameters cannot be bound is not viable, as one whose arity does not fit is not. Where ranks tie, a concrete position is preferred to a type parameter and a fixed parameter to an element of a variadic one, so route(e: Click), route<T: type extends Event>(e: T), and route<...Es: [].<type> extends [].<Event>>(...es: Es) layer from most to least specific and route(click) selects the first: a declaration that names the type is the one its author meant for it.

    Note 2

    Ranking by the worst match rather than by a sum keeps the rule from trading a bad match on one argument against a good one on another, which is where the ranking rules of C++ become hard to predict. A typed argument never ranks below 1: a typed argument of the wrong type is not viable at all, so it is never a question of how well it matches.

    An untyped function is a catch-all because its signature has [[Untyped]] true, which ranks last. Given function f() {} and function f(a: uint8) {}, the call f(1) selects the typed signature, since the literal ranks 2 against the catch-all's 4, while f(1, 2) selects the untyped one, since the typed signature's arity does not accept two arguments and it is not viable. A function that takes no arguments and is nonetheless typed is written by declaring the return type, as function f(): void {}, which makes [[Untyped]] false and so makes f(1) an error.

    The ambiguity rule reaches further than duplicate parameter lists. function f(a: uint8) {} and function f(a: uint8, b: string = 'b') {} are ambiguous, because the default makes the second viable for a single uint8 argument at the same rank; in contrast, function f(a: float32): void {} and function f(...a: [].<float32>): void {} are valid together. At the one-argument call their type ranks tie and the fixed position is more specific; other arities use the rest signature. A default or a rest parameter expands a signature into a family of arities, and it is the family that must not remain ambiguous after the same ranking and specificity judgments used at calls. Several rests multiply the family rather than changing the rule, and a signature with a rest of an untyped element collides with a great deal, which is a reason to type one.

    1.10.4 Named Arguments

    An argument at a call site may be written as a name and a value, name: AssignmentExpression, which supplies the value for the parameter of that name rather than for the parameter at that position. A named argument is a compact way to supply a later parameter while omitting earlier ones that have a default. The parameter names a signature carries (1.10.1) are what a named argument selects by.

    The Arguments grammar admits a named argument alongside the positional and spread forms. A named argument is an IdentifierName followed by : and an AssignmentExpression, at the top of an argument. This is new syntax: a call argument that is an identifier followed by : is a syntax error in the base language, so no existing call changes meaning, and the form is available only where the runtime types feature is enabled.

    ArgumentList[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ... AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ArgumentList[?Yield, ?Await] , AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ArgumentList[?Yield, ?Await] , ... AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] Argument[?Yield, ?Await] ArgumentList[?Yield, ?Await] , Argument[?Yield, ?Await] Argument[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ... AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] NamedArgument[?Yield, ?Await] NamedArgument[Yield, Await] : IdentifierName : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]

    This is the first restatement of ArgumentList, factoring the pinned edition's four alternatives through an Argument element exactly as FormalParameters is factored above, so that a new argument form is one added alternative rather than two. The references extension adds one such alternative, the ref argument, by restating Argument (2.1); per 1.1 that later block is the production's complete form.

    A call is bound to the parameters of the selected signature by BindArguments (1.10.4.4). It is a type error if a named argument's name is not a parameter of the signature, and it is a type error if BindArguments returns unmatched.

    For a named or object-spread call to an overload set, evaluate the argument contributions once in source order, preserving each contribution's name where present, source identity, value or original reference, and forwarding information. BindArguments is applied separately to each candidate; a losing candidate does not replay argument expressions, getters or iteration, run value parameter initializers, or convert an argument to make it viable. Preserve the candidate's successful binding map with its signature. Ranking and specificity compare the same supplied contribution at its receiving contract in each candidate, even where names place it at different parameter indices. Omitted defaults contribute no argument rank. Where repeated names replace an earlier assigned value under BindArguments, the earlier expression is still evaluated but its replaced contribution does not participate in ranking.

    After selecting an actual overload, invoke that member with its retained binding map and original argument contributions. Do not resolve the mapped list as a new positional overload call or redistribute its named groups by positional greediness. A named rest's selected count remains fixed even when an earlier rest could otherwise take its elements. Parameter initialization still performs the selected member's ordinary defaults, conversions, reference admission and liveness checks; retaining the assignment does not retain a proof that survives an intervening effect. Binding maps belong to their invocation and cannot be consumed by a nested or recursive call.

    When a positional argument is a reference, argument distribution uses the receiving parameter's contract. A reference position requires a compatible borrowed location, with the invariant type compatibility and no-conversion rule of 2.4; a value position uses the referent under its ordinary value-admission rule. Preserve the original reference through mapping so that final parameter binding still performs its required reference or value operation. Name placement does not require a storage read. Evaluating argument expressions, admitting their results, and binding parameters do not grant a reference new escape permissions, and successful admission does not establish liveness after intervening effects, including earlier parameter initializers. These requirements also apply when distributing non-final or multiple rests and forwarding a reference run.

    The signature selected is the signature in view. Where the callee expression is a reference whose binding has a declared type that is a function Type Record, or a nominal interface type whose structural form is one (1.4.2.9), the signature in view is selected from that type's [[Signatures]] by ResolveOverload, binding each candidate against the supplied names and positions before judging viability and ranking. A candidate is not selected merely because its parameters include the names; if no candidate is viable or no unique best candidate remains, the call is a type error. The call is bound against it as follows, and the callee receives the resulting positional list. Named arguments pin their parameters first. A positional argument fills the next unpinned position. A named argument fills the parameter bearing its name; it is a type error if no parameter does. A parameter filled by neither takes the signature's [[Initial]] where it has one, is left undefined where it is optional or a rest, and is otherwise a type error. An argument at a position whose parameter type is not any, where the argument is not an Object, is converted to that type as at a declared parameter (1.6). Where the callee expression has no such declared type in view, the signature in view is the callee function's own parameter list, read as before, and a skipped position is left undefined for the callee's own default.

    Note 1

    This is what makes an interface of call signatures usable as a declaration: interface I { (string = '5', named: uint32) } and function f(a: I) { a(named: 10) } bind by the interface's names and fill its default, so a function (a, b) => b passed to f receives ('5', 10) whatever it calls its own parameters. The interface supplies data the caller uses to assemble the argument list; it supplies no behaviour, and the function called is always the value itself. A parameter's declared type is carried on its binding (1.8.2), which is how a call through a parameter finds the signature in view.

    1.10.4.1 Named Arguments of Intrinsic Functions

    Where no declared callable signature is in view, the named parameter declaration of an intrinsic belongs to the actual function Object selected by ordinary evaluation of the callee. It is not obtained from the caller's property spelling, the receiver's inferred type, or the function's public name or length property. Aliasing or borrowing that function preserves its declaration; replacing a property selects the replacement function's declaration. A declared callable signature in view retains the names, defaults and admission rules specified above.

    The following declarations apply to the intrinsic Range methods and synchronous Iterator helpers. Parameters are listed in order. Unless marked optional, each must be supplied in a named or object-spread call. These are value parameters, with no reference rest.

    The static member signatures expose these same names. The reverse, toArray and self-iteration methods accept no named parameters. This table supplies no declaration for an unrelated built-in, a protocol request method, or an asynchronous helper.

    Evaluate argument contributions and apply BindArguments in the ordinary order. When materializing the positional argument List for an intrinsic's own declaration, omit an unfilled optional trailing position; supply undefined for an unfilled optional position preceding a supplied later position. An explicitly supplied undefined remains present. Thus a call to reduce naming only callback has no initial accumulator argument, whereas a call also naming initial with value undefined has one. This rule does not change materialization under a declared callable signature in view.

    Argument binding adds no conversion to an inferred receiver-dependent type. After binding, perform the selected intrinsic's ordinary receiver, value and callback admission, iterator operations and abrupt-completion handling. Retain original reference locations through binding and perform their existing value decay and liveness checks at the native boundary. No listed method admits a reference-rest forwarding occurrence, including an empty one. A Range helper delegates its materialized positional List to the normally selected Iterator helper; it does not bind the outer names a second time. Named parameter metadata alone supplies no generic callable capability and does not authorize ignoring explicit type arguments.

    A rest parameter is filled by name as well as by position. A named argument whose name is a rest parameter's supplies a value of that rest, and the positional arguments that follow it join the same rest in the order written, so function f(a: uint8, b: string = '', ...args: [].<string>) {} called f(8, args: 'a', 'b') binds a to 8, leaves b its default, and gives args the elements 'a' and 'b'. Where a parameter after that rest must still be filled, the rest gives back what the parameters after it require, which is the same rule BindArguments applies to a positional call.

    1.10.4.2 SequenceAssignment ( slots, n, admits [ , admitsRun ] )

    The abstract operation SequenceAssignment takes arguments slots (a List of Records with a [[Rest]] field (a Boolean) and an [[Optional]] field (a Boolean)), n (a non-negative integer), and admits (an Abstract Closure taking a non-negative integer and a Record of slots and returning a Boolean) and optional argument admitsRun (an Abstract Closure taking two non-negative integers and a Record of slots and returning a Boolean) and returns either a List of non-negative integers or unmatched. It distributes n items among slots in order, returning how many items each slot takes, or unmatched where no distribution admits every item. A slot whose [[Rest]] is true takes zero or more items, one whose [[Optional]] is true takes one or none, and any other takes exactly one. admits(i, slot) reports whether the item at index i may be taken by slot. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If slots is empty, then
      1. If n is 0, return a new empty List.
      2. Return unmatched.
    2. Let slot be slots[0].
    3. Let tail be a List of the elements of slots from index 1.
    4. Let limit be 0.
    5. Repeat, while limit < n and admits(limit, slot) is true and (slot.[[Rest]] is true or limit < 1),
      1. Set limit to limit + 1.
    6. Let min be 0.
    7. If slot.[[Rest]] is false and slot.[[Optional]] is false, set min to 1.
    8. For each integer m from limit down to min, in descending order, do
      1. If admitsRun is present and admitsRun(0, m, slot) is false, continue.
      2. Let shifted be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (index, which) that captures admits and m and performs the following steps when called:
        1. Return admits(index + m, which).
      3. Let rest be unmatched.
      4. If admitsRun is present, then
        1. Let shiftedRun be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (start, count, which) that captures admitsRun and m and performs the following steps when called:
          1. Return admitsRun(start + m, count, which).
        2. Set rest to SequenceAssignment(tail, n - m, shifted, shiftedRun).
      5. Else,
        1. Set rest to SequenceAssignment(tail, n - m, shifted).
      6. If rest is not unmatched, return the list-concatenation of « m » and rest.
    9. Return unmatched.
     Note

    This is leftmost-greedy matching with backtracking, which is what the design means by taking arguments greedily and giving them back to satisfy the signature: a slot takes as many items as it can and yields one at a time until the slots after it can be satisfied. A parameter list, and a tuple's element list, is a regular pattern over a sequence — a fixed slot is one item, an optional slot is one or none, a rest is zero or more — and this operation is the match.

    The result is deterministic. Because the search takes the greatest count first at each slot in turn, the assignment returned is the greatest in the lexicographic order on the count lists, so it does not depend on how an implementation searches; an implementation may use any method that agrees with it. The recursion terminates because each call passes a shorter slots.

    The design's own example is the one to check the rule against. For function f(...a: [].<uint32>, ...b: [].<uint32>, c: uint32) called f(0, 1, 2), the first slot takes all three, the tail cannot be satisfied, it yields to two, b then takes the one remaining and c cannot be satisfied, b yields to none, and the assignment settles at a: « 0, 1 », b: « », c: 2. Where the types differ the filter does the work with no further rule: in function f(a: string, ...args: [].<uint32>, ...args2: [].<string>, callback: () => void), args stops at the first argument that is not a uint32.

    1.10.4.3 ReferenceSequenceAdmits ( t, run, admits )

    The abstract operation ReferenceSequenceAdmits takes arguments t (a Type Record), run (a List of arguments), and admits (an Abstract Closure taking an argument and a Type Record and returning a Boolean) and returns a Boolean. It checks a reference rest's collected sequence, using admits for invariant reference admission at each receiving position. The Type Record is the resolved collected contract, after applicable generic substitutions. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. If t.[[Extent]] is an integer and the number of elements of run is not t.[[Extent]], return false.
      2. For each element arg of run, do
        1. If admits(arg, t.[[Element]]) is false, return false.
      3. Return true.
    2. If t.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. Let slots be a new empty List.
      2. For each element e of t.[[Elements]], do
        1. Append the Record { [[Rest]]: e.[[Rest]], [[Optional]]: e.[[Initial]] is not none, [[Element]]: e } to slots.
      3. Let one be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (index, slot) that captures run and admits and performs the following steps when called:
        1. If slot.[[Rest]] is true, return true.
        2. Return admits(run[index], slot.[[Element]].[[Type]]).
      4. Let many be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (start, count, slot) that captures run and admits and performs the following steps when called:
        1. If slot.[[Rest]] is false, return true.
        2. Let part be the sublist of run starting at start and containing count elements.
        3. Return ReferenceSequenceAdmits(slot.[[Element]].[[Type]], part, admits).
      5. Return true if SequenceAssignment(slots, the number of elements of run, one, many) is not unmatched, and false otherwise.
    3. For each element arg of run, do
      1. If admits(arg, t) is false, return false.
    4. Return true.

    A static use of admits applies the reference-argument judgment without reading storage; unresolved facts retain their existing deferred judgment. A runtime use requires a Reference Value, checks its live referent without conversion and preserves its available invariant location contract. A defaulted tuple position permits omission but supplies no location: a reference rest collects only the supplied borrows, creates no temporary for an omitted default, and retains bounds checks on subsequent indexing. A successful match is not proof of liveness after an intervening effect.

    1.10.4.4 BindArguments ( sig, args )

    The abstract operation BindArguments takes arguments sig (a Signature Record) and args (a List of arguments) and returns either a List of bindings or unmatched. It binds a call's arguments to a signature's parameters, giving each parameter the value or values it receives. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. For each named argument a of args, in order, do
      1. Let p be the parameter of sig.[[Parameters]] whose [[Name]] is a's name; if there is none, return unmatched.
      2. Assign a's value to p, and where p.[[Rest]] is true, assign to p the positional arguments following a up to the next named argument as well.
    2. If a positional argument after a named argument was not assigned to a rest parameter, return unmatched.
    3. Let positional be the positional arguments of args that precede the first named argument, in order.
    4. For each rest parameter r that a named argument assigned to, in parameter order, do
      1. Let required be the parameters not yet assigned to that are neither optional nor rest parameters and have no initial value.
      2. Let shortfall be max(0, the number of elements of required minus the number of elements of positional).
      3. Let nextRest be the next rest parameter after r that a named argument assigned to, if there is one.
      4. Let trailing be the elements of required that follow r in parameter order and precede nextRest if it exists.
      5. Let count be the minimum of shortfall, the number of elements of trailing, and the number of values assigned to r.
      6. Remove the last count values assigned to r and assign them, in order, to the last count parameters of trailing. These parameters are now assigned to.
    5. Let slots be a List containing, for each parameter p of sig.[[Parameters]] not yet assigned to, a Record { [[Rest]]: p.[[Rest]], [[Optional]]: p.[[Optional]] or p.[[Initial]] is not none }, in parameter order.
    6. Let admits be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (index, which) that captures positional and performs the following steps when called:
      1. Let p be the parameter which stands for.
      2. If p is a reference rest parameter, return true.
      3. Let target be p.[[Type]], or the element type of p.[[Type]] where p.[[Rest]] is true.
      4. If p is a reference parameter, return true if positional[index] satisfies the reference-argument judgment for target of 2.4, and false otherwise.
      5. Return IsAssignable(the Static Type of positional[index] in contextual type target, target).
    7. Let admitsRun be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (start, count, which) that captures positional and performs the following steps when called:
      1. Let p be the parameter which stands for.
      2. If p is not a reference rest parameter, return true.
      3. Let run be the sublist of positional starting at start and containing count elements.
      4. Let referenceAdmits be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (arg, target) that performs the following steps when called:
        1. Return true if arg satisfies the reference-argument judgment for target of 2.4, and false otherwise.
      5. Return ReferenceSequenceAdmits(the collected Type Record of p, run, referenceAdmits).
    8. Let counts be SequenceAssignment(slots, the number of elements of positional, admits, admitsRun).
    9. If counts is unmatched, return unmatched.
    10. Assign to each such parameter, in order, the number of elements of positional that counts gives it, a reference rest receiving their original locations, a value rest receiving an array of its type, and any other receiving the one element.
    11. For each parameter p of sig.[[Parameters]] that received nothing, do
      1. If p.[[Initial]] is not none, assign p.[[Initial]] to p.
      2. Else if p is a reference rest parameter, assign an empty reference run to p.
      3. Else if p.[[Rest]] is true, assign an empty array of p.[[Type]] to p.
      4. Else if p.[[Optional]] is false, return unmatched.
    12. Check each reference rest's assigned run against its complete collected contract using ReferenceSequenceAdmits; if any judgment fails, return unmatched.
    13. Return the bindings.
     Note

    A named argument pins its parameter before the positional match runs, so it prunes the search rather than widening it, and the positionals that follow a named rest join that rest as the paragraph above says. A rest that receives nothing is bound to an empty array rather than left unfilled, which is what makes b an empty array rather than an error in the design's example.

    A spread of an object, ...AssignmentExpression where the value is an object with no Symbol.iterator method, binds each of the object's own enumerable String-keyed properties by parameter name, as though each were written as a named argument. A spread whose value is iterable fills positions in order, as in the base language. Its static argument facts are the iteration contribution of 1.14.8, rather than facts assumed from indexed storage. Because the two are distinguished by the presence of an iterator, an object used to supply arguments by name is one that is not iterable; an iterable, including an Array, spreads by position.

    The spread protocol depends on the evaluated value, not on whether its expression is an object literal, an identifier, a property access or a call. Evaluate each argument expression once and finish its contributions before evaluating the next argument. A reference run retains the forwarding rules of 1.4.4, including an empty run's occurrence; it does not undergo property enumeration. A tuple Composite iterates by kind under 23.7.2. For any other Object spread value, perform GetMethod with %Symbol.iterator% once. If it returns undefined (including a nullish property value), use named properties. Otherwise use GetIteratorFromMethod with that already obtained method; a non-callable property or abrupt lookup is an abrupt completion, not a fallback to named properties. Non-Object values retain their ordinary iteration requirements.

    To collect named properties, call the spread value's [[OwnPropertyKeys]] once. Visit those keys in order. Skip Symbol keys without reading their descriptors or values. For each String key, call [[GetOwnProperty]] at that point; if the descriptor is present and enumerable, perform Get once and append the resulting named contribution. An earlier getter can remove a later property or change its enumerability or value before it is visited. Newly added keys absent from the captured key list are not visited. Do not enumerate first and then replay getters, and do not repeat collection for candidate signatures. Repeated fixed names retain BindArguments' sequential replacement rule; earlier expressions and getters still run.

    These evaluation rules apply to ordinary calls, optional calls that proceed, construction and super calls. An optional call that short-circuits evaluates no arguments. Subject to earlier checking errors, argument evaluation completes before the ordinary runtime callability or constructibility check, and binding uses only the resulting contributions. Abrupt argument evaluation stops later arguments and parameter initialization. Iteration retains the base language's IteratorStepValue behaviour, including its abrupt-completion behaviour; selecting a spread protocol does not add an IteratorClose when the base argument-spread evaluation would not perform one. An empty ordinary iterable or an object contributing no names supplies no argument and creates no default placeholder or named-rest scope. An empty reference run still carries its separate forwarding occurrence.

    Where the called value is overloaded (1.10.3), the parameter names are those of the selected signature, and a named or object-spread call that no signature can bind is a type error by the same rule as a positional call that matches no signature.

    Note 2

    Named arguments do not change a signature's identity: a parameter's name is carried but is not compared (1.10.1), so the same function reached through two declarations with different parameter names is one type, and a named call selects by whichever names the interned signature carries.

    1.10.5 Overloading on Return Type

    Because a signature is identified by its return type as well as its parameter types, two signatures may differ only in their return. The return type does not participate in ranking; it participates in viability, through the contextual type of the call (1.6.5). The return type read here is the DECLARED one: a published inferred return type (1.6.2) does not make a signature viable or non-viable, so which signature a call selects never depends on a function body.

    The contextual type of a call is the type its position requires. Where a call has no contextual type and more than one signature remains viable, the call is ambiguous and it is a type error.

    Note

    Given function f(): uint32 and function f(): string, the call f() alone is an error, const a: string = f(); selects the second, and g(f()) selects the first where g takes a uint32, because the parameter supplies the contextual type. h(f()) is an error where h is itself overloaded on uint8 and string, since an argument of a call with more than one applicable signature has no contextual type. The circularity is real and is resolved by rejecting the call rather than by guessing.

    Return-type overloading exists for the operators. A SIMD comparison returns either a vector of lane results or a compact mask, which Intel's intrinsics distinguish by name and which real types cannot: operator<(v: int32x4): int32x4 and operator<(v: int32x4): boolean8 are the same signature but for the return. const a: int32x4 = x == y; and const b: boolean8 = x == y; select between them, and the comparison written with no contextual type is an error rather than a default.

    1.10.6 The Literal Ranking Completed

    Table 21 orders the numeric types a literal may take. It is completed here for the types it omits, which are the ones a call may nonetheless select.

    Note

    Ranking number first is the repair 1.6.9 records. The design's ranking begins at float64 and justifies it on the ground that Number is a float64 and the conversion is exact, which is the argument for ranking number itself first: it is the type a literal takes with no contextual type, and the type an untyped program computes with. Without it, f(a: number) against f(a: float32) has no answer for f(1). This changes which function a call selects and so was a supplied repair when first recorded and is now load-bearing: 1.13.1 shows every untyped call into the overloaded standard library keeps its meaning only because number ranks first, so the ranking stands as a back-compatibility condition rather than a preference.

    Placing the rationals after the integers keeps a literal that is an integer selecting an integer signature, which is what a program that declares both would expect. Within a family a wider width ranks first, following the design's own order, which prefers the type that can represent the most.

    1.10.7 Arrow Functions

    An arrow function's parameters may carry annotations and its body may carry a return annotation. The annotations occupy the positions 1.4.4 gives them, within the cover grammar the arrow syntax already uses.

    ArrowFunction[In, Yield, Await] : ArrowParameters[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt [no LineTerminator here] => ConciseBody[?In]

    When the production ArrowParameters : CoverParenthesizedExpressionAndArrowParameterList is refined using ArrowFormalParameters, a parameter may carry the annotations of 1.4.4.

    Note

    (x: uint8): uint8 => x * x is therefore an arrow function of one uint8 parameter returning a uint8. The return annotation sits between the parameters and the =>, which is the only position available, and it is what distinguishes an annotated arrow from a function type: (uint8) => uint8 in a type position is a type, while (x: uint8): uint8 => x * x in an expression position is a function. An arrow function is not overloadable, since it has no name to overload.

    1.10.8 Annotations on the Remaining Function Forms

    Every function-shaped production takes the return annotation the same way: a TypeAnnotation between the parameter list and the body. The productions below restate their ECMAScript definitions with that insertion (1.1); parameter annotations need no insertion here, since a parameter of any of these forms is a FormalParameter or BindingElement and carries its annotation there. A method takes WhereClauses the same way a function declaration does (14), between that annotation and the body: a generic method specializes as a generic function does, so the rule 4.9 gives - "checked at each specialization once its parameters are bound" - applies unchanged. A method's clause may name the parameters of its CLASS as well as its own, since both are bound at the specialization the clause is checked at.

    MethodDefinition[Yield, Await] : ClassElementName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( UniqueFormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt WhereClauses[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] } GeneratorMethod[?Yield, ?Await] AsyncMethod[?Yield, ?Await] AsyncGeneratorMethod[?Yield, ?Await] get ClassElementName[?Yield, ?Await] (     A method may declare type parameters, as a function declaration may. They are in scope in the method's own signature and body, and a method of a generic class also reads that class's parameters there; where a method declares a parameter of the same name as one of the class's, the method's is the one its body reads. The arguments are supplied at the call, explicitly with . < > or inferred from the call's arguments, by the rules of 4.

    An accessor may not declare type parameters. A getter is never written as a call and takes no arguments, so a parameter it declared could be neither supplied nor inferred; a setter could infer one from the assigned value, but parameterizing one half of a property and not the other would leave the two halves of one construct with different rules. A method serves where a parameterized accessor would, and states which type it is applied to at the site rather than deducing it from a value. An accessor of a generic class reads that class's parameters as any other body of the declaration does; what it may not do is introduce parameters of its own.

    A set accessor declares no return type, so its production is restated unchanged; its single parameter is annotated through PropertySetParameterList. When CoverCallExpressionAndAsyncArrowHead is refined using AsyncArrowHead, a parameter may carry the annotations of 1.4.4, exactly as the synchronous cover is refined in 1.10.7. The static and runtime semantics of an annotation on any of these forms are those of 1.10: the annotation gives the declared return type, an async function's annotation types the promise the call returns, and a generator's annotation types the values the iterator yields. A generator's annotation is SHORTHAND: T names Generator.<T, ~void~, ~void~>, so a bare annotation types the yields and leaves the generator returning nothing, and a return with a value is refused unless the full Generator.<Y, R, N> is written. An async function's annotation is NOT shorthand in the same way and must be a promise type: the generator form fills its remaining arguments with void, which states truly that a generator yields and does not return, and there is no equally supportable filler for a REJECT type — 1.6.2 declines to infer one for the same reason. It is a Syntax Error for an async function to declare a return type that is not a promise type.

    Note

    The design writes async function f(): Promise.<uint8, Error> and typed generator methods throughout; this clause is where those parses come from. A class constructor is the one method that takes no return annotation, which 1.11.2 states.

    1.11 Classes, Interfaces, and Enums

    This clause defines the nominal and structural types a program declares: the object type and its identity and subtyping, which complete the last cases 1.2 defers; the rules that make a class a value type; interfaces; enums; and the sealed hierarchy that gives a closed union.

    1.11.1 Object Types

    It is a type error for a reached ordinary property operation to have a participating receiver whose Static Type consists only of null and undefined alternatives. Named and computed reads, stores, updates, deletion and invocation through a member share this receiver judgment, independently of whether the property key is known. Participation follows 1.9.7. Other primitive receivers retain ordinary boxing. An optional chain contributes no operation on its skipped path; parentheses end the chain, so an outer ordinary access checks the result it actually receives. Existing declared-member requirements on unions are unchanged. Unknown receivers retain runtime checking, and this judgment performs no property-key evaluation or reference read and changes no reference-liveness requirement.

    1.11.1.1 Typed Own-Property Initializers

    PropertyDefinition[Yield, Await] : ( PropertyName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await] ) : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]

    The annotation in { (x: uint8): 1 } declares the own property's storage type and supplies the contextual type of its initializer. It is a type error if the initializer's Static Type, after contextual literal propagation, is known and is not assignable to that declared type. The literal-fit and metadata rules of the declared type apply at this boundary. The judgment belongs to each definition independently of an outer object annotation or the final inferred shape, including when a later definition or spread overwrites the property, when the literal is discarded, and when it supplies a Composite.

    At evaluation the property key and initializer are evaluated once, in their ordinary property-definition order. The value crosses the declared property boundary of Table 23 before the property is installed. An any-typed initializer is checked there at runtime. The checking pass does not evaluate an ordinary computed key or initializer to decide assignability. The definition's context also governs decimal, rational and other representation-sensitive literal processing; inferring the final object shape does not replace that processing.

    A Property Type Record describes one member of an object type. It has a [[Key]] (a property key), a [[Type]] (a Type Record), an [[Optional]] field (a Boolean), a [[Readonly]] field (a Boolean), and an [[Initial]] field (an ECMAScript language value or none, the member's declared default).

    An Index Signature Record has a [[KeyType]] and a [[ValueType]], each a Type Record. No production of the type grammar writes one: an object type acquires index signatures through construction (1.12.4), they take part in identity below and in keyof (1.4.2.5), and their membership and subtype rules are parked with the objects work that will write the source syntax.

    1.11.1.2 SameObjectType ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation SameObjectType takes arguments s (an object Type Record), t (an object Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether s and t are the same object type. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If s.[[Properties]] and t.[[Properties]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
    2. For each element p of s.[[Properties]], do
      1. Let q be the element of t.[[Properties]] whose [[Key]] is p.[[Key]], or empty if there is none.
      2. If q is empty, return false.
      3. If p.[[Optional]] is not q.[[Optional]], return false.
      4. If p.[[Readonly]] is not q.[[Readonly]], return false.
      5. If p.[[Initial]] is none or q.[[Initial]] is none, then
        1. If p.[[Initial]] is not none or q.[[Initial]] is not none, return false.
      6. Else if SameValue(p.[[Initial]], q.[[Initial]]) is false, then
        1. Return false.
      7. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
    3. If s.[[IndexSignatures]] and t.[[IndexSignatures]] do not have the same number of elements, return false.
    4. For each integer j such that 0 ≤ j and j < the number of elements of s.[[IndexSignatures]], do
      1. Let a be s.[[IndexSignatures]][j].
      2. Let b be t.[[IndexSignatures]][j].
      3. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(a.[[KeyType]], b.[[KeyType]], assumptions) is false, return false.
      4. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(a.[[ValueType]], b.[[ValueType]], assumptions) is false, return false.
    5. Return true.
     Note

    Members are matched by key rather than by position, so the order in which an object type lists them is not part of its identity and { x: float32, y: float32 } and { y: float32, x: float32 } are one type. Canonicalization orders the [[Properties]] of an object Type Record by key, which is what allows the interning of 1.2.2.9 to give them one Type Object, and orders the [[IndexSignatures]] by the fixed total order on their [[KeyType]]s. That ordering serves identity; whether the source's own member order should additionally be preserved for display and reflection, carried outside the canonical form the way a parameter's name already is (1.10.1), is settled against a second channel: interning merges every spelling of a type into one object, so a non-canonical order would be the first spelling's, an accident of module load order, and the determinism this specification enforces elsewhere forbids exactly that kind of accident. A reflected object type lists its properties in key order whatever order the source wrote.

    1.11.1.3 IsObjectSubtype ( s, t, assumptions )

    The abstract operation IsObjectSubtype takes arguments s (an object Type Record), t (an object Type Record), and assumptions (a List of Records that have [[First]] and [[Second]] fields) and returns a Boolean. It determines whether every value of the object type s is a value of the object type t.

    A required target property needs independent evidence of presence in the source. An index signature constrains values at matching keys; it does not provide a missing named property, whether the key is a String or a Symbol. An optional target still permits absence. The same presence requirement applies to readonly targets; readonly affects value variance rather than existence.

    1. For each element q of t.[[Properties]], do
      1. Let p be the element of s.[[Properties]] whose [[Key]] is q.[[Key]], or empty if there is none.
      2. If p is empty, then
        1. If q.[[Optional]] is false, return false.
        2. Continue.
      3. If p.[[Optional]] is true and q.[[Optional]] is false, return false.
      4. If q.[[Readonly]] is false and p.[[Readonly]] is true, return false.
      5. If q.[[Readonly]] is true, then
        1. If IsSubtype(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
      6. Else,
        1. If SameTypeWithAssumptions(p.[[Type]], q.[[Type]], assumptions) is false, return false.
    2. For each element y of t.[[IndexSignatures]], do
      1. Let x be an element of s.[[IndexSignatures]] such that SameType(x.[[KeyType]], y.[[KeyType]]) is true and IsSubtype(x.[[ValueType]], y.[[ValueType]], assumptions) is true, or empty if there is none.
      2. If x is not empty, continue.
      3. If s.[[IndexSignatures]] is not empty, return false.
      4. For each element p of s.[[Properties]], do
        1. If y accepts p.[[Key]] and t.[[Properties]] contains no element whose [[Key]] is p.[[Key]], then
          1. If IsSubtype(p.[[Type]], y.[[ValueType]], assumptions) is false, return false.
    3. Return true.
     Note

    An object type is subtyped in width, so a type with more members is a subtype of one with fewer: an object that has everything { x: float32 } requires is usable where that type is required, whatever else it has.

    An index signature is covered by one of s's own, or - where s declares none - by s's properties. 1.4.2.9 gives the meaning the second case follows: { [key: string]: uint32 } is the type whose remaining string-keyed properties, beyond those declared, are uint32, so a type whose every such property fits is one of its values. This is what a boundary already does with a VALUE (1.7.3) and what an object literal is already checked against (freshly); stating it here is what lets a value that has a type reach such a position, and not only one written in place.

    The value type is covariant in both cases, which is not the rule a writable named member follows.
