A signature does not name a slot a program can be relied on to write through: a property it admits is admitted by its key, not declared, so the layout argument below does not reach it. The two cases agree deliberately - a source that declares a signature and one that does not should not be judged differently.

    A property t declares by name is judged by the property loop above and is skipped here, so a named member whose type differs from the signature's is t's own business.

    It is subtyped in depth only through a readonly member. A readonly member is covariant, since a value read from it and never written through it need only be of the required type. A writable member is invariant, because covariance there is unsound: were { x: Meter } a subtype of { x: float32 }, a bare float32 could be written through the supertype view into a slot the program believes holds a Meter. This is the same rule the reference and array kinds already follow in 1.2.3.1, and it is the point at which this proposal parts company with an erasable type system, which can afford covariance there because nothing depends on the claim. Here the layout does.

    A boundary that accepts a value into a position of an object type does not impose that type's members on the value. The value's own properties keep the types they were declared with, and a property the value declared without a type keeps the any type.

    Note

    This answers the question 1.7.2.1 raises and it answers it in the direction that admits the unsoundness, because the alternative is worse. Imposing the target's member types would mean that passing a plain object to a { x: uint8 } position silently retypes the object for every other holder of it, which is an action at a distance no other boundary performs, and would make the same object have different property types depending on where it had been. The consequence is that a check on a structural type is a statement about the value at the moment it crossed, not a guarantee about it afterwards, and a later write through an untyped alias can invalidate it. A program that wants the guarantee declares the property's type with the { (x: uint8): 1 } form of the object typing section, or uses a class, where the field's type is a property of the layout.

    A narrowing of a property, as in if (o.f instanceof T), follows from the same fact and is admitted only where the property cannot change between the test and the use: a readonly field of a sealed typed class, whose write is a type error after construction. Elsewhere the narrowing does not hold, since o.f may be a getter or may be assigned in between, and 1.8.5 therefore narrows bindings rather than paths.

    1.11.2 Typed Classes

    An established superclass constructor origin is preserved through parentheses and immutable lexical aliases, including aliases of closed specializations. Resolve the declaration by lexical identity and bind its type arguments before deriving inherited instance and static members, constructor signatures, override checks, abstract and interface obligations, operators, layout or access permissions. Initialization order and the class self-name's temporal dead zone remain in force. A mutable or erased alias, an unknown call result, mutation that invalidates the origin, or a cycle supplies no additional origin proof. A class carrying a decorator that may return a replacement supplies a bounded origin instead: the declared class or an unknown subclass of it (7.12). A bounded origin supports the prohibition on redeclaring an inherited typed field and the override and accessor checks against inherited members, which hold for every subclass; inherited members, constructor signatures, abstract and interface obligations, operators, layout and access permissions need an established origin. A decorator whose Static Type is callable only with a void or undefined return replaces nothing, and a class carrying only such decorators is established as itself. No superclass expression is executed by the checking pass.

    An effective own instance field that masks an inherited concrete method or accessor must preserve its participating capabilities. Its readable type must be a conversion-free subtype of an inherited getter's effective return type, and its callable type must accept the inherited method's arguments and supply its result. A function-valued field may satisfy this member-call capability without acquiring the method's receiver marker. An inherited setter also requires writable storage accepting every value the setter accepts. It is a type error when established contracts violate these obligations. Determine actual own-field/prototype precedence before comparison; an inherited own field still masks a derived prototype member. The independent prohibition on redeclaring an inherited typed field continues to apply. Unknown, any and entirely untyped contracts retain their existing treatment, and open contracts are checked when specialization establishes them. No wrapper, identity change or reference-liveness relaxation is implied.

    The accessor-pair declaration rule applies within each effective public, private, instance and static descriptor, even if no expression reads or writes it. The setter must accept every value of the getter's effective return type. Preserve private-name owner identity and separate static and instance namespaces. A field or method that replaces the descriptor is resolved before this comparison; an unpaired getter or setter remains valid. Establishing the pair invokes neither half.

    A paired object-literal accessor obeys the same declaration rule as a class accessor: its setter parameter type must accept every value of its getter's effective return type. The effective return is declared where annotated and published where inference establishes it. Resolve the effective descriptor in property definition order, using established String or Symbol key identity; a data property or ordinary method replaces accessor halves. A spread or unknown computed key prevents any conclusion depending on the descriptor it may replace. Unknown or any contracts remain dynamic. No getter or setter executes during this check.

    Within a static member or static initialization block, this has the constructor-side type of the enclosing class declaration or expression, including its effective static members. This identity belongs to the class declaration node and its specialization, not to the availability of an outer binding for its name. A nested arrow retains that receiver; an ordinary nested function establishes its own receiver context.

    It is a type error for a ClassHeritage expression to have a participating Static Type establishing only primitive values other than null, or a reliable typed invocation origin establishing that the value is not a constructor. The invocation-origin judgment used for new also applies here, including its lexical identity, alias and invalidation rules. A function type alone does not establish constructibility or its absence. null, a possible constructor, or an unknown alternative prevents an all-invalid type proof. Heritage is checked in its lexical scope before entering the class body, with the class self-name in its temporal dead zone and class parameters shadowing outer bindings. A self-name read does not establish an instance-layout cycle. For a participating non-null alternative not already known to fail constructibility, it is also a type error when the effective declared prototype member proves the subsequent prototype stage invalid: its type admits neither Object nor null. A possibly constructible base with such a prototype cannot complete heritage successfully. Combine these proofs over every possible selected path; a possible null base, an Object-or-null prototype, or an unresolved effective member/type prevents an all-invalid proof. An undeclared member of an open shape is unknown, not a proved undefined value. This is the heritage consumer's Object-or-null requirement, not the different prototype requirement of instanceof. The query executes no getter or Proxy trap and changes no runtime lookup, reference-liveness or storage check. Ordinary untyped JavaScript heritage retains its runtime checks, and this judgment adds no inheritance-cycle validation.

    A class is typed when at least one of its public or private fields, declared or inherited, carries a type annotation. A class expression bound to an immutable binding, or written inline where it is extended or constructed, is an established class: it is resolved as a heritage base as a class declaration is, and the Static Type of new of it is its instance type. Inherited counts because a subclass is a subtype: a typed class is automatically sealed, so a subclass that declared nothing and was therefore untyped would have EXTENSIBLE instances where its base has sealed ones, and those instances would still satisfy the base type. A class whose base is itself untyped is unaffected, and an untyped field or a dynamic modifier disqualifies a subclass exactly as it does a base. A typed class is automatically sealed and its prototype frozen, as 1.7.6 specifies. A class declared dynamic is not sealed and is not a value type.

    A typed class is a value type class when every one of its fields has a type that is a value type. Instances of a value type class are values in the sense of 1.5.1: they are laid out contiguously, they are stored inline in a field or an array element of that type, and assigning one copies it. It is a type error for a value type class to contain itself, directly or through a cycle of value type fields, since the layout would have no finite size (9.4). A field that closes such a cycle is written with a type that is a reference (1.11.10).

    Repeated field definitions in one class with the same established property key and placement share one storage contract. It is a type error for their explicit typed contracts to differ under SameType, or for their storage qualifiers (including readonly and layout controls) to disagree. Type metadata participates in that identity. Static and instance fields have separate keys; Symbol keys compare by identity. Compatible repeated contracts retain initializer order and last-value semantics while allocating one layout slot. A later unannotated initializer is still a store to the existing typed slot and must satisfy its contract. Entirely untyped duplicates keep ordinary ECMAScript behaviour. An unresolved computed key or dependent contract is checked when it is established; a determinable conflict is an Early Error. This rule does not permit redeclaring an inherited typed field.

    It is a type error for a class to declare a field whose name a class in its heritage chain declares as a typed field. 9.2 states the rule for a value type class, whose redeclared field would have no defined offset; it holds of every class because a typed field has one declared type, which subtyping, readonly permission and the typed store all read. A subclass that needs a different value for an inherited field assigns it in its constructor, or, for a value type class, declares a zero (1.11.5). A private name is per class and is not redeclared by a subclass's field of the same spelling, and a static field belongs to its own constructor.

    Note 1

    This clause once said that a field written T | null is a reference, which read against 1.11.4 as a claim about aliasing and is not one. A field declared A | null holding an A is reached by both sentences: this one calls it a reference, and the copying rule copies into a field of that type. They agree once the two are read as answering different questions - this one names a layout obligation, that the recursion stops rather than descending, while the copying rule names what a store does.

    What a store does is copy. A value type class in such a field is unshared in every channel a program can reach: storing into it copies, reading out of it copies, === compares fields rather than references, and the value cannot be held weakly (1.12.8). Aliasing would require an identity, and 1.5.1 has already given identity up for these values; a value cannot alias without one. Sharing is reached through a reference type instead, which has an identity precisely so that it can.

    An instance of a value type class REMAINS AN OBJECT. typeof reports "object" for one, and it has the identity an Object has: 1.5.1's "values that are not Objects" describes the types that clause ADDS, and this clause extends value SEMANTICS - copying and inline layout - to a class of Objects without removing them from the object type. A program that reads typeof sees what it saw before.

    IDENTITY is the other half, and it does not follow typeof. An instance of a value type class has none - that is what 1.5.1 means by indistinguishable - so it is refused at the positions that require one: it cannot be a WeakMap or WeakSet key, the target of a WeakRef, or registered with a FinalizationRegistry (1.15.4). The two answers are consistent rather than in tension: typeof reports what KIND of value it is, and a weak reference asks whether the value is one a collector can distinguish from a copy of itself.

    What value semantics does reach is EQUALITY. Two instances of one value type class are ===, Object.is and SameValueZero equal when their fields are, since 1.5.1 requires that "two values of the same value type that are the same value are indistinguishable" and a copy would otherwise be distinguishable from its source. Instances of DISTINCT value type classes are never equal, whatever their layouts, because the values of distinct value types are distinct.

    It is a Syntax Error if the MethodDefinition of a class's constructor has a TypeAnnotation. A constructor declares no return type, since the class is the type a construction yields — for a generic class, the specialization 4.8 binds. Three clauses said so and none said it as an early error, so an implementation could accept the annotation, check the constructor's body against it, and then ignore it at the construction site — enforcing in one place a rule it discarded in another.

    It is a Syntax Error if a typed class's constructor contains a ReturnStatement whose Expression is present and is not this. Bare return; and return this are the control-flow forms and remain legal.

    Note 2

    That the class is the type a construction yields is a claim about run-time behaviour, and the rule above is what makes it true. Without it JavaScript makes it false: [[Construct]] returns the constructor's own object when it returns one, so new C() need not be a C, a declared field reads undefined, and a private-name brand check fails.

    A refusal rather than a check, for two reasons. A base class's returning constructor breaks every subclass — a subclass that writes no return receives an object with neither its fields nor its prototype — and whether the base's returned object is assignable to a subclass is not knowable at the base, so no local check reaches the offence. And 1.7.6's layout guarantees are statements about what a construction produces; a constructor that may yield a foreign object makes every one of them conditional on reading a constructor body, including one the reader did not write.

    The exemption is on the operand's form, not on what it evaluates to: return _cond_ ? this : this is refused, because admitting it would require deciding return _cond_ ? this : _other_, which is the reasoning this rule exists to avoid. A primitive operand is refused for the same reason, though [[Construct]] would discard it. The replacement for a constructor that must yield something else is a static method.

    Scoped to a typed class so that this specification remains a superset: an untyped class keeps JavaScript's semantics unchanged, including a constructor that returns a proxy of its own instance. A class annotated only on a method, a getter, a constructor parameter, or a static field is not typed and is not reached, which is deliberate — only a field annotation makes an instance's shape a fact.

    A field with no initializer holds the default value of its type (1.8.3.1), and it is a type error to declare a field whose type has no default and give it no initializer.

    === on two instances of a value type class compares them field by field, since the identity of a value type is its value. === on two instances of a class that is not a value type compares references.

    A method a class declares whose parameter types are the same as an inherited signature's OVERRIDES that signature rather than overloading it. It is a type error if the effective return type of such a method is not a subtype of the inherited signature's effective return type (the declared type where present, and the published inferred type otherwise, under 1.6.2): an override may narrow a return, so that f(): B may stand over f(): A where B is a subclass of A (a covariant return), but may not change it, since a return that only converts to the inherited one, or is unrelated to it, would make b.f(0) mean two things for one receiver and one argument list. The signature is compared by parameter types alone, which is what a dispatch slot is keyed by; a method whose parameter types differ from every inherited signature's is an overload, as 1.10.3 describes. Java and C# state this rule as written; a Rust trait implementation must match the trait's signature, which is the same commitment.

    An override must also accept every argument sequence admitted by the inherited signature under ordinary parameter binding. Omitted arguments, optional parameters, defaults, rest parameters and reference modes participate in this comparison. The selected derived method evaluates its own defaults; it does not inherit a default expression merely because a base-view call omitted an argument. A derived required parameter therefore cannot replace an omittable inherited parameter unless its boundary admits omission. This is a compatibility obligation after identifying an override by parameter types, not a change to override identity. Apply the obligation again when specialization resolves a dependent contract.

    A field may be declared readonly, a modifier written before the field name and after static where both appear. A readonly field may be assigned only in its own initializer and in a body of a constructor of the declaring class. Every other assignment is a type error: at compile time where the type is known, and at run time otherwise, so an assignment from a method a constructor calls, from a constructor or method of a subclass, through a reference, or through reflection is a TypeError. The permission is the running constructor's, not the constructor's presence on the stack, so a method the constructor invokes cannot write the field even though a constructor is executing. readonly is shallow: it fixes the binding, not the object the field refers to, so a readonly field holding an object may have that object mutated.

    It is a type error to store through a class member whose effective accessor has a getter and no setter, where that member is statically known. Setter presence is independent of its parameter annotation and of the declaration order of a getter/setter pair. This permission applies to simple, compound and update assignments and to destructuring and iteration targets; invoking a declared compound operator that does not replace the member is not such a store. The judgment respects inherited members, specialization, private names, Symbol keys, and the distinction between static and instance members. An own field shadows a prototype accessor regardless of declaration order. A getter-only property does not acquire field-initialization permission in a constructor; a static field or a different private name does not supply that permission. An unknown receiver retains the runtime property checks.

    An effective accessor with a setter and no getter has the readable Static Type undefined. Its write contract remains the setter parameter type, or any where that parameter is unannotated. A getter/setter pair uses the getter result for reads and the setter parameter for writes, independently of declaration order. This applies to class and object-literal accessors, including static and private members and known Symbol keys. Resolve inheritance by the effective property descriptor: an own setter-only descriptor masks an inherited getter; the two descriptors do not supply halves of one pair.

    A member marked protected is accessible only within its declaring class and subclasses of that class. It is a type error to select a statically known protected declaration outside that scope. Apply this permission to fields, methods and accessors, static and instance, using the declaration that supplies the effective member. Dot access and a statically established finite set of String or Symbol keys use the same rule, as does a property of an object binding or assignment pattern, which reads the declaration its key selects, and a rest element or object spread, which reads every declared field of an established typed-class instance that is not otherwise named. Every known selected declaration of a union receiver must permit the access, after narrowing and optional-chain short-circuiting. An inherited member retains its declaring owner; a public override supplies its own permission. Unknown keys and any receivers do not establish a protected declaration. This is a static access rule, without a runtime visibility barrier or a change to layout.

    It is a type error to perform a selected private member operation when its participating receiver's Static Type proves that every remaining alternative is non-Object. This applies to private reads, writes, updates and calls. Optional access first excludes the nullish alternatives that skip the operation; an all-nullish optional receiver selects no access. A possible Object prevents this proof, irrespective of whether its static nominal type names the declaring class: private brands may be installed on other Objects. Unknown and any receivers retain runtime brand checks. This judgment does not change public primitive member access, private-name resolution, setter or readonly permissions, reference liveness, or the prohibition on borrowing private members.

    Performing SetIntegrityLevel with frozen on an instance of a typed class, as Object.freeze does, makes every field of the instance readonly at run time in addition to making its properties non-writable. A subsequent assignment to any field is therefore a TypeError in every mode, rather than the silent failure a non-writable property gives outside strict mode. This applies to an instance of a typed class, the same instances that are automatically sealed; freezing an ordinary object is unchanged.

    Note 3

    That a value type class defaults field by field means an instance can come into existence without its constructor running, which 1.8.3 flags. This clause endorses it, because the design already requires it in two places and the alternative would break both. let d: [10].<A>; must hold ten zero-filled instances for the memory layout extension's contiguous array to exist at all, and a conversion from a matching object literal, { ... } := Vector3, is specified to fill the layout directly and run no constructor. A value type class is therefore a shape with a zero, not an object with an invariant its constructor establishes, and a class that needs its constructor to run states that by holding a field whose type has no default, which makes the zero-filled form a type error. A parameterized field is one way to hold one: a class of unit-typed fields has a zero exactly where the base declares the cast that admits it (1.8.3), so a design that wants its vectors zero-fillable writes that cast, and one whose brand is meant to be reached only through the operators that produce it need not. This is a real constraint on what a value type class can promise, and it should be stated in the design rather than left to follow from the array case.

    1.11.3 Constructor Overloading

    Constructor declaration ambiguity is checked across signatures with different numbers of formal parameters. Optional parameters, defaults and rests can make their admitted argument counts overlap. Use the same viability and specificity rules as ResolveOverload: overlap alone is not ambiguity, and a fixed signature that outranks a rest remains valid. Report a proved ambiguity at the declaration even when no construction is written.

    A class may declare more than one constructor. The declarations are overloads of one construct signature set, resolved at a construction on the same terms as a call to an overloaded function (1.10.3).

    The base language makes a second constructor in a ClassBody a Syntax Error. That error does not apply where the declarations are DISTINCT SIGNATURES and at least one parameter across the set carries a type annotation. This is the relaxation 1.10 already makes for a function name declared twice, applied to the one member the base language singles out.

    The annotation is what admits the set. A class body carrying no annotation on any constructor parameter is exactly what it was: a second constructor is a Syntax Error, so a program with no types in it is unaffected in either direction.

    A signature is identified by its parameter types (1.10.5), and a construction yields the class rather than a declared return type, so two constructors whose parameter types are the same are ONE SIGNATURE DECLARED TWICE. That is a type error at the class, reported as it is for a function declared twice, and not deferred to the constructions that would be ambiguous.

    Note

    Reported at the class rather than at each construction because the mistake is in the class. Deferring it would name a fault at every new and at none of them — the shape 1.6 avoids for a converting constructor by the same reasoning.

    Every one-parameter overload is a converting constructor (1.6). Where more than one could represent a value, the conversion resolves by the argument's type exactly as a call does; it neither picks arbitrarily nor refuses for the ambiguity that resolution is there to settle.

    A VALUE TYPE class is not special here. Its default is built field by field and runs no constructor (1.8.3.1), and its layout is fixed by its fields (9), so neither depends on how many constructors it declares.

    1.11.4 Copying a Value Type

    Assigning a value of a value type, passing one as an argument, and returning one each COPY it. The copy is of the value's layout (9), padding included; it runs no constructor and no field initializer. There is no move that would leave the source invalid.

    The positions at which this occurs are: initializing a binding from a value of such a type, assigning to one, storing into a field or an array element of that type, passing an argument, and returning. A read of a field or an element into any of those positions is one of them, so _e_ in let _e_: _V_ = _arr_[0] holds a copy and writing to it does not disturb the element.

    CONSTRUCTION does not copy. A constructor call, an object-literal conversion, and a return of a newly constructed value build their result directly in the destination — a binding, a field, an array element, or the caller's receiving slot — so return { … } := _Matrix4_ writes the caller's storage in place, Matrix4 being a class that DECLARES a conversion from such a literal (1.6.8). An object literal does not convert to a class structurally: a class is satisfied by construction, not by shape, and the three declared forms are how a type states that a literal may become one. This is the copy elision that C++17 guarantees for prvalues, required here rather than permitted.

    A field in this clause is a class field carrying a declared type (1.11.2), and an array element is an element of an array carrying a declared element type. These are the storage that holds a value of a value type INLINE, which is why storing into one copies. A plain object's property and a plain array's element are not fields or elements in this sense: they hold a REFERENCE, as they do for a value of any other type, and a program that wants a copy into one writes a conversion.

    A SUBCLASS OF A VALUE TYPE CLASS IS NOT ASSIGNABLE TO ITS BASE. Where Sub extends Base, Base is a value type class, and Sub declares storage of its own, a value of Sub may not be placed in a position whose declared type is Base: not a field, an array element, a binding, an argument, or a return. The base's storage is _Base_.byteLength wide and the subclass does not fit, so the store could only keep part of the value; refusing it is what keeps a position of type Base holding a Base.

    Three things follow, and each is deliberate. A subclass that declares NO storage of its own has its base's layout exactly, so storing one loses nothing and is permitted. A REFERENCE TYPE base — a reference, sealed or abstract class (1.11.10) — holds any subclass by pointer and is unaffected; this is how a program expresses a hierarchy it means to be polymorphic. And the SUBTYPE RELATION IS UNCHANGED: Sub is a Base, _v_ is _Base_ and _v_ instanceof _Base_ both answer true, and a bound _T_ extends _Base_ instantiates at Sub carrying the whole value. Subtyping and storability come apart here, and only here: what a Base-sized slot cannot do is HOLD one.

    The conversion _v_ := _Base_ (1.6.7) is the widening, and the only way to obtain the base part. Its result is a value of Base — its prototype is Base's, its methods are Base's, and it may be stored wherever a Base may. The loss is written in the program, which is the distinction this clause exists to draw: a conversion between types is spelled explicitly rather than performed silently.

    A copy site is decided by WHAT THE SOURCE EXPRESSION IS, not by whether a type is written at it. A NAME, a field read and an element read each denote a value that already exists, so binding or assigning from one copies; a constructor call, a call, and a literal conversion each produce a value in place, so binding or assigning from one does not. let _b_: _V_ = _a_ and let _b_ = _a_ therefore copy alike, and _b_ = _a_ copies whether or not _b_ was declared with a type.

    An ARRAY LITERAL at a typed array's annotation stores each of its elements, so a literal naming an existing value copies it: const _arr_: [1].<P> = [_a_] and _arr_[0] = _a_ are one operation written two ways and hold a copy alike. The elision above does not reach this. It exempts an object-literal CONVERSION — a literal BECOMING a value of a value type, as { … } := _Matrix4_ does — and not a literal whose ELEMENTS are values of one; reading it the second way would elide the store this clause requires. A literal of CONSTRUCTIONS is unaffected, each element building in place.

    In particular the copy is NOT taken at a type boundary. A boundary is a check site (Table 23), and a check may be skipped where the source provably satisfies the target: a skipped check is nothing, while a skipped copy is an alias. An implementation that copies only where a check runs will alias exactly where a program is most explicit about its types, which is the opposite of what this clause requires.

    A ref binding (2.10) is the opt-out: it names a storage location rather than taking a value, so no copy and no allocation occurs, which is how a program passes a large value type without paying for it.

    A method's this value is the receiver's STORAGE and not a copy of it, so a method that writes to this writes through to the receiver, whether the receiver is a binding, a field, or an array element.

    Note

    The last rule is what makes a mutating method possible at all: were this a copy, _m_.bump() would compute a new value and discard it. C# reaches the same answer for a receiver that is a variable. Rust requires the receiver to be marked &mut self and this specification has no such marker, so the rule is stated rather than inferred — and the compound assignment forms of 1.9.9 depend on it: a declared compound operator is invoked as a method call and its target is not written, so the update it performs is a write through this, which a copied this would discard.

    A copy running no constructor is coherent with 1.11.2's reading of what a value type class is: "a shape with a zero, not an object with an invariant its constructor establishes". A class that needs its constructor to have run states that by holding a field whose type has no default.

    The copy carries the class's PRIVATE fields as well as its public ones, for the reason the default does: a private field is part of the shape. A copy that dropped one would leave a value of the type that its own methods could not read, and the identity rule above — two instances === exactly when their fields are, compared field by field — would compare a field one of them does not have.

    Copying is a property of ASSIGNMENT rather than of conversion, and the distinction is load-bearing for an implementation. A check inserted at a boundary (Table 23) may be skipped where the source provably satisfies the target, since a check that cannot fail does nothing. A copy is never nothing. An implementation that performs the copy as part of the boundary check will therefore copy or not according to what its checker happened to prove, which is one semantics decided by an optimisation.

    1.11.5 Declared Zeros

    A class may declare the value its bindings hold before assignment, in place of the one 1.8.3.1 derives field by field. The declaration is a static field named default:

    ClassElement[Yield, Await] : static default = AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ;

    The class's declared zero is that AssignmentExpression's value. It REPLACES the derived default rather than adding to it: a class that declares one is stating that the field-by-field value does not describe it, which is why 1.8.3.1 consults the declaration before every other step. A class that declares none is unaffected.

    The AssignmentExpression must be compile-time evaluable (1.2.7.1) and it is a type error otherwise, and it is evaluated ONCE, when the class is declared. The reason is the one 1.4.2.7 gives for a tuple element's Initializer: a type is interned, so one Type Object serves every use of it, and a zero that allocated per binding would either hand every value the same object or make the type's identity depend on when it was read. A compile-time evaluable zero is copied where it is used, so the sharing is unobservable — which is what a derived default already does, field by field.

    It is a type error if the declared zero is not a value of the class.

    Note 1

    The restriction is what keeps a declaration cheap. let d: [1000].<Transform>; takes Transform's zero a thousand times; evaluating a user expression that many times would turn a fill into a loop of calls, where copying one snapshot is the fill an engine would have emitted anyway.

     Note 2

    An interface cannot declare a zero, because it has no static member to declare it in. A binding of an interface type with no default remains a type error, as 1.8.3.1 already makes it.

    1.11.6 Abstract Classes

    An abstract obligation identifies an instance property key and a member kind: method, getter or setter. A same-named static member, field, or different accessor kind does not implement it. Property keys retain their identity, including Symbols and established computed keys. Compare full effective signatures, including parameter flags and generic parameters; normalize generator and async-generator implementation returns to their carrier types before comparison. An async implementation is compared using its declared Promise return. A compatible inherited implementation satisfies the obligation unless a nearer declaration masks it. An abstract redeclaration must itself satisfy the inherited signature and the ordinary override-return covariance rule; the nearest valid declaration governs subsequent implementations. Known violations are Early Errors, with the same judgment applied to contracts resolved during class-definition evaluation.

    A class may be declared abstract, sealed, or dynamic. The productions below restate their ECMAScript definitions with the modifier list (1.1); sealed is specified by 1.11.9, dynamic by 1.11.2, and the abstract method form is an alternative of the ClassElement restatement in 16. It is a type error if a modifier is repeated, and a type error if sealed and dynamic are declared together.

    ClassDeclaration[Yield, Await, Default] : ClassModifiersopt class BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] ClassTail[?Yield, ?Await] [+Default] ClassModifiersopt class ClassTail[?Yield, ?Await] ClassExpression[Yield, Await] : ClassModifiersopt class BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await]opt ClassTail[?Yield, ?Await] ClassModifiers : ClassModifier ClassModifiers ClassModifier ClassModifier : one of abstract sealed dynamic partial

    A member is abstract because it has no body; the abstract keyword before it is optional and says the same thing earlier. The absence of a body is what an implementation supplies, so the forms that have nothing to supply are not abstract members and remain a type error without a body, each for its own reason: a static member has no override site; a constructor is not implemented by a subclass but called by one through super(), and a class that cannot be constructed is what abstract on the class already declares; and an async or generator method's contract is written as an ordinary abstract method returning the type it produces, abstract m(): Promise.<T> rather than abstract async m(): T, so that a body's shape stays an implementation detail. A get or set accessor is an abstract member: it has an override site and its annotation types the implementations exactly as a method's does.

    An abstract method is a signature with no body, and its annotation types the implementations: it is a type error if a subclass implements an inherited abstract method with a signature the abstract declaration does not accept. It is a type error if a method with no body appears in a class not declared abstract, whether or not the abstract keyword is written, and a type error if a class not declared abstract leaves an inherited abstract method unimplemented. Where the Static Type of the constructor in new C(…) is an abstract class it is a type error; the [[Construct]] internal method of an abstract class's constructor throws a TypeError exception when NewTarget is that constructor itself, so a dynamic construction fails at run time while super() from a concrete subclass, arriving with a concrete NewTarget, runs the abstract constructor as a constructor body should.

    The direct-instantiation restriction follows a constructor identity proved through stable binding origins, including aliases, parentheses and specializations whose declaration is known. It does not remove the abstract constructor's construction capability: heritage and super() with a concrete NewTarget remain valid. Reassignment, shadowing, any, decorators and other unresolved transformations prevent an identity proof; a function's return type alone does not identify its result as a constructor declaration. The judgment executes no constructor or reference and changes no runtime liveness requirement.

    An abstract class is never a value type class (value type class). Its purpose is polymorphic dispatch through the hierarchy, which is reference behaviour, so an abstract class and every subclass reached through an abstract-typed binding are reference types.

    Note

    The design's Shape declares abstract area(): number; beside a concrete describe(), which is the division of labour: an interface is pure signature, while an abstract class carries the partial implementation a family of subclasses completes (design, README, Abstract Classes).

    1.11.7 Interfaces

    1.11.7.1 Interface Declaration Identity

    A source interface declaration introduces a nominal type at an actual lexical binding instance, not at a Parse Node alone. Associate one opaque interface declaration identity with that binding instance when declaration instantiation creates it. All Type Records formed for that source interface carry the identity in [[DeclarationIdentity]]. The identity is specification data, not an ECMAScript value, Reference or permission to access a location.

    1. Repeated type references, forward and recursive formation, checking preparation, ordinary Evaluation and any rebuilding of the same binding use its one identity. Rebuilding is not a new declaration instantiation.
    2. A fresh binding created by another function call, block entry, loop iteration or other lexical activation has a distinct identity, even if its Parse Node and captured values are the same. Reading an outer binding, returning its Type Object, or reaching it through an alias, import or re-export preserves its identity.
    3. A generic application retains the identity of its primary interface binding and adds the arguments established by ordinary generic binding. Equal arguments of that same binding denote one Type Object. Equal arguments of different binding instances do not. Rules relating applications of the same interface declaration, including variance, family matching and an erased argument, require the same declaration identity before comparing arguments.
    4. A partial interface contribution targets the actual resolved primary interface Type Object. It preserves that primary's identity and updates only its matching applications, including those already formed. A later activation of the same source declaration does not receive or overwrite another activation's contributions. Failure publishes no contribution to either activation.

    The member contract is formed using the lexical and generic inputs belonging to this declaration activation under 1.3.6. A class's runtime implements contracts retain the actual resolved interface identities, including through aliases and inherited class contracts. A symbolic checking record with no established binding identity is not a wildcard matching every activation. Publication of one constructor's resolved contracts must not overwrite those of a constructor created by an earlier activation. Interning, reflection reconstruction and successful-evaluation caches cannot substitute another activation's contract. A source location, spelling, Parse Node or matching member shape alone is insufficient to establish this identity. A checker may represent an as-yet uninstantiated binding symbolically; a shared Parse Node alone supplies no proof that distinct activations denote the same interface.

    Interface membership may still be structural, and structural aliases retain ordinary canonicalization. This identity rule changes neither the reference-liveness permissions of captured inputs nor the existing availability, evaluation and checking-phase rules. An implementation may share code and immutable structural summaries across activations when doing so preserves these identities and contracts. The identity itself need not retain an environment, a program value or a live reference.

    Self-referential, mutually recursive and forward-referenced interface contracts are formed under 1.3.6, preserving lexical binding identity and the complete member graph in nested scopes as well as at the source-checking boundary.

    Call signatures are obligations of an implements clause. It is a type error when established construction behaviour proves that the produced instance cannot be callable, as for an ordinary class with default non-callable construction. A method named call does not supply [[Call]], and the clause itself adds no call capability. An established callable construction result is checked by the ordinary signature relation. Function-derived construction with an unknown signature, unknown heritage, and replacement objects returned by constructors whose capability is unresolved retain the obligation at the eventual typed boundary. Do not execute constructors or infer callability merely from the claimed interface.

    Resolve each implements target by ordinary lexical type resolution, including transparent aliases and known imported identities. The resolved target must denote an interface; it is a type error if it denotes an established non-interface type. Alias chains do not create a new nominal identity. Bind generic arguments by BindTypeArguments, including names, packs, defaults, constraints and family-case selection, before verifying properties or operators. Retain the resolved interface declaration and bound arguments for subsequent nominal judgments; comparing source spellings or zipping arguments by written position is insufficient. Open applications retain their specialization obligations.

    Declaration-site verification includes each applicable index signature. Check established own enumerable instance fields, including inherited fields installed on the instance, against the signature's value type, except keys explicitly declared as interface properties, which retain their named contracts. Compare actual String and Symbol keys. Prototype methods and accessors are not enumerable instance fields. An index signature does not require every admitted key to exist. Unknown computed keys and dynamic additions retain their runtime checks; no constructor is executed to discover them.

    Declaration-site satisfaction includes the effective member's availability and read/write capability. A readonly field or getter-only property does not implement a writable interface property. Preserve optionality, readonly covariance, writable-property invariance and the ordinary function-signature relation, including inherited and specialized members. A declaration must not promise an interface that its effective property capabilities cannot satisfy.

    An interface is declared with the productions below; InterfaceDeclaration is an alternative of the Declaration restatement of 6.1, and ClassTail is restated with the implements clause (1.1).

    InterfaceDeclaration[Yield, Await] : interface BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt { InterfaceBody[?Yield, ?Await]opt } InterfaceBody[Yield, Await] : InterfaceMemberList[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberSeparatoropt InterfaceMemberList[Yield, Await] : InterfaceMember[?Yield, ?Await] InterfaceMemberList[?Yield, ?Await] TypeMemberSeparator InterfaceMember[?Yield, ?Await] InterfaceMember[Yield, Await] : TypeMember[?Yield, ?Await] OperatorDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] ClassTail[Yield, Await] : ClassHeritage[?Yield, ?Await]opt ImplementsClause[?Yield, ?Await]opt { ClassBody[?Yield, ?Await]opt } ImplementsClause[Yield, Await] : implements ImplementsList[?Yield, ?Await] ImplementsList[Yield, Await] : TypeReference[?Yield, ?Await] ImplementsList[?Yield, ?Await] , TypeReference[?Yield, ?Await]

    An interface's members are the TypeMember forms of an object type, index signatures and optional members with defaults included, and additionally operator members, as interface Ordered<T: type> { operator<(other: T): boolean; } written with declaration-site <…>; a type satisfies an operator member by declaring the operator. It is a type error if a class whose ClassTail carries an ImplementsClause does not satisfy every member, operator members included, of every listed interface.

    An interface declares a contract. Its type is a nominal type whose [[Declaration]] is the interface declaration, and a class that implements it is a subtype of it by 1.2.3.1, which follows the declared hierarchy. An interface may also type an object, an array, or a function structurally.

    A class that implements an interface cannot remove the contract: deleting a member the interface requires throws a TypeError exception, and this holds through a subclass, a reference, and reflection.

    The declaration is verified where it is made. It is a type error if a class declares that it implements an interface and does not declare every member the interface requires, an optional member excepted, with a type assignable to the interface's; a generic method satisfies the interface's through the identification SameFunctionType performs (1.10.2.1), so on<U: type> satisfies on<T: type> and on<T: type, U: type> does not. A member the class may leave out, an optional one, is supplied by the interface.

    Note 1

    An interface is nominal where a class declares that it implements one and structural where a value is checked against it, which are two questions rather than one contradiction: the first asks whether a declaration promised the contract, the second whether a value meets it. IsOfType decides the second by 1.7.2.1, so an object that has the members satisfies an interface-typed position whether or not any class declared it.

    Note 2

    The two questions divide by WHO ASKS, and the division decides a case that reads as a contradiction until it is named. A subtype question - is this type assignable to that one - is answered by 1.2.3.1, which relates two nominal types along declared inheritance and no other way; an interface's type is nominal, so a class reaches an interface-typed position by DECLARING implements and not by matching the shape. A value question - is this value of that type - is answered by IsOfType, which walks the members; a class instance that has them passes it whether or not the class declared anything.

    So class Rich { m(): uint8 { … } } without an implements clause gives new Rich() is Small the answer true, and let s: Small = new Rich() a type error. That is the same visible-and-blind split 1.7.3 describes: the checker can see that the source is a Rich, and refuses the claim a declaration never made; the same value arriving where its type is not visible is checked and admitted. new Rich() := Small states the claim in one token where a program means it.

    The alternative - a class satisfying any interface it happens to match - is what 1.2.3.1 forbids on purpose: a class states a construction and an identity as well as a shape, and it is the identity its type is for. A shape with no identity is written as an object type, and satisfies structurally in every position.

    1.11.8 Enums

    The missing-first-initializer rule is checked directly for every enum declaration in its lexical type scope. A known non-numeric underlying type requires an explicit first value even in a nested, unused body; closed enum evaluation is not a prerequisite. Empty enums, numeric default starts and valid later omissions retain their rules. An unresolved underlying type is checked when specialization or evaluation supplies it, without executing an ordinary enclosing function during checking.

    The enum switch judgment uses the enum declaration identified by the discriminant's resolved Static Type. A transparent alias, a known member read or a known call result preserves that identity; a shared underlying primitive type does not. Each enumerator label resolves in its own lexical scope and must name that same enum declaration. A default covers remaining values, and enumerator names sharing one value require coverage of that value only once. An unknown or any discriminant supplies no enum exhaustiveness proof.

    The labels of an enum switch are tested in order, so a label naming an enumerator whose value an earlier label of the same switch names, itself or through another name sharing that value, can never succeed, and it is a type error by 1.8.5.4. Coverage is of values, so a case for every value covers the enum however many names share one; a default that covers an enumerator without a label, a sentinel included, is live.

    An enum is declared with the productions below; EnumDeclaration is an alternative of the Declaration restatement of 6.1.

    EnumDeclaration[Yield, Await] : enum BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { EnumMemberList[?Yield, ?Await]opt ,opt } EnumMemberList[Yield, Await] : EnumMember[?Yield, ?Await] EnumMemberList[?Yield, ?Await] , EnumMember[?Yield, ?Await] EnumMember[Yield, Await] : IdentifierName Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt

    It is a type error if two enumerators of one declaration have the same name. Every initializer is evaluated in the compile-time evaluable fragment (1.2.7), since an enumerator is a constant of the program. An enumerator's initializer stands in a position whose contextual type is the underlying type, so a literal there takes it (1.6.6): enum D: decimal64 { A = 1.00 } holds the decimal 1.00 rather than a rounded double, and enum B: bigint { A = 1 } needs no n suffix. The contextual type is applied rather than required, since an initializer may also be a function of two parameters, which this clause calls rather than stores.

    It is a type error if an enumerator's value is already an enumerator of another enum of the same agent. What the source text shows of this rule is an Early Error: two enumerators of different declarations whose initializers are references to one immutable binding hold one value. A collision reached any other way, through a second binding or a value a call returns, is known only when the second declaration evaluates, and is a TypeError thrown there; identity is a fact about values, and a value built while checking is not the one the program later holds. Where the underlying type's values carry their own identity, that is an object, a function, or a symbol, an enumerator IS the value its initializer denotes, which is what makes it usable as that value without conversion. A value serving two enums would therefore be a value of two nominal types, and 1.5.1 admits none. Where the underlying type's values are compared by content, an enumerator is a distinct value of that content carrying its enum, so two enums may name the same content, and enum A { X = 0 } and enum B { Y = 0 } declare different values that this rule does not reach.

    Note 1

    The rule above is stated over values rather than over the form of an initializer. An initializer that constructs its value cannot conflict, but one that calls a function to construct it is equally sound, and no syntactic test separates the two. A declaration may therefore claim a value the program obtained elsewhere, including a shared or built-in one, and the effect of doing so is that 1.7.1.1 reports the enum for that value.

    An enum declaration introduces a nominal type whose values are its enumerators. The type after : is the enum's underlying type, and an enum declared without one has the underlying type int32. Any type may be an underlying type, including a function type and symbol.

    The first enumerator, when it has no initializer, takes 0, and it is a type error when the underlying type is not numeric, since a non-numeric enumeration must define its starting value. A later enumerator with no initializer takes the result of applying the underlying type's prefix increment operator operator++ to the previous enumerator's value, with the previous enumerator itself unmodified; where the underlying type declares no prefix increment, it takes a value equal to the previous one. An enumerator's initializer may name the enumerators declared before it in the same enum, each bound to its value as it is evaluated; it is a type error for it to name the enumerator it belongs to or one declared later, since the evaluation proceeds in declaration order and the binding does not yet exist. The enum's own name is not in scope there, being uninitialized until the declaration completes, so an earlier enumerator is named directly rather than through the enum. An enumerator initialized with a function of two parameters is given the result of calling that function with the enumerator's index and its name as a String, and a following enumerator with no initializer is given the result of calling the most recently given such function with its own index and name, until an initializer replaces it; an initializer that is not such a function sets its enumerator's value without disturbing the function for those after it. Such a function is not a closure.

    Note 2

    The increment above is the underlying type's own, not an operation on numbers. A bigint enumeration counts by 1n; an enumeration over a class whose declaration provides operator++ counts by calling it, with the previous enumerator unmodified; and a type declaring no prefix increment repeats, which is what gives B the value of A in enum S: string { A = "x", B }.

    An enum type is a subtype of its underlying type, so a value of an enum type is usable wherever the underlying type is required and no conversion is written. The reverse is explicit: calling the enum type with a value of the underlying type returns the enumerator whose value it is, and throws a TypeError when it is not one of them.

    A switch whose discriminant is a value of an enum type is checked at compile time. Each case label must be an enumerator of that enum, and it is a type error for a label that is not one; and where the switch has no default, it is a type error unless it has a case for every enumerator. Where it has a case for every enumerator, it is a type error for it also to have a default: the row of 1.8.5 gives the default its discriminant with every case's type removed, which is empty, so the default can never be taken (1.8.5.4), as a default after every atom of a match subject cannot (24.3.1). This is the enum row of the narrowing and exhaustiveness rules (1.8.5), the same closed-set reasoning a sealed hierarchy uses (1.11.9): the enumerators are a fixed set the declaration owns, so covering them is a claim the checker can prove.

    An enum's Type Object has %Enum.prototype% as its prototype, which has %Type.prototype% as its own, so an enum carries everything a Type Object carries and an enumeration surface besides. That surface is: toString, which takes a VALUE and returns the key of the enumerator having it, or undefined where no enumerator has it; keys, values, and entries, each returning an Array Iterator over the enumerators in declaration order, of the keys, of the values, and of two-element key-and-value Arrays respectively; and @@iterator, which is entries; and underlying, an accessor giving the Type Object of the type an enumerator's value is of. An enum's Type Object also has an own property for each enumerator's POSITION, so an enumeration is indexed by position beside being indexed by name.

    Note 3

    toString takes the value as an argument rather than being a method on an enumerator, because an enumerator IS a value of the underlying type: the one-way subtype rule above is what makes comp / 32 read directly, and it leaves an enumerator with no method of its own to override. String interpolation therefore sees the underlying value, and obtaining the key is what toString is for.

    @@iterator is entries rather than values, the choice Map makes and the opposite of the one Array and Set make, and for their reason: what an enumeration holds is named values, so yielding a bare value discards the name that distinguishes an enum from its underlying type. Indexing by position rather than by underlying value is the counterpart choice - a lookup BY VALUE is the reverse conversion and is already spelled Count(_n_), so an index that repeated it would leave the enumeration with no way to be read in order. forEach, filter, and map are deliberately absent: entries composes with the Array methods to give all three, and this specification has declined composable surface before.

     Note 4

    The one-way rule is the rule of C#, Rust, and Swift. It is what lets a bitmask index such as comp / 32 read directly while Component(id) remains a deliberate and validated step, and it is why an enum can be used for arithmetic, indexing, and comparison without a cast.

    An enum's subtyping is a further case of the primitive and nominal rules in 1.2.3.1, which follow a declared class hierarchy and a metadata parameterization but do not reach an enum's underlying type. It is stated here rather than there because it is the same shape of relation, a type that refines another and is subsumed into it, and the specification should ultimately give the three one rule rather than three.

    underlying is an accessor rather than a method because it reports something the type IS, as family and the layout properties do, where keys and values perform an enumeration. It lives on the Type Object rather than on a reflection node for the reason 1.12.3 gives for every named leaf: an enum shares the primitive node, whose payload is the interned Type Object itself, and a walker that needs to know a leaf is an enum reads family on that node rather than a kind of its own. An engine that emitted a distinct node kind for an enum instead would put a kind in reflection output that Table 33 does not list, and would have nothing for 1.12.4 to consume.

    Reflect.typeOf(Count.Zero) reports Count, by the rule of 1.12.1 that a value's runtime type is the most specific type of which it is a value. This does not make the enumerator anything other than a value the underlying type also accepts: membership in int32 follows from Count being a subtype of it, not from a second runtime type, so the uniqueness 1.7.1.1 requires is preserved and no conversion is performed. The case is exactly parallel to a metadata parameterization, where Reflect.typeOf of a Meter is float32.<{ m: 1 }> and not float32, while m instanceof float32 is nonetheless true.

    What remains is that this specification now has three relations of one shape: a metadata parameterization refining its primitive, an enum refining its underlying type, and a class extending its base. Each is a case of the refinement relation that 1.2.3.1 now names once, and the design would be better stating the enum case as subtyping rather than as an implicit conversion, which is what it is: describing it as a conversion is what makes it look like a fifth exception to Table 13 when it is not an exception at all.

    That an enumerator reports its enum is a requirement on the VALUE and not only on the type: an implementation must be able to recover the enum from the value. Where the underlying type's values are compared by content, an enumerator may be a distinct value carrying its enum. Where they carry their own identity, the enumerator is the value itself and the enum is recovered from it by other means, which is what the at-most-one rule above makes possible.

    1.11.9 Sealed Classes

    A class declared sealed may not be extended outside the module that declares it, so its subclasses are a fixed and known set. A sealed class is a reference type (1.11.10) rather than a value type, so a field of a sealed type holds an instance of any of its subclasses directly rather than through a nullable union.

    A sealed abstract class can be neither instantiated nor extended outside its module. Its concrete subclasses are therefore a closed set with no case among them for the base, and a switch over a value of its type is exhaustive when it has a case for each subclass. A default in such a switch is then a type error, for the reason 1.11.8 gives for an enum: it can never be taken.

    In a switch whose discriminant's Static Type is a sealed class, each case label is a class, and CaseClauseIsSelected selects a clause where InstanceofOperator(input, clauseSelector) is true rather than by strict equality, the labels being tested in source order. Each label is a narrowing form over what the labels before it left (Table 24), so a label for a class no value left can be of, a class outside the hierarchy, one an earlier label named, or a subclass of one an earlier label named, can never succeed, and is a type error by 1.8.5.4.

    Note

    This is the algebraic data type, assembled from parts the proposal has for other reasons rather than from a new construct. The cases are the subclasses, the case labels are their type objects, which are values because types are values, and the match is the switch the control structures section already defines. What makes it work is that the set is closed: exhaustiveness is a claim about a hierarchy no other module can extend, which is why it is reserved to a sealed class and an enum and is deliberately not available for a union of literal types, whose members are not a declaration anyone owns.

    That a sealed class is a reference type is what lets a field hold a subclass instance polymorphically. A value type class cannot, since its field embeds the base slice of the layout and has no room for a subclass, which is why the two forms differ. A T | *null* field is NOT the polymorphic spelling: an optional over a value type with a layout is inline (10), a discriminant and a payload sized for T, so it has exactly as little room for a subclass as the bare field does. It expresses ABSENCE, not polymorphism. Holding a value type class polymorphically is spelled by a reference type - a reference, sealed or abstract class - or avoided by giving each concrete class its own array, which needs no polymorphism at all since [N].<A> and [N].<B> each know their own stride.

    1.11.10 Reference Classes

    A class declared reference is a reference type. Its instances are held and passed by reference: assigning one aliases rather than copies it, === on two of them compares references rather than fields, a field declared with its type holds a reference of the implementation's width, and a field of that type may hold an instance of any of its subclasses.

    A class declared sealed or abstract is a reference type for its own reasons (1.11.9), so neither needs the modifier. The kind is inherited: a class whose base chain reaches a reference type is one.

    Because a reference type is reached through a reference, a field of one closes a cycle that would otherwise have no finite layout (9.4), and a reference type has no layout to report (Table 58) though a field of one occupies a reference's width.

    Note

    Two things need this modifier, and neither is served by the reference types that already exist. A class that contains itself has no finite inline layout, and sealed is the only existing way to say so - which forbids the extension an open class exists to offer. And a typed class meant to be subclassed by other modules is a value type class, so a field declared with its type embeds only the base slice and an instance of a subclass assigned to one loses everything the subclass added; such a class has always needed to be a reference type, and reference (1.11.10) is now the way to say it.

    The decision is made once at the declaration rather than at each use, which is what struct and class are in C# and in Swift. A per-use spelling, as Rust's Box<T>, &T and Rc<T> are, does not survive this specification's two commitments: an owned box would have to copy on store, since there is no move that leaves a source invalid (1.11.4), and a linked structure built from copying boxes copies its whole tail at every link; a box that instead aliased would have acquired an identity, and would be handing one to a value whose === this specification defines as structural. Rust can offer the use-site choice because it has no collector and ownership must therefore be written down. A language whose collector owns lifetime has one kind of reference, so the only question left is whether a given class is reached through one, which is a property of the class.

    1.11.11 Partial Classes

    The non-class-target judgment uses the actual lexical binding, not only declarations in the partial's statement list. An established ordinary-function or non-class value is a type error; immutable aliases preserve established class origins. A local declaration shadows an outer declaration in the ordinary way. A partial class creates no new binding for either lexical resolution or this judgment. Unknown, imported or dynamically supplied origins are not thereby proved non-class, and no type builder or constructor executes merely to classify the target.

    A class declared partial re-opens a class that is already declared, whether earlier in the same program, in another module, or as an intrinsic, and adds methods and operators to it. A partial declaration names an existing class; it declares no binding of its own, and its members are merged into the named class so that its instances and the class itself gain them. An instance method is added to the class's prototype, a static method to the constructor, and a named operator registers in the class's operator table, each as a fresh declaration of the member would place it.

    The partial keyword is required to extend a class this way. A class declaration whose name is already declared, and which is not partial, is an error, so a program cannot fork a class's behaviour by an accidental re-declaration. It is a type error if a partial declaration names a value that is not a class.

    A partial declaration adds behaviour and no cases: it introduces no subclass and no instance state, so it does not enlarge the closed set of a sealed hierarchy and does not change a class's layout. Extending a class with a partial declaration is therefore available from any module, including on a sealed class, which is the difference between it and a mixin: applying a mixin to a sealed class from outside its declaring module would create a subclass and is refused (1.11.9), while a partial extension adds no subclass and is allowed. A partial declaration over a CLASS does not re-open the constructor or add fields; it is a channel for methods and operators. A partial declaration over an INTERFACE may add members, and adds no instance state by doing so, since an interface declares a shape and constructs nothing: the three reasons above - no subclass, no instance state, no change to a layout - all hold of it, which is why the restriction a class needs an interface does not. A member already declared on the interface is a TypeError rather than an override, so the meaning of an interface does not depend on the order its declarations load.

    A partial declaration of a generic class or interface takes no parameter list of its own (1.4.3.1). With no list, its members are in the scope of the primary declaration's parameters: partial class Box { get(): T { … } } over class Box<T: type> adds a member to every application. A specialization list instead restricts the applications receiving the contribution. For example, partial class Box<uint8> contributes only to Box.<uint8>, and partial class Box<const E extends Numeric> contributes where the argument satisfies both the primary's bound and the capture's bound.

    The target is resolved through the partial's lexical binding, including an imported binding or immutable class alias. A partial need not share the primary's statement list; the placement restriction on replacement cases does not apply. Nested application patterns resolve the receiving constructor by declaration identity and expose its declared parameters, including argument labels, value domains, and defaults. Captures bind in the partial's member signatures and bodies; primary parameters continue to denote the target application's arguments. A wildcard imposes no additional condition and introduces no binding.

    Each partial is matched independently using the specialization-pattern rules. Every matching contribution is added; there is no most-specific winner among partials. Overlapping patterns are valid when they add distinct members. A member colliding with a primary member or another applicable partial's member is a type error, even when the signatures are identical. Overloads and paired accessors declared together within one contribution remain governed by their ordinary declaration rules. Instance and static member namespaces are distinct.

    An extension is available when its declaring module is loaded. Matching contributions apply to existing and future applications of the same declaration and arguments. The constructor and Type Object identities are preserved; instance storage, layout, and existing reference-liveness obligations are unchanged. New methods are checked with the same parameter, result, storage, and reference judgments as methods in the primary. An interface contribution extends the required contract without adding state or manufacturing members on existing objects.

    A statically established collision or incompatible member use is an early type error. Where the target or application is unavailable to the checker, the corresponding runtime operation performs the check. Loading an extension may require invalidating cached member and contract information; it does not authorize an engine to retain a proof based on the earlier member set.

    Note

    The metadata channel of the decorators and metadata extension is the principal use: a program adds typed Symbol-keyed members to an intrinsic metadata interface by declaring a partial interface over it, which is how a type's reflected metadata is extended without owning the declaration that carries it.

    1.12 Reflection

    This clause defines what a program observes of a type at run time: the operation that reports a value's type, the opacity of a Type Object, the operation that exposes a type's structure, and the effect of a declared type on the existing reflective operations.

    1.12.1 Reflect.typeOf ( value )

    This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return GetTypeObject(RuntimeTypeOf(value)).
     Note

    Reflect.typeOf reports the most specific type of which the value is a value, not every type it belongs to. For a uint8 binding it returns uint8; for a value of the metadata-parameterized Meter it returns float32.<{ m: 1 }>, the full parameterization, which is how reflection obtains constraint information at run time. Membership in a less specific type is not a second runtime type but a consequence of subtyping, which is why m instanceof float32 is true while Reflect.typeOf(m) is not float32.

    It is the companion of typeof, which is unchanged and reports the underlying language type: typeof a is "number" for a uint8 binding while Reflect.typeOf(a) is uint8. typeof on a Type Object is "object", since a Type Object is an Object, and typeof uint8 === "object" therefore doubles as feature detection for this proposal.

    1.12.2 The Opacity of a Type Object

    A Type Object exposes no property that reveals the structure of the type it denotes. Given the Type Object for Player | null no property yields its members, and given the one for [].<uint32> no property yields its element type or its extent. A Type Object's [[TypeRecord]] is an internal slot and is reachable only through 1.12.3.

    One exception is display: a Type Object has a toString method returning the canonical source form of the type it denotes, so calling String on the Type Object for 'a' | 'b' yields the String "'a' | 'b'". The printed form exists for diagnostics and authored error messages, not for inspection: its format follows the canonical form and is therefore stable, but parsing it is not the supported way to read a type's structure, which remains 1.12.3.

    A Type Object is callable: it has a [[Call]] internal method, so a type may be applied to an argument as T(v). For a plain type the call is the explicit conversion of 1.6, the same operation as v := T. For an enum type the call is the reverse conversion of 1.11.8, returning the enumerator whose underlying value the argument is. This does not make a Type Object a function to typeof, which reports "object" for it (1.12.1); the callability is the conversion surface, not a change of kind. Callability does not affect a Type Object's identity, so the interning of 1.2.2.9 is unchanged and two mentions of one type remain one callable object.

    A Type Object is any object carrying [[TypeRecord]], and that is the whole of the test: an array type object carries one, so [].<uint8> reflects as any other type does. A CLASS is the exception, and deliberately so - the design says a class's type object is its constructor, and a constructor is a function whose typeof ECMA-262 fixes as "function". Giving it [[TypeRecord]] would make it report "object" by the rule above, so a class denotes its type through an ASSOCIATION from the constructor to its Type Object, which the reflection operations resolve. A class is therefore the one denotation where the record is reached rather than carried.

    Note

    Opacity is what lets the interning of 1.2.2.9 be an implementation strategy rather than an obligation to materialize a graph. An engine that represents [].<uint32> as a tag rather than as an object with an element property is conforming, and a program cannot tell. It also keeps the type-object surface from becoming a second, weaker reflection API alongside the real one: there is one way to inspect a type, and it is named.

    1.12.3 Structural Reflection

    Reflect.getReflection.<Reflect.Type>(_t_) returns a reflection node describing the structure of the type t denotes. The node has a kind property whose value is a String naming the [[Kind]] of t's Type Record, and the further properties of Table 33. Every property of a node that denotes a type holds a Type Object, so a walker recurses by reflecting it in turn.

    Note

    The node kinds and the Type Record kinds of Table 1 correspond, and the correspondence now round-trips: every kind is readable, and writable through 1.12.4, with two deliberate wrinkles. The named leaves, primitive and nominal alike and with them any, void, and type, share the one "primitive" node, whose payload is the interned Type Object itself with a generic instantiation additionally decomposed, so a leaf is opaque to a walker exactly as 1.12.2 requires and a nominal type never exposes its declaration. And the deferred kind has no node at all, because specialization evaluates every deferred application before any code runs, so reflection cannot encounter one.

    A record's [[Origin]] (21) is not among these properties and is not reflected at all. It is a host-facing channel, and the reason is the one that clause gives: canonicalization unions origins across structurally identical declarations, so a program that could read one would observe its own type's origins change when an unrelated module declared the same shape. A tool reaches it by whatever means an implementation provides.

    The same Reflect.getReflection reflects a declaration's members, keyed on the declaration rather than on a type, which is how a class's fields, a function's parameters, and an enum's enumerators are exposed. That context and the rest of the reflection facility, including its metadata, are defined by 7. This clause defines only the type-object context it operates on.

    A union's arms are reflected in the canonical order rather than in the order written, since canonicalization has already reordered them and the Type Object is shared with every other spelling of the same type. A function's signatures are reflected in declaration order, which 1.10.2.1 preserves for this reason.

    For a concrete intrinsic application listed in Table 11, the generic property contains base, the intrinsic declaration's String name, arguments, its complete normalized arguments, and parameters, a List of records with name, domain, and default where one is declared. A generic reconstruction with such a String base binds and validates arguments by 1.5.25 before interning.
