Nominal applications, including library types such as Promise, retain their declaration Type Object base. A bare Promise type applies its defaults and is distinct from that declaration base; the base can be obtained as Reflect.getReflection(type Promise).generic.base. Reconstructing a library application completes and validates its arguments by 1.4.2.3 before interning. Preferred standard width aliases and explicit applications reconstruct to the same Type Object.

    A reflected function signature additionally has typeParameters, whose entries carry name, kind, variance, arity, variadic, constraint, and an opaque context preserving the declaration's parameter and default context. A family constraint is described by kind: "family-pattern" and application. An application entry has kind: "application", head (an intrinsic String name or nominal declaration Type Object), and arguments. A fixed entry has kind: "fixed" and type or value; a wildcard has kind: "wildcard" and a non-negative index. Repeated indices impose equality. A deferred declaration default has kind: "declaration-default" and its opaque declaration context; it is evaluated only after the preceding entries bind. A default already reduced to a fixed entry or a repeated wildcard is reflected in that equivalent normalized form. These descriptions are constraints, not concrete Type Objects. Reconstruction within a generic signature retains the declaration context and constraints; a standalone family-pattern description passed to Reflect.makeType throws a TypeError exception.

    1.12.4 Reflect.makeType ( node )

    The validity judgment includes every nested tuple rest operand: after canonicalization it must denote an array or tuple, subject to the same deferred requirement for dependent operands as 1.4.2.7. A violation throws a TypeError here; a required compile-time builder invocation is rejected by the checking pass.

    The input is structural: any object matching a node's shape in Table 33 describes that node, and a Type Object anywhere within it contributes its [[TypeRecord]]. This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. If node is not an Object matching a node's shape in Table 33, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. Let record be the Type Record that node, read as a description, describes.
    3. If record is not a valid type, throw a TypeError exception with the message the equivalent source declaration produces, or, where no declaration can write the type, a message naming the rule it violates.
    4. Return GetTypeObject(record).

    For every type T, Reflect.makeType(Reflect.getReflection.<Reflect.Type>(T)) is T. Construction canonicalizes and interns by 1.2.2.8 and 1.2.2.9, the same operations that give a source-written type its identity, which is what makes the round trip the identity function rather than an equivalence. Reconstruction is STRUCTURAL AND COMPLETE: a node's payload is rebuilt to its full depth, so a nested record within a parameterized node's metadata becomes a record again rather than remaining the object the node carried it in. A reconstruction that stops short produces a type that answers correctly to every question except identity — the same kind, the same base, the same field values, and stable under further round trips — which is why this paragraph states an identity and why a conformance suite that checks shape rather than identity does not test it.

    Note

    Canonicalization is where invalidity is caught: a node describing an infinite value-type layout, or an index signature with an illegal key type, fails exactly as the equivalent declaration fails, with the same message, so a builder's misuse reads as the misuse it is. An intersection whose members are disjoint is NOT among them, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than an oversight: the declaration is a type error (1.4.2.1) and the construction is never (1.2.2.8). A written intersection is an author naming two types that share no value, which is almost always & typed for |; a constructed one is the result of a computation over members the caller did not enumerate, and the empty type is the answer such a computation must be able to reach. An earlier draft of this clause claimed the two failed alike, and named a declaration rule that this specification did not then state. Validity is not syntactic reachability: a symbol literal type is a valid type with no declaration form at all, which is why it is constructed rather than written; an index signature has the declaration form of 1.4.2.9, and the declaration and a builder's construction reach the same Record. A recursive type is reached by a back-reference rather than a node, so construction ties its knot through the builder fixpoint rather than by accepting one; a constructed cycle arises only from the fixpoint of 1.2.7.3. The function is compile-time evaluable, and at run time it is an ordinary function returning the same interned objects, so String(Reflect.makeType(…)) prints the canonical form of 1.12.2.

    1.12.5 Reflect.isAssignable ( source, target )

    Its typed signature is (source: Reflect.Type, target: Reflect.Type): boolean (1.6.2.20).

    This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. If source is not a Type Object or target is not a Type Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. Return IsAssignable(source.[[TypeRecord]], target.[[TypeRecord]]).
     Note

    This is the checker's own judgment (1.2.3.2) exposed unchanged, so what a builder branches on and what the checker enforces cannot disagree; the conditional types of an erased system are written Reflect.isAssignable(T, U) ? X : Y inside a builder. It is deliberately the assignability relation rather than a new one: mutual assignability is composed from it, and identity is === by interning. That the relation is the checker's has a consequence a builder must account for: the any type satisfies it in BOTH directions and the never type in one, so Reflect.isAssignable(T, string) is true for T of any and of never alike, and a conditional written on it takes the same branch for both as it does for a string. Mutual assignability inherits this — any is mutually assignable with every type — so === is the relation that discriminates them, and a builder that must distinguish any or never tests for it first. This is not a defect in the relation: any IS assignable to string, and a judgment that answered otherwise would no longer be the checker's. The function is compile-time evaluable.

    1.12.6 Reflection and Declared Types

    The existing reflective operations respect a declared type. Reflect.set on a property with a declared type t performs RequireType(value, t) and throws where the value does not satisfy it. Reflect.get returns the property's value, which is of its declared type. Reflect.defineProperty accepts a type key in the property descriptor, whose value is a Type Object, and a descriptor with a type and no value gives the property the default value of that type (1.8.3.1), taken in the realm of that Type Object rather than in the caller's, since a parameterization's default is a crossing and a crossing consults a realm's declarations. Reflect.deleteProperty on a property with a declared type, and on a member required by an implemented interface, throws a TypeError exception.

    A Proxy constructed with a type argument T has a [[RuntimeType]] internal slot whose value is T's Type Record, so Reflect.typeOf reports T rather than the shape of its target, and its traps are checked against T. A Proxy constructed without one has no such slot and is of the any type. Each trap result for a property with a declared type, whether the type is declared by T or carried by the target as a typed own property, is checked against that type at the trap boundary. A trap is refused where its result would make the type T reports false: the get and getOwnPropertyDescriptor traps carry a value of a member's declared type out of the proxy and the set and defineProperty traps carry one in, so each is checked against that member's type; the has, deleteProperty and ownKeys traps may not deny, remove, or omit a member T declares and does not mark optional; and where T is a function type whose signatures agree on a return, the apply and construct traps are checked against it. The Static Type of new Proxy .<T> Arguments is T, and the Static Type of a Proxy constructed without a type argument is any, so the static and reported answers agree. Proxy is among the built-ins on which an application may write type arguments, and a construction that writes one has the construct signature (target: T, handler: ProxyHandler.<T>), checked as a user class's constructor signatures are; a construction that writes none declares no parameters, since its result is any and the base language admits any handler object.

    ProxyHandler.<T> is an interface of thirteen optional members, one per trap, each a function type over T: get and getOwnPropertyDescriptor returning what the base language does for the property named, set and defineProperty returning boolean, has, deleteProperty, setPrototypeOf, isExtensible and preventExtensions returning boolean, ownKeys and getPrototypeOf returning what the base language does, and apply and construct over T's signatures where T is callable. Every member is optional, since a handler declares the traps it means to intercept and the rest fall through to the target. A handler annotated with it, or passed inline to a construction that writes a type argument, is checked where it is written; the run-time checks at the trap boundary are made regardless, since a trap may return any and the annotation cannot see through it. The two are complements: one bounds what a proxy may do, the other says what its author has written. Constructing a Proxy whose target is an instance of a typed class or a typed array throws a TypeError exception: such a value is backed by a layout rather than a property table, a field access does not consult a handler, and there is no point at which a trap could correctly run.

    Note

    Reflection is a boundary in the sense of Table 23, not an exception to it. A value entering a typed position through Reflect.set is checked exactly as one entering through an assignment, which is what keeps a typed field's type a fact about its storage: were reflection able to write past the check, an engine could not lay the field out on the strength of its type, and the proposal's premise would not hold. That a typed property cannot be deleted is the same guarantee in the other direction, since a layout with a hole in it is not the layout the type described.

    A Proxy reporting the type it was constructed with rather than its target's shape is what makes the trap checks meaningful: the contract a proxy enforces is the one it was given, and reporting anything else would describe a value the program never promised.

    At a statically established intrinsic Proxy construction or Proxy.revocable operation, it is a type error if every possible target alternative has a typed-array stamp or sealed typed class storage that ProxyCreate forbids. Include inherited sealing; a dynamic subclass does not erase it, and reference identity supplies no Proxy exemption. Structural membership alone does not prove a physical layout. An unknown or ordinary-Object-compatible alternative prevents this negative proof. The target position must be established through the actual argument mapping.

    The intrinsic-origin proof is a prerequisite, not an assumption based on spelling. Resolve lexical declarations and aliases and account for mutable global bindings, property replacement, dynamic lookup, eval and unknown effects. Read only established intrinsic data; do not execute a getter, trap or other user code to obtain provenance. A run-time identity guard alone cannot justify an Early Error. Unresolved origins retain the run-time checks. The effect analysis is bounded in time as well as in kind: only an effect that can run before the selected construction can replace what the construction reads, so an operation after it in evaluation order, or in a function no counted region names, does not stand the proof down; and an operation whose every operand is a literal or a binding of one plain primitive type is the built-in operation, which no primitive block may replace (6.5) and which runs no user code, so it does not stand the proof down either. These requirements also govern the finite constructor-seed proof in 1.15.5.

    1.12.7 Library Constructor Contracts

    A proved intrinsic WeakRef construction checks the actual argument bound to target, independently of whether its result type was inferred or explicitly specialized. The argument must satisfy both CanBeHeldWeakly and the specialized parameter type T. Apply ordinary named and positional argument binding and established spread contributions. Unknown constructor identity or argument correspondence defers the affected judgment; a shadowed constructor receives its own contract. No collection or liveness observation is needed for the type judgment.

    FinalizationRegistry.<T> has constructor parameter callback: (heldValue: T) => void. Use the common library signature and ordinary contextual callback rules, including optional, defaulted and rest parameters. An established non-callable or incompatible callback is a type error, and an unannotated callback parameter receives the held-value type. The callback's result is ignored. Named construction uses the public name callback. At an any boundary the corresponding argument contract is enforced at runtime. Construction never invokes the cleanup callback to check it and promises no cleanup scheduling; the held value remains unconstrained by weak-target eligibility.

    1.12.8 Weak References and Typed Objects

    An instance of a typed class cannot be held weakly. Passing one to the WeakRef constructor, using one as a key of a WeakMap or a member of a WeakSet, or registering one as the target of a FinalizationRegistry throws a TypeError exception. This is CanBeHeldWeakly returning false for such a value: a value type has no identity (1.5.1), so there is no object whose liveness a weak reference could observe, and no cell a weak collection could key on. A value class rejected here also cannot be the target of a Proxy (1.12.6): the instance of a typed class that seals its instances, a value backed by a layout whose identity its type, not the reference, governs.

    Eligibility follows the effective class hierarchy. A subclass inherits a base's typed sealed storage even if the subclass declares no fields, and a dynamic modifier on the subclass does not undo sealing contributed by a base. A reference class kind anywhere in the hierarchy supplies reference identity and retains the reference-kind exemption. Static checking uses the resolved ancestry for this judgment; an unknown base that could supply reference kind retains runtime checking. Thus an empty subclass of class Base { x: uint8; } is refused in weak positions, while a subclass of reference class Base { x: uint8; } is admitted.

    Note

    A reference type, an ordinary object or a class that carries no typed field and is therefore not sealed, is held weakly as before, since it has the identity a weak reference is about. For a value class, sealing typed storage removes weak-reference eligibility. The reference-kind exemption concerns identity, whereas Proxy eligibility concerns physical storage: a reference class with sealed typed fields remains ineligible as a Proxy target. The two predicates therefore do not have identical boundaries. A composite object is refused in the same positions for the mirror-image reason, an identity that coincides with contents rather than none at all; 23.7 states the exclusion and merges both into CanBeHeldWeakly.

    The same judgment is made statically where the type is known. The type argument bound to the parameter that WeakMap, WeakSet or WeakRef holds weakly - K for WeakMap, T for the others - must be one every value of which CanBeHeldWeakly admits: object, symbol, any, an object, array, tuple or function type, a class that is not typed and sealed, or a union of these; it is a type error at the application otherwise, in every position an application can appear. A value type, a literal type, null, undefined, string, number, boolean, bigint, a composite type, and a typed sealed class are refused, and so is the nullable union of a typed sealed class, since the value a weak reference is checked against is the same instance under either binding type. The argument of the WeakRef constructor and the target and unregisterToken of FinalizationRegistry.prototype.register are checked the same way where their Static Type is known; FinalizationRegistry's type parameter is its held value and is unconstrained. Where the Static Type is not known, CanBeHeldWeakly decides at run time as before.

    1.13 The Numeric Library

    This clause defines the library the numeric types need: the overloading of the existing functions over those types, the named arithmetic forms that check or saturate rather than wrap, the floored division pair, the leading-zero count at the argument's own width, the parsing of a string into a numeric type, and the predicates that ask a numeric value about itself.

    1.13.1 Overloading of the Existing Functions

    The functions of the Math object, and the other library functions that TAKE a value of a numeric type, are overloaded for the numeric types by 1.10.3. A function that merely returns a number, with no parameter whose type could select a signature, is not overloaded and is unchanged. Table 34 lists the signatures: which functions, over which families, with what return, so that a call selects a signature as any overloaded call does and no conversion is written where the arguments already have a signature's types.

    Separately from the listing, a library function that takes a Number as a QUANTITY - a length, a count, an index, a position, a width of indentation - accepts a value of any numeric type in that position and reads it as its value. Such a parameter is not overloaded: there is one behaviour and one result, and the type of the argument selects nothing. The rule is stated because the alternative is silent: an operation that decides a branch by asking whether its argument is a Number takes the OTHER branch for a value of a numeric type, so Array(3) allocates three elements while a Array(_t_) for a uint32 t of 3 would build a one-element array holding t. What a quantity parameter must not do is change what it answers for an existing call, so a Number continues to be read as it is today.

    Note 1

    This is the reading side, and it does not create a conversion. An operation that REFUSES an implicit conversion from a Number refuses one from a value of a numeric type for the same reason and with the same error: ToBigInt throws a TypeError for a Number, and throws one for a uint32 as well, since ToBigInt performs no conversion from a sized integer type. The BigInt constructor's own Number step is unaffected and continues to answer for a Number. A program that wants a BigInt from a typed integer writes the conversion, u := bigint, and a boundary converts one exactly as it converts between any two numeric types (1.6).

    The listing ranges over the sized integer types int.<N> and uint.<N> for every N the type system admits, over bigint, over the binary float types of 1.5.3, over the decimal types of 1.5.4, and over the rational types of 1.5.5. Coverage is not conditioned on which types an implementation has values for: the float128 and decimal rows are as normative as the rest. number is not in the set, because the existing signatures over the Number type are unchanged and are what an untyped call selects. The vector types are not in the set, their arithmetic belonging to the SIMD extension's operators, and the complex numbers extension declares the rows of its own family, noted below the table.

    Every signature takes all of its numeric parameters at one type T. There are no mixed signatures and no resolution at a common supertype, because no numeric value type is assignable to another (1.2.3.2): a call mixing two typed widths is viable at no signature, and it is a type error, thrown as a TypeError exception where resolution happens at run time. The program states the conversion. A literal argument beside a typed one is ranked rather than typed and takes the parameter's type where it can represent it, so Math.max((1 := uint8), 3) selects the uint8 signature and is a uint8, while Math.max((1 := uint8), 300) is a type error, 300 being representable at no signature the uint8 argument leaves viable.

    A signature's declared return type is a boundary, and the boundary applies its family's own treatment of a result that does not fit. For an integer type, sized or bigint, the exact mathematical result is converted at T by the checked treatment of 1.7.3.1: a representable result is a value of T and an unrepresentable one throws a RangeError exception, so Math.pow((2 := uint8), (10 := uint8)) and Math.abs((-128 := int8)) throw, their results having no uint8 or int8 to be. For a binary float type the result is converted by the float rule of Table 19, rounded to the nearest value of T with a finite result beyond the type's range becoming an infinity of its sign, which is the treatment the type's own arithmetic applies, so Math.exp((100 := float32)) is the float32 positive infinity rather than an error. For a decimal type, precision rounding is silent and a result outside the exponent range throws a RangeError exception. For a rational type the result is exact, and a fixed-width result whose lowest-terms numerator or denominator does not fit its int.<N> throws a RangeError exception. Two domain errors are raised before any result exists: Math.sqrt of a negative value of an integer type throws a RangeError exception, and Math.pow over an integer type throws a RangeError exception when its exponent is negative, whatever its base.

    The semantics are stated on mathematical values. Where a row's result is exact, an implementation must produce it exactly at every width; an integer row computed through a binary64 intermediate that returns a wrong integer carrying the type does not conform. Where a row is implementation-approximated, the approximation is computed as if at the argument type's format or better and rounded once to that format. Math.sqrt is correctly rounded at every binary float and decimal width, as IEEE 754-2019 requires of the operation; at every width but one, the other approximated rows carry the latitude the Math functions have always had. At float128 they carry none: every implementation-approximated row is correctly rounded, its result the float128 value nearest the exact mathematical result, ties to even. A program chooses float128 for its precision, and a last bit that differs between implementations would give part of that precision back.

    NaN and the infinities are values of every binary float type and of every decimal type, and a NaN or infinite result at those types is a value of T, not an error: Math.log((-1 := float32)) is the float32 NaN. The integer and rational families have no such values, which is why their domain cases above throw instead. The existing conventions of the functions, among them the NaN and signed-zero handling of min and max and Math.round rounding half up, are unchanged and are evaluated at T.

    A family has a row for a function exactly where the operation has an answer in that family's own mathematics, with the return type leaving nothing to decide about the answer's representation. The integer roots are such answers: for an integer T, Math.sqrt and Math.cbrt return the exact root truncated toward zero as a value of T, the direction integer division truncates (1.9.6) and the semantics the BigInt Math proposal gives BigInt.sqrt and BigInt.cbrt. The transcendental functions have no integer counterpart, so they have no integer rows, and an integer-typed argument to one fails resolution; the program writes the conversion it means.

    The listing declares one signature per parameter list: no function of the numeric library is overloaded on its return type alone, so a bare call is never ambiguous (1.10.5 remains available to operators and to user code, where a call without a contextual type is legitimately an error). A contextual type participates in resolution as it does anywhere. Where a call's numeric arguments are untyped literals, the contextual type selects a typed signature and the literals take its parameter type, so the call is a computation at T rather than a conversion of a Number result: const a: uint8 = Math.pow(2, 10); resolves at uint8, computes the exact 1024, and throws a RangeError exception at the return, while uint8(Math.pow(2, 10)) is the untyped call followed by a wrapping cast and is 0, the distinction of Table 22 visible at one call site. Where an argument is typed and the contextual type is of another family, no signature is viable and it is a type error; the cast the program then writes selects the computation by its placement, float64(Math.sqrt(10n)) being the integer root converted, exactly 3, and Math.sqrt(float64(10n)) the real root of the converted argument. A cast constrains nothing here: a Type Object call accepts any numeric source, so it supplies no contextual type and a call within it resolves bare.

    The complex numbers extension declares the rows of its family beside its arithmetic: Math.abs of a complex.<T> is the real magnitude, a value of T; the transcendental functions the extension names return values of its types; and Math.conj and Math.arg are its additions. Math.random takes no numeric argument, and its typed form Math.random.<T>() belongs to the random extension. The value properties of the Math object, Math.PI among them, remain values of the Number type.

    The Static Type of a member access reading the length property of an array is the index type (1.2.6), as is the Static Type of a member access reading capacity. The value READ is a value of that type and not a Number, so a.length is index type is true where the array has an element type, and a count therefore carries its width into whatever it is used in. An array with NO element type is untouched: its length is a Number as it has always been.

    The Static Type of a COMPUTED member access on an array — a[i] — is the array's element type. It had been the any type, which left indexing untyped in both directions of the check: a store to an element was checked against the element type and a read from one was not, so let b: boolean = a[0] was accepted on an array of uint32. Indexing is the operation an array exists for, and it is checked in the same way whichever side of an assignment it appears on.

    Where the array has a fixed extent and the index is a numeric literal, a numeric literal preceded by a sign, or a reference to a const bound to one, the index is decidable before the program runs: an index that is negative, not an integer, or not less than the extent is a type error rather than the RangeError it would raise at run time. An index that is not a literal keeps the run-time check, which remains the rule for every index; the static case is the one an implementation may elide, the extent being a compile-time constant (1.4.2.7).

    Note 2

    The bound on which functions are overloaded is a compatibility rule, and it is the same one that leaves parseInt and parseFloat alone (1.13.5) and that decides the bigint predicate rows (1.13.6). An overload is selected by an argument's type, so a call written without one is unchanged; but a function with no numeric parameter has nothing to select on, and giving its result a value type would change what every existing call returns. 'A'.charCodeAt(0) === 65 is true today, and a uint16 result would make it false, since the values of distinct value types are distinct (1.5.1). The same reasoning covers indexOf and lastIndexOf, whose === -1 is the universal idiom, the Date getters, and the byte lengths. Where a typed result is wanted from such a function, the program writes a conversion.

    This is what makes the conversion rule livable rather than merely strict. Math.clz32 of a uint32 is a uint32, Math.min of two float32 values is a float32, and a uint32 loop counter compares against array.length without a cast, because the library meets the program where it is. A library that returned a Number from every function would force a conversion at every call and would make typed code read worse than untyped code, which is the failure mode the design is avoiding.

    The existing signatures are unchanged, so Math.min of two Numbers is a Number and every existing program means what it meant. The overloads are additions, and a call with untyped literal arguments and no contextual type selects among them by Table 21, which ranks number first and so keeps an untyped call on the signature it selects today.

     Note 3

    The bigint rows are those of the BigInt Math proposal: abs, sign, min, max, pow, sqrt, and cbrt, the roots truncated toward zero, sqrt of a negative throwing, and pow refusing a negative exponent. That proposal places the operations on the BigInt constructor rather than on Math, because in the base language a Math.sqrt whose result type depends on a runtime argument is a hazard every caller inherits. The objection does not transfer: here a signature is selected statically and the untyped surface is untouched, so the listing stays on Math, agreeing with the proposal value for value, and if the proposal advances, BigInt.sqrt(x) and Math.sqrt of a bigint are one mathematics with two spellings.

    The integer roots follow the shape integer division set. The result type leaves nothing to decide, so the type decides, and toward zero is the direction this specification's integer arithmetic already rounds: Math.sqrt((17 := uint8)) is (4 := uint8), and Math.cbrt of a negative integer value is defined, the cube root of -9 truncating to -2. A program that wants the real root of an integer writes the conversion, one cast that states the meaning.

     Note 4

    Math.pow and ** deliberately part ways at an integer type. (2 := uint8) ** (10 := uint8) wraps to 0, because the operators wrap (1.9.6); Math.pow((2 := uint8), (10 := uint8)) throws a RangeError exception, because a declared return is a checked boundary. This is the a + 1 against Math.addChecked(a, 1) distinction of 1.13.2 again, stated here so it reads as the design it is rather than as a disagreement: the operator is the cheap wrapping form and the function the checked one. What ** itself does with a negative typed exponent is a question for 1.9.6; this clause specifies the functions only.

    1.13.2 Checked and Saturating Arithmetic

    The operators wrap on overflow (1.9.6). Where wrapping is not wanted, the named forms of Table 35 are used. Each is overloaded for every integer type and returns a value of its operands' type.

    Each form performs the operation its corresponding operator performs, and differs from it only in what happens when the type cannot represent the answer. "The exact result" in Table 35 therefore means the exact result of THAT operation, not of an operation in the rationals: the division forms divide as / divides, truncating toward zero (1.9.6), so Math.divChecked(_a_, 2) on an int32 holding 7 is 3 and not an error. A division is the only one of the four whose result can fail to be representable for a reason other than magnitude, and it does so in exactly one case, the most negative value of a signed type divided by -1.

    That the operators wrap while a CONVERSION does not is the one place these rules look as though they disagree, so it is worth stating why they do not. A conversion is a value crossing into a type that cannot hold it, which is a mistake about the value: a store past an element type's range, or a binding initialized out of range, yields unrepresentable (Table 19) and raises. An arithmetic overflow is not a mistake about a value but an operation the type performs modularly by definition, which is what a fixed-width integer IS and what every use of one for hashing, checksums, or bit manipulation depends on. The two therefore meet without contradicting: in let z: uint8 = x + y with x 200 and y 100 the addition wraps to 44 and the conversion then has nothing to refuse, because the wrap happened at the operator and the value reaching the binding is in range. Where that is not wanted, Table 35 names the forms that refuse or saturate instead.

    A zero divisor produces no result at all, so neither treatment applies to it: Math.divChecked and Math.divSaturating both throw a RangeError exception when the divisor is zero. Saturating is a rule about a result the type cannot hold, and there is no result here to be nearest to.

    Note

    Silent wrapping is the wrong answer when the value is a count rather than a bit pattern, and the right answer when it is a bit pattern rather than a count. Neither is right always, so the operator takes the case that has to be cheap and the named forms take the rest: a + 1 on a uint8 holding 255 is 0, Math.addChecked(a, 1) throws a RangeError exception, and Math.addSaturating(a, 1) is 255.

    These forms exist for the integer types because only there is wrapping the default. A float already saturates, to an infinity, and a decimal already raises a RangeError, since a decimal's range is a property of the type rather than of the format (Table 19). A rational already raises a RangeError on an unrepresentable result. Each family's overflow behaviour is therefore the one its values make available, and the named forms give the integer types the two the others have built in.

    That a saturating form can still raise is worth stating plainly, because the name suggests otherwise. It raises for one reason only, and it is not an overflow: a division by zero has no result, and saturating chooses among the results a type can hold rather than inventing one where none exists. Every case that IS an overflow saturates, including the signed division that overflows, so Math.divSaturating of the most negative int8 by -1 is 127.

    1.13.3 Floored Division

    Math.divFloor(_a_, _b_) returns the exact quotient of a and b rounded toward negative infinity. Math.mod(_a_, _b_) returns the remainder whose sign follows the divisor. Both are overloaded for every integer type, and both also have a signature over the Number type.

    A zero divisor follows the family. At an integer type both throw a RangeError exception, since an integer type has no infinity and no NaN and so has nothing to return. Over the Number type both answer as the operators do: Math.mod(_a_, 0) is NaN, as _a_ % 0 is, and Math.divFloor(_a_, 0) is an infinity, as Math.floor(_a_ / 0) is.

    Note

    These are the other half of the pair 1.9.6 describes: Math.divFloor(_a_, _b_) * _b_ + Math.mod(_a_, _b_) = _a_ holds for the same reason the operators' identity holds, because the quotient and the remainder round the same way. They are named rather than assumed so that a program picks the pair it wants instead of receiving one by default.

    Unlike the checked and saturating forms, this pair is not restricted to the integer types. Those exist only there because only there is wrapping the default, and a checked form over the Number type would have nothing to check. This pair is not about overflow but about rounding direction, which is meaningful for any real, and its own motivating use is written in untyped code: array[Math.mod(_i_, _array_.length)].

    Math.mod is the % of Python, the mod of Kotlin, and the mod of Haskell. For a positive divisor, which is every case in which an index is being wrapped, its result equals the Euclidean remainder and is never negative, so array[Math.mod(i, array.length)] is always in range. Where the divisor may be negative and a non-negative result is still wanted, Math.mod(_a_, Math.abs(_b_)) gives it, which is why no separate Euclidean pair is provided.

    1.13.4 Counting Leading Zeros

    Math.clz is overloaded for the sized integer types, and for them alone. For a value of an integer type T of width N, it returns N less the bit length of the argument's mathematical value taken modulo 2**_N_, as a value of _T_, checked at the return as 1.13.1 checks every declared return. The operation is a question about an N-bit two's-complement encoding, so the families without one have no signatures: bigint has no width to count from the top of, and the float, decimal, and rational types have no integer encoding to count in. There is no untyped signature; Math.clz32 is already the 32-bit count.

    Note

    This is Math.clz32 freed from its width. The two agree at 32 bits, answering alike for every int32 and uint32, and differ below it: Math.clz((1 := uint8)) is 7 where Math.clz32((1 := uint8)) is 31, because clz32 counts in a 32-bit field whatever its argument's width and clz counts in the argument's own. Typed code that means the argument's width, which is most of it, writes clz; clz32 remains for the 32-bit field itself and for untyped callers.

    The count of a value of T always fits an unsigned T, and fits a signed T at every width past int.<2>; at the two narrowest signed widths a zero's count exceeds the type's greatest value and the checked return throws a RangeError exception, the same edge the clz32 row of Table 34 notes. bigint is excluded because the operation is width-relative and a bigint has no width; the width-free counterpart is a bit length, which is a different function and is not added here.

    A call whose argument is an untyped literal resolves like any other, by Table 21, which selects the widest width that can represent it. That is well defined and almost never meant, since the width is the semantics here, so a program writes the width it means, by a typed argument, by an annotation on the destination, or by a cast: const n: uint8 = Math.clz(1); is 7.

    1.13.5 Parsing

    Each numeric type has a parse function. For an integer type and for bigint its signature is parse(_string_, _radix_ = 10); for the Number type and the binary floating-point, decimal, rational, and complex types it is parse(_string_). The Number type's parse accepts what float64.parse accepts, fails as it fails, and returns a Number. It returns a value of the type the function belongs to.

    The accepted input is the grammar of a literal of that type, with optional leading and trailing white space and an optional sign. Numeric separators are accepted, and the form taking a radix accepts the prefix matching that radix. The entire string must be a literal of the type: no trailing text is consumed.

    parse throws a SyntaxError when the string is not a literal of the type, and a RangeError when it is a literal whose value the type cannot represent.

    Each type also has a tryParse function with the same parameters, returning a value of the type where parse would return one and null where parse would fail to parse its argument. Its return type is the union of the type and the null type. A call that is not a parse at all, because the receiver is not a numeric type, throws as parse does rather than answering null: that is a mistake in the program, and reporting it as a failed parse would name the wrong thing.

    Note

    parseInt and parseFloat are unchanged and continue to consume a prefix and to return NaN. The new functions do neither, because neither is available to them: an integer type cannot represent NaN at all, so a failed parse has nothing to return and must throw. Doing the same for the float types is a choice rather than a necessity, and it is the right one, since a failed parse that becomes a NaN surfaces far from its cause. Refusing trailing text follows: a function that cannot signal failure with a value has no reason to be lenient about what it accepts.

    Distinguishing the two errors is what makes the failure legible. uint8.parse('12abc') throws a SyntaxError exception, since the string is not a uint8 literal, while uint8.parse('256') throws a RangeError exception, since it is a literal and the value is out of range. This is the same distinction Table 22 draws between a value of the wrong type and a value of the right type out of range.

    tryParse returning a nullable union rather than a sentinel is what lets the failure be handled by narrowing (1.8.5): the result is a uint8 in the branch that tests it against null and needs no cast there. A string is deliberately not a conversion source for a numeric type, so let c: uint8 = '1'; is a type error and the parse is always written; 1.7.3.1 is where that is enforced, and it is enforced at the explicit conversion too, so '1' := uint8 is a type error for the same reason. The pair is what makes the strictness livable: a program that knows its input writes parse and lets the failure throw, and one that does not writes tryParse and handles the null.

    1.13.6 The Numeric Predicates

    The global functions isFinite and isNaN, and the functions Number.isFinite, Number.isNaN, Number.isInteger, and Number.isSafeInteger, are overloaded for the numeric types by 1.10.3. Each overload takes one value of a numeric type and returns a boolean, answering as Table 36 gives for the value's family. Where that answer is the same constant for every family of the argument's type, the overload's result is that literal type, true or false, so a test of it is judged by 1.8.5.4. The literal result is the ordinary Static Type of the selected call, available equally to inference, equality, match and switch. Its proof requires an established intrinsic origin and applicable argument contract; a shadowed binding, replaced method or unresolved origin must not borrow a result from the intrinsic's spelling. A merely untyped binding does not acquire an inferred contract from this rule. The existing signatures are unchanged: an untyped call coerces, or declines to, exactly as it does today.

    The bigint family is the one exception to the table's uniformity, and it is a compatibility rule rather than a semantic one: an overload taking a bigint is declared only for a function that has no defined answer for a BigInt today. isNaN and isFinite perform ToNumber on their argument, which throws a TypeError exception for a BigInt, so each declares one. The four Number statics already answer false for a BigInt, because a BigInt is not a Number, so none of them declares one and a BigInt passed to a Number static reaches that static's existing signature and is answered exactly as it is today.

    A complex answers the two classification predicates by its components, because a component can be NaN or infinite: isNaN is true exactly when either component is NaN, and isFinite exactly when both are finite, so a NaN component, not being finite, makes it false. These are the answers of Python's cmath.isnan and cmath.isfinite. It declares neither integer predicate, which ask about a place on the real line that a complex does not have; Number.isInteger and Number.isSafeInteger, which do not coerce, answer false for it as they do for any value that is not a Number.

    The complex numbers extension declares its family's rows for all four predicates. The expected shape is the componentwise one: a complex value is NaN where either component is, and finite where both are.

    Note

    The integer and rational columns are constants, and that is the point of them: a sized integer is a type whose isFinite has one answer, and the predicate saying so at the type is what lets a reader delete the check. The decimal columns are value tests even though the arithmetic of this specification never produces a decimal NaN or infinity, overflow raising a RangeError exception instead: the values exist in the type (1.5.4), so the predicate tests the value rather than asserting a constant the type system does not guarantee.

    Every test is of the mathematical or format value, never of a representation. At a width past 2*53, `Number.isSafeInteger` of an `int64` holding 260 is *false because the value is out of safe range, not because a payload lost precision.

    A plain BigInt value is a value of the bigint type, and it raises the one compatibility question in this table that the type system does not settle by itself. Every other row answers about a value that no existing program can write: a float32 NaN and an int32 need syntax this proposal adds, so giving them answers displaces nothing. A BigInt needs no new syntax at all. Number.isInteger(5n) is false in code running today, and making it true under the flag would change the meaning of a program that opted into nothing, which nothing else in this proposal does. The rows are therefore declared where they displace an error and declined where they displace an answer: isNaN(1n) and isFinite(1n) throw today, so the flag defines them, and the Number statics answer today, so the flag leaves them alone.

    The visible cost is that isFinite(1n) is true while Number.isFinite(1n) is false. The two functions differ in kind already, one coercing its argument and the other testing it, and this proposal closes only the case where the coercion threw; it does not make them agree, and it makes them disagree about no value that either answered before. Number.isInteger and Number.isSafeInteger have no global counterpart, so no surface takes a BigInt for those two questions at all. Their answers at the bigint type, were a surface for them to be declared on to exist, are true and true where the magnitude is at most 2**53 - 1; they are recorded here rather than in the table because a table of what the predicates answer should not carry an answer no call can obtain.

    The other rows repair a quieter hazard: without them, Number.isNaN of a float32 NaN is false and Number.isInteger of an int32 is false, each predicate silently testing representation where its name promises a value test.

    1.14 Arrays and Tuples

    This clause completes the array and tuple kinds: the membership test 1.7.2.1 defers, the default value of a tuple, and the checking of an element store.

    A Tuple Element Record describes one position of a tuple type. It has a [[Type]] (a Type Record), a [[Rest]] field (a Boolean, true for a ... element), and an [[Initial]] field (an ECMAScript language value or none, the position's declared default).

    1.14.1 Tuple Sequence Domains

    An established tuple sequence domain interprets a tuple's fixed elements, finite array rests and nested tuple spreads in order, when the result has at most one unbounded homogeneous array rest and obeys the effective default-placement rules of 1.4.2.7. A fixed element contributes one position of its [[Type]], retaining its declared default if any. A rest whose operand is an array with finite extent N contributes exactly N required positions of the array's element type; extent zero contributes none. A tuple rest contributes its ordered contents recursively. A dynamic array rest contributes a possibly empty homogeneous run. An unresolved extent or repeated active tuple in recursive spread expansion establishes no new positional domain.

    Several written unbounded rests may also establish this domain. After ordered tuple expansion, combine consecutive unbounded regions only when their element types are the same type and every required position between them has that same type. Retain the intervening required count: its positions may be represented at the end of the fixed prefix of the homogeneous region because every affected occupied position retains the same type at every admitted length. Repeat this judgment for further unbounded rests. Zero finite extents contribute no positions. Preserve the effective default-placement rules and the original default records. The result must have at most one unbounded homogeneous region; different intervening types, unresolved counts and active recursive expansion supply no such proof. This positional equivalence does not merge Type Objects, erase finite minima, or select a partition from current values. All established-domain rules below, including contextual conversion, retained backing and independent reference liveness, apply to this family. SequenceAssignment retains its original count judgment where the distribution among written slots is required.

    Let p be the full fixed prefix width and s the fixed suffix width. Without defaults the minimum is p + s. With defaults, the suffix is empty and the minimum is the number of required prefix positions. The maximum is p + s without an unbounded run, and unbounded otherwise. At an admitted length n, supplied prefix positions retain their indices, suffix positions start at n - s, and intervening positions have the unbounded run's element type. Omission never skips a supplied position. Several finite rests may contribute to a fixed region. Positions and lengths are determined from declarations and counts, never from current element values.

    This is a semantic expansion, not a requirement to allocate one Type Record per repeated position. Implementations may retain finite counts and declared run boundaries. It does not change CanonicalizeType: tuple operands still flatten there, while finite array rest records retain their existing reflected form and identity. Mutually assignable positional domains need not be the same Type Object.

    For two established positional domains, including the separately specified plain/defaulted-prefix domains, subtyping requires inclusion of their admitted length ranges and positional subtyping at every occupied index for every admitted source length. Repeated runs can be compared at their boundaries. An unresolved or general multiple-dynamic-rest domain supplies no new inclusion proof against an established finite or nested expanded domain. These judgments neither read elements nor weaken reference invariance.

    At a receiving boundary, use the established domain for arity, per-position membership, elementwise conversion and retained storage admission. Check an impossible length before indexed Gets. Retain selected callable and nested construction evidence, preserving the existing identity, ordinary-write, failure and publication rules. Default construction supplies each fixed position from its formed declared default, or independently from its element type's default if none is declared, and gives an unbounded rest zero elements. Omitted converting construction retains its logical output length and source default records by effective position, without expanding a finite count into type metadata. It reuses supplied observations and selected evidence, applies the existing overlapping-domain and publication rules, and produces a separately admitted Array before an enclosing setter receives it. A zero finite count does not request a default. Publish the complete domain on the produced tuple.

    Indexed stores, permitted length changes, intrinsic movement checks, search and reference liveness use the complete domain. Surviving indices must retain their contracts across resizing. A finite domain uses the existing bounded positional copying rules; the presence of a written finite rest does not turn it into an unbounded copy. Established literal lengths and singleton indexed-read proofs use its exact positional map and bounds. This does not establish the output of a replaceable iterator or broaden unknown-spread contextual typing.

    1.14.2 Ordinary Nominal Tuple Membership Storage

    This clause extends owned Array membership admission to ordered tuple patterns containing ordinary identity class types together with the scalar types of 1.14.5. Each class target is a resolved, non-generic source class with the permanent own prototype identity required by 1.7.3.2. Value class copying, metadata, union element types, defaulted positions, unresolved counts and active recursive expansion are outside this specialization. Required fixed positions, finite array rests, dynamic array rests and nested tuple spreads retain their ordered counts; zero contributes no position. Stable positional domains retain their existing location contracts and receive the same protection of nominal child membership.

    A successful receiving membership admission retains the complete ordered pattern on the owned Array, including admission reached through a selected structural property, union, intersection, parameter or return contract. Pure IsOfType retains no guard. Preserve any previously acquired storage contract and every independently acquired guard. At an otherwise unestablished location, derive its position projection from declarations, counts and admitted length as in scalar rest storage; do not narrow it to a child's current class or to the first successful partition.

    Before publishing the new guard, revalidate the retained own data observations and their current ordinary membership roles without a second observable source walk. An Object identity does not prove that an earlier nominal role remains true. Each class role is established by following ordinary internal prototype links to its required target. A path requiring an exotic prototype observation supplies no ordinary witness. Keep the existing selected evidence and earlier-effects rules; failure publishes none of this admission's new guards and does not undo an independently completed receiving boundary.

    A retained owner guard depends on the ordinary prototype links that support its accepting membership evidence. Before publishing a change to any such link, check every affected retained owner's complete sequence against all its acquired patterns, using the prospective replacement at that link. All other positions retain their current owned data values. A child may change roles, and the assignment may change, if the complete pattern remains satisfied. Apply independently acquired exact class obligations as well. Do not invoke a getter, conversion, constructor or Proxy trap during this check. If an affected owner has no accepting ordinary assignment, the ordinary [[SetPrototypeOf]] operation returns false before changing the link or any live dependency. Retain its existing same-prototype, extensibility and cycle checks and their order.

    After a permitted prototype publication, update the affected owner dependencies from the new accepting evidence without intervening user code. Previously unsuccessful roles need no independent dependency if the retained accepting evidence remains guarded; whenever that evidence changes, reconsider the complete pattern. A valid new prefix becomes guarded, and obsolete prefixes cease to constrain that owner. A target prototype's own outgoing link is irrelevant to a role that already reached it, but another role or owner may depend on that link.

    Ordinary element and length publication must preserve all retained ordered guards and existing location contracts. Refresh nominal dependencies from the actual resulting owned data without intervening user code. Replacement or removal retires only the removed owner's relationship to that occurrence; repeated occurrences, other owners and independently completed exact class boundaries retain their obligations. A partially failed length truncation retains dependencies for its actual surviving prefix and releases the removed suffix. Follow the existing staged insertion, removal, failure-precedence and reference-liveness rules. Repartition alone does not remove a location or retarget a reference. After user conversion effects, revalidate the prospective complete sequence rather than treating retained element identities as unchanged membership facts.

    Dependency bookkeeping must not strongly retain an owner or its child/constructor graph solely through a surviving prototype or child. The weak-clearance timing allowance of 1.7.3.2 applies to these owner dependencies. Cleanup invokes no ECMAScript code. This clause changes neither language-level weak-target eligibility nor independent reference removal or relocation semantics.

    Note

    For an admitted one-element tuple of type [...[].<C>, ...[].<D>], changing its ordinary child's prototype from C.prototype to D.prototype may preserve the tuple. It need not preserve an independently acquired exact C contract. For two initially C children, changing only the first to D produces an invalid ordered sequence and is refused; changing only the second may succeed. Removing an occurrence releases that owner's dependency, not another owner's promise.

    This membership and storage specialization is extended by the bounded selected constructor plans below. A constructor body or nominal default is never a speculative scalar computation. General constructor/operator applicability, initial Proxy/array-like backing, metadata, value-class copy transport and structural descendant roles require their separately specified rules.

    1.14.3 Selected Ordinary Constructors in Ordered Rests

    This clause extends the ordered conversion and store planner to the ordinary identity-class patterns of 1.14.2 when no established positional sequence domain applies. Existing complete unchanged membership takes precedence. Otherwise retain indexed observations, form candidates without executing constructors, and select a complete count assignment under the scalar-rest ranking and all acquired backing obligations. Required runs cannot be consumed by an earlier rest.

    A bounded constructor candidate requires an ordinary class target with one explicitly declared simple binding parameter and no optional marker, parameter default, rest, reference, or destructuring. Use the parameter Type Record resolved in its declaration context. An unavailable annotated signature supplies no proof, rather than an implicit any parameter. An unannotated or any parameter admits the supplied value. A primitive parameter may admit an existing member or an intrinsically pure checked conversion under the scalar-rest purity rules. An ordinary identity-class parameter may admit an existing ordinary member. Do not run a constructor, source conversion operator, metadata operation, getter, Proxy trap, reference read or effectful parameter conversion to discover applicability. Generic destinations and other parameter forms require a separate applicable plan.

    Retain a failed pure parameter conversion as an unavailable candidate and a failure fact in input-index and written-run order. It must not preempt another complete viable assignment. If no complete assignment exists, propagate the first retained pure failure or throw a TypeError exception if none exists. Constructor arity alone is insufficient proof of applicability. Selecting a constructor uses the existing constructor precedence; this clause supplies no speculative operator fallback.

    After selecting the complete assignment, invoke each selected constructor exactly once in input order with the retained supplied value. Its actual parameter boundary remains checked, including when the enclosing tuple conversion was explicit. Propagate an abrupt completion without trying another assignment or another conversion. Verify that its normal result is an ordinary member of its selected class; otherwise throw a TypeError exception. A successful selected class conversion completes its independent exact prototype obligation under 1.7.3.2. An unchanged nominal child does not acquire an exact class obligation merely from its selected tuple role.

    After the selected operations, validate the complete prospective sequence against every acquired ordered pattern. A later constructor effect may change the nominal membership of an earlier retained Object. Accept a valid repartition; refuse an invalid complete sequence before publishing it. On a fresh converted Array, install both the declaration-derived projection and the complete pattern, and establish its ordinary nominal dependencies before publication. On an existing owner, also revalidate the retained data, length, guard and backing observations before the current store. Preserve earlier effects and independently completed receiving obligations on failure. These checks do not grant new reference authority or restore a removed or relocated reference.

    For a staged insertion, only the destination value supplied by the current write may convert. Other entries of its previously prepared private tail are fixed values, whether relocated or supplied by earlier insertion writes. They participate in complete assignment and guard checking without another conversion. In particular, an insertion must not run a constructor on a retained movement value while planning the new supplied item. Existing SameType movement geometry and failure precedence remain applicable.

    Note

    For [...[].<C>, ...[1].<string>, ...[].<boolean>] and source [1, "s"], where C declares constructor(value: any), the selected conversion constructs C once and retains the required String. A constructor taking Boolean is not applicable merely because it has one parameter. A selected constructor that throws is not retried through another rest.

    The operator extension below adds bounded source and inbound plans. General effectful or composite parameter checks, nominal defaults, and generic specialization require separate plans. Their absence from this specialization is not a general language prohibition.

    1.14.4 Selected Ordinary Conversion Operators in Ordered Rests

    This clause extends the ordinary nominal rest planner with instance source and inbound conversion declarations from ordinary class definitions. Retain each declaration's resolved target Type Record, callable, form and parameter signature in the declaration's context. Target matching uses SameType, including nominal declaration identity; display spelling is not identity. Retain all same-form alternatives rather than overwriting the previous declaration. An unavailable annotated signature is not an unannotated any parameter.

    Source lookup follows ordinary internal prototype links without observable Gets or Proxy traps. For the exact target, use the nearest prototype's source declaration set; a nearer declaration for a different target does not hide it. Inbound candidates come from the target's own declaration set and must declare that exact target. Source declarations have no parameter. Inbound parameter applicability uses the simple checked proof of 1.14.3. Initially exotic lookup, partial additions, static forms and more general signatures require separate coverage.

    After complete unchanged membership has failed, prefer an applicable converting constructor, then an applicable source conversion, then an applicable inbound conversion. A proved inapplicable constructor may give way to a later form; a selected constructor's throw may not. A signature whose applicability is not established by this bounded proof must not be treated as proved inapplicable in order to skip a higher-priority form or a competing declaration. Within an inbound form, discard a candidate if another applicable parameter type is a proper subtype of its parameter type. An unannotated parameter has type any. More than one maximal applicable candidate is ambiguous; source declarations for the same selected target are likewise ambiguous when no unique declaration remains.

    Retain an ambiguous candidate during the complete count assignment. If the selected assignment includes an ambiguity, throw a TypeError exception before invoking any selected user conversion. Do not discard the ambiguous candidate to retry a less-greedy assignment. Whole unchanged membership and a run that contributes zero selected items do not invoke or select an unnecessary conversion. Pure parameter failures retain their existing unavailable-candidate and failure-order rules; ambiguity is a selection error, not such a parameter failure.

    Retain the selected callable and receiver or argument while planning. A source invocation calls that callable with the retained source value as receiver and no arguments. An inbound invocation calls its selected callable with undefined as receiver and the retained input value as its argument. Do not repeat operator lookup after earlier conversion effects. The actual inbound parameter boundary remains checked even inside an explicit tuple conversion. Invoke selected conversions once in input order, propagate selected abrupt completions without fallback, and verify every normal result against its selected ordinary class. A successful result completes the independent exact obligation required by the constructor-plan clause.

    Retain the same post-effect complete-pattern validation, owner/backing revalidation, publication order and reference authority/liveness rules as the constructor plan. A changed source lookup path does not replace a retained callable. A changed nominal role in an earlier resulting child still participates in final complete-pattern validation. Independently completed parameter and result obligations survive a later outer failure. Declaration registries must not globally retain an unreachable owning prototype solely because its declarations were recorded.

    Note

    This clause specifies the bounded ordered-rest extension, not a replacement of all general conversion dispatch. General signature evaluation, overload groups for constructors, metadata and generic contexts retain their separate proof obligations.

    1.14.5 Scalar Rest Storage

    This clause specifies the owned Array specialization for a tuple whose ordered expansion consists of required fixed positions, finite array rests and dynamic array rests over unparameterized number, string, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined, float16, float32, float64, or resolved int and uint types. Nested tuple spreads retain their ordered contributions. A finite count must be resolved and non-negative; unresolved counts and active recursive expansion supply no specialization. An element type carrying metadata, a union element type or a defaulted position is outside this specialization. An already established stable positional domain retains its existing rules. This specialization does not define the general heterogeneous rest conversion or storage algorithm.

    The tuple's ordered scalar pattern is a List of scalar Type Records with minimum and maximum counts. A required position has counts one and one; a finite array rest has its extent for both counts; a dynamic rest has minimum zero and unbounded maximum. Zero-count runs contribute no positions. A List of values satisfies the pattern if it can be partitioned into consecutive runs within those counts, each of whose values satisfies that run's scalar type. Repeated types retain their written run positions. For an admitted total length and occupied index, the position projection is the canonical union of the scalar destinations that can occupy that index in any complete count assignment of that length. Determine these possibilities from declarations and counts, independently of current values or a selected partition. The pattern, and not this union alone, constrains the sequence. Counts may be retained compactly without allocating one record per finite element.

    A successful owned Array admission retains its ordered scalar pattern as a guard together with the ordinary selected structural evidence. Direct admission and admission selected through a property, tuple or array element, union, intersection, parameter or return boundary have the same obligation. Pure membership acquires no guard. Publish no new guard from a failed admission. Before publication, revalidate the observed length, initialized own data elements and their values against the retained observations and every newly acquired pattern. Independently established backing is not evidence that those values remain unchanged. Existing narrower element, tuple and property contracts remain authoritative. A new guard adds an obligation and does not replace those contracts.

    A fresh owner with no established positional or element backing uses the position projection as its invariant location contract and retains the complete pattern separately. Guard acquisition neither freezes the current partition nor changes Type Object equality. Identical guard reacquisition does not reorder or replace a guard. Distinct guards are retained in successful acquisition order; guards acquired together retain the selected admission traversal order. The earliest guard supplies the written greedy ranking for later stores, subject to all guards and all existing backing obligations.

    Conversion to a tuple in this domain first retains ordinary complete membership success and its admission evidence. Otherwise obtain the source's length and indexed observations under 1.14.6, and select a destination for every item before executing effectful conversions. General rest assignment obtains its indexed input before searching; this clause does not introduce additional source Gets. An already admitted scalar is a viable candidate unchanged. For an intrinsically pure scalar conversion, its result and range failure may be determined and retained without invoking user code. For an effectful conversion, determine only whether the existing implicit or explicit rules supply an applicable operation; do not execute it during search. An implicit numeric-family prohibition remains a prohibition.

    Purity is a property of the selected conversion operation, not of an implementation's representation of its source. Intrinsic conversions from an unparameterized decimal, rational or binary floating-point value may supply retained results and failure facts, even if an implementation represents that value using an Object. A predictable failure, including a nonfinite value's conversion to bigint, makes that candidate unavailable without selecting it and prematurely propagating its failure when another complete assignment is viable. This does not permit speculative execution of a source class operator, a metadata operation, an ordinary Object coercion or a reference read. Establish that the conversion uses only the intrinsic numeric payload and applicable pure rules before retaining its result. An implicit numeric-family prohibition is still a failed candidate; this rule supplies no new implicit conversion. For example, an explicit conversion of a one-item sequence containing float128(Infinity) to [...[].<bigint>, ...[].<number>] selects the Number run after the pure BigInt failure. A required BigInt position cannot be erased by that giveback.

    Select the greatest count List in the existing leftmost-greedy order that accounts for every item and satisfies every acquired guard and backing obligation. On a conversion to a fresh tuple there is one pattern, the receiving tuple's. On a store, rank by the earliest acquired guard; additional guards constrain the result without replacing that ranking. Required counts must be filled. Retain every viable assignment of an additional guard, including alternatives where an earlier run gives an identical scalar back to a required later run; selecting only its earliest matching run is insufficient. Existing values not supplied by the operation cannot be converted. If the complete unchanged proposed sequence already satisfies these obligations, retain it without conversion. A missing new position contributes its selected scalar type's DefaultValueOf, where that is not none; a supplied undefined is a value and is not missing.

    If no assignment is viable, propagate the first retained pure scalar conversion failure in input-index and written-run order, or throw a TypeError exception if no such failure exists. After selection, execute each selected effectful conversion once in input order, retain pure results, and verify every result against its selected scalar destination. Propagate a selected conversion's abrupt completion without trying another assignment. A normal result outside that destination throws a TypeError exception. Publish a converted Array only with the projection and ordered guard needed by its successful target admission. Default construction gives each dynamic run zero elements and independently initializes each required scalar position from its scalar type's DefaultValueOf. If any required position has no default, the tuple has no default. A zero count does not request a default. The result carries the complete backing and guard.

    An indexed store, including a reflective data definition, plans against the full proposed sequence, every acquired guard and all existing location contracts. Only supplied destination values may undergo ordinary boundary conversion. Gap initialization and length growth select defaults consistently with the entire ordered pattern; they do not repeat the first rest's default regardless of surrounding values. An accessor cannot replace an owned typed element. Ordinary nonextensibility, length writability, fixed extent, descriptor compatibility and the existing initialization/publication rules remain applicable. Every proposed length must satisfy all acquired count ranges, including when earlier broader backing is retained. A resize must preserve SameType for every surviving location of the actual backing. Check these geometric obligations before indexed growth conversion or intrinsic element work. They do not establish that the eventual values satisfy the ordered guards.

    A finite scalar pattern need not admit every prefix of an admitted sequence. For owned Array truncation, after the existing nonwritable-length refusal and before deletion, determine the actual stopping length from current own descriptors and independently protected typed properties. This is the larger of the requested length and one more than the greatest index at or above it whose deletion would fail. Inspect no getters and execute no user code. Both the requested prefix and that stopping prefix must satisfy every guard, and the actual backing must preserve every surviving location contract at either length. Otherwise throw a TypeError exception before this truncation deletes any elements. If both qualify, perform ordinary descending deletion, partial-failure length restoration and requested writability handling. Do not roll back earlier effects, including independently completed length-conversion effects or earlier valid intrinsic writes.

    Retain the consulted current own data values, length, backing contracts and acquired guards before a receiving conversion. Revalidate them after effects and before publication. A changed consulted value, length, backing contract or guard invalidates that receiving operation with a TypeError exception; do not overwrite or undo the independent effect. An earlier abrupt completion retains its precedence. Reacquiring an identical guard is not a change. New independently acquired property obligations also apply to the final ordinary definition. No new guard or converted element from the failed receiving operation is published.

    Intrinsic movement requires the existing SameType relationship between declared source and destination locations and preserves the moved value. It must not use conversion to repair an ordered-guard violation. Keep ordinary reads, comparator calls, writes and abrupt-completion order. Check every actual published state; earlier valid writes survive a later failure. Growing insertion continues to retain only its designated private tail under 1.14.10.2, and removal retains 1.14.10.3. A successful geometric plan does not waive a subsequent guard or liveness check.

    A borrow uses the established invariant location contract, following reference aliases and Proxy aliases of an already guarded owner. The current scalar member does not narrow that contract. A known reference target other than any must be SameType with the known location contract other than any; value membership alone is insufficient. Existing narrower backing remains the source of this contract. Allocation generation and element-removal identity follow the actual owned backing even through a Proxy alias. Recheck the receiving borrow after conversion effects and immediately before its final own data definition, even when intervening growth or removal restored the original length. Replacement alone preserves identity, while removal/recreation and relocation retain the failures in 2.10.

    Note

    For [number..., string...], replacing the second value of [1, "s"] with a String is valid. Appending Number 2 may select ordinary String conversion and store "2". Reversing the same input does not convert movement values: its first write can leave ["s", "s"], and the second write then throws. The surviving state satisfies the guard.

    These rules do not justify a general first-rest fallback. Defaulted or non-scalar heterogeneous runs, object-valued role dependencies, metadata effects, fresh Proxy or array-like acquisition and general effectful intersection conversion require additional algorithms. Existing copying rules for an unbounded tuple without a determined result shape still produce an ordinary untyped Array.

    1.14.6 Source Observations During Sequence Conversion

    A concrete array or tuple receiving operation retains its own source observations across membership and subsequent elementwise conversion, for both implicit and explicit conversion. A failed membership result discards speculative admission evidence under the existing rules, but does not discard the source values already obtained by that operation. This rule concerns the sequence's own length and indexed properties; it does not combine separate candidate, member or child receiving operations.

    Associate an initially empty observation record with the source Object and this concrete operation. It has a retained length value, initially unobserved, an optional completed length conversion, and indexed entries. To obtain the sequence's length or an indexed value:

    1. If this observation record already has a value for the requested property, return that value.
    2. Let value be ? Get(the source Object, the requested property key).
    3. Retain value in the corresponding entry of the observation record.
    4. Return value.

    Use this operation at the sequence-read points of membership and conversion. Retain actual undefined as a value; it is not unobserved. Where the receiving operation converts the retained length to a count, retain that completed conversion as well and reuse it if needed again. A later source mutation does not replace a retained value or count. An abrupt Get or length conversion propagates immediately. This does not change the accepted length values, the existing count conversion, or the order of shape checks.

    Observation is lazy: retention performs no additional source Get. For a homogeneous array or an established positional tuple domain, membership visits indices in increasing order and stops at its first failed position. For general tuple rest matching, obtain the supplied indexed values in order before the assignment search and reuse those values for its alternatives. Conversion reuses the observations that membership obtained, then obtains any remaining supplied values in increasing order as their conversions are reached. An earlier abrupt conversion prevents later Gets that membership has not already performed. Preserve the existing impossible-length checks before indexed Gets.
