    Each independent or reentrant receiving operation owns a new observation record. A standalone membership test does not provide observations to a later conversion. Retained Object values preserve identity; they are not deep snapshots. Observation establishes no storage contract, descriptor stability, reference permission or liveness fact. Successful admission and produced-result publication retain their existing complete-backing rules. Failure preserves ordinary earlier effects, including independently completed nested receiving boundaries, without publishing the failed sequence's speculative backing.

    1.14.7 Membership

    For an array Type Record t, a value v is of the type t when v is an Object, v's length is t.[[Extent]] where that is not dynamic, and every element of v is of the type t.[[Element]].

    For a tuple with an established sequence domain (1.14.1), membership uses that domain's admitted lengths and exact position types. For a tuple Type Record t without a rest, or with a defaulted fixed prefix followed by one trailing unbounded homogeneous array rest, a value v is of the type t when it is an Object, its length is at least the number of required fixed positions, it has no surplus positions unless a rest collects them, and every supplied value is of its positional type. An index within the declared fixed prefix has that position's [[Type]]; every later index has the rest array's element type. Only unsupplied fixed positions are optional, exactly when their [[Initial]] is not none. A supplied value, including a hole's ordinary Get result, cannot skip an incompatible defaulted position. For rest shapes not covered by these domains, use SequenceAssignment (1.10.4.2) over t.[[Elements]] and v's length, retaining the same positional restriction on defaults before the first rest. The predicate checks each supplied value against its receiving fixed type or the collected rest's sequence type, and success requires an assignment other than unmatched.

    For general rest shapes, retain the collected sequence's count constraint inside SequenceAssignment's admitsRun predicate. A finite array rest of extent N accepts exactly N items, including zero when N is zero; an unbounded array rest imposes no exact count. A failed collected count continues the ordinary greedy giveback search rather than rejecting only the first unconstrained assignment. Expand tuple spread operands in their declared order before this judgment. A defaulted fixed position may take zero items only when the supplied sequence is exhausted at that position; it cannot skip a supplied incompatible value to let a later rest receive it.

    Declared count facts may establish a tuple length range even when several unbounded rests prevent a unique positional domain. Sum the ranges contributed by required fixed positions (one to one), defaulted fixed positions (zero to one), finite array rests (their exact extent), dynamic array rests (zero to unbounded), and nested tuple spreads. An unresolved count or active recursive expansion supplies no new range proof. If an established range excludes the observed length, membership returns false before indexed Gets, and tuple conversion throws a TypeError exception before indexed Gets or element conversion. A literal with an established exact produced count outside that range is a type error, including in an uncalled body; an unknown iteration count is not such a proof. A possible total length establishes neither a successful type assignment nor a unique positional backing contract. These count judgments do not select new storage contracts or weaken reference invariance.

    For a fixed prefix with defaults followed by a trailing unbounded homogeneous array rest, a converting boundary completes omitted fixed positions on a separate Array using their already formed defaults. A fully supplied compatible input retains the ordinary in-place admission rule. Retain the supplied observations and selected evidence, including nested construction, and the complete prefix/rest storage domain; do not replay source Gets to complete a successful admission. Apply the same overlapping-domain, failure and publication rules as omitted no-rest tuple construction. The produced Array is fully admitted before an enclosing setter receives it. Its storage minimum is the number of required prefix positions, its maximum is unbounded, and the rest starts after the full declared prefix even when some prefix positions are currently absent. Subsequent growth uses element-type defaults, not construction initializers. Independent membership and reference-viability tests do not construct the result.

    Note

    A tuple's length is a range rather than a number because a trailing position may carry a default and a position may spread an array type. [uint8, uint32 = 10] accepts a one-element and a two-element array, which is what lets a shorter array satisfy a longer tuple return, and [uint32, ...[].<float32>] accepts any length from one upward.

    Checking every element is linear in the array's length, which is the cost the any boundary has for an array and does not have for a uint8. It falls only where an array of unknown type reaches a typed position; an array whose static type is already the target is not checked at all (1.7.5), and a [].<uint8> passed to a [].<uint8> parameter costs nothing. Whether an implementation may instead check an element on each read, deferring the cost and spreading it, is the same question the object and function kinds raise, and it has the same answer here as there: the check as specified is eager, and a lazier one would need the wrapper the higher-order case would need.

    1.14.8 Static Iteration Contribution

    A possible non-terminal result with value?: T contributes T | undefined: reading an absent property supplies undefined. Optionality does not promise a value and does not by itself erase the known contribution. Use this read type consistently for synchronous, asynchronous and delegated iteration, including loop bindings, spreads and array patterns. Apply the selected operation's await stages afterwards. A terminal alternative contributes only where the operation consumes its completion value; no yield is invented for a done-only result. Unknown result shapes or any retain their existing uncertainty.

    Exclude an iterator-result alternative as terminal only when its done property is required and established truthy. In particular, done?: true may be absent and then reads as undefined, so that alternative's value remains a possible yielded value. Optionality and all viable union alternatives participate in the contribution. Use the same distinction for loops, spreads and array patterns.

    Apply the same conservative contribution judgment to every array-pattern destination: an explicitly annotated binding, a binding inferred at an existing participating site, an existing assignment location, and a collected rest destination. Preserve independently established fresh-literal or immutable-sequence positions. A done-only protocol contributes no yielded value. Iterator exhaustion, defaults and closing retain their existing semantics; a storage extent does not establish an iteration count. Store permission, reference decay and liveness judgments still apply to assignment locations.

    For for await, derive the contribution from the selected async or sync protocol. A real async iterator awaits the result of next and then contributes each possible non-done record's value type without separately awaiting that value. The async-from-sync adapter instead awaits the synchronous iterator's contributed value. Thus a real async iterator may contribute a Promise value, while a synchronous iterator yielding Promises contributes their assimilated values. Preserve optional-hook and union alternatives; any unresolved path leaves the contribution unknown. Done-only paths contribute no value. Apply this contribution to typed loop bindings, assignment heads and unannotated body bindings. Indexed storage alone supplies no exact iteration count.

    For a fixed parameter list and a single trailing positional spread, it is a type error when a required value parameter that no other argument can fill rejects both omission and every possible yielded value. Omission supplies undefined. Use the ordinary parameter boundary, including implicit conversions, rather than assignability alone. This proof needs no yield count. Defaults, optional parameters, admitted undefined, a viable overload or an unknown contribution prevent the proof; more complex mappings retain the judgments their available facts establish. The rule applies to ordinary calls, constructor calls and super calls.

    A value spread in a call, a constructor call, a super call or an array literal, and an array pattern, use the iteration protocol selected by evaluation. Their static iteration contribution consists of a known yielded element type, where the selected iterator's declared protocol establishes one, and a known ordered sequence of position types, where that protocol also guarantees the sequence. Either fact may be unknown. An element type alone establishes no minimum, maximum, or exact number of yielded values.

    It is a type error if a spread argument's Static Type proves that it can participate in neither positional iteration nor the named object-spread binding of 1.10.4. This judgment applies independently of whether the callee's signature is known, in an ordinary call, construction and a super call alike. A known numeric scalar therefore cannot be spread in new C(...n) or super(...n), just as it cannot in f(...n); unknown operands retain their runtime checks. This does not reject a non-iterable object merely because it supplies arguments by name.

    A declared iterable protocol (26) supplies the type of the values returned by its iterator's next method when done is false. The terminal return value contributes no element to a spread or an array pattern. A signature for an iterator method supplies these facts only where the method selected by the access is known to satisfy that signature; an unknown method lookup or an unconstrained replacement leaves the affected facts unknown.

    A mutable Array's array or tuple storage type does not by itself constrain its Symbol.iterator method. Its [[Element]], indexed position types, and storage extent therefore do not by themselves establish a spread's or array pattern's yielded types or count. In contrast, iteration of an immutable tuple Composite is specified to traverse its elements (23.7.2); a fixed tuple shape without optional or rest positions supplies those ordered position types and their exact count.

    The same contribution is used when checking call arguments, when checking an array literal against an array or tuple contextual type, when deriving an array literal's own Static Type, and when deriving an array pattern's position types. An array pattern uses a guaranteed sequence's corresponding position type, or the guaranteed yielded element type where only that fact is known; an unknown contribution leaves its unannotated binding's type unknown. An explicit sub-pattern annotation still tests and narrows the yielded value. Matching retains its iterator cache, effects, length test, and non-match behaviour. A successful length test establishes no indexed storage type or storage extent. A known sequence preserves positional correspondence for following arguments or elements. An unknown count loses correspondence from that position onward, but does not erase preceding known positions or the types of subsequent contributions. A contribution is checked against the destinations its known facts establish, including a homogeneous rest parameter or array element type; a positional or arity judgment requiring unavailable facts is deferred under 1.2.8. A value obtained from iteration is not a fresh literal expression and acquires no literal-propagation privilege merely because its indexed source once held a literal.

    Note

    Replacing an iterator may change both its yielded values and their count without changing indexed storage. For example, a tuple storing one String may have an iterator that yields two uint8 values; an ordinary spread observes those two values and the iterator's effects. A runtime guard used to optimize that lookup cannot justify rejecting a source text before the guard runs.

    This judgment does not change the separate index-based semantics of reference iteration (2.7), or the binding of spread type arguments (1.4.2.2). The additional eligibility rules for binding a variadic parameter (4.4) do not substitute indexed storage facts for the iterator's contribution to ordinary value arguments.

    1.14.9 The Static Type of an Array Literal

    Where a contextual type (1.6.5) requires an array or tuple type, an array literal is checked against it element-wise and the boundary converts, so the literal reports no Static Type of its own and the conversion that builds an Array carrying the element type is not elided.

    Where no such contextual type reaches it, the Static Type of an array literal is the array type whose [[Element]] is the join of its elements' Static Types, each widened as a contribution is (1.6.3), and whose [[Extent]] is dynamic. An elision contributes undefined and a spread element contributes the element type of its static iteration contribution (1.14.8), where known. Indexed storage alone does not determine that contribution. Where any element's Static Type is unknown the literal's is unknown, since an array holding something unspeakable is not an array of the join of the rest. An EMPTY literal likewise has no Static Type: it says nothing about its elements, and reporting an element type of never would say something false, since element types are invariant and a never-elemented array is assignable to no other array type.

    Note 1

    A literal every element of which is a literal does not ANCHOR an inference (1.6.2.2). [1] has a known type and states nothing a program annotated, exactly as 1 does, so function g() { return [1]; } publishes nothing and stays untyped.

     Note 2

    This rule changes the meaning of one shape of program that carries no annotation, and the change is intended rather than overlooked.

    1. [1n].includes(1) evaluates to true, where in the absence of this proposal it evaluates to false.

    The literal is a [ ] . < bigint >, so includes is read at that element type and its argument is a bigint position; literal propagation then builds the argument as a BigInt, and the search compares it against a BigInt element that holds the same mathematical value. Every step is a rule of this proposal applied where it says it applies.

    It is accepted because no program relies on it. A search of a BigInt array for a Number is a mistake in every case it can arise, and the value it evaluates to today is the one that hides the mistake. The alternative — leaving every array literal without a Static Type — costs an element read its type, costs a function returning a literal its inferred return, and leaves the non-convergence rule of 1.6.2.3 unreachable, since the shape that grows at every step is a literal containing a recursive call.

    The neighbouring cases report rather than change: [1, 2, 3].includes("2"), ["a"].includes(1), and [1, 2, 3].indexOf("2") are type errors, where they previously evaluated to false and to the not-found index. Each searches for a value the array's element type cannot hold, which is the mistake this proposal exists to report, and the answer they gave was the answer that concealed it. One diagnostic is weakened: an element whose value the callback's parameter type cannot hold, as in [300].map(f) where f takes a uint8, is now reported as a type error naming number and uint8 rather than a range error naming 300. The stricter report arrives earlier; the weaker one described the value better.

    1.14.10 Defaults and Stores

    An elision in an array literal occupies a position and contributes undefined to that position's contextual element judgment. It is a type error when that value is not assignable to the destination element type, for an array or tuple, including an argument or return context. A hole is supplied, so it does not activate a tuple position's default; only an omitted trailing position does.

    The default value of a tuple type is the array whose elements are, for each element of [[Elements]] whose [[Rest]] is false, its [[Initial]] where that is not none and the default value of its [[Type]] otherwise; a [[Rest]] element contributes no elements. It is none where an element has an [[Initial]] of none and a [[Type]] with no default.

    A store to an element of an array of element type t checks the value against t by Table 23. length is of the index type. Deleting an element of a typed array throws a TypeError exception.

    A store to a position of a tuple checks the value against the [[Type]] of the element that receives that position, by the same table; a position an element whose [[Rest]] is true collects takes that element's collected type. The type checked against is the one the VALUE carries rather than the one the reference through which it is reached would give it, which is what makes the covariance of 1.2.3.1 sound: a [uint8] seen as a [uint8 | string] is the same Array, and a String written through the wider view would otherwise land in a position declared uint8. The same reading governs the array store above, where [].<any> is a supertype of every array. A tuple's arity is part of its type, so a store to a position beyond it throws a TypeError exception rather than growing the Array, and so does an assignment to length that would leave fewer positions than the tuple fixes; a tuple with a rest element admits any length at or above its fixed positions.

    1.14.10.1 Initialization on Length Growth

    When an explicit definition or assignment to an Array's "length" increases its length and the Array carries typed array or tuple backing, apply the following rule after the typed count conversion, fixed-extent check and surviving-position contract check. An unchanged or decreased length retains the existing rules.

    1. Let oldLength be the Array's current length.
    2. Let newLength be the requested length.
    3. Let descriptor be the requested length Property Descriptor with its value replaced by the converted length.
    4. If the Array is not extensible, or IsCompatiblePropertyDescriptor returns false for descriptor and the current length descriptor, return false from the property definition, without computing defaults.
    5. Record the Array's current backing contracts and fixed extent, if any.
    6. Let values be a new empty List.
    7. For each integer index from oldLength (inclusive) to newLength (exclusive), in ascending order, do
      1. Let type be the actual backing type of position index at newLength, including every applicable conjoined contract.
      2. Let value be DefaultValueOf(type).
      3. If value is none, throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Append the value to be stored, with value-type copying as required by 1.11.4, to values.
      5. If the Array's current length differs from oldLength, or its backing contracts or fixed extent differ from those recorded, throw a TypeError exception.
    8. Recheck extensibility and compatibility with the current length descriptor as above. If either check fails, return false.
    9. Without executing user code between these checks and publication, create an own data property for each new position, with its corresponding prepared value and [[Writable]], [[Enumerable]] and [[Configurable]] all true, and apply descriptor to "length".
    10. Retain the current capacity if it suffices for newLength. Otherwise grow the allocation to sufficient capacity and invalidate references according to 2.10.
    11. Return true.

    Preparation does not publish the requested elements, length, capacity or relocation. Its failure does not roll back independent effects of default computation, including independent mutations, reservations or changes to property attributes. Such effects are not retried. Existing element value changes alone do not change the backing contract. A failed outer preparation does not itself invalidate references. A successful increase within capacity preserves references to existing elements.

    The new properties are present even when the default is undefined. Their creation invokes no inherited setter and does not repeat a conversion already performed by DefaultValueOf. A type without a default is not replaced by an untyped zero or undefined. This rule initializes an explicit length increase; it does not require defaults for insertions whose values are supplied by a caller or moved by an intrinsic.

    1.14.10.2 Initialization on Indexed Growth and Insertion

    For a typed Array's own indexed data definition that increases length, first apply the existing destination boundary conversion, fixed-extent and surviving-position rules. Prepare every new position in increasing index order, retaining the converted supplied destination value and computing DefaultValueOf of the actual backing type for each unsupplied position. Apply the preflight, conflict checks and publication rules of 1.14.10.1 to the complete new tail. The supplied destination retains the requested descriptor attributes; implicitly initialized gap positions are writable, enumerable and configurable own data properties. No element, requested length, capacity or relocation from this growth is published if preparation fails.

    Creating a new own typed element with a data or generic descriptor whose [[Value]] is absent uses the position's default, or throws a TypeError exception if it has none. An explicit undefined value is supplied and undergoes the ordinary boundary check. Omitting [[Value]] when redefining an existing property retains its existing value. A new accessor descriptor does not initialize a data position and throws a TypeError exception. Ordinary nonextensibility and length-writability refusal precede missing-default computation. A missing own element inside an existing extent uses the same default rule; if default computation independently creates that property or changes the published length or backing, throw a TypeError rather than overwrite the independent result.

    For a growing intrinsic unshift or splice on an owned typed Array, after ordinary receiver, length and index/count processing and the existing mutation-plan checks, record the current published length, backing contracts and fixed extent. Retain privately the operation's own data definitions at indices in the proposed new tail. Keep the ordinary order of property reads, conversions, species construction and setters; writes within the recorded extent occur immediately. Private definitions are not visible through reads, keys, descriptors, length or reference acquisition.

    The private definitions belong only to the specific intrinsic writes, not to code invoked by them. Getter, setter, species and conversion callbacks perform independent operations, including nested mutations of the same receiver. Before and after each intrinsic write and before final publication, if the published length, backing contracts or fixed extent differ from those recorded, throw a TypeError exception. Recheck after intervening lookup or conversion effects and before applying the write's own property definition, even if those effects have created its destination. Earlier abrupt completions retain their ordinary precedence. Existing-element value writes and capacity-only changes do not by themselves invalidate this plan. Failure discards private definitions and preserves prior ordinary writes and independent effects; it does not retry or roll them back.

    At the final length update, prepare the complete proposed tail using the retained descriptors. A position not supplied by an own data definition, including one whose setter consumed the supplied value, uses its actual backing type's default or throws if that default is none. Use the same default order, conflict checks and publication rules as explicit length growth. Recheck length-descriptor compatibility and extensibility; refusal is a failed final Set and therefore throws a TypeError for these intrinsics. Publish the complete tail and final length without user code between revalidation and publication. Inherited setters and successful conversions are not repeated.

    Update capacity and relocation only when initialized growth publishes, using current capacity. A failed definition, a discarded private tail, or an inherited setter that creates no element does not itself move backing or invalidate references. Growing beyond capacity invalidates references by 2.10; growth within capacity preserves surviving locations. These rules do not change untyped Arrays, non-Array receivers, or nongrowing intrinsic operations.

    1.14.10.3 Deletion and Removal of Typed Array Positions

    An owned typed Array's [[Delete]] throws a TypeError exception for an index in its backing contract's protected domain, regardless of the alias used, current occupancy, or the property's configurable attribute. The domain is every canonical array index for growable homogeneous backing, indices below a fixed extent, and indices admitted by the tuple backing's permitted length domain. Noncanonical keys, Symbols, and fixed nonpositions retain ordinary deletion behaviour. In particular, the string key "-0" is not an array index. Existing early deletion errors continue to apply where the receiver and key prove protection; otherwise property-key conversion and runtime refusal keep their ordinary timing. Refusal does not invalidate a reference.

    For a shrinking intrinsic pop, shift, or splice on an owned typed Array, after ordinary argument processing and mutation-plan validation, record the current published length, backing contracts, fixed extent, and proposed final length. Keep the ordinary order of element reads, movement writes, species work, replacement conversion, and setters. At each ordinary trailing-deletion step, revalidate the recorded plan and check the existing own descriptor's configurability. A nonconfigurable descriptor throws a TypeError at that step. Otherwise defer removal and reference invalidation until final truncation. Only indices in the recorded extent that leave the proposed extent receive this treatment; deletion of a surviving position retains the direct-deletion rule.

    Before and after each intrinsic element write, after intervening lookup or conversion effects and before applying its own property definition, at each deferred deletion, and before final truncation, if the published length, backing contracts or fixed extent differ from those recorded, throw a TypeError exception. These write checks belong to the specific intrinsic receiver, key and execution context; callback and nested operations execute independently. Earlier abrupt completions retain their ordinary precedence. Value-only or capacity-only changes do not by themselves invalidate the plan. On failure retain earlier writes, independent effects, and every tail location not actually removed; do not retry or roll back.

    At the final length update perform the ordinary typed length truncation, bypassing only the refusal of individual indexed deletion. Recheck length writability and the current element descriptors. Nonwritable length refuses before removal. Remove trailing elements in descending index order without intervening user code. A nonconfigurable barrier retains the ordinary failed-truncation state: length is one past the barrier, lower positions remain, and successful higher removals remain removed. Apply any requested nonwritable length as required by ArraySetLength. An earlier deferred-deletion refusal has removed no tail locations; earlier movement and replacement writes are not undone. Direct length truncation uses the same removal and barrier rules. A failed throwing Set still throws a TypeError.

    An independently acquired required object-property contract is not waived by sequence removal. Check its deletion protection at the ordinary deferred-deletion step. During length truncation, if deletion instead completes abruptly because of that protection, restore length to one past the protected index, apply any requested nonwritable length, and propagate the original abrupt completion. Completed higher removals remain. This rule also applies to an otherwise untyped Array carrying such required properties, and to a contract acquired during intervening effects.

    Actual removal, including a successful removal before a final descriptor barrier, invalidates that element's identity under 2.10. Surviving references retain their locations and observe moved or replaced values. Shortening itself does not change capacity or relocate backing; later regrowth does not revive removed references. These rules do not change ordinary untyped Array mutation or authorize deletion from callbacks, surviving typed positions, or unsupported non-Array backing.

    A method that writes a position takes its value at that position's type: with at the type of the position its index selects, and fill, push and unshift at the type of each position they reach, which is why they are refused on a tuple whose positions differ. A method that would MOVE a value between positions of different types throws a TypeError exception - reverse, sort, copyWithin and splice on such a tuple - because the Array would otherwise hold values its own type does not admit. Their copying forms are the way to do it and carry the shape the operation produced: toReversed answers the positions in reverse, slice the window it took, with the shape it was given, and toSorted the shape it was given where every position is the same type. Where the operation determines no shape - a comparator-driven sort of positions that differ, or any of these over a tuple with an unbounded rest - the result is an ordinary Array carrying no element type.

    For a bounded tuple without a rest, including one with trailing defaults, or a tuple whose rests all have finite expansion, including a defaulted effective tail, these copying shapes describe the positions actually produced at the operation's captured length. A slice retains its selected positions and a reversal reverses the occupied positions; these results have exactly the produced positions as required positions. A with copy retains the complete source storage domain after its replacement check. A sorted copy retains that domain when all occupied position contracts are the same. Omitted source defaults neither add output positions nor supply construction initializer metadata to the copy. The source retains its complete admitted length domain.

    For a proved intrinsic mutation, determine its permitted length and movement plan from the backing contracts after the ordinary receiver, length and index/count argument processing, and before element access, element conversion, callbacks, species creation, writes or deletion performed by the mutation. Existing comparator validation for sort precedes this plan. A planned final length outside a fixed array extent or the tuple's permitted length domain, or changing any surviving tuple index's backing type, throws a TypeError exception before element work. For an anchored suffix, compare each moved source contract at the old length with its destination contract at the proposed length. Earlier ordinary argument effects are retained. Where the intrinsic origin, contracts and arguments statically establish an impossible plan, the existing type-error rules apply.

    A planned move between tuple positions requires SameType for the source and destination backing types; value membership, subtyping or a possible conversion is not sufficient. For reverse, compare each mirrored pair. For copyWithin, compare the normalized source and destination runs. For shift, unshift and splice, compare every source/destination pair the operation moves. A same-length splice replacement does not move the remaining positions; each inserted value still crosses its own destination boundary. For sort, every position in the occupied range must have the same backing type because its permutation is not known before comparator execution. For fill, every position in the selected non-empty range must have the same backing type. Empty ranges impose no movement or uniformity requirement. These are restrictions on participating positions, not a blanket rejection of every method on a heterogeneous tuple.

    The plan is a pure judgment of contracts and index geometry. It does not read elements, attempt conversions, invoke user code, publish storage or change reference identity. A successful plan does not make the operation atomic or waive any subsequent check: ordinary reads, conversions, writes, deletions and length changes retain their order and effects, and a later abrupt completion does not roll back earlier effects or independently completed boundaries. An impossible pop therefore fails before removing an element, while an ordinary write failure after a valid plan may retain earlier writes. Reference liveness remains governed by 2.10. A user replacement for an intrinsic receives no intrinsic plan; invoking the intrinsic through another reference still executes its plan.

    A method of the array that takes or returns an ELEMENT takes or returns it at the element type. includes, indexOf, and lastIndexOf take their search element at t, where for a tuple t is the union of its position types, a rest position contributing its element type; fill, push, and unshift take the values they store at t; at returns t. A literal argument in one of those positions takes t by 1.6.6, so a.includes(65) finds the element 65 of a [].<uint16> rather than comparing a uint16 against a Number and failing. The same holds of a typed collection: the key and value positions of a Map.<K, V> and the element positions of a Set.<T> take their declared types, and so do those of a WeakMap.<K, V> and a WeakSet.<T>, whose key and element positions are constrained to the types a weak reference may hold and are checked against the declared type on top of that constraint. A method that STORES takes its value at the declared type however it is spelled, getOrInsert and getOrInsertComputed included, the latter checking the value its callback returns. A LOOKUP answers the value type or undefined, since a lookup that finds nothing answers undefined: the Static Type of get on a Map.<K, V> is V | undefined rather than V, so a binding of type V does not admit it without a test. An operation that RETURNS a collection carries an element type determined by where its elements can come from: intersection and difference on a Set.<T> draw only from the receiver and return a Set.<T> whatever the other operand holds, while union and symmetricDifference draw from both and return a Set.<T | U> for an other operand of Set.<U>. Where the other operand's element type is not known, the result's is not either, and the result carries none: a union with an unconstrained set is unconstrained, and answering Set.<T> would state more than the values support. isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom answer a Boolean. The count a collection reports, and the collection that reports none, are 1.15; a collection with no type arguments constrains none of these positions and is 1.15.7.

    These are ordinary parameters of a declared type, so Table 23 governs them and nothing further is needed: a literal that cannot take the element type is an Early Error, and a value of the any type is checked at the boundary. A search is not treated more leniently than a store. a.includes(70000) on a [].<uint16> is a type error rather than false, for the reason 1.8.5 gives for a narrowing whose test can never succeed: the answer is knowable from the types, so reporting it as an ordinary false would hide a mistake rather than answer a question. An UNTYPED array declares no element type and so constrains none of these positions.

    Note

    This reconciles the two rules 1.8.3 leaves in tension. A tuple defaults element-wise, but an element that carries a default already has a value for its position, so the initializer is used where there is one and the type's default only where there is not. [uint8, uint32 = 10] therefore defaults to [0, 10] rather than being rejected because the second position was already spoken for.

    The literal element store remains the open case 1.6.6 records: the design specifies array[0] = 300 on a [].<uint8> as wrapping to 44 on the grounds of matching Uint8Array, while the literal rule would reject it, and the compatibility argument does not reach new syntax. This clause resolves it against the design's example: a literal element store follows the literal rule and is rejected, because the compatibility argument does not reach new syntax, [].<uint8> exists nowhere today and Uint8Array is untouched, and a literal that does not fit its destination is the mistake every other literal rule here treats it as. A typed value stores by Table 22 as before, so the runtime wrap survives where it belongs.

    1.14.10.4 Relationship to %TypedArray%

    %TypedArray% and its constructors are UNTOUCHED by this proposal. A Uint8Array reports its length as a Number, wraps a store that does not fit, and behaves in every respect as it does today. Nothing here changes an object that already exists.

    The two are SEPARATE ARRAY SYSTEMS rather than one system with two spellings, and they do not mix directly: a Uint8Array is not a [].<uint8> and does not coerce to one, its elements being Numbers rather than values of a numeric value type. %TypedArray% is the system for byte-oriented work against existing APIs, and the array types are the system for typed storage; a program picks one per data structure rather than converting between them.

    Where they meet is a BUFFER, which both already understand. A %TypedArray% exposes its buffer, Span.<T>(buffer) (11) reinterprets those bytes at the element type T, and the result is a window — so writing through it writes the same bytes the %TypedArray% reads.

    An implementation SHOULD report the deprecation once per agent, on the first use of a %TypedArray% constructor or of %TypedArray.prototype%. Once per agent rather than per use: a diagnostic that fires inside a loop over binary data is noise, and the purpose is to tell an author that the family they are using has a successor, which needs saying one time. The report names the replacement rather than only the deprecation.

    Nothing about the report is observable to an ECMAScript program — no property, no altered result, no thrown completion — and an implementation that emits nothing is conforming. Deprecated says a program SHOULD move; untouched says no program BREAKS by not moving, and a deprecation that changed behaviour would be the compatibility event this clause exists to avoid.

    Note

    The alternative was to give %TypedArray% the counts and the growth of an array type, so that the two families were interchangeable. It was measured and declined. A length at the index type is a value of a numeric value type, and an untyped operand meeting one throws a TypeError at the operation, the checker deferring what it cannot see (1.8.2 gives an unannotated let the any type) — so for (let i = 0; i < u.length; i++) and total += u.length would raise in existing programs, and u.length === n against an untyped binding would silently answer false rather than raise. The first two are the ordinary way binary data is processed, and the third reports nothing at all.

    Two systems that each behave well, with a stated boundary and a buffer between them, is a smaller cost than one system that behaves well in new code and changes the meaning of old code. It is also legible: a reader can see which system a value belongs to from how it was written.

    1.14.10.5 Ordered Element Types

    Array.prototype.sort and Array.prototype.toSorted order by the String representation of each element when no comparator is given. Where an array's ELEMENT TYPE is known and carries an order of its own, that order is used instead, so [].<uint8> sorts as %Uint8Array%.prototype.sort does rather than as text. An array with no element type - an unannotated Array - is unaffected, as is any call that supplies a comparator.

    A type is ORDERED when it is one of the following. Anything else, including any, an object type without a declared comparison, and a union of unlike types, is not, and an array of it keeps the String comparison.

    Note

    An implementation compares with a two-way predicate rather than deriving a three-way result: a comparison sort needs to know only whether one element precedes another, and deriving "less, equal, or greater" from operator < would call it twice per comparison to no purpose.

    The order comes from the element TYPE, so it is fixed once for a whole sort rather than decided per pair.

    1.15 Keyed Collections

    For Map.<K, V> and WeakMap.<K, V>, getOrInsertComputed takes a key of K, a callback with contract (K) => V, and returns V. The callback's established parameters and produced result must satisfy these boundaries even when a particular map already contains the key. A fresh callback literal receives V as its contextual return type, preserving numeric-literal adoption. A callback result of any defers the produced-value check to insertion; its known parameter and receiver contracts are still checked. This per-call dynamic result rule does not make any a subtype of V. Runtime insertion enforcement is unchanged and no occupancy inspection is used to justify an early error.

    A member contract determined by a typed collection's resolved built-in identity and type arguments applies equally through a dotted name and a statically known String property key. This includes a constant alias or parenthesized key, and preserves the member's parameter, result and count types. A same-named user class does not acquire a library contract. This judgment supplies a Static Type, not a proof of intrinsic method identity; it does not elide property lookup, key evaluation, receiver binding or reference-liveness checks. Unknown keys and any receivers retain runtime checks.

    Map, Set, WeakMap and WeakSet take type arguments, and their members follow from them. 1.14.10 states what their key, value and element POSITIONS admit, alongside the array's; this clause states the count they report, the members that walk them, the type they report as their own, which values are of them, how they acquire their types, what their key positions admit, and the collection that has none of it.

    1.15.1 get Map.prototype.size, get Set.prototype.size

    Where the collection carries type arguments, size has the Static Type index type and the accessor returns a value of that type. Where it does not, size is a Number and the accessor is unchanged.

    size is an accessor property whose set accessor function is undefined, on a typed collection as on an untyped one. An array's length is assignable because an array is POSITIONAL and dropping a suffix is well defined; a keyed collection has no such operation that clear does not already name, and a count that deleted entries would be a mutator wearing the spelling of a report. Having a type does not imply having a setter: capacity (2.11.1) is of the index type and reports only.

    WeakMap and WeakSet have no size, and reading one from a value of either type is a type error rather than undefined. A member the type does not declare is a mistake the type can report, which is the treatment 11 gives the operations a window does not have.

    Note

    The accessor returns a VALUE of the index type and not 𝔽 of a count. The distinction is the one 2.11.1 states for a capacity, whose algorithm returned 𝔽 at every step while index type said the count it reports is of the index type; the dfn was the side that was right, and that clause now agrees with it. A count reported as a Number cannot be compared with one reported at the index type, which is the whole reason for naming the type.

    1.15.2 Iterating a Keyed Collection

    Where the collection carries type arguments, its entry type is the tuple type « K, V » for a Map.<K, V> and « T, T » for a Set.<T>, and the members that walk it carry the types below.

    A Map.<K, V> declares that it implements Iterable.<« K, V »> and a Set.<T> that it implements Iterable.<T>, in the sense of 26: the relation is a DECLARATION rather than a structural inspection, so it is decided by brand and a hand-written iterator entering the same position pays the structural check instead.

    On a Set, keys and values are the same function object, so they answer the same type; and entries yields a pair of the element with itself, which is what the language does and what a destructuring for-of over a set therefore binds.

    WeakMap and WeakSet have none of the members in the table above, nor size (1.15.1), and reading any of them from a value of either type is a type error rather than undefined, whether the read is a member access, a computed access whose key is statically established, or a property of an object binding or assignment pattern. The last is not a missing-key rule for patterns: it is this rule, applied to a read. A weak collection is not enumerable: what it holds may be reclaimed between one step of a walk and the next, so there is no order to report and no count to report it against. The absence is a consequence of weakness rather than an omission to be filled in.

    Note

    The return type is the Iterator of 26 rather than a per-collection type. There is no MapIterator or SetIterator, for the reason that clause already gives: the bare-argument shorthand carries the narrower element type that TypeScript needs those names for, so the family stays at six interfaces and two classes.

    forEach takes its VALUE first and its key second, which is the order the language chose and the order a reader most often gets wrong. Stating it is most of what typing forEach is worth.

    1.15.3 RuntimeTypeOf of a Keyed Collection

    A typed collection carries the Type Record it was built at, and 1.7.1.1 reports it: Reflect.typeOf of a Map.<K, V> is that type, and of a collection with no type arguments is the bare Map, Set, WeakMap or WeakSet.

    Note

    Carried rather than inferred, for the reason a window and a vector carry theirs: the type is not recoverable from the value. A Map.<string, uint8> and a Map.<string, string> have the same object shape and the same prototype chain, and a Map has no own properties at all - so inference read the literal type of an empty object and reported neither the specialization nor the bare nominal.

    1.15.4 Key and Element Positions

    A Map's or WeakMap's key, and a Set's or WeakSet's element, are identity-bearing positions. At such a position the conversions of Table 18 do not apply: a value that is not already of the declared type is a TypeError exception rather than a converted one. Every other position, including a Map's VALUE, is unaffected and converts as 1.6.1 states.

    This governs the positions wherever they are reached - the methods that store, the methods that search, and the entries a constructor's seed supplies (1.15.5) - because a rule enforced at some of them is one a program can route around.

    Note

    A boundary is a store, and the conversion rule reasons about stores: nothing is lost, since 5 is '5' and reads back as 5. A key is a store whose value is also an IDENTITY, and a conversion that loses nothing as a value can still lose an identity by mapping two distinct sources onto one key. Without this rule, _m_.set(_theNumberOne_, 1) followed by _m_.set(*"1"*, 2) left a Map.<string, uint8> holding ONE entry where a Map holds two - so giving a collection a type changed how many entries it had, silently, and only for the programs in which both spellings happened to occur.

    The numeric targets already have this property, which makes the rule a consistency correction rather than a new restriction: 1.7.3.1 admits a numeric source only where the target represents it exactly and raises a RangeError otherwise, so a Map.<uint8, V> could never merge two keys. The string target was the one boundary in this specification admitting a conversion that does not preserve identity.

    An ARRAY's element position is not identity-bearing and is unchanged: an array is addressed by an index, so _a_.push(5) on a [ ] . < string > still stores "5". What distinguishes a Set is that its element IS its key.

    1.15.4.1 Probes Performed by the Set Operations

    The set operations of 1.14.10 test each element of one operand against the other. Where the other operand's element type cannot hold the element, that test is false rather than a thrown exception. An exception arising from the other operand's has for any other reason propagates unchanged.

    Note

    A test a user writes with a needle the element type cannot hold is an error, because it can never succeed. A probe performed BY an operation is a different question with a known answer, and reading it as false is what makes the constant-folding this specification describes fall out of iterating: "an intersection of a Set.<uint8> and a Set.<string> is empty without iterating, and isDisjointFrom is true, since distinct value types share no values."

    Stated for both operands, which the earlier arrangement was not. An operation walks the smaller operand and probes the larger, and the probe ran through the converting path - so the fold held in the direction where the element could be converted and failed in the other, and which direction that was depended on which operand was smaller.

    1.15.5 Constructing a Typed Keyed Collection

    At a proved intrinsic collection construction, a non-nullish participating seed must satisfy the synchronous iteration protocol used by the constructor. It is a type error if established facts prove that this protocol cannot be obtained. Omitted, null and undefined seeds retain empty construction. A primitive category alone does not establish absence: boxed primitive prototype chains may supply the iterator, including through prior source texts. Establish the relevant lookup and effects without executing a getter. Unknown or replaceable protocol facts remain dynamic.

    Each iterated Map or WeakMap entry must be an Object before its key and value are read at property keys "0" and "1". It is a type error when established traversal reaches a non-Object entry; later duplicate keys cannot undo this failure. Entries need not be arrays, have length two or themselves be iterable. Ordinary data Objects may supply either position. An established missing positional read supplies undefined, but short array syntax alone does not prove absence of an inherited property. Preserve getters, proxies and intervening effects as unknown when their reads or traversal consequences are unavailable. Only after ordinary insertion are surviving entries checked for typed adoption, using the duplicate-key rule below.

    A collection acquires type arguments only where the entries it already holds satisfy them. Acquiring the type is therefore the same operation as checking that the value was already of it: each key, value or element the collection holds is converted at the corresponding type as by 1.7.3.1, and the converted value replaces the one held. Where any of them cannot be converted, the collection does not acquire the type and a TypeError exception is thrown.

    This is what checks a CONSTRUCTOR's seed. new Set.<uint8>(["a"]) is a type error, and new Set.<uint8>([1]) holds a uint8 rather than the Number the literal arrived as, so an element that entered through the constructor and one that entered through add are of one type afterwards.

    Where intrinsic construction, seed iteration and insertion behaviour are statically established, finite fresh literal seed facts may determine the contents at acquisition. It is a type error if an established surviving key, value or element cannot undergo the conversion required above. Apply the same judgment to explicit construction and immediate contextual adoption. For Map, preserve key/value positions and resolve proved duplicate primitive keys by the collection's equality rule before checking the surviving values: an overwritten value has no adoption obligation. A later unknown key that could overwrite a value prevents proof that that value survives. Seed expressions still evaluate in their original order; this judgment does not preconvert or omit transient entries.

    This bounded proof requires the intrinsic-origin conditions of 1.12.6 and established iterator/adder identity. General iterables, unknown spreads, getters, replaced operations, arbitrary mutation histories and unresolved effects retain run-time checking. Reuse the existing numeric-literal and declared-conversion rules; do not infer a permanent element type for an untyped collection, infer a closed shape from structural membership, or change weak-key eligibility. Empty and nullish seeds remain admitted.

    A class whose heritage names an instantiation constructs instances of it: for class M extends Map.<K, V> { }, an instance of M carries K and V, as does an instance of any class extending M. A class extending a bare Map or Set names no type arguments and its instances are 1.15.7.

    Note

    Checking on the way in rather than stamping before the seed is consumed. The latter is the more obvious rule and is not available: there is no object to carry the arguments until the construction has produced one, by which point the constructor has already consumed its seed. Checking what is found reaches further in any case, since it also governs the ANNOTATION spelling let s: Set.<uint8> = new Set(["a"]), where the construction names no type arguments at all.

    A collection that ALREADY carries type arguments does not acquire different ones, so annotating a Map of Strings as a Map.<string, uint8> is refused rather than silently re-labelled. Only a collection carrying none adopts, and only where its contents support the claim.

    1.15.6 Membership of a Keyed Collection Type

    A value is of the type Map.<K, V> when it is a Map and the type arguments it CARRIES are K and V, and correspondingly for the other three collections. An argument written any admits any instantiation in its position, matching the family top (1.2.3.1 Note 5). The any rule is not the collections' alone: it holds for two instantiations of any one generic declaration, a user class included, so Box.<any> is the family of every Box.<T> (1.5.20), and it is sound for the same reason — a store through the wider view is checked against the instance's own field type at run time (1.7.6), whatever the static type permitted. A collection carrying no type arguments is of the bare type Map and of no instantiation of it.

    This is what is, a when pattern naming an instantiation, a typed catch clause, and narrowing all read, so the four agree by construction.

    Note

    Decided by the arguments the value CARRIES rather than by inspecting its entries. Inspection would answer a different question: what a container currently holds is not what it will ACCEPT NEXT, and the instantiation is a claim about the latter. An untyped map whose entries happen to be Strings and uint8s will take anything on its next store, so calling it a Map.<string, uint8> would state a guarantee it does not make - and would licence exactly the unsoundness the invariance rule of 1.2.3.1 exists to prevent. Inspection is also unstable, since a single store invalidates the answer, and it costs a walk of the collection at each test.

    The prototype chain cannot decide this on its own: every Map has one prototype, so without the argument comparison every Map satisfied every Map.<…>. That is the same reason the ranges and the window forms carry their own membership rules rather than relying on the chain.

    Membership is asked at a CONVERSION BOUNDARY as well as by is, and the two want different things from it: the boundary asks whether a value is already of the type so that it may skip converting. A collection carrying no arguments ADOPTS the target's at such a boundary - which is what let m: Map.<string, uint8> = new Map() means - and is then of the type. A collection already carrying arguments does not adopt new ones, so a Map of Strings does not become a Map.<string, uint8> by being annotated as one.

    1.15.7 Collections Without Type Arguments

    A Map or Set written with no type arguments is unaffected by this clause and by every rule of 1.14.10 that concerns a collection. Its size is a Number, its keys and values are unconstrained, iterating it binds at the any type, and no program that does not use these types can observe any of the above.

    This is the collection reading of the rule an array already has, that "an array with no element type is untouched by any of this" (1.4.2.7). It is stated because a collection has no other place it would be stated, and because the two forms of one container are otherwise easy to conflate: a specialization adds nothing to a shared prototype and changes nothing about a constructor, so the typed and untyped forms coexist in one program without interacting.

    Note

    The rule is stated per family rather than as a general rule about an unparameterized built-in, because the families do not agree on what an unparameterized use means and a single sentence covering them would decide questions this clause has not asked. Proxy already has a different answer: without a type argument a proxy is of the any type and behaves as it does today.

    1.15.8 GetSetRecord ( obj )

    The abstract operation GetSetRecord takes argument obj (an ECMAScript language value) and returns either a normal completion containing a Set Record, or a throw completion.

    This operation reads the size of a set-like and converts it with ToNumber. Where the value read is of the index type, that conversion is not performed. It is revised to:

    1. If obj is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. Let rawSize be ? Get(obj, "size").
    3. If rawSize is a value of the index type, then
      1. Let sized be the mathematical value of rawSize.
      2. If sized is not a non-negative integer, throw a TypeError exception.
      3. Let intSize be sized.
    4. Else,
      1. Let numSize be ? ToNumber(rawSize).
      2. NOTE: If rawSize is undefined, then numSize will be NaN.
      3. If numSize is NaN, throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Set intSize to ! ToIntegerOrInfinity(numSize).
      5. If intSize < 0, throw a RangeError exception.
    5. Let has be ? Get(obj, "has").
    6. If IsCallable(has) is false, throw a TypeError exception.
    7. Let keys be ? Get(obj, "keys").
    8. If IsCallable(keys) is false, throw a TypeError exception.
    9. Return a new Set Record { [[SetObject]]: obj, [[Size]]: intSize, [[Has]]: has, [[Keys]]: keys }.
     Note

    A count is CHECKED rather than coerced, which is the discipline 2.11.2 states for the operations that ACCEPT a count: an operation that accepted a String as a count would disagree with the operations that report one. Without this revision a set operation between two typed sets would route a value of the index type through an implicit numeric conversion, which is the one thing the conversion rule (1.6.1) does not do.

    The ELSE branch matters as much, and is the existing steps unchanged. The argument to a set operation may be any set-like, whose size is an ordinary Number and whose failure modes have observable error kinds — a missing size is a TypeError by way of NaN, and a negative one a RangeError. Routing every set-like through ToIndexType would collapse both into a TypeError and change the behaviour of programs using no types at all, which 1.15.7 forbids.

    1.16 Extensions

    The design is organized as a core and a set of extensions, each of which adds types, operations, or syntax to the core rather than revising it. This clause states what an extension may do and records the hooks the preceding clauses have already named.

    1.16.1 The Extension Mechanism

    An extension may add types to 1.5, provided each is described by a Type Record of one of the kinds of Table 1. It may define the operations of 1.5.23 for a type it adds, and may declare operators for a type that does not define them (1.9.9). It may add syntax, subject to the constraint the whole proposal is under: the syntax must be an error in the current language. It may add library functions, overloaded by 1.10.3.

    An extension may not revise the type-checking framework of 1.2. In particular it may not add a kind to Table 1, may not change SameType or IsSubtype for a kind it did not introduce, and may not introduce an implicit conversion beyond those of Table 13.

    Note

    The last of these is the constraint worth stating explicitly, because it is the one an extension is most likely to want to break. A units extension wants Meter to become float32, a decimal extension wants a Number to become a decimal128, and a SIMD extension wants a scalar of a type other than a vector's lane type to broadcast into it. Each of these is available without an implicit conversion: the first is a metadata parameterization, which is a subtype of its base and so is subsumed rather than converted; the second is written; and the third is an operator the extension declares. The framework holds because every extension so far has been expressible within it, which is evidence that the four implicit cases are the right four rather than merely the ones that were listed first.

    1.16.2 The Hooks

    Table 39 lists the extensions the preceding clauses name and what each is relied on for. It is a map of the obligations this specification has incurred outward, not a specification of the extensions themselves.

    Note

    The extensions not listed, including composites, pattern matching, do expressions, the pipeline operator, serialization, structure of arrays, the regular expression types, Temporal, and the standard library, are specified in terms of the core and are relied on by nothing here. That is a claim about direction and not about importance: serialization is where a typed program meets a network, and it is built from the layout, the metadata hooks, and the where clauses this specification already gives, adding no rule any of them must accommodate. The one place the direction reverses is threading, whose heap sharing decides what a Type Object's identity means (40), which is why it alone among the outer extensions has a clause here.

    The dependency now runs in one direction without exception. The metadata parameterization that 1.2.3.1 once forward-referenced is core (1.5.20), as the refinement relation it shares with an enum's underlying type and a class's base always suggested it should be. What remains with the primitive metadata extension is the protocol's hook surface: the judgments beyond the branding default, and the conversion machinery.

    1.16.3 Coverage of the Design Documents

    Every document of the design has a disposition here: it is specified by clauses of this document, it is deferred to its own future clauses with a hook already named, or it is deferred outright, in which case whatever it adds must fit the mechanism above. The examples directory is a corpus this specification is checked against rather than a source of requirements.

    2 References and Borrowing

    A reference is a borrow: a handle to a storage location, a variable, an object property, or an array element, that reads and writes through to the original rather than to a copy. It is what lets a function mutate its caller's value and a loop write into an array in place. This clause specifies the borrowing forms of the design's references extension (Table 39): the ref argument and ref return, the ref parameter, the ref lexical binding and its rebinding, and the reference for-of loop. The ref type is already in the grammar; this clause adds the syntax of the borrowing forms and the runtime that the type describes.

    2.1 Syntax

    ref is a contextual keyword, not a reserved word, and every borrowing form claims it by one rule: ref is claimed only when the token that follows it, with no line terminator between, can begin the operand as written — an IdentifierReference or this for a RefExpression, whose operand is an expression, and a BindingIdentifier (an identifier, or yield or await where those are identifiers) for the binding forms, whose operand is a name. Everywhere else ref is the identifier it is today: f(ref) and f(ref, x) pass it, ref(x) calls it, ref[i] and ref.x read from it, ref = 1 assigns to it, and ref: labels a statement. The rule is what makes every addition below conservative: each new alternative derives only source text that is a Syntax Error in the base language.

    RefExpression[Yield, Await] : ref [no LineTerminator here] LeftHandSideExpression[?Yield, ?Await]

    The operand is a LeftHandSideExpression because a borrow names a place, and the claim rule restricts which tokens may begin it: ref a, ref a[i], ref o.x, and ref this.buffer are borrows, while ref (x) and ref [0] keep their base readings as a call and an element access of an identifier named ref. In argument position one further token is admitted, the pipeline topic %, not to make ref % mean anything but so that its refusal (39.3) carries its own diagnostic rather than surfacing as an unexplained token. A RefExpression appears in exactly two positions, an argument and a return; the rest of this clause gives each, and the binding forms, in turn.

    An argument may be a borrow. Argument is restated from 1.10.4 with the one added alternative; per 1.1 this block is the production's complete form.

    Argument[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ... AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] NamedArgument[?Yield, ?Await] RefExpression[?Yield, ?Await]

    A return may be a borrow. This is the first restatement of ReturnStatement.

    ReturnStatement[Yield, Await] : return ; return [no LineTerminator here] Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ; return [no LineTerminator here] RefExpression[?Yield, ?Await] ;

    return ref followed by a line terminator keeps its base meaning: the restriction inside RefExpression makes the new alternative unavailable, the Expression alternative derives the identifier, and automatic semicolon insertion completes the statement, exactly as it does today. return ref x derives only through the new alternative, since two adjacent identifiers have no expression reading.

    A lexical binding may be a borrow. LexicalBinding is restated from 1.4.4; the ref alternative requires its Initializer structurally, since an alias without a location to alias is nothing, and it joins neither the BindingPattern alternative, because the borrow binds one name to one location, nor the TypedInitializer alternative, because := infers a binding's type from a value and the initializer of a ref binding must denote a location.

    LexicalBinding[In, Yield, Await] : BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt Initializer[?In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypedInitializer[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] BindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] Initializer[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] ref [no LineTerminator here] BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt Initializer[?In, ?Yield, ?Await]

    It is a Syntax Error if the ref alternative of LexicalBinding is contained in the LexicalDeclaration of a ForStatement head.

    Note

    The per-iteration environment of a for statement copies each head binding by value into every iteration, which would silently decay the alias into a copy after the first. The form is refused rather than given that meaning; lifting the restriction awaits per-iteration semantics for a location binding, which no design document yet states.

    A mutable ref binding may be re-aimed by a statement of its own. This is the first restatement of Statement.

    Statement[Yield, Await, Return] : BlockStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] VariableStatement[?Yield, ?Await] EmptyStatement ExpressionStatement[?Yield, ?Await] IfStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] BreakableStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] ContinueStatement[?Yield, ?Await] BreakStatement[?Yield, ?Await] [+Return] ReturnStatement[?Yield, ?Await] WithStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] LabelledStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] ThrowStatement[?Yield, ?Await] TryStatement[?Yield, ?Await, ?Return] DebuggerStatement RefRebindingStatement[?Yield, ?Await] RefRebindingStatement[Yield, Await] : ref [no LineTerminator here] BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] = LeftHandSideExpression[?Yield, ?Await] ;

    The claim is the exact shape: after the same-line name, the next token must be =, and otherwise the identifier reading stands — ref = 1 assigns to a binding named ref, ref(x) calls one, and ref: labels a statement, all as today. The = itself may begin a new line, since ref b followed by anything but = has no reading in the base language either; an implementation that reads the name before deciding restores it on any other token. The production derives only strings an ExpressionStatement cannot, so no statement changes meaning.

    A reference for-of head marks its binding. ForDeclaration gains the marked alternative; the claim declines when the token after ref is of, so for (const ref of a) continues to bind an identifier named ref.

    ForDeclaration[Yield, Await] : LetOrConst ForBinding[?Yield, ?Await] LetOrConst ref [no LineTerminator here] ForBinding[?Yield, ?Await]

    It is a Syntax Error if the ref alternative's ForBinding is a BindingPattern. It is a Syntax Error if the ref alternative of ForDeclaration occurs in a for-in or for await alternative of ForInOfStatement: the borrow aliases an element slot, which the index-based for-of of 2.7 supplies, and which neither the property keys a for-in walks nor the values an async iterator yields can.

    A parameter's ref is already in the grammar (FormalParameter in 1.4.4, and the parameter lists of function types in 1.4.2.10); this clause adds its two Early Errors. It is a Syntax Error if a FormalParameter has ref and its BindingElement is a BindingPattern: the borrow binds one name to one location, and destructuring a borrow is the pattern's own (ref a) member form (2.2). It is a Syntax Error if a FormalParameter has ref and its BindingElement contains an Initializer: a default runs exactly when the caller supplied no argument, and a value the callee builds has no caller-side location to borrow, so the combination could never bind and is refused at the declaration rather than at the first defaulted call. The optional marker ? remains admitted, as the function type grammar already admits it; a call that omits an optional ref parameter fails the borrow at that call, a TypeError exception.

    An arrow function takes ref parameters through its covers. The parenthesized cover admits a ref parameter directly, refined exactly as 1.10.7 refines an annotated parameter, so (ref a: int32) => {} and the design's zip(a, b, (ref x, ref y) => { x = x + y; }) are covered; and through the async call cover a RefExpression argument refines to the same parameter, so async (ref a) => {} is the one form reached by the other road. A cover containing a ref parameter has no expression reading, so claiming it is arrow-only and conservative — (ref a) without a following => is a Syntax Error, as it is today. The Initializer Early Error above applies to the refined parameter as to a declared one.

    2.2 Typed Destructuring Members

    A nested annotation in a formal binding pattern contributes a binding obligation even when the formal has no whole-value annotation. Retain each obligation in its declaration's type and alias environment and apply specialization bindings before checking it. After ordinary named, positional, spread and rest argument mapping, check established property or iteration contributions at those member boundaries, recursively through defaults and nested patterns. A written whole-pattern default is independently checked against its nested annotations. This does not turn an object pattern into a closed object type or infer mutable iterator yields from indexed storage. Missing properties, getters, prototype fallback, iteration positions and collected rest shapes need their own proofs; unknown contributions remain dynamic. Existing conversion and borrowing rules apply.

    It is a type error for an object binding or assignment pattern to consume a participating source whose Static Type contains only null and undefined alternatives. Participation follows the operand-contract judgment of 1.9.7. Apply this source-eligibility judgment even to an empty pattern, and recursively to the selected contribution of each nested object pattern after an enclosing default or fallback. A property's default does not bypass RequireObjectCoercible on its container. A viable or unknown source alternative prevents the negative proof. Ordinary non-nullish primitive boxing, object-literal spread, borrowing permissions, reference decay and runtime liveness are unchanged; the checking pass reads no runtime reference. An unrelated annotation does not retime an ordinary JavaScript destructuring exception.

    A member of an object binding pattern may state the type of the binding it introduces, and may borrow the property rather than copy it. The annotation is written inside parentheses, because the position after a member's : is already taken: { a: uint8 } binds property a to a new name uint8, so an annotation cannot follow the colon. The parenthesized member leaves that colon free, so a member may be annotated and renamed at once.

    BindingProperty[Yield, Await] : SingleNameBinding[?Yield, ?Await] PropertyName[?Yield, ?Await] : BindingElement[?Yield, ?Await] ( refopt BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ) Initializer[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]opt ( refopt BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] ?opt TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ) : BindingElement[?Yield, ?Await]

    Without a rename the parenthesized name is both the property read and the binding introduced, so { (a: uint8) } binds a to the value of property a, enforced at that binding as an annotated declaration is (1.7). With a rename the parenthesized name is the property and the binding follows the colon, so { (a: uint8): b } reads property a and binds b. An Initializer supplies the value when the property is absent, as it does for any member.

    A member marked ? uses undefined as its missing-value sentinel, both for an absent property and for a present property whose value is undefined. Apply an Initializer first when that value is undefined. If the resulting value is undefined, bind it without enforcing the optional member's annotation; otherwise enforce the annotation normally. An optional member annotated with T therefore introduces a binding whose read type is T | undefined, including a renamed binding. A checked default known not to produce undefined makes the read type T. Check present contributions and defaults at their respective boundaries; the optional marker does not admit an incompatible non-undefined value. Ordinary narrowing may remove the undefined alternative. This rule does not admit optional reference bindings.

    An object rest may state the type of what it collects, { (a: uint8), ...rest: object }, which is an object type rather than a member type, as an array rest's annotation is the type of the array it collects rather than of an element. It is written without parentheses: the parentheses of a member exist because the position after a member's : is already taken, and a rest has no such collision.

    Object-rest collection produces a fresh ordinary, non-callable Object regardless of whether its source's Static Type is known. It is a type error if a rest annotation or an existing assignment destination is proved incompatible with that result category under the applicable boundary conversion rules. Unknown types and possible Object-compatible alternatives prevent that proof. The judgment does not manufacture a closed empty-object shape, restrict annotations to one Type Record kind, or infer enumerable own properties from structural membership alone. A collected property shape requires independently established copy facts; unknown exclusions and descriptor properties remain dynamic. Source coercibility, copying effects, reference decay and liveness are unchanged.

    An object binding or assignment pattern consumes known property-read contributions from typed arrays and tuples as it does declared structural members. Established count contracts and known position keys contribute at annotated destinations and the existing typed-parameter and participating-constant inference sites. Equivalent literal or known computed property keys agree; common known union contributions are joined. Unknown properties or alternatives retain the gradual judgment, and mutable unannotated bindings gain no permanent storage annotation from this rule. Property contribution extraction is distinct from iteration and does not use an overridden iterator to type an object-pattern read. The existing default, bounds, storage and reference-liveness rules are unchanged.

    A member marked ref borrows the property's location on the object being destructured, by the rule of 2.4.1, and binds its name to that location; reads and writes through the binding reach the property. It is a Syntax Error if such a member has an Initializer, for the reason a ref parameter may not have one (2.1): a default is a value the callee builds and has no location to borrow. It is a Syntax Error for such a member to be marked ?, and likewise for a ref parameter: the marker says the value may be absent, and a ref binds the location rather than the value, which is there whether or not the property is. A form that cannot honour what it declares is refused where it is written rather than at each use of it. An annotation on a ref member is checked against the referent and never converts it.

    A member of an object assignment pattern may be marked ref in the same parentheses, and then re-borrows: the named binding, which must already be a ref binding, is pointed at the location of the property on the object being destructured. ( ref r ) : x borrows the property x, and ( ref x ) without a rename borrows the property of the binding's own name. A target that is not a ref binding, and a value that is not an Object, are each a TypeError. This is the only destructuring form whose targets exist before it runs, which is what it is for: one borrow retargeted across the turns of a loop.

    An assignment member may not carry a type annotation. An annotation states the type of a binding the pattern introduces, and an assignment pattern introduces none; its targets already carry whatever type they were declared at, so an annotation here would be a second type for one target. A program that means to check a value writes is or :=.

    Note
