    The borrowed location belongs to the object, not to the caller's variable, so a function whose parameter is such a pattern takes an ordinary argument: g(o) suffices and g(ref o) is not required. ref o would state something different — that the callee may rewrite the caller's binding — and it could not reach the pattern in any case, since a parameter that is a BindingPattern consumes its argument as a value and a Reference Value decays there (2.3).

    2.3 Reference Values and the Absence of Identity

    A Reference Value is a value produced by a ref expression that holds a storage location: a Reference Record (in the sense of the base specification) whose base is an Environment Record for a variable or an Object for a property or an array element. A Reference Value is a primitive value in the sense that it is not an Object; nothing is allocated when one is created.

    A Reference Value has no observable identity. Every operation that reads a binding holding one dereferences to the value at the location, and a Reference Value that reaches any position consuming a value decays to the value at its location first. In consequence typeof, Reflect.typeOf, ===, and instanceof see the referenced value and never the reference, and a Reference Value cannot be stored in a binding that outlives its location, a property, an array, or a collection: the only bindings that hold one are the ref parameter and ref lexical binding below, which alias the location rather than store the reference. There is therefore no way to distinguish a reference from the value it refers to, which is what keeps it a location and an index rather than an object.

    Note 1

    Decay is where the absence of identity is realized. A reference reaches a value position at an ordinary call boundary, an operand of an operator, an argument to a non-ref parameter, or a conversion, and at each the value at the location is taken. The reference is observable only through the aliasing behaviour of the binding that holds it, not as a value in its own right, so no reflected type and no equality can name it.

    Decay is total, and the channels through which a Reference Value could otherwise be observed are these. A Reference Value decays when it becomes the base of a property access or of an optional chain, when it is the callee of a call, when it is gathered by a rest parameter, when it is the argument of a parameter that is a BindingPattern, when the arguments object of a call is created, and on entry to any built-in function. It decays at an ordinary call's return, so a call whose callee returned a borrow yields the referent's value at every position but the location-consuming ones, which 2.4 defers. The rule for each is the same rule: the position takes a value, so the value at the location is what it gets.

    A ref parameter makes a parameter list not simple, as a default value or a destructuring pattern does. The arguments object of a function with a ref parameter is therefore unmapped, and its elements hold the decayed values of the arguments; neither a read of arguments nor a store into it reaches the caller's location, and strict and sloppy code agree on this. The ref parameter itself is unaffected: it takes its location from the argument list, which the arguments object is a separate view of.

    Note 2

    Naming the channels is not a list of special cases but the closure of one rule over the places a value can go. Two of them are worth stating for what they exclude. A rest parameter gathers into an array, and an array cannot hold a reference, so a borrow forwarded through a variadic wrapper arrives as a value — the alternative, refusing the call, would make (...args) => f(...args) hostile to a borrow for no safety gained, since the forwarded reference could not have been written into the array anyway. And the built-in boundary is what makes the reflective call paths decay channels without naming them one by one: Function.prototype.call, apply, bind, and Reflect.apply are built-ins, so a Reference Value handed to one decays on entry, and the list such a function forwards, or stores as bound arguments, holds values.

    2.4 Reference Parameters and Arguments

    A ref argument f(ref e) evaluates e to a storage location and passes a Reference Value holding it. The location is obtained by RequireBorrowableReference (2.4.1), so it is a TypeError exception if e does not denote a location: a value, a private member, a super property, and a property of a primitive have no location a borrow could alias. A ref parameter binds its name to the location the argument carries, so a read in the callee reads through to the referent and a write in the callee writes through to it. It is a TypeError exception if the argument to a ref parameter is not a Reference Value, since a plain value has no location to borrow, and a Reference Value passed to a parameter that is not ref decays to its referent.

    At final binding of every reference rest, including a trailing rest reached through an unknown callable, check the actual run with ReferenceSequenceAdmits (1.10.4.3) before initializing its binding or entering the function body. Use the resolved collected annotation, retain positional tuple and nested-rest contracts and stated array extents, and require each supplied location's invariant type and current referent to satisfy its receiving contract without conversion. Omitted tuple defaults contribute no location. Failure is a TypeError exception; no partially admitted reference run is published. Recheck liveness after earlier parameter initializers and other intervening effects, even if distribution previously succeeded. The same sequence judgment applies statically where the run and its determining contracts are known; unknown iteration counts or unresolved inputs retain their existing runtime boundary.

    A type annotation on a ref parameter is checked against the referent and never converts it. The referent is of the annotated type or a TypeError exception is thrown; the value at the caller's location is not rewritten, because a borrow that converted its referent would silently change storage it does not own. A ref parameter's binding is not re-enforced by the parameter type pass of 1.7 for the same reason.

    Where the borrowed location's type is statically known, ref e contributes a reference Type Record whose [[Target]] is that location type. A return ref e is checked against the declared return type before the caller's value-context decay; reference compatibility uses the existing invariant target relation. At an ordinary value parameter the explicit reference argument instead contributes its referent type, after the specified decay, to argument checking, overload resolution and generic inference. Unknown location types retain runtime checks. These judgments read no location and do not alter borrow permission or reference liveness.

    Reference-argument judgments apply wherever the static argument binding proves the receiving parameter. A spread of unknown count does not suppress the check on a preceding required positional argument whose destination is independent of that count. It is a type error if such an argument does not supply a reference, or if its known referent type differs from the parameter's type. A mapping that depends on an optional parameter, a non-final rest, or a possible object spread binding names is deferred where those facts are unknown; indexed array storage alone does not establish an iterator's protocol or count (1.14.8).

    A function may return a reference with return ref e, evaluated as a ref argument is. The operand may denote storage of any lifetime, including a binding of the returning function itself: an environment is an object like any other and stays alive while anything refers to it, so a reference to a local outlives the frame that made it, exactly as a closure over that local does. At an ordinary call the returned reference decays to its referent, so a caller that consumes the call as a value observes the referent. A caller may instead consume it as a location, which is what makes first(a)++ write through to the element; 2.8 gives those positions.

    2.4.1 RequireBorrowableReference ( V )

    The abstract operation RequireBorrowableReference takes argument V (an ECMAScript language value or a Reference Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Reference Record or a throw completion. It returns V if V denotes a storage location a borrow may alias, and throws a TypeError exception otherwise. Every borrowing form — the ref argument, the ref return, and the ref binding — obtains its location through it, so all of them refuse the same operands. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If V is not a Reference Record, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. If IsUnresolvableReference(V) is true, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. If IsPrivateReference(V) is true, throw a TypeError exception.
    4. If IsSuperReference(V) is true, throw a TypeError exception.
    5. If IsPropertyReference(V) is true and V.[[Base]] is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    6. If V denotes a bit-field member of a laid-out aggregate (9.3), throw a TypeError exception.
    7. Return V.

    It is a type error when the syntax or Static Type of an operand to RequireBorrowableReference proves that it cannot denote a borrowable location: a non-location value, a private member, a super property, a property with a known primitive base, or a known bit-field member. This judgment applies to reference bindings, rebinding, reference arguments, and reference returns. A call with a known return type must return a reference; an unknown call or property base retains the runtime checks. A property is not rejected merely because its existence or descriptor is unknown.

    For a property selected from a union receiver or a statically established finite set of keys, the bit-field judgment rejects the borrow when every selected storage alternative is proved to be a bit-field without a byte address. A mixture containing an eligible or unknown alternative retains the runtime borrow check. Bit-field provenance comes from the selected class storage declaration, with inheritance and generic arguments resolved; the same small integer type on an ordinary structural property does not establish packed storage. This proof does not change reference liveness or create a temporary location.

    What counts as a storage location is decided at the Reference Record and not at the property behind it. A reference to an object property is borrowable whether the property is a data property, an accessor property, absent, or answered by a Proxy: reads through the borrow perform an ordinary Get and writes an ordinary Set, so a borrow of an accessor calls the getter and the setter, a borrow of an absent property reads undefined and creates the property when written, and a borrow of a Proxy-trapped property triggers the traps in the order those operations already specify. This is the only line that can be held, because the shape of a property is not stable for the life of a borrow — a data property can be redefined as an accessor, or deleted, between the borrow and the write — so a rule that admitted only data properties would have to re-check at every use and would still be wrong at the moment of redefinition.

    Note

    The exclusions are the cases where no location exists rather than the cases where one is inconvenient. A private member and a super property are not property references over an ordinary base; a property of a primitive is a property of a fresh wrapper that the write would discard; a bit-field is a run of bits within a byte, which is addressable only by reading and writing the containing scalar and so cannot be aliased as a location of its own. An unresolvable reference is a name that is not bound, and borrowing one would create the binding a plain read refuses.

    2.5 Reference Bindings and Rebinding

    For a RefRebindingStatement, it is a type error if lexical name resolution establishes that the destination is an ordinary binding or an immutable reference binding. A let ref binding and a reference parameter are rebindable; a const ref binding is not. The classification belongs to the nearest declaration, including binding-pattern and iteration declarations, and is independent of the referent's Static Type or its narrowing. A closure observes that same lexical declaration, and an ordinary var redeclaration does not change an existing reference parameter's binding kind. Where name resolution remains unknown or may be intercepted by an object Environment Record, the existing runtime rebinding check decides. This check neither converts an ordinary binding into a reference nor changes the source-location, assignability, storage-boundary or liveness requirements.

    A ref lexical binding aliases a storage location for its scope. let ref b = e and const ref b = e evaluate e to a location by RequireBorrowableReference (2.4.1), the same rule a ref argument applies, and bind b to it; it is a TypeError exception if e does not denote a location, and it is a Syntax Error for a ref binding to omit its initializer. A read of b reads through to the location. A let ref binding may be written through, so b = v writes v to the location, and may be rebound; a const ref binding may not be written through, so b = v is the ordinary assignment-to-constant TypeError exception, while a write to a member of the referent is permitted as for any const. An annotation on a ref binding is checked against the referent without conversion, as for a ref parameter.

    Preparing this binding's contract for a captured contribution uses the dependency and declaration-environment rules of 1.6.2.10. Availability of the contract does not establish runtime initialization or a current storage origin.

    The Static Type of a ref binding is its annotation where it has one, and otherwise the Static Type of the location its initializer denotes: a read of b reads through to that location, so it has the location's type, and a write through b meets that location's boundary. It is not widened, a borrow aliasing the location rather than copying out of it, so a store the location refuses is refused through the alias; where the location's type is not known the binding has none and the checks are the run time's. This is what a ref parameter, a ref return type and the binding of a reference for loop already state for themselves, said once for the form that writes no type of its own. Reassigning a let ref binding with ref b = e rebinds it: b is redirected to the location e denotes, and the location it previously aliased is not written. A binding's type is fixed at its declaration, so the rebinding must be to a location of that type: it is a type error if the Static Type of the location e denotes is not assignable to the Static Type of b, and where either is unknown the judgment is the run time's. Re-typing the binding at each rebinding is not the rule, since that would make a binding's type depend on the control flow that reached it, which no other binding of this specification does. It is a TypeError exception to apply the rebinding form to a name that is not a rebindable ref binding.

    Note

    Assignability on rebinding permits a wider alias to refer to a narrower location. In let a: uint8 | string = 1; let b: uint8 = 2; let ref r = a; ref r = b;, the binding r retains uint8 | string. A subsequent r = "s" is assignable to that view, but the write crosses b's uint8 boundary and throws a TypeError exception. The alias's type alone is not proof that the actual location accepts a store, so it does not justify eliding that boundary. This does not change the invariance of a reference Type Record or the separate rules for ref parameters, and every access remains subject to 2.10.

    2.6 Known Write Permission through a Reference Alias

    A reference binding's value type and the write permission of the location it currently denotes are separate facts. It is a type error to write through an alias where its known origin proves that the selected member is readonly and the actual write lacks that member's initializer or declaring-constructor permission. This includes simple, compound and update assignments and destructuring and iteration targets that store back. Reading the alias is permitted, and readonly remains shallow.

    Local alias chains preserve known origin restrictions. A reference to a reference binding follows that lexical binding's current location; rebinding that binding therefore changes the location reached through such an alias. Rebinding replaces the relevant origin without changing the alias's fixed declared value type. A control-flow join retains known readonly alternatives, and loop back edges participate in the judgment. A captured binding that can be redirected must not be judged using a stale definition-time origin. Where its origin cannot be established, runtime checks remain necessary.

    Constructor permission is evaluated at the write, not captured at the borrow. A callback invoked by a constructor does not gain its permission. Borrowability is unchanged: a readonly member still denotes a location, and a reference argument or return is not rejected merely because an unknown recipient might write. This rule introduces no public readonly-reference type, callee effect inference, new allocation pin, or exception to reference liveness. It does not permit eliding the actual location's storage or liveness checks.

    2.7 Reference Iteration

    Reference iteration requires array storage or the SoA storage specified by 2.9. It is a type error if the Static Type of the source proves that it has neither: in particular, a String, Set, Map, or generator is not eligible merely because it is iterable. A union is rejected by this rule only if every possible member is ineligible. An unknown source retains the runtime eligibility check. This judgment is distinct from the ordinary iterable check and introduces no user-defined reference-iterator protocol.

    A for ( LetOrConst ref p of e ) loop binds p to a reference to each element of the array e in turn, so the body writes into the array in place. The iteration is index-based: it reads the length of e once, evaluates the body once for each index below that length with p bound to a reference to the element at that index, and does not go through %Symbol.iterator%, so patching the iterator protocol does not affect it and no result object is allocated. A let ref element binding may be written through and rebound and a const ref element binding may not, as for a ref lexical binding. It is a TypeError exception if e has neither array nor SoA storage.

    The length read at the start of the loop is pinned for its duration. An operation that changes the length of the array while a reference into it is live, push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, or a store to length, is a TypeError exception, which a ref loop makes easy to reach since it holds a reference across the whole iteration. The rule is the loop half of 2.10, which gives the rule for a reference held outside a loop. A user-defined iterator that yields references is not supported and belongs to the design's extension (Table 39); a reference into an SoA column set is 2.9. The callback idiom needs no support of its own: a container that passes ref a[i] to a callback with a ref parameter composes from the argument and parameter forms above, which is how the design's zip writes through both arrays.

    Note

    The liveness rules are the whole of what the borrow needs, in place of a borrow checker with lifetimes. A reference cannot dangle in the Rust sense because the storage it points into is reachable from it and a garbage-collected object stays alive as long as anything refers to it; what remains to prevent is a reference into storage that moves, which 2.10 handles, and a reference escaping its location, which the absence of identity (2.3) already forecloses. Both are local checks and neither needs a lifetime system. This specification checks the length rule at run time; the design also permits a static rejection wherever the array's type makes the offending operation visible, which an implementation may add as a diagnostic without changing the meaning of any program this clause accepts.

    2.8 Location-Consuming Contexts

    A location-consuming context is a position that consumes the storage location an expression denotes rather than the value at it. A call that returns a reference does not decay in such a position, so the reference reaches the operation and the operation reads and writes through it. There are three, and each is a position in which the base language already refuses a call outright, so no existing program changes meaning.

    The first is the operand of ++ or --. The Early Error of the base language refuses a call there, because a call has no assignment target; that error is relaxed for a CallExpression whose Static Type is a reference type, and for such an operand the update reads the referent, computes the new value as it otherwise would, and stores it back through the same location. The design's element accessor is written this way:

    function first(a) { return ref a[0]; }
first(a)++; // Writes through to a[0]

    The second is a borrow source: the operand of a ref argument, the initializer of a ref lexical binding, or the source of a RefRebindingStatement. Each re-borrows the location a call returned, as in g(ref first(a)), let ref p = first(a), or ref p = first(a). The location the callee returned is passed on unchanged, including its existing liveness obligations; nothing is copied and no second borrow of a different location is created. Parentheses around the source preserve this context. Its referent type supplies the binding or rebinding type judgment, rather than treating the reference itself as a stored value.

    It is a type error for the operand of ++ or --, a borrow source as described above, or an assignment target to be a call whose Static Type is not a reference type. Where the callee's return type is not known statically the check is deferred to run time, per 1.2.8: it is a TypeError exception if the call's result in such a position is not a Reference Value.

    The third is an assignment target. first(a) = v stores through the location the call returned, and so does every form that assigns to a target: a compound or logical assignment, which reads the referent and stores the result back through the same location; an element or property of a destructuring assignment, at any depth; and the target of a for-in or for-of head. These all follow from one static semantic rather than from a rule stated per position.

    Where an explicitly typed union of callable alternatives supplies only reference returns, distinguish the possible locations from their value read type. A read joins the referent types. A store must satisfy the destination contract of every reachable known location after narrowing, with the ordinary conversion and fresh-literal judgment applied separately to each. A single reference whose target type is itself a union retains that union as one destination; it is not split into alternative locations. Local reference aliases and known rebinding/flow joins preserve these write obligations separately from the alias's declared read type. Captured rebinding and unknown origins follow the existing provenance-invalidation rules; no fact changes the runtime liveness of a reference. This applies at every store context listed above, including an update's write-back. An unknown callee or explicit any boundary retains runtime enforcement. Known non-reference alternatives remain invalid in a location-consuming context, and the decay rule for heterogeneous inferred reference returns in 1.6.2 is unchanged.

    The static semantic AssignmentTargetType of a CallExpression is ~invalid~ in the base language, which is what refuses a call as a target. It is instead ~simple~ when the CallExpression's Static Type is a reference type, and remains ~invalid~ where that Static Type is known and is not one. Where the Static Type is not known — the callee is reached through an unannotated binding, or its signature is otherwise unavailable — AssignmentTargetType is ~simple~ and the check is the deferred run-time one of the paragraph above, which is imprecise rather than wrong: a call that does not yield a Reference Value is a TypeError at the assignment rather than an Early Error at the source text. Every Early Error that governs an assignment target is phrased in terms of AssignmentTargetType, so each of the positions above inherits the rule without being named in it, and a call whose callee is KNOWN not to return a reference stays refused exactly where it is today.

    Note 1

    Which of the two the program gets therefore depends on what the checker can see of the callee, and that boundary moves as more of a program is typed: a callee whose return type is unavailable defers to run time, and the same call is refused before the program runs once that type is known. This is the ordinary gradual-typing direction — more type information turns a run-time failure into an earlier one, never a working program into a broken one — and it is why the two rules must be stated as one rule with a known and an unknown case rather than as a rule and an exception.

     Note 2

    A returned reference still decays everywhere this clause does not name, so first(a).x = v writes through the referent's property rather than the element's location, and let v = first(a) copies. What remains unspecified is a reference yielded by a user-defined iterator or callback (Table 39).

    2.9 References into a Structure of Arrays

    A borrow of an element of an SoA (13) denotes a column set and an index rather than a property slot. The element's fields are stored one column each, so the element has no single address a reference could hold, and the location is the storage together with the position within it. Reads and writes through such a reference go to the columns at that index.

    This is a location like any other, and every borrowing form produces it: ref s[i] as an argument or a return, and let ref or const ref as a binding, all yield the same reference, and all of them obtain it through RequireBorrowableReference (2.4.1). A ref parameter therefore accepts a borrow of an SoA element exactly as it accepts a borrow of an array element, which is what lets one function serve either storage: a parameter declared with a reference type receives a borrow without its caller stating which layout produced it.

    Reading through the reference yields the element, whose field accesses reach the columns; writing a whole value through it stores each of that value's fields into its column at the index. Decay is different from reading, and the difference is observable here: a Reference Value that reaches a position consuming a value decays (2.3) to the gathered element, the same detached copy the expression s[i] produces, so no aliasing survives a boundary that takes a value.

    Note

    For an ordinary reference these two coincide, since the referent of a variable or a property is just the value stored there, and nothing distinguishes reading a borrow from decaying one. An SoA element separates them: the element that field accesses must reach is a live position within the columns, while the value a boundary consumes must be a copy detached from them. The rule is stated in terms of what the position does — a position that goes on to read or write through the result dereferences, and a position that consumes a value decays — and it is only the second that copies.

    The liveness rules of 2.10 apply to such a reference however it was taken. The SoA is the container in this specification that relocates, so a borrow into one is invalidated when growth moves the columns, and a use through an invalidated borrow is a TypeError exception; a borrow of an element that has since been removed is invalidated in the same way; and within a reference for-of over an SoA, an operation that changes its length is a TypeError exception at that operation.

    2.10 Reference Liveness

    A reference is valid while the storage it aliases is where it was borrowed from. Two rules make that so, and they apply at different moments: the loop rule refuses the offending operation, and the relocation rule refuses the later use.

    The loop rule is the one above (2.7). Within a reference for-of, an operation that changes the length of the iterated container throws a TypeError exception at that operation. It applies to every container a reference loop can iterate, and it is structural: the loop holds a reference for its whole duration, so the length is pinned for its whole duration, and no accounting of individual references is needed to know that one is live.

    The relocation rule governs a reference held outside such a loop — a ref binding, or a ref parameter whose caller borrowed an element. A reference into storage that can be relocated is invalidated when that storage is relocated, and a read or a write through an invalidated reference throws a TypeError exception. A reference to an element of a container is likewise invalidated if that element is removed, since a reference names an element and not merely an address. Relocation is what an implementation does when a growable container outgrows its allocation, and the operations that can cause it include the ones that add elements and the capacity operations reserve and withCapacity.

    Note 1

    An implementation is not required to move an allocation that it need not move, but a program may not depend on its staying put: the rule is stated so that an implementation backing a [ ] . < T > with a packed allocation is conforming without having to track which references are live. That is the same reason the loop rule is structural rather than counted — the alternative would make growth depend on discovering every reference into the container.

     Note 2

    The rules divide this way because they can detect different things. A length comparison can see push but never reserve, which changes an allocation's capacity while leaving its length alone; a relocation test sees exactly the event that invalidates a reference, whatever operation caused it. Together they leave no gap: within a loop the length change is refused before anything moves, and outside one a reference that survives a move is caught at its next use. A reserve performed inside a reference loop is not itself a length change, so the loop rule does not fire, and the relocation rule then refuses the loop's own reference at its next use.

    Storage that cannot relocate needs no rule beyond the loop rule. A reference to a property of an ordinary object, including an element of an ordinary Array, aliases that property; properties do not move, so such a reference remains valid, and it continues to denote the same property even if the values around it are rearranged. a.shift() while a reference to a[0] is live is not an error and leaves that reference denoting a[0], whose value the shift has changed — the same thing the expression a[0] has always meant.

    Note 3

    The alternative design, counting live borrows and refusing a resize while the count is above zero, was not chosen. A reference reachable only from a suspended generator frame that is never resumed would leave a count that no execution decrements, so a container could become permanently unresizable through no fault of any running code. Both rules here are computed from state the container already keeps — its length, and whether its allocation has moved — and neither requires that a reference be discoverable from the container.

    The SoA of 13 is the storage for which these rules are presently normative in full, since it is the container in this specification that relocates: a reference into an SoA is a column set and an index (9), growth beyond the current capacity moves every column, and a reference taken before such a growth is invalidated by it. A growable [ ] . < T > is governed by the same rule. It has a backing allocation whose capacity is distinct from its length, reported by capacity and grown by reserve; growth beyond the current capacity, whether by reserve or by adding elements, relocates the allocation and invalidates every reference into the array, so a use through one is a TypeError exception. Reserving the needed capacity before taking a reference is how a program keeps its references valid across growth.

    2.11 Capacity Operations

    A growable [ ] . < T > has a backing allocation whose capacity is distinct from its length (2.10). Four operations concern it, and each is defined here on an array with an element type; on an array without one they are absent.

    2.11.1 get Array.prototype.capacity

    Array.prototype.capacity is an accessor property whose set accessor function is undefined. Its get accessor function performs the following steps:

    1. Let O be ? ToObject(this value).
    2. If O does not have a [[TypedElement]] internal slot, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. If O has a [[TypedExtent]] internal slot, return 𝔽(O.[[TypedExtent]])return the value of the index type whose mathematical value is O.[[TypedExtent]].
    4. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(O).
    5. If O has a [[TypedCapacity]] internal slot, return 𝔽(max(O.[[TypedCapacity]], len))return the value of the index type whose mathematical value is max(O.[[TypedCapacity]], len).
    6. Return 𝔽(len)Return the value of the index type whose mathematical value is len.
     Note

    An accessor and not a method: as a method, a.capacity answered the function object rather than the count, so if (a.capacity > 1000) was silently true and never reported the mistake. A fixed extent returns the extent itself and not the length, since such an array's storage holds exactly that many elements whether or not they have been written.

    The three returns produce a value of the index type and not 𝔽 of a count. They read 𝔽 while the dfn said the counts a container reports are of that type, and the dfn is the side that is right: it names capacity among the counts explicitly, and its closing sentence is that naming the type once is "what keeps capacity comparable with length without a conversion — the invariant that a capacity is at least a length is unstateable if the two are not one type". An algorithm returning 𝔽 makes exactly that comparison a conversion, so the clause contradicted the reason the type exists. sec-collection-size records the same distinction for size and points here.

    Unconditional, unlike size. A keyed collection reports a Number where it carries no type arguments, because an untyped Map is an ordinary Map and 1.15.7 requires that nothing about it change. capacity has no such form: it is reached only through a [[TypedElement]] slot, which this accessor requires before it reports anything, so every array that has a capacity at all is a typed one and there is no untyped reading to preserve.

    2.11.2 ToIndexType ( value )

    The abstract operation ToIndexType takes argument value (an ECMAScript language value) and returns either a normal completion containing a mathematical value, or a throw completion. It checks that value is a count and answers its mathematical value. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If value is not a value of the index type, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. Return the mathematical value of value.
     Note

    A COUNT passed to one of these operations is checked as a count rather than coerced like an ordinary argument. length and capacity READ at the index type, so a count that could be written as a String and silently converted would make the operations that accept a count disagree with the ones that report one — a.reserve("4") would be accepted while a.length could never be a String.

    This is stricter than ToLength, which these clauses previously specified: it refuses rather than converts.

    2.11.3 Array.prototype.reserve ( n )

    This method grows the backing allocation to hold at least n elements without changing the length. It performs the following steps:

    1. Let O be ? ToObject(this value).
    2. If O does not have a [[TypedElement]] internal slot, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Let wanted be ? ToIndexType(n).
    4. If O has a [[TypedExtent]] internal slot, then
      1. If wanted > O.[[TypedExtent]], throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Return undefined.
    5. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(O).
    6. Let capacity be max(O.[[TypedCapacity]], len), where a [[TypedCapacity]] that is absent is 0.
    7. If wanted ≤ capacity, return undefined.
    8. If wanted > 2*64 - 1, throw a *RangeError exception.
    9. Set O.[[TypedCapacity]] to wanted.
    10. Set O.[[TypedGeneration]] to O.[[TypedGeneration]] + 1.
    11. Return undefined.
     Note

    A request for room the array already has is a no-op and not an error, so a caller need not know the array's capacity to ask about it — which is why the comparison starts at the length rather than at zero. Growth increments [[TypedGeneration]], and that is what invalidates a reference into the array; a reserve that does not grow must not increment it, or a borrow into storage that has not moved would be refused.

    The RangeError is the range of the index type, not a statement about the element type. It is NOT the maximum length of an ordinary Array: that range is allocatable and usable, an array type not being bounded by ArrayCreate's limit. The check is on the growth path only, so a reserve within an existing capacity is unaffected.

    An implementation unable to reach a count the index type holds reports it as unimplemented rather than raising here. A RangeError says the LANGUAGE forbids the value; an implementation limit is a different statement, and collapsing the two would make a host's inability read as a rule of the language.

    2.11.4 Array.prototype.shrinkToFit ( )

    This method releases the backing allocation down to the length. It performs the following steps:

    1. Let O be ? ToObject(this value).
    2. If O does not have a [[TypedElement]] internal slot, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(O).
    4. Let capacity be max(O.[[TypedCapacity]], len), where a [[TypedCapacity]] that is absent is 0.
    5. If capacity ≤ len, return undefined.
    6. Set O.[[TypedCapacity]] to len.
    7. Set O.[[TypedGeneration]] to O.[[TypedGeneration]] + 1.
    8. Return undefined.
     Note

    It is the mirror of reserve and takes its shape from it: asking to release room the array does not have is a no-op rather than an error, so a caller need not know the capacity in order to ask. A fixed [N] . < T > needs no case of its own — its capacity is its extent and its length is its extent, so it is always already at fit and the step above returns.

    Where it does release, the allocation RELOCATES, so it invalidates every live reference into the array including references to elements that remain (2.10). That is what distinguishes it from shortening the length: removing an element invalidates the reference to the element removed and leaves the rest readable, because that storage has not moved, while releasing capacity moves all of it. The distinction is worth stating because the two read as the same operation from outside — both make an array smaller — and they differ in exactly the way the liveness rules are about.

    This is a BINDING release and not a request an implementation may decline, unlike the similarly named operation in some languages. An optional relocation would make an optional invalidation, and a program correct on one implementation would raise on another; the liveness rules can only describe an operation whose effect on references is fixed.

    2.11.5 withCapacity ( n )

    A call established to select this intrinsic has the index type as its parameter contract and the growable array type [].< T > as its result. A statically established invalid argument or result boundary is a type error, using the same literal admission and 2.11.2 rules as the runtime boundary. The proof follows 1.4.2.8: preserve the selected function's original identity and account for prior mutation and argument effects. A property name alone is insufficient. Unknown calls, accessors, escapes or future invocations that can replace a dependency prevent this proof; no getter or user function is executed to establish it. The property remains replaceable, and a runtime guard cannot justify an early error. Capacity is allocation state, not a fixed extent or a reference-liveness guarantee.

    The array type constructor of a growable [ ] . < T > has a withCapacity method that constructs an empty array of that type with room for n elements. It performs the following steps:

    1. Let T be the element type of the array type whose constructor is this value.
    2. Let wanted be ? ToIndexType(n).
    3. If wanted > 2*64 - 1, throw a *RangeError exception.
    4. Let A be ! ArrayCreate(0).
    5. Set A.[[TypedElement]] to T.
    6. Set A.[[TypedCapacity]] to wanted.
    7. Return A.
     Note

    It reserves rather than fills: the result has length 0, so a zero-filled array of a known length is a fixed [N] . < T > and not this. The array it returns is growable, the capacity being a property of the allocation and not of the type.

    3 Typed Regular Expressions

    A regular expression literal is a compile-time constant whose pattern an engine already parses before the program runs. This clause puts that parse into the type system: the Static Type (1.2.6) of a regular expression literal records the number and kind of its capture groups and the names of its named groups. This is the core of the design's regular expression types (Table 39); the fuller surface it enables, the typed match result and the group-name checking on it, the typed String methods, the flag-dependent result shapes, pattern composition, and string narrowing by pattern, is that extension's to complete and is specified in terms of this core.

    The Static Type of a regular expression literal is a nominal Type Record whose [[LibraryName]] is "RegExp" and whose [[Arguments]] are two Type Records, the Captures and the Groups, derived from the pattern:

    • Captures is a tuple Type Record with one element per capturing group, in the order the groups' opening parentheses appear, each element the type of that capture. Where the pattern has no capturing group, Captures is the empty tuple, as it is for every other pattern: a tuple with one element per group, of which there are none.
    • Groups is an object Type Record with one property per named group, its key the group's name and its type the type of that capture. A name that occurs on more than one capturing group, which the pattern grammar admits only across alternatives, contributes one property.
    • The type of a capture is the "string" primitive where every path through the pattern that produces a match enters the group exactly once, and the union of "string" with the undefined type otherwise. A group is in the second case when it is quantified with a minimum of zero, when it lies within a disjunction of more than one alternative, or when it lies within a lookahead or lookbehind, and when any group that encloses it is.

    A non-capturing group, a lookaround, and a backreference add no capture and contribute nothing to Captures or Groups. Because the type is a parameterization of the "RegExp" library type, it is invariant in Captures and Groups (1.2.3.1): a RegExp.<Captures, Groups> annotation whose arguments differ from a literal's inferred shape is a type error. A bare RegExp, the raw library type, is the supertype of every such parameterization, so it holds a literal of any shape while a written parameterization does not hold a value of another.

    Note 1
    Note 2

    An optional capture is string | undefined and not string | void. The two are not interchangeable here: void is the type with NO VALUES, "written to say that a result must not be depended on", while undefined "has the one value undefined and a binding may hold it" (1.5.17). A capture that no matching path entered holds undefined — /(a)?/.exec("")[1] is undefined, not absent — so a union with void has no arm that value belongs to, and the capture would have a declared type nothing could read it into.

    An earlier draft said void. It is the same slip this specification records elsewhere, where resolving undefined to void "made undefined unassignable to undefined, which took the whole T | undefined optional idiom with it" — and an optional capture is that idiom.

    The analysis is syntactic and reads only the pattern, which is why it costs nothing an engine does not already spend: the same parse that reports an invalid pattern yields the capture count, the group names, and the nesting that decides optionality. The rule for optionality is the design's, that a group is required exactly when every matching path enters it once; a group behind ?, *, or {0,n}, a group in one arm of an alternation whose other arm a match may take instead, and a group inside a lookaround are the cases a match may complete without entering, and each widens the capture with the void type.

    The empty-capture case is an empty tuple, which is what RegExp.<[], {}> names: a bare [] denotes the empty TUPLE in this grammar, an array being spelled [].<T>. An earlier draft made it the empty ARRAY type, which was correct when written: [] denoted the dynamic array then, and was reassigned to the empty tuple afterwards. The reassignment did not reach this clause, so the choice made to let RegExp.<[], {}> name a no-capture literal became the thing that refused it. Captures is a tuple in every case, and the no-capture case is the tuple with no elements rather than a case of its own. A pattern with captures is a tuple, so its arity is exact and a capture-count mismatch is caught. The flag-dependent result shapes, in particular the indices a d flag adds and the match overload a g flag selects, are part of the deferred match-result surface, so the inferred type carries the two arguments the annotation forms in common use write and not a third for the flags.

    4 Generics

    A generic declaration introduces parameters that a later application binds to types or values, and each distinct application is a distinct type with its own Type Object and its own specialized body. The core relies on this clause in three places already stated: the deferred applications of 1.2.7.2 carry the parameter Type Records this clause substitutes, the computed constraints of 1.4.3.4 bind parameters through the ordering this clause defines, and the invariance step of 1.2.3.1 is relaxed by the variance this clause declares. Named and spread arguments, and variadic parameters, are specified here (4.3, 4.4); the grammar of specialization lists and captures, and the kind of every parameter, are specified here (1.4.3.2, 1.4.3.3), and callable selection and specialized overload contracts are specified in 1.4.3.2.2. Replacement selection for class, alias, and interface families remains an extension hook (Table 39).

    4.1 Parameters as Types and as Values

    A generic parameter is a parameter Type Record whose [[Declaration]] is its TypeParameter. A type parameter, one whose domain is type (1.4.3.3), denotes that Record in a type position and, in an expression position, the Type Object bound to it, exactly as a type name does. A value parameter, one whose domain is a value domain, is the value generic parameter of the design: its argument is a value of the named type rather than a type, and this specification binds it to the literal type of that value (1.5.19) with the value recoverable as that type's one value. The literal-type binding is primitive and the value is its view, the decision 1.4.3.4 records: a body that reads V where a value is required, as 2 ** V, reads the [[Value]] of the literal type, and a body that reads V where a type is required, as Reflect.typeOf(V), reads the type itself.

    A generic declaration's type parameters are in scope, lexically, for its signature and body, including every function and class the body contains. Resolving an IdentifierReference in that scope reaches a type parameter after every binding of a scope nested in the body, the body's own top level and its parameter list being unable to bind the name (1.4.3.1), and before every binding of the environment that encloses the declaration, and so before the built-in type names of 1.5.27, which are consulted only when the scope chain is exhausted. A parameter named after a predefined type, uint32: type, therefore shadows that type in the body as it does in the signature, and let T outside function f<T: type>() does not reach its body. For a class the scope is its class scope, where the class binding is.

    Arguments to a computed type's builder are expressions and use this same lexical resolution and value view. A bare IdentifierReference to a value parameter reads its admitted value, including its declared numeric domain; a type parameter reads its Type Object even when that Type Object denotes a literal type. Parenthesizing an argument does not change which binding or view it reads. A value pack uses its specified array view. A nearer ordinary binding shadows an enclosing generic parameter; a generic parameter in its declaration's signature shadows an outer ordinary binding. Apply these rules when a constraint or default is evaluated as well as when the function body is evaluated. Resolving an argument does not initialize a captured ordinary binding or establish reference liveness.

    Note

    Two applications name one specialization when their arguments are pairwise the same: a type argument under SameType, and a value argument under SameValue, which is the identity the literal type already has, so A.<0> and A.<-0> are distinct and A.<NaN> is usable, following from identity rather than as special cases. A reference value cannot be an argument, since specialization identity would then turn on object identity; the permitted value types are the primitive value types the design lists.

    4.2 Constraint and Argument Environments

    Applying a generic signature uses two distinct source environments. The written arguments belong to the application; the domains, bounds, defaults and where clauses belong to the declaration. A returned function or an instantiated member retains the enclosing substitutions of its signature. Determine the obligations of each application as follows:

    1. Resolve each written type argument, including a named argument or spread operand, in the lexical and generic environments of that argument's source position. Assign the resulting arguments to the applied declaration's parameters by 4.3. The name of a named argument selects a parameter; it does not change the environment of the argument's Type.
    2. Resolve each parameter's effective constraint in its declaration environment. Retain the identities and bindings of free parameters captured from enclosing declarations or supplied by an instantiated class or interface. Apply the bindings established for this application in the order required by 1.4.3.4, preserving the existing rules for F-bounds and forward reads. The applied signature's own parameters remain distinct from enclosing parameters and from parameters of its caller.
    3. If the signature already has a completed description of that effective constraint, apply the remaining substitutions to that description. A description is reusable only for the same declaring environment and captured bindings. Re-reading its Parse Node in the caller's environment is not an alternative resolution rule. Retain the source and its declaration environment for a constraint whose computation is still deferred; a missing result does not discharge the obligation.
    4. Judge each supplied, inferred or defaulted binding against the resulting constraint by the existing admission rules, including the rules for value parameters, literal conversion and variadic collections. Use the same captured constraint when a pack's element bound participates in argument distribution. A statically established refusal is a type error at the application, including an application in an uncalled body. It is not postponed until invocation merely because the signature was returned by another function or obtained through a member.
    5. Resolve an omitted parameter's default and the declaration's where clauses in their original declaration environments under the applicable captured and preceding bindings. Neither publishing a signature nor reflecting it evaluates a default or executes a deferred constraint prematurely. A default supplied at its prescribed application is subject to the same constraint as an explicit argument. Existing compile-time evaluability, initialization and evaluation-limit rules still apply.
    6. When runtime inference is required because an argument's Static Type is any, that static lack of information is not an explicit binding of the generic parameter to the Type Object any. Infer from the actual argument under the existing runtime rules and enforce the constraint. A written type argument any remains an explicit argument and is judged by the existing gradual admission rule; this clause adds no prohibition on it.
    7. Keep distinct applications and captured function values independent. Completing a constraint for one application does not replace the declaration's symbolic constraint, change a different application, initialize a captured binding or prove a reference live. A failed application supplies no bindings to a subsequent application or to its caller.

    Callable admission uses the effective constraint descriptions of both signatures under their respective declaring environments and captured bindings. Before a required comparison, complete any constraint description whose determining inputs are available and whose value that comparison requires, subject to the existing evaluability and evaluation-limit rules. A missing description of a written constraint is not an absent constraint or the any type. The signature's own unbound parameters remain opaque: this preparation does not apply the signature, choose its type arguments or evaluate an unused parameter default. A source still requiring unavailable inputs retains its obligation under the existing deferred-computation rules.

    Apply 1.10.2.3 to the resulting descriptions, including its pairing of own binders and contravariant constraint comparison. This requirement applies to published callable returns and runtime callable admission through any, as well as to written callable positions. Completing a bound for one context does not replace the declaration's symbolic description or alter another activation. An implementation may share a completed answer only with the same determining inputs; it must not use the last concrete bound observed for that Parse Node. Abrupt completion or exhausted evaluation supplies no successful admission, and restoration supplies no initialization or reference-liveness fact.

    Instantiating a function value's published result first restores the free parameter bindings of that function value's creating environment, distinguished by parameter declaration and activation, and then applies the bindings of that function's own parameters when the function is applied. An own parameter shadows ordinary lookup of its name; it does not replace a retained capture of an enclosing declaration with the same name. Retain such captures through further returned signatures even when every visible enclosing parameter name is shadowed. Reflection restores the captured environment without applying the function's own binders or consulting an unrelated caller's generic bindings.

    Use that same instantiated publication for return admission and for the contextual result of a concise function body. A retained helper continues to denote its original closure and environment. Do not rebind the helper to make the source agree with an incorrectly instantiated target. Independent activations retain independent bindings, and failed admission does not alter another function value's captured context. These substitutions neither evaluate a bypassed default nor establish initialization or reference liveness.

    A selected method case retains the bindings of the receiver's instantiation of its declaring class. Apply those bindings to its parameter and result descriptions along with the selected case's own bindings, preserving the identities of the case's own parameters and captures. Selection does not restore an unspecialized declaring-class result after member lookup has established the receiver's arguments. An inferred binding initialized by that result is subject to its resulting contract, not to a fresh lookup of the declaring class's parameter names at the binding site.

    At a boundary with an instantiated class result, membership follows IsSubtype from the value's runtime class through its instantiated base types, preserving each base declaration and its arguments. A derived value is not refused merely because its most-derived declaration differs from the result's declaration. Nor does matching a declaration's name or members erase a mismatch in its arguments. This membership judgment does not discharge the separate value-storage restriction of 1.11.4: a subclass that adds storage cannot occupy a base value type position. RequireType applies that restriction to a runtime value reaching an annotated binding, parameter or return through any, just as it does to a field or array element. Reference-class targets keep their existing polymorphic admission and reference-liveness requirements.

    A default description follows the same free-parameter substitution as a constraint description. Substitute enclosing bindings wherever the default description refers to them, including within arrays, tuples and callable signatures, while preserving binders introduced inside the description. A default that itself denotes a generic function type remains generic. A default for a higher-kinded parameter denotes a constructor as a written argument for that parameter does; naming a generic declaration there does not apply it to an empty argument List. At the later application that uses the default, substitute the preceding bindings of that application and validate the resulting argument. Do not execute a computed type merely to obtain a description; retain an unresolved default and its declaring environment until its prescribed use. Supplying an explicit argument bypasses that parameter's default computation. This applies also to a computed type nested within a composite default.

    A recursively encountered default source supplies no completed result merely because its description is already in progress. Describing or publishing a generic declaration, including a class, does not apply its defaults. A default is required only when its parameter remains unbound at the default step of the applicable binding operation. If description is suspended, retain that application's source, parameter identities, preceding bindings and captured declaration environment. Neither a missing description nor repeated source syntax is a missing default, an implicit any binding or proof of a semantic cycle. A required closed default is evaluated under 1.2.7.4, including recursive argument binding, and its completed result is checked against its constraint and every dependent consumer. Exhaustion supplies no completed result and follows the containing checking boundary's existing failure rule. Restoration of the enclosing environment and bindings establishes no initialization or reference-liveness fact.

    Note

    For type R<T: type = R.<> > = T, declaring R alone or using R.<string> does not require the default. An application requiring R.<> cannot complete argument binding and exhausts the evaluation budget. In contrast, type R<T: type = R.<string>> = T has the finite default string. An implementation may suspend speculative description on source-node re-entry, provided that marker is not used as a completed query key or a source-level cycle verdict and the required application is still discharged.

    Determine whether a type source depends on an unbound parameter by its lexical binding dependencies. A declaration-local alias does not remove such a dependency: follow that alias's declaration and, for an applied generic alias, its own argument bindings. Repeat through dependent aliases while respecting binder identity and the existing recursive-type rules. An unbound dependency is retained for the application that can supply it; it is not a closed type computation with a missing global name. Once the application supplies the required bindings, discharge its constraint normally. Alias indirection does not weaken admission or postpone a statically established refusal.

    For a required constraint or omitted-argument default that remains computed, determine its inputs by lexical declaration identity, including dependencies reached through a helper function or alias. A helper retains its own declaration environment: a parameter of the applied signature with the same name does not replace the helper's captured parameter. Enclosing substitutions propagate through intermediate generic signatures even when an intermediate signature introduces a same-named parameter.

    A generic alias's parameter list does not hide its enclosing dependencies. Retain the free bindings reached through its body, constraints and defaults, while distinguishing the alias's own parameter declarations from captured declarations. Follow further aliases and helpers under the same rule. Retaining a dependency does not evaluate it: bind the alias's own arguments in order, evaluate only defaults required by that application, and keep captured bindings attached to the originating signature when a completed result reaches a consumer.

    1. Retain the source, its declaring environment, the captured parameter bindings and the preceding bindings required by the computation. For a value parameter, use the value admitted by its declared domain, with the conversion required by BindTypeArguments; its numeric domain is not replaced with Number merely because the source argument was a bare numeric literal.
    2. When those inputs are available at the required checking boundary, apply the compile-time evaluability judgment to the source and its transitive dependencies and evaluate the required source under those bindings. Do not enter an enclosing ordinary function body, execute its statements or initialize one of its local bindings in order to manufacture a captured input. Imported inputs retain the initialization and failure ordering of 1.3.8.
    3. An unresolved input retains an obligation; it is not a completed result of any. An abrupt required computation is a type error at this boundary under 1.2.8, and the evaluation-limit rules still take precedence when the computation exhausts its budget. A program-level try statement cannot catch a failure that must be reported before body evaluation.
    4. After a required computation completes normally, apply its resulting type to the owning application and repeat any dependent admission or default-completion judgment that lacked that result. A completed result may be reused only when the source, declaring environment and all determining bindings agree, including captured bindings and bindings established by this application. Distinct parameter declarations remain distinct even if their names agree.

    These requirements do not prescribe cache data structures, synthesized environments or a particular compiler pass. They do not introduce eager evaluation of unused defaults, deepen the admission of any, or establish initialization or reference liveness from the successful computation of a type.

    4.3 BindTypeArguments ( params, args, declaration )

    The abstract operation BindTypeArguments takes arguments params (a List of Type Parameter Records), args (a List of TypeArgument Parse Nodes), and declaration (a Parse Node) and returns either a normal completion containing a List of Records with fields [[Declaration]] (a TypeParameter Parse Node) and [[Value]] (a Type Record), or a throw completion. It binds an application's arguments to a declaration's type parameters — positional, named, spread, and variadic alike — and is the one operation every application site performs: a type reference, an expression-position application, new, a heritage clause, an explicit call, and the explicit half of a call whose remaining parameters are inferred. Its result is the bindings that SubstituteType consumes, and the identity of the specialization.

    Type aliases and interfaces perform this binding before expansion or canonicalization, just as classes and functions do. Parameter domains and bounds are obligations of the application even when the body does not use the parameter. Named arguments, defaults, packs and dependent bounds use the same ordered bindings. A statically established failure is a type error; an unresolved application retains its obligation until specialization supplies the missing information.

    Expansion or canonicalization of an alias's result does not discharge an unresolved obligation of that alias application. Retain the applied declaration, argument assignment, supplied arguments whose descriptions remain pending, and the declaring environment's captured substitutions independently of the expanded result. When the determining inputs become available, validate the retained application under the existing checking-boundary rules, including when an enclosing generic application supplies those inputs, the alias body omits a constrained parameter, or another alias expands to the same result. A statically closed invalid application in a published callable constraint is refused at that boundary even if the callable is never invoked. An input belonging to an unapplied inner generic declaration remains pending.

    Retained application descriptions remain associated with their producer's source declarations when another Script or Module specializes that producer. A consumer's bindings do not replace the producer's descriptions or the creating context of another application. Retaining an obligation does not create a distinct nominal type for a transparent alias, demand a bypassed default, execute an ordinary function body during type preparation, initialize a binding, or establish reference liveness.

    During checking, distinguish a parameter with no supplied argument from a parameter assigned an argument whose description is not yet available. The latter remains supplied and pending: do not select its default, infer a replacement solely because its description is missing, or report it as an omitted argument. Retain its source and argument-to-parameter assignment until the required inputs become available, then complete and validate that argument under the existing checking-boundary rules. An abrupt supplied argument is not replaced by the parameter's default.

    If an unresolved spread or argument-dependent distribution prevents establishing the supplied runs, retain the pending assignment; an empty set of completed bindings is not evidence of empty runs. A resolved empty spread follows the ordinary omission rules. Defaults for parameters established to be omitted remain subject to their own demand and input-availability rules, including dependencies on preceding bindings. Retaining dependencies reached through an alias's parameter list does not itself select or evaluate any default. None of these checking states is a completed binding of any, initialization, or evidence of reference liveness.

    For a function application, select defaults only after the applicable inference rungs. Retain each selected default's obligation with that application, its argument assignment, preceding bindings and declaration context, even if an unrelated supplied argument is still open or the callable's result does not mention the defaulted parameter. Availability depends on the selected default's determining inputs, not on all arguments of the application being closed. When enclosing specialization supplies a determining input, complete the retained obligation at the existing required checking boundary. An independent closed default is not suppressed by another parameter's pending description; a default that requires an unavailable input remains pending. Retaining this obligation does not evaluate a bypassed default or execute the ordinary enclosing or applied function body during preparation.

    Completing an application's defaulted bindings does not discharge value-argument checks that depended on those bindings. Retain the dependent consumer with its source-position inputs and argument-to-parameter assignment, and apply the ordinary admission judgment when the receiving contract is determined, including when an enclosing specialization supplies the determining inputs. Substitute the caller's source inputs separately from the applied declaration's bindings. Preserve contextual expression judgments, including literal propagation, fresh object and array creation, optional admission and rest positions; an unadapted source shape is not a substitute for such a judgment. A statically determined invalid consumer is refused at the existing required checking boundary even when it occurs in an unused caller. Distinct applications do not replace one another's source descriptions. This completion executes no ordinary body, establishes no initialization or reference-liveness fact, and is not by itself evidence that a runtime conversion can be elided.

    1. Interpret the type-source judgments below in the argument and declaration environments required by 4.2, retaining the applied signature's captured substitutions.
    2. Let entries be a new empty List.
    3. For each TypeArgument a of args, do
      1. If a is TypeArgument : ... Type , then
        1. Let t be ? the Type Record the Type of a denotes.
        2. If t.[[Kind]] is tuple, let elements be a List of the [[Type]] fields of t.[[Elements]], in order.
        3. Else if t is an array Type Record whose extent is stated, let elements be a List of that many copies of t.[[Element]].
        4. Else, throw a TypeError exception.
        5. For each element e of elements, append the Record { [[Name]]: none, [[Type]]: e, [[Node]]: none } to entries.
      2. Else if a is TypeArgument : BindingIdentifier : Type , then
        1. Append the Record { [[Name]]: the StringValue of BindingIdentifier, [[Type]]: none, [[Node]]: the Type of a } to entries.
      3. Else,
        1. Append the Record { [[Name]]: none, [[Type]]: none, [[Node]]: a } to entries.
    4. Let firstNamed be the least integer idx such that entries[idx].[[Name]] is not none, or the number of elements of entries if there is no such integer.
    5. Let positional be a List of the first firstNamed elements of entries.
    6. Let named be a new empty List.
    7. Let i be firstNamed.
    8. Repeat, while i < the number of elements of entries,
      1. Let e be entries[i].
      2. If e.[[Name]] is none, throw a TypeError exception.
      3. If params contains no element whose [[Name]] is e.[[Name]], throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Let p be the element of params whose [[Name]] is e.[[Name]].
      5. If named contains a Record whose [[Parameter]] is p, throw a TypeError exception.
      6. Let run be « e ».
      7. Set i to i + 1.
      8. If p.[[Variadic]] is true, then
        1. Repeat, while i < the number of elements of entries and entries[i].[[Name]] is none,
          1. Append entries[i] to run.
          2. Set i to i + 1.
      9. Append the Record { [[Parameter]]: p, [[Run]]: run } to named.
    9. Let slots be a new empty List.
    10. For each element p of params, do
      1. If p.[[Variadic]] is true, append a rest slot to slots.
      2. Else if p.[[Default]] is none and named contains no Record whose [[Parameter]] is p, append a fixed slot to slots.
      3. Else, append an optional slot to slots.
    11. Let prefix be the elements of params before the first whose [[Variadic]] is true, or all of params if there is none.
    12. Let admits be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (index, which) that captures named, positional, and prefix and performs the following steps when called:
      1. Let p be the parameter which stands for.
      2. If p.[[Variadic]] is false, return true.
      3. If named contains a Record whose [[Parameter]] is p, return false.
      4. If EffectiveConstraint(p) is none, return true.
      5. If EffectiveConstraint(p) reads any parameter not in prefix, return true.
      6. Let bound be the Type Record EffectiveConstraint(p) denotes, evaluated over the bindings of the elements of prefix to the corresponding leading elements of positional, as the binding loop below binds them.
      7. If bound is not an array or tuple Type Record, return true.
      8. Let element be the element type of bound (1.4.4).
      9. Let v be the Type Record positional[index] denotes.
      10. Return IsSubtype(v, element, a new empty List).
    13. Let counts be SequenceAssignment(slots, the number of elements of positional, admits).
    14. If counts is unmatched, throw a TypeError exception.
    15. Let bindings be a new empty List.
    16. Let cursor be 0.
    17. For each integer j such that 0 ≤ j < the number of elements of params, in ascending order, do
      1. Let p be params[j].
      2. Let supplied be a List of the counts[j] elements of positional beginning at index cursor.
      3. Set cursor to cursor + counts[j].
      4. If named contains a Record whose [[Parameter]] is p, then
        1. Let r be that Record.
        2. If supplied is not empty, throw a TypeError exception.
        3. Set supplied to r.[[Run]].
      5. If EffectiveConstraint(p) is none, let constraint be none; otherwise let constraint be ? the Type Record or Family Constraint Record EffectiveConstraint(p) denotes, evaluated over bindings (1.4.3.4).
      6. If p.[[Variadic]] is false, then
        1. If supplied is empty, then
          1. If p.[[Default]] is none, throw a TypeError exception.
          2. Let v be ? the Type Record the Type of p.[[Default]] denotes, evaluated over bindings.
        2. Else,
          1. Let v be ? the Type Record supplied[0] denotes: its [[Type]] where that is not none, and the type its [[Node]] denotes otherwise.
        3. If p.[[Kind]] is value and v.[[Kind]] is literal, set v to the literal type of v.[[Value]] converted to constraint as 1.4.3.4 binds a literal argument; if the conversion fails, throw a TypeError exception.
        4. Else if p.[[Kind]] is value and v.[[Kind]] is not parameter, throw a TypeError exception.
      7. Else,
        1. If supplied is empty and p.[[Default]] is not none, then
          1. Let v be ? the Type Record the Type of p.[[Default]] denotes, evaluated over bindings.
          2. If v.[[Kind]] is not tuple, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Else,
          1. Let elements be a new empty List.
          2. For each element e of supplied, do
            1. Let ev be ? the Type Record e denotes.
            2. If p.[[Kind]] is value and ev.[[Kind]] is literal and constraint is not none, set ev to the literal type of ev.[[Value]] converted to the element type of constraint; if the conversion fails, throw a TypeError exception.
            3. Else if p.[[Kind]] is value and ev.[[Kind]] is neither literal nor parameter, throw a TypeError exception.
            4. Append ev to elements.
          3. Let v be the tuple Type Record whose [[Elements]] are Records with [[Type]] the elements of elements, in order, none of them a rest and none carrying an [[Initial]].
      8. If constraint is not none and ? SatisfiesTypeConstraint(v, constraint) is false, throw a TypeError exception.
      9. Append the Record { [[Declaration]]: p.[[Declaration]], [[Value]]: v } to bindings.
    18. Assert: cursor is the number of elements of positional.
    19. For each where clause of declaration, evaluate it over bindings as 4.9 specifies; if the result is false, throw a TypeError exception.
    20. Return bindings.
     Note 1

    A value parameter takes a value (4.1): its argument is a literal type, converted to the domain, or a value parameter of an enclosing declaration, bound later. Any other argument denotes a type, and is refused before the constraint is consulted, since a type such as uint8 supplied for N: uint8 would otherwise pass SatisfiesTypeConstraint by being assignable to the domain it was meant to be a value of.

     Note 2

    An ordinary concrete constraint is checked with IsAssignable and not IsSubtype, which is the one place a gradual rule outranks a structural one. any is "the type of every value ... the type of a binding that carries no annotation" (1.5.15), and it is a subtype of nothing, so a subtype test would refuse every call a binding without an annotation makes to a constrained generic. That would make a constraint a wall between typed and untyped code rather than a claim about types, and untyped code calling typed code is the case this proposal is built to keep working. An argument of any other type is held to the constraint exactly as a subtype test would hold it.

     Note 3

    The positional half is the rest-parameter rule verbatim: 1.10.4.2 is the operation the design's "greedy, giving back to satisfy the parameters after" names for values, and a pack is a rest slot in it. A run ends where the next argument fails the pack's element bound; a non-variadic slot admits by arity alone, its constraint checked once bound, which keeps the split independent of what fixed parameters would accept — one rule for values and for types, and the same diagnostics. A parameter supplied by name is satisfied by its name, so for the split its slot is optional: id.<T: uint8> has no positional argument for T and is not unmatched. A pack whose bound reads a parameter declared at or after the first pack cannot help split, so it admits everything for the split and is checked in full once the assignment is fixed, the conservatism argument binding already applies to a parameter type that mentions a not-yet-bound type parameter. A literal is a type too: an unconstrained type parameter admits 0 positionally, so in <T: type, ...I: [].<uint32>> applied .<0, 1> the fixed T takes the literal type 0; the result is deterministic, and writing T: uint8 says what was meant.

    Two applications whose bindings are pairwise the same — SameType for a type, SameValue for a value — name one specialization whatever their spelling, positional, named, or spread; identity is the ordered bindings and never the text. Where the applied declaration is known statically, the refusals this operation performs for a positional argument after a named one, an unknown name, and a parameter supplied twice are the type errors of 1.4.2.2; a name written twice in one list is a Syntax Error there and never reaches this operation. The operation restates them for an application resolved at run time.

    4.4 Variadic Parameters

    A variadic parameter (1.4.3) binds a tuple Type Record: the elements are the Type Records its arguments denote, in order, and the tuple's length is the number of arguments.
