It is a type error if its TypeParameterConstraint does not resolve to an array or tuple type, the rule 1.4.4 states for a rest parameter's annotation; it is a type error if its TypeParameterDefault does not resolve to a tuple type; and it is a type error if two consecutive variadic parameters have constraints either of whose element type is the any type, which completes the early error of 1.4.3.1 for the bounds that need resolving. Two consecutive variadic parameters of one element type are admitted: the first takes what both admit, and the parameter after them says where the run must stop, as it does for two rest parameters of one type.

    Within the specialized body, a variadic value parameter — one whose [[Kind]] is value — reads as a frozen fixed-extent array, one per specialization, whose elements are the values of its literal types: I.length, I[k] for a constant k, and the array methods over them are compile-time expressions (1.2.7), and the same array answers every read, so I === I across calls of one specialization. A variadic type parameter reads as the Type Object of its tuple, as any type parameter reads as its type. This is the rule of 4.1 applied pointwise: a value parameter reads as its value, so a tuple of them reads as their array. A where clause over a variadic parameter (4.9) is checked once per specialization, every element being a constant.

    A variadic parameter is bound from a call's arguments wherever a scalar parameter is: through a rest parameter typed by it, from constant arguments as every value generic argument is; through a parameter of its tuple type, from one tuple; through a written tuple pattern, pairUp<T: type, ...Rest: [].<type>>(p: [T, ...Rest]), by the assignment BindTypeArguments performs on its positional half; through a callback's signature, structurally; and through a builder that stands between it and the arguments only by that builder's declared inverse (15.3), never by search. The ladder is that of 15 without exception. A spread argument, f(...xs), binds a variadic parameter only where the length of xs is statically known, as the type-argument spread of 1.4.2.2 requires. Where a parameter's binding depends on the variadic parameter's length — N: uint32 = I.length — it is a computed default of 1.4.3.4 and evaluates once the pack is bound.

    Note

    Transforming a pack is not a mapped-type sub-language. A value pack is an array in the body, so I.map(i => i * 2) inside a compile-time function transforms it; a type pack restructures by spread in a tuple type, [...Ts, T], and transforms per element through a builder (1.4.2.4) written once and named. The one modifier that distributes rather than maps is ref on a rest parameter (1.4.2.10), which is what lets a callback take a pack directly: (e: Entity, ref ...refs: Cs) => void. Most inversions are better avoided than declared: a declaration that binds the pack as what the caller passes, all<...Ps: [].<type> extends [].<PromiseLike>>(...ps: Ps): Promise.<awaitedAll(Ps)>, needs only the structural rung and yields the types the inverted spelling would, types being structural.

    Three rules follow the binding. A spread ARGUMENT, tup(...xs), binds a pack only where the spread's Static Type has a static length — a tuple, an array of stated extent, or a value typed by a pack, as ...xs for xs: Ts is when a pack forwards — and a spread of a dynamic array into a rest typed by a pack is a type error, the call-site twin of the spread type argument's rule (1.4.2.2): the check is static, since the run time would bind from whatever values it found. A parameter the call's explicit type arguments bind keeps that binding through inference, and the computed constraints and defaults of the parameters after it evaluate over it, so d.<0, 1, 2>() for d<...I: [].<uint32>, M: uint32 = I.length> binds M to 3. And typeof applied to a parameter's name reads what the name resolves to in the body: a Type Object for a type parameter, the value for a value parameter, the array for a value pack.

    A specialization chain that lengthens a tuple at each step — the reader of the design's binary packet example, read<T: type>(): Reader.<[...Ts, T]> — is finite per call site and costs what any specialization costs. A declaration that applies itself to a longer pack recurses without end and is stopped by the evaluation budget (1.2.7.4), as a recursive type alias is: a diagnostic naming the declaration, never an implementation's stack.

    4.5 Specialization as a Value

    A generic function applied in expression position, f.<uint8>, denotes a function object: the specialization of f at the bindings BindTypeArguments (4.3) yields for its arguments. Specializations are interned per function object and ordered bindings, so f.<uint8> === f.<uint8>, f.<uint8> === f.<T: uint8>, a Map keyed on one round-trips, and arr.map(f.<uint8>) runs the specialized body; two spellings of one binding list are one value because identity is the bindings and not the text. A specialization's where clauses are evaluated when it is created, as the last step of BindTypeArguments, and never per call. A specialization declares no type parameters, so applying type arguments to one is a type error. It does not capture a receiver: obj.m.<uint8> is the specialization of the function obj.m denotes, receiver-independent, and a call obj.m.<uint8>(x) supplies obj as this exactly as obj.m(x) does. The bare name keeps the generic signature: Reflect.typeOf(f) is <T: type>(x: T) => T, and Reflect.typeOf(f.<uint8>) is (uint8) => uint8.

    Determine the Static Type of a stored application from its completed bindings, including defaults evaluated in declaration order in the parameter environment of 4.2. A required checking-time default that has not yet completed is a dependency of the application and of judgments consuming its signature; it is neither the any type nor a missing explicit argument. Complete that dependency and reconsider its consumers at the prescribed checking boundary. This includes a := declaration whose initializer is the application. A later call uses the completed non-generic signature and does not infer the already bound parameters again. The requirements for available inputs, abrupt completion and evaluation limits remain those of the required default evaluation.

    When a binding is established to hold that application, retain the dependency for judgments consuming the value through that binding or an established alias. Apply the ordinary binding identity, stability, conversion and effect rules when establishing this relationship; a dependency of an initializer is not by itself evidence that its result is the same callable. Retaining the relationship does not publish an incomplete callable Static Type or restore the original generic signature as a new inference candidate. Reconsider dependent argument admission using the original application's completed bindings and each argument's source context, as required by 4.3.

    The producing application's enclosing generic bindings are identified by their declarations. A same-spelled parameter introduced by a consumer does not replace those inputs. The original application retains ownership of its default evaluation; storing or aliasing its result does not select defaults anew. These requirements execute no ordinary function body during checking, initialize no value binding, and supply no independent evidence of reference liveness.

    For argument binding, a specialization's own parameter list is the specialized function's list with its completed bindings applied: names, optionality, rest parameters and reference permissions are retained. In the absence of a separately declared callable type in view, named and object-spread arguments use that list and its completed parameter types under 1.10.4. A separately declared callable type in view retains the precedence given there, including its names and initial values. Reading the specialization's call metadata does not evaluate parameter initializers or select type arguments again. A skipped ordinary parameter is left undefined for the original function's initializer, which executes in its original environment at the ordinary call-time point.

    An implementation forwarding a specialization call to its original function does not introduce an additional value-consuming boundary for reference arguments. The original function's parameter binding retains the ordinary reference checks and value decay; actual calls through value-consuming built-ins retain their existing behaviour. This forwarding does not capture a receiver, change specialization identity or where-clause timing, or establish reference liveness.

    Note

    A call written with type arguments, f.<uint8>(x), creates or finds the specialization and calls it; finding one is a lookup keyed on the bindings, which is the cost of an interned record and not of a call. The design's swizzle.<0, 1>() and the reflection API's getReflection.<Reflect.Class, T>() are this form. Nothing here is new to a type parameter in a type position: a class application A.<uint8> has been a distinct type with its own Type Object throughout, and a function application is the same specialization with a function object as its value.

    4.6 Crossing a Boundary with a Generic Function

    A generic function that crosses into a binding of a concrete function type is specialized at the crossing: the bindings are those the instantiation step of 1.10.2.3 infers, the value that crosses is the specialization at them (4.5), its where clauses are checked there, and every call through the binding is a direct call of one body, so the crossing moves the decision to the assignment and costs the call nothing. A generic function that crosses into a binding of a generic function type crosses as itself. A call through such a binding, m.<uint8>(x), selects the specialization of whichever function the binding holds, by that function's identity and the call's bindings, and a call that infers its type arguments infers them against the held function's signature. This is the one place a specialization is selected by a callee not known where the call is written; the checks remain compiled away, and what is dynamic is the callee, which is dynamic at every indirect call already.

    For a crossing from one generic signature to one concrete signature, retain the bindings inferred by signature instantiation. Bind them against the held function's own declaration and materialize the same interned specialization as the equivalent explicit application. Perform its declaration checks before publishing the converted value. Evaluate specialization-time declaration expressions in that function's declaration environment, realm, private environment and captured generic context, not in the receiving caller's environment. This applies equally when the function was reached through any. The specialization captures no receiver.

    Compatibility and materialization are distinct operations. A successful IsOfType or signature relation does not itself create a specialization or run its where clauses; a receiving operation must use the converted value even when a compatibility check can be elided. The callable view's parameter names and defaults continue to govern calls through that view without changing specialization identity. The completed signature retains its declared narrowing guarantees with the same substitution. Existing reference modes and liveness requirements remain in force, and an abrupt crossing does not publish a replacement into its destination.

    For a union receiving a generic callable, retain the first compatible member selected in canonical order by the successful membership judgment. If it is a concrete callable contract, materialize at that contract; if it is generic, retain the generic value. Several compatible members do not form a combined callable contract. An abrupt declaration check after selection propagates before publication and does not cause selection to continue at another member. Retain the selected member as local admission evidence rather than repeating membership: unsuccessful alternatives contribute no selection, and a constituent property's selection is not a selection for its enclosing value. Check elision preserves this choice and its required materialization. A callable view with one non-nullish member retains that member's parameter names and defaults when invoked after nullish alternatives have been excluded; this does not combine multiple callable alternatives into an overload group or make a nullable value statically callable without the required proof.

    Note

    The cost is that of an indirect call together with a lookup keyed on callee and bindings, the dispatch C# performs for a generic virtual method, and it is paid only at calls through a binding of generic function type. The common case — a generic function handed to a slot that wants a concrete signature, arr.map(id) — pays nothing beyond the assignment. An implementation may cache the lookup at the call site as it caches any indirect call's target.

    4.7 SubstituteType ( t, bindings )

    The abstract operation SubstituteType takes arguments t (a Type Record) and bindings (a List of Records each with a [[Declaration]] and a [[Value]]) and returns a Type Record. It replaces the generic parameters bound by bindings throughout t and evaluates any deferred application thereby closed, the operation full specialization performs at each distinct application. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t.[[Kind]] is parameter, then
      1. For each Record b of bindings, do
        1. If b.[[Declaration]] is t.[[Declaration]], return b.[[Value]].
      2. If t has a [[Constraint]] field containing a Type Record, then
        1. Let constraint be SubstituteType(t.[[Constraint]], bindings).
        2. Return a Type Record with the same fields as t, except that [[Constraint]] is constraint.
      3. Return t.
    2. If t.[[Kind]] is deferred, then
      1. Let args be a new empty List.
      2. For each element a of t.[[Operands]], do
        1. If a is a Type Record, append SubstituteType(a, bindings) to args.
        2. Else, append a to args.
      3. If some element of args is a Type Record with a parameter within it, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: t.[[Operator]], [[Operands]]: args }.
      4. If t.[[Operator]] is keyof, return KeyTypesOf(args[0]).
      5. If t.[[Operator]] is indexed, return IndexedTypeOf(args[0], args[1]).
      6. Return the [[TypeRecord]] of the Type Object that results from evaluating the deferred application of t.[[Operator]] to args by EvaluateBuilderCall, which is a normal completion because args is now closed.
    3. Let u be a Type Record with the same fields as t, except that every Type Record reachable from t through its fields and the elements of any List or structured Record those fields hold, without descending into a nested deferred or parameter, is replaced by the Type Record that substituting bindings into it yields.
    4. Return CanonicalizeType(u).

    The [[Declaration]] identities in bindings determine substitution throughout a nested signature. An enclosing application supplies no binding for an inner signature's own parameter, even if the names are equal. A bound parameter's replacement is returned directly, without recursively applying the same bindings to the replacement. For an unbound parameter, substitution may change its effective constraint but preserves its declaration identity. Traverse effective constraint descriptions and the signature's parameter, declared and published result, receiver and narrowing records consistently. Retain unevaluated constraint and default Parse Nodes in their declaring environments; substituting their captured inputs does not evaluate them before the application that requires them. Preserve recursive record graphs when traversing these fields: revisiting the same record under the same bindings reuses its substituted record rather than unfolding the graph.

    Note

    Substitution and evaluation are one pass: a deferred application becomes evaluable exactly when substitution has closed every parameter it read, at which point 1.2.7.3 runs under the budget and memo already specified, so a builder used at two instantiations evaluates twice under two distinct memo keys and interns each result. A value generic contributes its literal type where a type is substituted and that type's value where the body computes, which is the one mechanism seen from two sides. Where substitution leaves a parameter in place, in the body of a still-generic outer declaration, the result is itself generic and specializes when the outer one does. A tuple element written with ... whose [[Type]] substitutes to a tuple Type Record is spliced element-wise into the containing tuple, so [...Ts, T] under Ts bound to [uint8, string] is [uint8, string, T] and not a tuple holding a tuple; CanonicalizeType performs the same splice, so the two spellings intern as one record.

    4.8 Constructing a Generic Class

    "The class is the type a construction yields" (1.11.2); for a generic class, the specialization is. A construction new C Arguments where C evaluates to the constructor of a generic class declaration, a target-typed construction new . Arguments whose contextual type is an instantiation of one (1.4.6), and a Reflect.construct whose target is such a constructor all construct a SPECIALIZATION of the declaration, never the declaration itself: its parameters bind, in order and left to right, by the ladder below, and the construction proceeds as new C.<…> Arguments would at those bindings. The declaration's own constructor has no body that can run, since its parameters are bound in no frame, and a bare construction that produced an instance of it produced one whose typed fields checked nothing.

    A generic function call also checks completeness after its explicit, contextual, value-argument and default inference steps, including a call with no value arguments. A required parameter that these steps provably leave unbound is a type error naming that parameter. Unknown argument contributions or an open specialization are not proof of a missing binding, and another viable overload remains eligible. No implicit any binding is invented.

    A parameter binds, taking the first source that fixes it:

    1. an EXPLICIT argument, by 4.3, where the construction writes TypeArguments;
    2. the CONTEXTUAL type of the construction (1.6.5), where that type is an instantiation of the same declaration, or a union one of whose members is: each argument of that instantiation binds the parameter in its position, an argument written any binding nothing. A binding so made is fixed before the value arguments are looked at and is treated exactly as an explicit one, so the arguments are then checked against it: const b: Box.<uint8> = new Box(1) binds T to uint8 and reads the literal 1 at uint8, and const b: Box.<uint8> = new Box("s") is a type error at the argument;
    3. INFERENCE from the value arguments, through the constructor's parameters as a call to a generic function infers through its parameters (1.4.3.4, 15): new Box((1 := uint8)) binds T to uint8, new Pair((1 := uint8), "s") binds A and C, and new G(4) for a value parameter N: uint32 binds N to the literal 4 converted to uint32. An untyped literal argument contributes its LITERAL type, and a parameter binds the JOIN of what every argument contributes to it: add(200, 100) for a parameter constrained uint8 binds 200 | 100, and pair("a", "b") for one constrained "a" | "b" binds 'a' | 'b'. The join is then checked against the parameter's evaluated constraint, which admits a literal that fits it on the terms 1.6.6 gives a literal in any other typed position, so 200 satisfies uint8 and 300 does not. Where the parameter has NO constraint the binding widens to the literal's base, so new Box(1) with no context is Box.<number>, as f(1) is for a generic function; a CONSTRAINED parameter keeps the literal, the constraint being the contextual type that clause speaks of. A rest parameter's arguments each contribute by the same rule and the parameter binds a tuple of them. Inference is one rung and does not join across rungs: a binding an earlier rung fixed stands, so a seed taken from the call's context is kept and an argument that contradicts it is dropped;
    4. the parameter's TypeParameterDefault, evaluated over the bindings so far;
    5. otherwise it is a TypeError exception naming the parameter and the declaration. A parameter no argument reaches and no default supplies is not bound to any or left open: "a parameter left by all three is an error" (4.3), and a signature "whose parameters cannot be bound is not viable" (1.10.3). The same holds of a call of a generic function.

    Within the construction new.target is the specialization, as it is for new C.<…>, and the instance's prototype and typed fields are the specialization's. The declaration's [[Construct]] is reached with newTarget equal to itself by every form above; a super() from a class extending a specialization never reaches it, that heritage having evaluated to the specialization; and Reflect.construct with the declaration as target and an unrelated newTarget is a TypeError exception, since running the declaration's body against a foreign prototype would produce the open instance by another route.

    Inference beats a default: new A(5) for a class A<T: type = uint8> { constructor(a: T) } is A.<number>, since the argument reaches T before the default is consulted; new A.<>(5) and let a: A = new A(5) are A.<uint8>, the default binding where nothing reaches the parameter or the context names it.

    Note

    The contextual rung is read BEFORE the arguments, not after them as a fallback, and the order is what makes the ordinary spelling work. An untyped literal binds number when it is looked at first, and Box.<number> is not a Box.<uint8>; read first, the context fixes T and the literal takes it, which is exactly what writing new Box.<uint8>(1) does. The context-first reading accepts strictly more than the argument-first one and never something the other would accept for a different reason: everything it produces has the context's type, and its arguments were checked against that type's parameters. The one visible difference — an argument whose own type contradicts the context — is reported at the argument, where new Box.<uint8>((1 := uint16)) reports it.

    The two sides of the checker and the run time compute the same bindings from the same inputs, the checker over Static Types and the run time over values, and a construction's Static Type is the specialization so bound (1.2.6). Where the run time is reached and the checker saw nothing — the class through an alias, Reflect.construct — the run time binds alone, by the same ladder.

    Collections are unaffected. Map's constructor declares no type parameters, so there is nothing here to bind, and an unannotated new Map() remains the untyped collection of 1.15.7; let m: Map.<string, uint8> = new Map() remains the adoption of 1.15.5, which reads the boundary AFTER the construction because a collection's arguments live on the instance. A class's live in its prototype, which is why a class must decide before it allocates and a collection may decide after.

    4.9 The where Clause

    A generic declaration may carry a where clause, written with the WhereClauses of 5.1 where 14 admits them: a compile-time-evaluable Boolean expression over its parameters, checked at each specialization once its parameters are bound. Where the expression is false for an application's bindings, that application is a type error, reported against the clause's source. A where over value generics, as where I.every(i => i < N) on a variadic pack, is the design's compile-time bound on the values a parameter admits; a where that inspects a runtime value rather than a generic parameter is the dependent record type extension's, checked at the boundaries Table 23 enumerates rather than at specialization; and a where naming return on a compile-time-evaluable function is a contract (14). One syntax carries all three because one rule does: a predicate is evaluated where its subject exists, which is at specialization for a parameter, at a boundary for a value, and at evaluation for a result.

    Source checking of a generic type alias application uses the declaration selected by lexical name resolution and the bindings produced by the ordinary type-argument binding rules. Resolve named arguments, defaults and variadic or spread arguments before judging a clause. A same-spelled declaration in another scope contributes no clause to that application. Omitting an argument list where defaults supply all arguments creates the same checking obligation as an explicit empty argument list.

    A closed specialization predicate whose inputs are available under the compile-time-evaluation rules is checked at the source's checking boundary, including in an uncalled function or an unreachable statement. Nesting depth and declaration placement do not remove this obligation. A predicate that is false produces the clause's type error before the candidate body is entered. Checking retains the clause's original source location, declaration scope and generic parameter identities; a temporary checking environment may not replace an unavailable nested binding with a same-spelled outer value or execute ordinary enclosing statements to obtain it.

    If an application's bindings still depend on an unbound generic parameter, retain its clause obligation along with that dependence. Apply the obligation when substitution establishes the required inputs, even if the alias's resulting type no longer mentions the parameter. A successful application with different bindings supplies no evidence for this one. Successful verification may be reused only for the same clause and semantically equivalent inputs, preserving type and value identity distinctions, including nominal declarations and signed zero. Identifier spelling and formatted diagnostic text do not establish that equivalence. Runtime-subject and unavailable-input cases keep their existing deferral rules; a resource limit follows 1.2.7.4, rather than silently treating an unvisited obligation as satisfied.

    Note

    The clause is evaluated by 1.2.7 like any other compile-time expression, so it may call builders and read a value generic's value, and its determinism and budget are those already fixed. A where is a check, not an inference: it narrows which applications are legal, and never changes what a parameter is bound to.

    4.9.1 Specialization Predicate Completion

    At a source-checking boundary, a closed specialization predicate is subject to the following rules. These rules apply to function and type alias applications, including applications retained inside enclosing generic declarations. They do not move a runtime-subject predicate or a result contract to that boundary.

    1. Establish the predicate's bound generic inputs and the availability of its external lexical dependencies, following the original declarations through helper calls and imports. Evaluability and availability are separate requirements. An admissible immutable initializer does not itself initialize its ordinary lexical binding. A class declaration's nominal identity does not supply a constructor, decorated members or layout that still require class evaluation. Do not execute ordinary enclosing statements, initialize a runtime binding, or replace a dependency with a same-spelled binding in order to obtain these inputs.
    2. If an explicit deferral rule applies, retain the obligation without evaluating the predicate or recording success. Unbound parameters, an uninstantiated enclosing environment and runtime-dependent inputs retain their existing deferral rules. A required imported input at a module boundary instead follows 1.3.8, including its failure rule for an uninitialized binding. A failed evaluation is not by itself evidence that a deferral rule applies.
    3. Otherwise evaluate the RefinementPredicate with its original lexical scope and the application's bound parameters, using 5.1 and the compile-time-evaluable fragment. Conditional and short-circuit forms evaluate only their selected operands. A throw handled within that evaluation contributes the handler's completion; a finally clause has its ordinary completion-replacement semantics.
    4. If the containing type evaluation exhausts its budget, apply 1.2.7.4. This outcome takes precedence over any incidental throw, caught exception, Boolean result or missing result. Record no successful verification.
    5. If evaluation otherwise completes abruptly, the application has a type-evaluation error reported against this clause's source, before the candidate source body is entered. This is distinct from a predicate that holds or fails normally. It applies regardless of the thrown value's class, properties or message. Do not suppress the error, convert it into a false predicate, or retry it after body entry.
    6. If evaluation completes normally and the predicate does not hold, report the unsatisfied-constraint type error against this clause's source. If it holds, verification may be reused only under the semantic-input identity rule above. An unavailable input, an abrupt completion and budget exhaustion never establish a successful verification.

    These rules classify the completion of a required checking-time evaluation. They do not wrap an ordinary runtime exception from a predicate whose evaluation is deferred until runtime. A helper's own uninitialized local read, once the helper is legitimately being evaluated, is an ordinary evaluation failure; it is not an unavailable external input. Likewise, catching an artificial premature read cannot establish a Boolean fact about a predicate that required an unavailable environment.

    4.10 Class Replacement Contracts

    A replacement class preserves its primary's effective public instance contract after substituting the arguments selected by its specialization pattern. It is a type error if an established required public member is absent, including a member with an established Symbol key. Resolve inheritance, own-field precedence and accessor descriptors before comparing capabilities. Private and protected implementation details are not public obligations, and this rule does not introduce static-member overriding.

    Every required readable member must supply a type assignable to the primary's promised readable type. A method must preserve its callable signatures, including receiver, argument and result contracts. Reference parameters preserve their mode and invariant target type; reference returns retain their existing invariant compatibility and liveness rules. Every primary field or accessor write capability must remain available and accept every value the primary accepts. Readonly storage cannot replace required writable storage; a setter's accepted type is compared independently of its getter's result. A replacement may add public members or change private representation without changing these obligations.

    Each substituted primary constructor signature must be accepted by a replacement constructor signature under the parameter-sequence compatibility rules, retaining the complete Parameter Records. Preserve accepted argument counts, optional positions, defaults, rest extents and reference permissions. A primary default admits omission; it does not execute before the replacement constructor is selected. The replacement must independently admit that omission. Constructors cannot discard required reference markers or change their invariant target types. An entirely untyped constructor retains the existing gradual treatment for copied arguments, without erasing a primary reference permission.

    Judge closed obligations when the declarations are checked. Retain obligations dependent on captures or unbound parameters and discharge them when an application establishes the bindings. Missing required members can be rejected without waiting for their types to close. No constructor, getter, setter, conversion or default expression is executed to compare contracts. Layout remains determined by the selected implementation, and successful compatibility establishes no additional reference-liveness permission.

    4.11 Declaration-Site Variance

    This clause states what a variance declaration means; a parameter carrying none is invariant, which is the rule 1.2.3.1 gives and the conservative default. A type parameter is declared covariant by the VarianceModifier out and contravariant by in (1.4.3). Where a parameter is covariant, one instantiation is a subtype of another along that position when the argument in the first is a subtype of the argument in the second; where contravariant, when the reverse holds; where neither is declared, the position is invariant, the default of 1.2.3.1. A covariant parameter is well-formed only where it appears in output positions of the declaration, a method return or a readonly field, and a contravariant parameter only in input positions, a method or constructor parameter; a parameter appearing in a position of the wrong polarity is an early error, since the variance would be unsound there for the reason the invariance note gives of a mutable container.

    Polarity composes recursively. Within a function type, its parameter types invert the enclosing polarity and its return type preserves it; a writable position imposes both. An occurrence refers to its declaring type parameter, so a nested declaration that binds the same name does not contribute an occurrence of the outer parameter.

    The variance of a nested application is read from the declaration resolved in its lexical scope, including a type alias. Named type arguments are associated with their declared parameters before polarity is composed; changing the written order of named arguments does not change variance. This judgment applies to a function or method's own generic parameters as well as to the parameters of classes, interfaces and aliases.

    Note

    This is the variance of C# and Kotlin, sound because the well-formedness rule confines a covariant parameter to positions a value is read from and a contravariant one to positions a value is written to. A Producer.<Dog> is usable as a Producer.<Animal> where Producer is declared covariant and only produces, which the container invariance of 1.2.3.1 forbids for a Map precisely because a Map also consumes. The relation composes with the others: an instantiation is a subtype along a covariant position by the ordinary subtyping of the arguments, so a covariant position holding another generic type carries the polarity inward, which the last two table rows state.

    A partial class or interface contribution is subject to its primary's variance promises. Check added signatures using the primary parameter identities and the captures to which the contribution's pattern maps them, composing polarity through variant nested parameters. A method-local type parameter shadows the outer binding. A fixed closed argument is not an occurrence of an open variant parameter. Loading a partial never changes the primary's declared variance, identity or layout. A forbidden occurrence is the same Syntax Error as it would be in the primary declaration.

    4.11.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors

    TypeParameter : VarianceModifier BindingIdentifier TypeParameterHolesopt TypeParameterDomain TypeParameterConstraintopt TypeParameterDefaultopt
    • It is a Syntax Error if any occurrence of the type named by BindingIdentifier within the declaration that introduces this TypeParameter is at a position whose polarity, as given by Table 41, is both or does not match VarianceModifier: output for out, input for in.
    Note

    A declaration is a claim rather than a derivation, so it can be wrong, and this is the rule that catches it: out on a parameter appearing in a non-readonly field is refused, since Table 41 gives that position both and only an invariant parameter may stand there. A parameter carrying no VarianceModifier is unconstrained by this rule, which is why invariance needs no check.

    4.12 Higher-Kinded Parameters

    A generic parameter with an [[Arity]] of zero stands for a type. A higher-kinded parameter has an [[Arity]] of n > 0 and stands for a generic declaration of n parameters: something that becomes a type once applied, rather than a type. This clause states how one is declared, what may be bound to it, what applying it means, and how the four clauses above read when a parameter is one (design, higherkindedtypes.md).

    A higher-kinded parameter's arity is written and never inferred. Each hole in its own parameter list contributes one:

    A parameter is higher-kinded when its BindingIdentifier is followed by a bracketed list of _ tokens, as W<_> for an [[Arity]] of 1 and W<_, _> for 2. The count of tokens is the [[Arity]].

    Note 1

    _ is the pattern wildcard of the pattern matching extension, and the reuse is positional in the way % already is: % is the remainder operator between two operands and the pipeline topic where an operand is expected, and here a type parameter list is a position where a pattern cannot appear. The token means a hole at both.

    Within the declaration that introduces it, a higher-kinded parameter may appear only applied, or as the argument for a higher-kinded parameter of the same [[Arity]], which forwards it. It is not a type, so a type position naming one unapplied is a type error, and the message states the arity the parameter expects. Applied, it is an ordinary application: the parameter is resolved to whatever the enclosing application bound it to, and that is then applied to the given arguments, so W.<X> means the same as writing the bound declaration applied to X directly.

    Before any application has bound it — while the declaration's own interior is checked — a higher-kinded parameter resolves to itself, exactly as a parameter of arity zero does. This is what lets a declaration be checked once rather than once per application.

    An application of a higher-kinded parameter supplies exactly its [[Arity]] arguments, positionally. It is a type error, at the declaration, for the application to supply another number, counting a spread argument by its statically known length, or to supply a TypeArgument of the named form, since the holes carry no names. The count is judged against the holes and not against a binding, which is what lets it be judged once: every declaration a binding may supply has exactly [[Arity]] parameters, so an application supplying [[Arity]] arguments reaches each of them, and after substitution it is an ordinary application whose arguments are checked against the bound declaration's domains and bounds as any other application's are.

    Note 2

    A bound declaration whose parameters carry defaults does not relax the count. W.<> for W<_> is refused even where every declaration the program binds to W happens to default its parameter, since that is a fact about the bindings and the rule is a fact about W; judging it per binding would need every admissible binding, the search the quantified constraint below is refused for. Rust reports the same mismatch on a generic associated type, whose applications name their full argument list.

    A higher-kinded parameter may carry a default, on the same terms as any other parameter and with the same well-formedness rule: a parameter carrying a default may not precede one that does not. This clause adds no exception, so a declaration wanting a defaulted wrapper places it after its required parameters, and Iterator.<T> reads as it did before the parameter existed.

    Note 3

    The rule is what decides the parameter's position rather than the other way round. A wrapper defaulting to the identity alias is the least interesting parameter at most use sites, so placing it last costs nothing and keeps every existing annotation naming the type unchanged; a design that needed the exception would be one whose parameter is in the wrong place. Where both forms want names, the second is an alias rather than a second declaration — type AsyncIterator<T: type, R: type, N: type> = Iterator<T, R, N, Promise> — so what is deduplicated is the members, not the names.

    An argument bound to a higher-kinded parameter must be a generic class, interface, or type alias whose parameter count equals the parameter's [[Arity]], or a higher-kinded parameter of that [[Arity]]. Two failures are distinguished, because they are different mistakes and a single diagnostic naming neither would leave a reader to work out which occurred:

    • An argument that is not a generic declaration at all is a type error naming the argument and stating that the parameter expects a declaration taking arguments.
    • An argument that is a generic declaration of the wrong parameter count is a type error naming both counts.

    Specialization (4.7) substitutes a bound declaration for the parameter and then applies it, so a specialized type contains no higher-kinded parameter and the resulting application is an ordinary one. Two applications binding different declarations are distinct types on the same terms as any other pair of applications, and interning follows from that with no rule of its own.

    A where constraint (4.9) on a higher-kinded parameter constrains its application at a stated argument, as in where W.<T> is Iterable`. A constraint quantified over every argument the parameter could receive is a type error.

    Note 4

    The quantified form is refused for a reason of correctness rather than of difficulty, and the reason is this specification's own. Type-position evaluation is metered (1.2.7.4): a budget of evaluation steps and type-construction requests bounds it, and exhausting the budget abandons the evaluation and reports. That bounds a computation, which either finishes or does not. A constraint quantified over every argument is not a computation but a search over the types that could be supplied, and truncating a search under a budget yields a WRONG answer rather than no answer — whether the constraint held would depend on how much budget remained when the search stopped. A rule whose truth varies with a host-defined limit is not a rule, so the form is refused rather than metered.

    Declared variance (4.11) applies to a higher-kinded parameter on the same terms as to any other, meaning at the applied form what it means for a parameter of arity zero, and a parameter carrying no annotation is invariant. An application binding one declaration is therefore not a subtype of an application binding another, which is what keeps a synchronous iterator from being accepted where an asynchronous one is expected.

    A higher-kinded parameter read as a value (4.1) is the unapplied declaration bound to it. Applying that value yields the same Type Object the corresponding type-position application yields, since both reach the same interned record.

    A higher-kinded parameter is bound only by explicit application. It is never inferred from an argument's type.

    Note 5

    Inference is declined for the reason the quantified constraint is. Recovering W and T from a single argument of type Promise.<uint8> admits at least two answers — W is Promise and T is uint8, or W is Identity and T is the whole promise — and both are consistent with the argument. Choosing between them is a search, and this specification meters computation rather than search. Requiring the argument costs a reader one type argument at each application and buys an evaluation that terminates with the same answer under every budget.

    5 Dependent Record Types

    A type alias declaration may carry where clauses, each a predicate over the value the type describes. What they state is what a property's own type cannot: that a credit card and a billing address are present together, or that a postal code's pattern follows from a country. The narrowing form v is T (Table 24) and the boundary checks of Table 23 are what this clause makes real.

    5.1 The where Clause

    The WhereClauses that 1.8.1 admits after a type alias's Type are given by:

    WhereClauses[Yield, Await] : WhereClause[?Yield, ?Await] WhereClauses[?Yield, ?Await] WhereClause[?Yield, ?Await] WhereClause[Yield, Await] : where RefinementPredicate[?Yield, ?Await] RefinementPredicate[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] if ( AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ) { RefinementPredicate[?Yield, ?Await] } if ( AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ) { RefinementPredicate[?Yield, ?Await] } else { RefinementPredicate[?Yield, ?Await] }

    A RefinementPredicate is evaluated with this bound to the value under test, and it holds when ToBoolean of its result is true. A match expression is an AssignmentExpression and so is a predicate like any other, where match (this.status) { ... }, and in this position it carries an implicit default: *false*; clause: a predicate that matches no clause has answered that the value is not of the type, which is the answer a predicate exists to give. It is therefore exhaustive by construction (24.3.1), and an explicit default overrides the implicit one. The conditional form evaluates its AssignmentExpression and then the predicate of the branch taken, and holds vacuously where that expression is falsy and no else is present. It is an early error for a RefinementPredicate not to be compile-time evaluable (1.2.7.1) as a function of this, which is what admits the same predicate at compile time, where it decides a constant, and at run time, where it checks a value.

    type N = T where P ; binds N to the Type Record { [[Kind]]: parameterized, [[Base]]: the Type Record T denotes, [[Metadata]]: OrdinaryObjectCreate with a where property whose value is P as a function of this }. Each further clause refines the type the clauses before it produced, so _T_ where _A_ where _B_ is the refinement by B of the refinement by A of T, and conjunction, subtyping, and membership follow from that nesting rather than from a rule of their own.

    The where meta type (6) claims the where key. Its validate of a value against a constraint is the evaluation of the constraint's where with this bound to that value; its subtype holds where the required constraint is unconstrained, so a predicate is shed, or where both carry the same predicate; its default is the unconstrained constraint, and it defines no other hook. A dependent record type therefore admits a value of its base only where every predicate holds of it, is a subtype of its base and sheds its predicates upward freely, and is reached from its base only by a crossing that runs them.

    Note

    The refinement is 1.5.20's, not a kind of its own, which is why nothing here restates layout, defaults, or the relations: a predicate changes no representation, and the branding rule of that clause is already the rule this one wants, that a Payment is usable wherever its bare object type is and that going the other way is a check. The design writes a postal code's pattern as string.<{ pattern: … }> in the same document that writes a payment's cross-field rule as where, and the two are one mechanism over two bases.

    Because a predicate is a function, the structural equivalence of 1.2.7.2 compares it by SameValue, so a dependent record type's identity is its declaration's identity: two modules that write the same where text declare two types, where two that write stringPattern(/^[0-9]{5}$/) declare one. That asymmetry is deliberate and is not an accident of the encoding. A predicate is code and may close over its scope, so where this.total < LIMIT in two modules means two things whenever their LIMIT differs; comparing predicate source would make those one type and would be unsound. A regular expression is data and carries no scope, so comparing it structurally is safe. A program that wants one dependent record type across modules declares it once and imports it, as it would a class.

    Conjunction by nesting also gives the diagnostics: a value failing _T_ where _A_ where _B_ fails at the innermost refinement whose predicate is false, so the clause that rejected it is the clause named.

    5.2 The is Operator

    v is T is true when the value of v is of the type T denotes and false otherwise. It performs IsOfType (1.7.2.1) and never throws for a value the type rejects, which is the difference between it and the check a boundary performs: a boundary requires, and is asks. Its grammar is given with the conversion operator (1.4.5), whose precedence it shares; the pattern matching extension widens its right operand to a full pattern, of which a type is one form (24.4), changing nothing written before it.

    Note

    is is the branch a program takes instead of the throw: if (payment is Payment) tests what example(payment) would have required. Against a dependent record type it runs the predicates, so it is also the only way to ask whether a value the program has been mutating is valid again. Against any other type it is the same structural test every boundary makes, so v is uint8 and v is { x: float32 } are ordinary questions with ordinary answers, and the accessor and higher-order reading of 1.7.2.1 is the reading here too.

    5.3 Discriminated where Chains

    A RefinementPredicate is a discriminating chain in either of two forms. In the conditional form, when: every condition is an equality comparison, == or ===, between one member access on this and a compile-time constant, every condition tests the same member; that member's declared type is a union of the literal types of exactly such constants, or an enum over them; and the chain is total, ending in an else or its conditions exhausting that type. In the match form, when the subject is one member access on this whose declared type is such a union or enum, every clause is unguarded with a pattern that is a constant of that type or an or of them, no two clauses name one constant, and the clauses name every constant of the type; each clause is then a branch, its condition being its pattern and its predicate its arm body. Such a chain denotes a union: one member per branch, and where a branch tests several constants one member per constant, each the type's base with the discriminant narrowed to the constant tested and with each shape assertion of the branch, this is T or this.p is T, applied by NarrowTo at the asserted path; a branch predicate that is not a shape assertion refines its member as a where of its own and contributes no members.

    The denoted union serves the exhaustiveness check of 24.3.1 and nothing else: the dependent record type remains one parameterized Type Record, Reflect.typeOf reports it, and assignability compares against it. A chain that does not qualify, a nullish or ordering condition, conditions over two members, a chain with no else over a type it does not exhaust, denotes nothing but itself and its match writes a default.

    Note

    The design's Address qualifies, one member tested against two literals with a final else, and it denotes exactly the discriminated union its document prints "for reference", so this clause writes down an equivalence the design asserts rather than inventing one. The qualification is syntactic so that no predicate reasoning enters the checker; the alternative was a prover with a budget, and no other rule here asks for one (design, patternmatching.md).

    5.4 Narrowing Through a Refinement

    Where the Static Type of v is a dependent record type whose predicate is the conditional form, and the narrowing facts in force at a position decide that predicate's AssignmentExpression, the branch so taken contributes its narrowing facts at that position, reading this as v: a branch predicate that is a narrowing form of Table 24 over a path rooted at this contributes what that form contributes over the corresponding path on v, so this is T contributes what v is T does, this.p is T what v.p is T does, and this.data !== undefined what v.data !== undefined does; a conjunction contributes both sides' facts; any other predicate contributes none. The conditional and match forms both take their branch this way, and the match form's chosen clause is the one whose pattern the facts decide.

    An expression is decided by the narrowing facts when evaluating it is compile-time evaluable given them, reading this as v and reading a path whose narrowed type is a literal type as that type's [[Value]]. No other means of deciding it is specified: a predicate the facts leave open contributes nothing, and the boundary check stands.

    Note

    This is what lets if (addr.country == 'US') narrow addr.postalCode to USPostalCode without the program writing a discriminated union, which is the case the design contrasts its where against. The chain is short and each link is already specified: the literal-equality row of Table 24 gives addr.country the Static Type 'US', that fact makes this.country == 'US' a compile-time-evaluable expression over a known value, deciding it selects the then branch, and that branch's this is { postalCode: USPostalCode } narrows exactly as the is would if the program had written it.

    The rule is deliberately not a prover. Where a predicate is not decided, nothing is narrowed and the boundary check runs, which is the design's own account of the case where a 'strict' name is assigned a 'loose' mode: the checker cannot know that one pattern's language contains the other's, so the check at the next boundary is what catches it. Sharpening that particular case is the pattern subtype judgment's business (1.5.20), not narrowing's.

    6 The Metadata Protocol

    A metadata parameterization carries a value that 1.5.20 gives one default meaning: a brand, shed upward freely and crossed downward only at a construction boundary. This clause is what lets that value mean more. A meta type teaches the checker the semantics of the fields it claims, so that float32.<{ m: 1, s: -2 }> is an acceleration whose dimensions combine under multiplication, float32.<{ bounds: 0.. }> is a bound that a comparison can narrow, and decimal128.<{ scale: 2 }> is a price that rounds where it is stored and not before.

    6.1 Meta Declarations

    The production below restates the Declaration of 1.8.1 and carries the declaration forms the extensions add (1.1).

    Declaration[Yield, Await] : HoistableDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await, ~Default] ClassDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await, ~Default] LexicalDeclaration[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] TypeAliasDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await] MetaDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await] PrimitiveOperatorDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await] InterfaceDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await] EnumDeclaration[?Yield, ?Await] MetaDeclaration[Yield, Await] : meta [no LineTerminator here] TypeName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt { MetaHookList[?Yield, ?Await]opt } MetaHookList[Yield, Await] : MetaHook[?Yield, ?Await] MetaHookList[?Yield, ?Await] MetaHook[?Yield, ?Await] MetaHook[Yield, Await] : default = AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ; MethodDefinition[?Yield, ?Await]

    A MetaDeclaration names an object type, the meta type's constraint shape, and supplies hooks for it. The MethodDefinitions it may contain are exactly those named in Table 42; a method of any other name is an early error, as is a second declaration for one type, a missing default or subtype, a default whose value is not of the constraint shape, or a hook whose signature does not match the table.

    Every hook is required to be a pure function of its arguments, compile-time evaluable (1.2.7.1), and deterministic, the obligation 1.5.20 states of the judgments they compose. It is an early error for a hook not to be compile-time evaluable.

    A type violation the checker can decide is likewise an EARLY ERROR, and the error is a StaticTypeError, whose prototype object inherits from %Error.prototype% and whose constructor is a global (1.3.11). It does not inherit from SyntaxError: the syntax of a program this rejects is well formed, and a host that catches a SyntaxError to mean "this source did not parse" must not be made to catch a type failure by doing so. Nor does it inherit from TypeError, which is reserved for the dynamic boundary; the two are disjoint, and a program wanting either phase tests both.

    The distinction it draws is WHEN, and it is observable: a StaticTypeError is thrown before any of the Script or Module runs, and a TypeError is thrown by a boundary during evaluation. let _n_: uint8 = "s" is decided without running and is the first; a value crossing a boundary the checker could not decide is the second.

    Every violation this specification calls decidable is therefore reported alike by every implementation, at the same moment and with the same class of error. An implementation that deferred one of them to evaluation would run a program that others refuse, which is the fragmentation early errors exist to prevent.

    Note

    The obligation is what makes one hook serve two phases. validate decides a literal at compile time and a value at run time; quantize folds a constant and rounds a computed result; subtype contributes only to the metadata subtype judgment: the checking pass (1.2.8) invokes it to decide a pair of portions, the decision is a pure function of its interned operands and is remembered, and the run-time operations that reach the judgment — a conversion between two parameterizations, an any-typed value arriving at a parameterized position — consult the remembered relation, invoking the hook only for a pair no check has yet decided. A hook that read the clock or a global would make a program's types depend on when it ran, which 1.2.7.4 already forbids of everything else in type position.

    meta is a contextual keyword under the restriction is takes (5.2) and for the same reason: meta T on one line is a Syntax Error today, and meta alone on a line is an expression statement that must stay one.

    6.2 Decomposition and the Judgments

    Before interning or comparing metadata, normalize every origin against the same instantiated constraint shape: the declaration's default, a written record, a builder result, a capture, and a reflected description. A written numeric literal leaf is read from its exact source digits in its declared numeric domain under literal representability rules; a runtime Number leaf denotes its actual Number value. Normalization never wraps an out-of-range integer or invokes a user conversion. An already typed numeric atom retains its domain and exact value. Normalize nested records and lists recursively, using their field, tuple-position, or element shapes; an optional numeric field supplies its numeric domain when present. A union with several numeric alternatives does not choose an alternative by order. Reject a completed claimed portion that does not satisfy its shape. Range endpoints use the declared endpoint-domain rule below. The unclaimed-key rule and base-form exception remain in force.

    Normalization is idempotent and independent of origin. Equivalent metadata must have the same interning key, and reconstructing a reflected type must produce the same Type Object. A typed view of a capture preserves its declared field types. Numeric atoms use the domain's SameValue rule, not composite SameValueZero: neither negative zero nor the distinction between an explicit default-pinned requirement and a bare type is erased.

    A metadata value is drawn from a closed language, given by Table 43. The top level is a flat record whose keys are claimed keys; the values under them may nest freely. Two metadata values are equivalent when they are equivalent by the comparison that table gives, and it is that comparison, and not object identity, that interning uses.

    The outer value supplied for a metadata record or claimed portion must be a record input under the admission rules below. A list, range, pattern or scalar is not such a record, even when it has no enumerable properties or when the base carries a base-form meta declaration. Determine this outer kind before reading its entries or replacing it with a snapshot. Nested lists remain metadata values; their indexed traversal is unchanged. An ordinary record does not become a list merely because its prototype is an Array.

    Projecting a written metadata argument preserves every supplied member and list position. Distinguish a completed value, an unresolved value dependency and a completed invalid form throughout nested projection. An invalid leaf invalidates the supplied value; omitting that leaf or replacing its containing record with an empty record is not permitted. A closed invalid leaf is a type error at the required source-checking boundary, including when another member remains dependent. An unresolved member retains its declaration and application dependencies until its value is available; no partial projection is a completed metadata record. An optional constraint member permits absence but does not admit a supplied undefined, and any in the constraint shape does not extend the metadata value language.

    A metadata argument denoting a meta-type family denotes the registered constraint shape itself. Possession of one of that type's claimed keys, or gradual mutual assignability through any, does not establish this identity. Keep this family interpretation distinct from supplied nested values and from ordinary type arguments to a generic declaration. A completed supplied value undergoes the same admission rules whether written directly, reached through an alias, computed, captured or reflected.

    Nothing else is a metadata value. A function, an object other than the forms above, and undefined are not: absence is the absence of a key rather than a key holding nothing.

    Admission precedes any copying that could erase the input's kind. Recognize supported numeric atoms, patterns and ranges by their actual kind, not by public tag properties or a user coercion. A record input is an ordinary Object with ordinary property access, without construction identity, private elements or additional opaque payload slots. Its prototype contributes no fields. Functions, class instances, boxed primitives, collection objects, typed-array objects and Proxies are not record inputs, even after a prototype change. Snapshot all metadata origins under these same admission rules before their completed values are normalized, interned or published.

    Composite record and tuple values and Span values are not metadata record or list inputs. Their admission does not depend on whether an implementation represents their special kind or backing state using object slots, value tags or side tables. Reject these kinds before entry reads, including empty values and values whose prototype has changed. A program may explicitly project contents to an ordinary record or Array before supplying metadata; that new input and every nested value still undergo the same admission checks. Typed owning Arrays remain list inputs.

    For a record snapshot, obtain its own key list once, and in that order inspect each key's current own descriptor. For each enumerable property, perform Get once and complete the resulting value's snapshot before proceeding to the next key. For a list input, capture the Array's length once and perform Get at each index from zero through that length minus one, in order, completing each element before reading the next. Index enumerability does not change list membership; named properties do not become elements. An indexed read yielding undefined, including an unfilled hole, fails admission. An inherited indexed value is the result of the ordinary Get. Getter effects and abrupt completions obey the existing type-position fragment rules; validation must not add a separate preliminary traversal that duplicates these reads.

    Record keys are String or Symbol property keys. Preserve their identity through every metadata origin, normalization, constraint-shape lookup, key claiming, default completion, capture, hook portion, computed result and reflected description. Distinct Symbols with the same description are distinct keys; no String spelling substitutes for a Symbol. Enumerable Symbol properties participate in record snapshotting in the own-key order described above, with the same reads and admission checks as String properties. Symbol properties of a list are not indexed elements. Record equivalence compares actual key sets and corresponding values without regard to insertion order. Canonical ordering distinguishes Symbol identities by the existing per-agent first-interning order, for both keys and Symbol values. Materialization exposes the original property keys.

    A cycle along the active record/list containment path is not a metadata value. Repeated references to an acyclic child are distinct snapshot occurrences, with the prescribed reads performed for each occurrence. An implementation may use an explicit worklist rather than host recursion. Snapshotting joins the surrounding type-evaluation budget, or begins one where none is active, and charges one logical step for each value visit and each container advance or completion. Getter and helper work also pays its existing charges. An exhausted or failed snapshot produces no completed metadata value and does not publish a declaration; earlier ordinary effects and completed declarations are preserved as specified above.

    When metadata reaches a hook or a reflected type description, materialize lists as Arrays, patterns as RegExp values, and ranges as Range values of their stored shapes. Ordinary records retain their ordinary member names: a property named __range or __pattern is not authority to create a different metadata kind. Reconstructing a reflected description uses the same admission rules and preserves the required Type Object identity.

    A range is admitted as a VALUE and not as an implementation of RangeBounds.<T>: the four shapes are the whole of what a metadata range may be. A class of a program's own that implements the interface has no structural comparison, could not be written into an expansion artifact, and would give interning no answer, which are the three reasons the language is closed at all. A meta type's constraint shape may still DECLARE such a field as a RangeBounds.<T>, since that is what a hook receives and what a hook returns; what this table closes is the set of values that may appear under it.

    Note 1

    Admission to the metadata value language does not bypass the declared field type. A Range.<T, S, E> field requires both endpoints at every origin, while a RangeBounds.<T> field admits all four range shapes. A written 0..<10 and a default .. have different shapes; comparing their admission does not test origin independence. The generic argument rules of 1.5.20 still apply: the required element type T is not supplied by writing a bare Range or RangeBounds.

    A present endpoint of a metadata range must itself be an admitted metadata atom: one of the scalar or numeric values in Table 43. The range's ordinary ordering requirements still apply. A built-in range carrying a live class instance, container or unsupported object as an endpoint is not a metadata value, even when it is a valid ordinary range. This restriction does not change range admission outside metadata. Check the start endpoint before the end using internal endpoint data, without public property reads, coercion or ordering calls. Each present endpoint consumes a value-visit step, and completion of the range consumes a container-completion step under the surrounding snapshot budget. Publish the range snapshot only after both present endpoints pass; omitted endpoints remain absent. Written range projection applies the same atom admission before completing its metadata value.

    Each present endpoint is a compile-time constant and is normalized against the endpoint type of the field's instantiated range constraint shape, using the same numeric-literal and runtime-value rules as other metadata leaves. The base supplies that endpoint type only through a declared meta parameter: a RangeBounds.<T> field uses the substituted T, while a RangeBounds.<uint16> field keeps uint16 endpoints on any host. A present optional range field supplies the same context. Where several union alternatives supply different possible range domains, do not choose by their order: there is no single contextual endpoint domain, and the supplied endpoints and range shape must satisfy one complete alternative. An unconstrained field supplies no host-derived endpoint domain. Already typed endpoints retain their domains and must satisfy the field type. A generic default is still evaluated and snapshotted once. An unbound endpoint parameter postpones its domain membership judgment until a concrete host is available; it does not establish completed membership. Normalize and check a completed default portion against the instantiated shape before a capture or hook reads it, and compare default participation against that same instantiated default, without reevaluating the default expression. SameValue retains domain distinctions and signed zero; omitted endpoints remain absent.

    Every present metadata endpoint, including an open endpoint, must be a value of that declared endpoint domain after normalization. Do not wrap, clamp, widen the declared domain, rewrite inclusivity, or invoke a user conversion to obtain it. A 0..<256 bound in a RangeBounds.<uint16> metadata field on uint8 is valid; the same bound in RangeBounds.<uint8> is invalid. This judgment concerns stored metadata endpoints, independently of the produced-element fit judgment for ordinary range iteration. Defaults, written arguments, builders, captures, hook results and reflected reconstruction apply the same rule before publishing a completed parameterization; failures retain their existing checking phase and declaration-publication rules.

    An empty range is a metadata value like any other, and it constrains its parameterization to no value at all: a validation admits nothing and the constraint lies below every bound. Equivalence over it remains structural, so two empty ranges with different endpoints are two types, both uninhabited. A range that constrains nothing is the full range, and a meta type whose key means an unconstrained bound says so in its default, which is what makes a parameterization that omits the key and one that writes the full range under it one portion by the completion rule below, rather than two spellings of one thing.

    Note 2

    The language is closed because three things depend on it and each would break for a different reason. Interning compares metadata rather than identity, which is what makes brand(uint32, 'UserId') written in two modules one type with no registry, and a form with no structural comparison would have no answer there. An expansion artifact (22) is a serialization of the interning table, so a form that cannot be written down and read back could not appear in one. And a hook receives the metadata, so every form must be presentable to a program.

    The representation is this specification's business and the cost is an implementation's. Metadata is settled where a type is written, so an implementation is expected to compare these forms directly and to materialize an object only where a hook is actually called. Nothing here is intended to cost a running program anything.

    An unregistered Symbol is admitted deliberately, and it is the one form whose equivalence is not structural. That is what it is for: a module that mints a Symbol it neither exports nor registers has a metadata key no other module can write, so its parameterizations are its own, and two of them are one type exactly when they carry that Symbol. A registered Symbol behaves the other way, being the same Symbol in every agent that asks for the key, and is the form to reach for where two libraries must agree. A type whose metadata carries an unregistered Symbol cannot appear in an expansion artifact and loses nothing by it: an artifact carries the concrete types a module graph's public surface produces, and a Symbol deliberately not exported is not part of one. An artifact is an optimization and never a semantics, so a consumer evaluates such a type as it evaluates any other.

    A MetaDeclaration may instead name a PRIMITIVE type rather than an object type, declaring a base-form meta type for it. Such a declaration has no constraint shape and so claims no keys: its hooks receive the WHOLE metadata of a parameterization of that base rather than a portion of it, and the judgments and conversions of this clause consult it in addition to the meta types that claim keys. Because it speaks for every key of such a parameterization, a metadata object whose base carries a base-form meta type is exempt from the unclaimed-key error below. This is how a brand is written: a meta type that constrains a base without naming any field of it.

    A MetaDeclaration may declare ONE type parameter, written with its domain as every parameter is, meta NumberBounds<T: type extends Ordered.<T>>, which is bound to the base at each parameterization the meta type governs. It is the name of what the base is, and it exists because a constraint shape whose fields live in the base's own value space cannot otherwise mention it: the shape is a type of its own that other code may name, so it is parameterized like any other. The parameter is never written at a use — uint8.<{ bounds: 1..=6 }> binds it to uint8 because uint8 is what is being parameterized — and it is the constraint shape that fixes how tightly it must be bounded, a shape holding a RangeBounds.<T> requiring an T that is ordered. A meta type that needs the base only within a hook declares no parameter, since a hook already receives values of the base; a bound expressed in the base's values is what the parameter is for. It is an early error for a MetaDeclaration to declare more than one type parameter, or for its constraint shape to take a number of type parameters other than the number the declaration takes.

    A meta type claims the property keys of its constraint shape. Claiming is global and flat, and is a property of the declaration rather than of an instantiation, so a parameterized meta type claims its keys once however many bases it governs: it is an early error, reported at the second MetaDeclaration rather than at any use, for two meta types to claim one key. A metadata object whose own key no meta type claims is a type error at the parameterization that writes it.

    The unclaimed-key judgment applies at every completed parameterization construction, including a reflected description. A published base-form meta type supplies the stated exemption for both String and Symbol keys; an incomplete or failed declaration supplies none. A construction reached at runtime reports an ordinary type error at that boundary. This does not defer a failure already required at a source-checking boundary.

    Declaration-time key claiming resolves a generic constraint shape in its declaring environment with its type parameters retained as binders. It does not apply the alias to fictitious arguments or require a self-dependent bound to hold of an unbound parameter. Key claiming does not discharge the constraints of a later application: the governing base must satisfy the applicable parameter constraints, and completed portions and defaults remain subject to their constraint-shape admission rules.

    Prepare a meta declaration's owner, constraint shape, keys, default snapshot and hooks before publishing that declaration's protocol. Check owner uniqueness, parameter count and key conflicts, evaluate and normalize the default once, and check its membership and the required hooks. Publish only after these operations complete successfully. A failed or incomplete declaration supplies no registered owner, key claims, shape, default, hooks or base-form exemption. Previously completed declarations retain their registrations; a later declaration or source-check failure does not roll them back. Effects of ordinary declaration instantiation and evaluation retain their existing rules.

    Conflict detection is distinct from protocol publication. Within one source check, an established owner and constraint shape already determine which later meta declarations would duplicate that owner or claim its keys, even if its default awaits permitted local initialization. Retain that information for checking subsequent declarations in source order, but do not expose it as a governing protocol or retain an incomplete declaration's reservation after the check ends. Revalidate ownership before publication if evaluating the default completed another declaration.

    At the checking boundary, a completed declaration failure is a StaticTypeError before source-body entry. An actually unavailable input and a failed computation using available inputs are distinct. Only a still-uninitialized direct binding belonging to the source being checked can justify deferring a local initialization dependency under the existing preparation rules. An exception from within a helper's own temporal dead zone, a previously retained exception, or an exception with the same class or message does not establish such a dependency. An uninitialized import needed at the module's required checking boundary remains a failure under 1.3.8.

    For a local declaration pending solely on such an uninitialized direct source binding, retain any already established constraint keys as private source-checking evidence. Detect a conflict between established pending claimants before body entry, even when no parameterization consumes the key. This evidence postpones only the unclaimed-key judgment for the matching key in that source; it does not register a claim, publish a default or hook, or supply the base-form exemption. A different unclaimed key still fails. A failed declaration or unavailable imported input supplies no pending local claimant. When evaluation reaches a parameterization, apply the ordinary ownership and admission checks against successfully published declarations and actual property-key identities.

    The default expression, its called helpers and the snapshot's getter evaluations are type-position computation. Apply the evaluable-fragment restrictions and the existing shared budget throughout that computation, including when the declaration is reached during evaluation. Exhaustion abandons the computation and cannot publish any part of the declaration; during the source check the evaluation-limit diagnostic retains precedence over incidental declaration errors. Successful preparation does not repeat the default computation when evaluation reaches the declaration's position.

    6.2.1 MetadataPortion ( m, M )

    The abstract operation MetadataPortion takes arguments m (an ECMAScript language value) and M (a meta type) and returns an Object. It returns the part of the metadata m that M governs. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let p be a copy of M's default.
    2. If m is an Object, then
      1. For each own property key k of m that M claims, set p's k to m's k.
    3. Return p.
