    Throughout this clause, a portion is M's default when the two are equivalent as Table 43 defines, not when they are the same object: MetadataPortion returns a fresh copy, so identity would make every meta type take part in every judgment and a brand refuse its own default.

    A value's effective portion is total: a value carrying no metadata of M has M's default portion, whether or not it carries another meta type's metadata. This is distinct from the constraint denoted by a type. A bare base type leaves M unpinned and admits parameterizations of that base; an explicitly written default portion pins M to that requirement. The latter remains a distinct Type Object. Admitting a particular bare value at that requirement does not make the bare base a subtype of the requirement.

    A default requirement applies at ordinary value boundaries as at operator arguments. When its effective source portion satisfies the required default without a conversion, the value is admitted unchanged, without acquiring a metadata carrier. Source metadata is inspected before considering the base or validation fallback: a value carrying a non-default portion cannot bypass that portion's subtype judgment merely because the required portion is the default. In particular, with exact dimensional subtyping, a plain scalar satisfies a written dimensionless requirement and a metre does not, including in an is test and after passing through a base-typed or any-typed binding.

    This value admission grants no permission to convert a borrowed location. A ref boundary retains its invariant location-type judgment and its reference-liveness checks, including when its callee is reached dynamically. The current value of a location satisfying a default requirement does not prove that the location has that type.

    Note 3

    Canonical metadata and the value presented to a program are separate views. A capture declared const D: Dimensions reads as a value of Dimensions; normalizing its numeric fields for metadata identity must not make D is Dimensions false. All metadata origins must use one normalization against the owning constraint shape before identity is established: defaults, written records, builder results and captured records. In particular, erasing the numeric tag of a typed default alone does not establish this invariant for an integer represented by a BigInt. Range endpoints retain the declared endpoint-domain normalization specified above, and an untyped Number and BigInt are not made equivalent.

    The metadata subtype judgment holds of two metadata values s and t when, for every meta type M declared in the surrounding realm for which MetadataPortion(s, M) or MetadataPortion(t, M) is not M's default, subtype of M holds of MetadataPortion(s, M) and MetadataPortion(t, M). The meta types declared in the surrounding realm are those declared as of the judgment's application: when the checking pass applies it, that is after the pass has processed the source text's own meta declarations (1.2.8) and after the evaluation of every source text evaluated before it.

    The validation judgment holds of a value v and a metadata value m when, for every meta type M whose MetadataPortion(m, M) is not M's default, M defines validate and it holds of v and that portion. A meta type that constrains and defines no validate therefore admits no bare value of the base at an annotation - the construction boundary, the cast or the Type Object call, is the way in, as it is for a brand - which is what makes a brand a brand and what makes const v: Velocity = 10; a type error until 6.5 gives number a way in.

    Note 4

    Decomposition is why one flat object serves every meta type at once: float32.<{ m: 1, s: -2, bounds: 0.. }> is read by the dimensions meta type as an acceleration and by the bounds meta type as a non-negative number, each seeing its own keys and the defaults of the rest, and neither seeing the other's. It also fixes what an omitted key means, since a portion is completed from default before any hook sees it: float32.<{ m: 1 }> is a metre because the remaining exponents default to zero, and a plain float32 is every meta type's default at once, which is what makes it dimensionless and unbounded rather than untyped. A meta type both of whose portions are its default takes no part in a judgment or a conversion, so declaring a meta type cannot change the relation between types that carry none of its metadata, and no hook is required to be reflexive at its own default.

    Claiming is global so that a key means one thing wherever it is written, and the diagnostic is at the declaration because that is where the collision is, not at the unlucky program that parameterized on m last. The cost is that a meta type cannot be extended by a third party: an extension ships as its own meta type with its own keys, and the Symbol keys of 1.5.19 are what keep two libraries from colliding at all.

    The where of a dependent record type (5), the brand, and the string pattern are meta types of this protocol declared by this specification rather than by a program, which is why nothing about them is special-cased above: a brand's subtype is the identity of its tag and it defines no validate, a pattern's validate is a full match and its subtype is the judgment 1.5.20 sanctions, and a where's validate runs its predicate while its subtype holds only where the required side is unconstrained or carries the same predicate.

    6.3 Conversion at a Boundary

    An implicit boundary to the bare base preserves metadata the supplied value already carries. An explicit conversion to the base may erase it. A bare annotation therefore supplies no proof that its value is plain. Neither value admission nor conversion changes the invariant type of a reference location or any reference-liveness requirement.

    A required metadata record pins each meta type for which it writes a claimed key, including a portion explicitly equal to that meta type's default. Pinning is independent of whether the completed portion governs a value. Unwritten portions do not constrain an argument and do not contribute a conversion factor.

    Two parameterizations of one base that differ in their metadata convert by this clause, which is the fourth case of Table 13 and applies at every boundary of Table 23, an operator's argument among them.

    6.3.1 ConvertParameterization ( value, from, to )

    The abstract operation ConvertParameterization takes arguments value (an ECMAScript language value), from (an ECMAScript language value), and to (an ECMAScript language value) and returns either a normal completion containing an ECMAScript language value or a throw completion. It converts value, whose metadata is from, to the metadata to. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let v be value.
    2. Let base be RuntimeTypeOf(value).
    3. If base.[[Kind]] is parameterized, set base to base.[[Base]].
    4. Let pinned be the meta types pinned by to.
    5. Let participating be a new empty List.
    6. For each meta type M of pinned, do
      1. If MetadataPortion(from, M) or MetadataPortion(to, M) is not equivalent to M's default, append M to participating.
    7. For each meta type M of participating, do
      1. Let fp be MetadataPortion(from, M).
      2. Let tp be MetadataPortion(to, M).
      3. If subtype of M holds of fp and tp, then
        1. NOTE: M admits the crossing, and requires nothing of the value.
      4. Else if fp is M's default and an implicit cast operator into M is declared on the base (6.5), then
        1. Set v to the result of applying that operator to v.
        2. If M defines validate and it does not hold of v and tp, throw a TypeError exception whose message names M and, where M defines describe, its description of tp.
      5. Else,
        1. Throw a TypeError exception whose message names M and, where M defines describe, its descriptions of fp and tp.
    8. Let f be the exact rational number 1.
    9. For each meta type M of participating that defines conversionFactor, do
      1. Let factor be ? the result of applying that hook to MetadataPortion(from, M) and MetadataPortion(to, M).
      2. If factor is not a finite real numeric scalar, throw a TypeError naming M and conversionFactor.
      3. Set f to the exact product of f and the mathematical value of factor, retaining any zero sign separately for the base's multiplication rule.
    10. Set v to ? ScaleMetadataValue(v, f, base).
    11. For each meta type M declared in the surrounding realm that defines quantize and whose MetadataPortion(to, M) is not M's default, set v to the result of quantize of M applied to v and MetadataPortion(to, M).
    12. Carry each unpinned source portion as described below, and retain every pinned target portion.
    13. If any meta type governing the resulting metadata defines a validation hook that rejects the resulting value and carried portion after scaling and quantization, throw a TypeError exception.
    14. Return v carrying the resulting metadata.

    Where the required metadata leaves a meta type unpinned, its source portion is preserved when f is one. Otherwise it is the normalized result of rescale applied to that portion and f, or its default when no rescale is declared. If every contributing factor was a Number or a binary floating-point value of width at most 64, the legacy rescale argument is the product rounded to Number; otherwise it is rational64 when the reduced exact product's numerator and positive denominator both fit int64, and rational.<bigint> otherwise. This is an explicit protocol presentation policy, independent of generic defaults. MetaProtocol defaults its Factor parameter to rational64, and the rescale factor parameter admits number | rational64 | rational.<bigint>. Representability is tested before construction; a caught error is not a signal to select the unbounded presentation. This presentation to a hook does not change the exact factor used to scale the value. A failed hook, invalid result, exhausted evaluation budget, or failed snapshot is never treated as an absent hook. A rescale result must satisfy the instantiated constraint shape; a quantize result must belong to the numeric base. These hooks propagate abrupt completions. Validation and quantization receive the raw numeric value.

    6.3.2 ScaleMetadataValue ( value, factor, base )

    The abstract operation ScaleMetadataValue takes arguments value (an ECMAScript language value), factor (a rational number), and base (a Type Record) and returns either a normal completion containing an ECMAScript language value or a throw completion. It scales in the base's numeric domain, without invoking user-language mixed-type multiplication or an operator definition. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If factor is 1, return value.
    2. If base is not a numeric primitive type, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. If value is finite and real, form the exact rational product of its value and factor.
    4. For a rational base, retain the exact product. For an integer base, truncate toward zero and apply the base's conversion overflow rule. For a binary floating-point or decimal base, round once to that base using its conversion rule.
    5. For a complex base, apply the corresponding real-component operation separately to its components.
    6. Preserve signed-zero and special-value behaviour under the base's multiplication rules. A special value of the input does not authorize a non-finite conversion factor.
    7. Return the resulting value of base.

    Each meta type gates the crossing independently, and there are exactly two ways through: subtype admits it, or the value carries nothing of that meta type and a cast supplies what it lacks. Meter reaches Kilometer by the first, since the exponents agree and only the ratio differs; a bare number reaches Velocity only by the second, which is why the design says that without a cast on number the assignment is a type error, and why a brand, for which no cast is declared, is reachable only by construction. validate is what the second way costs, and it is where a bound is enforced: subtype cannot prove an unconstrained value non-negative, so the cast into the bounds meta type checks it.

    The rest runs in the order above: the factor once, as the product over every meta type that contributes one; rescale on the portions that flow, so a bound stated in metres arrives stated in kilometres; and quantize after the scaling, so a value rounds onto the representation it will be stored in rather than one it passes through. Where every operand is a compile-time constant the whole of it folds and no check survives to run time (1.7.5).

    Note

    Kilometer(5) + Meter(300) is the worked case. The parameter is the receiver's dimensions, so the argument's metre constraint must pass subtype, which it does since the exponents agree; conversionFactor yields 1/1000, so the value becomes 0.3; the argument's bounds are not pinned by the parameter and so flow through rescale with that factor, arriving in kilometre space; and the operator body adds 5 and 0.3 with both operands in one unit system, which is the point of doing all of this before the body runs. Had the bound not been rescaled, a sum of bounds would have added a metre-space number to a kilometre-space one and produced a bound that means nothing.

    Taking the factor as a product over the meta types that contribute one, rather than applying each in turn, is a decision this specification makes where the design leaves an order: sequential application would make the result depend on the order meta types were declared in whenever a rescale is not linear, and an order-dependent type is the one thing the determinism invariant cannot have. Only the dimensions meta type contributes a factor in the design's own examples, so the two readings agree there and differ only where a second one appears.

    6.4 Narrowing a Constraint

    A comparison against a compile-time constant narrows the metadata of a parameterized value, as Table 24 records. The metadata it narrows to is NarrowMetadata(m, op, c), where m is the value's metadata, op the comparison, and c the constant: the metadata whose portion for each meta type M defining narrow is the result of narrow of M applied to MetadataPortion(m, M), the String naming op, and c, and whose portion for each other meta type is unchanged. The false branch narrows by the negation of op, pairing >= with <, > with <=, and == with !=, in both directions.

    Note

    This is what lets if (v >= 0) give v the type float32.<{ …, bounds: 0.. }> inside the branch, and a further if (v <= 343) intersect that bound to 0..=343, so that a return v into a type requiring both bounds passes subtype and needs no check at all. It is a narrowing and not a proof: a meta type that defines no narrow learns nothing from a comparison and keeps the constraint it had, which costs a check at the next boundary and nothing else.

    6.5 Operators on a Parameterized Primitive

    A declaration of the form primitive T P { … }, where T names a primitive type and P is up to two specialization lists (1.4.3.2), declares operators on T for each parameterization its parameters admit, and is the form that 1.9.9 allows an extension to supply. Its grammar, and that of the operator definitions within it, is 16's, which declares the same definitions on a class. What this clause fixes is what those definitions mean for metadata, which is this specification's to say because the metadata is.

    Each list of P is decided as a TypeArguments following a type is (1.4.2.2), by the type it follows: where that type declares type parameters the list matches them, the primitive's COMPONENTS; otherwise it is a pattern over METADATA, whose captures each bind the portion of the receiver's metadata claimed by the meta type its written domain names. float32 declares no parameters, so primitive float32<const D: Dimensions> captures metadata in its only list; complex declares its component type, so primitive complex<_><const T: P> matches every component and then captures metadata, and primitive complex<const E><const T: P> does the same while naming the component, a capture that takes its slot's domain, as the type complex.<float64>.<{ phase: 1 }> supplies its component and then its metadata; and primitive vector<float32.<const D: Dimensions>, const N: uint32> matches vector's element and lane count, capturing the element's metadata within. It is a Syntax Error for P to hold two lists where T declares no type parameters, since the first is already the metadata, or for a list of P to be a parameter list.

    These captures use MetadataPortion, including its default when the receiver carries none. An operator's own metadata parameters bind from its operand. A capture in a cast's destination is bound from the requested destination, not from the source's default. The projection rule is shared by specialization lists; repeating a capture compares completed portions, while admitting an operator argument uses the metadata subtype and conversion judgments for its pinned portions.

    Before consulting block definitions, a unary operation on a plain primitive value, or a binary operation on two plain primitive values of the same type, takes the primitive operation directly. No definition, including a definition without a body, contributes to that operation. A vector is plain for this purpose when its lanes carry no metadata. Compound assignment applies this rule to its underlying operation before checking the store. Mixed and parameterized operands continue through block dispatch.

    A bare Static Type is not proof of a plain runtime value: the binding may retain metadata admitted upward from a parameterization. The checker must not substitute defaults for these unknown portions. Where applicable definitions or their computed result metadata depend on such portions, the result is widened to a type admitting every possible result and the required boundary checks remain. The runtime fast path above is applicable statically only with a proof about the values, not from their bare annotations alone.

    The checking pass distinguishes an exact known portion, a known plain value whose projection is the default, an unknown portion, and a pattern that does not match. Unknown is not the default and is not failure. Its required local proof rules are: a numeric literal proves a plain value of its contextual base; parentheses preserve a fact; a conversion to a base proves plainness only from a proven plain numeric source; a parameterization supplies its written pinned portions but proves nothing about unpinned portions; ordinary unary and same-base plain arithmetic preserve plainness. A direct local initializer may copy these facts to a binding, and a direct assignment replaces its mutable fact. Calls, borrowing or possible aliasing, updates, control-flow boundaries, and entry to or exit from a nested function discard mutable facts. No fact is inferred from a bare parameter annotation or from an unknown property read. The proof walk is bounded to twenty nested expression steps, after which the fact is unknown.

    When only some captures are known, retain a result's numeric family, component type, lane count, and any result metadata independent of unknown captures. Widen metadata that depends on unknown captures. Join the possible successful return types of applicable value bodies and the built-in path when a plain pair remains possible; an unknown return requires an unknown result, rather than assuming the receiver's base. These rules determine the checking pass's baseline acceptance. Further optimization may elide checks already implied by that judgment; it may not introduce additional Early Errors.

    Operator evaluation first evaluates each original operand once, prepares candidate operand requirements, and selects a value definition. Receiver-block precedence and strict operand specificity take priority. For equal instantiated operand types, the existing fixed-over-captured preference applies. For different parameterizations that mutually admit one another and are otherwise tied, an exact match of every pinned portion beats one requiring a metadata crossing. Exactness compares descriptors, never the numeric payload or a computed factor; zero values and factor-one conversions do not affect ranking. Incomparable requirements and remaining ties are ambiguous.

    Convert the selected operand once before evaluating any metadata-only return builder. Rebind fresh operand captures from this effective operand, then check contribution applicability without selecting a different value body. With no value body, compatible metadata-only requirements combine into one conversion target; conflicting pinned portions are ambiguous. Independently captured portions already equal to their required portions impose no conversion. A result builder observes the converted and rescaled portions. Compare the completed, normalized portions from every applicable contribution, including the selected value definition and all definitions without a body. Equivalent repeated contributions are permitted; conflicting contributions to one result portion are a type error, independent of declaration order. The same rule applies to vector lane metadata. Detect a conflict before invoking the selected value body or storing a compound result. The raw value body receives this same effective operand with metadata removed.

    Note 1

    The rule is the one a type position already applies, so a block's header reads as the type it covers. A component slot is not a metadata position, so a capture naming a meta type there, primitive complex<const T: P>, restates the component's domain type as P and is refused by 1.4.3.2.3; its diagnostic offers primitive complex<_><const T: P>. Which lists a primitive's parameters make components is known from the primitive alone, since every primitive is predefined.

    An operator body evaluates on raw values: no operator declared by any block is re-entered within one, so return this + rhs; inside operator+ is the primitive addition rather than itself. The metadata of a result comes from the return type annotations alone. For one operator invocation, definitions are compared by the block that declares them: a block over the receiver's own primitive, primitive uint8, is more specific than a block over the family that primitive belongs to, primitive uint<const W>, since a fixed component is more specific than a capture (1.4.3.2), and a definition of the more specific block is chosen over one of the less specific whatever their order. Among the definitions of the most specific block that has a matching one, the definition with a body whose operand type is the most specific of those that match is chosen, whatever their order: one whose operand type is a subtype of every other matching one's, where of two equal operand types the one written without the block's captures, rhs: uint.<16>, is more specific than one naming them, rhs: uint.<W>; where no matching definition is the most specific, the invocation throws a TypeError, as a call no overload is most specific for is refused; any number of definitions without a body may match, each contributing its own meta type's portion of the result through its return type; where no definition with a body matches, the primitive operation runs; and the portions the matching return types evaluate to are merged into one flat metadata object, each meta type contributing its default where no matching definition mentions it.

    The raw-body rule removes result metadata obligations, not the declared base result obligation. The raw result type of a declared result is that type with its metadata parameterizations replaced by their bases, including through union and intersection alternatives and in vector lane types. Preserve numeric widths, component types, lane counts, literal restrictions, and ordinary structural member contracts. Judge each return, including implicit undefined on normal completion without a return, against that raw result type by the ordinary return checking rules. An unknown metadata capture does not obscure an independently known base. A statically decidable failure is an Early Error even if the operator is never invoked; unresolved obligations remain runtime checks.

    When established operand contracts determine a selected definition's component and metadata captures, a computed declared result is a checking obligation in that definition's lexical environment with those captures bound. Retain the identity of the definition, the operation and the determining arguments when reusing its answer. An open annotation at declaration does not make this closed application unknown. Resolve newly determined result dependencies, including an enclosing operation or a later binding that consumes a computed result, before admitting a source text. Unavailable inputs remain unresolved; the checking pass does not execute ordinary value bodies or initializers to supply them. Only the selected value definition and applicable bodyless contributions require their result computations, under the existing evaluation budget.

    After the selected value body completes normally, apply RequireType to its raw result and the raw result type of its resolved declared return. Perform this admission with operator-block re-entry still suppressed and the selected capture bindings still active. Use the declaration's captured environment, not same-spelled bindings at the invocation. Only after successful admission attach the already-composed result metadata. An abrupt body or admission completion propagates without publishing a result; restore the capture and operator-body state on every completion. Effects already performed by the body are not rolled back. An annotation such as any or a union describes admissible results; it does not replace the admitted value's primitive representation with an abstract contract tag. A definition without a declared result does not acquire the receiver's base as a return obligation.

    A String receiver consults its primitive string definitions before the built-in fallback, including when its representation carries a literal or refined String type. Literal refinement alone does not change the underlying primitive for protection of a pair of plain values: a broad operand definition cannot replace ordinary String/String operations merely because either value carries a literal type. Actual metadata parameterizations retain their dispatch eligibility. Boxed Strings remain Objects; do not perform ToPrimitive to discover a String receiver for block lookup. The raw-body and result-composition rules apply to parameterized String values too: remove operand metadata for the body and attach the merged declared metadata to its String result.

    A registered block that may apply prevents a checking pass from proving the built-in fallback solely from the absence of locally reconstructed declaration syntax. Recover a signature in its declaration and captured environment, including across source texts; where that proof remains unresolved, retain an unknown result and the required runtime result checks. A dynamically constructed function's own declarations participate in the source judgment as ordinary source declarations do.

    For this recovery, retain the identity of the declaring block and definition, its fixed operand and result descriptors, and its lexical and private environments and captured enclosing generic substitutions. This applies to definitions with and without a value body. Instantiate the definition's component and metadata captures from the established operand inputs. Resolve remaining type syntax in that declaration context, not in same-spelled consumer bindings or an unrelated active generic frame. Restore the consumer's evaluation context on normal and abrupt completion.

    Use the same plain-value protection, receiver precedence, operand admission and specificity as dispatch before applying built-in numeric-family exclusions. A definition that admits only part of a static operand domain is not disjoint from that domain: retain that possible selection instead of choosing a broader definition or fallback as if it were absent. Unknown metadata remains unknown. A statically established unique value definition supplies its declared result; a result of an unselected value definition need not be evaluated to answer this query and cannot cause its failure. Definitions without a body retain the result-contribution rules above.

    A required dependent result whose inputs are established is evaluated by the existing pre-evaluation fragment in the captured declaration context with those inputs substituted. Do not replay an earlier source or execute the ordinary operator body to recover its signature. Keep distinct queries for distinct consumer sites, declaring definitions, captured contexts or determining substitutions; reusing a completed result requires all its determining inputs to agree. Existing fragment resource requirements apply. Failure to evaluate a required type and an assignability failure established by the resulting type are distinct failures, both before consumer body entry. Where required inputs remain unresolved, preserve the existing deferred judgment and runtime checks. This signature recovery supplies neither reference permission nor proof of reference liveness.

    Two definitions declared for one operand are found at their declarations: it is an early error for two blocks of one level of specificity to define one operator with operand types that are the same, where a capture of either header is read by the role it plays, the component position it stands for or the meta type it captures, rather than by its name. So primitive uint<const W> { operator +(rhs: uint.<W>) … } and primitive uint<const V> { operator +(rhs: uint.<V>) … } declare one operand twice, while rhs: float64.<X>, the receiver's own metadata, and rhs: float64, any float64, are different operands.

    A definition chosen for an invocation is the meaning of that operator for its receiver and operand, not a conversion of either, so the rule that two different numeric types do not mix applies only where no definition speaks for the pair: with primitive float64 { operator *(rhs: uint8): float64 { … } } declared, (2 := float64) * (3 := uint8) is that definition, and its type is the definition's return type, while (2 := float64) * (3 := uint16) still does not mix. A static check chooses the definition as the invocation does, from the declared operand types, and counts every block of the program, as the operators are defined before any code runs.

    A block definition with a body replaces the operation for its pair, so the rule of 16 that an operator a type already defines may not be redeclared for it refuses a definition with a body whose operand type is the receiver's own type without metadata: primitive uint8 { operator +(rhs: uint8) … } redeclares uint8 addition and is an early error. Over a primitive that declares type parameters, a block covers every member, so an operand of the same family, rhs: uint.<W> or rhs: uint.<16> in primitive uint<const W>, coincides with some member's own pair and is refused alike. A parameterization is a type of its own, so rhs: float64.<X> declares an operator the base does not define, as do another type and another width; a definition without a body contributes metadata and replaces nothing. The comparison operators are dispatched as the arithmetic operators are, and != is the negation of the == a block defines, as it is for a class, so neither is declared on its own.

    Whether a definition matches an operand that its annotation writes with the block's captures, rhs: float32.<X> in primitive float32<const X: Dimensions>, is judged by the portions those captures speak for: the operand's effective Dimensions portion must be admitted by X under the metadata subtype judgment, and the metadata of every other meta type it carries is not the block's to judge. Any required conversion is performed after selection and before the raw body; this is argument admission, not the equality test for repeating a capture in a structural pattern. A block for one meta type therefore applies to a value that also carries another, and the result's metadata is merged per meta type as above, the portions the matching definitions give and the default of each meta type none mentions.

    Such a declaration may also define an implicit cast operator, written as an operator whose name is a parameterization of the primitive, which supplies the conversion of Table 13 from the bare primitive into a parameterization. At a boundary, one is invoked for each meta type the required metadata constrains and the supplied value's does not, and its absence is why such a boundary is otherwise a type error: const v: Velocity = 10; compiles exactly where number declares a cast into the dimensions meta type, and a bare number reaches a bounded type only through a cast whose boundary runs validate.

    An implicit cast likewise admits its raw result at the base of the actual target before attaching target metadata. Apply the base's ordinary checked conversion, without re-entering the metadata crossing. The metadata validation required by the receiving boundary still follows. The cast's target metadata is therefore not a return-boundary requirement inside its body, but its base representation remains a requirement.

    A block's COMPONENT capture is bound, for each invocation, from the receiver's own argument at that position, as its metadata captures are bound from the receiver's metadata: in primitive complex<const E> { operator +(rhs: complex.<E>): complex.<E> { … } } a complex128 receiver binds E to float64, and a uint16 receiver of primitive uint<const W> binds W to 16. A block over a primitive represented as an object, such as complex or rational, is consulted as any other is, before that primitive's own operation.

    A cast's name is a type, read as every type is (1.4.2.2), so where the primitive declares parameters the name supplies them before its metadata: complex.<T> names a complex whose component is T, never a metadata parameterization. A capture of the block's header in a cast's name stands for every value of its domain, so the name describes a family of parameterizations and the cast covers each of them: in primitive complex<const E><const T: Phase> { operator complex.<E>.<T>() { return this; } } the one cast serves a crossing into complex.<float64>.<{ phase: 1 }> and into complex.<float32>.<{ phase: 1 }> alike, and primitive float32<const D: Dimensions> { operator float32.<D>() { … } }, over a primitive that declares no parameters, needs no component.

    Note 2

    A cast's declared parameterization names what its result BECOMES, and is not a boundary its body must already satisfy. The raw-body rule above applies to a cast as it does to any other operator, so the body evaluates on raw values and the usual whole of one is return this;: its result is admitted at the target base and then taken AT the target metadata, rather than checked against that metadata inside the body. Reading the annotation as a boundary instead makes the plainest cast anyone will write fail inside its own body, because the return would re-enter the very crossing the cast defines - which is the case the raw-body rule exists to prevent, arriving from the other direction.

    What a cast does not do is replace the check. Its result reaches the boundary as any other value does, so a validate hook still judges it: a cast is how a value gets IN, not a way past what the metadata requires. A bounds meta type therefore still refuses an out-of-range value a cast produced, which is why const v: Velocity = 10; and a bounded type behave differently though both cross through one.

     Note 3

    The raw-body rule is what makes the whole protocol terminate: an operator body is the definition of the operation, so an expression inside it cannot mean the thing being defined. It is also why the boundary conversion of 6.3 happens before the body and not within it: a body sees operands already converted, quantized, and in one unit system, and needs to know nothing about metadata to be correct.

    Splitting a value definition from metadata-only definitions is what lets two meta types share an operator without either knowing of the other. The dimensions block computes the sum and says the exponents are unchanged; the bounds block says the sum's bounds are the sum of the bounds and computes nothing; the result carries both. A meta type that has nothing to say about an operator says nothing, and its portion of that result is its default, which is the correct answer for a constraint that the operation does not preserve.

    7 Declaration Reflection and Decorators

    The reflection of 1.12.3 reads a type. This clause reads a declaration: the fields a class declares, the parameters a function takes, the enumerators an enum lists, and what a decorator has recorded about any of them. The two are one facility under one name, selected by a first type argument, and they answer different questions: a type is shared by everything of that shape, and a declaration is the one place a program wrote it down.

    7.1 Token Records

    A Token Record is one token of source, as the lexical grammar produced it. It has the fields of Table 44.

    Tokens are what a decorator reads of the syntax it decorates, and what a replacement decorator returns. They are deliberately below a syntax tree: the lexical grammar of this specification is already normative and changes far more slowly than the syntactic grammar, so a token vocabulary is a surface that can be exposed without inventing one.

    Note 1

    [[LineTerminatorBefore]] is carried because a LineTerminator is semantically significant: automatic semicolon insertion depends on it, so text produced from tokens that emitted a space where the source had a newline would join a statement to the one above it. A separator is enough to keep two tokens from merging; it is not enough to preserve what they mean.

     Note 2

    regexp and punctuator are distinct kinds because the lexical grammar of this specification is not context-free: InputElementDiv and InputElementRegExp resolve / differently, so a token stream is parse-informed rather than purely lexical. A token a replacement decorator PRODUCES must therefore say which it means, and the kind carries it — the ambiguity is resolved by construction rather than by re-scanning the output.

     Note 3

    Delimited runs are grouped rather than flat, so a macro cannot produce unbalanced output: the delimiters of a group are the record's, not two tokens a producer must remember to pair. The engine already matches delimiters to find a decoration's boundary, so the grouping costs nothing it was not doing.

    A Span Record says where a token came from. It has the fields of Table 45.

    A Source Reference Record names a buffer. It has the fields of Table 46.

    Note 4

    A Span Record is not a source map. It says where ONE token came from, and it travels with that token wherever a replacement decorator moves it, so a chain of expansions needs no composition step: a token copied by one decorator and relocated by another still names the position a program was written at. The alternative — an offset map per expansion, composed across a chain — is where source-map correctness usually fails, and it fails silently.

    7.2 TokensOf ( node )

    The abstract operation TokensOf takes argument node (a Parse Node) and returns a List of Token Records. It returns the tokens of node's source text, with each token's [[Span]] naming the position it was written at. Delimited runs are returned as group tokens rather than as separate delimiters. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let text be the source text matched by node.
    2. Let source be the Source Reference Record for the buffer containing text.
    3. Let tokens be a new empty List.
    4. For each token t matched by the lexical grammar over text, in order, do
      1. Let span be a Span Record with [[Source]] source, [[Start]] the index of t's first code unit in that buffer, and [[End]] the index after t's last code unit.
      2. If t opens a run delimited by {, [, or (, then
        1. Let inner be the result of performing this operation over the tokens the run delimits.
        2. Append a Token Record with [[Kind]] group, [[Value]] t's source text, [[Span]] span, and [[Tokens]] inner to tokens.
        3. Advance past the run.
      3. Else,
        1. Append a Token Record with [[Kind]] the lexical form of t, [[Value]] t's source text, [[Span]] span, and [[Tokens]] empty to tokens.
    5. Return tokens.
     Note

    The lexical goal symbol at each position is the one the enclosing parse used, so / is already resolved to punctuator or regexp and no ambiguity reaches the caller.

    7.3 TokenStream Objects

    A TokenStream is an Array exotic object whose elements are Token Records exposed as objects, and whose prototype is %TokenStream.prototype%. It is what a reflection's syntax-valued fields hold and what a replacement decorator exchanges.

    7.3.1 TokenStream.prototype.toString ( )

    1. Let stream be the this value.
    2. Return the source text the tokens of stream were taken from, in order, including the trivia between adjacent tokens of one buffer.
     Note

    Comments and whitespace are recoverable rather than discarded: consecutive tokens of one buffer have the text between their spans, so the gap IS the trivia. This is why no separate source-text field exists on a reflection — a second field would be a second way to say one thing, and the two would have to agree forever.

    %TokenStream% is the intrinsic object holding the operation below; %TokenStream.prototype% is the prototype of every TokenStream.

    7.3.2 TokenStream.prototype.parse ( start, end, goal )

    Parses a range of this stream's source text and answers its tokens.

    1. Let stream be the this value.
    2. If stream is not a TokenStream, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Let source be the [[Source]] of the [[Span]] of the first element of stream's [[TokenRecords]]; if there is none, throw a TypeError exception.
    4. Let text be source.[[Text]].
    5. Let from be ? ToIntegerOrInfinity(start).
    6. Let to be ? ToIntegerOrInfinity(end).
    7. If from < 0, to > the length of text, or from > to, throw a RangeError exception.
    8. If goal is neither "expression" nor "statements", throw a TypeError exception.
    9. Let parsed be ParseText(the substring of text from from to to, AssignmentExpression if goal is "expression" and StatementList otherwise), with the [Yield], [Await], and [Return] parameters and the strictness of the region this stream came from.
    10. If parsed is a List of errors, throw a SyntaxError exception whose position is from within source.
    11. Return a TokenStream over TokensOf(parsed).
     Note

    This is what lets a replacement decorator define a syntax the implementation does not know. A macro captures its region, reads whatever it likes, and delegates the ranges that are ECMAScript - and what it gets back is threaded from THAT parse, so a RegularExpressionLiteral is one token and a TemplateLiteral is one token.

    It is the one thing a macro cannot do for itself. Whether / begins a regular expression or a division is not decidable lexically: after } it depends on whether the brace closed a block or an ObjectLiteral, which needs a parse. A macro re-lexing a range gets four tokens where there is one regular expression, and no way to tell it from a division.

    The context parameters come from where the REGION sits rather than from the caller. await, yield and return are legal only under a context the enclosing parse established, and a macro has nothing sensible to pass - passing anything would let it parse await into a synchronous function.

    "module" is not a goal: a range of a region is never one, and admitting it would put an ImportDeclaration inside a macro's region.

    7.3.3 TokenStream.gensym ( hint )

    The abstract operation TokenStream.gensym takes argument hint (a String) and returns a Token Record. It returns an identifier Token Record that cannot collide with any identifier in any source text or in any other stream. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return a Token Record with [[Kind]] identifier, a [[Value]] derived from hint that is distinct from every identifier produced by any other call and from every IdentifierName in any source text, and a [[Span]] whose [[Source]] names the caller.
     Note

    This is the hygiene mechanism. A replacement decorator uses it for every identifier it INTRODUCES, so a macro's temporaries cannot capture a binding at the position it is spliced into. It does not address a macro's REFERENCE to an identifier it did not create — a macro naming Date still meets a shadowing Date — which no mechanism short of syntax contexts on every binding addresses, and which the spans above make detectable even where they do not prevent it.

    7.4 Preprocessor Modules

    "preprocessor" is a supported import attribute key: 16.2.1.12.1 returns a List containing it. A module imported with an ImportAttribute Record whose [[Key]] is "preprocessor" and whose [[Value]] is "true" is a preprocessor module. Its exports may be used as replacement decorators in the importing module.

    A decoration whose IdentifierReference is a name a preprocessor import bound, and which is followed by {, takes that brace and its match as a region rather than decorating an ObjectLiteral. No attribute declares this: being a preprocessor decoration is what makes the braces a region, and preprocessor is as lexically visible as any other key - so a tool that does not resolve imports recognises a region exactly as it would have from a dedicated one.

    Note 1

    The cost is stated rather than left to be found: a preprocessor name cannot decorate an object LITERAL, so @m { a: 1 } is a region for every preprocessor m. Parentheses do not restore it, @name ( beginning an argument list, and the only way out is a second import of the same name without the attribute.

    A decoration on a declaration is unaffected. @m class C {} decorates the class, and @m function f() {} the function; only a { following the decoration directly is displaced.

    A replacement decorator's region is captured, always, because it is a replacement decorator: what such a decorator RECEIVES is a TokenStream (7.9), and the text of what it decorates is the only thing that can be. Capture is not a mode a macro selects; it follows from what a replacement decorator is. A decoration whose imported binding is NOT one — a function that does not take a TokenStream and return a token sequence — takes a Block, parsed, and its tokens are those of that parse. Its extent is found by matching delimiters, and its text reaches the decorator as tokens of the ordinary lexical grammar. A macro that wants a range of its region READ AS ECMASCRIPT asks for it, through TokenStream.prototype.parse (7.3), which is how a macro delegates the parts of its own syntax that are ECMAScript.

    Note 2
    Note 3

    The declaration is what is read, rather than a property set on the exported value. A macro that takes a TokenStream and returns a token sequence has SAID what it is, and its region's text is what such a decorator receives — so the signature already carries the answer, and a marker beside it could only agree or disagree with what the program wrote. The same reasoning decides which names a preprocessor import contributes (7.6.1): read the declaration, not an artifact of running it.

    It also settles WHEN the answer is available. A property must be read from an evaluated module; a parameter's type is in the text. The engine still evaluates a preprocessor module before parsing the module that imports it, so nothing turns on this today, but the rule no longer depends on it.

    A macro that annotates no context takes a parsed Block, which is what a macro declaring no capture took. No program written against an earlier edition changes meaning by this rule alone.

    The engine provides no grammars, so a decorator is not choosing among them. A macro whose region is not ECMAScript - a query language, a markup dialect - captures it, reads its text, and hands back the ranges that ARE ECMAScript through 7.3.2. That is what lets a variant of such a language be written without the implementation changing, which naming a grammar could never do.

    A preprocessor module is fetched and evaluated before the importing module is parsed. The loader blocks on it as it blocks for a module with top-level await; the preprocessor module itself cannot await, because 1.2.7 gives it nothing asynchronous to name.

    How the macro reaches the parse: the importing module's source is scanned for preprocessor imports before it is parsed, which is possible because an import declaration is at the top of a module and lexes as ordinary ECMAScript. Each module so named is loaded, linked and evaluated, and the value a decoration is spelled with is the export its import BINDS. import { jsx as h } declares @h and asks the module for jsx, and import jsx from declares @jsx and asks for "default" — a default import binds a name like any other, and the export it binds is the one a decoration spelled with that name resolves to. A NAMESPACE import and a bare ModuleSpecifier introduce no such name: the first binds one name to every export rather than to any one of them, and the second binds none at all, so a preprocessor module imported either of those ways provides no replacement decorators.

    The load is synchronous: an implementation completes it before the parse that is waiting on it, and a host that cannot answer in time is reported at the import rather than waited for. The specification says the loader blocks; what a host unable to block is owed is this.

    Note 4

    Blocking here does not require asynchrony. The loading operations call the host and the host calls back, re-entering the graph - a callback arrangement rather than an asynchronous one - so a host that answers before returning resolves the whole graph in time.

    A preprocessor module may itself import preprocessor modules, and they are loaded and evaluated before it is parsed, recursively. A preprocessor cycle - a preprocessor module that imports, directly or transitively, the module importing it - is a Syntax Error, reported at the import that closes the cycle.

    Note 5

    This is a stronger rule than ECMAScript modules have, which permit cycles, and the difference is worth stating rather than leaving a reader to assume the module graph's behaviour carries over. An ordinary cycle works because evaluation can observe a partially-initialised binding. Here the PARSE depends on the evaluation, and a partial parse is not a thing: to parse A you evaluate its preprocessor B, to parse B you evaluate its preprocessor A, and to evaluate A you parse A. Template Haskell's stage restriction refuses the same shape for the same reason.

    A preprocessor module is evaluated in the realm of the module importing it.

    Note 6

    Expansion is per-realm, a constant expression's cache is keyed per-realm (38), and Type Objects are interned per-realm. Evaluating a preprocessor elsewhere would put half of that somewhere else, and two realms importing one preprocessor would share a macro object across them.

    A preprocessor module and every export of it used as a replacement decorator must be compile-time evaluable. It is a Syntax Error otherwise, reported at the declaration that is not evaluable.

    Note 7

    Evaluability is the whole of the sandbox. An evaluable function reads only its parameters, constants, and other evaluable functions, so it cannot NAME the clock, randomness, I/O, or ambient state — Date.now, Math.random, WeakRef, and locale-sensitive operations are all unreachable by construction rather than withheld by a realm. Expansion is therefore a pure function of its input, which is what lets an implementation cache an expansion beside the code it compiled to, and what lets a build tool perform an expansion ahead of time and get the answer an implementation would.

    The constraint binds evaluation as well as expansion: a module that could read the network while evaluating would close over what it read, and its decorators would not be pure however pure their bodies were.

     Note 8

    Local mutation is evaluable — a Set of seen keys, an accumulator — and shared module-level mutable state is not, which is the same line 1.2.7 already draws for type builders and where clauses. A replacement decorator and a type builder are both user code an implementation runs while compiling, and they are one discipline.

    7.5 Captured Regions

    A captured region is the region a decoration on a REPLACEMENT decorator takes (7.4). The region begins at the { that follows the decoration, optionally preceded by do, and ends at the matching } as 7.5.1 finds it. Its contents are not parsed; its text reaches the replacement decorator as tokens of the ordinary lexical grammar, and the decorator reads it however its own syntax requires.

    Note 1

    7.5.1 counts brackets it does not interpret, so a captured region's text must BALANCE its brackets outside comments and literals. @m { <p>a } b</p> } ends at the brace in the text and not at the one the author meant, which is a property of capturing rather than of any grammar a decorator implements.

    The do is optional in every position and means nothing to the decorator: the token stream begins at the region, so @m do { ... } and @m { ... } deliver the same tokens. Both spellings are available wherever the other is.

    Note 2

    do { } exists because a { beginning an expression is an ObjectLiteral and a block that produces a value needs distinguishing from one. A captured region is parsed as neither - its extent is found by matching delimiters and its contents are never read as ECMAScript - so the distinction does not arise, and requiring do would buy nothing.

    It has a cost, which is stated rather than left to be discovered: a preprocessor name's { always begins a region, so the decorated object literal form - @name { a: 1 } - is unavailable for that name. Importing a name as a preprocessor therefore changes what @name { ... } means throughout the module. Parentheses do not restore it - @name ( begins an argument list, so @name ({ a: 1 }) is a decoration taking an object as an ARGUMENT - and the only way to decorate an object literal with a preprocessor name is to import it a second time without the attribute.

    A decoration's arguments are read as ECMAScript even where its region is read otherwise: a capture governs the region, not the decoration.

    A captured region is never evaluated. It is replaced by whatever its decorator returns, and what a decorator returns is ECMAScript however its region was scanned: a capture governs ingestion only. The grammar outside a captured region is unaffected, so a < b and a type argument list are read as they always were.

    Note 3

    Without this a region must be lexable as ECMAScript to reach a decorator at all, which forecloses most of what a syntax replacement is for. < cannot begin an expression, so <div/> fails at the < before the closing tag is reached - the same failure < 2 gives, and not the ambiguity the / in a closing tag raises. That second ambiguity is real and downstream of it: a </div>/ parses as a less-than the regular expression /div>/.

    7.6 settles the outgoing direction of that ambiguity, by having a decorator return a token whose kind resolves it. The incoming direction is what a capture settles, and the two are not the same problem: outgoing, the engine is told; incoming, it must decide before it has anything to be told by.

    Because a captured region is found rather than tokenized, an implementation records its source range and the tokens the region produced. Expansion replaces a decoration's target by source range (7.7), so a region that is scanned but not recorded cannot be replaced.

    A captured region's text reaches the replacement decorator as written. No entity is decoded and no whitespace is normalized, because both are conventions of the embedded language rather than facts about it: a whitespace run that one dialect drops another preserves, and two implementations of the same dialect ship different entity tables. A decorator applies whichever its language defines.

    7.5.1 ScanBalancedRun ( source, start )

    The abstract operation ScanBalancedRun takes arguments source (a String) and start (a non-negative integer) and returns an integer or unbalanced. It finds the end of a delimited run whose contents it does not interpret. It is used to find the extent of a captured region, whose contents are not ECMAScript and so cannot be found by scanning tokens. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Assert: The code unit at start within source is one of (, [, or {.
    2. Let stack be a new empty List.
    3. Let index be start.
    4. Repeat, while index < the length of source,
      1. Let c be the code unit at index within source.
      2. If c begins a single-line comment, a multi-line comment, a string literal, or a template literal, then
        1. Set index to the index just past that comment or literal. Within a template literal, each substitution is itself a delimited run and balances.
        2. If no such end exists, return unbalanced.
      3. Else if c is one of (, [, or {, then
        1. Append the matching close delimiter to stack.
        2. Set index to index + 1.
      4. Else if c is one of ), ], or }, then
        1. If stack is empty or the last element of stack is not c, return unbalanced.
        2. Remove the last element of stack.
        3. Set index to index + 1.
        4. If stack is empty, return index.
      5. Else,
        1. Set index to index + 1.
    5. Return unbalanced.
     Note

    Recognising comments and string forms is not optional: a } within one is not a delimiter, and counting braces without them ends a region in the wrong place.

    A regular expression is deliberately not recognised, and this is not an omission. Within a captured region the contents are not ECMAScript, so / is whatever the decorator says it is - in a JSX-shaped syntax it opens a closing tag - and a { within it is a real delimiter. Outside a region the opposite holds, which is why a </{/ scans a regular expression and swallows the brace. No single scanner serves both readings, which is the reason a region declares its mode rather than being guessed at.

    7.6 Replacement Decorators

    A replacement decorator is a decorator whose name was introduced by a preprocessor module's import clause. It receives the tokens of what it decorates and returns tokens that replace them, before the importing module is parsed.

    The name is decided syntactically

    A decoration names a replacement decorator if and only if its IdentifierReference is an element of ReplacementDecoratorNames of the Module.

    7.6.1 Static Semantics: ReplacementDecoratorNames

    The syntax-directed operation ReplacementDecoratorNames takes no arguments and returns a List of Strings. It returns the names a module's preprocessor imports introduce. It is computed from the ImportDeclarations alone, so it is available before the module is expanded and cannot be changed by expanding it.

    1. Let names be a new empty List.
    2. For each ImportDeclaration d of the ModuleItemList of this Module, do
      1. If d has a WithClause with an ImportAttribute Record whose [[Key]] is "preprocessor" and whose [[Value]] is "true", then
        1. If d has an ImportedDefaultBinding, append the StringValue of that ImportedDefaultBinding to names.
        2. For each ImportSpecifier i of d's NamedImports, append the StringValue of i's ImportedBinding to names.
    3. Return names.
     Note

    A namespace import and a bare ModuleSpecifier do not contribute: the first introduces only a name reached through a member access, which is not an IdentifierReference and so cannot appear in a decoration at all, and the second introduces no name. A DEFAULT import does contribute, because it introduces exactly the kind of name a decoration is spelled with. import jsx from "./jsx.js" with { preprocessor: "true" }; followed by @jsx { ... } is the shape a module with one macro takes, and it is the common one - a preprocessor module usually provides a single replacement decorator, which is what a default export is for.

    Static Semantics: Early Errors

    Module : ModuleBodyopt
    • It is a Syntax Error if the BoundNames of ModuleBody contains any element of ReplacementDecoratorNames of Module.
    • It is a Syntax Error if a decoration whose IdentifierReference is an element of ReplacementDecoratorNames of Module appears closer to the decorated declaration than a decoration whose IdentifierReference is not.
    Note 1

    The first makes a name introduced by a preprocessor import unshadowable, which is what lets the second be decided without resolving a binding. Both are computed from the module's own text, so neither depends on anything expansion produces.

     Note 2

    The rule is syntactic rather than scoped because a scope query would be circular: a replacement decorator may introduce declarations, so the scope to resolve against is not complete until expansion has finished, which is the thing the query would decide. Fixing the names by inspection breaks the cycle, and the cost is that a replacement decorator cannot be aliased or locally rebound.

     Note 3

    A consequence for the decorator's own output: a replacement decorator cannot emit a call to the name it is spelled with. A preprocessor import is an ordinary import declaration carrying an attribute, so the name it introduces is a live binding whose value is the macro, and the first rule above forbids the module binding it to anything else. Emitted code naming it therefore calls the MACRO at run time, and no runtime helper can take the name back - a global of that name is shadowed by the import as it would be by any other. A macro pairing itself with a runtime dispatch gives the two different names, which is what React's automatic runtime does from the other direction when it imports its dispatch as _jsx.

    Placement

    Note 4

    Replacement decorators are written outermost because they run first, so source order agrees with execution order between the two kinds. It also gives them the capability the arrangement exists for: a replacement encloses the runtime decorations, so it can rewrite them, or remove them together with what it replaces.

    Arguments

    The arguments of a replacement decorator are Token Records and are not evaluated. @f(0) passes a numeric token and @f(Serialize) passes an identifier token.

    Note 5

    This is an exception to the rule that decorator expressions are evaluated in document order (7.16): a replacement decorator runs before the module is parsed, so there is no scope to evaluate an argument against.

    One replacement decorator per name

    A name denotes one REPLACEMENT decorator. Selection among replacement decorators is not overload resolution: the arguments of every one of them are Token Records, so there is nothing for a type-directed rule to select on.

    A name may nonetheless carry an ORDINARY decorator as well, since the two are told apart by their signatures rather than by their arguments: a replacement decorator is the overload that takes a TokenStream and returns a token sequence (7.4), and an ordinary decorator is any other. Where a name carries both, the replacement runs at expansion and the ordinary one at decoration, in that order, and a decoration whose position the ordinary overload does not accept is a type error at that decoration. One name may therefore transform a construct and then decorate what it produced.

    Note 6

    Overload resolution selects on argument types, and the arguments of a replacement decorator are all Token Records. There is nothing for a type-directed rule to select on, and a macro that wishes to distinguish its arguments inspects them.

    Frequency

    A replacement decorator runs once for each decoration, at expansion. This includes a decoration on a block, which a runtime block decorator would run on every entry to that block.

    Note 7

    A replacement block decorator rewrites the block once and may emit whatever per-entry work is wanted inline, so the work happens per entry where the decorator does not. The per-iteration cost a runtime block decorator carries does not arise.

    7.7 Expansion

    Expansion is the phase in which replacement decorators run. It occurs after a module's source text has been scanned far enough to find its decoration boundaries, and before the module is parsed and checked.

    1. Let names be the replacement decorator names of the module (7.6).
    2. Let depth be 0.
    3. Repeat, while some decoration in the module names an element of names,
      1. If depth > the implementation's expansion limit, throw a SyntaxError exception naming the decoration and depth.
      2. Let d be the outermost such decoration in source order.
      3. Let result be ? ApplyReplacementDecorator(d).
      4. Replace the tokens d decorated, and d itself, with result.
      5. Set depth to depth + 1.
    4. Return the module's tokens.
     Note 1

    Expansion is a fixpoint: the tokens a replacement decorator returns may themselves contain decorations, and those are expanded in turn. The order is OUTERMOST first, so a replacement decorator receives the decorations it encloses UNEXPANDED and may rewrite or remove them. The alternative — innermost first — would make an outer decorator unable to remove an inner one, because the inner one would already have run, which is the capability conditional compilation depends on.

     Note 2

    Nothing is re-scanned. What a replacement decorator returns is already tokens, so the implementation walks the returned stream for further decorations rather than lexing it. This is why the phase costs one pass over what was produced rather than a re-lex of the region per expansion.

     Note 3

    names is fixed before the loop and nothing in the loop changes it, so a decoration that an expansion introduces cannot name a replacement decorator no import brought in. Such a decoration is an ordinary decorator and is resolved at run time, or is an error if nothing of that name exists. Re-resolving imports mid-expansion would be the alternative, and it is unavailable: 7.4 leaves an expansion nothing to fetch with.

     Note 4

    The expansion limit is an implementation limit, but a specified one: a program that expands in one implementation and not another because the limits differ is the failure a limit exists to make loud.

    7.7.1 When Expansion Happens

    ParseModule is modified: after a module's source text has been scanned and before it is parsed as a Module, if ReplacementDecoratorNames of the module is not empty, Expansion is performed and the module is parsed from the resulting token stream rather than from its source text.

    A module whose ReplacementDecoratorNames is empty is parsed unchanged, so a program that uses no replacement decorator observes no phase.

    Note 1

    ReplacementDecoratorNames is a static semantic of the ImportDeclarations, so deciding whether to expand at all needs the module's imports and nothing else — which is what lets an implementation skip the phase entirely for the modules that do not use it, and what lets a loader know from the import clauses alone which modules it must fetch first.

     Note 2

    Type checking follows parsing, so it sees only expanded code and never an unexpanded decoration. This ordering is normative: a program's validity depends on it, and an implementation that checked before expanding would reject syntax a replacement decorator was about to produce.

    7.8 ApplyReplacementDecorator ( d )

    The abstract operation ApplyReplacementDecorator takes argument d (a decoration) and returns either a normal completion containing a List of Token Records, or a throw completion. It calls the replacement decorator d names with the tokens d decorates and its own arguments, and returns the tokens the call produced. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let f be the function d's name denotes.
    2. Let target be the Token Records of the source text from the end of d to the end of the declaration d decorates.
    3. Let args be a List of the Token Records of d's arguments, unevaluated.
    4. Let result be Completion(Call(f, undefined, « target » followed by args)).
    5. If result is an abrupt completion, throw a SyntaxError exception whose message is result's value and whose position is d.
    6. If result is not a List of Token Records, throw a SyntaxError exception.
    7. If result does not match the grammar the position of d requires (7.9), throw a SyntaxError exception whose position is given by the [[Span]] of the first token of result that does not.
    8. For each Token Record t of result whose [[Span]].[[Source]].[[Generation]] is 0 and which did not come from target, set t.[[Span]].[[Source]] to a Source Reference Record with [[URL]] empty, [[Macro]] d's name, and [[Generation]] the current expansion depth.
    9. Return result.
     Note 1

    target is everything the decoration ENCLOSES, not the declaration alone. 7.7 replaces d together with what it decorates, so any decoration written between them is inside the replaced range - and handing the macro only the declaration would drop those decorations silently, which contradicts a replacement decorator being able to rewrite or remove the runtime decorations it encloses.

     Note 2

    A token the decorator COPIED from what it was given keeps the Span it arrived with, so it still names the position a program was written at however many expansions move it. Only a token the decorator CREATED is attributed to the decorator, which is what makes a diagnostic inside generated code point at the macro that generated it rather than at the splice — and why no offset map is needed anywhere: attribution travels on the token.

     Note 3

    A replacement decorator rejects its input by throwing, which is what a function does to reject its arguments and which cannot be ignored. The exception becomes a Syntax Error at the decoration site carrying the macro's own message, so a decorator applied to something it does not handle says so where it was written.

     Note 4

    A replacement decorator receives tokens and no reflection context. Every field of a context — a type, metadata, an initializer to add — needs either a resolved type or a running program, and expansion has neither.

    7.9 Syntax Replacement

    A replacement decorator is called with the tokens it decorates, a CONTEXT, and its own arguments where it has any - (tokens, context, args). Its TYPE is that reflection context: a macro may write context: Reflect.Block and have it mean what it says, which is what lets a name's overloads be told apart by the position each takes. The tokens argument likewise has the TokenStream type, not the type of whatever backs it.

    Where a name declares SEVERAL replacement decorators and none of them accepts the position a decoration is written in, there is no replacement to apply there: the decoration is left as written, for an ordinary decorator of that name at decoration time. This is not a decorator declining — no decorator ran — and it is not an error. It is the case a name carrying both a replacement decorator and an ordinary one exists for: @jsx { … } expands and @jsx class C {} decorates.

    Note 1

    Decided by resolution before the call rather than by reading the error one would throw. A macro whose own body calls an overloaded function with arguments no signature accepts fails for a real reason, and the two cannot be told apart by their messages.

    Only where the name declares more than one. A name whose single replacement decorator does not accept where it is written is an error, as it would be for any other call: there is no other declaration for the decoration to fall through to.

    The context is an ordinary object with one own property, kind, whose value names the position - the same name its reflection context has, "Class", "ClassMethod", "IfBlock" and the rest, with "Region" for a captured region. It is frozen, and it carries one other property only where the decorated statement is LABELLED, label, which is absent otherwise.

    Note 2

    label is carried because it is the one syntactic fact the tokens cannot hold. A label PRECEDES the decoration - lbl: then @m then the statement - so a span reaching back to include it would contain the decoration being expanded.

    Two positions are unreachable for a replacement decorator, though a runtime decorator reaches them: a preprocessor name's { always begins a region, so a decoration on a block reports "Region" rather than "Block", and one on a do block reports "Region" rather than "DoBlock". That is the same rule that makes @m { a: 1 } a region rather than an ObjectLiteral.

     Note 3

    Nothing else, because a replacement decorator receives the TOKENS OF WHAT IT DECORATES. A name, static, a for's binding, a match arm's pattern are all in those tokens already, and a field beside a token stream is two ways to say one thing. A runtime decorator needs them in its context because it is handed no tokens.

    Typing the context parameter declares WHERE a decorator applies, and a decoration in another position is then refused where it is written rather than inside the macro. It is optional: a decorator declaring no context is usable wherever its return parses, which is what lets one serve several positions without being told which it is in.

    A decorator answers a token sequence: an array-like of Token Records. Anything else is a Syntax Error, undefined included - a decorator ALWAYS replaces, and one that has nothing to change returns the stream it was given, which is a token sequence by this rule.

    An empty sequence is a replacement like any other, and is legal exactly where an empty token sequence parses: it removes a statement or a class member, and does not remove a formal parameter from the middle of a list or a region whose value is wanted.

    Note 4

    What a decorator RECEIVES is a TokenStream and what it RETURNS is a token sequence, and the asymmetry is deliberate. A TokenStream carries spans this specification assigns, and 7.3 refuses construction for that reason: a stream a caller built would carry spans locating nothing. So a decorator that rewrites assembles ordinary records, and one that does not returns what it was handed.

    There is no way for a decorator that RUNS to decline what it was given. A decorator that wants to inspect without rewriting returns its input, and that is the whole of the no-op - which is why undefined is refused rather than being read as one: a decorator that fell off the end of a branch would silently erase what it decorated.

    The tokens a replacement decorator receives are those of the region it decorates, produced as ECMAScript unless that region is captured (7.5). The tokens it returns must parse as the grammatical form the position it decorated requires. It is a Syntax Error otherwise, reported at the returned token whose [[Span]] locates the failure.

    Where the decorated position was a Statement, the replacement text is TERMINATED: a semicolon is appended unless what the decorator returned already ends in one, or in a block. A decorator may therefore return an expression in either position, which is what allows one decorator to serve both without being told which it is in.

    Note 5

    This is a rule about TEXT rather than about how the returned tokens are read, and it has to be. Expansion replaces a source range and the result is parsed again, so a decorator returning f() where a statement stood leaves f() against whatever followed it; with no LineTerminator between them, automatic semicolon insertion does not apply and the program does not parse. Reading the return as an ExpressionStatement would not help, because the adjacency is in the text.

    Every decorable position may be syntax-replaced, including the positions that do not admit value replacement: a block produces no value but has syntax, and so do a statement, a parameter, a return annotation, an enum, a tuple, a record, and a lexical declaration.

    Note 6

    This is a grammatical constraint where value replacement's is a typed one, and the two are different axes rather than one rule with exceptions. It is a Syntax Error for a decoration on a statement that declares nothing to name anything other than a replacement decorator: a statement has syntax to replace, but a runtime decorator runs when the declaration it decorates is evaluated and there is no declaration there to run at. A position may admit both: a do block's value may be replaced by a runtime decorator and its syntax by a replacement decorator, and which a return means is decided by which kind of decorator returned it.

     Note 7

    An empty result needs no separate permission. It parses where an empty token stream parses — as a statement, or as a class member — and does not where one does not, so removing a decorated statement is legal and removing a parameter from the middle of a list is the same error as returning a class declaration for one.

    7.10 Reflection Contexts

    A reflection context is a type in the Reflect namespace naming a kind of declaration or a part of one. Reflect.getReflection.<C, T>(…) reflects the part of T that the context C names, and is resolved by the specialized overloads of 4: the first argument selects among the signatures and the second is the declaration reflected, which is why one name serves every context with no any in it.

    A context that names a set of members has two signatures: one taking no name, returning an object keyed by member name, and one taking a name, returning that member alone. The forms and the options they take are given by 7.14.

    Note

    The contexts are the reason the facility needs no separate function per kind of declaration: getReflection.<Reflect.ClassField, Point>('x') and getReflection.<Reflect.Type>(Point) are the same call resolved by its selector, and the selector is an ordinary type. It is also the design's own demonstration of specialized overloads, one signature per context, which is why 4 records that form as the thing this extension needs from it.

    7.11 Reflection Shapes

    7.10 says which contexts there are. This clause says what each one answers, field by field. The shape of the one context the core defines, Reflect.Type, is given by Table 33 instead and is not repeated here.

    The rules of this clause hold of every reflection; the family clauses that follow give the fields.

    7.11.1 Rules Common to Every Reflection

    Every reflection has a kind property whose value is a String naming the context that produced it, "ClassField" for Reflect.ClassField and so on for each context of Table 47.
