A reader handed a reflection dispatches on it rather than inferring the context from which fields are present, which is what a decorator whose parameter is a union of contexts would otherwise have to do.

    The fields a family clause lists are all of a reflection's properties, and every one is present. An implementation may not omit a field, and it may not add a property beside them: anything an implementation exposes of its own goes under host, a single reserved property that is absent unless the implementation puts something there. So every bare property of a reflection is one this specification gives, and an implementation's own vocabulary is under one key a reader can see and ignore.

    Note 1

    A field an implementation may leave out is a field every reader tests for before using, and the tests are not written: a program is written against the implementation in front of it, and its portability is discovered later. Fixing the shape completely is what java.lang.reflect, System.Reflection, and inspect each do, and what makes a reflection worth reading at all.

    Reflect.getReflection returns a new ordinary object each time it is called. Two calls naming the same declaration return two objects, which are not the same value; a reflection is extensible and is not frozen. Type Objects are interned and a reflection is not (1.2.2.9), the difference being that a Type Object is the type while a reflection is a report about a declaration.

    A metadata object is the exception and is stable: reflecting one declaration twice reaches the same metadata object, and every decorator applied to one declaration is given that object. That identity is what makes a decorator's write visible to a later reader, and what lets a derived class's metadata inherit from its base's prototypically (7.15).

    Note 2

    Identity belongs to the thing that carries state and not to the report about it. The Block contexts show that it could not have been otherwise: a block decorator runs on every entry to its block, so its reflection is produced once per evaluation and there is nothing for an interning rule to key on. A rule that interned some contexts and not others would be worse than either.

    Where a family's reflection has a metadata property, the property is present and holds a metadata object even where nothing has written to it; it is never absent and never null. The contexts that carry no metadata at all, which are Reflect.Type and the Binding, Block, and Structural families of Table 47 as 7.15 gives them, have no metadata property, which is a different thing from an empty one.

    Note 3

    Present-and-empty is what keeps a read of a key that nothing set a missing key rather than a TypeError. The undecorated declaration is the ordinary input and the decorated one is the tested input, so a shape that is absent on the ordinary input fails where it is least likely to have been tried. It costs one object per declaration rather than one per reflection, since an undecorated derived class inherits its base's metadata object rather than being given a new one.

    An initial property holds a declared default only where that default is a constant, and undefined otherwise. Evaluating a non-constant initializer would run the program's code where the declaration is evaluated rather than where the value is wanted, so the declaration is reported through initializer as a TokenStream (7.3) instead. The two are a value and the expression that produced it rather than two spellings of one thing, and a reflection may carry one, the other, or both.

    7.11.2 The Class Family

    Every reflection of this family has the fields Table 48 gives it, together with the kind of 7.11.1. A type field holds a Type Object, an initial field is governed by the rule of that clause, and an initializer field holds a TokenStream (7.3) or undefined.

    A signature reflection, the element of a signatures List, has parameters, a List of parameter reflections of the family the declaration belongs to, and return, the return reflection of that family. Where the signature declares type parameters it has typeParameters, a List in declaration order of type parameter reflections, each reporting name, kind ('type' or 'value'), variadic, variance, arity, and constraint and default as the type objects the declared Types denote, or a deferred application where they read an earlier parameter — the declared data of the Type Parameter Record (Table 29), which is what lets a tool complete a named type argument at an application site. A parameter reflection is the same shape wherever it appears: ClassMethodParameter, ClassOperatorParameter, ClassSetterParameter, FunctionParameter, and ObjectMethodParameter differ in which declaration they reflect and not in what they report, and ClassSetterParameter carries no index because a setter has exactly one parameter.

    A constructor is reflected as a ClassMethod whose name is "constructor", and its parameters as that method's, so a construct signature needs no context of its own (7.10).

    Note 1

    A reflection and the decorator context built from it are not the same object. A context is a reflection with the fields a decorator needs to act rather than to read: addInitializer where 7.10 gives it, and a reference to the enclosing declaration's context, so a field's decorator can reach its class and a parameter's can reach its method. Everything a context reports about the declaration itself is this clause's, which is why the two are specified in one place and not two.

     Note 2

    offset and byteLength are undefined rather than absent where a field has no laid-out placement, since a field of a class that is not a value type has no offset to report and the shape does not vary with the class it came from. A reader wanting the full placement of a laid-out field, including its bit width and alignment, has 9; these two are here because a decorator that reorders or packs fields needs them at the declaration and should not have to reach for a second facility to get them.

    7.11.3 The Layout Family

    A ClassFieldLayout reflection reports where a field sits in its class, and is reached by Reflect.getReflection.<Reflect.ClassFieldLayout, T>(name). It is a TypeError exception where T has no layout: asking a class with none for a field's placement is the mistake, as reading byteLength from a string is (9). A program that does not know should ask hasLayout first.

    It carries no metadata, no type, and none of static, private, or protected: those are facts about the declaration and are reported by the ClassField reflection (7.11.2), which this one deliberately does not duplicate.

    Note

    The two are separate contexts because they answer different questions and are wanted by different readers: a decorator asks what a field was declared as, and a serializer or a vertex-attribute descriptor asks where its bytes are. Every system that offers both keeps the same seam - .NET has FieldInfo beside Marshal.OffsetOf, C's offsetof connects to nothing else, and Rust had no stable field-offset reflection at all until offset_of!.

    An accessor reports the name it was declared under rather than the private field it desugars to: the backing is unnameable, and a slot no program can name would leave a hole in a layout a program is trying to read.

    The two also answer differently for a class with no layout, and both are right. ClassField reports offset and byteLength as undefined, because a reflection's shape does not vary with what it reflects (7.11.1). This one throws, because it exists only to answer a question that has no answer there.

    7.11.4 The Function Family

    Note

    FunctionParameter and FunctionReturn report one signature's parameter and return, which is what a decorator on a parameter of an overloaded function needs: the decoration is written on one signature and reflects that one. signatures on the Function reflection is the whole set, so a reader wanting every overload takes it from there and one wanting the decorated position takes the parameter's own.

    7.11.5 The Binding Family

    Neither has a metadata property, this family being one of those 7.15 gives none.

    Note

    A const initialized with a constant always reports an initial, where a let's may be undefined; the rule is the same one (7.11.1) and it is the declarations that differ, a const with a non-constant initializer being as possible as a let with one. The two reflections have one shape rather than two because a reader of a binding wants the same four answers either way.

    7.11.6 The Object Family

    These reflections are reached from an instance rather than from a declaration: Reflect.getReflection.<Reflect.ObjectField>(instance, name) takes the object itself, where the Class family takes the class. An object literal has no declaration a second evaluation of it would share, so its metadata lives on the instance and so does the reflection that reports it (7.10).

    Note 1

    The family mirrors the Class family member for member and reports less of each: an object's members have no static, private, or protected to report, and its fields have no offset or byteLength, an object literal not being laid out. What is left is the same questions asked of a different kind of container, which is why a decorator written against one family reads almost unchanged against the other.

     Note 2

    Two objects of one literal are two instances and reflect separately, so what a decorator wrote about one is not visible through the other. That follows from the metadata living on the instance rather than on a declaration and is the one place this family's answer differs in kind from the Class family's rather than in detail.

    7.11.7 The Block Family

    A block reflection reports the syntax around the block rather than a type: every field but index and async holds a TokenStream (7.3) or undefined. A block has no type to report, and what a decorator on one wants is what the block is and what governs its running.

    Every reflection of this family has label, a String naming the block's label or undefined where it has none, and block, the tokens the block delimits. A field a particular block form does not have is present and undefined rather than absent, as 7.11.1 requires of every reflection: a for without an update clause reports update as undefined, so a reader walks one shape rather than testing which form it was handed.

    No reflection of this family has a metadata property, the Block family being one of those 7.15 gives none.

    Note

    A block reflection is produced on every entry to its block (7.16), so a block in a loop produces one per iteration. That is what a reflection being fresh per call amounts to here, and it is why the family carries no metadata: metadata is written once where a declaration is, and a block has no once.

    7.11.8 The Enum Family

    Note 1

    An enum reflection reports both a name and a type, as a class's does and for the same reason: the name is what a reader wants directly, and reaching it by reflecting the type and reading its display would be an indirection with nothing to recommend it. An object literal has no name to report, which 7.11.6 says by omitting one.

     Note 2

    An enumerator reflection reports its value and no type: the type is the enum's and is reached through the enum's reflection, where reporting it per enumerator would be the same Type Object repeated once per member. index is the declaration order rather than the value, which are different whenever a program assigns values explicitly.

    7.11.9 The Structural Family

    Neither has a metadata property, this family being one of those 7.15 gives none.

    Note

    These two reflect a composite VALUE where Reflect.Type reflects a type, and which of them a decoration selects is decided by the value rather than by the syntax: a composite built over a List selects Tuple and one built over a set of keyed members selects Record, the same division a composite's own kind already makes. A reader wanting the structure walks type with Reflect.Type (1.12.3), which is why one field is the whole shape.

    7.12 Replacement Values

    A decorator may return a value that replaces what it decorated. Returning undefined replaces nothing, so a decorator that only reads or only writes metadata returns nothing and is done. Where a value is returned, it replaces the decorated target and must be of the type Table 56 gives that context; a value that is not is a TypeError.

    Every other context admits no replacement, and a decorator on one that returns a value other than undefined is a TypeError. Those are the sub-target contexts, which name a part of a declaration rather than a thing that exists on its own - a parameter, a return - and the structural and binding contexts, and the blocks other than a do's.

    Note 1

    The Class row admits a subclass because a class type is nominal - a nominal Type Record (Table 1) is a subtype along its declared inheritance and not by its shape: a structurally identical class of another declaration is not a value of the decorated class's type, so "the same shape" would not have been a rule an implementation could check, where "the class or something extending it" is.

    The two do rows are the reason the block exclusion is stated over what a block produces rather than over blocks: a block produces nothing, so there is nothing to replace, and the exclusion was never about blocks being structural. A do expression produces a value and a do * produces a generator, so those two have something a replacement could be.

     Note 2

    This table and 7.6 are different axes, and a position may appear in both. A decorator of this clause runs when the declaration is evaluated and returns a VALUE; a replacement decorator runs at expansion and returns SYNTAX. The reasoning that excludes a block here does not carry there: a block produces no value, but it has syntax, and a replacement decorator on one rewrites it.

    7.13 addInitializer

    addInitializer(callback) registers callback to run once the declaration it was registered from is fully decorated. It is a TypeError if callback is not callable. The registered callbacks run after every decorator of that declaration has been applied, in the order they were added (7.16), and their return values are discarded.

    Only the contexts of Table 57 have an addInitializer property. On every other context it is absent, so a decorator written for a position that cannot register one finds nothing to call rather than a call that does nothing.

    Note 1

    The list is closed rather than derivable, and Function is the case that makes it so: a function declaration admits a replacement (7.12) and carries no addInitializer, so no rule of the form "whatever can be replaced can be initialized" holds. What the ten have in common is a declaration site inside a class or an object literal that something else constructs - an initializer runs at construction, and a free function has no construction to run at.

    ObjectField is the other case worth naming: it is a member of an object literal, and the literal is finished when the field's decorator runs, so there is no later moment for a callback to be later than.

     Note 2

    Callbacks running after every decorator of the declaration is what lets a decorator register work that depends on what a decorator applied closer to the declaration did, since application is innermost first (7.16) and registration is not application. Running them in the order added rather than in reverse is the ordinary reading of a queue, and the two orders together mean a stack of decorators applies outward and initializes forward.

    7.14 Retrieving a Reflection

    7.14.1 Reflect.getReflectionByIndex

    Reflect.getReflectionByIndex.<C, T>(…) answers the same reflections Reflect.getReflection of the same context and arguments would, as a List in declaration order rather than as an object keyed by member name. It exists for the positions a name does not order: a parameter list is read by position, and an object keyed by parameter name loses the order the positions have.

    It is defined for the contexts that name a set of members, and for a context naming exactly one thing it is not defined, there being no order to answer.

    7.14.2 The own Option

    Reflecting the members of a class answers the members it inherits as well as those it declares. Passing { own: *true* } in place of a member name answers only the members the class declares itself. Passing { static: *true* } answers the class's static members; an enumeration with neither option answers its instance members.

    An enumeration answers members of ONE staticness, because its result is keyed by name and a name does not identify a member: m and static m may both be declared in one class body, and both reach the same owner, a static member's home object being the constructor and an instance member's the prototype whose constructor names it. A program wanting both asks twice and merges the results BY VALUE, each reflection carrying its own name and static; merging them by key would lose one member per shared name, which is the collision the option exists to resolve.

    The enumerated methods of a class include its constructor (Table 47), a class always having one whether or not its body writes it. A program listing the methods it means to expose skips that name.

    Note

    Inherited by default because a decorator asking what fields a class has usually means all of them: an inherited field is a field of the instance, and a serializer or a validator that skipped it would be wrong in a way its author would not see until a subclass appeared. The option is for the reader that wants the declaration rather than the shape - a documentation generator listing what this class adds, say.

    7.14.3 Overloaded Targets

    A parameter of an overloaded function or method cannot be reached by name or by position, since neither says which signature it belongs to. Reflect.getReflection and Reflect.getReflectionByIndex of the ClassMethodParameter, ClassOperatorParameter, FunctionParameter, and ObjectMethodParameter contexts therefore throw a TypeError where the target is overloaded; the parameters are read through the signatures of the declaration's own reflection, each entry of which carries its own parameter and return reflections.

    Note

    This is the rule an ambiguous overloaded reference already follows at a call site, applied to reflection: answering one signature's parameter would be answering a question the caller did not ask, and answering all of them would not be a parameter reflection. Where the target is not overloaded the flat forms are defined and are the shorter way to write the common case.

    7.14.4 Reflect.getMetadata

    Reflect.getMetadata.<C, T>(…) performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let reflection be ? Reflect.getReflection.<C, T> of the same arguments.
    2. If reflection has no metadata property, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Return reflection.metadata.

    It is defined only for the contexts whose reflection carries a metadata property (7.15), which is the reading half of what a decorator writes. Where the reflection answers a set of members rather than one, the result is an object keyed as that reflection is, holding each member's metadata object.

    Note

    Sugar over Reflect.getReflection, and specified as such rather than independently, so the two cannot answer differently about the same declaration. The metadata object it returns is the stable one of 7.11.1, so a write through a decorator's context is visible through this and the reverse.

    7.15 The Metadata Channel

    A decorator may be written before a TYPE only in a position that has a reflection context of its own, which is a RETURN: a method's, a getter's, an operator's, an abstract method's, and a function's. Reflect.Type is a reflection target and not a decorator context - a bare type expression carries no decorator - so a decorator before the type of a binding, a field, a parameter, or an interface member is a Syntax Error rather than a decoration that names nothing.

    Note 1

    The rule is stated over positions rather than over spellings because the same text means different things in the two places: in m(): @f T the decoration is of the RETURN, whose context is ClassMethodReturn, and in let x: @f T there is nothing for it to be a decoration OF. Admitting the second and dropping it would read as support for a feature that does not exist.

    A reflection context of the Class, Function, Object, and Enum families has a metadata property holding the metadata object of what it names; the Type, Binding, Block, and Structural contexts have none, their reflections carrying no metadata. A metadata object is an instance of the intrinsic interface corresponding to its context, %ClassMetadata% for Reflect.Class, %ClassFieldMetadata% for Reflect.ClassField, and so on for each context of those four families; this specification declares the interfaces, and their names resolve in type position as the built-in type names do (1.5.27), which is what a partial declaration over one resolves. A program adds to one by declaring a partial interface over it whose members are typed and Symbol-keyed, and the members it adds are the only ones there are: the intrinsic interfaces declare none. An interface rather than a class, because a metadata object must be an ORDINARY OBJECT: the decorators extension has a subclass's metadata inherit its superclass's PROTOTYPICALLY, falling through for a key it does not set and shadowing without mutating for one it does, and an instance of a class with a typed field is not extensible (1.11.9) and so cannot be prototypically linked at all. An interface declares the shape without adding instance state, which keeps the whole set of keys and their types known at compile time - what an implementation needs to specialize access - while leaving a metadata object with only the members something set.

    Reflect.getMetadata.<C, T>(…) returns the metadata object that Reflect.getReflection of the same context and arguments would report, and is the reading half of what a decorator writes.

    A metadata object is inherited through the prototype chain. Where a derived class does not redeclare an inherited member, the member's metadata object is the base's, so a Symbol lookup finds what the base's decorators wrote. Where it redeclares the member and decorates it, the member's metadata object is a new one whose prototype is the base's, so what the derived class's decorators write shadows the base's without mutating it.

    Note 2

    Typed Symbol-keyed members on a partial interface are what make this a channel rather than a property bag: a key cannot collide, because a Symbol cannot; a value cannot be of the wrong type, because the member is declared; and nothing is reachable that was not declared, so a reader of %ClassFieldMetadata% sees exactly the vocabulary the program's decorators established. This is the same discipline the metadata protocol takes for a meta type's keys (6.2), reached from the other direction.

    Prototypal inheritance of the metadata object is what makes @tag('base') on a field of A visible on B's inherited copy and invisible once B redeclares and retags it, without either class knowing of the other. It also means metadata is read the way a property is read, so a key absent from a derived member's own object is not absent but inherited, which is usually what a decorator's reader wants and is worth knowing when it is not.

    7.16 Applying a Decorator

    A decorator is an ordinary function whose last parameter is annotated with a reflection context. Which function a decoration applies is decided by the overload resolution of 1.10.3.1 over the arguments written and the context of the position decorated, so @f, @f(0), and @f('a') may name three declarations of f and select among them the way any call does. @f and @f() are one form: both resolve with no explicit argument, and a signature taking the context alone is preferred over one whose remaining parameters are satisfied by defaults. Where no such signature exists and more than one is satisfied by defaults alone, the decoration is ambiguous and a TypeError is thrown where the decorated declaration is evaluated.

    It is a type error if an ordinary decorator's known application contract proves that it cannot receive the written arguments and the implicit context. The context is an Object supplied by value; it cannot satisfy a required reference parameter or a definitely incompatible scalar boundary where it is received. Bare and parenthesized applications use the same context-last placement, default and optional gaps, and rest rules. A missing prefix value is an error when the required parameter cannot accept undefined; untyped parameters retain their ordinary missing-argument behaviour. An extra context argument may be ignored. Within an overload set eliminate only demonstrably impossible candidates, preserving context-only preference and runtime resolution where context details remain unknown. Reachable union alternatives retain the per-alternative call judgment. Unknown context structure does not imply a closed empty-object type, an overload tie, or a selected reflection host. This judgment executes no decorator or getter, creates no borrow, and does not alter replacement-decorator expansion, context allocation, or liveness.

    A decorator runs when the declaration it decorates is evaluated, and what it may do there is write to the metadata of its context, register an initializer, and return a replacement for what it decorated. The replacement a context admits is given by 7.12, and the initializer registration by 7.13. So is the ORDER, which that extension now fixes in two phases: decorator expressions are evaluated in document order, and decorators are applied INNERMOST FIRST AND IN REVERSE SOURCE ORDER - several on one declaration apply closest-first, a declaration's parameters and return apply before the declaration itself, and members apply before their container, so a class decorator sees a class whose members are already decorated. Registered initializers run after every decorator of that declaration has been applied, in the order they were added (Table 39).

    A block is the exception, and it is the one position in this extension whose decorator runs more than once. A block decorator runs on every entry to its block rather than once where the block was written, so a block inside a loop runs its decorator once per iteration and a block inside a function once per call. This follows from the rule above rather than qualifying it - a block is evaluated each time control reaches it, and a decorator runs when what it decorates is evaluated - but it is worth stating, because the cost is real and is not visible at the decoration.

    Note 1

    What it buys is the reason the family exists: instrumentation, tracing, and scoped resources are per-entry questions, and a decoration that ran once at the declaration could not answer them. What it costs is a context and a call per iteration, which a decorator in a hot loop pays and the reader of the loop cannot see. A replacement decorator on a block runs once, at expansion, and can emit the same instrumentation inline - so the per-iteration work happens where the per-iteration decorator does not.

    This is also why a block reflection carries no metadata and cannot be interned (7.11.1): both would need a once for the block to have, and it has none.

     Note 2

    Types are what remove the (value, context) return from a decorator that takes arguments: an erased system cannot tell @f from @f(0) without one, since it cannot see which f is meant, and this proposal resolves it by the annotation on the last parameter. So a decorator looks the same whether or not it takes arguments, and giving one an argument is editing its parameter list rather than rewriting it into a factory.

    Both rules above are rules for decorators that run when the declaration they decorate is evaluated. A replacement decorator runs at expansion, and neither applies to it: its arguments are Token Records and are not evaluated, and its name denotes one function rather than a set of overloads.

    8 Declarative Checker Facts

    A signature carries two facts that no rule of the language computes and that a program states instead: the this a function expects, and what a call of it establishes about its arguments. They are data the checker reads, never code it runs, which is what distinguishes them from the meta protocol's hooks (6) and keeps them outside the boundary 1.2.7 draws: nothing evaluates, and each is consumed by machinery that already exists.

    8.1 The Expected this Type

    The receiver-presence rule also applies on the live path of an optional call. Thus const f = c.m; f?.() supplies no receiver, whereas c.m?.() and (c.m)?.() preserve the property reference. A comma expression, binding alias or destructuring extraction does not synthesize a receiver. No call occurs on a definitely nullish skipped path. A signature without [[ThisType]] remains callable without a receiver; a method's self [[ThisType]] does not disappear merely because its body does not read this.

    At a call with a selected signature carrying an explicit [[ThisType]], the supplied receiver must satisfy that type. A statically known incompatible receiver is a type error; an unresolved receiver is checked at entry before the body executes. Parentheses, explicit type arguments, optional calls and tagged calls preserve the receiver supplied by their member reference. This check preserves the receiver identity and does not convert it into a different object. The self [[ThisType]] continues to mean the receiver through which the method was reached, not the nominal class that declared it.

    A signature's [[ThisType]] is the type its this is required to have. It is contravariant, as a parameter is, so a signature with a [[ThisType]] is usable where one requiring a NARROWER this is required and never the reverse. A signature with none supplies no this rather than accepting any, so it is usable nowhere a this is required at all, and one that has a [[ThisType]] is usable nowhere a this is absent (1.10.2.3). A method extracted from its class and called free of it is the case this decides: its this is not of the type its body assumes, and the extraction is a type error at the boundary that took it, or at the call that supplies it no this, rather than a TypeError inside it.

    A method's signature has a [[ThisType]] although no syntax declares one: the self [[ThisType]], which stands for the receiver the method is reached through, whatever that receiver's declared type. Two methods agree on it, so a class satisfies an interface that declares the same method, and a method does not agree with a function type that has no [[ThisType]], which is what refuses the extraction at a boundary. It is not the class's own type: a method expecting its class would be narrower than the interface method it implements, and contravariance would refuse the implementation, although the interface's method is reached only through an object that has it.

    It is a type error for a call to supply no this to a callee whose every selected signature has a [[ThisType]]. A call supplies a this where its callee, once parentheses and explicit type arguments are removed, is a member access, an optional member access, or a super property; any other callee supplies none. So const f = c.m; f(), a destructured m(), and (0, c.m)() are type errors, while c.m(), (c.m)(), c.m.<T>(), f.call(c), and a call of a bound function are not. The boundary rule above refuses a method that reaches a position requiring a function type without a [[ThisType]]; this rule refuses the call through a binding that kept one, which crosses no such boundary.

    Where a non-arrow function literal's contextual type (Table 17) is a function type whose applicable signature has a [[ThisType]], the literal adopts it: this within the body has that type, and the literal's own signature has that [[ThisType]]. An arrow adopts nothing, since it has no this of its own to give a type to, and the this it closes over is already typed where it was written.

    Note

    This is the whole of what an erased system's ThisType<T> marker does, said as data rather than as a marker the checker recognizes by name. It is also why the design's options(Data, Methods) builder is three lines: it constructs an intersection of the data and the methods, and calls withThisType to put it on every method's signature, at which point a method written in the object literal has this typed as the finished object. Nothing about that reaches into inference; the type is built first and the literal is checked against it, which is the order 1.2.7 requires of everything.

    8.2 Declared Narrowing

    A call consumes the effective selected signature after type-argument substitution. Substitution applies to [[Narrows]] and [[ThisType]] as well as parameters and return type. Each narrowing target names the argument actually bound to that parameter by ordinary named, positional, default and rest argument binding; no fact is attached to an omitted value or an unestablished place. Method signatures retain the same declarations as free functions. If overload selection remains unresolved, no arbitrarily chosen signature supplies a narrowing. Boolean facts apply only in the corresponding guarded paths; void assertion facts apply only after successful return in positions dominated by the call, using the completion and join rules of 1.8.5.1. Ordinary assignment and effect invalidation still apply.

    A Narrowing Record has a [[Target]], a String naming a parameter of the signature or "this", and a [[Type]], a Type Record. A signature's [[Narrows]] is a List of them, and it says what a call establishes: that the argument passed at [[Target]] is of [[Type]]. Two forms follow from the signature's [[Return]], and no third is defined.

    Where the [[Return]] is boolean, the call is a test and its narrowings apply where its result is true, exactly as v is T applies (Table 24), so if (isFish(pet)) narrows pet in the branch it guards and narrows it away in the other. Where the [[Return]] is void, the call establishes its narrowings by returning at all, since there is no result to condition on, so they apply in every position the call dominates: the argument's Static Type there is NarrowTo(s, [[Type]]), which keeps a narrower s narrower. It is a type error where that is empty under the stability condition of 1.8.5.4, since the call can then never return normally; a void assertion that can never fail decides nothing, having no false branch, and is not an error. Where the [[Return]] is any other type, a non-empty [[Narrows]] is a type error: nothing would consume it.

    A narrowing declared by a signature is checked against nothing. It is a claim the declaration makes and the body is not required to honour, in the way that v is T is a question the language answers. This is the same reading a declared type of an unchecked boundary gets, and the same one an erased system's type predicate gets; what makes it sound here is that a value crossing a boundary is checked against its declared type regardless (Table 23), so a narrowing that lied costs a check that fails rather than a value that was never what it claimed.

    A fresh function literal whose return position is unannotated may adopt the contextual signature's narrowing declaration under 1.6.5, with parameter targets translated to its parameter names by position. This declares a contract on that new function; it does not prove its body. A pre-existing function value gains no narrowing declaration merely by crossing a guard-typed boundary. An explicitly written return contract is not replaced by contextual narrowing.

    Callable conformance preserves both branches of a Boolean test. A predicate for uint8 does not implement a predicate for uint8 | string over uint8 | string | boolean: it may answer false for a String, while the advertised predicate would remove String from that branch. A void assertion has only its successful continuation and may establish a stronger fact. These judgments compare declared contracts, not the truth of the body. An override cannot acquire or discard an advertised narrowing merely by returning a Boolean.

    Note 1

    The two forms are the type predicate and the assertion function of an erased system, and they are one field here rather than two spellings, because the difference between them is not in the fact declared but in what the declaration returns. A function that answers a question returns the answer, and its narrowing applies where the answer was yes; a function that establishes a fact returns nothing, and its narrowing applies once it has returned. Deriving the two from [[Return]] is why no asserts operator appears here.

    [[Narrows]] has a source spelling: the second form of TypeAnnotation (1.4.4), written in a return position. function isFish(pet: Pet): pet is Fish declares a signature whose [[Narrows]] holds one Narrowing Record, its [[Target]] the named parameter and its [[Type]] the type after is. The signature's own [[Return]] is boolean: the annotation says what a true answer PROVES, not what the function returns, so the body returns a boolean and a caller reads one. It is a type error if the BindingIdentifier is not the name of a parameter of that signature, since the narrowing lands on the argument in that position and a claim about anything else is one no caller could act on.

    A signature may also acquire [[Narrows]] and [[ThisType]] by construction (1.12.4), which is how the design's withThisType writes the latter, and a program uses the result by annotating with it: a binding declared of a constructed guard type narrows at every call through it. [[ThisType]] still has no spelling of its own, and joins the index signature and the symbol literal type as types this specification admits and no declaration writes.

    Note 2

    A spelling is what makes the [[Narrows]] step of 1.10.2.3 hold anything. A narrowing "is a claim the declaration makes and the body is not required to honour", so it is sound only while it is the DECLARATION's own: a rule that let any function of the right shape satisfy a guard type would hand the claim to code that never made it. Without a spelling the step had the opposite fault, since no written function could carry a Narrowing Record and so none was assignable to a guard type at all — the feature's own stated use, a guard a program writes, was unreachable.

    The lookahead is one token: a Type is never a BindingIdentifier followed by is, so the form is unambiguous against an annotation whose type happens to be named like a parameter. The [no LineTerminator here] restriction is the one the is operator already carries (5.2), and for the same reason.

    9 Memory Layout

    A value type has a defined layout in memory, and this clause defines it. It is what makes a [N].<T> a contiguous buffer rather than a list of references, what gives 1.8.3's zero-fill something to fill, and what a serializer, a placement construction over existing bytes, or a vertex descriptor reads. The default is the rule C, C++, and Rust follow, so a value type class is laid out as the same declaration is in those languages, and the controls below are their repr attributes together with the field offsets those languages keep to themselves.

    EVERY REFLECTIVE QUANTITY THIS CLAUSE DEFINES IS A uint64: a type's byteLength and alignment, an array's length, byteOffset and byteLength, and a window's length. They are the same kind of quantity and combine with one another, so _a_.length * _V_.byteLength is the size of a run and needs no conversion.

    Note

    They are typed rather than Numbers because a length and a stride are the operands of exactly the arithmetic the type system exists to check, and because a surface half of which was typed could not be combined with the other half at all.

    An exact width is still required of the OTHER operand: _count_ * _V_.byteLength where count is a uint8 is refused, as any mixing of widths is (6.1.6), and a program counting in a narrower type writes the conversion. Typing these quantities makes them combinable with each other; it does not and should not make the numeric family permissive.

    9.1 Layout Properties

    Install these fixed own data properties when the type's layout is complete, including on an applicable class or array constructor and on each completed specialization. A declaration or decorator cannot replace one with a user property: a conflicting own declaration fails before the completed type is published. An attempted write to an established fixed layout property is a type error, in every language mode, including a compound assignment or update. A logical assignment with an established skipped store remains valid. Immutable aliases preserve this permission; a value known only as type supplies neither a particular layout nor a general prohibition on writes to other members. Types with no layout retain their separate read behaviour.

    A Type Object whose type has a layout has three own properties. bitLength is the size in bits, which is what an arbitrary-width integer needs in order to describe itself; byteLength is the laid-out size in bytes, the bits rounded up to a byte and then to the type's alignment, so that every element of an array of the type is aligned; and alignment is the byte alignment. Each has the attributes { [[Writable]]: false, [[Enumerable]]: false, [[Configurable]]: false }, and each is compile-time evaluable (1.2.7), so [Vertex.byteLength * 1024].<uint8> is an array extent and T.byteLength inside a generic is a constant once T is specialized.

    A Type Object whose type has no layout has none of the three fixed own data properties. Reading one of these layout members through its layout-checking accessor throws a TypeError exception. The hasLayout member answers whether such a read is valid without throwing.

    A type's alignment is its byteLength rounded up to a power of two, and there is no upper bound on it: uint.<4> aligns to 1, uint.<24> to 4, uint.<128> to 16, and a float32x4 to 16. A value type class takes the alignment 9.2 gives it rather than this rule, since its size is a consequence of its fields rather than a width of its own.

    A Type Object has a family, a String naming the kind of value the type describes. Table 25 is organised by this concept already, deciding what an operator does by the family of its operands; family is how a program asks the same question.

    A type carrying metadata reports the family of the type it parameterizes, so float32.<{ m: 1 }> is "float" and uint8.<{ bounds: 1..=6 }> is "integer". A parameterization refines the type it parameterizes rather than replacing it (1.5.20), and reporting otherwise would put family at odds with instanceof, with the operator table, and with bitLength beside it, each of which already answers about the parameterized type.

    Note 1

    family names the family and nothing further. For a class it is "class", which is the name of the family and not of the declaration: a nominal type never exposes its declaration (1.12.2), and this exposes none of its fields, its name, or its shape.

    A program wanting the metadata a type carries rather than the family it belongs to reflects, where the "parameterized" node gives the base and the metadata (Table 33). The two are different questions - what kind of value this is, and what is known about it besides - and are answered in the two places that already describe them.

    family is not a substitute for is, for instanceof, or for Reflect.isAssignable. Whether a value may be stored at a type is those operations' question, and this proposal performs no implicit numeric widening, so two types of one family are no more assignable to each other than two of different families are.

    A Type Object has a min and a max, the least and the greatest value the type admits. They are the answer to the question a range check asks and a saturating operation obeys, and they are determined in this order.

    1. If the type carries bounds metadata (6), let r be that range. min is the least value of r and max is the greatest, each being a value the range ADMITS: an exclusive endpoint reports the last value on its side rather than the endpoint itself, so a bounds of 0 .. 10 over an integer type has a max of 9 where 0 ..= 10 has 10.
    2. Else if the type is an integer type, let w be the type's width in bits. min and max are the least and greatest values that width admits: 0 and 2w - 1 unsigned, and -2w-1 and 2w-1 - 1 signed. They are Numbers where w is 53 or fewer and BigInts above it, a wider integer having values no Number holds exactly.
    3. Else if the type is a binary floating-point type, min and max are the finite extremes of its format: min is the MOST NEGATIVE finite value and not the smallest positive one, and max is its negation.
    4. Else, reading either throws a TypeError exception, as reading byteLength from a string does.

    A binary floating-point type additionally has a minPositive, the least positive value its format represents, and an epsilon, the difference between 1 and the next value above it. An integer type has neither, rather than having them as undefined.

    Note 2

    The order of the first two steps is the substance: a refinement narrows what a type admits, so a narrowed type reports the narrowed answer, and a program asking what values a type holds gets one answer from one member whether the constraint came from the width or from the declaration. Without it, every reader that wants the question answered keeps a table of widths beside the code that reads the metadata, and the two say the same thing in two places.

    These are min and max and not MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, though the Number properties of those names are the nearest existing thing, because Number.MIN_VALUE is the least POSITIVE Number rather than the least: the most negative is -Number.MAX_VALUE. A float32.MIN_VALUE would have two defensible readings and no way for a reader to tell which was meant, and the integer and floating-point families would disagree about what the one name said. The lowercase names also match the members already on a Type Object, which are facts about the type rather than constants of a namespace, and minPositive gives the other reading a name of its own.

    min and max report values and carry no exclusivity of their own. A program that needs the endpoints as they were WRITTEN, which a schema emitter does in order to distinguish an exclusive bound from an inclusive one over the value below it, reads the range from the bounds metadata, where it remains whole. The two are not alternatives: the members are a projection for the reader who wants the extremes, and the metadata is there for the reader who wants the range.

     Note 3

    A Type Object also has an isPlainData property, true where the type has a layout and no position within it at any depth holds a reference, and false otherwise. Only such a type may be reinterpreted as bytes: viewed through a buffer (11), copied wholesale, overlapped at an explicit offset, or written to a wire format by offset. Like hasLayout it asks rather than asserts, so it never throws; a type with no layout is simply not plain data.

    isPlainData and hasLayout answer different questions and neither implies the other in the direction a program needs. A class every one of whose fields is typed string is a value type class with no layout, and a class holding a field typed D | null for a dynamic class D has a layout - a reference's - and is no value type at all. Reading "contains no references" off hasLayout therefore reaches the wrong answer in exactly the case that matters, the one whose layout is a reference's width, and a program that laid such a type over bytes it controls would read a forged reference back out of them and disclose a real one writing them the other way.

    The two questions a Type Object property answers have matching types in the type universe, so a generic may CONSTRAIN on them: value is the type every value type (1.5.1) is assignable to, and plain the type every plain-data type is assignable to. plain is the narrower: every plain-data type is a value type, and a class every one of whose fields is typed string is a value type that is not plain data. They exist as types rather than only as properties because a generic class constrains its type parameter through extends, a class-level where not being admitted, so a pool has no other way to state what it requires of its element. The three are separate because they vary independently, and the pair a given position needs differs: an array stride needs a layout, an assignment needs value-ness, and a byte view needs plain data.

     Note 4

    A Type Object has a hasLayout property, true where the type has a layout and false where it has none. Reading byteLength, bitLength, or alignment from a type with no layout throws a TypeError exception, which is right for a program that believes it has one; hasLayout is for the program that is asking rather than asserting, and answers without throwing.

    Note 5

    A generic serializer walking a heterogeneous structure asks this of every type it meets, and without a predicate its only route is to read one of the three and catch - control flow by exception for a question that is not a mistake, and a catch that swallows a misspelled type along with the answer. Testing for the property does not substitute: 'byteLength' in T is true for every type, the property being present and throwing when read.

    hasLayout sits beside the three it guards rather than in a function of its own, so it is compile-time evaluable for the same reason they are - which is what a serializer wants, the branch being one it would rather have folded away than taken. Whether a FIELD has a placement needs nothing new: its offset is undefined where it has none (7.11.2).

    This is the rule of C and of Rust, which the layout of this clause follows: each scalar is aligned to its own size, and Rust's u128 is 16-byte aligned in order to match C. Capping the alignment at 8 was considered and is not what this specification does, because it would make two types of one width disagree for no reason a program could observe - a 16-byte integer aligned at 8 beside a 16-byte SIMD vector aligned at 16 - and would need the vector to be stated as an exception. Uncapped, the vector is not an exception: a width that is already a power of two rounds up to itself. Raising an alignment past the natural one is what align is for (9.3), as #[repr(align(N))] is in Rust, and lowering it to 1 is what packed is for.

     Note 6

    These are properties of an interned Type Object rather than a sizeof operator, which is why they need no grammar and work wherever a type does, including on the result of Reflect.typeOf. The layout they report is the declared one, so the controls of 9.3 are accounted for in it: byteLength is what the program asked for, not what an implementation would have chosen.

    The alignment of a named numeric type is its byteLength. For an int.<N> or uint.<N> of a width no named type has, the alignment is the smallest power of two that is at least the bits rounded up to a byte; the design fixes only uint.<4>, whose byteLength is 1, and this rule agrees with it and with every named width. It is the general rule above restated for the widths no name covers, and it is uncapped for the reason that rule gives: an int.<96> aligns to 16 and pads to a multiple of it, which is the only reading on which an array of them stays aligned and the only one on which two types of one width do not disagree.

    9.2 Natural Alignment and Padding

    The layout of a value type class places its fields in declaration order. Let a bit cursor begin at 0, at the end of the layout of the class it extends where it extends one and at 0 otherwise. For each field in order:

    • Where the field's type has a bitLength under 8, it is a bit-field: it is placed at the cursor, or at the bit its offsetBit names, and the cursor advances by its bitLength.
    • Otherwise the cursor is first rounded up to a byte. The field is placed at the byte its offset names, where it has one; at the cursor, where the class is packed; and at the next multiple of its alignment otherwise, that alignment being the one its align names where it has one and its type's otherwise. The cursor advances to the end of the field.

    The class's alignment is the one its alignAll names, or 1 where it is packed, or the largest alignment among its fields otherwise. Its bitLength is the cursor's furthest extent, and its byteLength is the size its size names, or that extent rounded up to a byte and then to the class's alignment. It is a type error for a field to be placed outside the size a size fixes, or for an inherited field to be redeclared, since the redeclaration would have no defined offset.

    A field's offset is read through the reflection of its declaration rather than from the type, because it belongs to the field: Reflect.getReflection.<Reflect.ClassFieldLayout, T>(name) reports its placement, compile-time evaluable for the reason the layout is (7.11.3). The ClassField context beside it reports what the field was DECLARED as and carries offset and byteLength because those two are what a decorator commonly wants; the bit-level placement is meaningful only for a class that has a layout at all, which is why the two are separate contexts rather than one. This is the offsetof a serializer, a placement construction, or a vertex attribute descriptor needs.

    Note

    Rounding a class's byteLength up to its alignment is what makes an array of it an array: without the trailing pad, the second element would be misaligned. class A { a: uint8; b: uint16; } is therefore 4 bytes and not 3, and [10].<A> is 40.

    Because layout follows declaration order and this specification never reorders, field order is a performance decision the program makes: { a: uint8, b: float64, c: uint8 } occupies 24 bytes where { b: float64, a: uint8, c: uint8 } occupies 16. Reordering would be sound for a program that only reads its own fields and wrong for every one that does not, and views, serialization, and interop are exactly the cases that do not. Since byteLength is a constant, a program that cares can assert the size it meant to have.

    Inheritance appends, so a base's fields keep their offsets and a subclass's follow under the same rule, and class B extends A is laid out as the flattening of both. That is what lets a B be passed where an A is expected without copying: the prefix is an A already.

    9.3 Explicit Control

    Seven reserved names control the layout above. Each is a property-descriptor key and each has a decorator of the same name that sets it, so a program may write either and a tool that generates classes need not write decorators. A control's argument is a numeric literal: a layout is fixed at the declaration and byteLength is a constant a program may assert against, so the value has to be known there, and a literal is the form that guarantees it without bringing an evaluation order to a type position. This is #[repr(align(N))]'s rule in Rust for the same reason.

    These apply only where every field of the class and of its whole prototype chain is typed, since a class with an untyped field has no fixed layout to place a field within. A dynamic class may gain a typed field later through Object.defineProperty with a type key, and that field is part of no layout; on any other class such a call is a TypeError, because the layout closed at the declaration.

    Note

    An align replaces its field's alignment rather than strengthening it, which is the design's own reading: a float32x4 at @align(4) follows a float32 at byte 2 at byte 8, not at byte 16. That is what makes the control useful in both directions, and it is the program's to get right, since an implementation may hold a field's natural alignment to be a precondition of the instruction it would otherwise use.

    Two fields given one offset occupy one memory, which is the C union, and a negative offset overlaps a base's. That is deliberate reinterpretation, for reading a float32's bits as a uint32, and it is not how a program should write a tagged union: a sealed abstract class hierarchy is that, and the language checks it for exhaustiveness (1.11.8).

    Overlapping fields are the one place a typed read can produce a value the type system did not construct, and this specification permits it knowingly. The store check of Table 23 applies PER FIELD, against the type that field declares: a store through bits is checked against bits's type and a store through value against value's, and neither knows the other shares its bytes. So a program that writes a float32 through one field and reads a uint32 through another gets the bit pattern reinterpreted, which is exactly what it asked for and is the reason the C union is expressible at all. The type system's guarantee is over what a field ACCEPTS, not over what the bytes beneath it came to hold; a program that overlaps two fields of different types has taken responsibility for the correspondence, in the same way that a program writing through a DataView over a typed array has. Nothing else in this specification has this property, and nothing else needs it: it follows from offset placing a field outright, which is the point of offset.

    Reading or writing a bit-field is a shift and a mask, and taking a reference to one is a type error, since it has no byte address to refer to. A bit-field is also not a SIMD lane mask: boolean8 and its family are one bit per lane and belong to the vector types, where a bit-field is a sub-byte integer member of a class.

    Automatic packing reaches only a field under 8 bits, so a uint.<12> occupies 2 bytes unless an offsetBit places it, which is worth knowing for a wire format whose fields are 12 bits wide. The design states the rule for the sub-byte case and leaves the wider one to the explicit control, and whether automatic packing should follow bitLength rather than a byte is a question it should answer.

    9.4 Finiteness

    The layout of a value type class is defined exactly where the rule of 1.11.2 holds, that a value type class may not contain itself, directly or through a cycle of value type fields. The two are one condition. Computing a layout recurses from a class into the type of each of its fields; the recursion terminates exactly where that field relation is acyclic; and every field contributes a size of at least zero and at least one field of a cycle contributes more, so a cycle admits no finite fixpoint and every acyclic graph reaches one in as many steps as it has edges. The rule is therefore not a restriction placed on top of the layout but a statement of when the layout exists, and the diagnostic a program gets names the cycle rather than a size that could not be computed.

    A field whose type is a reference (1.11.10) closes a cycle, which Table 58 gives no layout and whose width is the implementation's; the recursion stops there rather than descending, which is why a linked list is expressible and a class containing itself by value is not.

    A field written T | null for a value type class T does NOT close a cycle, being laid out inline (10). A class that contains itself through one therefore has no finite layout, and is a type error like any other cycle of value type fields; the class is declared reference to close it.

    10 Optional Values

    A field or an element whose type is _T_ | *null* for a T that is a value type with a layout is laid out INLINE: a discriminant of one byte, placed so that the payload begins at T's alignment, followed by T's layout. The alignment of such a type is T's, and its byte length is T's byte length plus the discriminant, rounded up to that alignment. No storage is allocated for it separately and it is reached without indirection.

    null is the discriminant's zero, so a zero-filled allocation is a run of empty optionals and a typed declaration without an initializer needs no fill pass of its own.

    The discriminant is a declared byte rather than a spare bit pattern of T, EXCEPT where T's declaration excludes a pattern: an integer primitive whose bounds metadata (6) refuses a value its base could otherwise hold, or a type that is a reference and so cannot hold null. Where such a pattern exists it is the discriminant, and the optional is the width of T.

    A bounds range excludes a pattern where an endpoint is open, which excludes its own value, or where a closed endpoint does not reach the corresponding extreme of the base. A range with neither endpoint, or one whose closed endpoints reach both extremes, excludes nothing and declares no niche. Only an integer base is read: a floating-point type has no next representable value to reason about without rounding, so it declares no niche whatever its bounds.

    Note

    This is Option<T> in Rust and in Swift, std::optional<T> in C++, and Nullable<T> in C#. All four lay the payload out inline and all four reserve a separate spelling for the case reached through a pointer.

    The representation was a reference, and the change is a layout decision rather than a semantic one because the indirection was never observable: storing into such a field copies, reading out of it copies, === compares fields, and the value cannot be held weakly. Those are the channels through which a separate allocation makes itself known, and each is closed, so what remains is the layout this clause defines. A one-byte payload cost a reference's width and an allocation carrying an implementation's header; it now costs two bytes, and an array of a thousand of them one allocation rather than a thousand and one.

    An inferred niche, as Rust performs one, is deliberately not taken. byteLength is a compile-time constant this specification lets a program compute with, place in an array extent, and assert; a size that depended on whether some nested field's value range happened to have a hole would let a new enum member resize a structure declared elsewhere. A DECLARED exclusion does not have that property, being written in the type and checked at every boundary the value crosses, which is why it is the half taken - the same half Rust guarantees through NonZeroU32 rather than through inference.

    A cycle is not broken automatically. An inference that laid out inline where it could and indirected where it could not would have to choose an edge in a mutual cycle, and any choice makes one of those layouts a function of declaration order or of the order an implementation walks the graph; worse, it would make the choice invisible, so that a program adding a field that completes a cycle would find a structure elsewhere quietly grow. Rust and C++ both refuse the recursive declaration and require the author to name the indirection, and 1.11.10 is where it is named here.

    11 The Span Type

    A window's length is a non-writable, non-configurable own property. It is a type error to store through that known member, even if the assigned value equals its current length. The permission applies to updates, compound stores, destructuring and writes through reference aliases with known origins. It follows the window contract through array-window calls, buffer views and column projections; it does not make an owned array's length non-writable. Element writes remain permitted, with the ordinary bounds and reference-liveness checks.

    Span.<T> is a FIXED-LENGTH WINDOW over a run of elements of T that it does not own. A second argument is optional and states the length: Span.<T, N> is a window of exactly N elements, and Span.<T> one whose length is not stated. Its elements may be read and written; its length cannot change. An array view (12) is a Span.<T> over the bytes of a buffer, and a projection of an SoA column (13) is a Span.<T> over that column; both were this type before it had a name.

    The array types say what is known about an EXTENT: [N].<T> states one and [].<T> states that it varies. Ownership is a separate question, and Span.<T> answers it: the value does not own its storage, which is why it has no capacity, no reserve, and no shrinkToFit (2.11) — those describe an allocation, and a window has none. It is also why new Span.<T>() is a TypeError exception and a class may not derive from it: there is nothing for such a construction to allocate. Span.<T>(buffer) reinterprets bytes that already exist, which is why it is a call and not a construction.

    A Span.<T> is INVARIANT in T, for the reason the array types are (1.4.2.7): a Span.<uint8> used as a Span.<number> would admit a Number into storage typed uint8. Span.<any> is admissible on the same ground the array types admit [].<any>, that a store through it is checked against the storage's own element type at run time (Table 23).

    Note 1

    The window is writable, and calling it a read-only view would give the wrong answer here: a read-only type could be covariant in T and this one cannot, because a write through it reaches storage whose element type it does not get to choose.

     Note 2

    An access outside the window's length is a RangeError exception, for a READ and for a WRITE alike. The write is the part worth stating: a window's length is fixed, so a write past the end has nowhere to go. The three containers differ here, and the difference is the design rather than an accident — a write past a [N] . < T > is attempted GROWTH and a TypeError exception (1.14.10), a write past a [ ] . < T > GROWS the array, and only an array with no element type answers undefined to a read.

    11.1 Coercion to a Span

    [].<T> and [N].<T> are both assignable to Span.<T>, and a tuple is assignable to it when every position's type is T. The reverse never holds: a window is not assignable to either array type, since neither the storage nor the right to grow it is the window's to give. Span.<T> is a member of the array and tuple family, so a type parameter bounded by [] admits one.

    A source reaches Span.<T, N> only where its length is known to be N: a [N].<T> does, and a [].<T> does not, its length being a run-time fact. Span.<T, N> is assignable to Span.<T> and not the reverse, since forgetting a length is always safe and inventing one is not.

    Note

    The length is optional rather than always present because the two cases are genuinely different. A view over a resizable buffer cannot carry its length in its type — that is why 12 takes a count as an ARGUMENT — while a window taken over a known run of elements can, and something has to carry it for a bounds check to be elided.

    std::span<T, Extent> and &[T; N] are the same shape reached from the same pressure.

    A coercion MATERIALIZES: it produces a window value distinct from the array coerced, and two coercions of one array need not be the same value. An implementation may elide the construction where the window does not escape. Views and SoA projections already answer this way, and a coercion that instead passed the array through would make one static type stand for two different kinds of value, which is the confusion this type exists to end.

    A window does not confer ownership, so obtaining an owned array from one is explicit: a spread or a slice copies the elements into a new array, and no implicit conversion performs that allocation.

    11.2 Liveness of a Span

    A window names a run of elements in storage it does not own, so it is a reference in the sense of 2.10 and takes that clause's rules. A Span.<T> over a growable array is INVALIDATED when that array's allocation relocates — by a push that outgrows it, by a reserve that reallocates, or by a shrinkToFit that releases — and a read or a write through an invalidated window throws a TypeError exception. An operation that does not relocate does not invalidate: a reserve for room the array already has, and a shrinkToFit on an array already at fit, leave every window over it valid.

    A window over a [N].<T> is never invalidated, a fixed extent having nothing that relocates. A window over a buffer follows that buffer's rules instead: it tracks a resizable buffer's length, or detaches where a fixed view's bytes cease to exist (12).

    Note

    This is the same rule an SoA projection already states and the same one a ref into an array already obeys, which is what makes it one rule rather than three: a window is a reference to many elements where a ref is a reference to one, and relocation is what invalidates either.

    12 Array Views

    Span.<T>(buffer, byteOffset, count, byteElementLength) is a VIEW over bytes that already exist, as distinct from the allocations of 1.8.3. A view IS a Span.<T> (11) and this clause states the buffer-specific half of that type: how its length is derived, and what becomes of it when the bytes beneath it change. It was spelled [].<T>(buffer), which named the growable array type to produce a value that owns nothing and cannot grow; the spelling now says which type it makes. Each is a call on the type rather than a new, because nothing is constructed: a view aliases storage a program already has.

    buffer may be an ArrayBuffer, a SharedArrayBuffer, any typed array including another view, or a FIXED-extent owned array [N].<U>, whose bytes are the ones its buffer accessor gives it - so Span.<T>(a) is Span.<T>(a.buffer), and naming the array rather than its storage is a spelling rather than a different operation. A DYNAMIC [].<U> is not a source: its length is a run-time fact, and a window over bytes sized to the length it happens to have would either freeze the array or come to describe storage it no longer uses. Two views over one buffer alias the same memory - which is the point of reinterpreting a buffer, and why an implementation may not use the element types to rule aliasing out. byteOffset defaults to 0. A view holds WHOLE elements: where the bytes available from byteOffset are not a multiple of the stride, the count is the floor of their length over it and the trailing partial element is not part of the view. count decides whether the view is FIXED or LENGTH-TRACKING and is described below. byteElementLength defaults to T's byteLength and may be smaller or larger than it, so a view may read one field out of a larger element by giving the element's stride; an element is addressed at byteOffset plus its index times that stride. It comes last because no other view constructor in the language has it: %TypedArray% and DataView cannot address interleaved data at all, so a signature that puts the stride where they put a count would read as familiar and mean something else.

    A view with no count is LENGTH-TRACKING: its length is the bytes available past byteOffset divided by the stride, so it grows and shrinks as a resizable buffer is resized. A view given a count is FIXED at that many elements and records its byte extent at construction. This is the distinction %TypedArray% and DataView already make by the same means — new Uint8Array(buffer, 0) tracks and new Uint8Array(buffer, 0, 8) does not — and it is spelled the same way here so that a reader who knows one knows the other. A fixed view whose bytes cease to exist reports a length of +0𝔽, as a %TypedArray% in the same position does, and refuses every access; it is a RangeError exception if the buffer does not hold that extent past byteOffset, and if the buffer later shrinks below it the view is detached and any access throws a TypeError exception. Growth never invalidates a view, and a view over a SharedArrayBuffer never detaches, since a shared buffer never shrinks.

    A store through a view is checked against T as any store to a typed element is (Table 23), and the converted value is what reaches the bytes.

    Note

    A length-tracking view answers a shorter length where a fixed one detaches, and the difference is not a preference: a fixed view's extent is part of what it promised at construction, so bytes disappearing from under it invalidates the promise, while a tracking view promised only to describe whatever is there.

    13 Structure of Arrays

    SoA.<T, Length> stores its elements as one array per field of T rather than as a run of T. It is a built-in exotic in the same way [N].<T> is: no user-defined class can express it, because declaring one array per field of a type is a mapped type this specification does not have, and because a reference into one denotes a column set and an index rather than a byte offset.

    Length follows the array types: 0, which is the default, is growable, and a non-zero value is a fixed extent. T must be a value type class or a primitive. A primitive T degenerates to a single column, so a generic that may be handed one needs no special case; a class with a field of no layout has nothing to split and is a type error.

    The layout is the row Table 58 gives it: each field of T is a column of Length elements, padded and aligned on its own, in declaration order, and the type's byteLength is the sum of the columns rounded up to its alignment. The split is ONE LEVEL: a field that is itself a value type stays a single column, interleaved within itself, so a consumer wanting that field as a contiguous run of its own type has one and a consumer wanting each of its leaves contiguous flattens the class. Which is wanted is a property of the data's use, and this specification does not decide it.

    An element's fields are not adjacent, so there is no interior padding between them, and a T whose interleaved layout pads to a larger stride has a smaller byteLength here than [Length].<T> does. A Type Object of this type additionally has an elementByteLength, the per-element sum of the column strides, which for the same reason is not the interleaved stride.

    A growable SoA.<T> has no layout as a type, exactly as [].<T> has none; its instances have a byteLength.

    Each column is aligned to its element type's alignment, and to nothing wider. A vector width is a property of the host rather than of the type, so folding one into the layout would make the same SoA a different size on different implementations and would cost byteLength its place among the compile-time constants of 9.1. Where an SoA's allocation is PLACED is a separate question and the implementation's own: the base's address is not part of what the type describes, so an implementation may put every allocation on a vector or cache-line boundary and is encouraged to.

    Length is defaulted, so SoA.<T> and SoA.<T, 0> name ONE type, as a defaulted parameter does everywhere.

    An SoA and a [N].<T> are distinct types with distinct layouts and neither is assignable to the other, whatever their elements. Conversion is explicit and copies.

    fields projects each of T's immediate fields as a Span.<F> (11) over that field's column, and the views alias: a write through one is visible through the element operations and the reverse. A projection of a growable SoA is INVALIDATED by a growth that reallocates, and an access through it afterwards throws a TypeError exception, exactly as a reference into the same SoA does — a projection that kept reading the abandoned allocation would disagree with its container and say nothing. A projection of a fixed SoA.<T, N> can never be invalidated, since a fixed extent does not grow.

    Note

    Invalidating rather than preventing is what a garbage-collected language can express. A borrow checker refuses to compile a program that grows a container while a projection of it is alive, and pays nothing at run time for the guarantee; here nothing marks the end of a projection's life, so a container that could not grow while one had ever been taken could never grow again. The check is loop-invariant — the generation cannot change without a call — so it is hoisted rather than paid per element, and the fixed form has no check at all.

    14 Checked Contracts

    A function declaration may carry where clauses, the WhereClauses of 5.1, between its return annotation and its body. On an ordinary function they are the compile-time bound over its generic parameters that 4.9 describes. On a compile-time-evaluable function they are more, because such a function returns a type and a predicate over that type is a checked contract: a fact about the type the builder returns, stated at the declaration and checked at every evaluation.

    The production below restates the one 1.4.4 gives, with WhereClauses added (1.1).

    FunctionDeclaration[Yield, Await, Default] : function BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt WhereClauses[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] } [+Default] function TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt WhereClauses[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] }

    Within a WhereClause of a function declaration, return is a PrimaryExpression denoting the value the function returns. It is a Syntax Error for return to occur as an expression anywhere else, which costs nothing, since the token is ungrammatical in expression position today and no program can be using it.

    A contract is read two ways, and both are load-bearing. It is verified: at every concrete evaluation of the builder, once 1.2.7.3 has a result, each clause is evaluated with return bound to it, and a clause that is falsy is a type error naming the builder, the arguments it was given, and the clause. A contract is never trusted. It is assumed: before specialization, where the application is deferred and no result exists, the checker takes each clause as a known fact about the deferred Type Record. The second is sound because of the first: any specialization that would falsify an assumption is stopped at the builder, before the code that relied on it runs.

    Note

    This is the trade C++ concepts make, recovered inside a specialization model: the body of a generic is checked against declared bounds at its declaration, and per-instantiation verification is the backstop that makes the bounds safe to believe. function sanitize<T: type>(value: T): omit(T, ['password']) checks at its declaration because omit's contract says Reflect.isAssignable(T, return), and { ...value } is a T.

    Direction is the thing to get right and is easy to invert. An upper bound, that the result is assignable to something, serves a consumer holding the result. Checking a body that produces the result needs a lower bound, and for omit the true one is that T is assignable to the result, since removing properties yields a supertype. A contract stating the reverse would be both true of nothing and useless to the body.

    Two limits are worth stating rather than discovering. A contract is a proposition about one evaluation, so universally quantified knowledge, the variance of omit(T, K) in T or any parametricity fact, is not expressible as one and stays unavailable before specialization; after specialization the types are simply evaluated and compared, so nothing is lost where a program actually needs it.
