And a contract is checked only where the builder is evaluated, so one on a builder that nothing applies is checked nowhere: the ASSUMED reading can travel to a consumer while the VERIFIED one has not run anywhere. What closes that is a test that calls the builder, which is a library author's ordinary obligation rather than a mechanism this specification adds - and the gap is narrow, because a contract only misleads a consumer whose own code is never specialized, and code that is never specialized is never evaluated. Beneath contracts sits the cast, which is legal with a deferred application as its target and resolves at specialization into the ordinary checked conversion of Table 23; that is the honest division, with contracts stating what an author can promise and a checked cast bounding what an author merely asserts.

    15 Inference Through Computed Positions

    Inference reads plain parameter positions (1.4.3.4): a parameter under a deferred application is opaque, because binding it from the application's result would require running the builder backwards, and a builder is an opaque function. Where a computed type sits in a return position nothing is needed, since the argument infers plainly and the result is a function of it. This clause is the remainder, for a parameter that occurs only in computed positions, and it adds two rules that propose a binding and verify it forward. Neither runs a builder backwards and neither admits anything forward checking would not.

    15.1 Literal Freshness

    Known primitive object-spread contributions participate in the literal's final member facts. Null, undefined and non-String primitives contribute no enumerable own properties. A known String contributes its indexed UTF-16 code units; String length is not an enumerable contribution. Respect property replacement order and retain uncertainty for unknown Strings, Objects, getters or other unavailable contributions. A known empty spread does not conceal a missing required member.

    The required-member presence judgment includes established Symbol keys as well as String keys. Compare Symbol identity, not its description. Reject a missing required Symbol member only when both the final literal contributions and the relevant prototype lookup establish absence; an inherited property may satisfy the ordinary structural read. Optional members permit absence. Unknown computed keys, prototype effects and any retain runtime checking. Format a Symbol diagnostic without coercing the Symbol to a String value or executing user code.

    An object literal checked against an expected object type is checked freshly: an own property the expected type neither declares nor admits through an index signature is a type error, reported against the property. Freshness is a property of the literal and not of its type, so it is lost the moment the value is bound to a name and read back: f({ a: 1, b: 2 }) is checked freshly against f's parameter, and f(o) is not.

    Note

    Without this an all-optional shape is a supertype of nearly everything, and width subtyping admits any literal against it, which is correct for a value that reached the position through a binding and useless for one written at the position. A value type class already imposes the rule, since a literal converted to one fills a layout that has no room for a property it did not declare (9); freshness is that rule stated for the structural case, and it is what makes the trials below discriminate at all.

    15.2 Trial Specialization

    A generic parameter that ordinary inference leaves unbound and whose constraint, or for a value parameter whose domain, denotes a closed candidate set is inferred by trial. A value parameter has a domain and no bound, and M: 'fast' | 'safe' names the same candidates as M: type extends 'fast' | 'safe', so the two spellings infer alike. A constraint denotes one when it is a union of types, an enum of types, or a sealed class, whose candidates are the members in declaration order, the enumerators in declaration order, and the class with its direct subclasses transitively, the set that is fixed once the declaring module finishes evaluating (1.11.8). So do boolean, whose candidates are its two literals; a literal type, whose one candidate is itself; and an array of stated extent whose element denotes a closed set, whose candidates are the tuples of that length over the element's candidates in order — the form a variadic parameter (4.4) proposes through, [2].<boolean> proposing its four tuples — each tuple counted against the budget as a constructed Type Record. Any other constraint denotes none, and a parameter so constrained does not trial.

    A parameter is trialed against exactly the arguments whose declared types mention it and no other unbound parameter; an argument whose type mentions two or more is not separable and takes part in no trial. For each candidate in order, that candidate is substituted for the parameter throughout those arguments' declared types (4.7), which evaluates each deferred application under the memo already specified, and each argument is checked against the result, freshly where it is a literal. A candidate every argument satisfies survives. Exactly one survivor binds the parameter; zero or more than one is a type error asking for explicit arguments and naming the constraint.

    The count is a sum over the parameters trialed rather than a product across them, since each is trialed alone. Trials are counted against a ceiling of 64, which is this clause's own and not the host-defined budget of 1.2.7.4. Exceeding it is a type error asking for explicit arguments, and because the ceiling is fixed rather than host-tunable, whether a program's inference succeeds is a fact about the program.

    Note 1

    A fixed number here and a host-defined one at 1.2.7.4 is not an inconsistency but a difference in what is being bounded. That budget meters arbitrary evaluation, and the clause warns that "a limit must be one the implementation can actually reach"; a number fixed here would oblige every host to reach it for a computation whose cost the specification cannot see. A trial count is the opposite: it is a sum of candidate-set sizes, and each of those is fixed by a declaration the program contains — a union's members, an enum's enumerators, a class's subclasses — so the count can be read off the source before a single trial runs, it is small, and every implementation can honour it. A limit a reader can compute and a host can always meet is worth fixing; one that is neither is not.

     Note 2

    This is overload resolution's logic pointed at specialization: enumerate, evaluate forward, keep what checks. It terminates in as many memoized evaluations as the constraint has members and is sound because nothing is accepted that forward checking did not accept. apply({ kind: 'circle', radius: 3 }) against apply<T: Shape>(patch: partial(T)) trials Circle, whose partial the literal satisfies, and Rect, whose kind it contradicts, and infers Circle because exactly one survived.

    Separability is a determinism rule before it is a cost rule. merge<A: Shape, B: Shape>(a: partial(A), b: partial(B)) runs the members of Shape for A and again for B, never their product, and a site whose argument mentions both, as pair(A, B) does, asks for explicit arguments rather than searching a space whose size is the product of two constraints.

    15.3 Declared Inverses

    A compile-time-evaluable function may carry an inverse decorator naming another, which the checker consults for a parameter that ordinary inference and trial specialization both leave unbound. The declared inverse is applied once per site, memoized and counted against the budget, to the type of the argument whose computed type mentions the parameter, and what it returns is a proposal: for a builder with one inferable slot, a type; for one with several, a record keyed by parameter name, whose proposals are verified together.

    A proposal binds nothing until it is verified. It is substituted for the parameter, the deferred applications are evaluated forward, and the arguments are checked against the results, which is the check an explicitly specialized call would face and is performed by the same operations. Where it holds, the proposal binds. Where it does not, the parameter stays unbound and the site is a type error asking for explicit arguments. A declared inverse that does not invert can therefore only make inference fail, never make it succeed wrongly.

    Four details complete the rule. The argument's type, for a parameter reached through a REST (4.4), is the tuple of the collected arguments' types, a ref argument contributing its referent's; the inverse of a builder over a pack receives that tuple and returns the pack's tuple, one rule for scalars and packs alike. A proposal is a Type Object, or an object whose properties are Type Objects keyed by parameter name; anything else is a type error naming the builder. Where the builder is a member of an overload set, the inverse consulted is the one declared on the member the call resolves to (1.10.3), since resolution precedes binding. The two diagnostics name what they refuse: a builder with no inverse - "f declares no inverse, so T cannot be inferred through it; supply explicit type arguments" - and a proposal that fails forward verification - "f's inverse proposed X, which its forward evaluation does not accept for these arguments".

    The association is recorded through the declaration's own decoration and nowhere else: the inverse decorator's primitive accepts only the live decoration context of the declaration being decorated, so it cannot be called after the fact or on another declaration's behalf, which is what makes it a fact of the declaration rather than a registration. Because the checker consults the association before the source text runs, the checking pass processes an inverse decoration of a function declared in the source text with its other type declarations (1.2.8), applying it to the declaration's live decoration context there; a decoration the pass has processed is not applied again when evaluation reaches it. A builder that carries no inverse decoration declares no inverse, which the pass knows from the declaration alone.

    Note

    The association lives on the declaration because that is the only place with one possible author and no timeline: an imperative registration would make inference depend on module evaluation order and let unrelated modules contend for one builder's meaning, and a decorator has neither failure mode and is read where the checker is already reading. The proposal is what user code contributes, and it contributes it as an oracle whose answer is checked, which is why letting user code propose here does not reopen the boundary 1.2.7 draws.

    This rung is last on purpose. The first two need nothing from an author: a builder in a return position infers plainly, and a closed constraint trials. An inverse is for the remainder, and it should be adopted when porting demonstrates the need.

    16 Operator Declarations

    For numeric indexing whose effective selected operator [] is statically known, a store requires either a matching set operator [] or a read operator returning a reference location. A known value-returning read operator without a setter is not a writable location: assignment, compound fallback, update and destructuring or iteration stores to it are type errors. A declared compound operator that performs no store remains a call; a definitely skipped logical store is not judged as a write. Unknown selection defers to the runtime check. String-key property access remains ordinary property access, and a reference-returning operator retains all permission and liveness checks of 2.8.

    An operator is declared in one of three places, and they differ only in what the receiver is: on a class, where the receiver is the left operand; on a class reopened elsewhere, by the extension form, which appends operators to a type declared in another module; and in a primitive block (6.5), where the receiver is the primitive. This clause gives the form; 1.9.9 gives what an operator declaration means for the operators of the language, and 6.5 what it means for metadata.

    PrimitiveOperatorDeclaration[Yield, Await] : primitive [no LineTerminator here] TypeName[?Yield, ?Await] TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt { OperatorDefinitionList[?Yield, ?Await]opt } OperatorDefinitionList[Yield, Await] : OperatorDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] OperatorDefinitionList[?Yield, ?Await] OperatorDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] OperatorDefinition[Yield, Await] : staticopt operator OperatorName OperatorTypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] } staticopt operator OperatorName OperatorTypeParameters[?Yield, ?Await]opt ( FormalParameters[~Yield, ~Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ; operator Type[?Yield, ?Await] ( ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { FunctionBody[~Yield, ~Await] } * operator ... ( ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt { GeneratorBody } * operator ... ( ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ; OperatorTypeParameters[Yield, Await] : .< GenericEntryList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt > OperatorName :: one of + - * / % ** == < > <= >= & | ^ ~ << >> >>>

    An OperatorTypeParameters is classified and checked as the TypeParameters of a method definition is (1.4.3.1): operator+.<T: type>(rhs: T) declares a parameter, operator+.<uint32>(rhs: uint32) fixes the argument, and a mix of the two is a selector-prefixed overload. The leading . stays because the operator token may itself end in < or >.

    A PrimitiveOperatorDeclaration is a Declaration; 6.1 restates that production with it added. An OperatorDefinition is a ClassElement, restated below, and an interface member, so a class declares operators among its methods and an interface declares the operators a type must have, which is what makes an operator expressible as a constraint. The form without a body is the declaration-only one an interface and a metadata-only definition take. The cast production is the implicit cast operator of 6.5.

    The ... productions are the typed iteration protocol: a generator operator whose declared return type types the elements it yields, and whose declaration defines the class's Symbol.iterator method. Like any operator it may be overloaded on its return type, and untyped iteration uses the first declared overload. It yields values rather than references.

    ClassElement[Yield, Await] : MethodDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] static MethodDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] FieldDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] ; static FieldDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] ; ClassStaticBlock ; OperatorDefinition[?Yield, ?Await] abstractopt ClassElementName[?Yield, ?Await] ( UniqueFormalParameters[?Yield, ?Await] ) TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt ;

    The last alternative is the abstract method of 1.11.6, restated here because a later restatement carries a production's complete form (1.1). The abstract keyword is optional: what makes the member abstract is the absence of a body, and the class being declared abstract is what permits that absence. Writing the keyword is accepted and changes nothing.

    The alternative is written out rather than expressed as a MethodDefinition with its body omitted so that the forms it does not reach are visible in the grammar: it takes a ClassElementName and a parameter list and nothing else, so static, a constructor, and the get, set, async and generator forms of MethodDefinition are outside it. 1.11.6 gives the reason for each.

    An operator's own type parameters are written .<…> rather than <…> because the operator name may itself end in < or >: operator<.<D2: Dimensions> lexes where operator< <D2: Dimensions> would collide with the << token. This is the one place a declaration site uses the application spelling, and the reason is lexical rather than principled.

    Resolution reads the left operand's type alone. For a * b, the operators of a's type are searched for a signature whose parameter accepts b, and the operands are never reversed to find a match. Return type overloading applies as it does to any function (1.10.5), and two applicable definitions with the same parameter types and no expected return type is an ambiguity and a type error. A primitive block adds to a global operator table; two definitions for one pair of types is a type error at the second declaration. The pair is the type the block names and the type of the definition's parameter, and the return type does not distinguish two entries of the table, since dispatch through it selects by the right operand alone. The second declaration may be in a later source text: the checking pass of a Module runs after its dependencies have evaluated (1.2.8), and their blocks are in the table by then. A static operator defines an operator on the class object rather than on its instances, so that A += 5 may mean something, and takes no part in any of the above.

    |> may not be declared (39). Resolution reads the left operand's type and searches it for a signature describing the operation, and a pipeline has no operation to describe: it binds one operand and evaluates the other rather than computing a value from both. The same reasoning excludes any future operator that binds rather than computes, and is why the exclusion is stated here, where resolution is defined, rather than only where the operator is.

    Note

    Never reversing the operands is the rule that makes Matrix4 * Vector4 and Vector4 * Matrix4 different operations, which in a column-major library they are: one transforms a column vector and the other a row vector. A language that reverses operands to find any match makes that bug unfindable. It is also why 2 * v needs a primitive block rather than falling back to v's operators: the left operand is a number, and the declaration belongs where the library author can write it.

    The block is made generic by an interface constraint rather than written once per pair, so primitive float32 { operator*.<T: type extends ScalarMultiply.<float32, T>>(rhs: T): T } covers every type that defines scalar multiplication, including ones declared later. 2 * v reaches it because viability filtering precedes ranking (1.10.3.1): a Vector4 satisfies ScalarMultiply.<float32, Vector4> and not the number instantiation, so the number candidate is eliminated before the number-first order could prefer it. Division does not commute, so no such block exists for it and 2 / v stays a type error, which is correct, since it is not defined. The rule this states is general. It is a type error to apply an arithmetic, bitwise or ordered operator, unary or binary, to an instance of a typed class whose class declares neither that operator nor a primitive conversion of its own, a valueOf, toString or Symbol.toPrimitive other than those of %Object.prototype%: the conversion those inherited methods perform would succeed and produce NaN or a String, which is not the operation the program wrote. A + with an operand that may be a String is concatenation and is not reached. Where the instance is the right operand, the rule applies only where no primitive block could supply the operator, since dispatch reads the left operand. A class that is not typed is unaffected.

    A global table is why an operator-bearing type is a nominal class and not an alias. Were Vector4 an alias for float32x4, its operators would land on float32x4 itself and any other library aliasing that lane type would collide on every shared pair. Two libraries with two nominal Vector4 classes coexist, because the parameter types differ. The division the design draws is to alias for storage and accessors and to declare a class where the type carries operators.

    17 Vector Comparisons

    A comparison between two vectors of one shape yields one lane per input lane, and what it yields for each is decided by the expected type, since the comparison is overloaded on its return type (1.10.5). Three results are defined: the wide mask, a vector of the boolean type of the same width as the compared element, so a float32x4 comparison yields a boolean32x4 of lanes all-set or all-clear; the compact mask, a bit vector of one bit per lane; and the compared vector type itself, its matching lanes all-ones. Left with no expected type the expression is ambiguous among them and is a type error, so the result's type is written.

    Which comparison each operator performs on a lane is what it performs on a scalar. A hardware comparison of floating-point values chooses among predicates that differ on two axes: an ordered comparison is false when either operand is NaN and an unordered one is true, and a signaling comparison raises the invalid-operation flag where a non-signaling one does not. <, <=, >, >=, and == are ordered and != is unordered, which is the reading that makes a lane agree with the scalar operator of the same spelling: NaN == NaN is false and NaN != NaN is true. All are non-signaling, this specification having no floating-point exception surface to signal into. A comparison of integer lanes has no such choice, integers having no NaN. The predicates with no operator are not exposed; a program requiring the ordered test alone writes a == a && b == b.

    The lane counts the shorthand names cover are the register widths, which is why float32x4 has a name and a three-lane float vector does not. A vector of any other lane count is written vector.<T, N>, which is what a narrowing accessor produces, and a library wanting a name for one declares it.

    Note

    The three forms are three instructions, which is the point of the overloading rather than a consequence of it: the wide mask is what a comparison natively produces on SSE and NEON, the compact mask is an AVX-512 mask register, and the all-ones vector is what a program blends with. Choosing among them by the annotation lets one spelling reach each without an intrinsic per form, and makes the ambiguity rule load-bearing rather than pedantic: an unannotated a < b has no defensible default among three instructions, and a coin flip here is a performance cliff a program cannot see.

    The bit vectors are the one place a lane and a bit coincide, and the numbering is stated as a rule in 1.5.8 rather than here: a bit vector converts to and from an integer whether or not a comparison produced it. movmskps and vpmovmskb number their results the same way, which is why the rule costs nothing to honour. They are not the bit-fields of 9, which are sub-byte integer members of a class.

    18 Complex Numbers

    complex.<T> is a value type holding a real and an imaginary component of the real numeric type T. The width-named shorthands count total bits, following the convention of the numeric libraries the design cites, so a complex64 holds two float32 components; the bare name complex is complex.<number>.

    A numeric literal in a complex position takes the complex type, with the literal as its real component and zero as its imaginary one, so let r: complex = 5 is complex(5, 0) and an imaginary literal beside a real one reads as the mathematics does. A real VALUE does not convert on its own: _z_ + _x_ for a complex z and a number x is a type error, written _z_ + complex(_x_), which is the rule that holds between any two numeric types here. The literal's representability is the component type's, so a literal no float32 can hold is no complex64 either.

    ToBoolean of a complex is false where both components are zero and true otherwise, so complex(0, 0) is falsy as every other numeric zero is. A complex is not one of the existing language types, and ToBoolean of an object is otherwise always true, so this is stated rather than inherited: without it the origin would be the one numeric zero that is truthy.

    An imaginary literal (1.4.1.3) has the type complex, with the literal's value as its imaginary component and zero as its real one, so 4i is complex(0, 4). Literal propagation applies as it does to any numeric literal (1.5.19), so an imaginary literal in a complex64 position is a complex64. complex64 and complex128 convert to and from complex, and to each other, explicitly and not implicitly, exactly as float32 and float64 convert to and from number and to each other, and the treatment of a value outside the component type's range is Table 22's as it is for that component.

    Note

    Bare complex has number components for the reason the language keeps number and float64 distinct: number is what an untyped literal and every Math function produce, so a complex built from Math.PI composes without a cast, and the fixed widths exist for an interleaved buffer and for interop. Being a value type, a complex copies on assignment and lies inline, so a [].<complex128> is the interleaved buffer an FFT expects and 9 gives it the layout to be one.

    19 Ranges

    It is a type error if a present endpoint has a participating Static Type restricted to symbol, null or undefined, whose intrinsic domains supply no range ordering. A union establishes this failure only when every alternative is excluded. An omitted endpoint is not a present undefined value. Unknown types and unresolved class or metadata ordering capabilities do not establish this proof. No ordering operator is evaluated by this judgment.

    A range is a value type class over an ordered element type and a bound at each endpoint it has. There are four shapes: Range.<T, S, E> carrying both endpoints, RangeFrom.<T, S> and RangeTo.<T, E> carrying one, and RangeFull.<T> carrying neither. Each implements RangeBounds.<T>, which is the interface a consumer of an arbitrary range is written against and the type a bound-valued position takes. S and E are values of Bound, either Bound.Closed or Bound.Open, one for each endpoint the shape has, so the four intervals of a two-endpoint range, the closed, the two half-open, and the open, are the four pairs and nothing further is expressible. The four-way name of a pair is an Interval, which a range exposes and a diagnostic prefers over the parameterization, and which is never itself a parameter: a shape with one endpoint would otherwise carry a bound for an endpoint it does not have. A range is a value, so it allocates nothing and copies; and it is an expression, so it appears wherever one does, including a case label and an argument list, without further rule.

    19.1 Range Endpoint Domains and Membership

    The type parameter of a concrete range shape is its stored endpoint domain. Each present endpoint, including an excluded endpoint, is a value admitted by that domain. A fresh range expression in a range-family construction context reads its present endpoints at that context's domain using ordinary literal propagation and checked admission, in source order and once each. A statically established failure is an early type error, including in an unused body. A runtime-only failure occurs when that endpoint is evaluated; no range is published and contextual state is restored. A range obtained through a binding or call retains its domain and is not silently rebuilt by a target annotation.

    Real numeric endpoints use their intrinsic exact order, including object-backed decimal, rational and float128 values. Their representation does not require a user-declared ordering operator or ordinary conversion. NaN and complex values are not ordered range endpoints.

    Without a construction context, a range's endpoint domain is the canonical union of the runtime types of its present endpoints, or the one endpoint's type for a one-ended range. A full literal takes its domain from construction context, or any when none exists. Reflection reports the corresponding concrete range shape, this domain, and its actual bound arguments; it never derives the domain from only the first of two endpoints.

    Membership in a concrete range shape checks the shape, specified bound arguments, and invariant endpoint-domain identity. A bare shape or an any domain is an erased query. Membership in RangeBounds.<T> instead checks that the value is a range and that each present endpoint already satisfies T; it does not change the concrete specialization. A full range satisfies this view vacuously. These judgments perform no endpoint conversion, ordering comparison, iteration, or public endpoint property read, and grant no reference capability. Empty and descending ranges retain their endpoints and receive no exemption from these rules.

    Note

    (0..<5) is Range.<uint8> is false, while a fresh const r: Range.<uint8> = 0..<5 constructs typed endpoints. const r: Range.<uint8> = 0..<256 is a type error because the exposed end is not a uint8. Iterating the literal 0..<256 at uint8 remains valid under the separate produced-element rule.

    RangeBounds.<T> carries the operations that are total over the four shapes, because it is what a holder of an arbitrary range has. contains takes either a value or a range: against a value it is membership, and against a range it is containment of one point set in another, so an empty range is contained in every range and the full range contains every range. intersect is the point-set intersection of two ranges. It is commutative and associative with the full range as its identity; where two ranges share an endpoint the exclusive bound is the one the result carries; and where they are disjoint the result is the greater start with the lesser end, which is descending and therefore empty, so an empty intersection has no separate representation. The shape of an intersection follows from its operands rather than from either one, which is why the result is described by a RangeBounds view with the endpoint domain specified below: the intersection of a RangeFrom and a RangeTo is a Range, and the intersection of any range with the full range represents the same point set as that range.

    19.2 Domain-Preserving Range Selection

    Intersection, containment and emptiness are ordering operations. They use stored endpoints, not public endpoint property reads or an arithmetic reconstruction. Numeric comparison is exact mathematical comparison, including wide integer values; no intermediate Number conversion is permitted. A pair of class endpoints is compared using the left endpoint's declared < first and, if that is false, the right endpoint's declared < with exchanged operands. When both are false, the total-order contract makes the endpoints equivalent. An incomparable pair throws a TypeError. Abrupt comparison completion propagates immediately, before any result range is published. These operations do not invoke ordinary coercion methods, mutate the inputs, or grant reference capabilities.

    Intersection selects the greater lower endpoint first and then the lesser upper endpoint. An omitted bound contributes no constraint. At equivalent endpoints, retain the left input's endpoint value and choose an open bound if either input bound is open; otherwise choose a closed bound. Preserve selected endpoint values and their domains without conversion, rounding, wrapping or snapshotting. Disjoint operands retain the crossed endpoints and therefore produce an empty range.

    The result endpoint domain is the canonical union of both operand domains, independent of which endpoints are selected. A full range whose domain is any contributes no domain constraint and is neutral in this calculation; a full range with a specific domain participates normally. Thus equal domains remain equal, declared union domains remain present, and two RangeFull.<T> values intersect to RangeFull.<T>. The concrete shape and bounds follow the selected endpoints. The operation can be described as intersect<U>(other: RangeBounds.<U>): RangeBounds.<T | U>, subject to mutual ordering and the full-any identity rule. This does not change either input's concrete specialization.

    For emptiness, an endpoint-free range is not empty. A one-ended numeric range is empty when its only endpoint is positive infinity at an open start, or negative infinity at an open end; a closed extreme remains non-empty. Other one-ended ranges are not empty. For two present endpoints, compare the start with the end. It is empty when the start is greater, or when they are equivalent and either bound is open. For range containment, first determine whether the inner range is empty and, if so, return true. Otherwise test lower-bound coverage and then upper-bound coverage, stopping at the first failure. At equivalent bounds, an open outer bound does not cover a closed inner bound. A present endpoint is never treated as absent merely because its type lacks numeric conversion. A scalar NaN is not contained.

    Note

    Commutativity and associativity of intersection concern the represented point sets. Domain union is also commutative and associative. Equivalent endpoint representatives may have distinct signed-zero representations or class payloads: selecting the left representative does not assert that these values have identical representations or reference identity. No new canonicalization of endpoint payloads is implied.

    scale multiplies both endpoints by a scalar and is present on the instantiations whose element type defines scalar multiplication, which an ordering does not imply: a range over Temporal.Instant has an order and no arithmetic, and has no scale. A negative factor exchanges the endpoints and the bounds that go with them, since the image of a half-open range under negation is half-open at the other end, and exchanges RangeFrom with RangeTo for the same reason. A zero factor yields the closed range at zero rather than the result of multiplying each endpoint, which for a half-open range would be empty, and leaves an already empty range empty.

    19.3 Numeric Range Scaling and Reflection

    This clause defines the built-in numeric scale operation and unary negation of a range, which uses the same operation with factor negative one. Supported bases are number, bigint, sized signed and unsigned integers, binary float16, float32, float64 and float128, decimal32, decimal64 and decimal128, and rational types, including their numeric metadata parameterizations. This interval operation does not select an iterator item carrier.

    A call performs these steps in order. The ordinary evaluation of the receiver and argument expressions precedes the call.

    1. Require a range receiver; otherwise throw a TypeError. Read only its internal endpoints, bounds and stored or inferred endpoint domain. Require that domain to be a supported numeric type, a union consisting of supported numeric domains, or any. Require every present endpoint to have a supported numeric type and a finite real value or infinity. Otherwise throw a TypeError.
    2. Require the supplied factor to be a finite real numeric value. Omission, undefined, nonnumeric values, complex values, NaN and infinities throw a TypeError. Do not perform ordinary object or String conversion. Read the exact mathematical factor, independently of its representation or the endpoint widths.
    3. If the source is empty under 19.2, or the factor is exactly positive one, return a copy retaining the original endpoint values, bounds and domain. Do not repeat endpoint admission.
    4. If the factor is zero of either sign, select a zero type: the concrete numeric source domain if there is one, otherwise the original start's type if present, otherwise the original end's type if present, otherwise number for an endpoint-free any domain. If no type is determined, throw a TypeError. Construct canonical positive zero in that type and admit it by the rule below once. Return a closed singleton using the same admitted zero at both endpoints and the original source domain.
    5. For a non-zero factor, process the original start first and the original end second. An absent endpoint remains absent. A present infinite endpoint retains its numeric type and presence, with its sign multiplied by the factor's sign. For a finite endpoint, compute the exact mathematical product and represent it by the rules below. Admit each manufactured endpoint before processing the next; propagate the first abrupt completion immediately.
    6. If the factor is positive, publish the resulting endpoints in their original roles. If negative, exchange their roles and the corresponding bounds, including absence. Every result retains the original source endpoint domain, including a stored or inferred union. No result range is published before all required endpoint admissions succeed.

    An integer product must be integral and representable in that endpoint's original base; otherwise throw a RangeError. There is no truncation, wrapping, saturation or promotion. A rational product is exact, reduced to its canonical fraction, and checked against its existing numerator/denominator representation limits; a failure throws a RangeError.

    For a binary or decimal floating product, choose the greatest representable value no greater than the exact product for a final lower endpoint, or the least representable value no less than it for a final upper endpoint. The final role accounts for the factor's sign even though processing remains in original source order. If rounding moves the value, make its bound closed; otherwise retain its source bound. A finite product whose magnitude exceeds the base's greatest finite magnitude throws a RangeError, rather than manufacturing infinity. Binary subnormals participate. A non-zero decimal product whose adjusted exponent is below the base's supported minimum throws a RangeError; this operation does not introduce another decimal format. For binary zeros, including a non-zero product rounded to zero, retain the sign of the mathematical multiplication; the zero-factor singleton rule instead uses positive zero. These rules require no intermediate conversion through Number and no enumeration of interval members.

    Exact positive-one copies retain decimal cohorts. Exact negative-one reflection negates a decimal coefficient while retaining its exponent. Other decimal products use the reduced coefficient/exponent representation of their directed result, with zero represented canonically. This rule does not infer a preferred precision from an arbitrary rational factor. Infinite decimal endpoints preserve their numeric base and infinity sign under the preceding sign rule.

    To admit a manufactured endpoint, apply its full numeric parameterization's existing checked admission when it has one, propagating any exception. Admission must preserve the computed mathematical value, binary zero sign, and, for a decimal, coefficient and exponent. If it changes that representation, throw a RangeError. After successful admission and representation checks, the manufactured endpoint carries its full admitted numeric parameterization, even when the admission judgment accepted an otherwise bare base value. Attaching that already-admitted type does not invoke admission again and must preserve the same representation. Subsequent membership and reflection recognize the carried type by their ordinary rules; admission may not rescale or requantize the endpoint. For zero scaling there is one admission; for empty or identity copies there is none. Source ranges are never mutated, earlier hook side effects are not rolled back, and a later call can reuse the source. Success and failure confer no reference authority; borrowed locations retain all existing liveness checks.

    Note

    The floating result is a conservative enclosure of the exact image. (1..=1).scale(rational64(1,10)) has Number bounds 0.09999999999999999..=0.1. Metadata rescale hooks using bounds.scale(factor) inherit this enclosure rule, including possible widening. Ordinary scalar metadata conversion retains its existing conversion and rounding rules. Binary interval arithmetic, custom arithmetic domains and numeric iteration are separate operations; this clause does not supply a common promoted domain for two input ranges.

    19.4 Additive Numeric Interval Arithmetic

    The built-in + and - operations on two ranges compute coordinate addition and subtraction in the supported real numeric representations of 19.3. They use one agreed numeric endpoint type. These operations compute exact mathematical bounds followed by checked representation; arbitrary declared scalar operator bodies are not invoked as an interval enclosure algorithm.

    After ordinary left-to-right operand-expression evaluation, perform these steps in order.

    1. Inspect the left range's stored or inferred domain and present endpoint types, then the right's. Read internal values without public property access, ordinary coercion, or user ordering calls. A domain must be a supported concrete numeric type, including a numeric metadata parameterization, or any. A union or other domain throws a TypeError. Every present endpoint must have a supported numeric type and be finite real or infinity; otherwise throw a TypeError.
    2. Each concrete domain and each present endpoint's full numeric type contributes a type. An any domain contributes only its present endpoint types, so an endpoint-free full-any operand contributes nothing. Require all contributed types to be identical by SameType; otherwise throw a TypeError. Let the result domain be the agreed concrete type, or any if there are no contributions. No type is selected by magnitude, union-member order, or implicit numeric promotion.
    3. Determine emptiness of the left operand, then the right if needed, by 19.2. If an operand is empty, return a copy of that operand's endpoint values and bounds carrying the agreed result domain, preferring the left when both are empty. Do not manufacture or readmit its endpoints. Domain agreement is required even for these exits.
    4. For addition, calculate the lower result from the two lower endpoints. For subtraction, calculate it from the left lower endpoint minus the right upper endpoint. Represent and admit that endpoint by the rules below before proceeding.
    5. For addition, calculate the upper result from the two upper endpoints. For subtraction, calculate it from the left upper endpoint minus the right lower endpoint. Represent and admit that endpoint by the rules below.
    6. Publish the result range with the calculated endpoints, bounds and agreed domain. Propagate any earlier abrupt completion immediately; no result is published on failure.

    When either contributor to a result endpoint is absent, that endpoint and its bound are absent. Do not manufacture infinity or invoke endpoint admission for it. Otherwise both contributors are present. For finite values, compute their exact mathematical sum or difference with no intermediate Number conversion. Integer and rational results obey their exact representability checks; floating results round outward according to the final lower or upper role, with the same finite-overflow, binary-subnormal and decimal adjusted-exponent rules as numeric scaling. An exact result bound is open if either contributing bound is open; otherwise it is closed. If floating rounding moves a bound, make that bound closed.

    For present infinities, subtraction first reverses the right infinity's sign. Adding a finite value and infinity, or two infinities of the same sign, produces a present infinity of that sign in the agreed type. Opposite infinities in addition, and like infinities in subtraction, throw a RangeError at that endpoint calculation. Do not publish a NaN endpoint or replace an indeterminate calculated bound with absence. Missing bounds contribute no calculation, so their propagation is independent of arithmetic on explicitly present infinities. The empty-image exit precedes endpoint arithmetic.

    Exact cancellation produces positive binary zero. When both finite contributors are zero, addition produces negative zero only if both are negative zero; subtraction produces negative zero only for negative zero minus positive zero. Other exact zero results are positive zero. Decimal addition/subtraction uses the reduced coefficient/exponent representation of the calculated result. Neither operator has a zero-operand identity shortcut; manufactured endpoints receive ordinary admission even when their mathematical values equal old endpoints. Numeric scaling's explicitly specified identity and reflection rules remain unchanged.

    Apply the agreed full numeric parameterization's existing checked admission to every manufactured endpoint. Propagate its exceptions and require it to preserve the calculated mathematical value, binary zero sign and decimal coefficient/exponent, as in numeric scaling; a change throws a RangeError. Do not drop, merge or infer new endpoint metadata from arbitrary scalar operator bodies. Earlier hook effects retain their ordinary semantics, with no rollback. Source ranges remain unchanged and reusable. Neither the operation nor its failure extends reference lifetime or grants reference capabilities.

    Note

    An erased range with uniformly typed endpoints can establish the agreed carrier. A full-any range beside a byte range yields RangeFull.<uint8>; two full-any ranges yield RangeFull.<any>. Explicit union domains do not choose an arithmetic member. The result-domain rule selects the representation of a new computed range and does not convert either input. Multiplication and division are specified separately in 19.5; addition/subtraction alone does not determine the unit type of a product or the treatment of a divisor crossing zero. Custom interval enclosure declarations require their own contract.

    19.5 Multiplicative Numeric Interval Arithmetic

    The built-in * and / operations on two ranges compute coordinate enclosures in one agreed supported real numeric endpoint type. They do not invoke arbitrary scalar operator bodies as an enclosure algorithm or infer a quantity's result units from metadata. The agreed full numeric type is the result domain and its ordinary admission applies to manufactured bounds. These are coordinate interval operations, independent of the representable-member lattice used by iteration or length. Using the same range as both operands still supplies two independent coordinate choices.

    After ordinary left-to-right operand-expression evaluation, perform these steps in order.

    1. Validate both operand domains and present endpoints, establish one identical contributed numeric type, and select the first empty operand, exactly as the first three steps of 19.4. This includes full numeric parameterizations, rejection of unions, the erased any contribution rule, the left-first empty preference, and copying an empty operand with the agreed domain without readmission. Do not read public properties, invoke ordinary coercion or call user ordering operators.
    2. For division, if the right operand has neither a strictly positive lower endpoint nor a strictly negative upper endpoint, return an endpoint-free range in the agreed domain. An open zero endpoint does not satisfy this guard. This exit follows domain/empty checks and performs no endpoint admission, including when the numerator is zero.
    3. For multiplication, if either operand has a present infinite endpoint and the other contains zero or has a zero endpoint, throw a RangeError. This includes zero in the interior and excluded zero or infinity endpoints. For division, if both operands have present infinite endpoints, throw a RangeError, including excluded endpoints. Missing endpoints do not count as present infinities. Complete this indeterminate-coordinate preflight before any result endpoint representation or admission.
    4. Calculate exact candidates and select a lower and upper extreme by the rules below. This calculation performs no endpoint admission or intermediate representation rounding. Represent and admit the selected lower endpoint first, then represent and admit the selected upper endpoint. Stop immediately on abrupt completion.
    5. Publish the resulting range with the agreed domain, resulting endpoint presence and bounds. No partial result is published, and neither source range is mutated.

    For candidate calculation only, describe each present finite endpoint by its exact rational mathematical value, binary zero sign when applicable, and whether its bound is closed. Describe a present infinity by its sign and closedness. Describe a missing lower or upper endpoint by a private negative or positive infinite limit respectively, marked absent and not closed. These private coordinates are not values in the endpoint domain and are never admitted or stored as new infinity endpoints.

    Visit the four pairs in this order: left-lower/right-lower, left-lower/right-upper, left-upper/right-lower, left-upper/right-upper. A candidate starts closed only if both contributing coordinates are closed. Its multiplication or division sign is negative exactly when one contributing coordinate has negative sign, including a negative binary zero or negative infinite limit. Apply the following rules without intermediate conversion through Number.

    1. Two finite coordinates contribute their exact mathematical product or quotient. Division's guard ensures that a finite denominator coordinate is non-zero. Normalize its denominator to be positive.
    2. For multiplication, zero times a missing infinite limit contributes signed finite zero. Other products involving infinite coordinates contribute an infinity of the product sign; mark the candidate absent if any infinite contributor is absent. The preflight has already rejected products of zero and a present infinity.
    3. For division by an infinite coordinate, a finite numerator contributes signed finite zero. An absent numerator limit divided by a present infinite denominator also contributes signed finite zero. An infinite numerator coordinate divided by an absent denominator limit contributes no candidate. Two present infinities have already been rejected. These rules impose no constraint from a doubly unbounded quotient corner; other corners supply the extrema.
    4. For division with an infinite numerator coordinate and a finite denominator, contribute an infinity of the quotient sign and retain the numerator's absence mark.

    Select the mathematically least and greatest candidate, comparing exact fractions and signed infinite coordinates without narrowing. A non-empty operand pair passing the division guard supplies at least one candidate. At an extreme attained by several candidates, combine their closedness by disjunction. At a tied infinite extreme, combine absence marks by disjunction; a negative-infinite lower extreme or positive-infinite upper extreme marked absent produces no result endpoint or bound, even if another tied candidate was present. A positive-infinite lower extreme or negative-infinite upper extreme retains a present infinity bound even with absence provenance; it still constrains the result to that extreme, which a present source infinity necessarily established. Other selected infinities also produce a present infinity of their sign in the agreed type. At a tied exact finite zero, select negative binary zero for the lower result if any tied candidate has negative sign, and positive binary zero for the upper result if any has positive sign; retain the sole sign when all ties agree. Decimal zero is canonical.

    In addition to a closed corner, interior values can establish attainment of a selected extreme. A finite zero extreme in multiplication is attained when either operand contains zero. A finite zero extreme in division is attained when the numerator contains zero, or the divisor has a closed present infinite endpoint and the numerator has a finite coordinate value. A present infinite extreme in multiplication is attained when a closed present infinite endpoint in either operand can combine with a non-zero coordinate of the appropriate sign in the other operand; that coordinate may itself be infinite. A present infinite extreme in division is attained when a closed present infinite numerator endpoint can combine with a finite non-zero divisor coordinate of the appropriate sign. These tests use the coordinate intervals' intrinsic order and stored bounds, not enumeration or user callbacks. An absent result remains absent regardless of attainment. An exact present bound is closed if attained by any of these rules, otherwise open.

    Finite selected extrema use the checked representation rules of 19.3: integers must be integral and fit, rational fractions reduce before their numerator/denominator width check, and binary/decimal floating bounds round outward in their final lower or upper role. A moved floating bound is closed. Finite overflow throws a RangeError; binary subnormals and the existing decimal adjusted-exponent floor participate as specified there. A non-zero finite value rounded to binary zero retains its exact sign. Decimal results use the reduced coefficient/exponent form. No reciprocal, unselected corner or intermediate result receives these checks or admissions. Neither multiplication nor division has an identity-copy exemption.

    Every manufactured present endpoint receives the agreed full numeric parameterization's checked admission, with the mathematical-value, binary-zero-sign and decimal-cohort preservation checks specified for numeric scaling. Propagate hook exceptions; a representation change throws a RangeError. Missing endpoints receive no admission. Although candidate selection and indeterminate preflight precede representation, lower representation/admission precedes upper representation/admission: an upper overflow does not suppress earlier lower hook effects. Those effects are not rolled back. Sources remain reusable after failure. No success, failure, empty copy or full-range fallback grants reference authority or extends the lifetime of a borrowed location.

    Note 1

    (0..=0) * (0<..<1) is closed zero, and (Infinity..=Infinity) * (1<..<2) is a closed infinity singleton: endpoint exclusion does not make a constant image empty. (2..) / (2..) has an open zero lower bound and no upper bound. (0<..=1) * (1..<Infinity) throws because its explicit boundary coordinates are indeterminate; replacing the infinite endpoint with absence permits the private-limit calculation. (..) / (Infinity..=Infinity) is closed zero under this bound-information contract. Missing bounds do not enumerate implicit infinite inhabitants. These rules preserve the distinction between absent constraints and supplied endpoint values rather than defining an algebra of all subsets of IEEE values.

     Note 2

    The full-range division fallback deliberately retains the existing conservative contract. A divisor such as 0<..=1 can have a tighter one-sided quotient enclosure, but this operator does not switch to a partial-image or split-interval API. The result always has one RangeBounds view in the agreed domain. Custom scalar overloads or metadata alone do not establish a different enclosure or dimensional-arithmetic contract.

         Note 1

    The bound is per endpoint rather than one four-valued interval because a shape with one endpoint has one bound, and a RangeFrom parameterized by an interval would admit a type no value inhabits while still being nameable by an overload. The split also gives each marker in a literal one parameter to set, makes an operation that replaces one endpoint a substitution rather than a computation over an enumeration, and lets a signature fix one bound and quantify the other, which a single parameter could express only as a union of interval values.

    scale is conditional on the element type rather than declared for every range because an interface that advertises a member no instantiation of it can run is not a contract. The mechanism is the ordinary one for a member that exists on some instantiations, narrowing a parameter of a partial declaration, which 1.5.12 already uses to declare the mask operations on the vectors whose lanes are bits and on no others. A narrowing to an interface differs from that one only in admitting every element type that satisfies the interface rather than a single lane type.

    19.6 Range Literals

    It is a type error to use a value statically known to be a built-in range as a range endpoint, or as an operand on the built-in path of <, <=, >, or >=. A range's endpoints being ordered does not make the range itself ordered. A range literal has the corresponding range Static Type even when no outer contextual type is supplied; parentheses and participating constant aliases preserve it. Applicable declared and derived operators are considered first, so a declared comparison may accept a range argument. A union proves rejection only when every possible dispatch path establishes the prohibited built-in operation; an unknown left operand can still supply an applicable operator. Equality, containment and other interval operations are unaffected. The judgment uses the resolved built-in identity, not a user class's spelling, and dynamic failures retain their runtime checks.

    A range is written with a member of the .. family. The four two-endpoint forms a..<b, a..=b, a<..<b, and a<..=b produce the half-open, the inclusive, the open, and the open-start inclusive-end interval, and the open-ended forms a.., a<.., ..<b, ..=b, and .. omit an endpoint. A range that has an end always marks whether it includes it, and a range marks its start only where the start is exclusive, so there is no a..b and no ..b: a bare .. appears only where the endpoint it faces is absent and has no inclusivity to state.

    The family is six tokens, .., ..<, ..=, <.., <..<, and <..=, each taken whole by longest match and each decided by a fixed lookahead. At a . the second character separates the type argument list .< from the rest of the family and the third separates the spread ..., ..<, and ..= from ..; at a < the second character separates << and <= from the family and the fourth separates <..< and <..= from <... The .< that opens a type argument list and the ..< of a range are therefore told apart by their second character, before a third is read, and no input reaches a state where both are live. Claiming <.. costs the grammar one reading, a relational comparison whose right operand begins a range, and costs it nothing else, because generic application is spelled .< and a bare < is always relational or a shift.

    The family collides with the numeric literal grammar, since 1. is already a complete numeric literal, and the collision is resolved by one lexical rule: a . is not the decimal point of a numeric literal when the character after it is also a .. So 1..<6 is the three tokens 1, ..<, 6 rather than 1. then .6, while 1., 1.5, and the spread ... are unchanged, and a form that marks its start needs the rule not at all, since the < of 1<..<6 ends the literal before a decimal point is in question. The one construction the rule changes is an integer literal followed by .. and a member name, the 1..toString() idiom, which is a Syntax Error rather than a member access on a number, because 1.. is a complete from-range and an identifier cannot continue it. One further lookahead is extended by a character: ?. is not the optional chaining punctuator where a decimal digit follows it, and is likewise not the punctuator where a . follows it, so that cond?..<b:c is a conditional whose consequent is a range. The extension changes no program, since ?. followed by . is a Syntax Error under every production that consumes the punctuator.

    A range binds tighter than assignment and looser than || and ??, so its operands are ShortCircuitExpressions, and it is non-associative. The pipeline operator (39) binds looser still, so 0..<10 |> f(%) pipes the range rather than ranging over a pipeline. Continuing: a..<b..<c is a Syntax Error rather than a nesting. Member access binds tighter than the range, so 0..<arr.length is 0..<(arr.length) and a range reaches its own members through parentheses, as in (0..<10).length. Because a range is an expression it appears in a case label, an object literal, and an argument list with no further rule, and a statement that begins with .., ..<, ..=, or <.. continues the preceding expression, joining the other leading-operator forms on the list of automatic-semicolon hazards.

    Because each token is taken whole, the spacing of the family is significant at its edges. a..<b is the half-open range where a.. < b is a relational comparison against the from-range a..; a<.. is the open-start from-range where a < .. is a comparison against the full range; and a <.. < b is a comparison against a<.. rather than the open range, since <..< is one token and spacing it apart does not assemble it. None of the spaced readings is a program at all: a range binds looser than the relational operators, so a range is never a relational operand and each of these is a Syntax Error. Parentheses put a range back under them, and there a range is REJECTED as a relational operand: a range does not implement Ordered, so (0..<3) < 5 is a TypeError rather than the false an ordinary object's comparison would yield. Answering a meaningless comparison with false is the failure this rejection exists to prevent, and it is the only reading the family costs, so the cost is paid where it can be seen.

    The value carries its start and its end, and its bounds are in its type rather than in a field. Its start and end are the endpoints, absent for an omitted one, and interval is the four-way name derived from the two bounds of a two-endpoint range; contains tests a value against the endpoints and their bounds; An endpoint may be INFINITE, and an infinite endpoint is not the same as an absent one: 0..<Infinity has an end and 0.. has none, so they report different endBound and interval and only the latter is isFull when both sides are absent. They contain the same values and iterate the same, a positive infinite forward stop stopping finite progression nowhere exactly as an absent end does. length is the exact BigInt count of the members of a bounded integer range, which is one more than the difference of its endpoints less one for each endpoint whose bound excludes its own value, and never less than zero; and isEmpty is whether it has none, a descending range being empty rather than reversed and a range whose endpoints are equal being empty unless both of its bounds are closed; and reverse iterates the same members in the opposite order, which is how a descending traversal is written given that a descending range is empty. The nth value of an iteration is the start plus n times the step, counted from 0 where the start's bound is closed and from 1 where it is open, since a start that excludes its own value cannot yield it. A range iterates through its members by the rule of 19: over a bounded integer interval the step is 1 and implicit, and step supplies a step where the interval is not one an implicit step fits or widens the stride where it is. A range with no start is not iterable, and a range whose endpoints are not a whole integer interval is a TypeError to iterate without an explicit step, rather than a silent choice of 1.

    19.6.1 Static Types of Range Properties

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes the normal-result property types in Table 61. Recognize the resolved intrinsic identity, not the spelling of a user declaration. Let T be its endpoint type, S and E its bound arguments, B the intrinsic Range.Bound enum, I the intrinsic Range.Interval enum, and U the type undefined. Retain T's complete numeric metadata, generic parameter identity or class identity. An erased any endpoint remains any under the ordinary union rules. Existing generic-argument requirements still apply.

    Every receiver in the table contributes boolean for isEmpty and isFull, and bigint for length. A known bound selects a singleton based on the same intrinsic enum, not an unrelated Number literal or a newly declared enum. The interval members for closed/closed, closed/open, open/closed and open/open are respectively Closed, ClosedOpen, OpenClosed and Open. When a bound argument is not established, retain the whole corresponding enum; do not evaluate a generic argument to force a singleton.

    Use the same contribution for dot access, a statically established String property key, optional-chain access and object destructuring. Join every alternative of a statically established finite key domain; join receiver alternatives under the ordinary union-member rules. Optional-chain short-circuiting contributes undefined by the existing rules. An unknown key or unrelated property retains the existing gradual/member judgment. This table does not introduce types for untyped bindings or parameters independently of their existing participation rules.

    These are normal-result types, not proofs that the read completes normally. In particular, length retains the preconditions in 19.8, even for a statically known range. Empty and descending ranges retain their endpoint types. The judgment neither calls a getter, examines endpoint values, orders endpoints, acquires an iterator nor grants reference authority.

    The public read uses ordinary property access and its effects and abrupt completions. Its Static Type does not prove the identity or behaviour of a replaceable getter. Under 1.7.5.1, retain any required receiving or return boundary unless an independent proof establishes that the actual property implementation supplies that type. A guarded implementation may establish such a proof without changing observable property access or reference liveness. A replacement getter returning an incompatible value cannot silently initialize a binding whose required contract rejects that value.

    19.6.2 Static Types of Derived Ranges

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver with endpoint type T contributes a callable normal-result contract of RangeBounds.<T> for each of scale, take and drop. Retain the complete endpoint type, including metadata and generic or class declaration identity. Use this contract for dot access, established computed String keys, finite key domains, optional chains, extracted method values and receiver alternatives under the ordinary member and call rules. It neither binds the receiver to an extracted function nor introduces a typed contribution into an otherwise gradual binding.

    This clause supplies a result contract independently of argument admission and operation availability. The factor or count position retains the numeric validation, absence, failure and evaluation-order rules of the operation's runtime clause. In particular, do not convert a count to an index type or a factor to T as a consequence of this result judgment. Unsupported endpoint domains, invalid arguments and unrepresentable bounds may throw despite the known result view. Explicit iterator results are specified in 19.6.4; terminal forwarded helpers are specified in 19.6.6.

    After applicable declared operator dispatch, the built-in unary negation of a statically established range-family operand with endpoint type T contributes RangeBounds.<T>. For built-in binary +, -, * and /, establish both operands as built-in range-family values and read their endpoint types A and B. If A and B are the same type, contribute RangeBounds.<A>. Otherwise, if either endpoint type is any, contribute RangeBounds of the other endpoint type. If neither condition holds, this rule supplies no common result contribution. It does not unify different type parameters, strip metadata, promote numeric families or choose a union as an arithmetic carrier. A whole operand of any or unknown type does not establish built-in range dispatch and is not the endpoint-erasure case.

    For union operands, apply the result judgment to every alternative or alternative pair and join the results only when every alternative contributes. A cyclic or unresolved alternative supplies no independent result proof. The judgment examines types without evaluating operands, endpoints, generic computations, getters, comparisons or metadata hooks. It creates no reference authority. Applicable user-declared operators retain their declared return contracts.

    These contributions describe normal results, not proofs of normal completion or of the actual concrete shape. The runtime algorithms retain their domain validation before empty, zero and singular exits, full endpoint admission, failure order and reference-liveness checks. The actual value has the shape produced by the operation. A manufactured numeric endpoint retains its completed full-domain admission as specified for numeric scaling; an inferred receiving boundary must not lose that carried identity or repeat validation solely because the result gained a Static Type. Its static RangeBounds view contributes possible endpoint absence under 19.6.1; do not copy the operand's concrete shape or bounds into this result contract. Two-ended division can produce a full range, a negative scale can exchange one-ended shapes, and zero scaling can produce a closed point.

    A method's static return contract does not establish the identity or behaviour of its replaceable property implementation. Perform ordinary receiver evaluation, property access, argument evaluation and invocation. Retain any required receiving or return boundary under 1.7.5.1 unless an independent proof establishes the actual implementation's result contract. A failed inferred initialization preserves prior effects, leaves its binding uninitialized and does not permit subsequent uses to trust an unchecked replacement result. Optional short-circuiting and reference liveness retain their ordinary rules.

    19.6.3 Static Results of Range Selection Methods

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes a callable boolean normal-result contract for contains. Its candidate position is any, with omission supplying undefined under the runtime method's existing rules. A range candidate selects the subset operation; another candidate selects scalar containment. This result judgment neither converts the candidate to the receiver's endpoint type nor introduces an ordering-capability preflight or a narrowing predicate. Existing exact heterogeneous numeric comparison, declared class ordering, NaN refusal, short-circuiting, failure and evaluation-order rules remain applicable.

    The receiver's intersect member contributes a generic range-result view. Read the receiver's complete endpoint type T and the argument's established range-family view with endpoint type U. Normally contribute RangeBounds.<T | U> with a canonical endpoint union. When the receiver is statically established as RangeFull.<any>, contribute RangeBounds.<U>; when the argument is statically established as RangeFull.<any>, contribute RangeBounds.<T>. Both neutral shapes contribute RangeBounds.<any>. A full shape with a specific domain participates in the union normally. A RangeBounds.<any> view does not prove absence and is not neutral.

    A candidate whose range view or endpoint domain is unknown contributes any; the established method still contributes a RangeBounds.<any> result. For an argument union, include every alternative's contribution and canonicalize their endpoint union. An unresolved or cyclic alternative contributes any and cannot be omitted. Receiver alternatives use the ordinary union-member rules; a whole unknown receiver supplies no built-in contract. This is a normal-result judgment, not a proof that the argument is a range, that ordering succeeds, or that any result exists.

    Read these contributions from the established source types, independently of the destination annotation. A destination cannot remove a participating domain or cause endpoint conversion or reconstruction. Retain complete metadata and generic or class declaration identities. A method view retains its receiver contribution through generic substitution without capture by its own type parameter. Its actual normal result retains the selected endpoints, concrete shape, bounds and reflected domain specified by 19.2. Its static view exposes possible endpoint absence under 19.6.1.

    Apply the same contracts to dot access, established computed String keys, finite key domains, optional chains and extracted method values, including object patterns, under the ordinary member and call rules. Extraction does not bind a receiver. This judgment creates no typed participation for an otherwise gradual receiver. It evaluates no endpoint, getter, comparison or metadata hook and grants no reference capability.

    These contracts do not prove the identity of a replaceable method. Preserve ordinary property access, argument evaluation, invocation and abrupt completions. Under 1.7.5.1, keep required inferred-initialization and return admission unless an independent proof establishes the actual implementation's result contract. A replacement returning an incompatible result cannot initialize a checked binding; prior effects remain and that binding stays uninitialized after failure. Optional short-circuiting and reference liveness retain their ordinary rules. This clause does not supply iterator or callback result contracts.

    19.6.4 Static Results of Explicit Range Iteration

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes callable normal-result contracts for step and reverse. The step parameter is by: any = undefined; reverse takes no parameters. Their normal results are helper-bearing synchronous iterators with item contribution I, terminal contribution undefined, and an optional any input to next. The numeric cursor ignores incoming values. Omission of by supplies undefined and retains the numeric difference validation failure; it does not select implicit iteration. Its next result is the discriminated union { value: I, done: false } | { value: undefined, done: true }. Its self-iteration method contributes an Iterator with those same three protocol arguments. The terminal contribution is not void and a direct .value read must include possible exhaustion.

    Derive I without evaluating endpoints. For a concrete range shape, a complete supported numeric endpoint domain contributes itself, including metadata. The supported bases are number, bigint, sized int and uint, and float16, float32, and float64. A literal endpoint type contributes the endpoint-fallback contribution of its base. A union contributes the canonical union of every arm's endpoint-fallback contribution. A cyclic, unresolved, erased or unsupported alternative contributes any and cannot be discarded. This judgment supplies an upper bound on normal items, not proof that acquisition or any request completes normally.

    The endpoint-fallback contribution of a supported typed-numeric or BigInt type is its full type, including metadata. A Number type, including a Number parameterization, instead contributes number; a Number endpoint does not select a typed-number carrier in 19.7. Apply the same literal, union and unknown rules recursively. A RangeBounds receiver uses endpoint fallback even for a single numeric domain, because this endpoint-reading view does not prove the hidden stored domain. Thus a concrete range shape with a Number metadata domain retains that domain in I, while a RangeBounds view of it contributes number. Unresolved generic parameters contribute any at this judgment; a destination annotation does not select, reconstruct or retag a stored domain.

    Apply these contracts to dot access, established computed String keys, finite key domains, optional chains and extracted methods, including object patterns, under the ordinary member and call rules. Extraction does not bind a receiver. A whole gradual receiver gains no participation from its method's spelling. The result satisfies the structural iteration protocol; an implementation's internal helper carrier must not require resolving an unwritten global constructor. Existing helper contracts continue to apply to the helper-bearing result. This clause does not add those methods to arbitrary protocol objects.

    The contracts do not prove intrinsic method identity. Retain required inferred-initialization and return admission under 1.7.5.1, ordinary property access, argument evaluation and invocation. An incompatible replacement cannot initialize a checked binding; prior effects remain and a failed binding stays uninitialized. The result contract does not consume the iterator during checking or admission, add reference authority or extend reference lifetime. Numeric item admission, metadata hooks, fused exhaustion, failure order and step/origin validation remain as specified by 19.7. Default range iteration follows 19.6.5; terminal forwarded helper callbacks are specified in 19.6.6.

    19.6.5 Default Range Iterator Contracts

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes a callable [Symbol.iterator] member with no parameters. Its normal result has the helper-bearing synchronous cursor contract of 19.6.4: item contribution I, terminal contribution undefined, and optional any input to next. Derive I by that clause's concrete-domain, endpoint-fallback and uncertainty rules. The result's self-iteration method retains the same three protocol arguments. A direct next().value read includes possible exhaustion. Neither the destination context nor the member spelling invents a concrete stored domain.

    The original method acquires a fresh forward numeric cursor on every call, leaving the range reusable. The cursor's own self-iteration returns itself. This does not make a range a cursor or add a next member to it. Acquisition, missing-origin and unsupported-domain failures, item admission, progression and fused completion retain 19.7's rules. A known result contract does not prove successful acquisition, a non-empty sequence or termination.

    Apply the view when the well-known Symbol key is established under the ordinary property-key rules, including dot and computed access to the unshadowed Symbol intrinsic, constant keys and object-pattern extraction. Unrelated Symbols and a shadowed Symbol name do not establish the key. Optional reads retain short-circuiting; extraction does not bind a receiver. Whole gradual receivers and mutable callee bindings retain the ordinary participation and stability rules.

    Supply the same default protocol to established static iteration, flattening and delegation queries. A stored range's endpoint-literal set is not an item set: a ClosedRange.<1 | 3> can yield 2. Derive a consumer's yielded contribution from I, and a delegation's terminal contribution independently from undefined. Keep existing literal-loop counter facts and unresolved protocol uncertainty. A protocol contribution does not by itself promote an ordinary Array literal into typed storage or establish an Array's replaceable iterator from its indexed element type.

    Preserve a fresh range literal's produced-element fit judgment for contextual numeric spread destinations, including array, tuple-rest and function-rest positions. Its stored endpoint domain is not a second, broader item judgment that overrides that fit. A written unknown endpoint can select the runtime numeric carrier; another known Number endpoint alone does not establish Number items. Retain uncertainty absent an independently established context.
