For uncertain spread routing to fixed numeric parameters, the broad literal protocol alone does not prove every argument count impossible; distinct positions can have distinct numeric domains. Retain ordinary receiving checks rather than imposing one position's bound on the whole source interval. Receiving admission of a metadata-bearing item retains ordinary validation effects after next returns; it does not extend the cursor's active reentry guard through the receiving operation.

    The view is a property-read and normal-result contract, not a permanent storage declaration or proof of intrinsic identity. Preserve ordinary lookup, getter effects, invocation and required receiving admission under 1.7.5.1. Do not freeze or wrap a range, cursor or method to establish it. Checking executes no hook or next call. An incompatible replacement retains prior effects and leaves a failed initialization uninitialized. No part of this judgment grants reference authority or extends a reference lifetime.

    A simple loop binding whose type was inferred from the source protocol receives the ordinary inferred-binding admission before the body executes, with captured generic parameters substituted in the active type context. Retain that binding contract for subsequent stores. Explicit annotations retain their own checks, explicit any remains gradual, and destructured bindings use their ordinary extraction checks. Reference iteration retains its separate location and liveness rules. A failed loop-entry admission follows the existing abrupt-completion path, including environment restoration and iterator closing; a downstream elision may not rely on an inferred binding that was never admitted.

    19.6.6 Terminal Range Helper Contracts

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes the following callable contracts, where I is derived by 19.6.4, including its endpoint-fallback and uncertainty rules. This contribution does not assert successful acquisition, traversal or callback completion.

    Apply these member contracts to established computed String keys, finite key domains, optional access and extracted method views under the ordinary member and call rules. Extraction does not bind a receiver, and a whole gradual receiver gains no participation from the spelling. The callback positions provide contextual types under 1.6.5. A fresh literal's adopted bindings are enforced at initialization, including checked admission of the helper's counter to uint64; an already created uncontextualized function or a written any parameter is not retroactively annotated. Contextual void requires nothing of a discarded callback result. A predicate's contextual Boolean return remains a checked result boundary; an existing function with an explicit any return does not acquire that declaration by being passed as an argument.

    find includes undefined even for a non-empty range because the predicate may never match. The void result of forEach does not denote a value a binding may hold. The original forwarding methods acquire a fresh numeric forward iterator and read the corresponding helper by ordinary property access. toArray and forEach retain the refusal of an absent or positive-infinite stop before acquisition; some, every and find retain their short-circuit behaviour. Empty traversal does not invoke a callback to check its contract. Numeric acquisition and item admission follow 19.7.

    Neither the range method view nor the inherited helper name proves intrinsic identity. Preserve ordinary access and invocation effects and the required inferred-initialization and return checks under 1.7.5.1. A replacement that retains a contextually typed callback retains that callback's binding obligations on later calls. Failed admission preserves prior effects and leaves an unsuccessfully initialized binding uninitialized. Checking invokes no callback or iterator and grants no reference authority or extended lifetime. Lazy mapping and filtering are specified in 19.6.7, and flattening in 19.6.9; reduction recurrence follows 19.6.8. Default range iteration follows 19.6.5; argument-routing judgments remain separate.

    19.6.7 Lazy Range Mapping and Filtering Contracts

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes callable contracts for map and filter. Let I be its item contribution under 19.6.4, including endpoint-fallback and uncertainty rules. The mapper takes callback: (value: I, index: uint64) => U, where U is its generic output type inferred from the callback under 1.6.5. Its normal result is a helper-bearing synchronous iterator with item U. The filter takes callback: (value: I, index: uint64) => boolean; its normal result keeps item I. Filtering does not infer a narrowed item type merely from the predicate's body.

    Both results have terminal contribution undefined and an optional any input to next. Their next results are respectively { value: U, done: false } | { value: undefined, done: true } and { value: I, done: false } | { value: undefined, done: true }. Self-iteration contributes those same protocol arguments. Apply the inferred output substitution to the full result protocol as well as its item argument; a closed result must not retain an unbound output parameter in its self-iteration view. The results satisfy structural receiving contracts without resolving an unwritten global helper constructor, and retain the applicable synchronous helper contracts for subsequent calls.

    These judgments also govern mapping and filtering of an established helper-bearing synchronous iterator, using its established item contribution in place of I. They do not add helpers to arbitrary structural iterator Objects. A whole gradual receiver gains no participation from a method name. Established computed names, optional access and extracted method views use the same contracts under the ordinary member rules; extraction does not bind a receiver.

    The original range methods acquire a fresh numeric iterator and reach the corresponding helper by ordinary property access. Creating the helper does not invoke the callback. Traversal invokes it on demand, and filtering can consume several source items before yielding. An async mapper's returned Promise remains an item of the synchronous helper; it is not assimilated. Acquisition, callback failures, exhaustion, iterator closing and unbounded traversal retain their runtime rules. A result contract does not guarantee successful or terminating traversal.

    Contextual callback binding admission, written annotations and Boolean predicate result obligations follow 19.6.6. The views do not prove intrinsic identity: retain ordinary lookup, effects and required inferred-initialization and return admission under 1.7.5.1. A replacement that retains a callback retains its adopted binding obligations. An incompatible replacement result cannot initialize a checked binding; prior effects remain and that binding stays uninitialized. No contribution or admission consumes the iterator, executes the callback, grants reference authority or extends a lifetime. Flattening follows 19.6.9; reduction recurrence follows 19.6.8. Default range iteration follows 19.6.5.

    19.6.8 Range Reduction Contracts

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes a reduce callable contract with callback (accumulator: U, value: I, index: uint64) => U and normal result U. Let I be the cursor item contribution of 19.6.4, including its endpoint-fallback and uncertainty rules. An established helper-bearing synchronous iterator uses its established item contribution instead. This judgment does not add helpers to structural iteration interfaces or to a whole gradual receiver.

    Select one accumulator contract for the call after establishing argument routing. If there is no initial argument, let U be I. If an initial argument is present, a fresh callback's written non-any first parameter type anchors U; an existing callback with one established nongeneric signature may contribute its first parameter type on the same terms. A wider union in that position is an anchor, not a request to narrow U to the initial value. Use the input contract for the first supplied argument, not the collected rest binding: a fixed first tuple-rest position or a homogeneous array-rest element can contribute it. Unresolved leading-rest distribution supplies no anchor. Optional/default inputs include undefined before binding initialization. An ignored first parameter supplies no anchor. Otherwise derive U from the initial argument with ordinary binding widening and reference-value decay. A receiving result context may provide ordinary numeric-literal adoption but does not override a known incompatible initial type. A written any callback input does not erase an independently established initial contribution. Genuinely unknown contributions remain any. If unresolved spread count or routing leaves initial-argument presence unknown, do not choose either recurrence by guessing; retain independent item and index facts and leave the accumulator gradual.

    Check established initial values, callback inputs, callback results and completed results against the selected contract under the ordinary checking rules. Do not widen an anchored recurrence merely to accept a callback result. Apply contextual-function adoption under 1.6.5 to fresh callbacks; written annotations take precedence, and existing callbacks are not retroactively annotated. Preserve ignored callback parameters and symbolic types from enclosing generic contexts. These rules apply to established computed names, optional access and extracted method views. Each invocation selects its own accumulator contract. Extraction does not bind a receiver, and ordinary binding-stability rules remain applicable.

    A fresh callback's adopted parameters and result are enforced at their ordinary declaration boundaries. An explicit any result defers its produced-value check without discarding known parameter obligations: a subsequent typed accumulator binding checks its next input, and a required final receiving binding or return checks the completed value. A discarded final value creates no receiving obligation. An empty traversal does not invoke a callback to validate an unknown initial value. Do not wrap a callback, change its identity, or add an intrinsic accumulator-store check solely from this static view. Existing declaration checks and required receiving admission under 1.7.5.1 remain effective, including after method replacement.

    The original range method acquires a fresh forward numeric iterator and reads its helper by ordinary property access. It retains the refusal of an absent or positive-infinite stop before acquisition. Without an initial argument, the first item seeds the accumulator, callback indices begin at 1, and an empty iterator throws a TypeError exception. With an initial argument, indices begin at 0 and an empty iterator returns that argument. Explicit undefined is present, not omitted. Traversal, callback failure and iterator closing retain the base language's runtime order. No contribution guarantees successful or terminating traversal. Checking executes no callback, default, getter or iterator; it grants no reference authority or extended lifetime. An incompatible replacement retains prior effects and leaves a failed initialization uninitialized. These synchronous contracts introduce no await, public generic intrinsic capability or named-argument routing rule.

    19.6.9 Lazy Range Flattening Contracts

    A statically established built-in range-family receiver contributes a flatMap callable contract whose callback takes (value: I, index: uint64), where I is the item contribution of 19.6.4. An established helper-bearing synchronous iterator uses its established item contribution instead. First establish the callback's independent inputs, then infer its result R under 1.6.5. A written annotation takes precedence; an existing callback contributes its established signature and is not retroactively annotated. Observe the callback's declared or published inferred result through the ordinary inference dependencies. Do not adopt an inferred R as a new callback return obligation merely to derive flattened items; doing so can introduce observable structural-property reads. Written return annotations and independently required receiving admission retain their obligations. A contextual any result places no Promise-shaped return obligation on an async callback; it does not relax the requirements on a written async return annotation. Apply 30's flattening eligibility judgment separately from the item contribution below.

    Let F be the normal flattened item contribution of R under 19.6.10, or any when unknown. The normal result is a helper-bearing synchronous iterator with item F, terminal contribution undefined, and optional any input to next. Its result is { value: F, done: false } | { value: undefined, done: true }; self-iteration contributes those same protocol arguments. Inner terminal values are discarded. Only one iteration level is flattened: a yielded array or Promise remains an item, and an async callback result is not awaited to discover another iterable.

    This is an operation contribution carried by an established method view, including computed names, optional access and extraction. Extraction does not bind a receiver. It is derived after establishing the callback result, not by equating a receiving item context with the callback's whole result. A whole gradual receiver gains no participation from the method name. An unresolved callback protocol remains unknown; the judgment introduces no public dependent type operator and does not add helpers to arbitrary structural iterators.

    Creation does not call the mapper. Traversal invokes it and acquires inner iterators on demand, retaining ordinary lookup, failures, closing and termination behaviour. The view does not prove intrinsic identity. Required inferred-initialization and return admission, callback binding obligations after replacement, prior effects and unsuccessful initialization state follow 19.6.7. Neither inference nor admission traverses the iterator to discover its items. These contributions grant no reference authority and do not extend a reference lifetime.

    19.6.10 Static Flattening Contribution

    This judgment describes normal items reached by GetIteratorFlattenable with reject-primitives, followed by synchronous iteration. It is distinct from a negative proof that every callback result alternative fails. Inspect established type contracts only; invoke no callback, getter or iterator method.

    1. For each established callback result alternative, a proved primitive result has no normal items. For an Object with an established non-nullish @@iterator method, inspect the method's established callable result as the iterator. For an explicitly nullish hook, use the original Object as the direct iterator. An undeclared hook on an open shape is unknown, not proof of absence. An optional hook includes the direct-iterator fallback.
    2. Inspect each established iterator's next callable result. A proved non-callable selected method, non-Object acquired iterator or non-Object step has no normal items. Optional next absence is a throwing branch. A method signature whose argument or receiver contract proves that its actual zero-argument invocation cannot enter contributes no normal items. Use the same bounded proof as the eligibility judgment; a viable or unknown invocation is not excluded. Unresolved callable or generic protocol evidence is unknown. A void protocol result is also unknown: a void-returning callable type can conceal an Object result under 1.5.16, so it is not a primitive-category proof. Callable alternatives contribute their declared result, or their published inferred result when none is declared, under the ordinary stability rules.
    3. For each Object step, a required literal done: true contributes no item. Otherwise contribute the read type of value, including undefined for an optional property. An undeclared property on an open shape is unknown. This judgment does not infer a yielded value from a terminal value.
    4. A synchronous generator contributes its established yield argument. A finite Composite tuple contributes its established positions. An ordinary array or tuple storage type alone does not constrain its replaceable iteration protocol; separately established protocol evidence is required.
    5. Join all established normal-item alternatives. Proved throwing and definitely terminal alternatives contribute never. Any unknown alternative makes the contribution unknown. An empty collection of normal-item alternatives contributes never, not unknown. Recursive protocol evidence without a completed contribution is unknown. An established symbolic yielded type can remain symbolic, but an unresolved type for the entire callback result does not itself establish an item type.

    A precise normal-item contribution does not assert that traversal succeeds or terminates. In particular, a primitive alternative can throw even when another alternative establishes a precise item. The eligibility error still applies when every established result alternative fails. Helper exhaustion independently contributes undefined.

    A range literal consumed at an iteration element type T is a type error unless every element it produces is a value of T. A loop binding, array or rest spread, or collection seed supplies an iteration context, not a stored endpoint construction context. In the absence of an explicit iteration element type, a typed endpoint may supply it. This judgment does not change the range value's endpoint domain. A stored range annotation instead follows 19.1. Where T is a sized integer type, the elements run from the first to the last: the first is the start, or the start plus one where the start is open, and the last is the end, or the end less one where the end is open. So a..=b produces a through b, a..<b produces a through b - 1, a<..=b produces a + 1 through b, and a<..<b produces a + 1 through b - 1. An endpoint that is compile-time evaluable contributes its value; one that is not, but has a sized integer type, contributes only that its value lies within that type's range, and the range is judged by the lowest first element and the highest last element that range allows. A range whose first element exceeds its last for every such value produces nothing and fits every T. A range with no end, or with an infinite end, produces values without limit and fits no sized integer type.

    Where T is a binary floating-point type, a range whose endpoints are both whole integers iterates by 1, and its elements are the integers from the first to the last as above. Each must be exactly a value of T: a range of two or more elements fits only where its first and last element both lie within ±2p, p being the precision of T, and a range of one element fits where that element is a value of T. A range with an endpoint that is not a whole integer has no implicit step and so no elements; it fits unless an endpoint is outside the range of T, so that converting it would yield an infinity.

    Note 1

    The rule is over the elements a range produces and not over its endpoints, because a half-open range's end is not one of its elements. 0..<256 produces every value of uint8 and no other, though 256 is not a uint8; a rule over the endpoints would refuse it. The rule refuses 0..=256, 0..<257, and 0..<300 at uint8, each of which produces an element the type does not hold, so it verifies the consumer's iteration element contract rather than a stored endpoint contract. It does not decide a range whose endpoint is known only at run time and has no sized integer type, such as 0..<n for an untyped n; a typed store of an element that does not fit is refused where it happens.

    A typed endpoint's value is not known, but its type bounds it, and that is enough to decide. Iterating s..<300 at uint8, with s a uint8, produces 299 whatever s is and is refused, while s..<256 produces 255 at most and fits; reading the literal 256 at uint8 instead would refuse it, though 256 is the stop and never produced. 300..=e with e a uint8 produces nothing for any e, and fits as any empty range does.

    For a floating-point T the rule asks for exact values because a range rounds nothing: it yields the integer it steps to, so a float16 range reaching 2049 would yield 2049, which float16 cannot hold, and converting it would give 2048. A typed floating-point endpoint is not decided, since whether the range iterates at all depends on whether its value is a whole integer.

     Note 2

    The lexical rule is the whole of what the family costs the numeric grammar, and it is the trade Rust made in requiring 1.0 rather than 1. so that .. could be a range. The alternatives were weighed and set aside: ... reads as spread to every reader and Ruby's ../... pairing is a known hazard, and a contextual keyword reads poorly in an index position. An earlier draft set ..< aside as well, on the ground that .< already opens a type argument list; that was an error, since the two are told apart by their second character and never compete, and the syntax specified here rests on the correction.

    That every end is written is what makes for (const i of 0..<array.length) the loop written without thinking rather than one short. The reason is not that the reader recalls which reading of a two-dot form this language chose, but that there is no two-dot reading to recall: the languages that have a..b do not agree on what it means, half-open in Rust and inclusive in Kotlin, Ruby, Perl, Pascal, Ada, and Haskell, so a default would be a convention a reader has to carry rather than a fact the source states. The cost is charged where the disagreement is. An end is two characters longer in every range that has one, and a start, which every language spells inclusive, is marked only in the ranges that exclude it.

    A case whose label is a range matches where the range contains the discriminant, which is what a switch over a float discriminant needs, since a float has no enumerable cases to list. Matching is by containment rather than by ===, and the cases of such a switch are tested in source order, so overlapping ranges resolve to the first that contains the value rather than being an error.

    A range iterates where it has a step, which over an integer element type is 1 and implicit. Numeric iterator acquisition and requests follow 19.7. The counter of a for over a range has the range's element type refined by the range's interval (6), so for (const i of 0..<N) binds i at a type bounded below by 0 and above by N minus 1. Where N is a compile-time constant that refinement is one too, and an index of a [N].<T> by that counter needs no check, which is the case 1.7.5 names.

    Note 2

    The bound is the range's own interval, so nothing about the elision is special to a for: the counter's type carries the fact, and the ordinary subtyping of a bounded parameterization discharges the check the way it discharges any other. That the range states its end is what makes for (const i of 0..<array.length) right rather than off by one, and it is why the interval is part of the type rather than a convention a reader has to remember.

    The nth value of a stepped range is the start plus n times the step rather than the previous value plus the step, and iteration stops against the value rather than a computed count. Both halves matter over a float element type, where a computed count can round up and yield one value too many and repeated addition accumulates error; the arithmetic and final item-width rounding are specified below.

    19.7 Numeric Range Iteration

    This clause specifies forward implicit iteration, numeric step, and reverse for number, bigint, sized int and uint, and binary float16, float32, and float64 item types. A parameterization over one of these types uses its base for numerical progression and retains the full type at item admission. Other ordered domains require their own progression operation; a present unsupported endpoint must not be interpreted as an absent endpoint.

    The numeric range item type is the stored endpoint domain when that domain is a concrete numeric type or numeric parameterization covered by this clause. Otherwise it is the type of the typed start endpoint, or, if there is none, the type of the typed end endpoint, or otherwise number. A plain Number endpoint does not supply a typed endpoint for this choice; a BigInt endpoint does. This choice uses the original range's endpoints in both traversal directions. It does not change the range's reflected endpoint domain, and a union domain does not select an arithmetic operation over that union. Consumer iteration element checks remain the separate judgments of 19.6.

    Each acquisition produces a fresh iterator with internal state consisting of its item type and numeric base, origin, stop, stop bound, signed difference, direction, mathematical non-negative integer index, previous item if any, and exhausted and executing flags. Its state is not read from public properties of the range or iterator. Acquisition does not enumerate or admit future items. The range is unchanged by requests on any of its iterators.

    1. For forward traversal the origin is the start and the stop is the end. For reverse traversal the origin is the end and the stop is the start; bounds move with their endpoints. An absent or nonfinite origin is a TypeError. Each present endpoint must have a numeric value covered by this clause; no coercion or user-defined conversion is performed to discover it. A NaN endpoint is a TypeError. A missing stop alone is unbounded; an infinite stop retains its sign.
    2. Implicit forward traversal and reverse require each present finite endpoint to be integral. Their differences are respectively 1 and -1 in the mathematical integers. A nonintegral endpoint is a TypeError at acquisition.
    3. step performs forward traversal. Its argument must be a positive finite numeric value covered by this clause; otherwise acquisition throws a TypeError. An integer item base additionally requires an integral origin and integral difference. The difference need not be representable at the item width, and its numeric type need not equal the item type. No object-to-number or string-to-number coercion is performed.
    4. If origin and difference are integral, progression is exact integer progression. Otherwise both operands must enter binary64 without loss of their numeric values, or acquisition throws a RangeError. This exact-entry requirement matters for an integer wider than binary64 in an otherwise fractional calculation.
    5. The initial index is 0 for a closed origin bound and 1 for an open origin bound. For an open bound the origin is also the initial previous value, so a first rounded item that fails to move past that excluded value is refused. The executing flag is initially false. After the preceding validation, the exhausted flag is initially true if the original interval is descending, or if both endpoints have equal numeric values and either bound is open; otherwise it is false. An empty interval is completed without attempting to advance a rounded candidate.

    A numeric range iterator's next method performs the following steps:

    1. If the receiver has no numeric range iterator state, throw a TypeError. If its executing flag is true, throw a TypeError. If its exhausted flag is true, return CreateIteratorResultObject(undefined, true).
    2. Set executing and exhausted to true. All exits from this request clear executing. An abrupt completion leaves exhausted true, and propagates the original completion. A reentrant request that is caught by an admission hook does not itself abort the outer request.
    3. For exact progression, let the candidate be origin + index × difference in the mathematical integers, without modular reduction or rounding. Otherwise, at index 0 let the candidate retain the origin's binary64 representation; at a later index convert the index to binary64, perform binary64 multiplication by the difference, and then binary64 addition of the origin, in that order. Round this fractional candidate to the item base's format, using round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. These separate binary64 operations must not be replaced by a fused operation that changes the result.
    4. Compare the candidate to the stop before admitting it as an item. In forward traversal a value greater than a closed stop or greater than or equal to an open stop finishes the iterator; in reverse traversal the inequalities are reversed. If finished, return CreateIteratorResultObject(undefined, true). There is no comparison for an absent stop. For fractional progression the compared candidate is the rounded value the consumer would receive.
    5. Construct a value at the item base from the candidate. A sized integer candidate must lie within that type's bounds. An exact integral candidate at a binary floating-point base must be finite and exactly representable, rather than rounded to a different integer. A fractional floating candidate must be finite. Failure of any of these conditions throws a RangeError. A closed origin at index 0 preserves the sign of zero. An excluded candidate that finished the iterator in the preceding step need not inhabit the item base.
    6. If a previous value exists, the item must be strictly greater than it for forward traversal, or strictly less for reverse traversal. Otherwise throw a RangeError. This condition also prevents rounding from repeatedly producing a value without progress.
    7. If the item type is a parameterization, apply its existing checked admission to the constructed value. Propagate any abrupt completion. Admission must retain the candidate's numeric value, and the zero sign at a floating base; if it changes that value, throw a RangeError. Thus metadata admission does not silently rescale or move a computed item past a bound.
    8. Record the item as the previous value and increase the mathematical index by 1. Set exhausted to false, unless the item is equal in numeric value to the present closed stop, in which case leave it true. Return CreateIteratorResultObject(the item, false).

    Once exhausted, an iterator remains exhausted, whether exhaustion followed the bound test, return of a closed endpoint, or an abrupt request. Carrier overflow is not implicit range completion: an unbounded byte progression from 255 yields 255, then throws RangeError, then returns done on subsequent requests. A bounded closed byte range ending at 255 instead finishes normally. A new iterator over the same range starts independently. Any metadata checks retain their existing effects and error classes; numeric iteration neither establishes nor extends the liveness of a reference later accessed by a consumer.

    Note

    The cursor may use checked machine arithmetic when that produces the same sequence; mathematical integer state does not require a particular allocation or representation. Range-returning take and drop and exact BigInt length are defined in 19.8. Numeric scaling is defined in 19.3. Interval arithmetic and nonnumeric progression domains have separate contracts and are not defined by substituting this cursor's private state.

    19.8 Numeric Range Counts and Adapters

    A newly manufactured cut carries its full admitted numeric endpoint domain after successful admission and representation checks, under the retention rule of 19.3. Reusing an original endpoint does not admit it again. Attaching a completed admission neither changes its numeric representation nor waives any failure or reference-liveness check.

    The length getter and range-returning take and drop operations use the supported numeric endpoint representations of 19.7. All integer computations in this clause are mathematical integer computations: they do not wrap, round to an endpoint width, or coerce objects. These operations do not enumerate members or invoke per-item iteration checks.

    The length getter first requires a range receiver, then two present finite integral supported numeric endpoints; otherwise it throws a TypeError exception. It returns the BigInt value of the greater of zero and the end minus the start plus one, less one for each open bound. Its result type is always bigint, including a property read of a statically known range-family type by a dot, known String key, or object binding pattern. It is the cardinality of the unit integer lattice. It is independent of the representation or metadata admission of intermediate items and does not prove that iteration succeeds. Missing, infinite, fractional, or unsupported endpoints have no length in this numeric contract; isEmpty retains its interval-ordering judgment.

    A numeric take or drop call performs these steps in order. The usual evaluation of the receiver expression and argument expressions precedes the call.

    1. Require a range receiver; otherwise throw a TypeError exception. Read its internal endpoints and bounds, without reading public properties.
    2. Require a present finite integral supported numeric start. If the end is present, require a supported numeric value that is integral or is positive or negative infinity. Otherwise throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Require the supplied count to be a supported numeric value; an omitted argument, undefined, and every nonnumeric kind throw a TypeError exception without conversion. If the count is negative, fractional, NaN, or infinite, throw a RangeError exception. Let the non-negative mathematical integer count be n; negative zero counts as zero.
    4. Retain the source endpoint domain: the stored domain if present, otherwise the same inferred endpoint domain that Reflect.typeOf reports for the source. Every result below carries that domain, even when an endpoint contributing to an inferred union is replaced. A copy retains both original endpoint values and their bounds, including absence and the sign of infinity. The canonical empty result uses the stored start for both endpoints, with closed start and open end.
    5. If n is zero, return the canonical empty result for take, or a copy for drop.
    6. Let first be the exact integer start plus one if its bound is open, or the start otherwise. For a finite end let last be the exact integer end minus one if its bound is open, or the end otherwise. If the end is negative infinity, or first exceeds a finite last, return a copy.
    7. If last exists and n is at least last minus first plus one, return a copy for take, or the canonical empty result for drop.
    8. Let cut be first plus n minus one. Select the original range's numeric item domain by 19.7. If the cut equals the stored start's integer value and the stored start already has that item type, reuse the stored start, including its zero sign and metadata, without new admission. Otherwise manufacture an endpoint of that type with exact integer value cut. Throw a RangeError exception if it does not fit the numeric base exactly. Then apply the full parameterized type's existing admission, propagating any exception. Require the admitted value to retain the exact computed integer and, for zero, positive zero; otherwise throw a RangeError exception.
    9. For take, publish a range with the original start and start bound, and the admitted or reused cut as its closed end. For drop, publish a range with the cut as its open start, and the original end and end bound. No result is published before the required endpoint admission completes.

    The operations never mutate the source range or confer reference permissions. Validation-hook side effects retain their ordinary semantics, and later accesses to borrowed locations still perform their existing liveness checks. Only manufactured endpoints are newly admitted; skipped or selected interior items are not visited. A fresh call after a failure observes the same source range. Closed carrier maxima require no successor. The partial results of (0..<10).take(3) and (0..<10).drop(3) are 0..=2 and 2<..<10, respectively; fractional membership follows those bounds. Iterator-returning helper operations retain their own count-conversion and consumption contracts.

    20 Structural Matching

    Reflect.inferSlot(name) returns a fresh slot, a Type Object standing for a position a match is to bind. Reflect.matchType(pattern, subject) performs one-sided structural unification of pattern against subject: where every slot in pattern can be bound consistently so that the pattern becomes subject, it returns an object mapping each slot's name to the Type Object bound there, and otherwise it returns null. A slot occurring twice binds once and must bind alike. A constraint on a binding is an ordinary check of the result afterwards, so Reflect.isAssignable supplies what an infer S extends string says.

    A pattern is structural: it is a node, and its slots stand where a Type Object would. A slot inside an deferred Type Record is a type error at the match rather than null, because evaluating a builder against an unbound slot is exactly the inversion no operation of this specification performs (15). A pattern for the result of a builder is therefore written against the shape the builder produces, an optional property or a wrapped element, and never against the application.

    Note

    This closes the question of whether anything an erased system's infer does is out of reach, and the answer is that it is not. A library author who wants an explicit inverse has one that is ordinary code (15.3 is where the checker will consult it).

    The operation was proposed as optional on the measurement that the design's catalog needed it exactly zero times. That measurement has since changed: the decorators extension dispatches on the structure of a type it is handed, which is what a decorator that emits a schema, a validator, or documentation does, and there is no way to write that without this operation. The extends pattern of 24.2.4 is its syntactic form, standing to it as is stands to IsOfType, and consumes the unification defined here rather than defining a second one. Reflective use remains available and remains the escape hatch for what the syntax does not spell.

    21 Provenance

    A Property Type Record and a Type Record may carry an [[Origin]], a List of references to the declaration sites the record came from. It is not part of any type's identity: SameType does not read it, IsSubtype does not read it, and CanonicalizeType neither reads it nor writes it into the comparison that decides whether two Records are one. What canonicalization does with it is union it: where two Records that differ only in [[Origin]] are merged by interning, the merged Record's [[Origin]] is the union of theirs, ordered by 1.8.5.2. It is a HOST-FACING channel: an implementation makes it available to a tool, and no program reads it. That is a deliberate restriction rather than an omission. Because canonicalization unions origins, a reflected origin would change what a program observes about its own type when an unrelated module declared a structurally identical shape, which is a surprise with no upside for the program and none for the tool, since a tool already has the whole program in view. A builder that spreads a property record therefore spreads no origin, and one that mints a record has none to spread.

    A record a builder mints carries no [[Origin]], which is the correct answer rather than a missing one: nothing declared it. An implementation is likewise free to hold an origin as an opaque handle, a source and a position, rather than as a reference to the declaration itself, and is encouraged to: retaining the declaration would keep a parse tree alive for as long as the type is interned, which in an agent that does not exit is a leak and not a cost. Documentation is not carried here and is not carried in the node model at all. It stays with the source, and a tool resolves it from an origin at the moment it displays something, falling back for a minted record on the application that produced it, which is the expression a diagnostic already names.

    Note

    The reason to want this is that partial(User) should not cost an editor its memory of where name came from. The reason not to put a documentation string in the node instead is worth stating, because it is the same argument this specification makes twice already: anything inside a node rides the round trip through 1.12.4, so a doc string either joins the canonical form, and two structurally identical types with different comments become different types, or interning crowns one winner and the rest is lost silently and by load order. Provenance escapes both because it is a reference rather than a payload and because it unions rather than wins.

    That union is also why [[Origin]] does not reopen what 1.10.1 forecloses. The rule there is not that no second non-canonical field may exist; it is that no field may depend on the order modules loaded. A [[Name]] is first-won and so does depend on it, which is tolerated because a parameter has one name and there is nothing else to do. An [[Origin]] accumulates every site and is ordered canonically, so the same program produces the same origins in the same order however its modules were reached, and the accident the rule exists to prevent does not arise.

    22 The Expansion Artifact

    Because evaluation is deterministic and its results are interned canonical forms, they may be computed once and shipped. An expansion artifact is a serialization of the interning table for the concrete types a module graph's public surface produces, every closed application among them pre-evaluated, keyed by a hash of the module graph that produced it. A consumer verifies the hash and reads the types out of it rather than evaluating them; on a mismatch it evaluates, and determinism is what makes the two agree.

    An artifact contains no open application. partial(T) inside an exported generic evaluates against the consumer's T, at the consumer, so the evaluator is not removed by the artifact and cannot be: what the artifact removes is the common path, a dependency's concrete surface, which is the part that would otherwise be recomputed by every tool on every build. An artifact is an optimization and never a semantics: a consumer that ignores every artifact computes the same types, and one that reads a stale artifact detects it by the hash rather than by disagreeing. More generally it carries no UNBOUND TYPE PARAMETER, wherever one stands: an exported generic signature is unbound for the same reason partial(T) is, since what takes the parameter's place is the consumer's type. A name whose type carries one is omitted from the artifact rather than the artifact being refused — an artifact contains no open application, which is not the same as a module holding one being unable to have an artifact — and the omitted names are carried, so a producer says what it left out rather than a consumer inferring it from absence. A consumer that finds nothing for a name evaluates, which is always correct.

    Note

    This is what makes the standalone conformance of A pay. A tool that reads an artifact is trusting that whoever produced it computed what this specification says, and the conformance suite is what makes that claim checkable rather than hopeful; the hash is what makes the trust revocable. The artifact also carries the extracted documentation for the origins of 21, since a dependency's sources are exactly what a consumer does not have on disk, which is the one thing provenance alone cannot supply.

    The format is fixed here, because a consumer that can only read one producer's artifacts is not reading an artifact, it is reading that producer. An artifact is a TABLE of entries. An entry is the reflection node Table 33 gives for its type, with every nested Type Object replaced by a reference to another entry, written as an object whose sole key is $ref and whose value is that entry's index. A table rather than nesting, because a primitive record refers to itself and a recursive type reaches itself through a member, so a form that carried nested types by containment would not terminate on the simplest type this specification defines. A tagged reference rather than a bare index, because a literal carries a value and a member carries an initializer, either of which may be a number.

    Entries are ordered as the interning table orders the records they came from, so an artifact does not depend on the order a producer enumerated a module's exports; two producers over one graph write one artifact. A nominal type is carried as its module specifier and its declared name, never by value: its record holds a declaration and a constructor, and neither crosses a boundary. A consumer resolves that name against its own copy of the module. Every other leaf is a value, encoded as itself. A symbol is not encodable and a producer refuses rather than carrying one: an unregistered symbol has no name that survives a boundary, and a registered one would need the consumer to agree about identity across a wire, which is not a question a serialization answers. An artifact carries a version, and a producer writes it from the first artifact it writes.

    A consumer verifies the hash, and declines anything it does not understand — a version above the one it knows, a name it cannot resolve, an entry whose shape it does not recognize — and evaluates instead. This is what makes "nothing in it can change what a program means" a rule rather than a hope: a consumer either reads an artifact it understands entirely, or it evaluates, so no artifact changes what a program means however it was produced. Declining is also what makes the format evolvable, since an addition a reader has never seen is refused by the same step that refuses a stale one.

    The key is the SHA-256 digest of a canonical encoding of the module graph: for each module in the graph, reached transitively and ordered by specifier, the specifier and the source text, each written with its length before it. Length-prefixed rather than delimited, because a specifier and a source may contain any separator, and two graphs that encode alike would be one key. The digest is fixed alongside the encoding rather than left open: a shared input with an unshared digest is half a guarantee, and two implementations would then agree on what to hash and still not read each other’s artifacts. The key is written as the ASCII text sha256: followed by the digest in lowercase hexadecimal, for the same reason and to the same end: a reader compares keys as text, so a form left to the producer is a mismatch reported as staleness. Nothing precedes the entries — no count and no version — since the entries are self-delimiting and a version belongs to the artifact rather than to the graph it keys. Replacing the digest later is a change of version, which a reader already declines.

    What is not fixed here is what carries the bytes and how a producer finds a module graph. Neither affects whether two artifacts are mutually readable, which is the whole of what fixing a format is for. What is fixed besides the format is the contract: the key is a hash of the module graph, the contents are canonical forms, a mismatch re-derives, and nothing in it can change what a program means.

    23 Composites

    A composite is a frozen object with a null prototype that is interned: two composites created from the same contents are the same object. Equality of contents is therefore identity, and ===, Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes compare composites structurally with no change to any collection or operator, because the comparison each already performs finds one object where the contents are one. This clause specifies the design's composites extension, which integrates the Composites proposal under this type system; where the two differ, 23.8 records the difference.

    Interning is defined over SameValueZero, and SameValueZero under this specification requires its operands to be values of one type before it compares them (1.5.1). Interning inherits that: a uint8 field and a Number field of the same mathematical value are different keys, so the value read back from a composite is the value that was stored, at its type, however many creation sites produced the object. The nondeterminism the upstream proposal resolves for -0 by normalization cannot arise between types here, because values of two types are never SameValueZero-equal; within a type it is resolved by 23.4.2, of which the -0 normalization is one instance.

    const a = Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 });
const b = Composite({ y: 4, x: 1 });
a === b; // true, one object
new Map([[a, 'ship']]).get(Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 })); // 'ship'

Composite({ (x: uint8): 1 }) === Composite({ x: 1 }); // false: a uint8 field and a Number field

    23.1 Composite Objects

    A composite object is an object contained in the Composite Registry of its heap (23.3). Composite objects are created only by FindOrCreateComposite and FindOrCreateTupleComposite, which are the only operations that add an object to a Composite Registry. Membership in the registry is what an object's status as a composite consists of, so the status cannot be forged: a Proxy exotic object whose target is a composite object is not itself a composite object.

    There are two kinds of composite object. A record composite is an ordinary object whose [[Prototype]] is null, whose [[Extensible]] is false, and whose properties are own data properties with String keys, each with [[Writable]] false, [[Enumerable]] true, and [[Configurable]] false. A tuple composite is an Array exotic object whose [[Prototype]] is null and whose [[Extensible]] is false, whose integer-indexed properties are own data properties with [[Writable]] false, [[Enumerable]] true, and [[Configurable]] false, and whose "length" property is non-writable, non-enumerable, and non-configurable. Array.isArray answers false for a record composite and true for a tuple composite, and typeof answers "object" for both.

    Every composite object has a [[RuntimeType]] internal slot holding the composite type of its contents (23.2), which is what RuntimeTypeOf (1.7.1.1) reports for it. A composite object is frozen from its creation, so the slot never becomes stale.

    Note 1

    Being frozen has a consequence at a boundary: a composite whose member needs CONVERTING to cross cannot be narrowed, because the conversion of an object's members happens in place (1.6.7.1) and a frozen member cannot be written. Composite.<{ n: number }> does not cross to { n: uint32 }; one whose members already hold the target types crosses, no write being attempted. The refusal names the member and the type rather than reporting a failed assignment.

     Note 2

    A record composite holds what upstream's composites hold. The tuple kind is this design's addition: an array-shaped composite whose "length" is own and non-enumerable, so that Object.keys lists the elements, and whose iteration 23.7 supplies without a prototype to carry %Symbol.iterator%. The two kinds never intern together (23.4.9): Composite([1]) and Composite({ 0: 1 }) are different objects, because a record with the entry "0" and a tuple of one element disagree about shape even where they agree about every entry.

    23.2 Composite Types

    A Type Record is a composite type when its [[Kind]] is primitive and its [[Name]] is "Composite". The composite type over a shape S, where S is an object, tuple or array Type Record and where an interface type contributes the object Type Record of its structural form, has [[Arguments]] « CompositeTreeShape(S) », and that record is called its shape. A shape is read as a composite tree: since a composite object is frozen from its creation and the value it holds at a structural position is itself a composite (a composite's contents are a tree terminating in non-composite leaves), CompositeTreeShape(S) is S with every Property Type Record's [[Readonly]] set to true and every [[Type]] of a property, tuple element or array element that is an object, tuple or array Type Record replaced by the composite type over that record, recursively; a member type that is not one of those kinds is unchanged, and the operation is idempotent. The reading is made where the composite type is constructed and nowhere else, so that every spelling of the type — an annotation, the typed creation Composite.<S>(source), a parse target, the record Reflect.typeOf reports — denotes one type. An array shape is the variable-length tuple composite: a composite of that type is a tuple composite of any length each of whose elements is of the element type. The top composite type, written Composite with no arguments, has [[Arguments]] « », states no shape, and is the type of every composite object. Composite joins the built-in type names of 1.5.27, resolving in type position by the rule stated there, and Composite.<T> is a TypeReference with TypeArguments like any other parameterized family. That the shape is a TYPE ARGUMENT and not a metadata record follows from the general rule (1.5.20) and needs no special case here: Composite declares a parameter, so its arguments are types. The rule matters at this clause in particular because a composite type's [[Kind]] is primitive, so a reading that asked what KIND the base was — rather than whether it declares parameters — would take the shape for metadata and put it in [[Metadata]], where 1.2.3.1 does not look for it. These Type Records canonicalize by canonicalizing the shape in [[Arguments]] (1.2.2.8), so Composite.<{ x: int32; y: int32 }> written anywhere is one Type Object. The Static Type of a call of the Composite function is the top composite type where the call supplies no TypeArguments and no contextual type reaches it, and the composite type over T's structural form for the typed creation Composite.<T>(source); Reflect.typeOf on a composite returns the Type Object of its [[RuntimeType]], the same object either spelling denotes. A const binding whose initializer is such a typed creation, or any call that writes its type arguments, takes the call's Static Type as its own, as a const initialized by a construction does: in each case the type is one the program wrote at the initializer, not one inferred from a literal, so const t = Composite.<[uint8, uint8]>([1, 2]); let a: [].<uint8> = t; is the type error the subtyping rule states rather than a binding the checker cannot see.

    Composite Type Records use the primitive representation but describe frozen Objects and a family of overlapping contracts. Their disjointness is decided before the scalar primitive rules of AreDisjoint (1.2.2.6). The top composite type overlaps every shaped composite type, and different shapes are not disjoint merely because their Type Records differ. Common-kind, required-member and admitted-length contradictions are judged by CompositeShapesAreDisjoint. A composite may also satisfy a structural object or tuple contract or an interface; absence of a subtype proof does not prove these contracts disjoint. Mutable array contracts exclude composite values, and a composite is neither callable nor a scalar or enum value. This judgment does not merge Type Objects, convert stored members, decide equality of particular values, or alter reference permissions or liveness. Equal contents still intern according to their stored types and composite kind.

    The shape recorded for a composite object is derived from its stored contents by CompositeShape (23.4.6), so that objects with the same contents have the same shape and interning is coherent. The type of each field is the runtime type of its value, except that a field whose value is an Object records the any type, a field whose value is a composite object records that composite's own type, and a field whose value is a Type Object records the type type. An ordinary object's structural runtime type describes the properties it happens to have and can change as the object does, which is why it is not recorded: a frozen object's recorded type must not go stale, and the identity a reference field contributes is the reference, not a snapshot of its shape.

    The subtype rules for composite types are stated in IsSubtype (1.2.3.1), where they precede the step that separates the kinds: every composite type is a subtype of the top composite type; a composite type over a shape is a subtype of a composite type over a wider shape; and a composite type over a shape is a subtype of that shape's object or tuple type and of an interface whose structural form it satisfies.

    A composite type is therefore a subtype of the object type of its shape, which is what makes a composite satisfy an interface: const q: IPoint = p holds for a p of type Composite.<IPoint> with no cast and no write, since a frozen object trivially cannot be modified out of an implementation. Composite types are covariant in their shapes, which the frozenness of every composite makes sound: no store can later violate a wider reading. A composite type over a tuple shape is a subtype of the tuple types its shape is a subtype of; it is a subtype of no array type, because an array type describes a mutable container and every mutating operation on a composite throws. It is, however, a subtype of the composite type over an array shape whose element type each of its elements is a subtype of (the step in IsSubtype above): Composite.<[uint8, uint8]> is a subtype of Composite.<[].<uint8>>, since both are frozen and the array shape is the variable-length tuple composite.

    Note

    IsOfType (1.7.2.1) needs one step. A composite value reaching an object target is checked structurally by the existing steps, reading its properties as it would any object's; a composite target is decided by the operation's final step, IsSubtype of the value's runtime type, which the rules above extend; and a composite value reaching an array target is false, for the reason the subtyping rule gives: an array type describes a mutable container, and a tuple composite, though it is an Array, is not one. Without that step the structural read admitted a tuple composite as a [].<T> and the first mutation through the binding threw where the binding itself was the error. A tuple target is not so refused, a tuple composite being a subtype of the tuple types its shape is. The conversion of a composite to an array type at a typed position, where IsOfType is false, proceeds as for any array-like source and builds a new array of the type; the composite is not bound and is not modified. A record composite created without type arguments has Number fields where its source had numeric literals, so checking it against an interface of uint32 members fails on those fields by the no-implicit-conversion rule of 1.6; the remedy is to type the creation, which is the same advice every boundary of this specification gives.

    23.3 The Composite Registry

    Each heap has an associated Composite Registry: a List of Objects, initially empty, whose elements are exactly the composite objects of that heap. Objects are added to it only by FindOrCreateComposite and FindOrCreateTupleComposite. The registry is a property of a heap in the same way the type-object intern table is (1.2.2.9): agents that share a heap share one registry, so composites are === across every realm and every agent of one heap, like symbols obtained from Symbol.for, and an agent that does not share the heap is not reached by it (40). A composite object has a [[Prototype]] of null and so bears no relationship to the realm whose Composite function created it; only its contents matter.

    Note 1

    Under the agent model of the pinned edition each agent has its own heap and the registry is per-agent, which is the upstream proposal's rule. The threading extension is what makes the scope worth stating as the heap's: it gives several agents one heap, objects cross between their threads by reference with no serialization step, and a registry scoped more finely than objects are reachable would put two composites of equal contents, both reachable from both threads, in one heap, falsifying the invariant the feature is. Creation against a shared registry must accordingly be safe under concurrent callers; the observable requirement is only the one FindOrCreateComposite states, that equal contents yield one object, and implementations are expected to reach it without serializing unrelated creations through one lock.

     Note 2

    Membership in the registry does not keep a composite object alive; an implementation may remove one that is no longer live. The removal is unobservable, because composite objects cannot be held weakly (23.7) and so cannot be placed in a WeakMap, WeakSet, WeakRef, or FinalizationRegistry, which are the only instruments that observe liveness.

    23.4 Abstract Operations for Composite Objects

    23.4.1 IsComposite ( value )

    The abstract operation IsComposite takes argument value (an ECMAScript language value) and returns a Boolean. It returns true if value is a composite object. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If value is not an Object, return false.
    2. If the Composite Registry of the surrounding agent's heap contains value, return true.
    3. Return false.
     Note

    The operation is defined by searching the registry; an implementation is free to answer it any faster way, such as a bit on the object, that yields the same result.

    23.4.2 CanonicalizeCompositeValue ( value )

    The abstract operation CanonicalizeCompositeValue takes argument value (an ECMAScript language value) and returns an ECMAScript language value. It returns the canonical representative of the SameValueZero equivalence class of value within its type: the one value stored for every value the class contains, chosen so that the contents of a composite do not depend on which member reached the creation. Values of distinct types are never SameValueZero-equal (1.5.1), so the class is always within one type. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If value is -0𝔽, return +0𝔽.
    2. If value is a negative zero of a binary floating-point type (1.5.3), return the positive zero of that type.
    3. If value is a finite value of a decimal floating-point type (1.5.4) whose type does not restrict the exponents of its values, then
      1. Let c be the coefficient of value.
      2. Let q be the exponent of value.
      3. Let qMax be the largest exponent of value's type.
      4. If c = 0, return the value of value's type with positive sign, coefficient 0, and exponent 0.
      5. Repeat, while c modulo 10 = 0 and q < qMax,
        1. Set c to c / 10.
        2. Set q to q + 1.
      6. Return the value of value's type with the sign of value, coefficient c, and exponent q.
    4. If value is a negatively signed zero of a decimal floating-point type whose type restricts the exponents of its values, return the positively signed zero of that type with the exponent of value.
    5. Return value.
     Note

    The rule generalizes the upstream proposal's normalization of -0, which is its Number instance. A SameValueZero class with one member canonicalizes to itself, which covers most of the type universe with no step naming it: every integer, String, BigInt, Boolean, Symbol, and Object value is alone in its class; a rational is because its type keeps every value in lowest terms (1.5.5), so each rational number has exactly one representation. The classes with more than one member are the signed zeros, handled above for the Number type and each binary float width, and the decimal cohorts.

    A decimal type whose metadata fixes the exponents of its values, such as one parameterized by a DecimalContext scale (1.5.20), has collapsed each cohort before this operation sees a value: conversion into the type quantizes at the boundary, so the only remaining choice is the sign of a zero, which the fourth step settles. A bare decimal type stores the reduced cohort member, trailing zeros stripped, which is the one member computable from the numerical value alone and the value any hash of the field must be computed from in any case. The division of labour is deliberate: canonicalization is the type's wherever the type has an opinion, and this operation's only where it does not. A value whose significance matters to a program belongs in a type that declares its scale, at which point a composite stores exactly that scale; an unconstrained decimal in a composite does not carry significance, as it would not survive any other typed boundary either.

    Each floating-point type of this specification has a single NaN value, so a NaN canonicalizes to itself and no step names it. Where an implementation nonetheless distinguishes NaN encodings, as the pinned edition permits and the byte views of the memory layout extension can observe (12), the NaN stored in a composite must have one fixed encoding per type, the canonical quiet NaN with positive sign and zero payload, so that reading a stored NaN's bytes reveals nothing about which creation interned the composite or what payload it supplied. This is the requirement the upstream proposal states for the Number type, applied to every float width the byte views reach.

    A program that needs a signed zero, a specific cohort member, or a NaN payload to participate in a key carries it as data, a sign field or an exponent field, which keys correctly with no special case. No option restores the distinction: an argument that changed interning identity would fragment the registry into flag-keyed families, so the preserveNegativeZero option the upstream FAQ floats is not adopted.

    23.4.3 Composite Entry Records

    A Composite Entry Record is a Record value describing one key/value pair of a record composite. It has a [[Key]] field (a String) and a [[Value]] field (an ECMAScript language value).

    23.4.4 CompositeCanonicalOrder ( entries )

    The abstract operation CompositeCanonicalOrder takes argument entries (a List of Composite Entry Records) and returns a List of Composite Entry Records. It returns entries in the canonical key order of record composites, which does not depend on the order in which the entries were provided. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let integerEntries be a new empty List.
    2. Let stringEntries be a new empty List.
    3. For each Composite Entry Record entry of entries, do
      1. If entry.[[Key]] is an array index, append entry to integerEntries; otherwise, append entry to stringEntries.
    4. Sort integerEntries into ascending order by the numeric values of the array indices their [[Key]] fields denote.
    5. Sort stringEntries into ascending lexicographic order of their [[Key]] fields, compared code unit by code unit.
    6. Return the list-concatenation of integerEntries and stringEntries.
     Note

    This is the ordinary own-key order except that the non-index String keys sort lexicographically rather than by creation order, which is what makes a record composite a canonical form of its contents.

    23.4.5 CompositeFieldType ( value )

    The abstract operation CompositeFieldType takes argument value (an ECMAScript language value) and returns a Type Record. It returns the Type Record recorded for a composite field holding value. The result is a function of value alone and is stable over the composite's lifetime, which interning requires. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If IsComposite(value) is true, return value.[[RuntimeType]].
    2. If value is a Type Object, return the Type Record for type (1.5.21).
    3. If value is an Object, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: any }.
    4. Return RuntimeTypeOf(value).
     Note

    A value of a value type contributes its runtime type, so a uint8 field is a uint8 field and an untyped creation's numeric literals are Number fields, which is where the typed and untyped boundary of this clause's introduction becomes visible to reflection. An ordinary object contributes any rather than its structural runtime type, because that type is a mutable object's current shape and a frozen composite must not record something that can go stale; the identity a reference field contributes to interning is the reference itself. A nested composite and a Type Object are frozen and interned, so their types are stable and are recorded.

    23.4.6 CompositeShape ( kind, contents )

    The abstract operation CompositeShape takes arguments kind (record or tuple) and contents (either a List of Composite Entry Records or a List of ECMAScript language values) and returns a Type Record. It returns the shape of a composite with the given contents: an object Type Record for a record composite and a tuple Type Record for a tuple composite. contents is a List of Composite Entry Records where kind is record and a List of ECMAScript language values where kind is tuple. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If kind is record, then
      1. Let props be a new empty List.
      2. For each Composite Entry Record entry of contents, do
        1. Append the Property Type Record { [[Key]]: entry.[[Key]], [[Type]]: CompositeFieldType(entry.[[Value]]), [[Optional]]: false, [[Readonly]]: true, [[Initial]]: none } to props.
      3. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: object, [[Properties]]: props, [[IndexSignatures]]: « » }).
    2. Let elements be a new empty List.
    3. For each element v of contents, do
      1. Append the Tuple Element Record { [[Type]]: CompositeFieldType(v), [[Rest]]: false, [[Initial]]: none } to elements.
    4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: tuple, [[Elements]]: elements }).

    23.4.7 FindOrCreateComposite ( entries )

    The abstract operation FindOrCreateComposite takes argument entries (a List of Composite Entry Records) and returns a record composite. It returns the interned record composite for the key/value pairs of entries, creating it if none exists. No two elements of entries have the same [[Key]], and every [[Value]] is already the result of CanonicalizeCompositeValue. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let sortedEntries be CompositeCanonicalOrder(entries).
    2. Let registry be the Composite Registry of the surrounding agent's heap.
    3. For each composite object c of registry, do
      1. If CompositeMatch(c, record, sortedEntries) is true, return c.
    4. Let c be OrdinaryObjectCreate(null).
    5. For each Composite Entry Record entry of sortedEntries, do
      1. Perform ! DefinePropertyOrThrow(c, entry.[[Key]], PropertyDescriptor { [[Value]]: entry.[[Value]], [[Writable]]: false, [[Enumerable]]: true, [[Configurable]]: false }).
    6. Set c.[[Extensible]] to false.
    7. Set c.[[RuntimeType]] to the composite type over CompositeShape(record, sortedEntries).
    8. Add c to registry.
    9. Return c.
     Note 1

    The search over the registry describes the required observable result and is not an implementation model. Interning must be implemented by hash tables or other means whose cost per creation is, on average, sublinear in the registry's population; a typed creation site whose shape is statically known additionally admits a fixed hashing sequence with no key sorting and no descriptor walk, since the order and the field types are known before the program runs.

     Note 2

    No step of canonicalization, matching, or interning calls user code. The creation algorithms read the source's values once, getters included, and everything from CanonicalizeCompositeValue onward operates on the values read, over objects that cannot be Proxy exotic objects, so a composite's identity is a function of its contents and of nothing a program can interpose on. What a collection treats as one key is a separate question from what a composite is, and only the second is settled here.

    23.4.8 FindOrCreateTupleComposite ( elements )

    The abstract operation FindOrCreateTupleComposite takes argument elements (a List of ECMAScript language values) and returns either a normal completion containing a tuple composite or a throw completion. It returns the interned tuple composite whose elements are elements, creating it if none exists. Every element is already the result of CanonicalizeCompositeValue. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let registry be the Composite Registry of the surrounding agent's heap.
    2. For each composite object c of registry, do
      1. If CompositeMatch(c, tuple, elements) is true, return c.
    3. Let len be the number of elements of elements.
    4. If len ≥ 232, throw a RangeError exception.
    5. Let c be ! ArrayCreate(len).
    6. Set c.[[Prototype]] to null.
    7. Let i be 0.
    8. For each element v of elements, do
      1. Perform ! DefinePropertyOrThrow(c, ! ToString(𝔽(i)), PropertyDescriptor { [[Value]]: v, [[Writable]]: false, [[Enumerable]]: true, [[Configurable]]: false }).
      2. Set i to i + 1.
    9. Perform ! c.[[DefineOwnProperty]]("length", PropertyDescriptor { [[Writable]]: false }).
    10. Set c.[[Extensible]] to false.
    11. Set c.[[RuntimeType]] to the composite type over CompositeShape(tuple, elements).
    12. Add c to registry.
    13. Return c.

    23.4.9 CompositeMatch ( c, kind, contents )

    The abstract operation CompositeMatch takes arguments c (a composite object), kind (record or tuple), and contents (either a List of Composite Entry Records or a List of ECMAScript language values) and returns a Boolean. It returns true if c is a composite of the given kind with exactly the given contents. contents is a List of Composite Entry Records where kind is record, in the canonical order of CompositeCanonicalOrder, and a List of ECMAScript language values where kind is tuple. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If kind is tuple and c is not a tuple composite, return false.
    2. If kind is record and c is a tuple composite, return false.
    3. If kind is tuple, then
      1. Let len be ! LengthOfArrayLike(c).
      2. If len ≠ the number of elements of contents, return false.
      3. Let i be 0.
      4. For each element v of contents, do
        1. If SameValue(! Get(c, ! ToString(𝔽(i))), v) is false, return false.
        2. Set i to i + 1.
      5. Return true.
    4. Let keys be ! c.[[OwnPropertyKeys]]().
    5. If the number of elements of keys ≠ the number of elements of contents, return false.
    6. Let i be 0.
    7. For each Composite Entry Record entry of contents, do
      1. If entry.[[Key]] is not keys[i], return false.
      2. If SameValue(! Get(c, entry.[[Key]]), entry.[[Value]]) is false, return false.
      3. Set i to i + 1.
    8. Return true.
     Note

    Both sides are canonicalized before this operation runs, so within one type SameValue and SameValueZero coincide here, and across types both are false because the values are distinct. Comparing with SameValue is therefore comparing with SameValueZero, stated with the finer relation so that the assertion is checkable.

    23.5 The Composite Function

    The Composite function:

    • is %Composite%.
    • is the initial value of the "Composite" property of the global object.
    • has a [[Prototype]] internal slot whose value is %Function.prototype%.
    • returns a composite object when called as a function, creating one only when no interned composite of the same contents exists.
    • does not have a [[Construct]] internal method; new Composite(...) throws a TypeError exception.
    • does not have a "prototype" property.
    • is the head of the composite type family: applying TypeArguments to it, in type position or in expression position (1.4.6), yields the Type Object of the composite type over the argument. It is a type error if the argument is not an object, tuple, array, or interface type, or if it has a Symbol-keyed member, since a composite's keys are Strings. Calling that Type Object is the typed creation of 23.5.2, the construction boundary a parameterized type already has (1.5.20).

    23.5.1 Composite ( source )

    This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. If source is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. Let isArray be ? IsArray(source).
    3. If isArray is true, then
      1. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(source).
      2. Let elements be a new empty List.
      3. Let i be 0.
      4. Repeat, while i < len,
        1. Let v be ? Get(source, ! ToString(𝔽(i))).
        2. Append CanonicalizeCompositeValue(v) to elements.
        3. Set i to i + 1.
      5. Return ? FindOrCreateTupleComposite(elements).
    4. Let entries be a new empty List.
    5. Let keys be ? source.[[OwnPropertyKeys]]().
    6. For each element key of keys, do
      1. Let desc be ? source.[[GetOwnProperty]](key).
      2. If desc is not undefined and desc.[[Enumerable]] is true, then
        1. If key is a Symbol, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Let v be ? Get(source, key).
        3. Append the Composite Entry Record { [[Key]]: key, [[Value]]: CanonicalizeCompositeValue(v) } to entries.
    7. Return FindOrCreateComposite(entries).
     Note 1

    The kind is decided by Array.isArray on the argument: an array source creates a tuple composite from its elements 0 through length - 1, and any other object creates a record composite from its own enumerable String-keyed properties. Inherited and non-enumerable properties are ignored, getters are invoked eagerly and exactly once each in the order the keys are reported, and an own enumerable Symbol-keyed property is a TypeError; a Symbol remains an ordinary value. The source is never itself converted; it only supplies values, and Composite(template) !== template for any non-composite template. Composite is idempotent as a consequence of interning: Composite(c) on a composite reads c's own contents, an array source for a tuple and enumerable entries for a record, and interns to c itself.

     Note 2

    The upstream proposal reads every array through the record path, where length, being own but non-enumerable, is dropped, so its Composite([1, 2]) yields the record { 0: 1, 1: 2 }. The tuple kind is therefore a behavioural change to an existing call rather than an addition, recorded in 23.8. It resolves the reservations upstream states against a list form, an enumerable length and a missing %Symbol.iterator%, by making length own and non-enumerable and by supplying iteration without a prototype (23.7); the reservation about creation cost growing with element count stands, and a long list remains a poor key.

    23.5.2 Calling a Composite Type Object

    Calling the Type Object of a composite type over a shape S, written Composite.<T>(source) for the S that is T's structural form, returns the result of CompositeFromShape(S, source), where source is the call's first argument, or undefined where none is supplied. This is the construction boundary of the composite types, as calling any parameterized Type Object is its type's (1.5.20). The same boundary is reached by the conversion of a value to a composite type at any typed position (1.6): an Object that is not a composite, reaching a position whose type is a composite type over a shape, is converted by CompositeFromShape of that shape, and a value that is already a composite is passed through, the typed creation being idempotent on one.
