Since a shape's structural members are composite types (23.2), this is what builds the nested composites of a composite tree: Composite.<S>(source) with an ordinary object or array at a structural position of source converts it, at the member's type, into the composite it must be, and the typed creation of a document interns with the typed parse of the same document.

    23.5.2.1 CompositeFromShape ( S, source )

    The abstract operation CompositeFromShape takes arguments S (an object, tuple or array Type Record) and source (an ECMAScript language value) and returns either a normal completion containing a composite object or a throw completion. It performs the typed creation of a composite: each supplied value is converted to its member's type, a required absence throws, an undeclared property throws, and an optional member's declared default is filled, before canonicalization and interning. S is a SHAPE (23.2), which is what the three kinds it may be have in common. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If source is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
    2. If S.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(source).
      2. Let elements be a new empty List.
      3. Let i be 0.
      4. Repeat, while i < len,
        1. Let v be ? Get(source, ! ToString(𝔽(i))).
        2. Let converted be ? the conversion of v to S.[[Element]], as at a typed argument (1.6).
        3. Append CanonicalizeCompositeValue(converted) to elements.
        4. Set i to i + 1.
      5. Return ? FindOrCreateTupleComposite(elements).
    3. If S.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(source).
      2. If len is not a length S admits (1.14.7), throw a TypeError exception.
      3. Let elements be a new empty List.
      4. Let i be 0.
      5. Repeat, while i < len,
        1. Let v be ? Get(source, ! ToString(𝔽(i))).
        2. Let converted be ? the conversion of v to the [[Type]] of the element of S that receives position i, as at a typed argument (1.6).
        3. Append CanonicalizeCompositeValue(converted) to elements.
        4. Set i to i + 1.
      6. For each element e of S.[[Elements]] whose position is not less than len, do
        1. If e.[[Rest]] is false, then
          1. Assert: e.[[Initial]] is not none, since a tuple's defaults are trailing (1.4.2.7) and len is a length S admits.
          2. Append CanonicalizeCompositeValue(e.[[Initial]]) to elements.
      7. Return ? FindOrCreateTupleComposite(elements).
    4. Assert: S.[[Kind]] is object.
    5. If any Property Type Record of S.[[Properties]] has a [[Key]] that is a Symbol, throw a TypeError exception.
    6. Let entries be a new empty List.
    7. Let keys be ? source.[[OwnPropertyKeys]]().
    8. For each element key of keys, do
      1. Let desc be ? source.[[GetOwnProperty]](key).
      2. If desc is not undefined and desc.[[Enumerable]] is true, then
        1. If key is a Symbol, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Let memberType be empty.
        3. Let p be the Property Type Record of S.[[Properties]] whose [[Key]] is key, or empty if there is none.
        4. If p is not empty, then
          1. Set memberType to p.[[Type]].
        5. Else,
          1. Let sig be the first Index Signature Record of S.[[IndexSignatures]] that accepts key, or empty if there is none.
          2. If sig is not empty, set memberType to sig.[[ValueType]].
        6. If memberType is empty, throw a TypeError exception.
        7. Let v be ? Get(source, key).
        8. Let converted be ? the conversion of v to memberType, as at a typed argument (1.6).
        9. Append the Composite Entry Record { [[Key]]: key, [[Value]]: CanonicalizeCompositeValue(converted) } to entries.
    9. For each Property Type Record p of S.[[Properties]], do
      1. If no element of entries has [[Key]] p.[[Key]], then
        1. If p.[[Optional]] is false, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. If p.[[Initial]] is not none, append the Composite Entry Record { [[Key]]: p.[[Key]], [[Value]]: CanonicalizeCompositeValue(p.[[Initial]]) } to entries.
    10. Return FindOrCreateComposite(entries).
         Note

    Typed creation is the untyped algorithm with each supplied value converted to its member's type at the boundary, which is what makes the resulting fields carry T's types and the result's Static Type Composite.<T>. It is that algorithm literally: the read set is the same one, the source's own enumerable String-keyed properties in the order its [[OwnPropertyKeys]] internal method reports them, each read exactly once, so the two spellings hold the same data and run the same getters in the same order. What the shape adds is the conversion of each value, the two rejections, and the defaults; what it does not add is a second way of finding a value. Three of its rules deserve their reasons. A required member that is absent throws rather than filling the type's default: a composite is a key, and a key half of whose contents were invented silently would collide with the key that stated them. A property the type does not name throws for the mirror reason: dropping it silently would intern two different sources to one object. And an optional member's declared default, the [[Initial]] of page?: uint8 = 0, is written here, before freezing and before interning, so Composite.<CacheKey>({ id: 7 }) and Composite.<CacheKey>({ id: 7, page: 0 }) are the same object; an optional member with no declared default simply stays absent. A default is a construction feature (1.4.2.9), typed composite creation is a construction site, and a check of a composite that already exists writes nothing to it, which for a frozen shared object is not a preference but the only possibility.

    The contextual type of source is T's structural form (1.6.5), so numeric literals in the source take the member types by 1.6.6 and the conversions above are checks rather than coercions at a literal creation site. A binding annotated Composite.<T> gives an unadorned Composite(...) initializer the same treatment through the return-type direction of overload resolution (1.10.5). An unannotated, uncontextualized Composite({ id: 7 }) in typed code produces Number fields; code that means anything else says so at the creation site.

    That the read set is the enumerable own properties, rather than everything a lookup would answer, is a decision and the alternative is worth naming. A boundary check (1.7.2.1) reads through accessors and the prototype chain, because it asks whether a value can be used as the type; a creation asks what the new value's contents are, and every operation in the language that copies contents, Object.assign, object spread, JSON.stringify, and structured cloning among them, reads the enumerable own properties. A composite is a copy, so it reads what a copy reads. The cost is that a member supplied only by a prototype accessor or a non-enumerable own property does not satisfy the shape; the benefit is that the case fails loudly, with a TypeError naming the absent member, where the untyped creation silently produces a composite without it. Reading through the chain instead cannot be made symmetric in any case: the rejection of an undeclared property needs a finite set of keys to walk, and a lookup has none, since every object inherits "toString".

    A rejection therefore throws part way through, after the getters preceding it in key order have run, exactly as the untyped creation's Symbol-key rejection does. A trailing tuple position the source does not supply is filled from its declared default, as an absent optional member is, and for the same reason: Composite.<[uint8, uint32 = 10]>([1]) and Composite.<[uint8, uint32 = 10]>([1, 10]) are one object. A position the source does not supply always carries a default, since a tuple's defaults are trailing and the admitted lengths stop only where one begins (1.4.2.7). One consequence of filling is worth stating: Composite.<T> is not idempotent where T declares an optional member with a default, since Composite.<CacheKey>(_c_) fills page onto a composite c that lacks it and so returns a different object. That is the rule working rather than failing, because every creation through Composite.<CacheKey> fills it and they therefore agree with each other; a composite lacking the member satisfies the type by width subtyping and is a different key, which is what it is.

    23.5.3 Composite.isComposite ( arg )

    This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return IsComposite(arg).

    23.5.4 Composite [ %Symbol.hasInstance% ] ( value )

    This function performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return IsComposite(value).
     Note

    The Composite function has no "prototype" property, so without this method value instanceof Composite would throw through OrdinaryHasInstance. With it, instanceof against the bare function answers membership in the top composite type, and instanceof against Composite.<T>, a Type Object, answers membership in that type by 1.7.7, narrowing the static type on success as any type-object instanceof does.

    23.5.5 Composite [ %Symbol.customMatcher% ] ( subject, hint )

    The function performs the following steps when called:

    1. Return IsComposite(subject).
     Note

    Composite needs this method because it is a function, not a Type Object: a name pattern that evaluates to a Type Object tests membership, but a plain function is a constant compared by SameValue (24.2.1), so without the matcher when Composite: would compare the subject against the function itself, a test nothing sensible ever passes. With it, the bare name means what Composite.<T> already means narrowed: is this value a composite. In an ecosystem whose default matcher instead invokes a callable as a predicate, the method is load-bearing rather than merely useful, since a bare when Composite: would there call Composite(subject), match every object, run the subject's getters, and intern a composite as the side effect of a test. A composite constant used as a pattern remains one pointer comparison, since a constant pattern tests SameValue and an interned composite's SameValue is its contents.

    23.6 Composites and JSON

    JSON.stringify requires no change: a record composite is an object whose own enumerable properties are its contents, and a tuple composite is an array, so each serializes as its data. Interning is deliberately not on the wire; it is an identity within one heap, not a serialization format.

    The typed parse re-interns: CoerceJSONValue (43.1) carries a case for composite types, placed before its primitive case since a composite type is of that kind, which coerces the parsed value against the shape, canonicalizes each resulting value, and obtains the result through FindOrCreateComposite or FindOrCreateTupleComposite. The order is load-bearing: the coercion against the shape is where the document is validated — a member token that does not fit its integer type, or a missing required member, is a TypeError exception there, exactly as it is for JSON.parse.<T> of the same text — and only a validated value is interned. Converting first and validating never would let a uint8 member wrap 300 to 44 and intern the wrong document silently. Because the shape's structural members are themselves composite types (23.2), the coercion of the shape reaches this same case for every nested object and array of the document, so the whole document is interned as a tree with no further step, and an array shape yields a tuple composite as CompositeFromShape does. The top composite type is rejected there with a TypeError exception, because it states no shape to validate against.

    Note

    JSON.parse.<Composite.<T>>(text) therefore validates against T by the walk of 43 and interns the result, so whether a configuration has changed between two polls is === between two parses. This answers the mapping the design's serialization document left open for composites. Absent members follow the construction rule of 1.4.2.9 through the coercion of the shape, since the shape's own coercion is what fills them: an optional member's declared default is filled and an optional member without one stays absent, and a document whose array is shorter than a tuple shape takes that shape's trailing defaults. A parsed composite therefore interns with the typed creation of the same document.

    A host that serializes objects for transfer between heaps, as the HTML structured clone algorithm does, must serialize a composite as its kind and its contents and, on deserialization, obtain the result through FindOrCreateComposite or FindOrCreateTupleComposite in the receiving heap, each value having been deserialized and canonicalized first. Equality between composites is thereby preserved within every heap, two messages carrying equal contents arriving ===, and never across heaps, whose registries are disjoint; a composite is never the same object on two sides of a boundary that copies.

    23.7 Modifications to Existing Abstract Operations

    23.7.1 CanBeHeldWeakly ( v )

    The abstract operation CanBeHeldWeakly takes argument v (an ECMAScript language value) and returns a Boolean. It returns true if and only if v is suitable for use as a key of a WeakMap, an element of a WeakSet, the target or unregister token of a FinalizationRegistry, or the target of a WeakRef. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If v is an Object, IsComposite(v) is false, and v is not an instance of a typed class that seals its instances (1.12.8), return true.
    2. If v is a Symbol and KeyForSymbol(v) is undefined, return true.
    3. Return false.
     Note

    The one operation gates every weak position, so this change makes each of WeakMap, WeakSet, WeakRef, and FinalizationRegistry reject a composite with a TypeError exception. A composite is excluded for the reason a value type is (1.12.8), reached from the other side: its identity coincides with its contents, so the registry may always resurrect an equal object and there is no liveness for a weak reference to observe, only the registry's own entry, which holding weakly would keep alive. A cache that must not retain composite keys holds their constituent trackable objects weakly instead.

    23.7.2 GetIterator ( obj, kind )

    The abstract operation GetIterator takes arguments obj (an ECMAScript language value) and kind (sync or async) and returns either a normal completion containing an Iterator Record or a throw completion. It obtains an iterator for obj. The algorithm restates the pinned edition's, with the inserted steps marked. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If obj is a tuple composite, then
      1. Let iterator be CreateArrayIterator(obj, value).
      2. Let nextMethod be ! Get(iterator, "next").
      3. Let iteratorRecord be the Iterator Record { [[Iterator]]: iterator, [[NextMethod]]: nextMethod, [[Done]]: false }.
      4. If kind is async, return CreateAsyncFromSyncIterator(iteratorRecord).
      5. Return iteratorRecord.
    2. If kind is async, then
      1. Let method be ? GetMethod(obj, %Symbol.asyncIterator%).
      2. If method is undefined, then
        1. Let syncMethod be ? GetMethod(obj, %Symbol.iterator%).
        2. If syncMethod is undefined, throw a TypeError exception.
        3. Let syncIteratorRecord be ? GetIteratorFromMethod(obj, syncMethod).
        4. Return CreateAsyncFromSyncIterator(syncIteratorRecord).
    3. Else,
      1. Let method be ? GetMethod(obj, %Symbol.iterator%).
    4. If method is undefined, throw a TypeError exception.
    5. Return ? GetIteratorFromMethod(obj, method).
     Note

    A tuple composite has a null prototype, so no %Symbol.iterator% can reach it by lookup, and being frozen it cannot receive one. The inserted step recognizes the kind directly, so for-of, spread, and array destructuring iterate a tuple composite's elements with no method on the object; the manual protocol spelling is Array.prototype.values.call(m), which builds the same iterator. In typed code the iteration is additionally type-directed, an index loop over known element types, exactly as an array of statically known element type iterates; the step above is what extends that behaviour to untyped code, where nothing else could. Record composites are unaffected and are not iterable, matching ordinary objects.

    The non-mutating array generics apply to a tuple composite explicitly, as Array.prototype.map.call(m, f), or through the typed signatures the standard library gives them; the mutating ones throw on a frozen receiver as they do for any frozen array, and delete and every store throw as 1.14.10 already provides for typed elements.

    23.8 Deviations from the Upstream Proposal

    For feedback in both directions, the deltas between this clause and the upstream Composites proposal, in one place:

    • Interning is type-sensitive, because SameValueZero is: Composite({ (x: uint8): 1 }) and Composite({ x: 1 }) are distinct objects. Upstream has one number type and no such distinction to make.
    • Canonicalization is stated as a rule over SameValueZero equivalence classes, of which upstream's -0 normalization is the Number instance; the decimal cohorts and the per-width float zeros are further instances, the NaN encoding requirement extends upstream's to every width a byte view reaches, and the preserveNegativeZero option is not adopted.
    • The tuple kind is added, and it changes the result of Composite on an array source, which upstream reads through the record path with length dropped.
    • The registry is scoped to the heap rather than to the agent. The two coincide under the pinned edition's agent model; they come apart exactly where the threading extension shares one heap among agents.
    • Typed creation through the composite Type Objects, the Composite.<T> types with their subtyping and interface satisfaction, and the [[RuntimeType]] a composite carries for reflection are added; they change nothing observable about an untyped creation beyond what canonicalization states.
    • Composite[%Symbol.hasInstance%] is added so that instanceof answers membership rather than throwing, and Composite[%Symbol.customMatcher%] is added so that the pattern Composite tests membership rather than invoking the function as a predicate; the latter applies to the upstream proposal as it stands and is independent of types.
    • The typed JSON parse and the host serialization requirement of 23.6 are defined.
    • Everything else, the creation semantics and eager getters, the Symbol-key refusal, the canonical key order, frozenness and the null prototype, Composite.isComposite, the weak-position refusal, the cross-realm identity within one registry, and the impossibility of cycles, since a composite is frozen at birth and can reference only values that already existed, is adopted as upstream specifies.

    24 Pattern Matching

    This clause specifies the design's pattern matching extension: the match expression, the pattern grammar, the widening of is to take a pattern, and the exhaustiveness and narrowing rules that make a match over a closed type checked complete. A pattern is a test, a destructuring, and a proof at once; the runtime semantics here perform the first two, and the static semantics hand the third to the narrowing machinery of 1.8.5.

    24.1 The match Expression

    PrimaryExpression[Yield, Await] : MatchExpression[?Yield, ?Await] MatchExpression[Yield, Await] : match [no LineTerminator here] ( Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ) { MatchClauses[?Yield, ?Await] } match [no LineTerminator here] all [no LineTerminator here] ( Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ) { MatchAllClauses[?Yield, ?Await] } MatchAllClauses[Yield, Await] : MatchAllClause[?Yield, ?Await] MatchAllClauses[?Yield, ?Await] MatchAllClause[?Yield, ?Await] MatchAllClause[Yield, Await] : when MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchGuard[?Yield, ?Await]opt : MatchArmBody[?Yield, ?Await] MatchClauses[Yield, Await] : MatchClause[?Yield, ?Await] MatchClauses[?Yield, ?Await] MatchClause[?Yield, ?Await] MatchClause[Yield, Await] : when MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchGuard[?Yield, ?Await]opt : MatchArmBody[?Yield, ?Await] default : MatchArmBody[?Yield, ?Await] MatchGuard[Yield, Await] : if ( Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ) MatchArmBody[Yield, Await] : AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ; throw AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] ; Block[?Yield, ?Await, ~Return]

    The Block of a MatchArmBody carries the [Return], [Yield], and [Await] permissions of the function enclosing the match, so return, break, continue, await, and yield inside a block arm mean what they mean in that function; the Return above is notational for the production and the permission is threaded in the obvious way by the enclosing contexts. The ; of an expression arm is subject to automatic semicolon insertion as the ; of an expression statement is.

    The second form answers with every clause that matched rather than the first, as an Array in clause order. It differs from the first in three ways and in no others - patterns, guards, bindings, per-clause narrowing, arm bodies, and the single evaluation of the subject are all the same:

    • the value is an Array of the matched clauses' values, empty when none matched;
    • exhaustiveness is not required (24.3.1);
    • subtraction narrowing between clauses does not apply, since a later clause is reached whether or not an earlier one matched.

    A MatchAllClause admits no default. default and the wildcard pattern are interchangeable in a MatchClause, and a form in which one meant "always" and the other "only where nothing else did" would give the same spelling two meanings one form apart. A clause that always contributes is written when _.

    Note 1

    all is a contextual keyword: it is the modifier only where a ( follows it on the same line, and it remains an ordinary identifier everywhere, including as a binding, a property, and a function name. The [no LineTerminator here] restriction before it is what keeps match on one line followed by all(x) on the next meaning the two statements it means today.

    It is a Syntax Error if a default MatchClause is not the last of its MatchClauses.

    Note 2

    match, when, and, or, and not are contextual keywords, treated as keywords only in the positions above and in the pattern grammar, which are Syntax Errors today. match(x) {} remains a call followed by a block, because MatchClauses requires at least one clause; in statement position the braced sequel of match (…) is parsed under a cover, as the type operator's parenthesized operand is (1.4.5), and refined to MatchClauses where they parse as such, otherwise remaining the block it is today. Every program the refinement accepts was a Syntax Error: a clause's pattern is never empty, so the label when: never reads as a clause, default is reserved and cannot label a statement, and when followed by a pattern is not a statement sequence. In expression position there is no overlap at all, since a call followed by { is a Syntax Error there.

    24.1.1 Runtime Semantics: Evaluation

    A Match Cache Record has a [[Reads]] field, a List of Records { [[Object]], [[Key]], [[Present]], [[Value]] }, and an [[Iterations]] field, a List of Records { [[Object]], [[Elements]] (a List), [[Done]] (a Boolean), [[Iterator]] (an Iterator Record) }. It memoizes what a match reads of its subject, so that a property is read at most once and an iterator is obtained at most once however many patterns look, and every pattern of one match sees the same values.

    1. Let subject be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of Expression).
    2. Let cache be the Match Cache Record { [[Reads]]: a new empty List, [[Iterations]]: a new empty List }.
    3. For each MatchClause clause of MatchClauses, in source order, do
      1. Let outerEnv be the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment.
      2. Let env be NewDeclarativeEnvironment(outerEnv).
      3. For each element name of the BoundNames of clause, do
        1. If the MatchBindingPattern binding name has const, perform ! env.CreateImmutableBinding(name, true).
        2. Else, perform ! env.CreateMutableBinding(name, false).
      4. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to env.
      5. If clause is a default clause, let matched be true.
      6. Else, let matched be Completion(PatternMatches(the clause's MatchPattern, subject, cache, env)).
      7. If matched is an abrupt completion, set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv and return ? matched.
      8. Set matched to ! matched.
      9. If matched is true and clause has a MatchGuard, then
        1. Let guard be Completion(GetValue(Completion(Evaluation of the MatchGuard's Expression))).
        2. If guard is an abrupt completion, set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv and return ? guard.
        3. Set matched to ToBoolean(! guard).
      10. If matched is true, then
        1. Let result be Completion(MatchArmEvaluation of the clause's MatchArmBody).
        2. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv.
        3. Return ? result.
      11. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv.
    4. Throw a TypeError exception.

    The second form collects rather than returning:

    1. Let subject be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of Expression).
    2. Let cache be the Match Cache Record { [[Reads]]: a new empty List, [[Iterations]]: a new empty List }.
    3. Let results be a new empty List.
    4. For each MatchAllClause clause of MatchAllClauses, in source order, do
      1. Let outerEnv be the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment.
      2. Let env be NewDeclarativeEnvironment(outerEnv).
      3. For each element name of the BoundNames of clause, do
        1. If the MatchBindingPattern binding name has const, perform ! env.CreateImmutableBinding(name, true).
        2. Else, perform ! env.CreateMutableBinding(name, false).
      4. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to env.
      5. Let matched be Completion(MatchPatternMatches of the clause's MatchPattern with arguments subject and cache).
      6. If matched is an abrupt completion, set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv and return ? matched.
      7. Set matched to ! matched.
      8. If matched is true and clause has a MatchGuard, then
        1. Let guard be Completion(GetValue(Completion(Evaluation of the MatchGuard's Expression))).
        2. If guard is an abrupt completion, set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv and return ? guard.
        3. Set matched to ToBoolean(! guard).
      9. If matched is true, then
        1. Let result be Completion(MatchArmEvaluation of the clause's MatchArmBody).
        2. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv.
        3. Append ? result to results.
      10. Else,
        1. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to outerEnv.
    5. Return CreateArrayFromList(results).
     Note 1

    The subject is evaluated once and the cache is shared across clauses, exactly as in the first form, so a property is read at most once however many patterns look at it.

    An abrupt completion from any clause propagates, which is what makes an arm that throws abort the collection: the clauses before it have already evaluated their arm bodies, and those values are lost with the expression. An arm that RETURNS a failure rather than throwing one is what collecting failures looks like, and needs nothing further - the value is the failure and the result is already the collection.

    Reaching the end without a match returns an empty Array rather than throwing, which is the whole of why exhaustiveness is not required of this form.

    MatchArmEvaluation of AssignmentExpression ; returns ? GetValue(? Evaluation of AssignmentExpression). Of throw AssignmentExpression ;, it evaluates as the throw statement does. Of a Block, it is the evaluation of a do expression's Block (37): the block is evaluated and the result is its completion value.

    Note 2

    An arm's block was given a narrower rule than this while do expressions were outstanding - its value was its final statement's only where that statement was an ExpressionStatement, and void otherwise - and that rule was a strict subset of this one, so no program changes meaning by its replacement. What it could not do was let an arm end in an if with an else or a try, and what it did badly was make an arm ending in a declaration a silent void rather than the Syntax Error 37.1 now gives. The bindings of a clause are created immutable and are initialized by the pattern as it matches; a clause that does not match discards its environment, so a binding never leaks between arms, and the guard and body of the arm that runs see exactly what its own pattern bound.

    24.2 Patterns

    MatchPattern[Yield, Await] : MatchOrPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchOrPattern[Yield, Await] : MatchAndPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchOrPattern[?Yield, ?Await] or MatchAndPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchAndPattern[Yield, Await] : MatchUnaryPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchAndPattern[?Yield, ?Await] and MatchUnaryPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchUnaryPattern[Yield, Await] : not MatchUnaryPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchPrimaryPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchPrimaryPattern[Yield, Await] : ( MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ) _ extends TypePattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ${ Expression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] } ObjectMatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ArrayMatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] ( MatchPatternList[?Yield, ?Await]opt ) MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] ObjectMatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] ArrayMatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchLiteralPattern[?Yield, ?Await] Type[?Yield, ?Await] MatchBindingPattern[Yield, Await] : let BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt const BindingIdentifier[?Yield, ?Await] TypeAnnotation[?Yield, ?Await]opt TypePattern[Yield, Await] : Type[?Yield, ?Await] MatchNamePattern[Yield, Await] : IdentifierReference[?Yield, ?Await] MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] . IdentifierName MatchNamePattern[?Yield, ?Await] TypeArguments[?Yield, ?Await] MatchPatternList[Yield, Await] : MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchPatternList[?Yield, ?Await] , MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ObjectMatchPattern[Yield, Await] : { } { MatchPropertyList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt } { MatchPropertyList[?Yield, ?Await] , ... MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] } { ... MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] } MatchPropertyList[Yield, Await] : MatchProperty[?Yield, ?Await] MatchPropertyList[?Yield, ?Await] , MatchProperty[?Yield, ?Await] MatchProperty[Yield, Await] : PropertyName[?Yield, ?Await] : MatchPattern[?Yield, ?Await] MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ArrayMatchPattern[Yield, Await] : [ ] [ MatchPatternList[?Yield, ?Await] ,opt ] [ MatchPatternList[?Yield, ?Await] , ... MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ] [ ... MatchBindingPattern[?Yield, ?Await] ]

    The identifier _ is the wildcard wherever a pattern is expected, taking precedence over its MatchNamePattern reading, so a program that binds the name _ and wants its value writes ${_}. A MatchProperty that is a MatchBindingPattern is the shorthand: let x is x: let x. Within a MatchPattern, ${ is recognized as a punctuator, a lexical goal the pattern context sets as the template contexts do; outside one it lexes as it does today. A MatchLiteralPattern is a ShortCircuitExpression restricted by the early errors below to a literal-like form; the restriction is applied after the cover parse, as the parenthesized operand of type is refined (1.4.5).

    MatchLiteralPattern[Yield, Await] : ShortCircuitExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await]
    • It is a Syntax Error if a MatchLiteralPattern's ShortCircuitExpression is not one of: a NumericLiteral, optionally preceded by + or -; a StringLiteral; a NoSubstitutionTemplate; true, false, or null; a RegularExpressionLiteral; or a range literal of 19.6, each of whose present endpoints is one of the preceding forms or a MatchNamePattern form.
    • It is a Syntax Error if the two alternatives of a MatchOrPattern do not have the same BoundNames.
    • It is a Syntax Error if the BoundNames of a MatchPattern contain any duplicate entries, except that the same name bound by both alternatives of an or is one binding.
    • Within a TypePattern, a CaptureBinding in a TypeArgument position is the pattern slot, the syntactic form of the slot that 20 creates reflectively: Box.<const T>, or under the nested parameter's name, Map.<K: string, V: const T>. It binds what stands in its position, and is meaningful only where a type is being matched rather than written, which is the type-subject pattern the Early Errors of 1.4.3.2 admit a CaptureBinding in. The BindingIdentifier : Type form of TypeArgument is a named type argument (1.4.2.2) in a TypePattern as everywhere else; the marked capture is what keeps the two readings apart without consulting the context.
    • It is a type error if the MatchNamePattern of a juxtaposition or of an extractor form resolves to a binding that does not denote what the form requires: the juxtaposed head must denote a type, and the extractor head must denote a value with a %Symbol.customMatcher% method, decided at the site where the head's Static Type is known and at run time otherwise. Every name resolves to some binding, a class declaration's included, so the rule turns on what the binding denotes. A type, a class and a Type Object are Objects, so a juxtaposed head whose Static Type establishes only non-Object values denotes no type.
    • A JUXTAPOSITION matches where the value is of the type its MatchNamePattern denotes and the ObjectMatchPattern or ArrayMatchPattern then matches it, and its PatternType is the head's type narrowed by the shape's. This follows from the overlap rule above rather than qualifying it: P tests membership, so P { ... } must agree with P about whether a P matches, and the head's test is also what gives the preceding rule anything to enforce.
    • No LineTerminator may appear between a juxtaposition's MatchNamePattern and its ObjectMatchPattern or ArrayMatchPattern. A pattern is the right operand of is, which is an ordinary expression, so without the restriction an expression statement followed by a block would read the block as the pattern's shape.
    • MatchNamePattern ArrayMatchPattern and an IndexedAccessType are ambiguous after a name: P [x] may be read as a juxtaposition or as an index into P, and unlike the overlap above the two readings do not agree. The juxtaposition is taken only where an element is something a Type cannot express, such as a binding or _, and the index is taken otherwise. This is the rule the braced and bracketed patterns already carry on their own - a shape every one of whose elements is a type is read as the type, the two readings agreeing there - and it is decided on the FORM of each element rather than on what it denotes, so it is settled before any name is resolved.

    A MatchNamePattern and a Type overlap where a name is both; the name form is preferred, and the two readings agree wherever both exist, since a name denoting a type matches by membership under either. The Type alternative exists for the forms only a type can spell, a union of literal types being the or-pattern for constants with no combinator: 'GET' | 'HEAD' is one type pattern whose test is two comparisons. A MatchLiteralPattern and a literal Type likewise coincide; the literal form is preferred and the semantics are one.

    24.2.1 PatternMatches ( P, subject, cache, env )

    The abstract operation PatternMatches takes arguments P (a Parse Node), subject (an ECMAScript language value), cache (a Match Cache Record), and env (an Environment Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It decides whether the pattern P matches subject, initializing the bindings P declares in env as it does. Sub-patterns are tried in source order and the operation returns at the first failure, so user code a pattern can reach, a getter, a matcher, an interpolation, runs at most once and only up to the deciding test. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If P is MatchOrPattern : MatchOrPattern or MatchAndPattern, then
      1. Let bindings be the states of the bindings named by the BoundNames of the first alternative in env.
      2. Let left be ? PatternMatches(the first alternative, subject, cache, env).
      3. If left is true, return true.
      4. Restore those bindings in env to bindings. This restoration does not undo observable effects or discard entries in cache.
      5. Return ? PatternMatches(the second alternative, subject, cache, env).
    2. If P is MatchAndPattern : MatchAndPattern and MatchUnaryPattern, then
      1. Let left be ? PatternMatches(the first operand, subject, cache, env).
      2. If left is false, return false.
      3. Return ? PatternMatches(the second operand, subject, cache, env).
    3. If P is MatchUnaryPattern : not MatchUnaryPattern, then
      1. Let inner be ? PatternMatches(the operand, subject, cache, env).
      2. If inner is true, return false; else return true.
    4. If P is a parenthesized pattern, return ? PatternMatches(its MatchPattern, subject, cache, env).
    5. If P is MatchPrimaryPattern : _, return true.
    6. If P is MatchPrimaryPattern : extends TypePattern, return MatchTypePattern(the TypePattern, subject, env).
    7. If P is a MatchBindingPattern, then
      1. If P has a TypeAnnotation, then
        1. Let ok be ? IsOfType(subject, the Type Record it denotes).
        2. If ok is false, return false.
      2. Perform ! env.InitializeBinding(the StringValue of P's BindingIdentifier, subject).
      3. Return true.
    8. If P is ${ Expression }, then
      1. Let v be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of Expression).
      2. Return MatchConstant(subject, v).
    9. If P is a MatchLiteralPattern, then
      1. Let v be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of its ShortCircuitExpression), except that a numeric literal takes the contextual type of the pattern's position (1.6.6).
      2. If v is a Range, return ? MatchRange(subject, v).
      3. If v is an Object with a [[RegExpMatcher]] internal slot, return ? MatchRegExp(subject, v, none, cache, env).
      4. If P's ShortCircuitExpression is a NumericLiteral with no preceding + or - whose value is a zero, return the result of the sameValueZero comparison of subject and v within their type, false where their types differ.
      5. Return MatchConstant(subject, v).
    10. If P is a Type, then
      1. Let t be the Type Record P denotes.
      2. Let structural be ? MatchStructuralType(t, subject, cache).
      3. If structural is not not-applicable, return structural.
      4. Return ? IsOfType(subject, t).
    11. If P is a MatchNamePattern alone, then
      1. If P resolves to a type, then
        1. Let t be the Type Record it denotes.
        2. Let structural be ? MatchStructuralType(t, subject, cache).
        3. If structural is not not-applicable, return structural.
        4. Return ? IsOfType(subject, t).
      2. Let v be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of P read as the member expression it spells).
      3. If v is a Type Object, return ? IsOfType(subject, the Type Record v reifies).
      4. If v is a Range, return ? MatchRange(subject, v).
      5. If v is an Object with a [[RegExpMatcher]] internal slot, return ? MatchRegExp(subject, v, none, cache, env).
      6. If v is an Object, then
        1. Let matcher be ? GetMethod(v, %Symbol.customMatcher%).
        2. If matcher is not undefined, then
          1. Let r be ? Call(matcher, v, « subject »).
          2. If r is an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
          3. Return ToBoolean(r).
      7. Return MatchConstant(subject, v).
    12. If P is MatchNamePattern ( MatchPatternList? ), then
      1. Let v be ? GetValue(? Evaluation of the MatchNamePattern read as the member expression it spells).
      2. If v is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
      3. Let matcher be ? GetMethod(v, %Symbol.customMatcher%).
      4. If matcher is undefined, throw a TypeError exception.
      5. Let r be ? Call(matcher, v, « subject »).
      6. If r is null, return false.
      7. If r is not an Object, throw a TypeError exception.
      8. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(r).
      9. If len ≠ the number of patterns in the MatchPatternList, or the list is absent and len ≠ 0, throw a TypeError exception.
      10. Let i be 0.
      11. For each pattern p of the MatchPatternList, in order, do
        1. Let e be ? Get(r, ! ToString(𝔽(i))).
        2. If ? PatternMatches(p, e, cache, env) is false, return false.
        3. Set i to i + 1.
      12. Return true.
    13. If P is a juxtaposition of a MatchNamePattern and an ObjectMatchPattern or ArrayMatchPattern, then
      1. Let t be the Type Record the MatchNamePattern denotes; it is a TypeError exception at run time if it denotes none.
      2. Let ofType be ? IsOfType(subject, t).
      3. If ofType is false, return false.
      4. Return ? PatternMatches(the structural pattern, subject, cache, env).
    14. If P is an ObjectMatchPattern, return ? MatchObjectPattern(P, subject, cache, env).
    15. Assert: P is an ArrayMatchPattern.
    16. Return ? MatchArrayPattern(P, subject, cache, env).
     Note

    NaN needs no rule of its own: it is a name pattern holding a Number, so MatchConstant compares it with the type's sameValue, under which a NaN equals a NaN, and a float32 NaN does not match a float64 one because their types differ. MatchConstant(a, b) is the sameValue comparison within one type: false where the types of a and b differ, and the type's T::sameValue otherwise, with SameValue for values that are not of a numeric type. For an interned composite that is one pointer comparison, and for a value type class instance it is the fieldwise comparison its === performs. The bare-zero step is the one SameValueZero literal: 0 matches both zeros of the position's type at every width, while an explicit +0 or -0 distinguishes them, the design's rule stated per type.

    The name form dispatches on what the name turns out to hold, so a range or a regular expression bound to a constant matches as the literal spelling would, by containment and by whole-subject match; the escape to identity in every case is ${name}. A boolean-returning matcher reached without parentheses is a membership test, the form Composite uses (23.5.5); a matcher that returns an object there is a TypeError, as parentheses on a boolean matcher are, so the two protocols cannot be confused silently. Matchers and interpolations are the patterns that run user code, and they run in source order at most once each per match attempt.

    24.2.2 MatchObjectPattern ( P, subject, cache, env )

    The abstract operation MatchObjectPattern takes arguments P (a Parse Node), subject (an ECMAScript language value), cache (a Match Cache Record), and env (an Environment Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It matches an ObjectMatchPattern: each named member must be present, by the in test, and its value must match its sub-pattern; the rest binding, where present, collects the remaining own enumerable members. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If subject is not an Object, return false.
    2. For each MatchProperty prop of P, in order, do
      1. Let key be the property key prop names.
      2. If no element of cache.[[Reads]] has [[Object]] subject and [[Key]] key, then
        1. Let present be ? HasProperty(subject, key).
        2. If present is true, let value be ? Get(subject, key); else let value be undefined.
        3. Append the Record { [[Object]]: subject, [[Key]]: key, [[Present]]: present, [[Value]]: value } to cache.[[Reads]].
      3. Let read be the element of cache.[[Reads]] whose [[Object]] is subject and whose [[Key]] is key.
      4. If read.[[Present]] is false, return false.
      5. If ? PatternMatches(the sub-pattern of prop, read.[[Value]], cache, env) is false, return false.
    3. If P has a rest MatchBindingPattern, then
      1. Let rest be OrdinaryObjectCreate(%Object.prototype%).
      2. Perform ? CopyDataProperties(rest, subject, the List of the property keys the MatchProperty list names).
      3. Perform ! env.InitializeBinding(the StringValue of its BindingIdentifier, rest).
    4. Return true.
     Note

    The cache is why arms agree: a getter named by three patterns runs once, and the presence test and the read are one cached touch, a HasProperty and at most one Get per key per match. A composite subject makes the cache unnecessary rather than the guarantee weaker, since its every read is idempotent, and an implementation may skip it there (23). An absent optional member fails the pattern rather than matching undefined, which is the design's presence rule; matching the absence is a guard's job. A member the pattern does not name is ignored, since this type system has width subtyping and no exact object type, so a pattern has nothing to say about members it did not name and no token it must spell to stay silent about them; a member whose value does not matter is named against the wildcard, which tests presence and reads nothing.

    24.2.3 MatchArrayPattern ( P, subject, cache, env )

    The abstract operation MatchArrayPattern takes arguments P (a Parse Node), subject (an ECMAScript language value), cache (a Match Cache Record), and env (an Environment Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It matches an ArrayMatchPattern through iteration rather than through an array test, which is what reaches every array-shaped value of this proposal - a [N].<T> need not be an Array exotic object, a tuple composite is iterable by kind rather than by prototype, and a typed view answers no array predicate - memoized per subject: elements are pulled as patterns need them, a pattern without a rest element requires the iterator exhausted at its length, and a rest binding collects the remainder into a fresh Array. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If subject is not an Object, return false.
    2. If no element of cache.[[Iterations]] has [[Object]] subject, then
      1. Let iteratorRecord be ? GetIterator(subject, sync).
      2. Append the Record { [[Object]]: subject, [[Elements]]: a new empty List, [[Done]]: false, [[Iterator]]: iteratorRecord } to cache.[[Iterations]].
    3. Let it be the element of cache.[[Iterations]] whose [[Object]] is subject.
    4. Let n be the number of patterns in P's MatchPatternList, or 0 where it is absent.
    5. Perform ? MatchIteratorFill(it, n + 1).
    6. If P has no rest MatchBindingPattern, then
      1. If the number of elements of it.[[Elements]] ≠ n or it.[[Done]] is false, return false.
    7. Else,
      1. If the number of elements of it.[[Elements]] < n, return false.
    8. Let i be 0.
    9. For each pattern p of the MatchPatternList, in order, do
      1. If ? PatternMatches(p, it.[[Elements]][i], cache, env) is false, return false.
      2. Set i to i + 1.
    10. If P has a rest MatchBindingPattern, then
      1. Repeat, while it.[[Done]] is false,
        1. Perform ? MatchIteratorFill(it, the number of elements of it.[[Elements]] + 1).
      2. Let restList be the List of the elements of it.[[Elements]] from index n onward.
      3. Perform ! env.InitializeBinding(the StringValue of its BindingIdentifier, CreateArrayFromList(restList)).
    11. Return true.

    24.2.4 MatchTypePattern ( P, subject, env )

    The abstract operation MatchTypePattern takes arguments P (a TypePattern Parse Node), subject (an ECMAScript language value), and env (an Environment Record) and returns a Boolean. It matches a type against a pattern of types: subject must be a Type Object, its type must be within the type P writes, and each pattern slot of P binds the component of subject that stands where it does. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If subject is not a Type Object, return false.
    2. Let t be the Type Record subject reifies.
    3. If P contains no pattern slot, return IsAssignable(t, the Type Record P denotes).
    4. Let pattern be the Type Record P denotes with each pattern slot replaced by a fresh slot (20).
    5. Let bindings be the one-sided structural unification of pattern against t (20).
    6. If bindings is null, return false.
    7. For each pattern slot s of P, do
      1. Let v be the component bindings binds for s: the Type Object where that component is a Type Record, and the component itself where it is a metadata object or another value.
      2. If IsAssignable(RuntimeTypeOf(v), the Type Record s's Type denotes) is false, return false.
    8. For each pattern slot s of P, perform ! env.InitializeBinding(the StringValue of s's BindingIdentifier, the value bound for s above).
    9. Return true.
     Note

    The two halves answer different questions and both are needed. Without slots the test is assignability, so when extends string: matches a string and every refinement of one, which is what the keyword promises to a reader who has met it in a type position. With slots the test is unification, because a slot has to bind the component that stands where it does, and unification is the operation that finds it; a slot is a CaptureBinding (1.4.3.2), and its written domain or bound is then an ordinary check on what it bound, exactly as 20 says an infer S extends string is a check afterwards.

    The consequence worth stating is that a slotted pattern matches structurally where an unslotted one matches up to subtyping: extends [].<const E> does not match a [5].<uint8>, whose extent is 5 where the pattern's is dynamic, although extends [].<uint8> does match it. Unification up to subtyping is a different and much larger operation, and this specification does not perform it anywhere; a pattern is written against the shape it expects, which is the same discipline 20 already imposes in refusing a slot inside an deferred.

    The positions a slot may stand in are the ones this specification fixes: the [[Metadata]] of a parameterized Type Record and the [[Arguments]] of a nominal one. A slot standing where the generics extension rather than this specification defines the position, a variadic pack among them, reaches as far as that extension does (4), and a slot inside a deferred record is refused outright, which is the boundary 20 already draws for the same reason: a position no operation here can invert is a position no pattern can bind.

    A slot binds a value rather than always a Type Object because the positions of a parameterized type do not all hold types: float32.<const B: NumberBounds> binds the metadata object, which is what makes { ...B } in the design's constraintsFor an ordinary spread, while Map.<K: type, V: type> binds Type Objects. RuntimeTypeOf of the bound value is what the constraint is checked against in either case, and it is also the binding's Static Type (24.3).

    24.2.5 MatchIteratorFill ( it, count )

    The abstract operation MatchIteratorFill takes arguments it (a Record of a Match Cache Record's [[Iterations]]) and count (a non-negative integer) and returns either a normal completion containing unused or a throw completion. It advances the memoized iteration until it.[[Elements]] has count elements or the iterator is exhausted. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Repeat, while it.[[Done]] is false and the number of elements of it.[[Elements]] < count,
      1. Let next be ? IteratorStepValue(it.[[Iterator]]).
      2. If next is done, set it.[[Done]] to true.
      3. Else, append next to it.[[Elements]].
    2. Return unused.

    24.2.6 MatchStructuralType ( t, subject, cache )

    The abstract operation MatchStructuralType takes arguments t (a Type Record), subject (an ECMAScript language value), and cache (a Match Cache Record) and returns either a normal completion containing either a Boolean or not-applicable, or a throw completion. It matches a structural object type MEMBER BY MEMBER, reading each member through cache, so that the guarantee in 24.1 — that a property is read at most once however many patterns look — holds for a type pattern as it does for an object pattern. It returns not-applicable where t is not a type this treatment applies to, and the caller then uses IsOfType. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If t is not an object Type Record and is not a structural nominal type whose [[Structure]] is one, return not-applicable.
    2. Let shape be t or its [[Structure]], as applicable.
    3. If shape has any index signature, return not-applicable.
    4. If any member of shape.[[Properties]] is optional or is not named by a String, return not-applicable.
    5. If shape.[[Properties]] is empty, return not-applicable.
    6. If subject is not an Object, return false.
    7. For each element p of shape.[[Properties]], do
      1. If no element of cache.[[Reads]] has [[Object]] subject and [[Key]] p.[[Key]], then
        1. Let present be ? HasProperty(subject, p.[[Key]]).
        2. If present is true, let value be ? Get(subject, p.[[Key]]); else let value be undefined.
        3. Append the Record { [[Object]]: subject, [[Key]]: p.[[Key]], [[Present]]: present, [[Value]]: value } to cache.[[Reads]].
      2. Let read be the element of cache.[[Reads]] with [[Object]] subject and [[Key]] p.[[Key]].
      3. If read.[[Present]] is false, return false.
      4. If ? IsOfType(read.[[Value]], p.[[Type]]) is false, return false.
    8. Return true.
     Note

    Three kinds of object type are excluded, and each is excluded because a member-by-member test cannot express it. An OPTIONAL member is satisfied by its absence, where this test requires presence. An INDEX SIGNATURE names no members to walk. A NOMINAL type rejects a value that merely has the right members, so it can never become a structural test; an interface is structural and is not excluded.

    Without this, IsOfType reads the subject outside the cache, and two clauses of one match could see different values of one member. That is observable as a WRONG ARM rather than as a slower one: given a getter whose value changes, when { g: 2 } followed by when { g: 1 } reads twice and matches neither, where a single read matches the second.

    24.2.7 MatchConstant ( a, b )

    The abstract operation MatchConstant takes arguments a (an ECMAScript language value) and b (an ECMAScript language value) and returns a Boolean. It is the sameValue comparison within one type: false where the types of a and b differ, the type's T::sameValue where they are of one numeric type, and SameValue otherwise. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If a and b are not values of one type, return false.
    2. If a is a value of a numeric type, return the sameValue comparison of that type applied to a and b.
    3. Return SameValue(a, b).

    24.2.8 MatchRange ( subject, r )

    The abstract operation MatchRange takes arguments subject (an ECMAScript language value) and r (a Range) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It matches a range pattern by containment. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If subject is not a value of a type ordered with the element type of r, return false.
    2. Return ? the result of the containment test the range's contains performs on subject (19), which is at most two comparisons.

    24.2.9 MatchRegExp ( subject, r, sub, cache, env )

    The abstract operation MatchRegExp takes arguments subject (an ECMAScript language value), r (an Object with a [[RegExpMatcher]] internal slot), sub (a Parse Node or none), cache (a Match Cache Record), and env (an Environment Record) and returns either a normal completion containing a Boolean or a throw completion. It matches a regular expression pattern against the entire subject, and matches the juxtaposed structural pattern sub, where present, against the match result. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If subject is not a String, return false.
    2. Let result be ? RegExpExec(r, subject) restricted to a match of the entirety of subject: the match must begin at index 0 and end at the length of subject, as the whole-string discipline of a pattern constraint requires (3), so a search is spelled as one.
    3. If result is null, return false.
    4. If sub is none, return true.
    5. Return ? PatternMatches(sub, result, cache, env).
     Note

    The match result's Static Type is the exact result type the regular expression's captures give it, so groups: { let year } binds the typed group and a misspelled group name is a type error against that type. The result is constructed once and its reads enter the cache as any subject's do.

    24.3 Static Semantics of Patterns

    The pattern type of a pattern P, PatternType(P), is the Type Record a successful match establishes, defined by the form of P: a Type, the type it denotes; a name resolving to a type or evaluating to a Type Object of known type, that type; a literal, its literal type at the position type by 1.6.6, so that a numeric literal at a position with no numeric member keeps its base number; a name denoting a constant of literal or enumerator type, that type; a binding with an annotation, the annotated type, and without one, any; a range whose endpoints are compile-time constants, the position type refined by the interval's metadata (19); a regular expression, string; an extractor whose head denotes a type, that type, which is the narrowing its matcher's author asserts and the checker takes, as it takes a declared narrowing predicate's, and any for a head that denotes no type; a juxtaposition, PatternType of its structural part narrowed to its head's type; an ObjectMatchPattern, the object Type Record whose properties are the named members, each required, at the PatternType of its sub-pattern; an ArrayMatchPattern, any, since testing iteration establishes no indexed storage type; its sub-patterns retain the position types established by the static iteration contribution; an and, the NarrowTo of its operands' pattern types in order; an or, the union of its alternatives'; an extends pattern, the type type (1.5.21), since what a successful match establishes of the subject is that it is a Type Object; a wildcard, a not, or an interpolation of non-literal type, any.

    A pattern test divides the Static Type s of its position in two: MatchNarrow(s, P), the type of a value of s that P can match, and MissNarrow(s, P), the type of a value of s that P can miss, each empty where there is no such value. PatternType alone does not give both, because it is any both for a pattern that matches every value and for one that establishes nothing, and because the miss of not Q is the match of Q. They are defined by the form of P, a parenthesized pattern being its MatchPattern:

    • A Type, a name denoting a type or a constant of literal or enumerator type, a literal other than a regular expression or a range, an interpolation of literal type, and a binding with an annotation that does not denote any, each of which matches exactly the values of its PatternType: MatchNarrow is NarrowTo(s, PatternType(P)) and MissNarrow is NarrowFrom(s, PatternType(P)).
    • The wildcard, and a binding with no annotation or one denoting any, each of which matches every value: MatchNarrow is s and MissNarrow is empty.
    • not Q: MatchNarrow is MissNarrow(s, Q) and MissNarrow is MatchNarrow(s, Q).
    • Q or R: MatchNarrow is the union of MatchNarrow(s, Q) and MatchNarrow(s, R), and MissNarrow is MissNarrow(MissNarrow(s, Q), R).
    • Q and R: MatchNarrow is MatchNarrow(MatchNarrow(s, Q), R), and MissNarrow is the union of MissNarrow(s, Q) and MissNarrow(MatchNarrow(s, Q), R).
    • An ObjectMatchPattern or ArrayMatchPattern: MatchNarrow is empty where the structural impossibility rule below holds, and otherwise NarrowTo(s, PatternType(P)) for an object pattern and s for an array pattern; MissNarrow is s with every atom the pattern covers by the structural rules of 24.3.1 removed.
    • Every other form, each of which may miss a value of its PatternType - a regular expression, a range, an extractor, a juxtaposition, an extends pattern, and an interpolation of non-literal type: MatchNarrow is NarrowTo(s, PatternType(P)) and MissNarrow is s. For a range, MatchNarrow is empty where no member of s is of a type ordered with the range's element type, since MatchRange answers false for such a value whatever the interval; a Number and a BigInt are ordered with each other. Where every endpoint the range has is a compile-time constant, MatchNarrow is also empty where the interval holds no value of any member of s, an empty interval holding none (19.6), and MissNarrow is empty where every member of s is an integer type, or a literal type over one, every value of which the interval holds; a floating-point member is never wholly held, since its NaN lies in no interval. Apply these range rules separately to each known union member and canonicalize the union of the surviving results: on success remove a member whose domain cannot intersect the interval, and on failure remove a member whose entire domain is held by the interval. A partially overlapping member retains its existing type unless an existing refinement represents a narrower result. Unknown endpoints, unresolved domains or metadata, and an inexact endpoint representation supply no member-exclusion proof. This filtering introduces no new public Type Record or reflected type identity.

    Either operation applied to empty gives empty, and the union of empty with a type is that type. Where MatchNarrow or MissNarrow is empty the pattern test can never succeed or can never fail, and 1.8.5.4 judges it, under its stability condition, where the test decides a branch.

    For an interpolation pattern, it is a type error if the expression's Static Type and its position type are established to share no values. This judgment is separate from PatternType: a non-literal interpolation may contribute any to narrowing while still having a provably impossible comparison. Interpolation compares the value actually produced, without adopting the position type or performing a conversion. Unknown or overlapping types do not establish failure. The judgment applies at nested pattern positions and after preceding narrowing.

    An array pattern's PatternType of any records the absence of additional indexed-storage information; it is not a test covering every value. Neither matching nor failing the pattern establishes a different indexed-storage type. It is therefore not a pattern that matches every value of its PatternType, and MissNarrow does not remove a subject atom through it: exclusion of an entire atom requires the array-pattern coverage rule of 24.3.1. The same restriction applies to array patterns within combinators and structural sub-patterns.

    Within a pattern, each sub-pattern's position type is the subject's Static Type at that position, computed left to right: the subject narrowed by the preceding operand of an and, a named member's type in the members of a union position the pattern has not eliminated, an array-pattern element's type from the subject's static iteration contribution (1.14.8), an extracted position's type from the matcher's declared return. A binding's Static Type is NarrowTo of its position type and its PatternType. A pattern slot's Static Type is its written domain, or its position's domain where none is written, so const B: NumberBounds binds a NumberBounds and const K in a type position binds a type; a slot is a binding of the clause for every other purpose, immutable, in scope in the guard and the arm, and subject to the duplicate-name and or-consistency errors above. It is a type error if MatchNarrow of a sub-pattern's position type and the sub-pattern is empty under the stability condition of 1.8.5.4, the impossible-test rule applied within a pattern, in every position the pattern occurs in: each alternative of an or is a sub-pattern at the position of the or, so an alternative that can match nothing there is an error although another alternative can match, and a pattern that can match nothing is dead code wherever it is written, as an unreachable operand is. It is a type error if an ObjectMatchPattern or ArrayMatchPattern occurs at a position whose Static Type is known and none of whose members can be an Object, by the first boundary of that condition, or if an ArrayMatchPattern of n elements occurs at a position every member of whose type has a static iteration contribution with a number of positions other than n, since MatchObjectPattern and MatchArrayPattern answer false for a value that is not an Object and MatchArrayPattern for a sequence of another length; this structural impossibility rule applies at the top of a pattern as well as within one; and it is a type error if a numeric literal's position type is a union of two or more numeric types, since the literal has two types it could take, resolved by and with a type or by an interpolation.

    Impossible and irrefutable pattern judgments read a generic parameter through an established upper bound, as 1.8.5.4 requires. This includes range tests and match-clause selection. A verdict must hold for every value of the bound; an unknown bound, partial overlap, uncertain endpoint or unresolved metadata supplies no universal verdict. The projected bound is a proof domain only: surviving bindings, stores and result types retain the parameter's identity.

    The rows this clause adds to Table 24: in the arm of a when P, MatchNarrow(s, P); in the arms after it, MissNarrow(s, P) where the clause is unguarded; and v is P narrows as when P does, in the positions the test governs. For ordinary match, the Static Type is the canonicalized union of its arm types, a throw arm and a diverging block contributing nothing (25) and a block arm contributing CompletionTypeOf of its StatementList (37.2); a contextual type on the match is the contextual type of each arm body.

    For match all, each clause starts with the original subject type and applies only its own pattern and guard; no earlier clause subtracts from a later clause's subject type, and exhaustiveness is not required. Its Static Type is an array Type Record with [[Extent]] dynamic. An array contextual type supplies its element type as the contextual type of each arm body and as [[Element]] of the result: each collected value is admitted at that type, with an unknown contribution checked at run time. Without an array context, [[Element]] is the canonicalized union of the value-producing arm types; an unknown contribution makes [[Element]] any, without losing the known array result. A throw arm or diverging block contributes no element; a block arm contributes CompletionTypeOf of its StatementList. A scalar context supplies no arm context. The number of clauses does not establish an extent. The ordinary array element and reference-escape restrictions apply; contextual construction does not change array subtyping or make [].<any> assignable to an array of a more specific element type.

    24.3.1 Exhaustiveness

    A match whose subject is a Type Object has no atoms, the types being an open universe, so 24.3.1 requires such a match to carry a catch-all. The atoms of a Type Record t are: for an enum, its enumerators; for a sealed class, its direct subclasses and, where instantiable, itself; for boolean, true and false; for null and undefined, themselves; for a union of two or more members each of which is one of the preceding, an object type, a tuple type, or a composite type, the atoms of each member, an object, tuple, or composite member being its own atom; for a lone composite type, itself, so the coverage a union member gets applies to it alone, a composite being frozen with its members; for a dependent record type whose predicate is a discriminating where chain, the atoms of the union that chain denotes (5.3); for an intersection one or more of whose members is a union, the atoms of the union formed by distributing it, one member per choice of one arm from each such union intersected with the remaining members; and none otherwise. A union with a member of literal kind has atoms none: a closed set of literals that wants the check is an enum over its base, the standing decision of 1.11.8, restated rather than reopened.

    An unguarded clause covers an atom a when: for a non-structural pattern P, MissNarrow(the type of a, P) is empty, which for a Type is IsSubtype(the type of a, PatternType(P), « ») and for not Q is MatchNarrow(the type of a, Q) being empty, reading an enumerator atom's type as its enumerator, covered by the constant pattern naming it or a type pattern naming its enum, and reading true, false, null, and undefined atoms as their literal patterns and types; an object or record-composite atom is covered by an object pattern each of whose named members is declared required by the atom and whose sub-patterns each cover the member's declared type; an array pattern covers an atom only where its static iteration contribution guarantees a sequence admitted by the pattern's length test and each sub-pattern covers its contributed position type, the subsumption the impossible-test rule computes run in the other direction. For structural patterns these conditions apply instead of the PatternType test, including within combinators: an and covers an atom only when both operands cover it, and an or when an alternative covers it. A default covers every atom, and a guarded clause covers none.

    A pattern is irrefutable when it matches every value: the wildcard; a MatchBindingPattern with no TypeAnnotation, or one whose annotation denotes any; a parenthesized irrefutable pattern; an and both of whose operands are irrefutable; and an or either of whose alternatives is. A clause is a catch-all when it is a default, or is unguarded with an irrefutable pattern.

    A match is exhaustive when it has a catch-all clause, when the atoms of its subject's Static Type are not none and every atom is covered by some clause, or when the Static Type folded by MissNarrow over its unguarded clauses' patterns is empty, as it is for match (1) { when 1: ... }, whose literal type the literal pattern names. It is a type error for a match whose subject's Static Type is not any not to be exhaustive; an untyped subject is not judged, and the TypeError of 24.1.1 remains its backstop. Neither this rule nor the one that follows applies to the match all form (24.1): no clause of a match all need match, since its value is the List of those that did and an empty List is an answer rather than a missing case; and a later clause there is reached whether or not an earlier one matched, so it is narrowed by nothing the earlier clause failed to establish. A clause of a match all is still a narrowing form, and it is a type error if MatchNarrow of the subject's Static Type and the clause's pattern is empty under the stability condition of 1.8.5.4, since that clause can never contribute to the result; the sub-pattern rules above apply to its pattern as to any other. It is a type error if a clause can match nothing the preceding unguarded clauses have left: where MatchNarrow of the subject's remaining type, the Static Type folded by MissNarrow over the preceding unguarded clauses' patterns, and the clause's pattern is empty, or where every atom the clause covers is covered before it; a default whose preceding clauses cover every atom of a subject with atoms is that error's instance, so a covered match and a defaulted one cannot silently coexist. A default after an unguarded clause that matches every value the subject can hold, as when let x does, is another instance: the remaining type is empty, so the default can match nothing, and a match that already cannot fall through gains nothing from one.

    Note 1

    The last two rows are derived forms, and they are derived for this check alone. A discriminating where chain denotes a union and an intersection over a union distributes into one, but neither changes what the type is: Reflect.typeOf reports the dependent record type and the intersection, CanonicalizeType flattens an intersection without distributing it (1.2.2.8) so identity and interning are untouched, and assignability compares against the type as written. What they change is only that the checker sees the cases the reader sees, which is what the check is for. Distribution is bounded by the type expression, since it multiplies the arm counts of the unions an intersection names, and it needs no new subtyping: IsSubtype already decides an intersection on the left by finding one member within the target, so an arm naming A covers an atom A & C.

    Requiring exhaustiveness of every match is what makes the TypeError of 24.1.1 unreachable from typed code: a match whose subject holds a value of its Static Type has a clause for it, so the throw is left for an untyped subject and for a value that has drifted out of its type, where the boundary check is the backstop as everywhere else (Table 23). The rule pairs with unreachability into one statement a program can be told: exactly one of "this match needs a catch-all" and "this match must not have one" holds of it, since a closed subject covered atom by atom rejects the default it does not need and everything else requires one. Naming the atoms is also what lets an implementation report which pattern is missing rather than only that one is.

     Note 2

    Decoration cannot falsify a coverage claim, which is worth stating because a decorator may replace what it decorates and a reader has no reason to assume the interaction was considered. Three rules of the decorators extension carry it, one per way an atom set could move.

    An atom set is read from a declaration, and no context rewrites one. The enum, enumerator, tuple, record, block, let, and const contexts admit no return replacement at all, so the enumerators a match covers are the ones the declaration lists; a decorator that mutates an enum object at run time changes no declared type and so moves no atom.

    A class replacement is a subclass. The Reflect.Class context does admit a replacement, and the design's singleton returns class extends T, but the declared return type is T and a class type is nominal (Table 1), identified by the declaration that introduced it, so a structurally identical class of another declaration is not a T and only T's own declaration or a subclass satisfies the return. Coverage is IsSubtype over the atom's type, which is closed downward, so an arm naming a class matches an instance of whatever the decorator returned. Where the class decorated is a sealed base rather than one of its cases, a decorator in another module cannot return a subclass at all, since extending it outside its module is what sealed forbids (1.11.9), and one in the same module declares a case the checker reads like any other, so the check is stricter rather than wrong.

    A field replacement is a value, not a type. Reflect.ClassField replaces the field's initial value at type T, and the accessor contexts replace a getter at () => T and a setter at T, so a discriminant declared with a literal type still holds a value of it and a member a pattern reads still has the type it was declared with.

    What is outside the claim is what is outside every claim here: a decorator running arbitrary code may write a value that has drifted out of its type, and the backstop is the one Table 23 already provides, not a property of match.

     Note 3

    The switch exhaustiveness of 1.11.8 and 1.11.9 is the two-atom-kind instance of the coverage half of this rule, and nothing about switch changes; a switch remains able to fall through to no case, which is the difference between a statement that may do nothing and an expression that must produce a value. What patterns add is the members a pattern can provably blanket, which is what makes a discriminated union of object types and the T | null of every tryParse checkable with no default, and what a lone object or tuple type deliberately does not get, its atoms being none absent a qualifying where chain, because a subset pattern is the point of matching on one. Coverage is syntactic over declared types; the checker evaluates no guard and no predicate.

    24.4 The is Operator Takes a Pattern

    The right operand of is (1.4.5) is widened from Type to MatchPattern, of which a Type is one form, so every existing is keeps its parse and its meaning. v is P evaluates PatternMatches(P, the value of v, a fresh Match Cache Record, env) and returns the Boolean, where env is a new declarative Environment Record in which P's BoundNames are created as immutable bindings; the bindings are in scope in exactly the positions the truth of the test governs, the positions 1.8.5 enumerates, each such position evaluating in env. It is a type error to reference one of those bindings anywhere else, and it is a type error for a binding-carrying is to occur where no position is governed by its truth, since the bindings would then exist nowhere.

    Note

    subject is P is the one-arm match, exactly: it matches, binds, and narrows as when P would, which is what makes while (read() is Ok(let chunk)) a loop whose body sees chunk and whose exit is the miss. The dependent-record is of 5.2 is the Type case of this operator, unchanged.

    24.5 %Symbol.customMatcher%

    This extension adds the well-known symbol %Symbol.customMatcher% (Symbol.customMatcher), the method a name and an extractor pattern consult. The typed protocol is a method from a subject to a tuple or null, or to a Boolean for the parenthesis-less membership form; its declared signature is the whole contract, overloads select on the subject's Static Type, and a generic matcher infers its parameters from the subject as any generic call does, which is how an extractor's bindings are typed with nothing annotated (design, patternmatching.md).

    A statically established custom matcher must be callable. Finding the symbol-named property alone does not satisfy the method requirement. It is a type error when the established member type has no callable or unknown alternative; callable intersections and overloads retain their ordinary judgments. No getter or matcher runs during this check.

    25 Divergence

    This clause, like 31, is owed elsewhere and stated here because this is the first clause that computes with it. The design defines divergence in its switch chapter, and 24.3 already reads a match arm's type by it - "a throw arm and a diverging block contributing nothing" - without the notion having been defined.

    A statement diverges when no path of control through it completes normally. The analysis composes statement completions, established immediate call-result contracts and effective awaited-result contracts; it does not execute expressions or infer termination from arbitrary callee bodies:

    • A return, a throw, and a break or continue targeting an enclosing statement diverge.
    • An evaluated call whose established effective selected result is never has no normal successor. Apply callee and argument effects in order and preserve its possible exceptional path for handlers and finalizers.
