A possible returning or unknown signature prevents the proof; a provisional inference seed is not an established contract. A call returning a Promise or generator object returns normally even when a contained value type is never. Compose this absence of normal completion through the enclosing expression's actual evaluation paths.
    • An evaluated await whose established effective fulfillment type is never has no normal resumption. Preserve possible rejection and the paths through handlers and finalizers. An unknown assimilation path, a possible fulfilled alternative, or a provisional inference seed prevents this proof. This rule consumes the awaited result contract without inferring termination from an async body or treating an unawaited Promise as non-returning.
    • A Block diverges when any statement in it diverges.
    • An if statement diverges when it has an else and both branches diverge.
    • A switch statement diverges when it is exhaustive - every enumerator, every direct subclass, or a default - and every clause diverges.
    • while (true) and for (;;) diverge when no break targets them.
    • A do statement diverges when its body does and no break targets it, whatever its condition, since the body runs before the condition is read.
    • A try statement diverges when its finally block diverges; otherwise, when its try block diverges and, where it has one, its catch block diverges too. A try block that diverges says nothing on its own, since the path that threw reaches the handler.
    • A labelled statement diverges when the statement it labels diverges and no break targets the label.

    Two consequences follow, both of which the design states. A switch clause whose body diverges needs no break and is not a fallthrough; and a function whose body diverges satisfies a non-void return type with no trailing return.

    Note

    Apart from an established immediate or awaited never result, the listed syntactic forms bound the judgment: while (cond) does not diverge however plainly cond is true to a reader, because a rule that reasoned about the condition would have to reason about values, and the design's analyses do not. That is why the list names while (true) and for (;;) as forms rather than describing a condition.

    26 The Iteration Types

    It is a type error to consume a value through an iteration protocol when its effective declared entry-hook type proves that every possible selected hook is invalid. This applies to for-of, for await, array spreads, array binding and assignment patterns, and yield*, using each consumer's synchronous or asynchronous protocol. The proof uses the actual well-known Symbol key and the effective member contract, including inherited and specialized members. A known non-object hook value is non-callable; an open object-shaped hook does not prove non-callability merely by lacking a declared call signature.

    A nullish synchronous hook supplies no iterator. For asynchronous selection a nullish async hook instead selects the synchronous fallback, while a present non-callable async hook fails without fallback. Optional and union members are judged over these selection paths. A missing declaration on an open object, an unrelated Symbol, a Symbol index signature alone, or an unknown alternative supplies no proof of failure. The checker does not call a getter or an iterator to answer the judgment. Argument spread's separate named-property protocol is unaffected: an invalid iterator alone does not disqualify an object from named argument spreading. Reference iteration retains its separate index-based rules.

    The negative iteration proof also follows effective callable contracts through the stages reached by the consumer. A known non-object entry-hook result fails iterator acquisition. If a step is requested, a known non-callable next or known non-object step result also proves failure. An empty array binding or assignment pattern acquires the iterator but does not call next; an element, elision or rest requests a step. The result Object need not statically declare value or boolean done: an empty Object can satisfy the base-language step-result requirement.

    For an actual asynchronous iterator, apply the step-result Object judgment to the awaited result of next. Do not await the entry-hook result. For synchronous fallback, apply the Object judgment to the raw synchronous step result; awaiting a yielded value is a later stage and does not await that step result. Unknown returns, open members, or unresolved overload results prevent a closed proof at that stage. Reject only when every possible selected path is known to fail a stage reached on that path. These checks invoke no getter, hook or step and change no iterator-closing or reference-liveness requirement.

    The bounded assimilation judgment of 1.6.2.19 also applies to a real asynchronous iterator's next result, including initial async yield* forwarding, and to its return result only where the closing judgment below proves that close is reached and its failure is not suppressed. During async-from-sync stepping, first require an Object raw synchronous step result, then apply the assimilation judgment to its effective value contract, even when done is true. Do not assimilate the raw iterable, entry-hook result or raw synchronous step. A real async iterator's value is not separately awaited by for await. Combine argument-boundary, assimilation and required Object-result failures within each selected alternative, and reject only when every selected path is disproved. Unknown contracts, viable signatures, non-callable then and intrinsic Promise paths retain their existing treatment. Arbitrary later delegation resume requests are not made unconditional errors by this initial-step proof. No hook runs during checking, and promise scheduling, cleanup precedence and reference liveness are unchanged.

    Iterator closing contributes a separate negative protocol judgment. It is a type error when a consumer is known to reach a closing stage whose effective contract fails on every selected path and whose failure is not suppressed by the incoming completion. A known present non-nullish non-callable return fails the method stage; a callable close with a known non-Object result fails the result stage. A nullish return is a valid no-op. An empty array binding or assignment pattern acquires and closes with normal completion without requesting a step. A definitely-yielding first step followed immediately by break also supplies a bounded closing edge. So does an array binding or assignment pattern with no rest element whose every requested step definitely yields, since it ends with the iterator not done, when each element is a hole or a target whose store cannot throw first: a binding identifier with neither an Initializer nor an annotation, or an assignment to a let binding with no annotation. Possible exhaustion, unresolved control flow, or an incoming throw completion that takes precedence over the closing failure prevents this proof at that edge.

    For IteratorClose, judge the raw result Object; a Promise is an Object and is not awaited. For AsyncIteratorClose on an actual async iterator, judge the awaited result. Unresolved async-from-sync adapter paths remain dynamic. Use effective inherited and specialized contracts, the actual entry-hook Symbol, and the participating-source judgment above; unknown and viable alternatives prevent a closed proof. These checks execute no close method, getter or step. Accepted executions retain all required cleanup side effects, completion precedence, reference decay and liveness checks.

    The negative iteration judgment includes the typed argument boundary of each reached implicit call. Entry hooks, ordinary consumer steps and IteratorClose or AsyncIteratorClose supply an empty argument List. Initial yield* forwarding supplies « undefined »; later forwarding is judged only where its actual argument contract is established. Apply the ordinary parameter-boundary rules, including optional/defaulted parameters, admitted undefined, implicit conversion, reference markers, generic substitution and rest distribution by SequenceAssignment. A possible applicable signature prevents an argument-failure proof; a valid result on a signature whose arguments cannot be supplied does not. Implicit calls may ignore surplus arguments as their runtime parameter boundary does. This rule imposes no canonical declaration shape, does not request a step for an empty pattern, and retains closing reachability and completion precedence. Async/sync adapter arguments are judged only along established forwarding paths. Unknown later resume arguments remain dynamic. Named argument spreading and index-based reference iteration keep their separate protocols.

    This clause is owed to the iteration protocols the core already defines, not to any extension. for-of asks whether [Symbol.iterator] is callable and never asks what a value declared; the design writes Iterator.<T> throughout and this specification has named no such type, so what a helper returns and what a hand-written iterator satisfies have both been undescribable. It precedes 31 because the generator types are stated in terms of it.

    The iteration result type IteratorResult.<T, R> is the union of two object Type Records, one with members value of T and done of the literal type false, the other with value of IteratorCompletionValue(R) and done of the literal type true. It is discriminated by done, so a match over an iteration result binds value at T in one arm and at IteratorCompletionValue(R) in the other (24.3.1), and reading one requires no narrowing rule of its own.

    Note 1

    Structurally, and therefore not by identity: a generator object, an Array, and a hand-written object with the right members all satisfy Iterable.<T>, and none of them was constructed as anything named Iterable. An implementation that also keeps a nominal type of that name — for the carrier a helper chain returns, say — must not let the two share a name, or one annotation means a shape in one place and an identity in another, and which one a program gets depends on the order its resolution happens to consult. That divergence is invisible where a boundary check is elided (1.7.5), because nothing then asks the question at run time.

    The protocols are interface types, satisfied structurally through their structural form (1.4.2.9):

    • Iterator.<T, R, N> declares next, taking an optional argument of N and returning IteratorResult.<T, R>, and optionally return and throw.
    • Iterable.<T> declares [Symbol.iterator], returning Iterator.<T>.
    • IterableIterator.<T, R, N> inherits both and its self-iteration hook returns Iterator.<T, R, N>, preserving all three arguments.
    • AsyncIterator.<T, R, N>, AsyncIterable.<T>, and AsyncIterableIterator.<T, R, N> are the same three with [Symbol.asyncIterator] in place of [Symbol.iterator] and protocol methods returning promises of the iteration result; the self-iteration hook of AsyncIterableIterator preserves all three arguments.

    Iterator is also a built-in class, the one on which the iterator helper methods are defined, and it declares that it implements IterableIterator. AsyncIterator is the same for the asynchronous protocol. Both join the built-in type names of 1.5.27. A value of the class satisfies the interface by refinement rather than by inspection (1.2.3.1), so it is decided by the declaration; a value that merely has the members satisfies it through the structural form.

    A bare argument is the first: Iterator.<uint8> is Iterator.<uint8, void, void>, and likewise for the other five. This is the shorthand 31 states for the generator families, and it is one rule rather than two.

    Note 2

    R and N default to void as they do in the generator families. A generator's body return obligation and its operation results are distinct: conformance to a structural iterator follows 32, including ordinary exhaustion. Equal default spellings do not establish an unconditional same-argument implementation relation.

    There are no per-collection iteration types. TypeScript names ArrayIterator, MapIterator, and SetIterator because it needs somewhere to carry a narrower return type; the shorthand carries it here, so the family stays at six interfaces and two classes. The absence is a decision rather than an omission.

     Note 3

    The element parameter is invariant, as every generic in this specification is (1.2.3.1), so an Iterable.<Circle> is not an Iterable.<Shape> for a Circle that extends Shape. Covariance would be sound for these types and for no container: an iterator produces its element and never accepts one, which is the condition the invariance rule states for a mutable container and which these types do not meet. Admitting a declared variance is the generics extension's to make, and the invariance rule already names C# and Kotlin as the precedent; both spend that feature on exactly these types. It can be admitted later without invalidating a program, since a variance annotation only adds legal conversions, which is how .NET added covariance to its enumerable interfaces after they had shipped invariant.

    27 Fixed String Properties

    Where an operation's receiver is established to be a primitive String and the operation reaches a write to its fixed own length property, it is a type error. Deleting that property is also a type error. The same judgments apply to a character-index property only when its existence is established, using the String's UTF-16 length and the base language's canonical property-key rules. Non-writability and non-configurability are separate reasons for these judgments.

    An unknown receiver, key or reached store does not establish failure. In particular, a logical assignment whose store is skipped is not refused by this rule. The rule does not classify every primitive member, structural lookalike, boxed object or configurable property as immutable; an inherited setter on another member can be callable. No getter is evaluated to establish a descriptor. Accepted code retains the ordinary runtime property operations and reference-liveness checks.

    28 IteratorCompletionValue ( R )

    The abstract operation IteratorCompletionValue takes argument R (a Type Record) and returns a Type Record. This operation separates a discarded completion contract from the value carried by a completed iteration result. It is a built-in type computation, not a new global binding or source operator. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If R.[[Kind]] is void, return the any Type Record.
    2. If R.[[Kind]] is deferred and R.[[Operator]] is iterator-completion, return R.
    3. If R.[[Kind]] is parameter or deferred, return the Type Record { [[Kind]]: deferred, [[Operator]]: iterator-completion, [[Operands]]: « R » }.
    4. Return R.

    Substitution into the deferred operation substitutes its operand and applies IteratorCompletionValue again. The existing identity and reflection rules for deferred Type Records apply. An open operation grants no more precise bound than any. This rule does not change an ordinary property of type void, rewrite the yielded component, or distribute a discard interpretation into other type constructors. An explicit undefined completion remains undefined.

    The next, optional return and optional throw methods share the iteration result type, wrapped in a Promise for async protocols. Their inputs remain separate: next takes optional N, return takes optional R, and throw takes an optional gradual value. Normalizing the completed result does not widen either R or N at an input boundary. The nominal generator type retains its original arguments, and its body's written return obligation is unchanged. In particular this operation does not admit a non-undefined body return at a written void obligation.

    A nominal generator delegation's terminal contribution is GeneratorCompletionValue(R) (32); structural delegation reads the corresponding value component of the selected result shape. Self-iteration of IterableIterator and AsyncIterableIterator preserves T, R and N. Ordinary iterable shorthand retains its default discard contract. Existing async-from-sync assimilation, async return assimilation, ordinary lookup, receiving admission, effects, failed state and reference-liveness rules remain in force. The type computation executes no hook, iterator method or callback and extends no reference lifetime.

    29 Explicit Intrinsic Mapper Specialization

    The intrinsic Range and synchronous Iterator map functions declare one type parameter, U. Applying explicit type arguments uses the ordinary named, positional and fixed-extent spread rules. U has no default for a stored application. Resolve the actual callee by ordinary lookup, and bind its type arguments once before evaluating value arguments. A nongeneric replacement does not inherit intrinsic generic capability from the property name.

    A stored intrinsic mapper specialization is interned by its original function Object and completed output Type Record under SameType. It is independent of the receiver. Equivalent named, positional, alias and spread applications have the same identity; distinct nominal declaration identities and distinct original function Objects remain distinct. A direct member application preserves its already evaluated receiver and selected callee without a second getter invocation. Public name and length properties do not determine the declaration.

    The completed callable signature takes callback: (value: any, index: uint64) => U and returns the helper-bearing synchronous iterator contract with item U, completion undefined and optional any next input. A statically established receiver retains its more precise input contribution under 19.6.7 and 30; specialization does not bind a receiver or replace its item type with U. An internal rename used to avoid capture does not change a declaration's public parameter name: named type argument selection and reflection use its declaration spelling, while substitution retains the distinct binding identity.

    For the selected intrinsic Iterator mapper, capture the completed U in the existing mapping closure. After Call of the mapper completes normally and before Yield of that mapped value, admit the normal result to U by the ordinary value-boundary rules, including their permitted conversions. If admission is abrupt, perform the same IfAbruptCloseIterator step as for an abrupt mapper call. Preserve the existing close precedence, completion state and subsequent-resume behaviour. Do not execute the callback at specialization or helper creation, wrap or alter the callback, or add an iterator facade.

    For U equal to void, retain the callback-result discard interpretation: it supplies no claim that the actual mapped value is undefined. For any, retain the value unchanged. An empty traversal has no mapped value to admit. A Promise or thenable result is an item; this synchronous operation introduces no Await. Admission and suspension retain all existing reference decay and liveness checks.

    An explicit intrinsic Range mapping acquires its ordinary fresh cursor, performs ordinary lookup of that cursor's map, and forwards the completed U as an explicit positional type argument to the selected function, with the original callback and materialized positional argument List. A selected user generic function or overload set uses the ordinary generic selection, constraint, where-clause and invocation rules; a nongeneric replacement fails before its body. Admit the delegated normal result to the helper-bearing U protocol by the existing receiving rules. This boundary neither executes replacement protocol methods to prove their future values nor strengthens a gradual user declaration beyond the existing callable contracts. Plain inferred mapping retains its ordinary forwarding behaviour.

    30 Iterator Helper Callback Contracts

    These contracts apply to the synchronous intrinsic Iterator helpers on a resolved helper-bearing receiver, rather than to an arbitrary user method with the same name. The iteration interfaces alone do not declare these helpers.

    The result domain of a flatMap callback is an Object accepted by GetIteratorFlattenable with reject-primitives. It includes object iterables and direct iterator Objects whose next method is used when @@iterator is nullish; it excludes all primitive results, including Strings. It is a type error when every established callback result alternative fails the reached flattening protocol. A viable or unknown alternative prevents the negative proof. Eligibility is separate from inference of the flattened element type (19.6.10), and does not use Array.prototype.flatMap's scalar-result rule. No callback, getter or iterator method runs during checking.

    Reduction follows 19.6.8, using the established iterator item contribution. One accumulator contract governs the initial value when present, recurrence inputs, callback result and completed reduction. The clause specifies anchoring, genuine uncertainty, explicit any results, empty traversal and ordinary declaration and receiving admission.

    These synchronous contracts do not specify future asynchronous helpers. In particular, they do not add awaits to callback results or change generator suspension, protocol effects or reference liveness.

    31 The Generator Types

    When inferring a generator's completion component, including for a generator do-expression, preserve an established undefined contribution as the undefined value type. The ordinary-function inference rule that collapses wholly valueless results to void does not apply to this protocol component. Written generator annotations and their shorthand defaults are unchanged by this inference rule.

    For structural yield* operands, derive separate yielded and terminal contributions from the selected iterator protocol. Non-completed records contribute to the enclosing yield boundary; completed records contribute to the delegation expression's result. A definitely completed record contributes no yielded value, and a definitely non-completed record contributes no terminal value. Preserve the value types of possible paths, leaving a contribution unknown where method selection, overloads, required properties or result types do not establish it. For a real async iterator, await the step result; the typed async yielded-value boundary separately assimilates an outgoing value as specified below. Async-from-sync adaptation assimilates both yielded and terminal values. A terminal value is checked when used at a typed destination, including a return, and is not itself a yield error when discarded. This does not extend the bounded proof of subsequent resume, throw or return forwarding, or execute a protocol method.

    This clause is owed to the generator forms the core already parses, not to the extension that follows it. 1.10.8 admits a return annotation on a generator and says what it means in prose, that "a generator's annotation types the values the iterator yields", and the design writes Generator.<Y, R, N> throughout; the type itself has not been stated. It is stated here because 37 is the first clause that computes one.

    Generator names the built-in generic whose instances are the objects a generator function returns, and AsyncGenerator the same for an async generator. Generator.<Y, R, N> is the nominal Type Record for the first with those arguments, and AsyncGenerator.<Y, R, N> for the second. Y is the type of the values the generator yields, R the type of the value it returns, and N the type of the value a caller sends to next. Both are generic classes, so each is invariant in its arguments by the rule of 1.2.3.1: a Generator.<uint8, void, void> is a subtype of no other instantiation.

    A generator's return annotation is read as follows, which is the design's shorthand made precise. Where the annotation denotes a Generator instantiation, and an AsyncGenerator instantiation for an async generator, it is the declared type as written. Where it denotes any other type T, the declared type is Generator.<T, void, void>, or AsyncGenerator.<T, void, void>, so that function* f(): int32 declares a generator of int32. It is a type error for the annotation of an async generator to denote a Generator instantiation, or for a synchronous generator's to denote an AsyncGenerator instantiation.

    The Static Type of a call of a generator function is its declared type. Within the body, the Static Type of a YieldExpression without * is N, and it is a type error if the operand's type is not assignable to Y. The Static Type of a yield* is GeneratorCompletionValue(R) for its operand's generator type, since delegation can receive the body return or ordinary exhaustion, and the operand's Y must be assignable to the enclosing Y.

    A YieldExpression in a deciding position is judged by the truthiness of its established normal resumed result, as any other operand under 1.8.5.4. A plain yield reads N, and delegation reads the established terminal result of the selected protocol, not its yielded element type. A constant-answer value query remains permitted. Suspension does not preserve arbitrary pre-yield place relations; possible thrown or external return resumptions, catch handlers and finalizers remain separate completions. Unknown protocol or assimilation results supply no new verdict, and reference-liveness and scheduling requirements are unchanged.

    When the running async generator has a resolved declared, contextual or published return contract that supplies a generator yield type, its yielded-value enforcement first applies Await to an Object value and then requires the resulting value to be of Y. An unresolved return type parameter supplies no such contract. This enforcement also applies to the outgoing value of yield* after a non-completed step. It does not add assimilation to untyped delegation or to a real async for await step's value.

    For a concrete established typed async yielded-value boundary, the bounded first-step proof follows the selected real async iterator, the awaited Object step result and a known false done to the effective value. It is a type error when every selected path fails a reached stage, including a yielded value whose callable then cannot accept the resolving callbacks under 1.6.2.19. A possible completed result, unknown done or value contract, viable overload or intrinsic Promise path prevents this new assimilation proof. Async-from-sync retains its separate value-assimilation rule. No getter or callback runs during checking; accepted programs retain their scheduling and reference-liveness obligations, and arbitrary later delegation requests are outside this bounded proof.

    Note

    A generator satisfies the corresponding Iterable or AsyncIterable element view. Its more precise structural iterator relationships follow its operation signatures, including exhaustion, under 32. The nominal R remains the body return obligation and is not widened in the generator's identity.

    Reading a bare annotation as the yield type rather than as the whole generator type is the design's choice and is the useful one: a generator's return and next types are void in almost every generator anyone writes, and requiring Generator.<int32, void, void> at each of them would make the common case the verbose one. The full form remains available and is what a generator with a meaningful return or a two-way protocol writes.

    That yield* has the delegated generator's GeneratorCompletionValue(R) as its type, while contributing its Y to the enclosing generator's, is the one part of the protocol a reader is likely to get backwards. It follows from the run time: yield* drives the operand to completion and evaluates to its return value.

    32 GeneratorCompletionValue ( R )

    The abstract operation GeneratorCompletionValue takes argument R (a Type Record) and returns a Type Record. A generator operation can observe ordinary exhaustion separately from its body's return. This operation computes its completed-value view without changing the body's obligation or the nominal generator arguments. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let completed be IteratorCompletionValue(R).
    2. Let absent be the Type Record of undefined.
    3. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: « completed, absent » }).

    The read signatures of next, return and throw on Generator.<Y, R, N> each return the union of the result shape with done false and value of Y, and the shape with done true and value of GeneratorCompletionValue(R). The corresponding AsyncGenerator methods return a Promise of that union. All three methods are present; their optional synchronous inputs remain N, R and any respectively. Async next and throw retain those inputs; async return uses the raw input contract in 34. These signatures describe normal results and do not imply that a request fulfills or that return cannot yield during cleanup.

    The self-iteration hook returns the same nominal generator instantiation. Dot access, an established computed String key, optional access, object-pattern member reads and the actual well-known self-iteration Symbol use this read contract. Ordinary lookup and receiver binding remain in force; extraction does not bind the receiver. A shadowed Symbol, unknown key or opaque receiver supplies no intrinsic identity. These read judgments do not make the members readonly or execute a getter.

    Derive structural iterator conformance from these signatures, not an unconditional same-argument implementation claim. An optional R input already admits undefined; the generator's declared structural view may equivalently spell that input as optional _R_ | undefined, retaining the same operation result. This declaration rule does not change general signature identity or nominal invariance. In particular a body with R of string supplies the result view needed by Iterator.<Y, string | undefined, N>, but not the narrower Iterator.<Y, string, N>. Ordinary iterable element views remain available.

    A nominal generator delegation uses GeneratorCompletionValue(R) as its terminal contribution, since the operand may already be exhausted. Structural delegation retains the terminal type of the selected structural result. Async-from-sync retains its existing assimilation stage. A source-local call alone does not establish a more precise lifecycle or immutable intrinsic identity. Open generic operands retain the deferred IteratorCompletionValue computation within the union until substitution and canonicalization resolve it.

    This operation does not widen a written IteratorResult, admit undefined as a body return under a non-void R, itself change external request admission, or rewrite runtime result values. Synchronous request admission is specified separately in 33. Receiving checks, failed-state effects, queue order, cleanup, Promise scheduling and reference-liveness rules remain applicable. A completed result grants no reference permission across suspension.

    33 Synchronous Generator Return Request Admission

    A generator retains its resolved declared, contextual or published protocol at creation, including the captured generic context. For a synchronous intrinsic return request, first perform the ordinary receiver, brand and executing-state validation. Then admit its payload against the retained optional R: undefined, whether omitted or explicitly supplied, passes this input; a non-undefined payload crosses the ordinary RequireType boundary for R. An absent or gradual obligation has its existing behaviour. The void discard interpretation of a completed operation result does not widen this input. Erasing the receiver's static type, borrowing the intrinsic method, or reaching a suspended-start or completed generator does not remove the obligation.

    Admission occurs before this request changes the generator state, resumes a body or performs its cleanup or delegate lookup. A validation failure precedes admission effects. An admission failure propagates without this request's state transition; effects of ordinary admission, including permitted conversions and property access, are not rolled back. Since those effects can re-enter the generator, after successful admission repeat the ordinary validation and read the current state before performing the native state-dependent continuation. Do not resume using the pre-admission state or add a lock that forbids otherwise valid reentrancy.

    The admitted return completion is associated internally with the generator that admitted it. Propagation of that completion, including through normal finally evaluation and suspension, preserves its external provenance. At that generator's final completion, such an unchanged external completion is not checked as a return executed by the body. The ordinary body-return obligation still applies to normal fallthrough and fresh body return completions, including replacements produced by finally. A second admitted external return has its own provenance. A failed request does not overwrite the provenance of an already suspended completion. Equal payload values do not establish provenance, and an association for one generator does not authorize another generator's body return.

    For synchronous delegated yield receiving such an external completion, an absent delegate return method propagates the same completion. When the selected delegate return method produces a completed result, preserve the native lookup, call, Object validation, done read and value read order, then independently admit that replacement value against the enclosing generator's optional R. The resulting external completion belongs to the enclosing generator. Admission is performed even if its payload equals the incoming one; it is not treated as an executed body return. Abrupt lookup, call, result access or admission follows the body's ordinary abrupt path, including catch and finally.

    A non-completed delegate return result retains ordinary yield enforcement and suspension. Subsequent normal resumption follows the native delegation algorithm and can complete the delegation normally; a later return statement is a new body obligation. Neither a permanent closing flag nor payload equality transfers an external permission to that statement. No method, getter or callback is executed to prove a static judgment. Established request-input incompatibility retains the ordinary early error, and gradual paths retain the runtime backstop.

    This clause adds no runtime result wrapper, readonly member, reference authority or extension of a reference lifetime. Ordinary receiving, suspension and reference-liveness checks remain in force. It specifies synchronous request admission only; 34 retains asynchronous return assimilation, queue order and native rejection stages rather than replacing them with this synchronous pre-resumption sequence.

    34 Async Generator Return Request Admission

    An async generator retains its resolved declared, contextual or published protocol at creation, including its captured generic context. Its intrinsic return request admits a resolved payload against that protocol's optional R: omitted and explicit undefined pass; a non-undefined payload crosses the ordinary RequireType boundary for R. The void discard interpretation of completed operation results does not widen this input. An absent or gradual obligation retains its existing behaviour. Erasure, borrowing the intrinsic method or reaching completion does not remove an established obligation.

    The optional raw input in the AsyncGenerator return member's read signature is the canonical union of direct R (the type of undefined for void), Promise.<any, any>, and a structural object with a required callable then member accepting the ordinary resolver and rejector arguments and having a gradual result. For any, the input remains gradual. This is a raw request contract, as for typed Promise resolvers, not a proof of fulfillment with R. Promises and nested thenables retain runtime admission of the eventual resolved value; an incompatible Promise fulfillment can reject the request. Known incompatible direct scalar and plain-object inputs retain ordinary static checking. Unknown objects are not all declared thenable. The read contract follows ordinary member lookup, extraction and structural conformance, without adding immutable intrinsic identity or receiver binding.

    Preserve native receiver and brand validation, enqueue, state transitions and scheduling. Do not await or admit the raw operand before enqueue. In AsyncGeneratorUnwrapYieldResumption, after the native Await fulfills, admit its value against the captured optional R and produce an admitted external return completion for this generator. Await rejection retains its native throw resumption. Admission failure is also a throw resumption at the suspended yield, so the body's ordinary catch and finally processing applies; it may catch the error, yield, return a replacement or reject the current request.

    In AsyncGeneratorAwaitReturn, preserve native PromiseResolve and rejection paths. In the fulfillment reaction, admit the resolved value before AsyncGeneratorCompleteStep. On success, complete the queue-head request with a normal completion containing the admitted payload. On admission failure, complete that request with the throw completion. In either case continue with AsyncGeneratorDrainQueue. An unstarted body is not entered, including on failure. The earlier transition to draining-queue is not rolled back. Admission effects can enqueue additional requests; the current request stays at the head until its completion, and subsequent requests retain their order. No conversion, getter or thenable effect is rolled back.

    Associate each admitted external completion with its owning generator as in 33. Propagation through normal finally evaluation, Await and yield preserves its external provenance; the generator's final completion does not reclassify it as a body return. Fresh body returns, normal fallthrough and abrupt replacements retain their ordinary obligations. Equal payload values do not establish provenance. A failed second async request at a yielding finally follows the reached throw-resumption path and can replace the pending completion; it is not synchronous pre-resumption rejection.

    For async delegated yield receiving an admitted external completion, preserve native lookup and assimilation order. If the delegate has no return method, perform the native additional Await, then admit its actual result against the enclosing optional R and produce an external completion for that generator. Otherwise call the selected return method, await its result object, validate Object, read done and then value in native order. For a done-true result, independently admit that replacement value against the enclosing optional R without adding an Await of the value property. A Promise-valued property is the payload at this boundary, not its eventual fulfillment. Async-from-sync adapters retain their own native assimilation. Abrupt lookup, call, await, result access and admission follow the body's ordinary abrupt path. Done-false results retain ordinary yielding and resumption; a later body return is a fresh obligation.

    These rules add no wrapper, public result property, global type operator or reference authority. Every native suspension retains the existing reference-liveness rules; successful admission cannot extend a lifetime or revive an invalidated reference. General function and callback context transport is governed by its existing rules, not inferred from a mutable caller spelling.

    35 Proven Generator Resume Forwarding

    A bounded static proof may establish a later normal resume forwarded by synchronous yield*. Its initial supported case is a direct source-local generator with no parameters or decorators, whose first statement delegates to a direct source-local generator with no parameters or decorators and an immediate literal yield. The enclosing generator is created in a fresh top-level immutable local and directly resumed twice in source order. The selected iterator and next methods must be established intrinsics, with no unknown call, getter, escape, reflective mutation or other intervening effect that could replace a dependency.

    At that established forwarding boundary, it is a type error if the enclosing generator's declared input type is not assignable to the delegated generator's established input type. This compares one forwarded input contract, not the invariant identity of whole generator types. The initial request is separate from the later forwarded value. A known immediate completion, unknown completion or selected method, open input type or any cannot establish this mismatch.

    An uncalled generator body alone does not establish future intrinsic identity and is not refused by this proof. Replacing the protocol in an earlier script also prevents the proof. No generator, getter or callback is executed while checking. This rule does not extend to arbitrary later requests, asynchronous delegation, or throw and return forwarding. Runtime conversions, cleanup, scheduling and reference-liveness checks at suspension and resumption remain in force.

    36 Typed Resource Management

    A using declaration admits the same type annotations as a const declaration. Its initializer crosses the declared type boundary as an ordinary immutable binding does. The resource is still acquired and disposed by the base language's explicit resource-management semantics: null and undefined register no disposal, and a non-nullish resource requires a callable Symbol.dispose method.

    When an explicit annotation is present, use its declared post-boundary type for the acquisition and disposal-call judgments below, including explicit any or a broad Object type. Otherwise, use the known Static Type of a participating initializer. This use does not infer or install a declared storage type on the resource binding. Resolve each initializer in its lexical environment and declaration order, including earlier bindings in the same declaration. Plain untyped initializers and unknown contracts retain runtime protocol discovery. This extension changes neither cleanup order nor suppressed-error and reference-liveness semantics.

    It is a type error if the resource type used for this judgment proves that resource acquisition cannot succeed. A non-nullish primitive type or void cannot supply a disposal method. For an object or class type, a declared Symbol.dispose member whose type is known to be non-callable proves the same failure. Member lookup includes inherited members with the base's type arguments substituted, and a getter contributes its declared result type without executing the getter. For example, using r: { [Symbol.dispose]: uint8 } = value is a type error.

    It is also a type error when the effective declared synchronous disposal method is callable but every signature rejects the empty argument List supplied by disposal. This judgment uses the ordinary parameter boundary, including default and optional parameters, admitted undefined, reference markers, rest distribution and implicit conversions. A viable or unresolved signature prevents the proof. The normal result of synchronous disposal is ignored. This failure is determined before evaluation, even when the declaration occurs in an unused body.

    This is a check of known impossibility, not a requirement that every annotation explicitly declare a disposal member. An open object type, any, an unknown member or callability, and a dynamically supplied method retain runtime protocol discovery. A union is refused by this judgment only when every alternative proves acquisition or the disposal call impossible; an admitted nullish alternative, a callable method not proved to reject the empty argument List, or an unknown alternative prevents that proof. A known callable member does not by itself justify eliding mutable method lookup, cleanup, or reference-liveness checks.

    Note

    For await using, a corresponding impossibility judgment must consider asynchronous acquisition, including Symbol.asyncDispose and the base language's synchronous-disposal fallback. Absence of an asynchronous member alone does not establish failure.

    37 do Expressions

    A do expression is a block that produces a value: its statements are evaluated and its value is the completion value, the value of the last statement that completed normally. This clause specifies the design's do expressions extension, which integrates the do expressions proposal under this type system and adds the generator forms of that proposal's issue 76.

    PrimaryExpression[Yield, Await] : DoExpression[?Yield, ?Await] DoExpression[Yield, Await] : do Block[?Yield, ?Await, ~Return] do * { GeneratorBody } async [no LineTerminator here] do * { AsyncGeneratorBody }

    The Block of the first form carries the [Return] permission of the function enclosing the do, as a MatchArmBody's does (24.1), so return, break, and continue inside it mean what they mean in the surrounding code; the Return above is notational and the permission is threaded by the enclosing contexts. The [no LineTerminator here] is what keeps async a contextual keyword: async on one line and do * on the next must remain an identifier reference followed by something else, which is the restriction the productions above already carry before function.

    It is a Syntax Error for a DoExpression to appear where a Statement is admitted, since do there begins a do-while. In statement position a program writes a Block, or parenthesizes.

    Note

    do is a reserved word, so this form costs the grammar less than match did (24.1): there is no cover grammar and no program whose meaning changes, only a position where the word was previously a Syntax Error. The do * and async do * forms need no statement-position rule of their own, since * cannot begin a Statement and so cannot be a do-while body; they are refused there with the first form anyway, because a do * evaluated as a statement discards the generator it built, and a reader should not have to know which form the collision applies to.

    37.1 Early Errors

    The following apply to the first form only. A do * has no completion value, its body being a generator body whose completion is discarded, so nothing here restricts it: a do * may end in a loop or a declaration, and the design's own motivating example does end in a loop.

    • It is a Syntax Error if EndsInIterationOrDeclaration of the Block's StatementList is true. That operation is the upstream proposal's and is adopted unchanged: it holds when the completion value of the list can be the completion value of an iteration statement or of a declaration, which reaches through nesting, so a Block whose last statement is an if with an else one of whose branches ends in a loop is a Syntax Error too.
    • It is a Syntax Error if the Block's StatementList ends in an if statement with no else.
    • It is a Syntax Error for a VariableStatement to appear within a DoExpression that occurs in a parameter expression, since the function body its binding would hoist into does not yet exist.
    • It is a Syntax Error for an unlabelled break or continue to appear within a DoExpression in the head of an iteration statement.
    • It is a Syntax Error for a return to appear within a DoExpression in a computed property name in a class body, which is inside no function.
    Note

    Each of the first two is about a completion value a reader would not predict rather than about a shape being hard to evaluate. A declaration's completion is empty, so do { 'before'; let x = 'after'; } would be "before"; an if with no else is its consequent's value or undefined by a condition the reader has to trace; and a loop's is the last iteration's value, or undefined for none. The upstream proposal records that it intends to pursue changing the completion value of declarations in the base language, and this specification's rule follows whatever that settles: the restriction is stated in terms of EndsInIterationOrDeclaration rather than restated, so it moves with it.

    37.2 CompletionTypeOf ( list )

    The abstract operation CompletionTypeOf takes argument list (a StatementList Parse Node) and returns a Type Record. It returns the type of the completion value of list: the union of the types of the statements that can be the last one to complete normally.

    A completion summary records each possible completion's kind, target and value type, distinguishing an empty value from the type undefined and from an unknown type. It is computed structurally, without executing expressions. Sequential composition evaluates a following statement only on normal paths; an empty resulting value inherits the preceding value as UpdateEmpty does. An expression statement supplies its expression's Static Type. A targeted break retains the carried value, and the matching labelled statement converts that break into a normal completion. A break or continue not consumed by a construct remains abrupt.

    Blocks compose their reachable statements in order. Conditional branches are joined, applying the base language's replacement of empty values by undefined. A switch joins possible entry clauses and their reachable fall-through successors, consumes its unlabelled breaks, and includes the no-entry completion only when it is not exhaustive. A try statement includes its block and reachable handler outcomes; a normally completing finally preserves the incoming outcome, while an abrupt finally replaces it. Return and throw outcomes remain abrupt. Unsupported or budget-limited analysis yields an unknown fact, never proof that a path is absent. The separate restrictions on declaration and loop completions of a value-producing do still apply.

    1. Let outcomes be the completion summary of list.
    2. Let members be a new empty List.
    3. For each normal outcome outcome of outcomes, do
      1. If outcome's value type is unknown, return the Type Record for any.
      2. If outcome's value is empty, append the Type Record for undefined to members.
      3. Else, append outcome's value type to members.
    4. Return CanonicalizeType(the Type Record { [[Kind]]: union, [[Members]]: members }).
     Note

    The Static Type of a DoExpression of the first form is CompletionTypeOf(its Block's StatementList). For do { done: { 's'; break done; 1; } }, the string supplies the value; the numeric tail is unreachable. Reachability without the carried value would not suffice to type the expression.

    A do all of whose paths diverge has the empty union, which is never (1.5.18) and is a subtype of every type, so const port: uint16 = do { throw new ConfigError('no port'); }; is accepted. This is the first construct in this specification where ordinary code produces never rather than a type computation producing it, and it is the answer a program wants: the binding is unreachable, so its declared type constrains nothing.

    The switch step is the one place this operation is not the obvious rule, and it is the design's own. An exhaustive switch takes no path where no clause ran, so it contributes no undefined, which is the conclusion 1.2.7 already draws for a switch that maps a value to a type: "because enum and sealed-class exhaustiveness is checked, a switch used to map a value to a type covers every case its argument can take and therefore yields a Type Object rather than undefined". The same expression must not type one way inside a compile-time builder and another inside a do. A switch that is not exhaustive does contribute undefined, which is what makes const u: uint8 = do { switch (s) { case 'a': 1; } }; a type error.

    Exhaustiveness here is the switch's, which this specification reserves to enums and sealed hierarchies (1.5.18 restates the reservation), and it is deliberately narrower than the atoms a match reads (24.3.1). A switch over a boolean covering true and false is therefore not exhaustive for this operation, and a do ending in one has undefined in its type, while the corresponding match is checked complete. The asymmetry is between the two constructs rather than introduced here: match was given a wider analysis when it was added, and widening switch to meet it is that clause's decision to make rather than this one's. A do that wants the narrower answer writes the match.

    An empty do {} is undefined, the value void 0, and not void: void is the absence of a value and is a return type, while do {} produces one.

    37.3 Contextual Typing

    A contextual type on a DoExpression of the first form is the contextual type of every expression that can supply a normal completion value in CompletionTypeOf, including a value carried through a targeted break consumed within the expression. Unreachable lexical tails supply no value. A numeric literal at such a producing position takes the expected type by 1.6.6.

    Read each producing expression in its own lexical scope and incoming flow environment, with that contextual type, before joining the result types. Retain that value type when UpdateEmpty carries the value across an empty completion or a matching label consumes a break. A normally completing finally does not replace the captured value or reinterpret it in the finally block's environment; an abrupt finally replaces the incoming outcome and its value producer. Read switch coverage from the discriminant's environment at that switch, not from the environment after its clauses or after leaving their scopes. A type query exports no additional execution effects; the ordinary flow transfer accounts for the expression's effects and escaping abrupt completions.

    Note

    Without this the form would be typed and not usable: every literal inside a do would need the annotation the surrounding declaration already carries, so const level: uint8 = do { if (verbose) 3; else 0; }; would hold Numbers. It is the same propagation a match gives its arms, reaching the same kind of position, the one that carries the value out.

    Narrowing needs no rule of its own. A test inside a do narrows inside it by 1.8.5, and no fact survives the expression, since which path ran is not visible outside it; what leaves is the type, and the union over the tails is what carries the narrowing outward.

    37.4 do * Generators

    A do * evaluates to a generator object, as a call of a generator function does, and its body is a generator body. The Static Type of do * { GeneratorBody } is Generator.<Y, R, N> (31), and of the async form AsyncGenerator.<Y, R, N>, where the three are found rather than declared, there being no annotation site:

    • Y is CanonicalizeType of the union of the type of each YieldExpression operand in the body that is not a yield*, and of the Y of each yield* operand's generator type.
    • R is CanonicalizeType of the union of the types of the body's return operands, or void where it has none.
    • N is void unless a contextual type supplies it, in which case it is that type's N. A contextual type also supplies Y and R, and it is a type error if what the body yields or returns is not assignable to them.

    A contextual type on a do * is the contextual type of each YieldExpression operand, so a literal yielded takes the expected type as one in a plain do's tail does.

    Computing Y and R from the body makes distinct yielded-result and completion-result queries under 1.6.2.5 and 1.6.2.6, with this DoExpression as their common source owner. Combining their computation in one traversal does not combine their accounting: each recomputed component spends an evaluation unit and remains active until its query returns. Record each completed component answer before constructing or publishing the generator carrier; an unanswered prerequisite records no completed answer. A contextual type can supply the components without those inference queries, but does not waive operand checks or inference required by a nested expression. These requirements apply to both the synchronous and asynchronous forms.

    A do * is a function boundary and a do is not, which is where the two forms part company. this, arguments, and new.target inside a do * are the enclosing function's, as they are in an arrow: the design's motivating example exists to delete a function* () { … }.call(this), and binding this any other way would reintroduce it. But the body is a generator body, so yield belongs to the do * rather than to the enclosing function, return sets the generator's return value rather than returning from the enclosing function, and an unlabelled break or continue cannot leave the body.

    Note

    That return means one thing in do and another in do * is the sharpest edge in this clause and is worth stating rather than deriving. In a do it returns from the enclosing function, which is what the upstream proposal's own getUserId depends on; in a do * it completes the generator. Nothing else in the language turns on a single token that way, and a reader who has just read the first form will assume the second.

    The typed form is what the IIFE it replaces cannot easily give. Promise.all takes an iterable of promises, so Y is checked against what it awaits and a do * yielding the wrong thing is refused at the yield; through function* () { … }.call(this) the same relation holds but is read through a call whose this is supplied separately.

    37.5 Modifications to Existing Clauses

    A match arm's Block (24.1) is a DoExpression's Block of the first form: its value is CompletionTypeOf(its StatementList) and it carries the Early Errors of 37.1. This replaces the rule that clause stated, under which an arm's value was its final statement's only where that statement was an ExpressionStatement and the arm was void otherwise, and it correspondingly replaces the sentence in 24.3 that gave such an arm void.

    Note 1

    No program changes meaning. The arm rule accepted a strict subset of this one - a block ending in an ExpressionStatement has the same value under both - and its own note reserved the difference, recording that it "errors exactly where full completion-value semantics would permit" so that a later general form could only make errors legal. Two things improve. An arm may now end in an if with an else, a try, or a switch, which the arm rule made void and therefore unreadable at the use site. And an arm ending in a declaration or a loop is now a Syntax Error naming what it ended with, where it was a silent void and a complaint at whatever read the match's value.

    An arm's block is the first form and never do *: an arm produces the arm's value, and a do * there would produce a generator.

    The Block family of Table 47 gains DoBlock and DoGeneratorBlock, which are two contexts rather than one because what the block is differs, a block in one case and a generator body in the other, as ForBlock and ForOfBlock are two. They are the first block contexts to admit a return replacement: a DoBlock decorator may return a value of the do expression's type, and a DoGeneratorBlock decorator a Generator.<Y, R, N>, replacing what the expression produced. The exclusion of blocks from replacement was never about their being structural positions but about their having no value to replace, and these two have one.

    Note 2

    With the per-entry rule that family already carries - a block decorator runs on every entry rather than once where the declaration is evaluated - a replacement makes memoization, caching, tracing that substitutes, and stubbing expressible at an expression as small as one wants. The generator context is the more useful of the two, since what a do * decorator receives is an iterator and wrapping one is what a decorator over a sequence is for.

    38 constant Expressions

    A constant expression is a block whose value belongs to its site: it is evaluated at most once for a given ConstantExpression in a given realm, and every later evaluation reaching it answers with the value already produced.

    PrimaryExpression[Yield, Await] : ConstantExpression[?Yield, ?Await] ConstantExpression[Yield, Await] : constant [no LineTerminator here] Block[?Yield, ?Await, ~Return]

    constant is a contextual keyword rather than a reserved word, so an existing program that uses it as an identifier keeps its meaning. The [no LineTerminator here] restriction is what keeps the two apart: without it, constant alone on a line followed by a block would be an ExpressionStatement and a Block under automatic semicolon insertion.

    Note

    This is the rule ECMA-262's GetTemplateObject applies to a tagged template's strings array - it looks the site up in the realm's [[TemplateMap]] and returns the array already built for it - generalized from a frozen List of Strings to the value of a Block. Both answer the same question - what belongs to a position in the source rather than to an evaluation of it - and both answer it by keying on the Parse Node.

    The guarantee is IDENTITY, not speed. Two closures produced by two calls to one factory share the value, and a site inside a loop yields the same value on every iteration, because the key is the site and not any evaluation reaching it. A binding hoisted to enclosing scope cannot do that: it is re-created whenever the declaration containing it is evaluated again.

    A Realm Record has an additional field for this purpose.

    38.1 Static Semantics: Early Errors

    ConstantExpression : constant Block
    • It is a Syntax Error if the Block contains an IdentifierReference that does not resolve to a binding declared within the Block.
    Note

    The Block must be CLOSED: it reads nothing from outside itself. Its value is then a property of the site and of nothing else, which is what makes "evaluated once" unobservable except through identity.

    Without this rule, function f(x) { return constant { x + 1 }; } would answer every call with the first call's argument, and nothing would signal it. The rule is stated over free references rather than over non-determinism because the two differ in both directions: a parameter is not ambient state, and reading Math.max is ambient but cannot observe how many times it ran. Being closed subsumes the non-determinism a replacement decorator is held to (1.2.7), since an ambient name is a free reference too.

    It refuses a Block that calls a helper declared outside it. Admitting a reference to an immutable outer binding would relax the rule soundly and is deliberately not specified here.

    38.2 Runtime Semantics: Evaluation

    ConstantExpression : constant Block
    1. Let realm be the current Realm Record.
    2. For each Record { [[Site]], [[Value]] } entry of realm.[[ConstantMap]], do
      1. If entry.[[Site]] is the same Parse Node as this ConstantExpression, return entry.[[Value]].
    3. Let completion be Completion(Evaluation of Block).
    4. If completion is an abrupt completion, return ? completion.
    5. If completion.[[Value]] is empty, let value be undefined; otherwise let value be completion.[[Value]].
    6. Append the Record { [[Site]]: this ConstantExpression, [[Value]]: value } to realm.[[ConstantMap]].
    7. Return value.
     Note

    Evaluation is LAZY: the Block runs when an evaluation first reaches it, not when the module containing it is evaluated. A branch never taken therefore costs nothing. Because the Block is closed, the choice between lazy and eager is unobservable except in whether it runs at all.

    An abrupt completion is NOT recorded. Nothing was produced, and a stored failure could not be told from a stored value, so a later evaluation reaching the same site evaluates the Block again.

    The value belongs to a realm as well as to a site, so a module evaluated in two realms builds two, and neither is reachable from the other.

    39 Pipeline Operator

    x |> f(%) evaluates its left operand, binds it to the topic, and evaluates its right operand with that binding in scope. This clause specifies the design's pipeline operator extension, which integrates the pipeline operator proposal under this type system.

    PipelineExpression[In, Yield, Await] : ShortCircuitExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] PipelineExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] |> ShortCircuitExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] ConditionalExpression[In, Yield, Await] : ShortCircuitExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] ShortCircuitExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] ? AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] : AssignmentExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] PipelineExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] PipelineExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] ? AssignmentExpression[+In, ?Yield, ?Await] : AssignmentExpression[?In, ?Yield, ?Await] PrimaryExpression[Yield, Await] : IdentifierReference[?Yield, ?Await] TopicReference TopicReference : %

    |> is left-associative, binds looser than ?? and tighter than the conditional operator. The upstream proposal names ShortCircuitExpression as its operand, which assumes the base language's precedence table; this design has placed ranges at that level (19), so a pipeline's operands are ranges and |> binds looser than ... 0..<10 |> sum(%) pipes the range, which is what it reads as; the other order would make it 0..<(10 |> sum(%)), which nothing writing it means. Otherwise the placement is the proposal's: a |> f(%) |> g(%) is (a |> f(%)) |> g(%), and c ? a |> f(%) : b needs no parentheses. The token % is the remainder punctuator, and the two are told apart by position — a TopicReference stands where an operand is expected and the remainder operator between two — which no operator declaration can change, since 1.9 lets a type supply a meaning for the binary form and never a new arity.

    Note

    The upstream proposal records its grammar as incomplete (issue 290) and its topic token as unsettled after the longest bikeshed the committee has run (issue 91). This clause takes %, which is the proposal's current spelling; every rule below is stated in terms of the topic rather than the token, so a different token is an edit to the grammar and to nothing else.

    An expression language with operator overloading has fewer free tokens than one without, which is a fact about this design that the committee's discussion has not had before it. # is a private name, ? is optional chaining and the optional marker of 1.4.4, @ is a decorator in about twenty positions, _ is the pattern wildcard (24.2), and % and ^ are operators a class or a primitive block may declare. The design's own token would be _ and it cannot be: one glyph meaning "anything at all" in a pattern and "this exact value" in a pipeline is a worse collision than the remainder one.

    39.1 Early Errors

    • It is a Syntax Error if a TopicReference is not contained within the right operand of a PipelineExpression. Outside one, % is the remainder punctuator and a % where an operand is expected is the ordinary Syntax Error it is today.
    • It is a Syntax Error if the right operand of a PipelineExpression contains no TopicReference that the operand binds. A step that does not mention the topic discards the value piped into it, which is not a pipeline and is more likely a mistaken tacit call than an intention.
    • It is a Syntax Error if a TopicReference is the target of an assignment, an update expression, or a destructuring pattern. The topic is an immutable binding: a step that reassigns what is being piped leaves the next step an input it cannot predict.
    Note

    The second error is what keeps the tacit form from arriving by accident. x |> f() is refused rather than read as f(x), so a program that means the call writes x |> f(%) and a program that meant something else is told. 39.3 records what a typed language could do about a tacit form and why this specification does not.

    "That the operand binds" excludes a topic belonging to a nested pipeline: in a |> f(b |> g(%)) the only TopicReference is the inner pipeline's, so the outer operand contains none of its own and is a Syntax Error. It is written a |> f(%, b |> g(%)) or not at all.

    39.2 Runtime Semantics

    Evaluation of PipelineExpression : PipelineExpression |> ShortCircuitExpression:

    1. Let ref be ? Evaluation of PipelineExpression.
    2. Let value be ? GetValue(ref).
    3. Let oldEnv be the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment.
    4. Let topicEnv be NewDeclarativeEnvironment(oldEnv).
    5. Perform ! topicEnv.CreateImmutableBinding(the topic, true).
    6. Perform ! topicEnv.InitializeBinding(the topic, value).
    7. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to topicEnv.
    8. Let result be Completion(Evaluation of ShortCircuitExpression).
    9. Set the running execution context's LexicalEnvironment to oldEnv.
    10. Return ? result.

    Evaluation of TopicReference : % returns the value bound in the nearest enclosing topic environment.

    Note

    The left operand is evaluated once however many times the topic appears, which is the difference between a binding and a substitution and is what expensive() |> [%, %] rests on. An immutable binding in its own environment also gives the shadowing rule for free: a nested pipeline creates a second topic environment, so its steps see its own value and the outer one is unreachable from within it.

    39.3 Static Semantics

    The Static Type of the topic is the Static Type of the PipelineExpression that binds it, and the Static Type of a PipelineExpression is the Static Type of its right operand evaluated with that binding. The topic is a binding for every purpose of this specification: it is narrowed by the tests that govern it, it is shadowed by an inner pipeline's, and it is immutable, which the early errors above enforce syntactically rather than through the assignability rules.

    A tested pipeline propagates its body's result environments and, where proved, the topic's captured input-place identity by 1.8.5.1. The input is still evaluated once. A write to that place or a prefix, or another invalidating effect, prevents publishing a fact about its new value from the old topic.

    A contextual type (1.6.5) on a PipelineExpression is the contextual type of its right operand, so a numeric literal in a step takes the expected type by 1.6.6 rather than defaulting. Without this the form would be typed and unusable, which is the failure 37 had to avoid in the same way.

    It is a type error for a TopicReference to be the operand of ref (2). A reference parameter binds the caller's location; the topic holds the value the left operand produced, so o.a |> f(ref %) would bind a reference to a temporary and a write through it would reach nothing the caller can observe. It is refused rather than admitted and useless, because the expression reads as though the pipe were transparent to the place it came from.

    Three consequences follow from the topic being an ordinary binding and are stated because a pipeline reads like a substitution. Overload resolution (1.10.3.1) selects on the topic's type as on any argument. Generic parameters are inferred through it, and may be supplied explicitly as x |> f.<uint8>(%). And the topic is admitted wherever an expression is, including a spread and the argument positions a rest parameter distributes (1.10.4.4).

    A PipelineExpression whose right operand diverges has the type of the empty union (25, 1.5.18). A PipelineExpression is compile-time evaluable exactly when both operands are: it introduces a binding and substitutes, reading nothing the surrounding code could not, so it is admitted in a type builder on the same terms as any other expression.

    Note

    The tacit form the proposal calls F# style — x |> f, calling f with the value and no topic — is refused by the second early error, and the reason is worth recording precisely, because it is not the reason usually given. That reason is that a language cannot see what a function expects, so a two-parameter function piped one argument fails somewhere else. It does not hold here: a function has a Signature Record with Parameter Records (1.10.1), so a tacit call could be checked, the topic tested against the first parameter and an under-supplied signature rejected at the pipe.

    What survives is narrower and is enough. A tacit form cannot express the steps that are not calls — % + 1, [%, %], await % — and await is not a function, so no signature rescues it. A pipeline whose steps are sometimes tacit and sometimes not would be two forms sharing an operator, and the second early error is what keeps them from being confused.

    39.4 Modifications to Existing Clauses

    Table 24 gains a row: a test governing a TopicReference narrows it in the positions the test governs, by the same rows the table gives is, typeof, instanceof, in, and a discriminant. shape |> (% is Circle ? %.radius : 0) is the case, and it is the rule a pipeline cannot do without — a substitution has no identity to narrow, which is a second reason the topic is a binding.

    1.9 gains a sentence: |> may not be declared as an operator. Resolution reads the left operand's type and searches it for a signature, and a pipeline has no operation for a signature to describe — it binds one operand and evaluates the other rather than computing a value from both. The same reasoning excludes any future operator that binds rather than computes.

    40 Types Across Agents

    The threading extension gives a program more than one executing thread over one heap. There is no copying step between them: a value is shared by being referenced, and no structured clone, no message, and no byte buffer stands in between. The threads of such a program are agents of one agent cluster that share a heap rather than only a block of memory, and the intern table of 1.2.2.9 is a property of that heap, as the Composite Registry is (23.3). They therefore share both. A type constructed on one thread is the same Type Object on every other, === answers on any thread what it answers on the thread that built it, and nothing about interning, canonicalization, or the total order is per-thread. This is what that clause's note defers to, and the answer is that the extension does not carry a Type Object across a boundary; it removes the boundary.

    An agent that does not share a heap is the other case, and a Type Object does not reach it. A value that crosses to one crosses as data, and the receiving agent types that data by its own declarations and interns the result in its own table. Two structurally identical declarations in two such agents are two Type Objects and are not ===, which is correct rather than a defect: identity is what interning within one heap establishes, and there is no third table above them in which to establish more. A program that needs the same type on both sides declares it on both sides, and every structural rule of this specification then agrees about it, because structure is what those rules read.

    Two consequences follow for the types whose identity rests on something an agent holds. A symbol literal type (1.5.19) over a registered Symbol has a counterpart in another agent, because the registry is shared and the key is what identifies it; over an unregistered Symbol it has none, and the type does not travel, because the Symbol does not. The canonical order of symbol values is by first interning within an agent (1.8.5.2), which is a per-heap fact for the same reason the table is, and two agents may order the same two symbols differently without either being wrong.

    A value type is copied by assignment (1.11.2), and that copy is not atomic. A value wider than a single primitive, or an update spanning several fields, may be observed torn or half-applied by a thread that races it. Atomicity is obtained only through Atomics operations, whose compareExchange compares with SameValueZero so that a loop cycling through NaN terminates; there is no rule making some assignments atomic and others not, because leaving that set undefined would make a racing program unspecifiable and would tax every shared write. The shared modifier marks the state a program expects to cross threads, which is what lets the boundary be reasoned about statically rather than discovered.

    Note

    The proposal makes no claim to prove races away. A race here is a stale value and never a corrupted heap, which is the position Java and Go take rather than Rust's; what the types offer in place of a proof is the discipline that shared marks what crosses and that mutable shared state is reached through an atomic or a lock. Retrofitting a Send/Sync proof onto a shared mutable heap without a borrow checker would make this a different language, and the memory safety the core guarantees is unconditional either way.

    That tearing is possible is worth stating next to the value type rules rather than only here, since it is the one place the core's "a value type copies" meets a second thread. It is also why the layout extension's guarantees are the ones a concurrent program leans on: a shared SoA.<T> allocates each field its own column, so two threads writing two fields of one element never contend for a cache line, which no interleaved layout can promise.

    41 Threading

    The clause before this one settles what a shared heap means for the identity of a type. This one specifies the surface that puts a second thread on that heap: how a thread is created and when it ends, where a promise reaction runs when the thread that settles a promise is not the thread that attached to it, what the shared modifier claims about storage and about what a checker may assume of it, the Atomics operations over typed values, the Lock, Condition, and ThreadLocal objects, and parallel iteration over a range.

    The whole of it rests on one decision the core has already made elsewhere and this clause only carries through: memory safety is unconditional and race freedom is not. A program that races produces a stale or surprising value, never a corrupted heap and never a value that is not of its declared type. Everything here that constrains an implementation constrains it in service of that line, and everything here that constrains a program is a discipline the program may keep or break without the engine's guarantees depending on which it does.

    Note

    The clauses that follow are ordered as they depend on each other. 41.1 and 41.2 establish what a thread is and where a job runs, which 41.3 then uses. 41.4 gives shared its meaning in the type system and its placement, which 41.5 turns into the events the memory model of the pinned edition already reasons over, and only then can 41.6 say what an atomic operation on a typed value is. 41.7 and 41.8 are built from those. Cancellation is not a clause of its own: it is an AbortSignal observed at points the operations that can observe it each name.

    41.1 Threads and the Agent Cluster

    A thread is an agent. The threads of one program are the agents of one agent cluster, and what distinguishes that cluster from the one an ECMAScript program has today is that its agents share a heap rather than only a block of memory: one realm, one global object, one already-executed module graph, one intern table, one Composite Registry (40). Nothing is copied between them, so no rule of this specification describes a value crossing from one to another. There is nowhere to cross to.
