    Each thread holds what an agent already holds, per-thread: an execution context stack, the microtask queue its jobs are drained from, and its Agent Record fields, of which [[CanBlock]] is the one this extension consults (41.7). Each thread drains its own queue, and a job of one thread's queue never runs on another. The main thread is the agent that evaluated the program; it is a thread like the others in everything this clause says, and hosts commonly give it [[CanBlock]] false.

    A thread runs to completion and then ends. CreateThread (41.3.3) gives the steps; the shape is that the function is called, a thenable result is adopted, the thread's own microtask queue is drained, the settlement is posted, and the agent is removed from the cluster. The drain comes before the post, so everything the thread did, its trailing microtasks included, happens-before the thread that awaits the result observes it.

    Whether a thread may receive host-defined work — a timer, an I/O completion, a host job of any kind — and what becomes of such work still pending when the thread's function has settled, is host-defined. A host that keeps a thread alive to run it does not thereby change what the thread's handle means: the handle settles when the function does, which is the rule the thread's caller was given.

    Note

    A thread costs a native stack and the per-thread allocator state an agent needs, and not another evaluation of the program: the module graph is already executed and is shared, so nothing about starting a thread re-runs it. That is what makes a thread per request or per connection a reasonable structure rather than one to be pooled around, and it is the concrete difference from an agent that does not share a heap, which must be given its own copy of everything before it can run a line.

    41.2 Job Scheduling Across Threads

    A promise is an ordinary object of the shared heap, so any thread that holds one may settle it and any thread may attach to it. Where the reaction runs is a separate question, and this clause answers it: a promise reaction runs on the thread that created it.

    A PromiseReaction Record gains an [[Agent]] field, set to the surrounding agent when the record is created. PerformPromiseThen creates the reactions it appends to a pending promise's lists, and the Await machinery creates the reaction that resumes a suspended execution context, so in both cases [[Agent]] is the agent that attached. NewPromiseReactionJob returns its job paired with [[Agent]] rather than with the settling agent, and HostEnqueuePromiseJob enqueues a job on the microtask queue of the agent it is paired with. Attaching a handler to a promise that has already settled enqueues on the attaching agent, which is the agent running PerformPromiseThen at that moment, so that path needs no rule of its own.

    Settling a promise from another thread therefore posts to the reaction's home queue. The post carries a happens-before edge: every operation the settling thread performed before the settle happens-before every step of the reaction. This is the ordinary release-acquire pairing the memory model already gives a synchronizing operation (41.5), and it is what makes a value written before resolve visible to the code that awaits it.

    The handle returned by callThread is not an exception to this rule. It settles on the thread that created it, which is the thread that called callThread, because that is where its reactions were attached — the same reason every other promise behaves the way it does.

    Note

    The alternative rule — run a reaction on whichever thread settled the promise, saving the post — does not survive await. An await resumption IS a promise reaction, so under that rule the continuation of an async function runs wherever the awaited promise happened to settle. await lock.asyncHold() would resume the waiter on the thread that released the lock, stacking every waiter's critical section onto the releasing thread; a main-thread function awaiting anything another thread can settle would silently continue off the main thread, which is fatal to a thread-affine host API and invisible at the await that caused it; a ThreadLocal read would not survive an await; and placement would become a race, since a handler attached before a settle would run on one thread and the same handler attached after it on another.

    It would also separate await from .then, which this language specifies in terms of each other. A threading model in which rewriting one into the other changes which thread runs the body is one a programmer cannot hold in mind. The cost of the rule chosen here is a cross-thread enqueue, and settle-side execution is never needed, since the settling thread may always do the work before it settles. Recovering it where a program wants it is a matter for an explicit opt-in, not for the default.

    41.2.1 Weak References Across Threads

    A target is live while it is reachable from any thread of the cluster. Reachability is a property of the heap, and the heap is one, so no thread's stack is privileged in deciding it and a target held only by a thread other than the registering one is not collectable.

    A cleanup callback registered with a FinalizationRegistry is called on the thread that registered it, whichever thread's collection observed the target become unreachable. This is the rule of 41.2 applied to a callback rather than to a reaction: the work runs where it was attached. What may be held weakly at all is unchanged — an instance of a typed class may not be (1.12.8).

    41.3 Function.prototype.callThread

    callThread calls a function on a new thread and returns a promise for its result.

    41.3.1 Function.prototype.callThread ( ...args )

    This method performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let func be the this value.
    2. If IsCallable(func) is false, throw a TypeError exception.
    3. Let options and callArgs be the result of ClassifyThreadArguments(func, args).
    4. Let signal be undefined.
    5. If options is not empty, then
      1. Set signal to ? Get(options, "signal").
      2. If signal is not undefined and signal is not an AbortSignal, throw a TypeError exception.
    6. Return CreateThread(func, callArgs, signal).

    The declared type of this method is (options?: { signal?: AbortSignal }, ...args) => Promise.<Return, any>, where Return is the declared return type of the function it is called on. The rejection type is any because a function may throw anything.

    41.3.2 ClassifyThreadArguments ( func, args )

    The abstract operation ClassifyThreadArguments takes arguments func (a function object) and args (a List of ECMAScript language values) and returns a pair of an Object or empty and a List of ECMAScript language values. It decides whether the first element of args is the options bag or the first forwarded argument. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If args is empty, return the pair (empty, args).
    2. Let first be args[0].
    3. If first is not an ordinary Object, return the pair (empty, args).
    4. For each signature sig of the declared type of func, do
      1. Let p be the type of the first parameter of sig, or unresolvable if sig has no parameters or that type is not resolvable at this point.
      2. If p is not unresolvable and ! IsOfType(first, p) is true, return the pair (empty, args).
    5. If first has no own property keys, return the pair (first, the List of the elements of args from index 1).
    6. If first has an own property "signal" whose value is an AbortSignal, return the pair (first, the List of the elements of args from index 1).
    7. Return the pair (empty, args).

    The bag is recognized by the brand of the value it carries and not by the shape of the object carrying it, because a brand is the stronger evidence: an ordinary object whose signal is an actual AbortSignal is an options bag in every program that is not deliberately constructed to look like one. An empty object is admitted so that a bag may be passed explicitly with nothing in it.

    The declared signature overrides the brand, which is the step no untyped resolution can perform. A function that declares a first parameter admitting the object receives it as an argument, whatever it carries, so a program that wants to forward a signal-carrying object as data annotates the parameter and is answered exactly. Argument count plays no part: rest parameters and overloads make a declared length useless for this.

    Admission is membership and not assignability. The operation holds a value rather than a type, so IsOfType is what it can ask, and asking it means an object is admitted by a parameter type it actually satisfies rather than by one it could be converted to. Any signature suffices, not only a sole one: an overloaded callee that can receive the object in at least one of its shapes is a callee the program meant to hand it to, and choosing among the shapes is the ordinary work of overload resolution at the call rather than of this operation.

    A parameter type that is not resolvable at this point — the unbound type parameter of a generic function, which names a type the call has not yet bound — does not admit. Both answers are defensible and neither is more correct, but refusing keeps the bag reachable on a generic function, and a program that wants the other reading has the concrete annotation available to say so.

    Note

    One case is left over, and it is the intersection of three opt-outs: an untyped variadic function whose one intended argument is an object carrying a real AbortSignal under the key signal sees it taken as the bag. Annotating the parameter resolves it, and so does wrapping the value.

    This operation counts own property keys, while callThread reads the option with Get, which walks the prototype chain. The asymmetry is deliberate and is what makes callThread's validation step reachable: an object with no own keys is an explicit empty bag, so one created with an inherited signal is classified as a bag and the inherited value is then read. An inherited AbortSignal is used, and an inherited value that is not one throws rather than being silently ignored. Were both steps to consult only own properties, no object could reach that step with a bad signal and the check would be unreachable.

    41.3.3 CreateThread ( func, args, signal )

    The abstract operation CreateThread takes arguments func (a function object), args (a List of ECMAScript language values), and signal (an AbortSignal or undefined) and returns a Promise. It creates an agent of the surrounding agent's cluster, calls func on it, and returns a promise for the result. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. Let capability be ! NewPromiseCapability(%Promise%).
    2. If signal is not undefined and signal is aborted, then
      1. Perform ! Call(capability.[[Reject]], undefined, « the abort reason of signal »).
      2. Return capability.[[Promise]].
    3. Let thread be a new agent of the surrounding agent's agent cluster, sharing its heap and its realm. The [[CanBlock]] field of thread is host-defined.
    4. Let finish be a new Abstract Closure with parameters (completion) that captures capability, thread, and the surrounding agent and performs the following steps when called:
      1. If completion is a normal completion, perform ! Call(capability.[[Resolve]], undefined, « completion.[[Value]] »).
      2. Else, perform ! Call(capability.[[Reject]], undefined, « completion.[[Value]] »).
      3. Remove thread from the agent cluster.
    5. Enqueue on the microtask queue of thread a job that performs the following steps:
      1. Let result be Completion(Call(func, undefined, args)).
      2. If result is a normal completion and result.[[Value]] is an Object with a callable "then" property, then
        1. Let inner be ! PromiseResolve(%Promise%, result.[[Value]]).
        2. Perform PerformPromiseThen(inner, a function that calls finish with a normal completion of its argument, a function that calls finish with a throw completion of its argument).
        3. Return unused.
      3. Perform finish(result).
    6. Return capability.[[Promise]].

    The capability is created on the calling thread, so its reactions are that thread's reactions and the handle settles there (41.2).

    Adopting a thenable is a suspension of the thread and not a step it runs through. An async function returns a pending promise the moment it reaches its first await, so a thread that settled its handle with the returned value and ended would end while its function was still suspended: the body past the await would never run and the handle would resolve with a promise rather than with a result. The reactions on inner are created on thread, so they are thread's reactions and run on it, and thread is therefore alive and running its own continuation until the adoption completes. That is the whole of what "the thread ends when the completion settles" means.

    There is no separate step draining the thread's microtask queue. The settlement is delivered by a job on the spawning agent's queue, enqueued when finish runs, and by then every job the thread queued before it has already run — the drain is a consequence of the queue rather than an operation performed on it. What the clause promises, that everything the thread did happens-before the spawner observes its result, holds for that reason.

    41.3.4 Cancellation

    The signal option is an AbortSignal, the mechanism the platform already has. A signal already aborted when callThread is called rejects the handle with the signal's abort reason and starts no thread.

    Otherwise the thread observes the abort at a cancellation checkpoint, and the checkpoints are the points at which it is between things or waiting for one: when it takes a job from its microtask queue, at the resumption of an await, and in a wait — Atomics.wait and Atomics.waitAsync (41.6), and the Lock and Condition waits (41.7). A wait that is already parked when the abort happens is woken by it. A wait that could only be observed on entry would leave a parked thread uncancellable, which is most of what cancellation is for.

    Observing it throws the signal's abort reason from whatever operation was pending. That is an ordinary abrupt completion and unwinds ordinarily: finally blocks run, using declarations dispose, a lock held through hold is released, and a reason that reaches the top of the thread's function rejects the handle.

    Those two sentences have an order, and it decides what a host may throw away. A thread parked on a wait is not idle: the abort is delivered through the wait, which completes abruptly with the reason. A thread that has been delivered an abort is not idle either: it is unwinding, and its remaining jobs are the finally blocks and catch clauses of that unwinding. So an abort abandons a thread's queued work only where the thread has nothing pending to deliver it through and has not already been delivered it — a thread that has not yet begun, or one between jobs. Abandoning the work of a thread that is unwinding would discard exactly the steps the paragraph above promises will run.

    There is no checkpoint at a loop back-edge. A computation with no suspension point is cancelled cooperatively, by reading the signal's aborted state, which crosses threads because the signal is an object of the shared heap and because an abort on one thread and the read that observes it on another are ordered by 41.5.

    Note

    Cancellation interrupts; it does not destroy. A thread torn down where it stands would leave broken exactly the invariants a lock was protecting, which is why Thread.stop and Thread.Abort were both removed from the languages that had them, and why the surviving design everywhere is an exception thrown at a point the thread can be caught at.

    41.4 The shared Modifier

    shared before a type produces the Type Record { [[Kind]]: shared, [[Target]]: the Type Record of its operand }. The grammar that admits it is PrimaryType : shared PrimaryType, given with the array and tuple types (1.4.2.7).

    It is a type error if the operand is not a value type (1.5.1): the sized numerics, the vector types, a value type class, a fixed-length array of a value type, and the SoA.<T> of the structure-of-arrays extension are what the modifier admits. It is a type error if the operand is itself shared, and a type error if it is reference, since ref denotes a location rather than a value and a location is already reached from wherever the thread that holds it can reach.

    An open operand retains this formation obligation. Substitution that establishes a closed operand discharges the same value-type, non-reference and non-nested-shared requirements, including through aliases and nested type positions. A resolved violation is a type error even in an unused signature. An unresolved generic operand or class layout retains the existing deferral; formation does not imply atomicity or reference liveness.

    An object needs no modifier and is not given one. There is one heap, so a thread that can reach a reference reaches the object it denotes; shared would claim nothing of an object type that is not already true of every object type, and would falsely suggest that a marked collection is a concurrent one when what the design offers is the ordinary collection under a Lock. A composite (23) is refused for a stronger reason: it is frozen, so the question the modifier answers does not arise for it.

    A shared type is invariant in its [[Target]], as a reference is, and for the same reason: the storage it describes is read and written, so a mismatch in either direction is unsound. Between a shared type and a type that is not one, the modifier is instead transparent, because it is not observable in the value. IsSubtype (1.2.3.1) reads, before its comparison of kinds: if s.[[Kind]] is shared and t.[[Kind]] is not shared, return IsSubtype(s.[[Target]], t, assumptions); if t.[[Kind]] is shared and s.[[Kind]] is not shared, return IsSubtype(s, t.[[Target]], assumptions). A value of type T is therefore assignable to storage of type shared T, which is how a value is published, and a read of that storage yields a value of T.

    The unwrapping is one-sided on purpose. Two shared types meet under the invariant rule, and SameType holds of shared T and T for no T, which is what keeps the distinction load-bearing exactly where it has to be: a writable member is invariant (1.11.1.3), so { x: shared uint32 } is not viewable as { x: uint32 }, and the regime a slot is under (41.4.2) cannot be laundered by aliasing the slot through an object type that drops the marker.

    RequireType (1.7.3.1) enforces a shared type by enforcing its [[Target]]: publishing a value into shared storage applies the same check and the same conversion as storing it in unmarked storage of that type. The conversion is the part that matters. A boundary that tested membership without it would refuse let a: shared uint32 = 5 while accepting let a: uint32 = 5, since a Number is not a member of uint32 but converts to one, and no rule of this clause asks for those two to differ.

    41.4.1 Placement

    Storage of a shared type is backed by a Shared Data Block, laid out at the offsets Table 58 gives its [[Target]]. The modifier decides placement and nothing about layout: shared T and T have the same size, alignment, and field offsets, so a value moves between marked and unmarked storage by copying and no representation changes.

    A shared SoA.<T> allocates each of its columns its own region. Two threads writing two different fields of one element therefore write two different regions, and no false sharing arises between them, which an interleaved layout cannot promise at any alignment.

    Note

    Unmarked storage of a value type is not thereby unreachable from another thread, and this clause does not make it so. A binding a function closes over is reached by whatever thread runs that function. What the modifier buys is that the storage is shared-capable from the start: an implementation that discovers a second thread touching unmarked storage may place it in a Shared Data Block at that point, at a cost the marked case does not pay. That is an implementation's affair, and no operation of this specification consults the modifier to decide whether it is permitted (41.6).

    41.4.2 Stability and Narrowing

    Narrowing a binding or a field (1.8.5) records at one program point a type narrower than the declared one and carries it to a later point. Carrying it assumes the storage did not change in between. The two regimes of this clause are the two answers to whether that assumption may be made.

    For storage that is not shared, it may. A narrowing established before an operation that no thread of this agent can have changed the storage through survives that operation, and a check the narrowing makes redundant is elidable exactly as 1.7.5 allows in a program with one thread. If another thread writes the storage anyway, the narrowing may be stale, and a stale narrowing is a branch taken on old information: the value read is still of the storage's declared type, because a write from any thread passes the same boundary check every write passes (1.7.6), so what the program loses is the refinement and never the declared type.

    For storage that is shared, it may not. The slot carries no narrowing across any operation: each read of it yields its declared type, and a program that wants a narrowing reads once into a local binding, which is unmarked storage, and narrows that. A program with no reachable second thread is unaffected in either regime, since a narrowing is only lost where another thread could have written.

    Note

    Declared types hold in both regimes, so every elision 1.7.5 justifies at a declared type is justified here unchanged, and that clause needs no threading caveat. What differs is only how long a narrowing lives, which is a claim about refinement and not about type.

    This is the position a C or C++ compiler takes on non-atomic storage, transplanted into a language where the failure it permits is bounded. There, a compiler that assumes no concurrent mutation and is wrong may produce anything at all. Here the memory safety the core guarantees is unconditional, so the same assumption, when wrong, costs a value that is out of date and nothing else. That bound is what makes the assumption affordable, and it is why the modifier can be a claim the program makes rather than one the implementation must verify.

    41.5 Shared Typed Memory

    This clause adds no memory model. The one the pinned edition defines already says what a racing program may observe, in terms of a candidate execution over a set of events and the agent-order, reads-from, and synchronizes-with relations among them. What was missing was only that its events were reachable exclusively through a TypedArray over a SharedArrayBuffer. Typed storage has byte addresses too (9), so this clause names the events that typed accesses are, and everything that clause proves then applies to them unchanged.

    Let a shared typed slot be storage of a shared type, which 41.4.1 places in a Shared Data Block at a known offset for a known number of bytes. Then:

    • A read of a shared typed slot is a ReadSharedMemory event whose [[Order]] is unordered, whose [[Block]] is that Shared Data Block, whose [[ByteIndex]] is the slot's offset, and whose [[ElementSize]] is the laid-out size of the slot's type.
    • A write of a shared typed slot is a WriteSharedMemory event with the same fields and [[Order]] unordered.
    • An Atomics operation on a shared typed slot (41.6) is the corresponding event with [[Order]] seq-cst, a read-modify-write being a ReadModifyWriteSharedMemory event as it is over a TypedArray.

    A slot whose type is one of the sized numerics or boolean has [[NoTear]] true: a read of it reads the bytes of a single write and never a mixture of two. A slot whose type is an aggregate — a value type class, a fixed-length array, a vector — has no such guarantee, and a read of it concurrent with a write may compose bytes of both. This is what 40 states in prose and this clause states as events.

    Note

    Tearing is bounded in a way it is not in an unmanaged language. A torn read of an aggregate composes bytes that were each written by some thread through the typed-storage boundary (1.7.6), so every field of the result holds a value of that field's declared type. What the program loses is the relation between the fields — a point whose x is from one write and whose y is from another — and never the type of either. A program that needs the whole aggregate at once either takes a Lock (41.7) or builds the value, freezes it, and publishes it by a single reference store, which is the composite idiom (23) and is tear-free because a reference is one slot.

    Accesses to storage that is not shared are not events of this model, and a program with no shared storage and no Atomics has the memory model of the pinned edition unchanged. Where such storage is nonetheless reached by two threads, an implementation that has placed it in a Shared Data Block gives its accesses the same event vocabulary; where it has not, the accesses are not shared-memory accesses and the checker's assumption of thread stability (41.4.2) is what governs. Either way the outcome is bounded the same way: a stale value of the declared type, never an unsafe one.

    Two threads are ordered by the relations of the memory model and by nothing this extension adds. Settling a promise whose reaction belongs to another thread synchronizes-with the running of that reaction (41.2), and the release of a Lock synchronizes-with the acquisition that follows it (41.7); those are the edges an ordinary program is built from, and each is an ordinary seq-cst pairing rather than a new kind of ordering.

    41.6 Atomics on Typed Values

    The Atomics operations of the pinned edition take a TypedArray and an index. This clause admits two further targets: a typed binding reached through a reference, and a typed own data property of an object. A program that has a uint32 may operate on it atomically without first arranging for it to live inside a byte buffer.

    41.6.1 Reference Arguments

    An Atomics operation whose first argument position is written ref binding receives a Reference Record rather than the value of the binding, as a call to any function declaring a ref parameter does (2).

    A built-in function is therefore able to declare a parameter position as taking a reference, and each of the operations of this clause declares its first. This is a change to the references extension, which until now needed no such thing: a built-in had no ref parameter, so a reference argument decayed to its referent at every built-in boundary without exception. The exception is unavoidable here, since operating on a copy of the binding is not the operation the program asked for. Nothing else changes, and in particular the reflective call paths remain decay channels: f.call(*null*, ref x) decays at %Function.prototype.call%, which declares no such position, so what it forwards carries a value.

    The borrow is validated where the ref argument is evaluated, by RequireBorrowableReference (2.4.1), which is how every ref argument reaches every callee. A reference that arrives at one of these operations has already passed it, so these operations do not apply it a second time.

    41.6.2 ValidateAtomicTarget ( args, operation )

    The abstract operation ValidateAtomicTarget takes arguments args (a List of ECMAScript language values) and operation (integer-only or any-value-type) and returns either a normal completion containing an Atomic Target Record or a throw completion. It resolves the shapes an Atomics operation admits to one description of a place in memory.

    An Atomic Target Record has fields [[Block]] (a Data Block or Shared Data Block), [[ByteIndex]] (a non-negative integer), and [[Type]] (a Type Record).

    1. If args[0] is a Reference Record, then
      1. Let ref be ? RequireBorrowableReference(args[0]).
      2. Let type be the declared type of the storage ref denotes.
      3. Let block and byteIndex be the Data Block and offset at which that storage is placed.
    2. Else if args[0] is an Object that is not a TypedArray, then
      1. Let key be ? ToPropertyKey(args[1]).
      2. If args[0] does not have a typed own data property whose key is key, throw a TypeError exception.
      3. Let type be the declared type of that property.
      4. Let block and byteIndex be the Data Block and offset at which that property is placed.
    3. Else,
      1. Return ? ValidateIntegerTypedArray(args[0], args[1]) as an Atomic Target Record whose [[Type]] is the element type of the TypedArray.
    4. If type is not a value type, throw a TypeError exception.
    5. If operation is integer-only and type is not an integer type, throw a TypeError exception.
    6. If the laid-out size of type (9) is not one the implementation performs atomically, throw a TypeError exception.
    7. Return the Atomic Target Record { [[Block]]: block, [[ByteIndex]]: byteIndex, [[Type]]: type }.

    The shared modifier is not consulted. A binding carrying it and one not carrying it are equally valid targets, and the restrictions this operation enforces are restrictions of type: an integer type where the operation needs bit patterns, a value type of a size the implementation can operate on atomically, and a typed own data property rather than an ordinary one, an any-typed slot having no width for an operation to be atomic over.

    Note

    Requiring the modifier would buy no invariant. Unmarked storage is not unreachable from another thread — a binding a function closes over is reached by whatever thread runs that function — so plain racing writes to it are possible whether or not the synchronized ones are permitted, and forbidding only the synchronized ones would leave a program the worse tool for the same storage. It would also fracture generic code: a function taking ref uint32 would have to know whether its caller's storage carried a marker, and expressing that would mean a sharedness dimension through the reference types for no gain. What the modifier changes is cost, not legality (41.4.1).

    41.6.3 The Operations

    Atomics.load, Atomics.store, Atomics.exchange, and Atomics.compareExchange accept any target ValidateAtomicTarget (41.6.2) admits with operation any-value-type. Atomics.add and Atomics.sub accept the integer types and the floating-point types. Atomics.and, Atomics.or, Atomics.xor, Atomics.wait, Atomics.waitAsync, and Atomics.notify are integer-only: a bitwise operation on a floating-point value has no meaning the program intended, and a wait compares bit patterns.

    A value stored through any of these operations passes the typed-storage boundary (1.7.6), so a store of a value not of the target's type throws as an ordinary assignment to that storage would, and the same conversion applies.

    41.6.3.1 Floating-Point Addition

    Atomics.add and Atomics.sub on a target whose [[Type]] is a floating-point type perform the read-modify-write as a sequentially consistent compare-exchange loop: read the current value, compute the sum, and attempt to replace the value read with the sum, repeating until the replacement succeeds. Each attempt is one ReadModifyWriteSharedMemory event.

    The result is therefore atomic but not deterministic across interleavings, floating-point addition not being associative. A program that needs a reproducible sum accumulates per-slice partials and combines them in a fixed order, which is what 41.8 does.

    41.6.3.2 The compareExchange Comparison

    Atomics.compareExchange converts the expected value to the target's [[Type]] and then compares it with the value read using SameValueZero. The conversion is not optional: a comparison of an unconverted operand against a typed value read from the target never succeeds, so every compare-exchange would silently fail and a claim loop would spin rather than throw. The TypedArray form of the operation converts for the same reason. On an integer target this is indistinguishable from every other candidate. On a floating-point target it is the choice that makes a compare-exchange loop terminate, which 40 already states normatively and this clause does not restate.

    Note

    Strict equality would not terminate: NaN is not strictly equal to itself, so a loop whose observed value is NaN would retry against the very value it read, forever. A comparison of representations would terminate but is not specifiable, since an implementation may write an implementation-chosen NaN encoding when it stores a floating-point value, which would leave the success of a compare-exchange varying by implementation. SameValue terminates and distinguishes +0𝔽 from -0𝔽, which breaks the commonest use of the operation in the subtlest way: a computed -0𝔽 fails to match a +0𝔽 sentinel, so a claim loop intermittently refuses a slot that is arithmetically zero. SameValueZero is also the language's own storage equality, the predicate of Map, Set, and Array.prototype.includes, which is the role an expected-value comparison plays.

    41.6.3.3 Waiting

    Atomics.wait, Atomics.waitAsync, and Atomics.notify on a typed target use the WaiterList of the pinned edition, keyed by the target's [[Block]] and [[ByteIndex]] as they are keyed for a TypedArray. A wait on storage the implementation has not placed in a Shared Data Block places it in one, which is the promotion 41.4.1 describes and the one case in which it is forced rather than discovered.

    Atomics.wait throws a TypeError exception where the surrounding agent's [[CanBlock]] is false, as it does today. A wait is a cancellation checkpoint (41.3.4): a signal aborted while a wait is parked wakes it, and the wait then throws the signal's abort reason. The reactions of Atomics.waitAsync run on the agent that created them, as every reaction does (41.2).

    41.7 Synchronization Objects

    Atomics covers a single location. For anything larger — a multi-field update, a shared collection, a handoff — this clause specifies three ordinary objects: a Lock (41.7.1), a Condition (41.7.2), and a ThreadLocal (41.7.3).

    Where the surrounding agent's [[CanBlock]] is false, Lock.prototype.hold, Lock.prototype.acquire, and Condition.prototype.wait throw a TypeError exception, as Atomics.wait does. They throw rather than quietly becoming their async counterparts: an operation returning T on one thread and Promise.<T> on another would have a return type that depends on which thread is running it, which is not a thing a typed language can say.

    41.7.1 Lock Objects

    A Lock has internal slots [[Owner]], an Agent Record or none, and [[Waiters]], a List of waiting agents in the order they arrived.

    A Lock is not reentrant. Reentrant monitors buy tolerance of self-nesting at the price of owner-and-count bookkeeping on the fast path, a Condition that must release and restore a nesting depth, and the silent tolerance of a layering violation that a non-reentrant lock reports the moment it appears.

    It is therefore a TypeError exception for an agent to acquire a Lock it already owns through hold or acquire. Those forms block, so the acquisition cannot make progress: the agent that would have to release is the agent now parked, which is a certain deadlock, and the owner is known because Condition.prototype.wait must check it anyway. A specification cannot leave the outcome unstated, and the platform's answer for an operation that can never proceed is to throw — the same choice made when Atomics.wait on a host's main thread became an error rather than a frozen page.

    asyncHold while holding is not a deadlock and is permitted. The acquisition queues, and the holder may release from a later job before anything awaits the pending promise.

    41.7.1.1 Lock.prototype.hold ( callback )

    It acquires the Lock, calls callback with no arguments, releases the Lock, and returns what callback returned. If callback returns an abrupt completion, the Lock is released and the completion propagates, so the release has the force of a finally.

    The closure does not escape the call, so an implementation may allocate nothing for it and may inline the critical section. It may not be marked inline, for the reason a ref callback may not (2).

    41.7.1.2 Lock.prototype.acquire ( )

    It acquires the Lock and returns a lock guard, an object with a [Symbol.dispose] method that releases it. using guard = lock.acquire() therefore holds the Lock for the enclosing block, which reads better than hold where the critical section wants an early return or spans a try.

    Disposing a guard twice is a TypeError exception, as calling a release function twice is, and for the same reason.

    Note

    A guard is where the type system can do what a callback cannot. A guard type the checker requires to be consumed by a using declaration, or disposed on every path, turns forgetting to release into a type error rather than a deadlock at run time. That refinement is not specified here, the guard being an ordinary disposable, but the shape is chosen so that it can be.

    41.7.1.3 Lock.prototype.asyncHold ( )

    It returns a promise for a release function, fulfilled when the Lock has been acquired for the calling agent. The promise's reactions run on the agent that created them, as every reaction does (41.2), so the critical section that follows the await runs on the thread that asked for the Lock.

    The release function may be called once, by the agent that received it. A second call, or a call from another agent, is a TypeError exception. Tolerating a stale release would unlock a critical section that by then belongs to somebody else, which is the one failure a Lock exists to prevent.

    41.7.1.4 Ordering

    Releasing a Lock synchronizes-with the acquisition that next obtains it, in the sense of 41.5. Everything an agent did while holding the Lock therefore happens-before everything the next holder does, which is what makes a Lock a way to publish a multi-field update that 41.5 would otherwise permit to tear.

    Which waiter obtains a released Lock is implementation-defined. An implementation is not required to be fair, and a program that requires fairness builds it rather than assuming it.

    41.7.2 Condition Objects

    A Condition has an internal slot [[Waiters]].

    41.7.2.1 Condition.prototype.wait ( lock )

    It is a TypeError exception if lock is not a Lock owned by the surrounding agent. It releases lock and parks the agent in one step, so no notification can be missed between the release and the park, and reacquires lock before returning.

    An implementation may wake a waiter that was not notified. A program therefore tests its condition in a loop rather than assuming that returning from wait means the condition holds — which is the discipline every condition variable requires, and which this clause states rather than leaving to be discovered.

    41.7.2.2 Condition.prototype.asyncWait ( lock )

    It returns a promise fulfilled when the waiter has been notified and lock reacquired, so the code after the await holds the Lock exactly as the code after wait does. Its reactions run on the agent that created them.

    41.7.2.3 Condition.prototype.notify and Condition.prototype.notifyAll

    notify wakes one waiter, notifyAll wakes every waiter. Which one notify wakes is implementation-defined. Neither requires the calling agent to hold any Lock, since the Lock a waiter reacquires is the waiter's and not the notifier's.

    41.7.2.4 Cancellation

    A wait and an asyncWait are cancellation checkpoints (41.3.4). An abort delivered while a waiter is parked wakes it, and the wait then completes abruptly with the signal's abort reason — after reacquiring the Lock, so that the unwinding runs with the invariant the waiter was holding. A Lock acquisition is a checkpoint on the same terms.

    41.7.3 ThreadLocal Objects

    ThreadLocal.<T> is a generic intrinsic, in the manner of SoA.<T> and Composite.<T>. An instance holds storage per agent: reading its value reads the storage of the surrounding agent, and writing it writes that agent's, so no two threads see one another's.

    An agent that has not written the storage reads DefaultValueOf(T) (1.8.3.1), taken in the realm in which the ThreadLocal was created rather than in the reading agent's. Where T is a parameterization its default is a crossing, and a crossing consults the declarations of a realm; taking the reading agent's would let two agents read one storage and receive different values, or one of them a TypeError, for a write neither performed. An agent's storage is unreachable once the agent is not, so a ThreadLocal does not keep the values of ended threads alive.

    Note

    A ThreadLocal is coherent here because a reaction runs on the thread that created it (41.2). Were a continuation to resume on whichever thread settled the promise it awaited, a ThreadLocal read before an await and one after it could answer differently in the same function, and the primitive would be a trap rather than a tool. The two rules stand or fall together, which is why one specification carries both.

    None of these is compile-time evaluable (1.2.7). Each is either shared mutable state or a question about which thread is asking, and neither survives being answered at compile time.

    41.8 Parallel Iteration

    The Thread namespace object carries two operations over a range of integers. They exist because the alternative — spawning a thread per slice by hand and joining it — is both more code and worse, since a thread per call is a thread the pool would have reused.

    41.8.1 The Partition

    Both operations cut begin through end into slices: disjoint contiguous sub-ranges covering the whole range, numbered from zero in ascending order of the elements they contain. How many, and where the cuts fall, is implementation-defined as a function of begin and end alone. Nothing else may influence it — not how many threads the host has, not how many are idle, not how long a body took on a previous call.

    Which agent executes which slice is not fixed and may vary between runs of one program. An implementation may move whole slices between agents freely, which is what lets it balance work; what it may not do is cut differently because of what its agents are doing.

    Note

    The constraint is what gives parallelReduce a reproducible answer over floating-point values, and it is chosen at the level where it costs least. Fixing the partition in this specification would deliver reproducibility across implementations too, but any constant this clause named would be arbitrary today and wrong on the hardware of a few years from now. Leaving the partition entirely to the implementation would deliver nothing: a result that changed with core count, or with whether a machine was busy, is not what a program means by deterministic. A partition that depends only on the range gives an implementation every tuning decision that matters and takes away only the one that would make the answer move.

    41.8.2 Thread.parallelFor ( begin, end, body )

    It calls body once with each integer in the range, in slices (41.8.1), and returns undefined when every slice has finished.

    The calling agent participates: it executes slices itself, and when none remain to claim it waits out the slices still in flight without parking on a WaiterList. A call therefore never blocks in the sense 41.7 uses, and is permitted on an agent whose [[CanBlock]] is false — a host's main thread included, which is where a frame loop lives and which is the reason the operation is shaped this way.

    Two properties follow, and both are normative. Executing every slice on the calling agent, in ascending slice order, is a conforming implementation: a host with no threads to give still runs the program, and gets the same answer. And a body that itself calls parallelFor cannot deadlock by exhausting the pool, since the inner call participates on the same terms; the worst case is that the inner range runs on the agent that entered it.

    A reference into an element is valid for the slice that borrows it (2.10), and it is a TypeError exception to change the length of an array a slice holds a reference into for the duration of the call. Because slices are disjoint, writes to distinct elements never contend; over a shared SoA.<T>, writes to distinct fields do not contend either, each field being its own region (41.4.1).

    41.8.3 Thread.parallelReduce ( begin, end, initial, perElement, combine )

    Each slice (41.8.1) folds perElement over its own elements, starting from initial, producing one partial. The partials are then combined with combine in ascending slice order, left to right. The calling agent participates as it does for parallelFor.

    The result is therefore a function of the range, the body, and the callbacks — and not of the scheduling. Given one implementation, the same begin and end and the same callbacks produce the same value on a busy machine and an idle one, on four cores and on sixty-four. This holds although combine need not be associative, which matters because floating-point addition is not and is the case the operation exists for.

    The guarantee is only as strong as the callbacks. A perElement or combine that consults a ThreadLocal, asks which agent is running, or observes the scheduling in any other way reintroduces exactly the variation the partition rule removes, and this clause promises nothing about such a program.

    41.8.4 Errors

    If a call to body or perElement completes abruptly in slice k, slices numbered above k are cancelled, slices numbered below k are allowed to finish, and the operation completes abruptly with the completion of the lowest-numbered slice that failed. A combine that completes abruptly is attributed to the later of the two slices it was combining.

    That is the completion a sequential execution would have produced, since a sequential execution reaches the lowest failing index first and stops there. Failures are therefore as reproducible as results, and for the same reason.

    Note

    Reporting whichever failure happened first in time would be simpler and is what an unordered pool naturally does, but it would make the error a program sees depend on scheduling — so a program with two bad elements would report one of them on a fast machine and the other on a slow one. Collecting every failure would run work already known to be doomed, and the set collected would be scheduling-dependent anyway unless every slice ran to completion.

    41.8.5 The Pool

    The agents these operations execute slices on are a resource of the agent cluster, sized and managed by the host, and reused across calls. Creating a thread per call would make the operations too expensive for the loop they are meant to sit inside.

    Neither operation is compile-time evaluable (1.2.7).

    42 UTF-8 Conversions

    A string has no layout, its size being a property of the value rather than of the type (9.1), so a string held in a fixed-width record or written to a wire format is held as bytes. Three operations convert between the two, and they are specified here rather than left to a host encoder because what they REFUSE is part of the language.

    String.fromUtf8(bytes) returns the String the given bytes encode. bytes is any array-like of byte values, which is what lets a [N].<uint8>, a [].<uint8> and a Span.<uint8> all reach it. An element that is not an integer in the inclusive range 0 to 255 is a TypeError.

    String.prototype.toUtf8(into) encodes the String as UTF-8 into into and returns the number of bytes written. The target is a PARAMETER rather than the receiver, and is so that an owned array reaches it: a [N].<uint8> coerces to a Span.<uint8> at a boundary and a parameter is a boundary, where a method's receiver is not.

    String.prototype.utf8Length is the number of bytes the String's UTF-8 encoding occupies. It is not length, which counts UTF-16 code units: a single astral code point is two code units and four bytes, and a slot is sized in bytes.

    42.1 What the Conversions Refuse

    A value whose encoding does not fit into is a TypeError, and NOTHING IS WRITTEN. This is the rule 1.6.6 states for a literal a type cannot represent — "a type error rather than a silent truncation" — applied at the other end of the same conversion. The second half is as load-bearing as the first: a partial write would leave a record holding the front of one value and the back of another, which is worse than either, and a caller that caught the error would have no way to know.

    Only WELL-FORMED text encodes. A String may hold an unpaired surrogate, which has no UTF-8 encoding; toUtf8 and utf8Length both raise a TypeError for one rather than encoding it as WTF-8 or substituting U+FFFD, either of which lets a value that cannot round-trip appear to have done so. String.prototype.isWellFormed is the question to ask first and String.prototype.toWellFormed is the program's explicit escape — the pair 9.1 draws between hasLayout and byteLength, where the property that ANSWERS guards the one that ASSERTS.

    Decoding is strict, and the refusals are the four ways a decoder is usually lax: a TRUNCATED sequence whose continuation bytes run past the end; an OVERLONG encoding, C0 80 for U+0000 being the classic, which would let one code point have several spellings and is a security defect wherever a filter runs before a decoder; a surrogate encoded as three bytes, which is CESU-8 and would let a lone surrogate survive a round trip the encoder refuses to produce; and a code point above U+10FFFF, which is not a code point. A stray continuation byte and a lead byte no sequence begins with are refused for the same reason.

    A zero byte decodes to U+0000 like any other, and fromUtf8 decodes every byte it is given. Trimming padding is a property of a FORMAT rather than of UTF-8, so it belongs to whatever overlays the bytes; keeping it out of the conversion is what lets one codec serve a zero-padded record, a length-prefixed wire format, and a tag with no padding convention at all.

    43 Typed JSON Parsing

    JSON.parse gains a generic overload, written JSON.parse.<_T_>(_text_), that parses and validates in one pass. The Static Type of the call JSON.parse.<_T_>(_text_) is T, since the value it produces has been converted against T; the two-argument reviver form is the untyped overload and has the Static Type any. It parses text as JSON, which is a SyntaxError on malformed input exactly as the untyped JSON.parse is, and then converts the resulting value against T by 43.1. Well-formed JSON that does not satisfy T is a TypeError naming the path at which the mismatch occurred, so a typed catch (_e_: SyntaxError) and catch (_e_: TypeError) separate a malformed document from a well-formed one of the wrong shape.

    A JSON array coerces against an array type, whose extent it must match where that is fixed, and against a tuple type, whose admitted lengths it must be one of and whose positions type its elements one by one, with a short array taking the trailing positions' declared defaults. Validation is otherwise layered as any other boundary in this specification: a leaf is checked against its type as it is reached, a parameterized type consults its metadata's validation judgment (1.7.2.1), and a class or record where clause runs once the target is filled, as the construction boundary check. Unlike the general boundary of 1.7.3.1, which distinguishes a RangeError for a numeric value the target cannot represent, every failure here is a TypeError: in a parsed document the type is the schema, so a value outside a field's range violates the schema rather than overflowing an arithmetic. The overload takes no reviver, since a reviver observes the intermediate untyped graph this feature exists not to build.

    43.1 CoerceJSONValue ( value, type, path )

    The abstract operation CoerceJSONValue takes arguments value (an ECMAScript language value), type (a Type Record), and path (a String) and returns either a normal completion containing an ECMAScript language value or a throw completion. It converts the JSON value into type, or returns a throw completion whose value is a TypeError describing path. It may call user code, since converting a structural type reads and writes properties. It performs the following steps when called:

    1. If type.[[Kind]] is any, return value.
    2. If type.[[Kind]] is reference or type.[[Kind]] is shared, return ? CoerceJSONValue(value, type.[[Target]], path).
    3. If type is a composite type (23.2), then
      1. If type is the top composite type, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Let shape be the shape of type.
      3. Let data be ? CoerceJSONValue(value, shape, path).
      4. If shape.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
        1. Let elements be a new empty List.
        2. Let len be ! LengthOfArrayLike(data).
        3. Let i be 0.
        4. Repeat, while i < len,
          1. Append CanonicalizeCompositeValue(! Get(data, ! ToString(𝔽(i)))) to elements.
          2. Set i to i + 1.
        5. Return ? FindOrCreateTupleComposite(elements).
      5. Let entries be a new empty List.
      6. For each own property key k of data, in the order returned by ! data.[[OwnPropertyKeys]](), do
        1. Append the Composite Entry Record { [[Key]]: k, [[Value]]: CanonicalizeCompositeValue(! Get(data, k)) } to entries.
      7. Return FindOrCreateComposite(entries).
    4. If type.[[Kind]] is primitive, then
      1. If type is a numeric type, then
        1. If value is not a Number, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. If type is a sized integer type and the mathematical value of value is not an integer in the range of type, throw a TypeError exception.
        3. If type is the number type, return value.
        4. Return value converted to type by Table 19.
      2. If type is the string type, then
        1. If value is not a String, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Return value.
      3. If type is the boolean type, then
        1. If value is not a Boolean, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Return value.
      4. If type is the null type, then
        1. If value is not null, throw a TypeError exception.
        2. Return value.
      5. Throw a TypeError exception.
    5. If type.[[Kind]] is literal, then
      1. If SameValue(value, type.[[Value]]) is true, return value.
      2. Throw a TypeError exception.
    6. If type.[[Kind]] is union, then
      1. For each element m of type.[[Members]], do
        1. Let r be Completion(CoerceJSONValue(value, m, path)).
        2. If r is a normal completion, return r.[[Value]].
      2. Throw a TypeError exception.
    7. If type.[[Kind]] is array, then
      1. If value is not an Array, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(value).
      3. If type.[[Extent]] is not dynamic and type.[[Extent]] ≠ len, throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Let elements be a new empty List.
      5. Let i be 0.
      6. Repeat, while i < len,
        1. Let element be the element of value at index i.
        2. Let elementPath be the string-concatenation of path, the code unit 0x005B (LEFT SQUARE BRACKET), the decimal representation of i as a String, and the code unit 0x005D (RIGHT SQUARE BRACKET).
        3. Let converted be ? CoerceJSONValue(element, type.[[Element]], elementPath).
        4. Append converted to elements.
        5. Set i to i + 1.
      7. Return CreateArrayFromList(elements).
    8. If type.[[Kind]] is tuple, then
      1. If value is not an Array, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Let len be ? LengthOfArrayLike(value).
      3. If len is not a length type admits (1.14.7), throw a TypeError exception.
      4. Let elements be a new empty List.
      5. Let i be 0.
      6. Repeat, while i < len,
        1. Let element be the element of value at index i.
        2. Let elementPath be the string-concatenation of path, the code unit 0x005B (LEFT SQUARE BRACKET), the decimal representation of i as a String, and the code unit 0x005D (RIGHT SQUARE BRACKET).
        3. Let converted be ? CoerceJSONValue(element, the [[Type]] of the element of type.[[Elements]] that receives position i, elementPath).
        4. Append converted to elements.
        5. Set i to i + 1.
      7. For each element e of type.[[Elements]] whose position is not less than len, do
        1. If e.[[Rest]] is false, then
          1. Assert: e.[[Initial]] is not none, since a tuple's defaults are trailing (1.4.2.7) and len is a length type admits.
          2. Append e.[[Initial]] to elements.
      8. Return CreateArrayFromList(elements).
    9. If type.[[Kind]] is object, then
      1. If value is not an Object or value is an Array, throw a TypeError exception.
      2. Let result be OrdinaryObjectCreate(%Object.prototype%).
      3. Let keys be ? value.[[OwnPropertyKeys]]().
      4. For each element k of keys such that k is a String and no Property Type Record of type.[[Properties]] has key k, do
        1. Let accepted be false.
        2. For each index signature s of type, do
          1. If accepted is false and s accepts k, then
            1. Let kv be ? Get(value, k).
            2. Let keyPath be the string-concatenation of path, the code unit 0x002E (FULL STOP), and k.
            3. Let converted be ? CoerceJSONValue(kv, s's value type, keyPath).
            4. Perform ! CreateDataPropertyOrThrow(result, k, converted).
            5. Set accepted to true.
        3. If accepted is false, throw a TypeError exception.
      5. For each Property Type Record p of type.[[Properties]], do
        1. Let present be ? HasProperty(value, p's key).
        2. If present is true, then
          1. Let pv be ? Get(value, p's key).
          2. Let fieldPath be the string-concatenation of path, the code unit 0x002E (FULL STOP), and p's key.
          3. Let converted be ? CoerceJSONValue(pv, p's type, fieldPath).
          4. Perform ! CreateDataPropertyOrThrow(result, p's key, converted).
        3. Else if p is optional, then
          1. If p's [[Initial]] is not none, perform ! CreateDataPropertyOrThrow(result, p's key, p's [[Initial]]).
        4. Else,
          1. Throw a TypeError exception.
      6. Return result.
    10. If type.[[Kind]] is parameterized, then
      1. Let base be ? CoerceJSONValue(value, type.[[Base]], path).
      2. If ? IsOfType(base, type) is false, throw a TypeError exception.
      3. Return base.
    11. If type.[[Kind]] is nominal, then
      1. If type is an enum type, then
        1. If value equals the value of an enumerator of type, return that enumerator.
        2. Throw a TypeError exception.
      2. If type has a structural form, return ? CoerceJSONValue(value, that form, path).
    12. Throw a TypeError exception.
         Note

    The physical form the extension describes, writing straight into contiguous typed storage with no intermediate graph, is an implementation strategy and not observable, so an implementation that parses to the untyped JSON value and then converts it conforms.

    The conversions this operation does not perform are the deferred part of the extension: a class target that fills a sealed layout without running its constructor, the exact wide numeric types (the 64-bit integers, decimal128, and bigint) whose digits must convert without first rounding through a Number, the complex types, for which JSON has no syntax at all — a number carries no imaginary part, so admitting one would be a decision about what the absent part means rather than a conversion, and the enforcement of the built-in refinement judgments, which parameterized validation consults but which are themselves specified with the primitive metadata they belong to. An intersection target is deferred with them, and deliberately: coercion must produce one value, so an intersection of object types needs a rule merging its members into the single shape the walk fills, including what a key both members declare converts to, and that rule belongs with the objects work rather than with serialization. A function target throws, since no JSON value denotes a function, and the remaining kinds cannot reach a specialized type.

    Annex A (normative) The Compile-Time Evaluable Fragment

    This annex fixes the compile-time-evaluable subset of the language as an implementation target in its own right, so that a tool that is not an ECMAScript engine can evaluate types and prove that it agrees with one. The determinism this specification already requires, one result or failure and never a different result (1.2.7.4), is what makes that agreement a checkable claim.

    A.1 The Grammar of the Fragment

    The fragment is the ECMAScript grammar less the following, together with the reading discipline of 1.2.7.1, which is what excludes input, output, and ambient state, since code in the fragment cannot name them.

    • AwaitExpression and YieldExpression, and every async and generator form of function, method, and arrow.
    • ClassDeclaration and ClassExpression: a builder transforms and constructs types but does not mint a nominal one (1.5.20).
    • A direct or indirect eval, the Function constructor, the construction of a Proxy, and a dynamic import(), which the library rule below also excludes.
    • The debugger statement.

    Everything else is within the fragment: functions and closures over evaluable bindings, local bindings and their mutation, the ordinary operators and control forms including try, subject to 1.2.7.4's carve-out, template literals, destructuring, spread, and regular expression literals.

    A.2 The Library Surface

    A built-in is within the fragment when its result is determined by its arguments, it performs no observable mutation outside values the call created, and it depends on no host or ambient state. The floor the fragment guarantees: the type operations of 1.12, Type Object identity and toString, regular expression construction and matching, Map and Set, whose keys Type Objects serve as by interned identity, Symbol and its registry, and the pure methods and functions of String, Number, BigInt, Math, Array, Object, and JSON. Symbol is within the fragment although a fresh symbol is not determined by its argument: a fresh symbol is a value the call creates, as a fresh array or Map is, and the determinism the fragment requires is of the types a program computes and the order it observes them in, both of which the same source fixes by creating the same symbols in the same sequence. Symbol.for is within it by the ordinary rule, its result determined by its key. Excluded by the same rule: Math.random, Date, every locale-sensitive method, Atomics and shared memory, and weak references and finalization. The conformance suite fixes the exact enumeration.

    A.3 Semantics and Conformance

    The fragment's semantics are this specification's own, restricted to the fragment; no second evaluator is defined. A standalone implementation of the fragment conforms when, for every program of the fragment, it produces, position for position, the same interned types this specification produces, or fails where this specification fails, under the budget invariant of 1.2.7.4 and with the memoization of 1.2.7.3 or anything observably equivalent to it.

    Note

    The subset is deliberately small as a language: a conforming standalone evaluator is a small tree-walking interpreter, not an embedded engine, and because evaluation is memoized, an interactive tool evaluates each distinct application once. Regular expressions are the one sizeable obligation, and the pattern metadata of 1.5.20 requires them anyway.

    A.4 The Conformance Suite and the Acceptance Corpus

    A conformance suite accompanies this annex, and conformance to the fragment is conformance to it together with this annex's text. Its seed is the design's acceptance corpus: one hundred and ninety programs, the whole of the type-challenges repository, the warm-up, thirteen easy, one hundred and four medium, fifty-five hard, and seventeen extreme, each pairing the erased-language solution with a builder solution whose assertions must hold under this specification's semantics. The assertions include type identity written ===, which interning supplies and which the erased corpus can only imitate through unspecified checker behaviour.

    Note

    The corpus is maintained with the design, and the symbol literal types its eleventh challenge exercises are now those of 1.5.19, so no challenge is gated on an unadopted extension. The questions and divergences the corpus surfaced are recorded in its own notes and tracked with the design documents.

    Annex B (informative) The Standard Builder Kit

    The primitives are normative and live in the core: construction, relations, never, keyof, and the evaluation semantics. The kit is the 313 non-comment lines of ordinary evaluable code written over them, and it ships as source under one standard module, spelled std:types here and reconciled with the standard library extension by observing that the two do not overlap: that extension gives typed signatures to methods that already exist and introduces no module, where the kit is new code and needs one. The kit is therefore the single new specifier, and a signature listing is never one until its final home is reconciled with the standard library extension. Shipping it as source is the proof that no construct in it is engine magic, gives the ecosystem one interned vocabulary, so that partial(User) in two packages is one type, and makes the definitions themselves the reference documentation. A codebase that cannot assume the module can polyfill it verbatim.

    The surface is Table 64: 71 exports in nine families. Each row gives the name, its signature as the module declares it, and what it answers. The definitions are the normative text — that is what shipping as source means — and the table is the index into them, so a reader can find an export without reading three hundred lines and a conformance suite has one place to enumerate. Three exports the table does not list are worth naming for the same reason: suffixed and stringPattern are written in the module and NOT exported while the pattern meta key remains a provisional claim, and instanceType was withdrawn because a class is its own instance type, so the export was the identity for every input anyone would bring it.

    The style is visible in the definitions. The four property mappers are one line each, the union filters two, and the brand three:

    export function partial(T: type): type { return mapProperties(T, p => ({ ...p, optional: true })); }
export function required(T: type): type { return mapProperties(T, p => ({ ...p, optional: false })); }
export function readonly(T: type): type { return mapProperties(T, p => ({ ...p, readonly: true })); }
export function mutable(T: type): type { return mapProperties(T, p => ({ ...p, readonly: false })); }

export function exclude(T: type, U: type): type {
  return union(arms(T).filter(arm => !Reflect.isAssignable(arm, U)));
}
export function extract(T: type, U: type): type {
  return union(arms(T).filter(arm => Reflect.isAssignable(arm, U)));
}

export function brand(T: type, tag: string | symbol): type {
  return Reflect.makeType({ kind: 'parameterized', base: T, metadata: { brand: tag } });
}
    Note

    Where the kit and the core describe one operation, they must agree, and the corpus checks that they do: the corpus's library blocks assert each shipped helper against the exercise it solves. A helper that REBUILDS a type is held to the identity of 1.12.4 rather than to equivalence: reflecting a type, transforming its node, and constructing the result must yield the same Type Object where the transformation changed nothing. The distinction is invisible to any check short of === — a type rebuilt incorrectly answers with the same kind, the same base and the same fields — so a conformance suite that compares shape does not test it. The key operation is not among them - keyof is a primitive, and type keyof T reaches it from a value position, so the kit has no key helper to keep in step. The kit's normative status is this annex's status: informative, with the primitives it is written over carrying the normativity.
